Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.

p.seg: The Six Classics are all history.
The ancients did not write books;
the ancients never discussed principles apart from actual affairs.
The Six Classics are all the political statutes of the former kings.
Someone may say:
"Regarding the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, Yuè, and Chūnqiū,
I have already heard your explanation.
But the Yì is used to expound yīn and yáng.
I wish to hear why it is considered a political statute,
and why it is classified together with history." I reply:
I have heard it from the words of the Master.
"The Yì opens up things and accomplishes tasks,
encompassing the ways of the world."
"It knows the future and stores the past,
sharing fortune and misfortune with the people."
Its Way indeed encompasses what political teachings and statutes cannot reach.
Imitating heaven and modeling earth,
"thus it brings forth spiritual things,
to guide the people in their use."
Its teachings indeed precede political teachings and statutes.
The Zhōuguān states that the Grand Diviner was in charge of the methods of the three Yì:
the Xià dynasty called it the Liánshān,
the Yīn dynasty called it the Guīcáng,
and the Zhōu dynasty called it the Zhōuyì.
Each had its own images and numbers,
each differed in its changes and divinations,
and they did not follow one another.
Yet the three Yì each had their own origins:
as stated in the Dàzhuàn, referring to Fúxī, Shénnóng, Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn.
The Guīcáng originated from Fúxī, the Liánshān from Shénnóng, and the Zhōuyì from Huángdì.
Looking from their origins,
not only did the Three Sovereigns not follow one another,
but the Three August Ones and Five Emperors also did not follow one another.
When sages first emerged to govern the world,
they renewed what people saw and heard,
established teachings through spiritual ways,
to supplement what rituals, music, punishments, and governance could not cover.
This was entirely based on the natural principles of heaven,
unlike later generations who relied on strange and ominous things,
prophecies and numerological techniques,
to deceive the world.
The Master said:
"I studied the ways of the Xià,
but Qǐ was insufficient for evidence.
I obtained the Xià calendar.
I studied the ways of the Yīn,
but Sòng was insufficient for evidence.
I obtained the Kūnqián."
The Xià calendar
is the book of Xià's calendar.
The Kūnqián
is of the Yì category.
The Master regretted that the documents of Xià and Shāng could not be verified,
yet the Kūnqián, together with the Xià calendar, were obtained from studying Xià and Shāng.
Thus, what enriched the people's livelihood and benefited their use
was akin to regulating the calendar and clarifying the seasons,
both being the legal statutes of a dynasty.
They were not the personal thoughts of a sage,
separated from affairs and written as a book
to claim to illuminate the Way.
Displaying images and establishing teachings,
and regulating the calendar and assigning seasons,
are matters of heavenly principle.
The Lǐ, Yuè, Shī, and Shū,
together with punishments, governance, teachings, and decrees,
are matters of human affairs.
Heaven and humans interact,
and this is the great authority of kings in governing the world.
When Hán Xuānzǐ visited Lǔ,
he viewed books at the Grand Historian's office,
and saw the Yì images and the Chūnqiū,
believing that Zhōu rituals were preserved in Lǔ.
The Chūnqiū was the old statutes of Duke Zhōu,
so it could be said that Zhōu rituals were in Lǔ.
The Yì images were also called Zhōu rituals.
That they were political teachings and statutes,
closely related to the people's use and not empty words of an individual,
handed down from a glorious age and not merely old systems,
is even clearer.
The Master said:
"The rise of the Yì,
was it in the middle antiquity?
The author of the Yì,
did he have worries and troubles?"
Gù Yánwǔ once said that the Liánshān and Guīcáng
were not called Yì.
The three Yì mentioned by the Grand Diviner
were named by association with the Zhōuyì.
Now, observing that the Eight Trigrams originated with Fúxī,
the Liánshān was composed in the Xià dynasty,
yet the Master said the Yì rose in middle antiquity,
and the author of the Yì specifically referred to King Wén,
then the Liánshān and Guīcáng not being called "Yì"
is further evidence.
Someone may say:
"King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
never attaining a position to practice the Way.
How could he be said to have composed the Yì to establish political statutes?" I reply:
The Eight Trigrams were common to the three Yì.
King Wén himself attached explanations to the Eight Trigrams.
During the decline of the Shāng dynasty,
King Wén shared the people's worries and troubles.
Thus, he repeatedly discussed the way to handle worries and troubles,
focusing on avoiding blame,
but he did not create a new system.
After King Wǔ of Zhōu stabilized the world,
he named it the Zhōuyì
and established the teachings and statutes of a dynasty,
which was not initially intended by King Wén.
The Master was born without a position,
unable to create systems and establish laws
to guide the people's use.
Seeing that the Zhōuyì in terms of the Way and laws
was perfect and could not be improved,
he feared it would be lost over time.
Thus, he composed commentaries such as Tuàn, Xiàng, and Wényán
to elaborate its meanings,
which is called transmitting without creating.
It was not that he lacked the ability,
but the circumstances made it inappropriate.
Later Confucians imitated the Yì,
which was reckless and thoughtless!
Did their so-called principles and numbers
go beyond the Zhōuyì?
Since they did not go beyond it,
they only changed the images, numbers, and methods
to show they did not follow antiquity.
This is like when kings ruled the world,
renewing what people saw and heard,
similar to the Hàn system's use of yellow as the color and five as the number,
which is the same as changing the calendar and altering ceremonial colors.
Yáng Xióng created without understanding,
using eighty-one
to change the sixty-four.
Later great Confucians
often praised him,
because his numbers related to calendar regulation,
and his divination stalks matched fortune and misfortune.
Numbers are common to all ages.
Anyone skilled in calendar studies
could deduce them.
Why must it be the Tàixuán to match?
That divination stalks match fortune and misfortune
is the ultimate principle of yīn and yáng's naturalness.
With utmost sincerity,
even drawing lots or drilling tiles
can reveal fortune and misfortune.
Why must the text be convoluted
and the characters obscure,
only then to know fortune and misfortune?
The Yuánbāo falsely claimed to be the Guīcáng,
not worth discussing.
Sīmǎ Guāng's Qiánxū
again used fifty-five to replace eighty-one,
showing that even the worthy could be meddlesome.
Thus, the Six Classics cannot be imitated.
Earlier Confucians only discussed fearing the former sages and the need for reverence.
This refers to Yáng's Fǎyán
and Wáng's Zhōngshuō,
truly hitting their flaws.
As for the Six Classics,
they are all traces of the former kings attaining position and practicing the Way,
ordering the world,
and not empty words.
Thus, even with the Master's sageliness,
he still transmitted without creating.
If one creates recklessly without understanding,
not only is there suspicion of imitating the sages,
but also the crime of usurping royal statutes.
Should one not be cautious!
Kǒng Zhòngdá said:
"The term 'Yì'
is the general name for transformation and change,
a special designation for alteration and exchange."
Among earlier Confucian scholars' explanations of the meaning of the Yì,
none were as clear and comprehensive as Master Kǒng's.
Taking his explanation and advancing it further,
the Yì is the great classic for kings and rulers to reform institutions,
its affairs and the establishment of calendars and clarification of seasons are mutually complementary,
its meaning is as clear as if held aloft.
Xǔ Shūzhòng explained the character "Yì"
as:
"The lizard,
the gecko,
is a pictograph.
According to esoteric texts,
'sun and moon form Yì,'
representing yīn and yáng."
The Grand Diviner in the Zhōuguān,
was in charge of the methods of the three Yì.
Master Zhèng's commentary states:
"Yì means
the numbers derived from manipulating yarrow stalks for divination, which are subject to change."
Master Zhūzǐ said, "The Yì contains the meanings of exchange and transformation."
These all generate interpretations based on the text,
each speaking from one perspective,
and are not the original intent behind naming it the Yì.
The name "three Yì,"
although it began with the Zhōuguān,
and the Liánshān and Guīcáng
can both be named Yì,
the Yì cannot be appended to the Liánshān and Guīcáng to be called 'three Lián' or 'three Guī,'
truly because the meaning of Yì
actually encompasses the numerical methods that have not been passed down unchanged since Fúxī and Shénnóng.
The earliest appearance of Yì in writing
is in the Diǎn's "píng zài shuò yì,"
Kǒng's commentary says it refers to the yearly change,
and the Zhōu people then took it to name the book of hexagram manipulation,
thus the great principle of kings and rulers reforming institutions and renewing
is clearly evident.
The Dàzhuàn says:
"The production of life is called Yì."
Hán Kāngbó said, "Yīn and yáng alternate and change,
thereby accomplishing transformation and generation."
This is the source from which Master Zhūzǐ's meanings of exchange and transformation derive.
Although the texts of the three Yì are not transmitted,
observing now that the Grand Diviner in the Zhōuguān had their methods,
and the Zuǒzhuàn records divinations with their statements,
then the Liánshān and Guīcáng
both contained the meanings of exchange and transformation.
Thus since Fúxī and Shénnóng,
although the name Yì was not yet established,
the idea of Yì was already operating within them.
In high antiquity, simplicity and substance prevailed,
written characters were few,
there certainly were things that possessed the reality but had not yet been given a name.
Later people consequently determined their names,
then penetrating both before and after,
all took this as their main principle,
as if their names had long been established,
this is also one aspect of it.
Qīnmíng means reverence,
yǔnsè means sincerity,
lìxiàng means calendrical calculation (the 'lì' in lìxiàng is explained as推算, not the name for a calendar book).
All first possessed the reality and later were given the name.
The Yì, Gé hexagram, Xiàng says:
"Fire in the lake,
the nobleman uses this to establish the calendar and clarify the seasons."
Its Tuàn says:
"Heaven and earth undergo change, and the four seasons are formed.
Tāng and Wǔ undertook revolutionary mandate,
complying with heaven and responding to the people."
Calendars since the Huángdì era,
have been altered generation by generation,
and the Master thus took the image from the lake and fire,
and moreover took heaven and earth changing the seasons, and Tāng and Wǔ's revolutionary mandate as the meaning of the Gé hexagram;
then the Yì's being discarded or revived according to the times,
how could its principle be any different?
The Yì began with Fúxī and Shénnóng,
and was completed by the time of the accomplished Zhōu;
calendars began with Huángdì,
and successively changed in later ages;
high antiquity emphasized the way of heaven,
and from middle antiquity onward emphasized the major aspects of human affairs.
However, the theory of hexagram qi,
although created by Hàn Confucians,
the sequence and positions of the hexagrams
already contained their beginning and end;
thus one suspects that before Dànáo created the heavenly stems and earthly branches,
Fúxī and Shénnóng already used hexagram lines as calendrical symbols,
what is called the unity of heaven and humanity.
The Dàzhuàn says:
"In ancient times,
when Páoxīshì ruled the world,
he looked upward and observed the images in heaven,
looked downward and observed the patterns on earth,
observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land,
taking from near his own body,
taking from afar the myriad things,
then for the first time created the eight trigrams,
to penetrate the virtue of the spiritual and bright,
to categorize the circumstances of the myriad things."
This was created before Huángdì made the stems and branches.
Observing the separate commands to Xīhé,
then images, patterns, markings, and suitability,
their way was all-encompassing,
all were used to give the people the seasons.
From this we know that the sages of high antiquity,
opening heaven and creating institutions,
establishing laws to govern the world,
the creation of the Yì and the making of calendars
came from the same source,
one cannot forcibly separate which came first or later.
Therefore the Yì says:
"Opening up things and accomplishing tasks,
covering the ways of the world."
The Shū says:
"Orderly regulate, respectfully bestow,
act and transform, accomplish change."
All are one principle.
The Master said:
"Add a few years to my life,
and at fifty to study the Yì,
I could be free from major faults."
He also said:
"I study the Zhōu rituals,
they are used today,
I follow the Zhōu."
Studying the Yì
is the means to study the Zhōu rituals.
Hán Xuānzǐ saw the Yì Xiàng and the Chūnqiū,
and considered the Zhōu rituals to be in Lǔ.
The Master studied the Yì and recorded the Chūnqiū,
which is called studying the Zhōu rituals.
The Master said to Yán Yuān:
"Follow the Xià calendar,
ride the Yīn carriage,
wear the Zhōu ceremonial cap,
for music, the Sháo dance."
This is weighing and considering the hundred kings,
adding and subtracting from the four dynasties,
to be the standard for ten thousand generations.
Calendars and symbols changed successively,
yet the Master exclusively took the Xià calendar;
divination methods differed,
yet the Master exclusively took the Zhōuyì.
These are what, after the three dynasties,
have been followed and practiced without abandonment until now.
However, after the three dynasties,
calendars became prominent and the Yì became subtle;
calendars were preserved by official custodians,
while the Yì flowed through master-disciple transmission;
therefore Confucians dared to imitate the Yì,
but did not dare to create calendars.
The eclipses, fullness, and waning of calendars
have phenomena that can be verified,
while the good fortune, misfortune, regret, and distress of the Yì
have no traces to be constrained by;
thus calendar officials cannot force interpretations through private cleverness,
while Yì masters each set forth their own theories,
resulting in endless confusion.
Therefore, those who study the Yì

cannot but understand heaven. Observing this, one further understands that works like the Tàixuán, Yuánbāo, and Qiánxū are utterly without any reason to have been created; the reason always lies in not knowing they were for royal institutions.
The images of the Yì,
the evocative analogies of the Shī,
transform and change and cannot be categorized as things.
The offices of the Lǐ,
the precedents of the Chūnqiū,
are meticulous and strict and cannot be borrowed.
The Master said:
"The world reaches the same destination by different paths,
attains the same result through a hundred considerations."
The nobleman's approach to the six arts,
is to thread them together with one principle,
this is sufficient.
Things intermingle and form patterns,
affairs gain comparison and have their categories.
Knowing that the names and meanings of things and affairs emerge in complexity and are situated by comparison,
without patterns they cannot be expressed,
without categories they cannot be comprehended;
the patterns of the six arts,
can be encompassed in a single statement.
As for images,
evocative analogies,
precedents,
offices,
they are as unrelated as wind, horse, and ox,
their language can be called patterned,
their principle is simply said to be comprehending categories.
Therefore the essential point for learners,
lies in valuing the understanding of categories.
The concept of "xiàng" (symbolic imagery) encompasses a broad scope,
not limited to the Yìjīng alone;
all Six Arts incorporate it,
for it represents the Dao's substance on the verge of taking form yet not yet fully manifest.
The ospreys symbolizing a good match,
the bending trees representing chaste virtue,
and even the bears and snakes signifying men and women—
these are instances of xiàng's connection to the Shījīng.
The correspondence of the Five Phases to the Five Affairs,
the verification of rain and wind by the constellations Jī and Bì,
and even Fù Yán appearing in a dream to bestow a mandate—
these are instances of xiàng's connection to the Shūjīng.
The ancient officials recording clouds and birds,
the Zhōuguān modeling itself on heaven, earth, and the four seasons,
down to dragons and pheasants adorning robes,
bears and tigers marking archery—
these are instances of xiàng's connection to the Lǐjīng.
Songs harmonizing with yīn and yáng,
dances distinguishing civil and martial,
down to stone chimes recalling boundaries and hexagrams,
drums contemplating generals and commanders—
these are instances of xiàng's connection to the Yuèjīng.
Recording and editing did not omit calamities and anomalies,
and the Zuǒzhuàn subsequently expanded on omens and portents—
these are instances of xiàng's connection to the Chūnqiū.
The Yìjīng takes heaven and earth as its standard,
thus it can fully encompass the Dao of heaven and earth.
All things and affairs,
as they transition from stillness to motion,
before their traces become clear, their xiàng appears.
Therefore, the Dao cannot be seen;
when people seek the Dao and seem vaguely to perceive something,
it is all its xiàng.
There are xiàng of heaven and earth's spontaneous nature,
and there are xiàng constructed by the human mind.
The xiàng of heaven and earth's spontaneous nature
are roughly exhaustively covered by passages in the Shuōguà such as "for heaven, for roundness."
The xiàng constructed by the human mind,
like the carriage in Kuí carrying ghosts,
or the flying sound ascending to heaven—
wherever the intention reaches,
nothing is impossible.
However, the mind is empty and functions spiritually;
humans dwell within heaven and earth,
and cannot but receive the waxing and waning of yīn and yáng.
The constructions of the mind
are produced by the transformations of emotions.
The transformations of emotions
are stimulated by interactions in the human world,
and ride upon the mutual dependence and latent forces of yīn and yáng.
Thus, the xiàng constructed by the human mind
also originate from the xiàng of heaven and earth's spontaneous nature.
Although the xiàng of the Yìjīng encompass the Six Arts,
they are especially interconnected, like exterior and interior,
with the bǐ and xìng of the Shījīng.
The various genres of Shī
flourished in the literary culture of the Warring States period,
being renowned for their excellence in allegory and admonition.
As the saying goes, "Without studying the Shī, one has no means to speak" (detailed in the "Shījiào" chapter).
Moreover, the literature of the Warring States period
is profound in its use of bǐ and xìng,
which is precisely its profundity in employing xiàng.
The allegories in Zhuāngzǐ and Lièzǐ
allow for states to be established on the horns of a snail,
or lawsuits to be heard concerning a straw deer.
The Lísāo's expression of grievance
can ascend to the ninth heaven to reach the emperor's gate,
or probe the ninth earth to discern ghostly sentiments.
Others, like the rhetoricians of the Vertical and Horizontal alliances,
the masters of persuasion and manipulation,
the strategems of moving snakes and leading tigers,
the dialogues of peachwood figures and clay dolls—
become increasingly marvelous and
beyond comprehension.
Yet, in guiding the perplexed toward the Dao,
they certainly have their merit;
in embellishing wickedness and peddling deceit,
they also inflict their poison.
Therefore, the xiàng constructed by the human mind
can be auspicious or inauspicious;
one ought to examine the xiàng of heaven and earth's spontaneous nature
and align them with principle.
This is how the teachings of the Yìjīng serve to model the world.
The various masters and hundred schools,
not aligning with the great Dao,
yet are able to uphold their views with grounds and articulate them rationally,
is because their origins
all lie within the custodial institutions of the Zhōuguān.
Those that are fragmented and not in accord with the Dao
result from teachers losing their official custodianship,
and later derivative studies
each arbitrarily expounding their theories according to private intentions.
It is not that they gained nothing at all from the Way of the former kings,
and independently established a school of learning.
As for the learning of Buddhism,
coming from the Western Regions,
regardless that it is not a legacy of our world's official custodianship,
and moreover, it originated outside of China,
with languages not mutually intelligible,
and upon entering China,
its script was not yet understood.
Yet its doctrines and its scriptures,
being upheld with grounds and articulated rationally,
perhaps even surpass the various masters and hundred schools in abundance.
Upon repeated examination,
one realizes its fundamental origin lies in the teachings of the Yìjīng.
For what it terms mind, nature, principle, and Dao,
though the names differ,
inferring their intended meanings,
initially do not differ from the words of the sages.
Where it differs from the sages
lies solely in discarding actual affairs and separately perceiving something called the Dao.
As for the sixteen-foot golden body,
the majestic forms and appearances,
down to the clear brightness of heaven,
the gloomy misery of hell,
the heavenly maidens scattering flowers,
the yakṣas with dishevelled hair—
all such bizarre illusions,
unseen by humans,
Confucians denounce as false.
They do not realize that Buddhism teaches through xiàng,
no different from the Yìjīng's "dragon's blood is dark and yellow"
or "drawing the bow, the carriage carries ghosts."
Thus, the transformed appearances of Yama
are all spoken in terms of xiàng constructed by the human mind,
not fabrications and deceptions created by them to delude the world.
As for later corruptions and misinterpretations in transmission,
concretely interpreting them literally,
the ignorance of common men and women,
occasionally seeing forms and relying on sounds,
and drawing forced analogies therefrom,
then claiming that under the bright heavens
there exists another realm.
Confucians, again not examining the root and branches,
roll up their sleeves to dispute,
indignant as if sharing not the same sky,
yet do not realize this is not its true reality.
If what they learn,
and what their scriptures point to and analogize,
were only to切入 into the daily use of human relations,
it would be the Dao of the sages.
Teaching through xiàng
is not without foundation.
The xiàng of the Yìjīng interconnect with the bǐ and xìng of the Shījīng;
the phrases of the Yìjīng interconnect with the principles of the Chūnqiū.
Strictly distinguishing between heaven and marsh, then the second line [of a hexagram] often brings praise,
the fourth line often brings fear.
Carefully noting the border between order and chaos,
then yáng represents the noble person,
yīn represents the petty person.
Blocking the beginning of subtle encroachments,
the Gòu hexagram with one yīn line
already warns of the woman's strength.
The Lín hexagram with two yáng lines
immediately anticipates the eighth month.
Being cautious about the borrowing of names and vessels,
the fifth line warns against yīn softness,
the third line often indicates danger and caution.
As for the honor of the Four Virtues,
Yuán has no differing designation,
Hēng has lesser Hēng,
Lì Zhēn has lesser Lì Zhēn,
Zhēn has auspicious Zhēn and inauspicious Zhēn,
Jí has supreme Jí,
Huǐ has vanishing Huǐ,
Jiù has absence of Jiù.
The shift of a single character
is more rigorous and strict than the Chūnqiū.
For the sage, regarding the relationship between heaven and humanity,
considered it greatly awe-inspiring.
The Yìjīng uses heavenly principles to address human affairs;
the Chūnqiū uses human affairs to accord with heavenly principles.
The principles and examples manifested in their texts
are where the sage's mind was cautious.
The Outer Historian of the Zhōu Guān
was in charge of the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Now only the bamboo slips of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu remain;
of the Five Emperors, only two are preserved,
and of the Three Sovereigns, none are heard of.
The so-called Sānfén and Wǔdiǎn mentioned in Zuǒshì
are now unknown;
it is uncertain whether they were indeed those books.
If we infer the principles and examples of the Three Sovereigns and various emperors from the oaths, proclamations, tributes, and models of the Three Dynasties,
then in high antiquity, simplicity and plainness prevailed;
the knot-typing era was not far removed,
and writing had just begun to flourish.
Documents were merely sufficient to convey subtle meanings and communicate forms and names.
They were composed according to events,
inherently without fixed rules,
and could not be expected to be as comprehensive as later histories,
constrained by rigid definitions.
The Master edited and transmitted them,
selecting those that were broad, penetrating, and far-reaching,
sufficient to serve as teachings for posterity.
Confucian scholars of later times failed to understand this
and believed that the true origin of historiography
lay in the Shàngshū.
Consequently, they took the established historical methods of later generations
and recklessly tried to emulate the Shū.
This was all misguided.
The nature of history before the Three Dynasties
and after the Three Dynasties
can be understood through their similarities and differences.
Before the Three Dynasties,
recording and annotation had established methods,
but composition had no fixed names.
After the Three Dynasties,
composition had fixed names,
but recording and annotation lacked established methods.
When recording and annotation lack established methods,
gathering materials becomes difficult.
When composition has fixed names,
completing books becomes easy.
When completing books is easy,
form overwhelms substance.
When gathering materials is difficult,
falsity confounds truth.
When falsity confounds truth and form overwhelms substance,
historiography, though not extinct, is as good as extinct.
Talented historians appear only once in several generations;
they patch up deficiencies and remedy flaws,
yet are exhausted and unable to sustain the effort.
It is not that later scholars’ knowledge and insight are inferior to those of earlier times,
but that the methods of the Zhōu Guān were lost
and the teachings of the Shàngshū were cut off.
The situation inevitably became this way.
The Zhōu Guān had three hundred sixty offices,
encompassing the finest details of the world.
Yet the methods were embodied in the offices,
and the offices safeguarded the books.
Observing the principle of the six ministers working in concert,
we know that the ancients, regarding classics and records,
did not shy away from complexity and thoroughness
to ensure the completeness of recording and annotation.
For example, the texts of the six codes
were so detailed and voluminous
that the Grand Steward oversaw them,
the Lesser Steward assisted,
and the Directors of Accounts, Scribes, and Grand Historians each kept duplicate copies.
Thus, the texts of the six codes
had perhaps five times as many duplicates
stored in the archives.
Other texts and records
must have been similar.
Thus, if one office lost its charge
or one code was lost to fire or flood unexpectedly,
other departments could still rely on duplicate copies for reference.
Was this not an established method of recording and annotation,
more detailed than in later times?
From Hàn to the Yuán-Chéng period,
classics and records could be said to be complete.
Yet Liú Xiàng’s Qī Lüè,
though tracing the origins and categories of the six codes,
could no longer fully account for the offices.
Statutes and decrees were stored in the legal offices,
regulations and precedents were kept in the old repositories,
and court rituals were preserved by the Tàicháng.
It was unheard of for the Shíqú and Tiānlù libraries to store duplicate copies
