the model of annals arranged chronologically
has existed
since the advent of writing.
"Shàngshū" (The Book of Documents) represents a distinct form of historical writing;
if one applies the method of Zuǒshì (the Zuǒ Commentary),
integrating it with chronological arrangement,
it becomes a "zhuàn" (commentary or biography).
Using the principles of "Shàngshū"
to create commentaries for "Chūnqiū" (The Spring and Autumn Annals),
then Zuǒshì would not have to sacrifice literary quality for the sake of formulaic rules,
and much of the superfluous prose could be eliminated.
Using the principles of "Shàngshū"
to create biographies for Sīmǎ Qiān's "Shǐjì" (Records of the Grand Historian),
then the eight treatises and thirty hereditary houses
would not need to be categorized separately;
all could follow Zuǒshì's model and be collectively named "zhuàn."
Some would examine institutions and creations,
some narrate the beginnings and ends of human affairs,
some investigate the conduct of an individual—this is the essence of biographies.
Some combine affairs of the same category,
some record the speeches and instructions of a particular time (such as proclamations and edicts).
Some document the writings of an era,
determining the chapters according to events,
to complement the annals.
Compared to Zuǒshì's support of the classics,
this would avoid the constraint of being bound by chronological sequence;
compared to the separate categories in Sīmǎ Qiān's "Shǐjì",
it would avoid the complexity of overlapping and cross-referencing.
The prose would be more concise while the events become clearer,
the format simpler while the meaning becomes more refined.
Is this not the appropriate balance between substance and ornament,
the middle way between antiquity and the present?
As for personal names and categories of events,
when integrated into narratives of beginnings and ends,
they become difficult to check and examine.
Therefore, compile separate tables
to organize them systematically.
Celestial phenomena, geographical features,
carriages, attire, and instruments,
which cannot be fully covered in narratives,
and are also difficult to describe in words,
should be drawn as separate charts
to illustrate them clearly.
Generally, to comprehend the origins of "Shàngshū" and "Chūnqiū",
and to remedy the shortcomings in the traditions of Sīmǎ Qiān's "Shǐ" and Bān Gù's "Shū" (Book of Hàn),
there is no better method than this.
As for creating new formats,
delineating and distinguishing categories,
comparing ancient and modern writings,
and establishing the framework for a single work,
these are separately discussed in the "Yuántōng" (Comprehensive and Penetrating) chapter,
and will not be elaborated here.
Shào Jìnhán said:
"The format of annals and biographies in history,
modeled after Yuán Shū,
is similar in appearance but different in essence.
Using it to connect with the tradition of the 'Shàngshū' school,
is different in appearance but similar in essence.
What this chapter deduces,
is a branch of the Six Classics,
but a major school in historiography;
a pillar of strength amidst the flow of previous histories,
and a pioneering effort for later scholars."
With the decline of the Zhōu dynasty, literary practice deteriorated,
the Way of the Six Classics ceased to flourish,
and the various masters contended.
By the Warring States period, the transformation of literature was complete,
by the Warring States period, the composition of writings became specialized,
by the Warring States period, the literary genres of later ages were fully formed.
Therefore, discussing literature from the Warring States period,
one can understand the reasons for its rise, fall, prosperity, and decline.
The literature of the Warring States period,
with its strange and heterodox proliferation,
and its fragmentation of the Way,
is known to people;
that its sources all stem from the Six Classics,
is not known to people.
The literature of later ages,
whose genres were all fully formed in the Warring States period,
is not known to people;
that its sources largely derive from the teachings of the "Shī" (Classic of Poetry),
is even less known to people.
Only by knowing that literary genres were fully formed in the Warring States period,
can one begin to discuss the literature of later ages.
Only by knowing that the various schools are rooted in the Six Classics,
can one then discuss the literature of the Warring States period.
Only by knowing that the Warring States period largely derived from the teachings of the "Shī",
can one then discuss the literature of the Six Classics.
Only by being able to discuss the literature of the Six Classics,
can one then transcend the literature to perceive the Way.
Only by being able to transcend the literature to perceive the Way,
can one then uphold the Way to critique the writings of the various schools.
The literature of the Warring States period,
its sources all stem from the Six Classics.
What does this mean? It is said:
The substance of the Way encompasses everything,
and the Six Classics are sufficient to exhaust it.
The writings of the various masters,
those that are well-grounded and reasoned in their arguments,
must have grasped one aspect of the substance of the Way,
and only then could they freely elaborate their theories,
to establish the doctrines of their own school.
What is called 'one aspect'
is invariably encompassed by the Six Classics;
therefore, tracing it back, all find their origin.
This does not mean that the various masters truly followed the teachings of the Six Classics,
and that their words necessarily conformed to them.
"Lǎozǐ" explains based on Yīn-Yáng,
"Zhuāngzǐ" and "Lièzǐ" use allegories and borrowed images—
these belong to the teachings of the "Yì" (Classic of Changes).
Zōu Yǎn's extravagant discourses on heaven and earth,
Guān Yǐn's elaboration of the Five Phases—
these belong to the teachings of the "Shū".
The legalist systems of Guǎn Zhòng and Shāng Yāng,
whose principles lie in governmental statutes—
these belong to the teachings of the "Lǐ" (Classic of Rites).
The penal and names doctrines of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi,
whose aim is reward and punishment—
these belong to the teachings of the "Chūnqiū".
Other theories like those of Yáng Zhū, Mòzǐ, and Yīn Wén,
the strategies of Sū Qín, Zhāng Yí, Sūnzǐ, and Wú Qǐ,
distinguishing their origins and developments,
drawing out their main ideas,
the divisions of the Nine Schools,
the discussions in the "Qī Lù" (Seven Records),
all, in their specialized functions and official roles,
achieve a consistency,
without themselves realizing they are remnants of the Six Canons.
The literature of the Warring States period,
while originating from the Six Classics,
is also said to largely derive from the teachings of the "Shī".
What does this mean? It is said:
The Warring States period
was an era of纵横家 (Vertical and Horizontal Alliances strategists).
The learning of the纵横家
originated from the ancient office of the 'xíngrén' (envoys).
Observing the diplomatic rhetoric of the Spring and Autumn period,
ministers of the various states,
visiting and inquiring of feudal lords,
dispatched on missions requiring adept responses,
merely sought to embellish their speech to convey their intent.
By the Warring States period, through persuasive debate and揣摩 (weighing and揣摩),
they promoted their theories to seek wealth and honor.
Their language became elaborate and exaggerated,
transforming its original form and becoming even more grandiose and extraordinary.
It cannot be said that this was not the ultimate development of the envoys' rhetoric.
Confucius said:
"Though a man may be able to recite the three hundred poems,
if he is given administrative responsibilities,
he cannot carry them out;
if sent on missions to the four quarters,
he cannot give appropriate replies by himself—
what is the use of his multitude of poems?"
Thus, the intent of comparison and stimulus (bǐxìng),
the meaning of indirect admonition (fěngyù),
were certainly practiced by the envoys.
The纵横家 school,
extending and elaborating this,
were thus able to be曲折 (subtle and circuitous) and accord with human feelings,
implicit and adept at indirect criticism.
The learning of the Nine Schools,
inheriting specialized functions from the Six Canons,
although some originated from the "Shū", "Yì", or "Chūnqiū",
their substance mostly stems from the teachings of the "Lǐ",
because its substance is comprehensive.
When they emerged to be applied in the world,
they necessarily incorporated纵横家 techniques,
to embellish their substance.
In antiquity, substance and ornament were unified.
By the Warring States period, each possessed its own substance;
when applied,
they necessarily incorporated the rhetoric of the纵横家 to embellish it—
this is the effect of the literary decline in the late Zhōu.
Therefore it is said:
The Warring States period
was an era of纵横家.
The literary genres of later ages were all fully developed during the Warring States period.
Why is this so? It is said:
As the traditions of the masters and historical records declined, the genre of collected works flourished;
as original composition declined, the study of ornate writing arose.
Collected works
are not the domain of specialists in ornate writing,
but rather gather literary compositions,
forming a mixed repository, as detailed in the chapter "Collected Works."
Later scholars inherited this and did not abandon it,
for once rivers are channeled, their momentum cannot be restrained again.
Classical studies are not the domain of specialists,
yet collected works contain exegeses of the classics;
historical studies are not the domain of specialists,
yet collected works contain biographies and records;
the establishment of doctrines (i.e., the writings of the various masters) is not the domain of specialists,
yet collected works contain discourses and disputations.
In the collected works of later ages,
aside from the three genres of classical exegesis, biography/records, and discourse/disputation,
the rest all belong to the category of ornate writing.
And ornate writing was indeed fully developed during the Warring States period,
inheriting its flow while each generation transformed its forms.
Scholars are unaware of this,
and trace back to Zhì Yú's compiled "Liúbié" (Zhì Yú authored the "Wénzhāng Liúbié Zhuàn").
Some even regard the "Wénxuǎn" of the Xiāo Liáng dynasty
as the progenitor of ornate writing,
which shows they do not understand the principle of the evolution of genres from ancient to modern times.
Now, taking the various genres in the "Wénxuǎn,"
we can verify their comprehensive development in the Warring States period (Zhì Yú's "Liúbié" and Kǒng Huàn's "Wényuàn" are no longer extant, hence we rely on the "Wénxuǎn").
The various rhapsodies on capital cities
derive from Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí's纵横捭阖 among the Six States,
extravagantly describing strategic situations.
"Shànglín" and "Yǔliè"
stem from Ānlíng's following the hunt,
and Lóngyáng's shared fishing.
"Kè Nán" and "Jiě Cháo"
derive from Qū Yuán's "Yúfǔ" and "Bǔjū,"
and Zhuāng Zhōu's questioning of Huì Shī.
Hán Fēi's "Chǔ Shuō,"
with its comparative events and paired evidence,
initiated the genre of "Liánzhū" (some predecessors have already mentioned this).
Yet some believe it began with figures like Fù Yì (according to Fù Xuán's words),
which is not its essence.
Mèngzǐ's questioning of the King of Qí about his great desires,
enumerating light warm clothing, rich food,
music and beautiful colors,
inspired the "Qī Lín";
yet some attribute its creation to Méi Chéng,
forgetting its origin.
Zōu Yáng's defense against slander before the King of Liáng,
Jiāng Yān's pleading before Jiànpíng,
derive from Sū Qín's self-defense of loyalty and trustworthiness leading to offense.
Essays like "Guò Qín," "Wáng Mìng," "Liù Dài," and "Biàn Wáng,"
with their rises and falls, repetitions,
embody the satirical intent of poets,
the way Mèngzǐ and Xúnzǐ cited ancient sages
to admonish contemporary rulers (Qū Yuán's works also praised Emperor Kù above, recounted Tāng and Wǔ in the middle, and spoke of Qí Huán below, which is similar).
The guests of Huáinán,
the literary figures of the Liáng garden,
were grand gatherings like those of Yuán, Cháng, Shēn, and Líng.
Dōngfāng Shuò and Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
attendants in Xījīng,
Xú Gàn, Chén Lín, Yìng Yáng, and Liú Zhēn,
sought and followed in Yèxià,
were wondrous spectacles of cosmological debate and ornate rhetoric.
Encounters had rises and falls,
times had gains and losses,
extraordinary talents converged in a declining age,
wealth and status concentrated their innate spirit,
from court to mountain forests,
from rivers and lakes to the palace gates,
across generations they resonated,
not knowing whether to feel sorrow or joy,
the deep emotion of literary men in the "Shī" and "Sāo"
is the same across ancient and modern times.
By the Warring States period, the transformation of literary writing was complete,
by the Warring States period, the literary genres of later ages were fully developed,
this statement is credible and well-supported.
By the Warring States period, the act of composing writings became specialized.
Why is this so? It is said:
In antiquity, there was no such thing as composing writings;
officials and masters upheld their statutes and regulations,
historiographers recorded their duties and accounts.
The way of writing,
used by all officials to govern,
and by the myriad people to observe,
was already fully utilized.
Therefore, sage kings standardized writing to bring peace to the world,
never failing to apply it to governance, education, statutes, and regulations,
rather than using writing for the personal compositions of an individual (detailed in the outer chapter "Xiàochóu Lüè: Zhùlù Xiānmíng Dàdào Lùn").
When the Way was not practiced, teachers and Confucians established their teachings,
which is why our Master's achievements surpassed Yáo and Shùn.
However, the Master wished to remain silent,
yet his actions were always instructive;
the Six Arts preserved the old statutes of the Duke of Zhōu,
and the Master never composed writings himself.
The "Lúnyǔ" records the subtle words of the Master,
while Zēngzǐ and Zǐsī
both had expositions to transmit teachings,
and by Mèngzǐ, the writing became grand and expansive.

This clearly shows that composing writings became specialized only by the Warring States period (the "Lúnyǔ" records Zēngzǐ's death; Wú Qǐ once studied under Zēngzǐ, so Zēngzǐ died in the early Warring States period, and the "Lúnyǔ" was completed during the Warring States period, which is clear).
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Guǎnzǐ once had writings,
"Yùzǐ" and "Yànzǐ"
were later forgeries.
However, recording the statutes, regulations, and governance of an era
is like the Duke of Zhōu having the "Guānlǐ."
Recording Guǎnzǐ's words and deeds
was compiled by those who studied Guǎn's methods,

and not composed by Guǎn Zhòng himself (some say Guǎn Zhòng's writings should not refer to Duke Huán by his posthumous title; Yán Ruòqú also said they were added by later people, not the original text of "Guǎnzǐ"; all these views do not understand that in antiquity, there was no practice of private composition; all were compiled by later people, as detailed in the chapter "Zhūzǐ").
The military strategists' "Tàigōng Yīnfú,"
the physicians' "Huángdì Sùwèn,"
the agriculturalists' "Shénnóng" and "Yělǎo,"
earlier Confucians considered them later forgeries,
falsely attributed to ancient people;
this view seems plausible,
but examining their intent,
it is not entirely complete.
For even minor skills and techniques,
their origins all began with the sages.
Without the transmission of subtle words and essential principles,
they could not have been utilized for millennia.
In the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties,
each guarded the hereditary professions of officials and crafts,
thus transmission was oral,
and before Confucius and Mèngzǐ,
their writings were never seen.
By the Warring States period, the way of official guardianship and master transmission was abandoned,
and those who mastered the learning
recorded old knowledge and wrote it on bamboo and silk.
Among these, there may inevitably be gains and losses,
but considering their origins,
they cannot be hastily dismissed.
For people of the Warring States period
to record the sayings of Huángdì and Shénnóng,
earlier Confucians thus discerned through literary style
and judged them as forgeries;
they did not know that in earliest antiquity, there was no composition of writings,

and it was only in the Warring States period that bamboo and silk replaced oral transmission (the Outer Historiographer was in charge of the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, as well as records of the four regions, and the Six Arts old statutes recounted by Confucius, all of which were not categories of composed writings; this has been discussed earlier).
In reality, they were not deliberate forgeries.
Thus, the specialization of composing writings began in the Warring States period,
which also arose from inevitable circumstances.
Composing writings inevitably evolved into literary expression,
and literary expression inevitably gave rise to its own preferences.
Later people lacked the compulsion of earlier people,
and merely pursued literary expression out of preference.
Yet they still proclaimed themselves as composing writings.
Thus, while the Warring States period was the zenith of literary writing,
the seeds of decline were already sown in the Warring States period.
Someone says:
If this is the case, then after the Three Dynasties,
among the Six Arts, the teaching of the *Book of Songs* is the most extensive.
May I ask, is there any use of literature
more flourishing than that of the *Book of Songs*? I reply:
How could this only be true after the Three Dynasties?
Even before the Three Dynasties,
the teaching of the *Book of Songs* was never not extensive.
The Master said:
"If you do not study the *Book of Songs*,
you will have no means to speak."
In ancient times, there were no private writings,
yet there were never no words expressing inner feelings.
They were only entrusted to sound,
and not recorded in writing,
so when the Qin people banned the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
the *Book of Documents* suffered gaps and interruptions,
but the poems of the *Book of Songs* were not lost.
In later ages, the achievement of bamboo and silk
surpassed that of mouth and ear;
while in ancient times, the transmission through sound
surpassed that of writing;
this is because times differ between ancient and modern,
and the principles and circumstances are also different.
Since ancient times, sage kings governed the world through rituals and music,
the refinement and substance of the Three Dynasties
came from a single source.
In times of flourishing,
institutions and regulations were preserved by the officials,
this is the substance of ritual;
emotions and aspirations were harmonized in songs and poems,
this is the refinement of music.
When decline came,
institutions and regulations scattered,
and the various masters expressed themselves through their arts.
Thus, specialized arts of governance
were all transformations of the *Official Rituals*.
Emotions and aspirations became unrestrained,
and retired scholars engaged in reckless debates,
so the hundred schools expounded their theories,

all being transformations of the *Book of Songs* in name. Schools such as Legalism, Logicians, Military, Agriculture, and Yin-Yang, which focus on practical application, are called specialized arts of governance. Originally, each had its own official duties, thus belonging to the officials, and are transformations of ritual. Schools such as those discussing cosmology, rhetoric, sophistry, and paradoxes, which focus on abstract principles, are called the hundred schools expounding theories. Their words merely express their emotions and aspirations, thus belonging to poetry, and are transformations of music.
The literature of the Warring States period

was a transformation of the former kings' rituals and music. The Six Arts are the legacy of the *Official Rituals*, this theory is also detailed in the *Discussion on Clarifying the Great Way* in the *Collation and Criticism Section* of the outer chapters.
However, the reason for specifically saying that the teaching of the *Book of Songs* was extensive during the Warring States period
is that specialized arts were few,
while persuasive and eloquent speeches were many.
In later ages, books on specialized arts ceased (spurious works of the masters are not worth mentioning), and literary collections flourished.
Although there are differences in purity, flaws, and quality,
in the end, they are nothing more than expressing their own emotions and aspirations.
Therefore it is said:
the literary styles of later ages
were all complete by the Warring States period,
and the teaching of the *Book of Songs* can be said to have reached its greatest extent then.
If scholars can truly broadly examine the literary collections of later ages,
and imagine the beginnings of the former kings' rituals and music,
they may then establish themselves and be able to speak (having a foundation in learning is establishment, not entirely as Zhūzǐ said, merely binding skin, flesh, sinews, and bones).
They can then participate in understanding the instruction of studying the *Book of Songs* and studying ritual.
Scholars only confine themselves to considering poetry as that which has rhyme,
and do not know that literature expressing emotions and aspirations,
elaborating and admonishing,
modulating and immersing,
all originate from the teaching of the *Book of Songs*.
Therefore, later literary collections flourished,
and the various inherited and used writings
followed its style,
without knowing its essential unity.
As for rhymed literature,
the ancients did not entirely equate it with the *Book of Songs*,
and later inherited uses such as poetry and fu
also did not entirely derive from the teaching of the Six Arts.
The reason for this is also fully present in the Warring States period.
Therefore, understanding the evolving styles and trends of the Warring States period,
then the distinction between ritual and music can be clarified,
and the teachings of the Six Arts can be differentiated;
the theories of the *Seven Summaries*, the Nine Schools, the various masters, and the hundred schools
can be traced to their sources and their streams explored;
the literature of the Liǎng Hàn, Liù Cháo, Táng, Sòng, Yuán, and Míng dynasties
can be divided by fields and demarcated by ridges;
official duties and specialized arts,
songs, poems, lyrics, and discourses,
the transitions from oral transmission to written records,
can all be settled while seated.
Expounding the categories of the *Great Plan*,
the admonitions and proclamations that are rhymed,
are for the convenience of chanting and recitation,
to remember and not forget.
The six images and explanatory words,
the rhymed parts of the *Yáo* and *Xì* [appendices to the *Yìjīng*],
are for communicating with divination,
and elucidating the obscure and mysterious.
Not all of the Six Arts can be equated with the *Book of Songs*,
yet rhymed language was not abandoned,
so harmonizing sound and coordinating rhythm
cannot be exclusively attributed to the teaching of the *Book of Songs*.
Historical records like the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and *Guóyǔ*,
philosophical works like the *Lǎozǐ* and *Zhuāngzǐ*,
where writing follows sound and thus becomes harmonious,
and language responds to rhythm and suddenly becomes coordinated,
must they necessarily conform to the comparisons and associations of the *Book of Songs* teaching?
Jiāo Yán's *Yì Lín*,
Shǐ Yóu's *Jí Jiù Piān*,
are rhymed texts in the classics category not involving the *Book of Songs*.
The seven-character lines of the *Huángtíng Jīng*,
the broken-character style of the *Cāntóngqì*,
are rhymed texts in the masters and arts category not involving the *Book of Songs*.
Later miscellaneous arts and hundred schools,
collecting terms and numbers,
mostly used five- or seven-character lines,
developed into songs and formulas,
all for the convenience of memorization and recitation,
none matching the meaning of the poets.
Yet the literary intent lies in lyrical expression,
the adopted meaning close to comparison and association,
sometimes lengthy as ten thousand words,
sometimes brief as a few phrases,
not necessarily harmonizing rhyme and sound,
yet discerning people elegantly appreciate them as legacies of the *Guófēng* and *Chǔcí*.
Therefore, those skilled in discussing literature
value seeking the author's intent,
and must not be confined by external form.
The tradition says:
"That which is recited without singing is called fu."
Bān Gù said:
"Fu is a branch of ancient poetry."
Liú Xié said:
"A vassal of the Six Arts,
flourished into a great state."
This is a transformation of prolonged lyrical expression,
and unrhymed literature that can communicate with poetry
also thereby became more extensive.
The twenty-five pieces of Qū Yuán,
recorded by Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù,
are considered the *Fu of Qū Yuán*.
The words of *The Fisherman*,
though not rhymed,
are included among the fu,
so the inherited distinctions of literary genres
must be understood gradually.
Literature that is elaborate and vigorous,
are all transformed styles of fu,
not only did a vassal become a great state,
but also like after Chén Wán,
leaving the old capital of Wǎnqiū,
and greatly opening territory on the shores of the Eastern Sea.
Later hundred schools and miscellaneous arts,
also used the fu style for recitation and collection (e.g., Dòu's *Shū Fù*, Wú's *Shìlèi Fù*, medical herb property fu, astrology, fortune-telling, and physiognomy arts fu, etc.).
These, like songs and formulas, emerged outside the Six Arts.
However, the fu writers,
still retained the legacy of the various masters,
confidently establishing themselves as a school of thought,
each with its own guiding principles.
They are certainly not like later poetry and fu writers,
confined by form without substance,
vaguely indistinguishable in their lineage.
Therefore, Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù's *Summary of Poetry and Fu*
divided into five categories,
and established Qū Yuán, Lù Jiǎ, and Xún Kuàng
as the three schools of learning (discussed in detail in the *Discussion on the Hànshū Treatise on Poetry and Fu* in the *Collation and Criticism Section* of the outer chapters).
The two histories by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
regarding the fu writings of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Yáng Xióng, and others,
all recorded them in detail in their biographies,
since Liú Zhījī and after,
those who consequently criticized and ridiculed them
are too numerous to count,
but essentially, they did not understand the words.
For they laid the foundation for the later literary garden,
and the literary garden must present the actual traces of literary brilliance.
Compared to Fàn Yè's history and after,
which merely labels a literary garden and only narrates the conduct of literary men,
they are far superior.
However, the fu of the Hàn court
were indeed not carelessly composed.
Long pieces were recorded in full in the biographies,
sufficient to show the extreme thought of the person,
almost like Jiā Yí's memorials and Dǒng Zhòngshū's policies,
their uses were different,
but similarly aimed at transmitting the person through literature.
Thus, the fu writers,
belonging to the Persuaders school,
and also inheriting the remaining style of the various masters,
this is why they differ from later literary scholars.
Therefore, when discussing literature from the Warring States period onward,
it is essential to seek the author's intent,
and not be confined by external form.
The flaw of judging literary works by their formal appearance reached its extreme in the anthologies of later generations.
This was due to the lack of discernment of the compilers,
and also because they did not understand the different schools of the ancients or the authors’ intended meanings,
so they had no choice but to judge the works by their formal appearance.

Although collected works began with Wèi Wén of the Jiàn’ān period compiling the writings of Xú, Chén, Yīng, and Liú into one collection—this being the beginning of literary collections, with Zhì Yú’s *Liúbié Jí* coming later—
they actually flourished during the Qí and Liáng dynasties.
The ancient learning could not be restored,

and by the Qí and Liáng periods it had completely vanished. Zhì Yú’s *Liúbié Jí* was a later person collecting the works of earlier people. Personal collections began with Qí’s *Wáng Wénxiàn Jí*, and Zhāomíng’s *Wénxuǎn* further exemplified the flourishing of general anthologies.
In the histories of Fàn, Chén, and those of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
the biographies of literary figures
always summarize their writings
by stating how many pieces of poetry, fu, inscriptions, admonitions, eulogies, and elegies they composed, but never mention how many volumes of collected works they produced.
Thus, it is evident that the writings of the ancients were scattered among various texts and were not forcibly categorized by type.
Sūn Wǔ’s book originally had eighty-two chapters (as detailed in the *Xiàochóu Lüè* of the outer chapters, in the *Hànzhì Bīngshū Lùn*),
but Hé Lǘ said, “I have already seen your thirteen chapters.”
This shows that the thirteen chapters from “Initial Calculations” onward were originally circulated separately and independently,
and were only combined by later generations—clear evidence of this.
Hán Fēi’s book now survives in fifty-five chapters,
but when the King of Qín saw his “Five Vermin” and “Solitary Indignation,”
he regretted not being able to live in the same era as him.
This shows that “Five Vermin” and “Solitary Indignation” were originally circulated separately and independently,
and were only combined by later generations—clear evidence of this.
The self-preface to *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* states that a gentleman asked about the twelve annals,
indicating that the eight overviews and six discourses were not originally included in the sequence.
Dǒng’s chapters “Qīngmíng,” “Yùbēi,” and “Zhúlín” were recorded by Bān Gù alongside *Fánlù* with their chapter titles,
showing that these chapters were not originally part of the *Fánlù* book.
Now, the specialized books of the various masters, which focus solely on their own topics without digressing, still cannot be forcibly categorized by type.
How much more so for literary collections, which gather works of varying forms and differing intents?
Without deeply investigating the intended meanings behind them, how can one forcibly judge them by their titles and formal appearances?
Fu preceded poetry, and *sāo* is distinct from fu.
Fu often begins with questions and answers, which were mistakenly treated as prefaces to fu—a clear example of earlier critiques of the *Wénxuǎn*.
As for “Fēngshàn,” “Měixīn,” and “Diǎnyǐn,” they are all eulogies.
If praising merits and virtues by citing auspicious signs is classified separately as “auspicious mandate,”
then Wáng Zǐyuān’s praise of the auspicious meeting where a sage ruler obtained worthy ministers should also be separately classified as “ruler and minister.”
Bān Gù’s rhyming summaries are actually the self-preface to the *Hànshū*.
His statements “Narrating ‘Annals of Emperor Gāo,’ First” and “Narrating ‘Biographies of Chén and Xiàng,’ First” were meant to explain his original intent in writing the book.
Since Sīmǎ Qiān had already written such works earlier, Bān Gù humbly referred to his own work as “narrating.”
Now, aside from historical discourses, a separate category called “historical narrative praises” has been created.

If so, then Sīmǎ Qiān’s self-preface, which states “Composing ‘Annals of the Five Emperors,’ First” and “Composing ‘Biography of Bóyí,’ First,” should also have a separate category called “historical composition praises.”
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn’s edicts examining the worthy and virtuous were essentially policy questions.
Now, because they were issued by the emperor, they are separately named “edicts” apart from policy questions.
If so, then the responses to imperial policy questions should be separated from policy questions and given a different name, such as “memorials.”

Jiǎ Yì’s “Guò Qín” was originally a chapter title in *Jiǎzǐ* (the transmitted *Jiǎshì Xīnshū* begins with the two chapters “Guò Qín,” but this was compiled by later people and is unreliable. The *Hànshū Yìwénzhì* records fifty-eight chapters of *Jiǎ Yì* and seven fu, with no other works mentioned, so it is clear that “Guò Qín” was a chapter of *Jiǎzǐ*).
Because Lù Jī’s discourse “Biàn Wáng” imitated “Guò Qín,”
and citing Zuǒ Sī’s statement “composing discourses based on ‘Guò Qín’” (Zuǒ Sī’s statement about composing discourses should be interpreted flexibly, not rigidly),
the genre was labeled as “discourse.”
Wèi Wén’s *Diǎnlùn* is similar to Huánzǐ’s *Xīnlùn* and Wáng Chōng’s *Lùnhéng* in using “discourse” in the book title.
“Lùnwén” is its chapter title.
Now it is grouped together with chapters like “Liù Dài” and “Biàn Wáng” under the category of “discourse.”

If so, then Zhāomíng’s self-preface, which states, “The works of Lǎo and Zhuāng, and the school of Guǎn and Mèng, take establishing meaning as their essence, not literary skill as their foundation,” and thus excludes the chapters of the various masters—does this mean that because these writings were selected, they could be excerpted and labeled as “discourse,” thereby transforming masters’ works into collected works?
The writings in *Qī Lín* are all in the form of questions.
Now, because Méi Shēng posed seven questions, they are labeled as “seven.”
If so, then “Jiǔ Gē,” “Jiǔ Zhāng,” and “Jiǔ Biàn” could also be labeled as “nine.”
“Nàn Shǔ Fùlǎo” is also in the form of questions.
Now, because the title contains “nàn” (difficulty), it is separately classified as the “nàn” genre.

If so, then “Kè Nàn” should be compiled together with it, while “Jiě Cháo” should be separately classified as the “cháo” (ridicule) genre, and “Bīn Xì” should be separately classified as the “xì” (play) genre.
The *Wénxuǎn* is the standard for literary compositions and the criterion for collected works,
yet it is confused, cluttered, and cannot be fully interrogated.
When browsing various collections, who can deeply perceive and grasp the different schools of the ancients and the authors’ intended meanings?
If even collecting others’ writings fails to capture their intended meanings,
how much more chaotic are those who compile their own works into collections?

As for the classification of general and individual collections, the merits and flaws of editing and compilation, the appropriateness of ancient and modern details and brevity, and the correctness of recording, selecting, evaluating, and transcribing, these will be discussed in separate dedicated chapters and will not be fully addressed here.

The Six Classics do not call themselves “classics,” and the Three Commentaries do not call themselves “commentaries”—just as each person has a self but cannot assert that self as exclusively their own.

Commentaries exist in relation to classics, and the self exists in relation to others. Thus, the names “classic,” “commentary,” “person,” and “self” arose out of necessity, not because they are inherently so.
The *Yì* says: “In ancient times, they governed by knotting ropes; later, sages replaced this with writing, so officials could govern and the people could understand.”
Governing and understanding were meant to reveal the hidden and clarify forms and names, disseminate governance and teachings, and standardize laws and regulations.
There was no such thing as using writing for private family statements.
The *Yì* says: “Clouds and thunder symbolize difficulty; the nobleman uses this to order the world.”
“Ordering the world” refers to governing the universe.
Zhèng’s commentary says: “Discussing and compiling books, rituals, and music to implement governance.”
This is the origin of the term “classic”!
Yet it still refers to ordering and managing, not explicitly pointing to the *Shī*, *Shū*, or the Six Arts as “classics.”
With the decline of the Three Dynasties, governance and teachings separated.
The Master was born in the Eastern Zhōu, virtuous but without position.
Fearing that the accumulated laws and perfected ways of the former sage kings, which reached their peak in the Chéng Zhōu period, would have no one to continue and uphold them and thus be lost,
he took the institutions of the Duke of Zhōu, which embodied the workings of heaven and humanity and preserved the traces of governance and transformation,
and together with his disciples, elucidated and clarified them.
This is why the Six Arts, though they lost their official guardians, still relied on master-disciple transmission.
Yet in the Master’s time, they were still not called “classics.”
After the Master passed away, subtle words ceased and great meanings began to diverge.
Then, disciples and followers, based on what they had seen, heard, or been told,
either took from bamboo slips or passed on orally,
recording the texts and deriving meanings.
Zuǒ’s *Chūnqiū* and Zǐxià’s chapters on mourning garments were all called “commentaries.”
Moreover, surviving texts from earlier times not part of the Six Arts were also referred to as “commentaries” when discussed,
such as Mèngzǐ’s responses about Tāng, Wǔ, and King Wén’s hunting parks.
Thus, the name “classic” arose because of “commentaries,” much like establishing the title “father” because of “sons.”
When officials and teachers became distinct,
and scholars without official positions engaged in unrestrained debates,
various masters emerged in great numbers,
writing books and establishing doctrines,
then writings began to include private discourses,
not entirely derived from statutes, regulations, and governmental teachings.
The school of the Ru (Confucians),
revered the Six Arts and honored them as Classics,
thus not only using the term in contrast to commentaries.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Learning begins with reciting the Classics,
and ends with practicing ritual."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Confucius spoke of governing the Six Classics: the *Shī*, *Shū*, *Lǐ*, *Yuè*, *Yì*, and *Chūnqiū*."
He also said:
"I have read the Twelve Classics,
to meet Lǎozǐ."
Both Xúnzǐ and Zhuāngzǐ came from the disciples of Zǐxià,
and what they said is as above;
the name "Six Classics"
clearly originated from the disciples of Confucius.
However, what they referred to specifically as the Six Classics
were the statutes, regulations, and governmental teachings of the ancient kings,
which upheld order in the world.
Therefore, the *Jīngjiě* distinguishes the Six Classics,
considering that upon entering a state, one can understand its teachings.
The *Lúnyǔ* records the words and deeds of the Master,
the *Ěryǎ* provides glosses for the various Classics,
the *Xiàojīng* was compiled by disciples of later generations,
and works like the *Zīyī*, *Fáng*, and *Biǎo* chapters
are similar in nature.
Scholars like Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù
categorized them into nine classes,
yet referred to the arts as six,
thus treating the other three as commentaries,
and attaching them to the Classics.
These are the so-called commentaries separated from the Classics,
not arranged together with commentaries attached to the Classics.
At that time, various masters in their writings
often distinguished between Classics and commentaries themselves,
such as the compilers of the *Guǎnzǐ* separating the "Classical Sayings,"
the *Mòzǐ* also having "Classic" chapters,
and the *Hánfēizǐ* containing "Stored Sayings" as Classics and commentaries.
This was likely due to establishing meanings according to the times,
using their own doctrines to form a framework,
not imitating or presumptuously using the name.
"Classic" was a term of respect,
its meaning also implying comprehensiveness and essence,
not as strict as in later ages.
Even a sage like the Master
did not necessarily have his works called Classics.
The various masters had Classics
to connect their commentaries,
each with its appropriate meaning.
Later bibliographers,
due to the abundance of writings
not all related to fundamental principles,
then took the subtle words of ancient sages
and works supporting the various Classics,
and all called them Classics.
Such as the *Lúnyǔ*, *Mèngzǐ*, *Xiàojīng*,
and the distinctions of the *Dàdài Lǐjì* and *Xiǎodài Lǐjì* from the *Lǐ*,
the *Zuǒzhuàn*, *Gōngyáng*, and *Gǔliáng* distinctions from the *Chūnqiū*,
all were titled as Classics,
leading to Nine Classics, Ten Classics, Thirteen, Fourteen Classics, etc.,
considered specialized categories,
honoring the Classics and including their branches.
And Confucian scholars in their writings
began to strictly uphold the name "Classic,"
not daring to violate it,
thus respecting the teachings of the sages and carefully avoiding improper use of the name,
similar to after the Three Dynasties,
when none but the sovereign could refer to themselves as "zhèn."
However, what are now called Classics
are mostly what the ancients called commentaries.
What the ancients called Classics
were the statutes, regulations, and legal systems
of the prosperous era of the Three Dynasties,
manifested in the realities of governance and conduct,
not texts intentionally created by sages to transmit to later generations.
Affairs have concrete evidence,
while principles have no fixed form.
Therefore, the Master's transmission of the Six Classics
all drew from the statutes and regulations of the ancient kings,
never separating affairs to expound principles.
Later Confucians, taking the words and deeds of the sage teacher as models for the world,
also designated their books as Classics,
which is natural according to reason.
However, if one can arbitrarily honor them,
then one can also arbitrarily usurp the name.
Since the distinction between officials and teachers,
officials had governance,
and those of low status dared not forcibly interfere,
because there was evidence.
Teachers had teachings,
and the unworthy dared to presumptuously claim authority,
because there was no evidence.
In Mencius's time,
Yáng and Mò were considered heterodox.
Yáng had no writings;
Mò Dí's writings
initially were not called Classics (though there are "Classic" chapters and "Classic Explanations," the entire work was not named a Classic).
Yet Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Followers like Huò and Dènglíng
all recited the *Mòjīng*,"
thus his disciples themselves revered and called it a Classic.
When Qín Jǐng of the Eastern Hàn was sent to Tiānzhú,
the *Forty-Two Chapters*
were not called a Classic;
Buddhist scriptures were all translated in China; Indian texts had no character for "classic." Later, when translated into Chinese,
they were arbitrarily called Classics,
which was also embellished language.
The two chapters of the *Lǎozǐ*,
recorded by Liú and Bān,
were initially not called a Classic.
The *Suíshū* bibliography, following Ruǎn's *Catalog*,
called it the *Lǎozǐjīng*.
It is likely that Ruǎn's *Catalog* came from the Liáng period,
when Emperor Wǔ of Liáng revered heterodox teachings,
thus both Buddhist and Daoist works were classified as Classics,
which was imitated.
And adding *Dàodé Zhēnjīng* to the *Lǎozǐ*,
and *Nánhuá Zhēnjīng* to the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
and *Chōngxū Zhēnjīng* to the *Lièzǐ*,
was due to the Xuánjiào (Mysterious Teaching) establishment of categories during the Kāiyuán era,
with added embellishments,
becoming even more pronounced later.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
"The Way they speak of
is not the Way I speak of."
Since the teachings and names differ,
why prevent them from calling what they consider Classics,
which are not what I call Classics?
As for state institutions,
they are originally regulatory systems.
Lǐ Kuī's *Fǎjīng*
was the origin of later laws and decrees;
the Táng people established legal categories,
the Míng founder promulgated the *Dàgào*,
scholars and teachers lectured on it,
considering it statutory law,
which aligns with the meaning of "managing" in the *Yì*,
state instructions and codes,
revered by officials and people as Classics,
not contradicting ancient meaning.
Mencius said:
"To practice benevolent governance,
one must start with defining boundaries."
Boundaries referred to as "jīng,"
takes the meaning of ordering and managing.
Therefore, geographical books
often use "jīng" in their names.
The *Hànshū* bibliography has the *Shānhǎijīng*,
the *Suíshū* bibliography then has the *Shuǐjīng*,
later regional geographies
often called "tújīng,"
all based on the meaning of boundaries,
the books themselves preserve precedents,
not in the same category as literary compositions,
and thus do not conflict
with the writings of the Six Arts.
As for the various schools of techniques and calculations,
all originated from the creations of the sage schools.
The Duke of Zhōu managed and transmitted codes,
all adhering to official duties and material principles,
without losing their transmission.
When the officials lost their responsibilities,
and the Way scattered and categories vanished,
then those who studied these doctrines
discussed and transmitted them among themselves,
similar to the transmission and study within the Confucian school out of necessity.
However, oral learning
cannot last long without errors,
thus recording on bamboo and silk
to transmit to others (discussed in detail in the "Shījiào I" chapter),
is also reasonable.
Therefore, by the Warring States period, books attributed to Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Huángdì
emerged混杂ly.
These books all referred to ancient sages,
such as the astronomical Gān and Shí's *Xīngjīng*,
the medical *Língshū*, *Sùwèn*, *Nànjīng*,
and similar works were numerous.
This is like carpenters offering sacrifices to Lǔ Bān,
soldiers offering sacrifices to Chīyóu;
it is not necessary that the authors were truly sages,
but those who practiced these arts,
revering them as authorities,
also had to honor them as classical sayings.
Furthermore, after the "Treatise on Literature" in the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
various works from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods emerged,
such as Shī Kuàng's *Classic of Birds*,
and Bó Lè's *Classic of Horse Physiognomy*.
Works of this kind are also numerous,
but they are merely the creations of enthusiasts
who attached them to famous figures,
or those with some knowledge of the methods
who invoked ancient authorities to elevate their status.
This is similar to how Confucian scholars transmitted the *Book of Documents* attributed to Méi Fú,
or the "Great Preface" to the *Book of Songs* attributed to Zǐ Xià.
Others, such as Lù Yǔ's *Classic of Tea*,
Zhāng Nán's *Classic of Go*,
the *Classic of Sweet Dew* on wine,
and the *Classic of Shell Appraisal* on goods,
are merely literary diversions,
and fundamentally unsuitable for inclusion in bibliographic records.
They are akin to writing biographies for a writing brush,
treatises on crabs,
histories of the qin,
or manuals on lychees and peonies.
These are all ambiguous and insubstantial,
not worthy of serious discussion.
Now, considering the aforementioned categories:
The scriptures of heterodox teachings,
like the various states of the Warring States period each claiming kingship,
ignore the authority of the Zhou Son of Heaven.
Yet the principles of name and status in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
are known to all,
and they cannot be usurped and appropriated.
As for the classics of institutions,
the laws of the ruling dynasty,
unified in doctrine and custom,
need not all bear the name "classic."
Moreover, ritual adapts to the times,
and as subjects of the contemporary era,
one must naturally follow them without overstepping.
Even devotion to the Six Arts
is but one aspect of adhering to the king's institutions.
Regarding the classics of arts and techniques,
each has its adherents
who uphold them collectively,
so there is no fear of transgressing boundaries.
As for diversions that also bear the name "classic,"
this is like what Zhào Tuó called arrogating an imperial title
merely for self-amusement.
They can be treated as playful diversions;
the Way of the Six Classics,
radiant as the midday sun,
is surely not harmed by such things!
For heterodox schools to call their works "classics" to rival the Six Arts
is foolish.
For Confucian scholars to presumptuously label works as "classics" to emulate the Six Arts
is arrogant.
The Six Classics were not originally honorific titles;
their meaning lies in governing and serving as models for the world.
The Six Arts were all governmental statutes of the Duke of Zhōu,
hence they were established as classics.
Though the sagehood of Confucius
is no less than that of the Duke of Zhōu,
the chapters such as the *Analects* are not called classics
because they are not governmental statutes.
Later Confucians, out of reverence, elevated them,
categorizing them under classics,
considering commentaries as wings supporting the classics.
The books of Buddhism and Daoism
are originally the teachings of individual schools,
lacking governance and administrative matters.
Their followers, wishing to honor their teachings,
may elevate their school's teachings
above the Six Classics—
there is nothing wrong with that.
But to forcibly apply the name "classic" to draw parallels
is no different from actors imitating the prime minister of Chǔ.
This, too, is foolish.
Yáng Xióng and Liú Xīn
were Confucians well-versed in the classics.
Yáng Xióng's *Model Sayings*,
it is said, responded to contemporary inquiries
with normative answers—
this is acceptable.
But to claim it imitates the *Analects*—
how erroneous!
Nevertheless,
this is still the teaching of one school,
and its flaw is minor.
What is more astonishing
is his composition of the *Great Mystery* to parallel the *Book of Changes*.
People only know to call it presumptuous emulation of a classic,
but they do not realize that the *Book of Changes* was a governmental statute of the ancient kings, not empty words.
Yáng Xióng thus committed the crime of arrogating royal statutes—
a grave lack of reflection. See the chapter "The Teaching of the *Changes*."
Wèi Yuán's *Primordial Wrapper*,
Sīmǎ Guāng's *Hidden Void*,
even sought to imitate the *Great Mystery* in their compositions,
not realizing that the *Great Mystery*'s imitation of the *Book of Changes* was already mistaken.
Liú Xīn composed the *Great Announcement* for Wáng Mǎng—
his actions offended Confucian teachings,
and there is certainly no excuse for that.
But to imitate the *Book of Documents*—
how could it go this far?
As for the six classics of Héfén,
some say they were embellished by enthusiasts,
and Wáng Tōng might not have been so presumptuous.
If such things truly occurred,
then the criticism of being "slaves to the Six Classics"
still does not capture the full truth.
Slaves do serve their masters,
but how did Wáng's six classics
serve the house of Confucius?
Where is the evidence?
Shù Xī's "Supplemented Odes for the Shēng",
Pí Rìxiū's "Supplemented Nine Xià",
and Bái Jūyì's "Supplemented Tāng's Expedition",
may be considered literary playfulness without malice—
calling them imitations
is acceptable.
But to label them as "supplements"—
what place do the words of literary writers have
in filling the gaps of the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*?
As for the *Classic of Filial Piety*,
though named a classic,
it is actually a commentary.
Confucians, valuing the Master's legacy,
attached it to the classics section.
Mǎ Róng, earnest in promoting loyalty,
could have presented his own teachings,
citing classics and commentaries,
expounding freely and repeatedly,
pushing his arguments to their limits.
Yet he insisted on titling it *Classic of Loyalty*—
this is indeed peculiar.
Moreover, dividing it into eighteen chapters,
quoting the *Airs* and adorning it with the *Elegantiae*,
mimicking them one by one—
how is this different from Zhāng Zǎi's "Imitating the Four Sorrows"
or the *Seven Forests* imitating the "Seven Stimuli"?
Truly, it is not Mǎ's work
but a forgery by vulgar Confucians.
Sòng Ruòzhāo's *Women's Classic of Filial Piety*,
and Madame Zhèng's *Women's Analects*—
to acknowledge women's talent
and praise their aspirations is fine.
But if they wished to clarify women's education,
they could have established their own doctrines.
Instead, they invented Bān Zhāo and Huì Jī
conversing with other women—
this treats the work as a canonical instruction
while first relying on fictional characters like Zǐxū and Wúshì,
leaving readers at a loss.
Their intention was to make it resemble classics and commentaries,
but can classics be imitated?
If one seeks resemblance to classics,
then even jesters have hexagrams. See *Notes Taken While Ploughing*.
Boots beginning to store sound
have their "Monthly Ordinances"— all playful matters.
As for Qū Yuán expressing his grievances
in twenty-five poetic pieces,
Liú Xiàng and Bān Gù, in their records,
generally called them *The Poetry of Qū Yuán*.
Yet when Wáng Yì wrote his commentary,
the piece "Encountering Sorrow"
already bore the name "classic."
Wáng explained "classic" as "path,"
but he did not know who first
titled it as a classic.
By the time Sòng dynasty scholars annotated Qū Yuán,
they said, "One edition has 'commentary' after the 'Nine Songs'."
Though the origin of the name is unknown,
it likely established the name "commentary" based on the classic,
and this did not begin in the Sòng.
Now, Qū Yuán's poetry
naturally emphasizes "Encountering Sorrow,"
and from Sīmǎ Qiān onward,
the entire collection was even named after "Sorrow,"
as it still is today.
Yet the themes of the various pieces
are fundamentally undifferentiated.
Merely because the first piece is emphasized,
to forcibly divide them into classic and commentary,
trying to equate the standard *Elegantiae* as classics
and the altered *Elegantiae* as commentaries—
this would mean the seven chapters of *Mencius*
should be divided into the "King Hui of Liáng" as classic,
and "Gōngsūn," "Téng Wéngōng," and others as commentaries.
When the Master composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
Zhuāngzǐ considered it as offering judgments without making definitive decisions,
for its principles are embedded within its events and its prose,
without imposing rewards or punishments on its own.
From the Hàn and Wèi dynasties onward,
those who imitated the Spring and Autumn Annals
were indeed numerous.
Among them, some succeeded while others failed,
and it would be impossible to enumerate them all.
Later commentators
even compared the works of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward
to the Shàngshū;
and the various chronicles
to the Spring and Autumn Annals.
They did not realize that the basic annals of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
were originally rooted in the tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
while their treatises, tables, and biographies
were akin to the internal and external commentaries of the Zuǒzhuàn and Guóyǔ, which elucidated and complemented the main text.
The various works titled Yángqiū
emerged in a scattered fashion over time,
some using the name but altering the form (such as the Shíliù Guó Chūnqiū),
others avoiding the name while imitating the substance (such as the Tōngjiàn Gāngmù).
In essence, they all failed to recognize that the works of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
were fundamentally continuing the tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and were not modeled after the Shàngshū.
Therefore, those who understand the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals
should only examine the prose and events in the works of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward,
to discern what principles are embedded within them.
If one wishes to compile events
and arrange them by year,
then the examples of Xún Yuè and Yuán Hóng are readily available,
and they can certainly be emulated.
But if one insists on creating a new Spring and Autumn Annals
outside the frameworks of annals-biographies and chronicles,
then it would merely be a continuation of Wáng Tōng’s Yuánjīng.
When heterodox schools resist the classics,
they are not worth discussing.
But if Confucian scholars, who devote themselves to the Six Classics,
do not realize that the classics cannot be imitated,
then their understanding as Confucians is shallow indeed!

The great origin of the Way comes from Heaven,
but does Heaven indeed command it with earnest words? It is said:
Before Heaven and Earth existed,
I cannot know.
When Heaven and Earth gave birth to humanity,
the Way was already present,
though not yet manifested.
When three people lived together in a dwelling,
the Way began to take shape,
though not yet fully evident.
When people multiplied from tens and fives to hundreds and thousands,
and a single dwelling could no longer contain them,
they were divided into groups and classes,
and the Way became evident.
The names of benevolence, righteousness, loyalty, and filial piety,
and the institutions of punishments, governance, rituals, and music,
all arose out of necessity.
Human life possesses the Way,
but people are unaware of it;
when three people live together in a dwelling,
they must open and close the doors morning and evening,
and fetch firewood and draw water for meals.
Since it is not a single individual,
there must be division of responsibilities.
Some attend to specific tasks,
others take turns on shifts—
this is what is called the inevitable tendency,
and from it emerges the principle of fairness and order.
Fearing mutual neglect and contention,
they must defer to the eldest to maintain balance—
again, an inevitable tendency,
and from it takes shape the distinction between elder and younger, honored and humble.
When it comes to tens, fives, hundreds, and thousands,
divided into groups and classes,
there must be leaders for each group of tens and fives,
and as they accumulate into hundreds and thousands,
the multitude relies on capable management.
They must defer to the most talented to handle complexity,
and as situations grow chaotic, requiring guidance,
they must defer to the most virtuous to oversee transformation—
this too is an inevitable tendency;
and from it emerge the roles of rulers and teachers,
the division of land into regions,
and the ideas of the well-field system, feudalism, and schools.
Therefore, the Way
is not something created by the wisdom or power of sages;
it is all a natural outcome of circumstances,
gradually taking shape and becoming evident,
emerging out of necessity.
Thus it is said to come from Heaven.
The Yìjīng says:
"The alternation of yīn and yáng is called the Way."
This means that before humanity existed, the Way was already present.
"What continues it is goodness;
what completes it is nature."
This means Heaven manifests through humanity,
and principle attaches to vital force.
Therefore, what can be given form and named
are all manifestations of the Way,
but not the Way itself.
The Way
is the reason why all things are as they are,
not the way all things ought to be.
What humans can perceive
is only the way things ought to be.
From the beginning of human life,
to the formation of tens, fives, hundreds, and thousands,
and the establishment of rulers and teachers,
the division of regions and demarcation of land—
there must first be a need, and then provision follows;
first a blockage, and then release follows;
first a flaw, and then remedy follows.
The creations of Fúxī, Shénnóng, Xuānyuán, and Zhuānxū
were initially no more than this.
Laws accumulated and became refined and complete,
reaching perfection in the time of Táng and Yú;
the Yīn built upon the Xià, learning from them,
until the Chéng-Zhōu era left no regrets.
It is like a trickling stream accumulating to become rivers,
or mounds of earth accumulating to form mountains—
this too is the natural tendency of principle and circumstance;
it is not that the sagehood of Yáo and Shùn
surpassed that of Fúxī and Xuānyuán,
or that the divine prowess of Wén and Wǔ
excelled that of Yǔ and Tāng.
Later sages followed earlier sages,
not because they followed the earlier sages themselves,
but because they followed the Way that gradually took shape and became evident.
The Three Sovereigns governed through non-action and natural transformation,
the Five Emperors initiated things and accomplished tasks,
the Three Kings established institutions and handed down laws—
later people see these as differences in governance and transformation.
When the sages of those times created institutions,
it was like needing linen in summer
and furs in winter—
not because they harbored any intention
to think, "I must be like this to differ from the sages,"
or "I must be like this to match the earlier sages."
All this is the inevitable outcome of the alternating cycles of yīn and yáng,
but it cannot be equated with the Way of yīn and yáng itself.
The alternating cycles of yīn and yáng
are like the turning of a wheel.
The sages' creation of institutions,
resembling linen in summer and furs in winter,
is like the tracks left by the wheel.
The Way operates spontaneously,
while the sage cannot but act as he does.
Are these two situations the same?
They are not.
The Way does nothing yet acts spontaneously;
the sage has insight and thus cannot but act as he does.
Because the sage has insight,
he cannot but act as he does;
the common people lack insight,
so they act without knowing why they do so.
Which is closer to the Way?
Acting without knowing why,
that is the Way itself.
It is not that there is nothing to see,
but that it cannot be seen.
That which cannot but be so
is how the sage aligns with the Way;
it cannot be taken as the Way itself.
When the sage seeks the Way,
the Way cannot be seen;
it is through the common people’s acting without knowing why
that the sage is able to perceive the Way.
Thus, acting without knowing why
is the trace of the alternating yīn and yáng.
Learning from the sage
makes one a worthy.
Learning from the worthy
makes one a gentleman.
Learning from the common people
makes one a sage.
It is not that the common people can be learned from directly,
but that the Way must be sought in the traces of the alternating yīn and yáng.
From the beginning of heaven and earth
down to the times of Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng,
traces multiplied, and the principles of adaptation and continuity became fully developed.
Zhōu Gōng, a sage endowed by heaven with innate knowledge,
happened to live at a time when ancient traditions had accumulated
and the methods of the Way were fully完备,
thus in planning and instituting,
he gathered the great achievements of a thousand ages.
This too was due to the circumstances of the time,
not because Zhōu Gōng’s sagely wisdom could make it so.
For since ancient times, all sages
have learned from the common people’s acting without knowing why,
and Zhōu Gōng moreover thoroughly examined the unavoidable actions of sages since antiquity,
thus understanding why they were so.
Though Zhōu Gōng was indeed a sage endowed by heaven with innate knowledge,
this was not due to his own intelligence or ability;
it was the circumstances of the time that made it so.
Just as spring, summer, autumn, and winter
each govern a season,
and winter marks the completion of the year,
this too is due to the circumstances of the time,
not because winter surpasses the other three seasons.
Thus, sages who create institutions and manifest achievements
are alike throughout the ages.
But to gather the great achievements—
this is unique to Zhōu Gōng.
The times happened to be right for it,
and even Zhōu Gōng himself did not know why it was so.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Confucius may be called one who gathered all the great achievements."
Now if we say that it was Zhōu Gōng who gathered the great achievements,
does this not contradict Mèngzǐ’s meaning?
To "gather" means
to collect what everyone has and unify it.
From the beginning of heaven and earth
down to the times of Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng,
all were sages who held the position of Son of Heaven,
planning governance and transformation,
all arising from the natural suitability of the substance of the Way.
Zhōu Gōng completed the virtue of King Wén and King Wǔ,
just when the imperial way was fully完备 and the kingly way complete,
with Yīn building upon Xià and serving as a mirror,
reaching a point where nothing more could be added.
Thus he was able to draw upon this to establish institutions and regulations,
and with the Way of Zhōu, gather the achievements of the ancient sages.
This is what is meant by gathering the great achievements.
Confucius had virtue but no position,
so he had no means to obtain the authority to institute,
and could not be counted among those who completed a single achievement;
how could there be great achievements for him to gather?
It is not that Confucius’s sageliness
was inferior to Zhōu Gōng’s;
it was the circumstances of the time that made it so.
What Mèngzǐ meant by gathering the great achievements
was said in relation to Bó Yí, Yī Yǐn, and Liǔxià Huì.
Fearing that learners might think Confucius’s sageliness
was the same as these three men’s,
and having no other analogy,
he analogized to the great completion in making music.
Thus the saying that Confucius achieved great completion
can be applied in relation to those three men,
but cannot fully encompass Confucius.
To use it to fully encompass Confucius
would instead diminish Confucius.
Why?
Zhōu Gōng gathered the great achievements since Fúxī, Xuānyuán, Yáo, and Shùn;
Zhōu Gōng indeed learned from the successive sages and gathered them.
Without the methods of the Way of the successive sages,
he certainly could not have become the Zhōu Gōng he was.
Confucius did not gather the great achievements of Bó Yí, Yī Yǐn, and Liǔxià Huì;
Confucius certainly never learned from Bó Yí, Yī Yǐn, and Liǔxià Huì,
and even without the deeds of Bó Yí, Yī Yǐn, and Liǔxià Huì,
would he then have had nothing with which to become the Confucius he was?
Mèngzǐ’s words
each have their appropriate context,
how can one take the text literally and harm the meaning?
A man from Dáxiàng village said:
"Great is Confucius!
He is broadly learned, yet has no specialized reputation."
Now people all laugh at the villager for not understanding Confucius;
but do they know what reputation Confucius actually achieved?
Thinking that a sage endowed by heaven with innate knowledge
cannot be discussed or compared,
and thus cannot be given a fixed name,
they then invoke heaven and spirits,
considering the sage unknowable and leaving it at that.
How does their insight
differ from the villager’s?
The greatness of heaven and earth
can be exhausted in a single phrase.
Though Confucius is great,
he does not surpass heaven and earth;
can he alone not be exhausted in a single phrase?
If asked how to exhaust him in a single phrase,
the answer is:
He learned from Zhōu Gōng, that is all.
Was there nothing else to learn besides Zhōu Gōng?
It is not that there was nothing to learn and Confucius failed to reach it;
since Zhōu Gōng had already gathered the achievements of all the sages,
beyond Zhōu Gōng
there was simply nothing more to learn.
Zhōu Gōng gathered the great achievements of all the sages;
Confucius learned and fully embodied the Way of Zhōu Gōng.
This single phrase
is sufficient to cover the entirety of Confucius.
"He transmitted the doctrines of Yáo and Shùn"—
this was the aspiration of Zhōu Gōng.
"He took Wén and Wǔ as his models"—
this was the work of Zhōu Gōng.
Once he said:
"Since King Wén is gone,
does not culture reside here?"
Again he said:
"How I have decayed!
I no longer dream of Zhōu Gōng."
He also said:
"I study the Zhōu rituals,
which are now in use."
And also:
"How rich and elegant is the culture!
I follow Zhōu."
When Duke Āi asked about governance,
he said:
"The governance of Wén and Wǔ
is spread out on bamboo and wooden tablets."
When asked, "From whom did Zhòngní learn?"
Zǐgòng said,
"The Way of Wén and Wǔ
has not yet fallen to the ground."
"Transmitting without creating"—
this refers to the old statutes of Zhōu Gōng.
"Loving antiquity and diligently seeking"—
this refers to the surviving texts of Zhōu Gōng.
The villager lived in the same age but did not know this,
saying he had no specialized reputation;
yet he was not entirely without insight.
Later people read the records
and do not know what the Master learned;
this is inferior to the villager’s insight.
Yet they still laugh at the villager for not knowing—
is this not like one who has run a hundred steps laughing at one who has run fifty?
Thus, since ancient times, sages
though alike in sageliness,
the reasons for their being sages
need not be entirely the same;
this is due to the circumstances of the time.
Only Confucius and Zhōu Gōng
were both born after methods had accumulated and the Way was完备, with nothing more to add.
Zhōu Gōng gathered the achievements to practice the Way;
Confucius fully embodied the Way to illuminate its teachings.
They fit together like tally tokens,
as if coming from a single person,
with not the slightest difference or discrepancy.
Then, for those who wish to honor Confucius,
what need is there to invoke heaven and spirits
with vague and unreliable theories?
Someone says:
Since Confucius shared the same Way as the Duke of Zhōu,
and the Duke of Zhōu synthesized the great achievements,
is Confucius alone not considered a great synthesizer? I reply:
Confucius’s great synthesis,
is not what Mencius meant either.
It is rather that he shared with the Duke of Zhōu the synthesis of the accomplishments of Fúxī, Shénnóng, Xuānyuán, Zhuānxū, Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties,
and not the synthesis of the accomplishments of Yí Yǐn and Liǔxià Huì.
It is because the roles of ruler and teacher separated, and governance and instruction could no longer be united in one person,
which is a matter of the vital force and destiny that comes from Heaven.
The Duke of Zhōu synthesized the accomplishments of the governing tradition,
while Confucius illuminated the ultimate standard for establishing instruction.
Both were necessities dictated by the nature of affairs and principles,
and not because the sages differed from their predecessors.
This is the Way and the model that comes from Heaven.
Therefore, before the Suí and Táng dynasties,
schools jointly sacrificed to Zhōu and Kǒng,
taking the Duke of Zhōu as the Former Sage,
and Confucius as the Former Teacher.
This was to say that creating institutions makes one a sage,
while establishing instruction makes one a teacher.
Thus Mencius said:
"The Way of the Duke of Zhōu and Zhòngní is one."
If so, then the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
by the circumstances of their times, established the ultimate standards for their respective traditions.
Do sages indeed rely on the circumstances of their times?
Zǎi Wǒ held that the Master was "worthier than Yáo and Shùn";
Zǐgòng held that "among the people born there has never been one like the Master";
Yǒuruò, comparing the Master to the ancient sages,
said he "stood out from his class and rose above the crowd."
These three disciples all set aside the Duke of Zhōu,
and uniquely honored Master Kǒng.
Master Zhū held that their achievements in affairs differed,
which is correct.
However, governance manifests in actual deeds,
while instruction transmits empty words.
Later people, based on the words of these three disciples,
greatly exalted Confucius,
placing him above Yáo and Shùn.
Consequently, they revered the nature and destiny and belittled achievements in affairs.
Thus, the statecraft of a thousand sages

was deemed insufficient to match the idle discussions of Confucian scholars. Yíchuān, discussing Yǔ, Jì, and Yánzǐ, said Yǔ and Jì were coarser compared to Yánzǐ. Master Zhū also closely compared the two Chéngs with Yán and Mèng, weighing their strengths and weaknesses. Such sectarian views are unavoidable even among the worthy, a common affliction throughout the ages.
Now, in honoring the Master,
nothing is better than being close to human feelings.
Not knowing the reality,
and only striving to exalt him,
makes it mysterious and even more mysterious.
The sage becomes merely a lofty title like a spirit or Heaven.
What benefit does this bring to the world’s instruction?
Therefore, Zhōu and Kǒng cannot be ranked as superior or inferior.
"Dust and dirt, chaff and husks,
could mold and cast a Yáo or Shùn" —
Zhuāngzǐ even called this a parable.
How could Confucian scholars adopt such a saying?
Therefore, one who wishes to know the Way
must first know why Zhōu and Kǒng were Zhōu and Kǒng.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
"From the Duke of Zhōu upward,
upward they were rulers,
therefore their affairs were implemented;
from the Duke of Zhōu downward,
downward they were ministers,
therefore their doctrines are prolonged."
Now, the prolonging of doctrines
is how the Way is illuminated,
but the prolonging of doctrines
is also how the Way becomes obscured.
The Master illuminated instruction for ten thousand generations,
yet the Master never created doctrines for himself.
He elucidated and honored the Six Classics,
preserving the old statutes of the Duke of Zhōu.
Therefore he said:
"I transmit and do not create;
I am faithful to and love antiquity."
He also said:
"There are probably those who create without knowing,
but I am not one of them."
"The Master’s standard speech concerned
the Odes, the Documents, and the performance of the Rites,"
which means he illuminated the Way of the former kings to guide people.
It was not that the Master, in deferring to the former kings,
intended to be humble and refrain from creating himself;
rather, the Master had nothing to create.
Having virtue but no position,
he lacked the authority to create institutions.
Empty words cannot instruct people;
this is what is meant by 'without evidence, there is no trust.'
The matter of instruction,
since the times of Fúxī and Xuānyuán,
has already existed.
Observing what is described in the "Great Treatise" of the Yì,
one knows that the sages demonstrated the model through their own persons,
established instruction according to affairs,
and never, apart from administering government and implementing order,
had something called a separate teaching method.
In the instruction at the court of Yú,
there were specialized officials;
what the Minister of Education respectfully disseminated,
what the Director of Music consulted and commanded;
down to the establishment of schools,
which extended through the Four Dynasties;
the duties of the Director of Education and the guardians and tutors,
were detailed in the Zhōu official system.
However, once they were listed among the offices,
then the practice of studies resided with the archivists.
What they learned
was the Way of self-cultivation, family regulation, state governance, and bringing peace to the world,
and those they took as teachers
were people who upheld official duties and classical laws.
Governance and instruction were not two things;
officials and teachers were united as one.
How could there be empty words to preserve their private doctrines?
The school of the Confucians,
honoring and revering Confucius,
as if they would privately make him the founding master of the Confucians,
also did not understand Confucius.
Confucius established the ultimate standard for the human way;
did he intend to establish the ultimate standard for the Confucian way?
The Confucians
were worthy scholars who did not encounter the flourishing age of enlightened rulers and good ministers,
did not obtain position to greatly implement their Way,
and thus guarded the Way of the former kings,
awaiting later learners.
This arose from a situation of having no alternative.
What ought to be done for the human way
is broad
and great.
How could it be that in one’s own life one encounters nothing,
and must resort to guarding the former and awaiting the later,
never again engaging with human affairs?
Studying the Yì traces back to Fúxī’s diagrams;
one need not wear grass clothing and dwell in the wild like him.
Reading the Documents begins with the Canons of Yú;
one need not cry out to Heaven and weep like them.
It is because the situations in which they found themselves
were each different.
If so, then those who study the Master,
should they say they abandon achievements in affairs,
anticipating that the Way will not be practiced and thus transmit their instruction?
The Book of Changes says:
"That which is above form is called the Way;
that which is within form is called the vessel."
The Way does not exist apart from the vessel,
just as a shadow does not exist apart from the form.
Later generations who received the teachings of the Master began with the Six Classics,
believing that the Six Classics are books that convey the Way,
without realizing that the Six Classics are all vessels.
The Book of Changes, as a text,
serves to reveal things and accomplish tasks,
and was overseen by the Grand Diviner of the Ministry of Spring,
so it naturally had official custodians and was listed among the historical records.
The Book of Documents was under the Outer Historian,
the Book of Songs was overseen by the Grand Master,
the Rites came from the Minister of Rites,
Music had the Director of Education,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals were each maintained by the state historians.
Before the Three Dynasties,
the Six Arts, including the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents,
were always used to teach people,
unlike later generations who revered the Six Classics,
treating them as a separate branch of Confucian learning,
and exclusively calling them books that convey the Way.
This is because what scholars learned
did not extend beyond the duties and custodianship of officials,
or the governance and teachings of the state;
and their application
was also confined to the norms of human relations and daily life.
Thus, they only saw them as matters of necessity,
without separately recognizing the Way conveyed within them.
The Master compiled the Six Classics to instruct later generations,
also stating that the Way of the ancient sages and kings could not be seen directly,
and that the Six Classics were the visible vessels of that Way.
Later people could not see the ancient kings,
so they should rely on the tangible vessels to contemplate the intangible Way.
Therefore, he highlighted the governance and teachings of the ancient kings,
along with the duties and custodianship of officials, to show people,
rather than composing his own theories,
so as to avoid discussing the Way apart from the vessel.
When the Master explained why he composed the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he said:
"I would rather convey it through empty words,
but it is not as profound and clear as demonstrating it through actions."
Thus, beyond governance, teachings, institutions,
human relations, and daily life,
there is no other way of composing writings,
which is already clear.
The Qin people prohibited private discussion of the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents,
and said, "If you wish to learn laws and ordinances,
take officials as your teachers."
What the Qin did that contradicted antiquity
was prohibiting the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents.
As for saying that those who study laws and ordinances
should take officials as teachers,
this also reflects the unity of the Way and the vessel,
and the principle that governance, teaching, officials, and teachers
were never separated into two.
Later, when governance and learning became divided,
they could no longer be unified,
which was fate.
Officials guarded the historical records of their time,
while classical scholars transmitted and taught the texts,
which was also a matter of necessity.
However, throughout the generations,
the Confucian profession was never abandoned,
because it preserved the Way of the ancient kings.
Yet the Confucian school,
guarding the Six Classics,
believed they were merely books conveying the Way.
