How could there be discussing the Way apart from the vessel,
or preserving a shadow apart from the form?
Those who abandon the affairs of the world, human relations, and daily life,
and guard the Six Classics to discuss the Way,
truly cannot be spoken to about the Way.
The Book of Changes says:
"The benevolent see it and call it benevolence;
the wise see it and call it wisdom;
the common people use it daily without knowing it."
Yet not knowing the Way, the Way exists;
claiming to see the Way, the Way is lost.
The great Way is hidden,
not hidden from the ignorant,
but hidden because the wise and talented see it in fragmented ways.
When governance, teaching, officials, and teachers are united,
the intelligence of the world is guided as one,
so the Way exists within the vessel,
and people's minds do not wander beyond it.
When governance, teaching, officials, and teachers are divided,
intelligence and talent
are no longer within bounds,
so the interplay of yin and yang
enters into the biases of human nature,
and each takes what they see as the truth,
which is inevitable.
The officials of rites and music,
each guarding their specialized duties,
even with the keen sight of Lí Lóu
or the sharp hearing of Shī Kuàng,
could not but conform to the norms and rules.
Now it is said that the official custodianship has been lost,
and I use morality to clarify its teachings,
so everyone believes they possess morality.
Thus, the Master transmitted without creating,
and highlighted the Six Arts
to preserve the old institutions of Zhōu Gōng,
not daring to discuss the Way apart from the vessel.
Yet the various philosophers, in great numbers,
already spoke of the Way.
Zhuāngzi compared them to ears, eyes, mouth, and nose,
Sīmǎ Tán distinguished them into six schools,
and Liú Xiàng categorized them into nine streams.
Each believed they had reached the ultimate,
and sought to change the world with their Way.
From the perspective of the noble person,
these are all views of benevolence and wisdom,
not the Way itself being so easily grasped.
The Way is manifested through the vessel,
not named after people.
Once people began to speak of the Way,
the Way started to be named differently according to individuals.
The benevolent see it and call it benevolence,
the wise see it and call it wisdom,
this is so.
People naturally follow the Way in their actions,
but the Way is not something people can possess.
Once each person speaks of their own Way,
and acts according to what they call the Way,
the Way begins to be possessed by people.
The Way of the Mohists,
the Way of Master Xǔ,
and others are all like this.
The Way first took shape in the daily life of three people sharing a household,
and was fully developed by Zhōu Gōng and Confucius.
The sages of the past never separately named it the Way,
just as within a household,
one does not label one's own surname.
When the hundred schools emerged and spoke of the Way,
the Confucians had no choice but to elevate their own origins.
First, they spoke of the Way of Yáo and Shùn,
then the Way of Zhōu Gōng and Zhòngní,
hence Hán Tuìzhī said, "The Way and virtue are empty positions."
That "the Way and virtue are empty positions"
marks the decline of the Way and virtue.
When people gather together,
the distinction between guest and host is established.
When diverse opinions arise,
the distinction between right and wrong is established.
Since the various masters spoke in profusion about the Way,
the Way itself became afflicted.
The school of the Ru (Confucians),
then revered the Way of Yáo, Shùn, the Zhōu, and Kǒng,
considering it to be "our Way."
The Way originally has no "us,"
but people make it their own,
thinking this might distinguish it from ways that are not the Way.
They do not realize that each makes it their own,
just as the multitude of a three-army host
can be called "our army"
when facing an enemy state;
but when not facing an enemy,
each of the three armies again has its own "us."
Now, the Six Arts
are where the sages preserved the Way within the vessels;
yet the three schools' interpretations of the *Yì* (Book of Changes),
and the four masters' interpretations of the *Shī* (Book of Songs),
those who attack and study them
are endlessly partisan, esteeming their own master and despising others.
They do not understand that the ancients, regarding the Six Arts,
wore them like clothes and consumed them like food,
everyone practiced them as a matter of course,
and never specialized in them to become famous masters.
Later Confucians merely focused on a single corner of one classic,
exhausting their energy throughout their lives,
still fearing they might not achieve a single success.
Is this because ancient and modern people are incomparable?
The circumstances made it so.
In antiquity, the Way resided in the vessels,
officials and teachers were united,
what the scholars learned
was either the state's statutes and regulations,
or the precedents and practices of the offices,
their ears and eyes were accustomed to them, with no need for deep inquiry,
hence they acquired them easily.
Later Confucians sought the Way from the vessels,
having teachers but no official positions,
matters came from hearsay,
not from personal observation,
the texts required exegesis, not plain speech,
therefore they acquired them with difficulty.
Now, the Six Arts are equally important,
one cannot stop at guarding just one classic;
the meaning of the classics is vast and profound,
it cannot be limited to a corner;
yet the various Confucians specialized in a corner of one classic,
necessarily doubling the effort compared to the ancients' ability to master all Six Arts,
thus being far removed from the sages in time,
it is certainly not strange in such matters.
But having exhausted the intelligence of their minds, ears, and eyes,
they must have uniquely perceived the height and depth of heaven and earth within,
and therefore said that of all under heaven,
no one surpasses me;
this is also human nature.
They do not realize they are merely focused on a corner of one classic,
insufficient to glimpse the complete substance of the ancients.
Exegesis and parsing of sentences,
explaining meanings and principles,
investigating names and objects—
none are sufficient to speak of the Way.
Taking these three and combining them,
then using the power of aggregation
to supplement the effort of tracing back from afar,
one might perhaps come close.
But the classical masters themselves could not avoid contradictions,
and those who transmitted their learning
again divided into their own schools,
no less distinct than the debate between Confucians and Mohists;
thus, by distinguishing guest, the host is determined,
yet within the host there are again guests,
by establishing what is wrong, what is right is set,
yet within what is right there is again wrong.
The paths become more divergent,
and the great Way becomes more hidden.
"In high antiquity, they governed by knotting cords;
later sages replaced this with written contracts.
The hundred officials used them to govern,
the myriad people used them for clarity."
Now, the use of writing
was for governance and clarity;
the ancients never took it as a means for writing treatises.
Using writing for treatises
arose from the separation of duties between officials and teachers,
and the divergence of governance and instruction.
The Master said:
"I wish to be without words."
Wishing to be without words
means he could not avoid having something to say.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Do I love disputation?
I have no choice."
Later scholars who wield the brush,
composing literary works
to be trusted in the present and transmitted to the future,
should also remember the intent of wishing to be without words,
and the feeling of having no choice,
so that perhaps the words come from me,
but the reason for speaking
is not originally from me.
Now, the Way is fully present in the Six Classics;
the hidden meanings contained in earlier times
can be illuminated by exegesis and parsing.
Events and changes arising later,
the Six Classics cannot speak of,
thus it is essential to grasp the intent of the Six Classics,
and compose writings according to the times to investigate the great Way.
The highest is to establish virtue,
next to establish achievements,
next to establish words.
Establishing words is equivalent to establishing achievements.
For there must be a need, and then one supplies it;
there must be pent-up feelings, and then one expresses them;
there must be弊端, and then one remedies them;
it is not merely to boast of sound and color,
for the sake of one's own fame.
The *Yì* says:
"Spirit is used to know the future,
wisdom is used to store the past."
Knowing the future
is the yang aspect.
Storing the past
is the yin aspect.
One yin, one yang—
that is the Way.
The use of literary writing
is sometimes to narrate events,
sometimes to clarify principles.
Events trace the past,
which is yin.
Principles elucidate the future,
which is yang.
The highest achievement
is to narrate events while principles become clear,
to speak of principles while events provide models;
then the host is not biased,
and the writing is in accord with the Way.
The histories of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
the writings of Dǒng Zhòngshū and Hán Yù—
do they perhaps have that sense of having no choice in speaking?
Not knowing the reason,
but merely沉迷 in literary embellishment,
such a person is not worth discussing.
Even those who make lofty claims,
saying that writing should value illuminating the Way,
what need is there for sound, emotion, and color to give pleasure?—
these are also not words that understand the Way.
Now, in the governance of non-action, the warm breeze is played;
with the achievement of the Spiritual Terrace, bells and drums bring joy;
and further, playing the qin to encounter culture,
singing in the wind at the Rain Altar to express aspirations—
then when emperors and kings achieve governance,
and sages and worthies cultivate merit,
have they not had the pleasure of delighting the eyes and gladdening the heart?
And to say that the use of literary writing
must lack the charm of chanting, sighing, rising and falling?
Zǐgòng said:
"The Master's cultural accomplishments
can be heard and learned.
The Master's discourses on human nature and the Way of Heaven,
cannot be heard and learned."
This is because everything the Master spoke of,
was none other than human nature and the Way of Heaven,
yet he never explicitly labeled them as such, saying
'this is human nature, this is the Way of Heaven.'
Thus, it is not that human nature and the Way of Heaven
cannot be heard;
rather, it is that explicit discourses on human nature and the Way of Heaven
cannot be heard.
Everything he spoke of was none other than human nature and the Way of Heaven,
yet he did not explicitly label them as such,
fearing that people would abandon the vessel to seek the Way.
He could speak of the rituals of the Xià,
he could speak of the rituals of the Yīn,
but always said, 'Without evidence, there is no trust.'
Thus, what the Master spoke of
necessarily drew evidence from things and affairs,
and was not merely empty words
used to illuminate the Way.
Zēngzǐ, through genuine accumulation and prolonged effort,
was told:
"All is unified by a single thread."
Zǐgòng, through extensive learning and broad knowledge,
was told:
"All is unified by a single thread."
Without genuine accumulation and prolonged effort,
or extensive learning and broad knowledge,
there would indeed be no basis for this unifying thread.
Exegesis and the study of names and objects
aim to trace the traces of the ancient sages,
yet those who indulge in memorization
resemble merchants in a marketplace.
Composing writings and literary expressions
seeks to elucidate the minds of the ancient sages,
yet those who are enamored with brilliance
resemble those who play with curios.
Heterodox doctrines and partial learning
proclaim their own Way,
and uphold their own Virtue,
and thus are certainly insufficient to determine the gains and losses of this Way.
The learning of memorization,
the talent for literary expression,
cannot but take this Way as their sovereign,
yet those who act like merchants and players are numerous and forget their origin.
The Sòng Confucians arose and contended,
saying that all these are mired in vessels and do not know the Way.
For those mired in vessels and not knowing the Way,
one can simply use the vessel to show them the Way;
this would suffice.
Yet their flaw
was to want people to abandon the vessel and speak of the Way.
The Master taught people to be broadly learned in culture,
yet the Sòng Confucians said:
"To toy with things leads to the loss of purpose."
Zēngzǐ taught people to keep their words far from vulgarity and perversity,
yet the Sòng Confucians said:
"Skillful writing harms the Way."
Are not the words of the Sòng Confucians
good medicine for the ills of later generations?
Yet medicine is meant to cure diseases of the internal organs.
The intention of the Sòng Confucians
seems to be that seeing the disease in the organs,
they then wish to remove the organs altogether.
Seeking human nature and Heaven,
they belittle memorization and disdain literary composition;
how is this any different?
Yet their precision in analyzing principles,
and their steadfastness in practice,
were unheard of among the Hàn and Táng Confucians.
Mèngzǐ said:
"The delight that principles of righteousness bring to my mind
is like the delight that rich meats bring to my mouth."
Principles of righteousness cannot be spoken of emptily;
they must be substantiated through broad learning,
and expressed through literary composition.
When these three are united as one,
then perhaps, though the Way of Zhōu and Kǒng is distant,
it is not unlike reaching it through successive translations.
Yet classical scholars disparage each other,
literary men look down upon each other,
and among the Confucians discussing nature and principle,
there are the differences between Zhū and Lù,
and the mutual attacks between followers of Zhū and followers of Lù.
And those who speak of learning and literary composition
merely chase trends without understanding,
as Zhuāngzǐ said, 'The hundred schools go forth and do not return;
they are certainly not in harmony.'
Alas!
Shào Jìnhán said:
"When this piece first appeared,
and the manuscript circulated in the capital,
friends who had always admired Zhāng's writings were all dissatisfied,
saying it followed the mannerisms of Sòng dynasty语录,
inevitably appearing stale and off-putting,
and unlike his usual style of writing.
Some even sent letters to admonish him.
I examined it carefully,
and said to Zhū Shàobái (named Xīgēng):
'This is to clarify that everything written in his Tōngyì,
its original ideas and distinctive theories,
all arise naturally,
without any forced affectation.
Though the language is holistic,
the ideas are mostly profound and incisive;
it cannot be criticized.'"
My nephew Tíngfēng said:
"Uncle's Tōngyì
is widely admired and enjoyed,
but do people truly grasp its intent?
They merely find its refined discourse and lofty theories
novel and pleasing,
or use it as material for elegant conversation.
They do not know that Uncle often regretted his excessive use of clever phrasing,
which loses the ancient spirit.
The title of this piece
may seem pedantic and impractical,
but its meaning is truly original and insightful.
For instance, saying the Way begins with three people living together,
and that rulers, teachers, governance, and teaching
all originate from Heaven;
that the worthy and wise learn from the sages;
that the sages learn from the common people;
that the one who synthesized the great achievements
was the Duke of Zhōu, not Confucius;
that scholars should not arbitrarily separate Zhōu and Kǒng;
that those who learn from Confucius
should not first aim to teach for ten thousand generations;
that the greatness of Confucius
can be wholly encompassed by the phrase 'learning the rituals of Zhōu'—
these ideas are startling upon first hearing,
yet profoundly accurate upon deep reflection.
Before the Tōngyì,
no one had ever expressed them.
How can they be called stale?
The gentlemen who at the time disparaged it as stale
probably read the title too familiarly
and did not carefully examine the text."
The Book of Changes says:
"That which completes the images is called Qián;
that which imitates the patterns is called Kūn."
Learning is
what is called imitating the patterns.
The Way is
what is called completing the images.
The Master said:
"Learn from below and reach upward."
This means learning from the concrete vessels of the lower realm,
and thereby reaching upward to the Way of the higher realm.
Scholars aspire to become worthies,
worthies aspire to become sages,
and sages aspire to become like Heaven.
To aspire to become worthies and sages
is to grasp their principles.
"The workings of high Heaven
are without sound or smell"—
how then can sages aspire to become like Heaven?
For when Heaven gives birth to humans,
it invariably endows them with the nature of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom—
these are the virtues of Heaven;
it invariably places them within the relationships of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, elder and younger brother, and friend—
these are the positions of Heaven.
To cultivate the positions of Heaven with the virtues of Heaven—
even before things and affairs interact in the subtle and hidden realm,
there already exists the standard of what is appropriate and fitting,
without excess or deficiency—
this is what is called completing the images.
In daily life, embody these images;
when affairs arise and things interact,
act in accordance with this standard to meet them—
this is what is called imitating the patterns.
This is how sages aspire to become like Heaven,
this is how sages learn from below and reach upward.
Yī Yǐn said:
"Heaven, in giving birth to the people,
causes those who first know to awaken those who later know,
and causes those who first awaken to awaken those who later awaken."
Human beings receive their vital breath unevenly;
there are inevitably those who cannot know for themselves the standard of what is appropriate and fitting.
Thus, those who first know and first awaken
instruct and guide them—
this is what is called teaching.
Teaching is
teaching people to know for themselves the standard of what is appropriate and fitting;
it is not teaching them to abandon themselves and follow me.
Therefore, scholars aspire to become worthies,
and worthies aspire to become sages—
they aspire to imitate the patterns of the completed images,
not to abandon what they inherently possess in their aspiration.
But then, how can they be made to know the standard of what is appropriate and fitting?
How can they be made to know the completed images and imitate their patterns?
They must observe those who, since the birth of the people,
have fully possessed the purity of Heaven's virtues,
and have reached the utmost of Heaven's positions.
Seek their former words and past deeds,
how they dealt with extremity, change, penetration, and endurance, and become broadly acquainted with them.
Only then can they attain for themselves what is called the completed images,
and skillfully imitate their patterns.
Therefore, imitating patterns
must be manifested in practical affairs.
Reciting and reading the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents
is the means to seek resources for imitating patterns;
it is not itself the imitation of patterns.
Yet the ancients did not regard practical affairs as learning,
but regarded reciting and reading the Book of Songs and the Book of Documents as learning—
why is this?
It is because without investigating things to extend knowledge,
one cannot make the will sincere;
action then proceeds according to one's knowledge.
Therefore, regarding reciting and reading as learning
is spoken from the perspective of what teaching can reach;
it does not mean there is no learning beyond this.
Zǐ Lù said:
"There are the people and their affairs;
there are the altars of soil and grain—
why must one read books
to be considered learning?"
The Master rebuked him as being glib,
because when Zǐ Gāo was made steward,
he did not speak like this;
it does not mean that learning must be exclusively reciting and reading.
To regard learning as exclusively reciting and reading
is the narrow view of worldly Confucians.
The learning of the ancients,
did not neglect practical affairs,
for governance and education were not yet separated,
officials and teachers were united as one,
and thereafter it was relatively easier to carry out.
The Minister of Education disseminated the five teachings,
the Director of Music instructed the noble youth,
and the schools of the Three Dynasties,
all were manifested in the institutions.
At that time, those engaged in learning,
entered to recite their texts,
and upon exiting, immediately encountered the implementation of governance, education, and canonical regulations,
thus their learning was trustworthy and verifiable,
and not merely empty words exchanged in instruction.
However, that knowledge was easy to acquire,
but its practice was difficult to match,
which has been the case since ancient times.
When Yáo condemned Gònggōng,
he said:
"He speaks smoothly but acts contrary."
Now, to be calm and able to speak,
is not the mark of an unlearned person.
But when tested in action, he acted contrary,
which differs from emulating established models.
When Fùyuè enlightened Gāozōng,
he said:
"It is not that knowing is difficult,
but that doing is difficult."
Gāozōng had long studied under Gānpán,
and toiled extensively abroad,
how could he be unlearned?
Not having been tested in action,
he feared that his practice might not inspire confidence.
He also said:
"One seeks broad knowledge,
timely to establish affairs,
learning from ancient teachings yields gain."
Though these words come from ancient texts,
they must have been based on some received wisdom.
To seek broad knowledge and substantiate it by establishing affairs,
then what is called learning from ancient teachings,
is not merely recitation and discourse,
as can be seen.
When governance and education were united and officials and teachers undivided,
acquiring knowledge was easy, yet practical implementation was already difficult;
how much more so when officials and teachers separated,
and what scholars studied,
were all the remnants of past generations?
The Master said:
"Learning without thought is labor lost;
thought without learning is perilous."
He also said:
"I have spent whole days without food,
and whole nights without sleep,
in thought,
but it was of no benefit.
It is better to learn."
Now, thought is also part of the scholar's endeavor,
yet distinguishing thought from learning,
as if thought cannot be called learning,
means that one must be practiced in affairs,
before one can speak of learning.
This is the Master's way of teaching the unity of knowledge and action.
The doctrines of the various masters and hundred schools,
arose from thought alone without learning.
Thus their tenets all had something inherited,
yet could not be without flaws.
What Liú Xīn called a certain school of thought,
its source lay in the charge of a certain ancient office,
its flow became the learning of a certain school,
its deviation became the fault of a certain affair.
The charge of a certain office,
was the canonical laws and institutions of the former kings.
Flowing into the learning of a certain school,
then the official duties were lost in transmission,
and each, according to where thought reached,
formed their own separate streams.
Deviating into the fault of a certain affair,
then thought was extreme but not practiced in affairs,
though they held to it with reasons,
and spoke of it with principles,
they could not know that their practice was flawed.
Thus in the flourishing of the Three Dynasties,
learning emerged from unity,
what was called learning,
all referred to human effort.
Speaking comprehensively,
ten years was called childhood learning,
this is so.
then at thirteen one learned music,
at twenty one learned rites,
this is so.
The state, based on the names of human effort,
named its institutions,
thus called local schools and state schools,
learning then was shared by the Three Dynasties,
this is so.
There was not yet learning attributed to individuals,
and distinguished as names of personal attainment.
When officials and teachers separated and the doctrines of the various masters and hundred schools arose,
then learning began to be named according to personal attainment,
what is called the learning of a certain Mr. Jiǎ,
the learning of a certain Mr. Yǐ,
this is so.
Learning differing in name according to individuals,
learning thus became erroneous.
This is not due to an excess of practice reaching this point,
but arises from an excess of thought.
Therefore, the Master spoke of the fault of neglecting either learning or thought,
and immediately followed with:
"To attack heterodox doctrines,
this is harmful indeed."
Now the rise of heterodox doctrines,
all stems from an excess of thought,
and not being practiced in affairs.
The affliction of the various schools of thought and the hundred philosophers
arises from thinking without learning;
the affliction of the worldly Confucians
arises from learning without thinking;
this is because the separation of officials and teachers has caused learning to differ from that of the ancients.
Later rulers, believing that Confucian teachings could not be abolished,
thus established the position of Erudites,
appointed disciples,
and set up examinations to select scholars,
intending to encourage the recitation and emulation of the former kings.
At its inception,
they used wealth and rank to encourage Confucian teachings,
but in the end,
Confucian teachings were subordinated to the pursuit of wealth and rank.
This, of course, is not worth discussing.
Yet from this emerged great Confucian masters and eminent teachers,
which cannot be said
to be unrelated to the influence of the court's teachings and customs.
Human nature
cannot be moved without something to admire;
once engaged in something,
one then strives to achieve its substance,
seeking to match the name.
Those of average ability and above
can strive and aspire to this.
Through schools and imperial examinations,
thousands of talented individuals vie for success;
could it be that not even one in ten rises above the average?
As we are far removed from antiquity,
unable to learn what the ancients learned,
the recitation and study of Confucian teachings
have become the ultimate goal of learning.
Moreover, the difficulty of mastering them
is inevitably greater than for the ancients.
Therefore, for those who specialize in Confucian studies,
if they can indeed distinguish themselves
and are not merely ordinary and vulgar,
I have no criticism.
Those with extensive learning excel in investigation and inquiry—
is this not the accumulation of substance within the Way?
Yet those who chase after breadth
exhaust their spirit and labor their minds in its pursuit all their lives,
without considering what purpose such breadth serves.
Those with formidable talent excel in composing writings—
is this not the expression of the substance of the Way?
Yet those skilled in writing
toil with anxious thoughts to construct it all their lives,
without considering what use such writing has.
Those who discuss principles and meanings seem capable of thought,
but they do not realize that principles and meanings, when suspended in emptiness without foundation,
also fail to align with the Way.
These all know that it is so,
but do not know why it is so.
Master Chéng said:
"In all matters, to think about why they are so
is the foremost learning in the world."
Should not people also seek to think about why things are so?
The world cannot be without trends,
and trends cannot avoid cycles;
the principle of one yīn and one yáng
manifests in the patterns of vital energy and numbers.
What is valued in the learning of the noble person
is the ability to uphold the world and correct biases;
the principle of one yīn and one yáng
is suited to balancing and harmonizing.
When a trend emerges,
there must be a reason for its adoption;
the emphasis on learning, literary composition, and principles
is why imbalances and disproportions inevitably occur.
When a trend becomes established,
there must be a reason for its decline;
human nature tends to follow the times and seek fame,
pursuing the trivial without knowing the fundamental.
Therefore, although the initiators may not avoid bias,
they must adopt its essence
to welcome new vitality;
even if the declining trend is called orthodox,
it will inevitably inherit its falseness,
becoming a refuge for the decadent;
this too is a natural tendency.
Yet those in the world who discuss learning
do not know how to uphold trends,
but only know how to follow them,
and even claim that without this, one cannot gain reputation.
This is simply a lack of thought.
Shěn Fēngchí wrote to me inquiring about learning,
feeling ashamed that in the company of learned individuals and large gatherings,
he was unable to engage in dialogue with them.
I replied that learning lies in self-reliance;
what others are capable of,
I need not feel ashamed for not being able to do.
I then drew an analogy with commerce:
those who deal in cloth and silk
need not be knowledgeable about grains and beans;
those who store medicines and remedies
need not be familiar with gold and pearls.
The concern is whether one can establish oneself as an expert.
For instance, if one sells cloth but lacks materials for clothing,
or sells medicine but is deficient in prescriptions,
that would be unacceptable.
Someone said:
"This is the same method Sū Zǐzhān taught for reading the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
which many scholars today are aware of."
I replied:
"The words may seem similar, but they differ;
a slight deviation at the start
can lead to errors of a thousand miles."
Someone once asked Sū Jūn:
"Your broad and profound knowledge—
can it be learned?"
Sū Jūn replied:
"Yes,
I once read the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
going through it several times until I mastered it.
For topics like military affairs, agriculture, rites, and music,
I focused on one theme each time I read,
and after a long time, I achieved thorough understanding."
He then used the analogy of market goods,
meaning that goods are endless,
but one's purchasing power is limited,
so one must know how to choose.
Many scholars recite Sū's words,
considering them an excellent method,
not realizing this is merely ordinary excerpting of sentences,
like modern compilations of categorized examination strategies.
The questioner only sought broad and profound knowledge,
with no deeper meaning.
Sū's response
was nothing more than the work of a classical scholar preparing for examinations.
Today, those who pay slight attention to examination preparation
can mostly do this;
it cannot be elevated to the level of true learning.
Yet scholars regard it as an excellent method,
showing how few truly understand learning.
Learning must have a focus.
If Sū's intention
was to take Bān's book as the object of learning,
then one could never complete such a task in a lifetime—
how could several readings suffice to master it?
If the intention was to take the sought-after rites, music, military affairs, and agriculture as the objects of learning,
then each category has its own depth and complexity—
how could one reading exhaust a single category?
Using Sū's analogy
of purchasing goods with limited funds,
focusing on one theme per reading
is like going to the market first for gold and pearls,
then for cloth and silk,
and then for rice, grains, and medicines,
seeking them in sequence by category.
If one seeks to exhaust all categories,
even with the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn,
one could not afford it.
If one roughly estimates the cost
and buys a little of each type,
then one accumulates nothing substantial.
Sū's words
lack solid ground in either direction,
yet scholars today are so busy following Sū
that they use his words
for learning, which is insufficient,
but for examination preparation, it is more than enough.
Examination preparation is known and recited in every household,
but few can achieve what Sū did.
Occasionally, someone does,
and they stand out among the vulgar trends,
making others look upon them with awe.
Such individuals then consider themselves
to be engaged in true learning,
not mere examination preparation,
unaware that they are mistaken.
Sū's learning
originates from the School of Diplomacy.
His strength lies in
assessing worldly affairs,
being practical and nearly useful,
but what he relies on for expression
is policy essays and discourses.
Policy responses must have clear points,
discourse arguments must cite historical examples.
Unless one is a specialist with long-standing learning,
one must consult books to verify.
If one truly applies the effort Sū used to read the *History of the Han Dynasty*,
then one can also respond to sudden demands and prepare for inquiries,
with no difficulty.
Hán Chānglí said:
"For recording events, one must extract the essentials;
for compiling words, one must probe the profundities."
Probing profundities and extracting essentials
has been praised as a fine saying for millennia;
yet the profound and essential words Hán himself wrote
are not only unseen today,
but also never circulated in his time.
They must have been mere excerpts and phrases,
prepared for use in writing.
Yet people want to imitate the idea of probing profundities and extracting essentials to produce writings—
this is like mistaking Sū's categorical seeking
for true learning,
and can be viewed as analogous.
Someone said:
"According to your words,
are Hán and Sū not worth emulating?" I replied:
"Hán and Sū used their efforts
as aids for literary composition,
not considering this as learning."
Someone said:
"Examinations are meant to gauge one's learning.
If examination preparation diverges from learning,
that is a failure of later generations.
If one prepares something for the examination,
isn't that what the *Records* call 'broad learning and strong memory to await questions'?
How can that not be called learning?"
I replied:
"Broad learning and strong memory
are the concerns of Confucians.
But to consider this the foundation of self-reliance
is mistaken.
Learning values breadth but also the ability to synthesize;
one cannot synthesize without breadth.
Speaking of narrow-minded and crude Confucians,
they confine themselves to the words of one master,
and cannot be called experts.
Yet one also cannot achieve breadth without synthesis.
Speaking of vulgar Confucians who memorize indiscriminately,
reaching endless extremes,
they recklessly seek to know everything,
unaware that even Yáo and Shùn's knowledge had limits.
Broad learning and strong memory
can indeed prepare one for questions,
but without synthesizing and upholding principles,
and only preparing for questions,
then if no one asks,
will Confucians have no learning?
Moreover, questioners seek to hear our reputation and seek our substance;
reputation is established
only through specialized, accomplished learning.
Thus, no one can achieve learning without specialization."
Someone said:
"Sū's categorical seeking
and Hán's probing profundities and extracting essentials
are both learning for answering questions.
You say they are insufficient to establish expertise.
Wáng Bóhòu searched, selected, and excavated,
exploring the obscure and minute;
regarding classics, commentaries, philosophies, and histories,
names, objects, institutions, and numbers,
he connected and ranged widely,
truly addressing what earlier Confucians had not covered.
The books he compiled and edited
are still relied upon by scholars today—
how can learning for answering questions be overlooked?"
I replied:
"Wáng Bóhòu
sought substance through reputation.
It was said that Hán Chānglí perceived the Way through literature;
once he perceived the Way,
he transcended literature.
Wáng sought learning through preparing for questions;
once he understood learning,
he transcended preparing for questions.
However, Wáng's various books
can be called compilations,
but not original writings;
they can be called the efforts of a scholar seeking knowledge,
but not the accomplished scholarship of an expert.
Today's broad and elegant gentlemen,
exhausting their spirits on classics, commentaries, philosophies, and histories,
yet gaining no true learning in their lifetimes,
precisely because they revere Wáng
and mistakenly cling to the efforts of seeking knowledge,
thinking that this is learning.
Learning and effort
are similar but different.
Learning cannot be achieved abruptly;
one should devote oneself to effort, that is acceptable.
To point to effort and call it learning
is like pointing to sorghum and calling it wine."
In learning, there is innate nature,
and within reading and studying the ancients,
there are insights grasped from the very beginning
that remain unchanged throughout one’s life.
In learning, there is also profound emotion,
and within reading and studying the ancients,
there are moments of joyful or poignant resonance,
where one suddenly does not know whether to sing or weep.
If one’s effort is abundant
but one’s innate nature and emotion are insufficient,
this cannot be called true learning.
If one possesses innate nature and emotion
but does not deepen them through effort,
this is what is called having fine qualities without learning.
The Master said:
“So intent upon enlightening that I forget to eat,
so happy that I forget sorrow,
not knowing that old age is approaching.”
One cannot tell which is effort
and which is innate nature and emotion.
This is indeed the ultimate aim of learning.
How did the Master achieve this?
He said:
“It is because I am fond of antiquity and diligent in seeking it.”
Nowadays, vulgar Confucians
regret not seeing the unrevised *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the Master,
and regret that Dài Gōng obtained the *Shāng Sòng*
but did not preserve the missing titles of the seven chapters,
considering this lofty sentiment and superior taste,
and even praising it among themselves.
Carrying their biased views to the extreme,
they seem to think that the Master’s editing and revising
was not as good as Wáng Bóhòu’s skill in searching for lost texts.
This is because they chase after current trends
and mistakenly believe that piecing together fragments is sufficient to exhaust the capabilities of heaven and earth.
Fortunately, they live in later ages.
If they had lived before the Qin burning of books,
when all texts were preserved
and there was no need for supplementation,
they would have had no use for their learning.
Someone may say:
You speak of scholarship,
insisting that effort must be combined with innate nature and emotion.
As for the method of learning,
you do not establish fixed rules,
but only let learners recognize their natural inclinations and what they can strive for,
and apply their effort accordingly.
This is probably the legacy of Wáng’s theory of innate knowing.
In ancient teaching,
from numbers and directional names
to reciting poetry and dancing with the Sháo,
each had a fixed curriculum,
regardless of whether one’s natural inclinations matched it
or whether one could strive for it.
Yet you say that each person has abilities and inabilities,
and they should not be forced.
Are the teachings for ancient and modern people different?
I reply:
Modern people do not learn,
and cannot be the same as the ancients,
not because their talent is inferior,
but because circumstances make it so.
Since officials and teachers separated,
teaching methods have not been unified.
Learners privately pass on what they themselves can do,
which is the first difference.
Moreover, since officials and teachers separated,
learning relies solely on written texts.
The Way is not manifested in objects,
and affairs are not upheld through professions,
which is the second difference.
Thus, learning lost the transmission from teachers.
The six scripts and nine numbers,
which the ancients mastered in childhood,
are now studied by later generations’ aged scholars and experts
who exhaust their lifelong energy
yet still cannot fully match the ancients,
which is the third difference.
The times and human affairs
cannot be forcibly made the same for ancient and modern,
and this is not something human intelligence can achieve.
However, the great principles of the Six Classics
are as clear as the sun and stars.
The modifications of the Three Dynasties
can be inferred for a hundred generations.
The brilliant follow the general outline and diligently seek,
while the profound follow measures and gradually attain.
Natural inclinations and the ability to strive
are possessed by everyone,
so everyone can attain it for themselves.
How can one enforce fixed standards to force others?
Wáng’s theory of extending innate knowing
is the legacy of Mèngzǐ’s teachings.
Innate knowing must be extended,
so it certainly does not neglect effort.
Zhūzǐ wanted people to clarify through what is manifested,
which is what Mèngzǐ called examining the beginnings and expanding them.
Both follow the same Way.
Yet worldly Confucians, when speaking of learning,
often avoid mentioning innate knowing,
perhaps due to caution against the failures of later followers,
but does this mean the essence differs from what was said in ancient times?
Someone may say:
What Mèngzǐ called expansion
certainly attains the entirety of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.
Yet you want people to recognize their own strengths
and thereby specialize in their own school and establish their own name,
even cautioning against dabbling in other areas.
Is this compatible with the comprehensive Way?
I reply:
Words cannot be so rigid.
The Way should be comprehensive,
but one’s work must be specialized.
These two principles coexist without contradiction.
Among the disciples of the Sage, seventy-two were proficient in the six arts,
yet from Yán, Zēng, Cì, to Shāng,
their paths were not the same.
After two generations,
Xúnzǐ spoke of the *Rites*,
while Mèngzǐ excelled in the *Odes* and *Documents*.
Some were broad, others detailed;
their paths differed,
but they all returned to the Way.
Later Confucians’ paths
lie either in moral principles,
in institutions and numbers,
or in literary expression.
These three are the main categories.
To achieve one of them,
one cannot but neglect the other two—
such is the nature of circumstances.
Knowing that what one achieves is one aspect of the Way,
and not neglecting the other two that are set aside,
then one is not far from the Way.
Adhering to one bias
and claiming nothing in the world surpasses it
leads to factionalism and rivalry,
which is what is called being rigid and unadaptable.
Therefore, learning must seek personal understanding,
work must value specialization and refinement,
categories must be expanded,
and the Way must reach its full measure.
Innate nature and emotion are expressed through worry, joy, indignation, and pleasure;
principles and circumstances are understood through exhaustion, change, penetration, and endurance.
Be broad but not杂乱,
concise but not遗漏.
Then scholarship may become pure and solid,
and the way of preserving the past and awaiting the future
may perhaps be glimpsed.
The words of the ancients
were meant for the public good;
they never took pride in literary expression
or privately claimed them as their own.
Their aspirations were directed toward the Way,
words were used to clarify their aspirations,
and writing served to complete the words.
If the Way was truly made clear to the world,
and their aspirations were all fulfilled,
it was unnecessary for the words to be truly their own.
The Yú Shū says:
"Present your words in reports,
and clearly test them through achievements."
This marks the beginning of judging people by their speech.
If one must rely on testing achievements to secure submission,
then what is valued lies not in words and rhetoric.
The forms of oaths and proclamations
are words crafted into writing.
If they suffice to establish governance and spread order,
sovereign and ministers never separately claimed credit for establishing the words.
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"The king speaks thus to the many regions."
This is the text of the proclamation to the four states.
Commentators believe the Duke of Zhōu conveyed the king's command,
not knowing that these words originally came from the Duke of Zhōu,
and King Chéng approved and enacted them—
thus they became King Chéng's words.
When a sage minister establishes words for a worthy ruler,
it is called the worthy being able to employ the sage;
this too is the governance of a sage.
Zēng Gǒng said:
"The Diǎn and Mó documents record the achievements of Yáo and Shùn,
and also record their subtle and profound intentions—
how could this be matched by ordinary people?
The historians who recorded them at the time
were also disciples of the sages."
From this perspective,
when worthy ministers narrate affairs for sage rulers,
it is called the worthy being able to understand the sage;
this too is the words of a sage.
Writing and the Way form a single thread,
words and affairs share the same principle,
just as the eight tones depend on each other to create harmony in music—
one cannot attribute it solely to the excellence of a single instrument.
The five flavors blend to create harmony in the cauldron—
one cannot single out the sweetness of one ingredient.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients
were meant for the public good;
they never took pride in literary expression
or privately claimed them as their own.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The three hundred poems of the Shī
were largely composed by worthies and sages to express their indignation."
Thus, the words of longing between men and women
are寄托 for missing one's lord or cherishing friends.
The laments of soldiers on campaign and separated wives
are寄托 for loyalty to the state and concern for the times.
If one rigidly clings to the words
and treats them as the literal speech of those individuals,
then "Chīxiāo" would truly be the mournful sound of a bird—
why wonder that the crucian carp reproached Zhuāng Zhōu in anger?
"Chángchǔ" would be a happy plant without a home—
why wonder that the female wind sighed with emotion in Sòng Yù?
The aim of the poet
is gentle and sincere,
emphasizing literary elegance and indirect remonstrance:
the speaker is without fault,
the listener is sufficiently warned.
They give vent to their indignation
and contribute even a ten-thousandth part to moral instruction—
this is their aspiration.
To seek fame because of this
is to contend over artistic skill and craftsmanship—
the ancients had no such practice.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients
were meant for the public good;
they never took pride in literary expression
or privately claimed them as their own.
The Master said:
"I transmit rather than create."
The Six Arts were all old texts of the Duke of Zhōu;
the Master had nothing to create.
The Lúnyǔ records the Master's words.
"Not constant in his virtue"—
citing it to explain shamans and physicians—
he never explicitly noted it as text from the Yì.
"Neither envious nor covetous"—
praising Jì Lù—
"truly not because of wealth"—
sighing over Bó Yí and Shū Qí—
he never stated it came from the Shī.
"Sincerely hold fast to the Mean"—
narrating the words of Yáo—
"with the dark bull I clearly announce"—
narrating the oath of Tāng—
he never stated it came from the Shū.
The Lúnyǔ records the subtle words of the Master,
yet the Shī and Shū are initially undifferentiated—
this too reflects the principle that transmission and creation are not distinct.
The Master's words
appear in the citations of various schools—
yet the Lúnyǔ never attempted to collect them all—
this too reflects the principle of mutual寄托 between detail and brevity.
The Six Arts are the origin of writing,
the Lúnyǔ is the essence of sage words:
creating the new and transmitting the old,
they never concerned themselves with it,
for it sufficed to clarify the Way and establish teaching.
Thus, the sage's creation and the wise transmission
never separately claimed credit for establishing the words.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients
were meant for the public good;
they never took pride in their literary expression
or privately claimed them as their own.
With the decline of Zhōu, writing became corrupted;
the various masters contended to be heard,
after the Master had passed away,
when subtle words ceased and the great meaning was already distorted.
Yet the various masters sought to change the world with their learning;
they certainly wished to use what they called the Way
to contend for supremacy in the world.
As for language and writing,
they never privately claimed their origins.
Ancient precedents and old statutes
were preserved and recorded without distinction—
such as the chapters "Yòu Guān" and "Dì Zǐ,"
and the instructions "Yuè Lìng" and "Tǔ Xùn."
Compiling words and deeds
need not all be what they themselves discussed—
such as Guǎn Zhòng discussing events after his death,
or Hán Fēi recording Lǐ Sī's "Counter-Argument."
The chapters "Ràng Wáng" and "Yú Fù" in the Zhuāngzǐ,
Sū Shì called them forgeries;
they are not forgeries,
but additions by scholars of the Zhuāng school.
The Yànzǐ Chūnqiū
Liǔ Zōngyuán believed contained Mohist words.
It is not that Yànzǐ was a Mohist,
but Mohist scholars narrated Yànzǐ's deeds
to name their book,
just as Mencius named his chapters "Gào Zǐ" and "Wàn Zhāng."
The Lǚshì Chūnqiū
earlier scholars grouped with the Huáinán Hóngliè as similar compilations,
meaning they were composed by gathering many guests,
unable to claim expertise themselves—
this is indeed so.
Yet Lǚ Bùwéi and Liú Ān
never concealed that they gathered many,
unlike later generations who掩盖 others' strengths as their own.
These two certainly exercised the authority of final裁定,
claiming their works as school doctrines;
thus their guiding principles
were never without a consistent uniformity.
This, moreover, arose from what the guests did not participate in.
The rise of the various masters
was due to the splitting of the Way and its methods;
each, relying on their particular intelligence and talent,
gained one aspect of the great Way
and then sought to change the world with it.
Those who had grounds for their views
and reasoned arguments
naturally wished to expand their scholarship
and transmit it to their disciples.
If it sufficed to manifest their methods and establish their school,
then those who drew upon earlier accounts
and those who appended and elaborated later
never separately claimed credit for establishing the words.
Therefore it is said:
The words of the ancients
were meant for the public good;
they never took pride in their literary expression
or privately claimed them as their own.
Alas!
When the teachings of the world decline,
when the Way is insufficient and people contend over literary form,
then speech can be appropriated for private ends;
when substance is lacking and people contend over reputation,
then writing can be used for self-aggrandizement.
When speech can be appropriated for private ends,
and writing can be used for self-aggrandizement,
then contentious minds arise and the methods of the Way are fractured.
The words of the ancients
were intended to enlighten the world;
whereas the words of later people
are intended to deceive the world.
It is not that their hearts are at ease with deceiving the world,
but because they have something private to cherish and boast about,
they cannot help but be this way.
The words of the ancients
were intended to improve others;
the words of later people
are intended to show off themselves.
It is not that the ancients did not wish to show off,
while later people are particularly inclined to do so;
rather, it is because they have deficiencies and insufficiencies
that they cannot help but be this way.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Is the arrow-maker less humane than the armor-maker?
One cannot but be cautious in the craft one practices."
The ancients established their words from an easy position;
later people establish their words from a difficult position.
How can this be made clear?
What the ancients wished to communicate
was the Way.
When they had no choice but to speak,
it was like joy within that compelled laughter,
or illness afflicting the body that compelled groaning—
how could they have calculated the skill or clumsiness, quickness or slowness,
and forced themselves to imitate such effects?
As for where the Way resides,
one studies to approach it;
where learning resides,
like-minded people gather.
If the ancients had words
that first captured the shared understanding of my heart,
then those are my words.
Why?
Because their Way is the same.
If transmitted to others,
and they can grasp my discourse and adapt it flexibly,
then those are my words.
Why?
Because their Way is the same.
To exhaust a lifetime of study, reflection, and discernment on a constant Way,
and above, to connect with people of the same Way throughout the ages as a foundation,
and below, to await people of the same Way throughout the ages as support—
when they establish their words,
is it not indeed easy?
Only those with unguided intelligence,
who strive for insubstantial writing,
then without joy force a smiling appearance,
without illness deliberately produce groans—
they themselves cannot bear the toil and exhaustion;
how much more so when harboring a private fear of being exposed,
usurping and arrogating empty fame for themselves,
with no foundation ahead,
and no support behind,
placed in an isolated and precarious position without security—
is it not difficult indeed?
Words that are externally adorned
and words that emerge from within—
the difference in their ease and difficulty can be known.
Words not intended to contend for fame
and words determined to contend for fame—
the difference in their ease and difficulty
can also be known.
Words that connect past and present, before and after,
and are shared with others publicly,
versus words privately claimed as one's exclusive possession,
insisting they must originate from oneself—
the difference in their ease and difficulty
can also be known.
Those who establish words—
will they aspire to the Way,
and follow what is public and easy?
Or will they merely compete in literary form,
and follow what is private and difficult?
Between public and private, easy and difficult,
there must be a distinction.
Alas!
How can we find those who understand words,
and with them strive to advance in the Way?
In antiquity, there were none who stole others' words and claimed them as their own.
Bó Zōng's response regarding Liáng Shān—
he not only received ridicule for having no descendants,
but also incurred the crime of obscuring the worthy.
In antiquity, there were none who stole others' writings and claimed them as their own.
When Qū Píng's draft was not yet finalized,
Minister Shàngguān saw it and wanted to seize it—
not only did he intend to deceive his lord,
but also to slander his friend.
Stealing others' excellence
is equivalent to the theft of property—
Lǎozi spoke of this unequivocally.
The flaw arises from selfishly guarding one's own talents and wisdom,
and not knowing to return them publicly to the Way.
If Bó Zōng had recommended the worthy charioteer,
and employed the established saying of mourning in plain white at the temple,
that would have been Bó Zōng's words to prosper the state,
and his achievement would not have been limited to the affair of Liáng Shān.
If Minister Shàngguān had praised Qū Píng and assisted in drafting the ordinances,
that would have been Minister Shàngguān's words to build Chǔ,
and his achievement would not have been limited to the excellence of the ordinances.
When Hán Qí was prime minister,
Ōuyáng Xiū was a Hanlin academician.
Some said that Duke Hán had no literary compositions;
Hán replied, "With Qí as prime minister employing Xiū as academician,
in all under heaven, whose literary compositions
are greater than Qí's?"
Alas!
Someone like the Hán clan
can be said to have understood the intent of the ancients' public-mindedness in words.
Those who steal others' words
and claim them as their own—
desire for fame is the gravest motive,
and contention for achievement is secondary.
Achievement deceives for a time,
but fame deceives for a thousand ages.
Those who forge their own compositions
and falsely attribute them to the ancients—
fraudulent gain is the gravest motive,
and meddlesomeness is secondary;
meddlesomeness confines the crime to one's own person,
but fraudulent gain encourages imitation and obscures customs.
Qí Qiū stole the *Huà Shū* from Tán Qiào;
Guō Xiàng stole the commentary on the *Zhuāngzi* from Xiàng Xiù—
the gentleman considers them frivolous and without integrity.
If the authors were aware,
they would only wish their ideas to be made clear to all under heaven,
and not necessarily that the clarity come from themselves.
Yet they cannot but grieve in their hearts over those who steal,
for the cunning of burglars and pilferers
must involve alteration and revision to cover their tracks,
and thereby lose the original meaning.
Liú Xuàn's *Lián Shān*,
Méi Zé's *Ancient Text Shàngshū*—
presented in response to imperial summons,
were intended to seek salary and profit.
Insulting the words of the sages,
and presumptuously comparing themselves to the searches of Héjiān and Hénèi—
the gentleman considers their crimes beyond punishment.
Since the ancient texts were lost,
and forgers collected and patched together, as with the ancient texts gathering lost documents scattered in records and commentaries, almost without omission,
it is not necessarily that nothing at all was preserved.
Yet one cannot but deeply detest the forgers,
for lost chapters and scattered phrases,
attached as missing texts,
still preserve their meaning;
but when forced into a complete book,
their meaning is lost.
If they had directed the effort spent on forgery
toward collecting and supplementing as their own achievement,
then would their achievement have been inferior to the *Rites* of Héjiān
or the *Shū* of Hénèi?

Wáng Bóhòu's *Examination of the Three Schools' Shī* and Wú Cǎolú's *Lost Rites*, produced between the Sòng and Yuán dynasties, far removed from antiquity, still contributed to classical studies. When Six Dynasties ancient texts were not greatly scattered and lost, their achievement, compared to later people, must have been easier to accomplish. It is regrettable that they did not adopt this approach, but instead used it for forgery. Guō Xiàng's explanations of "Autumn Floods" and "Full Understanding of Life"
were not without refined words and famous principles that could make him second to Xiàng;
if he had elaborated their intent,
and let Xiù's commentary
and his own proceed side by side,
readers would not have distinguished which was Xiàng's and which was Guō's—
how could he have abruptly descended to the methods of burglary?
Not understanding the intent of public-mindedness in words,
and wishing to selfishly seek profit as achievement—
the great Way is hidden, and the workings of the mind can no longer be questioned.
All scholars aspire to achieve immortality,
but do they understand that immortality indeed has its own path?
When words are made public to the world,
even if the books themselves may perish over time,
the learning they contain does not abruptly vanish.
For when a school of thought is fully developed,
its influence spreads and endures,
and those who study it can examine and discern its essence.
Although the ancient texts of the Kǒng family were lost,
Sīmǎ Qiān sought instruction from Kǒng Ānguó,
and now Sīmǎ Qiān’s works are preserved in full,
so the Kǒng family’s version of the *Shū*
is not entirely lost.
Although Hán Yīng’s version of the *Shī* was lost,
Xǔ Shèn studied the *Shī* and incorporated Hán’s interpretations;
now the *Shuōwén Jiězì* is fully preserved,
so Hán Yīng’s *Shī*
is not entirely lost.
Although Liú Xiàng’s *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng Zhuàn*
and the *Qī Lüè Biélù* were lost,
Bān Gù’s historical scholarship derived from Liú Xīn;
Liú Xīn’s *Hàn Jì* served as the basis for the *Hànshū*. Now the treatises on the Five Phases and Arts and Letters are fully preserved,
so the learning of the Liú family is not lost.
There are also later scholars who relied on earlier masters:
Chǔ Shǎosūn drew inspiration from Sīmǎ Qiān,
Péi Sōngzhī relied on the light of Chén Shòu—
not merely clinging to their coattails,
but because their own strength was insufficient to survive independently.
There are also cases where the Way was the same and the methods similar,
and though the books were unfortunately lost,
they were preserved through fellow practitioners:
the *Lièzǐ* was fragmentary,
but half of it is recounted in Zhuāngzǐ’s works;
the writings of Yáng Zhū were lost,
but much survives in the *Hánfēizǐ*;
for Zhuāngzǐ and Lièzǐ both emerged from the Daoist school,
and Yáng Zhū’s doctrine of “for oneself”
naturally aligns with the methods of the School of Names and Legalism.
There are also those who relied on their own talents and intellect,
yet fell short of establishing a school,
but because they encountered the Way,
their unpolished substance fortunately survived:
Gàozǐ’s debates on the willow and the rushing water
were transmitted thanks to Mèngzǐ;
Huì Shī’s discourses on white horses and three-legged creatures
were made prominent through Zhuāngzǐ;
though they served as targets for critics,
they also reveal untrammeled talent,
not merely vanishing into obscurity.
There are also trivial sayings,
initially lacking lofty discourse,
but which fortunately resonated with understanding minds,
and ultimately became enduring classics:
the song of the child washing his feet
applies to family and state;
the common saying about seedlings and ears of grain
is verified in body and mind.
Those that illustrate principles
can be profound despite their simplicity;
and those that survive
are never vulgar but always refined.
All such cases
are not necessarily because the ancients had it easy and later people find it difficult,
nor because the ancients were clever and later people are clumsy,
nor because the ancients were right and later people are wrong.
The circumstances of name and reality differ,
the sentiments of public and private diverge,
and those who speak with intention and those who speak without intention
cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Thus it is said:
“Without intention for literary refinement, the writing endures;
with intention for literary refinement, the writing perishes.”
Now consider the lawsuits of common folk:
both parties present their statements,
and the officials accept them,
relying on these statements to reward the right and punish the wrong.
Are the statements presented
necessarily composed by the common folk themselves?
Yet the judgments of right and wrong, rewards and punishments,
are not applied to those who composed the statements,
but to the litigants,
emphasizing the intent behind their words,
while the words themselves need not be scrutinized for their origin.
In matters of grave plots and fields,
ancestral temples and lineage branches,
inspecting steles and tablets,
no rustic or crude source is disregarded,
for it is believed that to adjudicate right and wrong,
without these, one cannot grasp the essentials.
Are there no bronze vessels from the Three Dynasties,
or stone inscriptions from the Qín and Hàn,
with archaic and unusual inscriptions,
elegant and profound characters,
unattainable by later generations?
Yet for resolving disputes,
even the mundane cannot be discarded;
what is irrelevant to the matter at hand,
no matter how extraordinary, is not worth contending over.
Thus, later scholars
who seek refinement in the superficial aspects of writing
and wish to claim it as their private possession
are not worthy of discussing the Way.
Some may say:
“Pointing to the distant with elegant words”
is the teaching of the *Dàzhuàn*.
“Avoiding vulgarity and perversity in speech”
is the saying of the wise and enlightened.
“If words are not refined,
they will not travel far”—
thus, literary expression cannot be neglected.
Now you say that seeking refinement in the superficial aspects of writing is wrong;
what then should be the principle for establishing one’s words? The reply:
This is not what I meant.
The *Yì* says:
“Cultivate words to establish sincerity.”
Sincerity does not require the ultimate perfection of a sage’s utmost sincerity
to be worthy of establishing through cultivated words.
When scholars engage in literary composition,
regardless of the words used,
if they uphold them for a reason,
and not merely as empty ornamentation,
that is sincerity.
Having a reason,
and cultivating words to match it—
this pursuit of refinement
is precisely to express that sincerity.
“The *Yì* is extraordinary yet patterned;
the *Shī* is upright yet flowery”—
“the *Yì* expresses yīn and yáng,”
the *Shī* expresses emotions and nature.
The reason they are cultivated to be extraordinary and flowery
is precisely because it was believed that without this,
they could not manifest the principles of yīn and yáng or the expression of emotions and nature.
Thus it is said:
it is not a pursuit of refinement.
Without substance but with ornamentation,
even the words of the Six Classics
would be of no value,
let alone others.
Writing is
an empty vessel; the Way
is the substantial aim.
To desire refinement in writing
is like desiring excellence in bows and arrows.
Bows and arrows can defend against bandits,
but can also be used by bandits—
this has nothing to do with whether the bows and arrows are excellent or not.
Writing can illuminate the Way,
but can also betray the Way—
this has nothing to do with whether the writing is refined or not.
When Chén Lín drafted the proclamation for Yuán Shào,
denouncing Cáo Cāo’s crimes,
the literary style was undoubtedly vigorous and fervent.
Later, when he met Cáo Cāo,
he compared himself to an arrow that must follow the bowstring.
Had he drafted a proclamation for Cáo Cāo against Yuán Shào,
its refinement would surely have been the same.
Thus, merely excelling in literary expression
without aligning with the Way
is like having excellent boats and carriages—
indeed convenient for travel,
but whether they head to Yān or Yuè
remains unknown.
The words of the sage,
when recounted by the worthy,
may sometimes lose their original intent.
The words of the worthy,
when recounted by ordinary people,
may also sometimes lose their original intent.
Human minds differ,
just as their faces do.
Yet it is said that words are entrusted to the public,
and need not all originate from oneself—
why is this?
It is because the Way is the same and virtue is aligned,
and in the end, they do not diverge completely.
Moreover, when composing poetry, one may quote a passage out of context,
as if it came from one’s own mouth,
without being constrained by its original meaning.
When citing words to debate each other,
even if the meaning seems contradictory,
the ancients preserved them without discarding them.
When predecessors spoke,
later generations invoked their words to lend weight to their own arguments—
this is aligning oneself with the ancients.
When predecessors spoke,
later generations expanded upon their words—
this is attaching oneself to the ancients.
The benevolent see benevolence,
the wise see wisdom.
Words may appear similar yet differ,
or differ yet converge—
much like the feathers of autumn birds,
too numerous to list exhaustively.
Thus, when later generations recount the words of their predecessors,
they do not discard the old ways of those predecessors.
They believe that both coexist under heaven,
and matters of right and wrong, gain and loss,
are left to the discernment of the wise—
this is what makes it public.
The gentleman detests those who steal others’ words
and hastily erase the traces,
to satisfy their selfish desire to conceal.
If the words of predecessors have been lost,
and one has no choice but to draw from the discussions of later generations,
this is an unavoidable circumstance—
like those who have lost their ancestral rites
finding a clan member to preside over them,
so that the spirits may still be appeased.
Without understanding the principle of public discourse,
one cannot grasp this.
Thus, one wanders through the forest of literature,
soars in the garden of arts;
transcending form to capture essence,
casting off restraints and breaking free;
looking upward to discern the intent of the authors,
and downward to gather the writings of contemporary trends.
Oral transmission declines,
while written records gain prominence.
Dwelling in caves and nests,
one begins to carve jade;
using fur and leaves for warmth,
one eventually weaves brocade.
Famous words are forgotten in antiquity,
while schools of thought arise in recent times.
Like drawing water from a bubbling spring,
one lifts the hem to cross the ford;
to save from raging floods,
one must board a boat to navigate the chaos.
Extending the principle of public discourse,
one attains the unity of our Way.
Though used daily without awareness,
like forgetting the pellet while savoring roasted owl.
Try to trace the flow of the stream,
and behold the lush greenery of spring fields.
As for the lofty emperor enthroned in ninefold majesty,
unifying the six directions under one custom.
Imperial edicts are issued,
like the primal energy filling the world.
Ministers holding power and adjusting the cauldron,
assist in planning within the palace halls;
scholars wielding brushes and holding tablets,
receive decrees under the imperial maple.
Thus, in the Western Secretariat, drafts are written,
and in the Northern Gate, documents are reviewed.
The wind of heaven reaches the four directions,
the thunder from the abyss resounds across the eight regions.
Spreading overflowing virtuous words,
expressing diligent and concerned thoughts.
Promoting culture, it is like the Sháo and Huò music of mountains and seas;
strengthening military might, it is like grooming steeds at Tàishān and driving at Bīn.
Administering governance, it is like clouds and dragons following rhythm;
relieving disasters, it is like doves and cranes returning to plumpness.
These are all stored in stone chambers and golden caskets,
archives revered and preserved as precedents;
while silk-bound scrolls and yellow cases,
are compiled by scholars into family books.
The records of the left and right historians,
show no partiality of the ruler;
the collections of internal and external decrees,
are not monopolized by literary officials.
Though the wooden tower is secluded and pure,
public discourse has its dedicated officials;
and under bamboo mats and thatched eaves,
preserving and exchanging words does not hinder external transmission—such is the public nature of imperial decrees.
As for promoting culture and examining antiquity,
purchasing classics and extending brilliance.
The Luántái recounts history,
the Hǔguān discusses the classics.
Debates in the academies and schools,
on the six heavens, five emperors, three systems, and nine categories,
are contested by various experts;
disputes over the Rites and Documents,
theories of Qí and Lǔ traditions, Kǒng’s wall, and Liáng’s tombs,
are settled by imperial decree.
The Correct Meanings are established by one school,
the Jìn History is condensed into a hundred volumes.
Six hundred years of commentaries and annotations on the Five Classics Correct Meanings, drawing from the theories of Hàn and Six Dynasties experts and unifying them.
Eighteen schools of annals and biographies on the Jìn History.
Like the Zhāng River dividing and the Jiāng River merging,
the Jì River flowing underground and the Héng River crossing,
the Huái River extending and the Miǎn River winding,
all converging toward the valley king;
kingfisher feathers and azurite,
indigo blue and purple ganoderma,
aquamarine and cinnabar sand,
brilliantly displayed in colorful splendor.
All to unify writing and chariots, and harmonize sight and sound,
to standardize measures and suppress heresy and excess.
Though collectively called imperially sanctioned,
they are truly the work of Confucian officials.
Leaders of high rank,
present memorials with their names inscribed at the forefront;
while many officials collaborate,
their names are often forgotten over time.
Just as when a new temple is completed,
who counts the many craftsmen rushing about,
and records their contributions?
When solemn rituals are performed,
who discusses the cooks preparing the offerings,
while the priest chants the prayers!
Moreover, the three ministries and eight high offices,
hundreds of positions and various departments,
regional commanders and unified divisions,
prefectures and counties governing separately.
Like stars scattered across the autumn sky,
or grains sprouting in eastern fields.
Documents pile up densely,
scrolls and records spread in disarray.
The civil and military repositories,
the dazzling offices of rites and music,
are like spokes converging and turning the wheel’s axle;
military affairs, lawsuits,
currency, and farmland regulations,
are like chess pieces arranged on a square board.
Official documents advance like geese in formation,
following statutes and formats in writing;
summoning followers like holding a bull by the ear,
adhering to precedents and approving with a stroke.
Thus, the brush is wielded like a knife,
and writing is called clerical script.
Words are dispatched by clerks,
while gains and losses rest with senior officials.
For the hundred officials govern and the myriad people observe,
hence knotted ropes were replaced by written contracts.
The ignorant argue over trivialities,
while the wise understand the original intent—such is the public nature of official documents.
As for the marquises, kings, generals, and ministers,
the regional governors and assembled dignitaries.
In their offices, they handle affairs,
at their gateways, they manage military matters.
They possess the lofty prestige of wealth and rank,
and wield the awe-inspiring authority of both civil and martial prowess.
Then there are the graceful secretaries,
the refined and celebrated scholars,
the advisors in the command tents,
the literary aides and clerks.
Like the osprey striking by the seaside,
Zhòng Lián sent swift missives across the desert;
like the eagle soaring over Hé Shuò,
Kǒng Zhāng sped urgent proclamations to Dāngtú.
Wáng Càn, impassioned and reliant on Liú,
composed rhapsodies that spread through the Jīng court;
Bān Gù, untrammeled and following Dòu,
inscribed steles at Lángjū Mountain.
With haystacks crushed and roads destroyed,
the wandering soul was moved by Huì Lián's elegy;
with orioles singing and flowers blooming,
the living spirit returned through Xī Fàn's letter.
Such cases may involve sincerity piercing the firmness of metal and stone,
or loyalty and fervor stirring the energy of wind and clouds.
To convey emotion is like green grass sprouting in spring,
to soar in argument is like yellow waves boiling in summer.
To stir the hidden is like mountain ghosts weeping at night,
to reveal the clear is like sea spirits clearing at dawn.
All can pursue the obscure and enter the profound,
transmit the heart and convey the will.
They transform and adapt to others,
bending and flexing as desired.
Since the paths to profit and rank are broad,
the efforts of揣摩 (assessing and adapting) subtly arrive.
The collections of mid and late-period literati,
are largely filled with ghostwriting skills.
Since they harmonize the reins and the carriage bells,
how can they part ways and contend with separate banners?
It is heard that when the desire for wealth and rank is satisfied,
then one yearns for immortality.
When the arts of alchemy (yellow and white) prove deficient,
the esteem for literary composition becomes specialized.
Considering the immortality of human life,
long life is not as good as the transmission of one's name;
since it punishes folly and displays wisdom,
it thus allows the later to surpass the former.
Then there are those who monopolize the seven sable insignia of rank,
or perhaps households enfeoffed with a hundred thousand,
during the leisurely pace after retiring from court,
or in the idle feasts during rest periods.
Ashamed to be submerged in worldly glory,
they then earnestly admire writing praises and commentaries.
Thus, in the Western Garden they gather the elegant,
in the Eastern Pavilion they host Confucian scholars,
they arrange lead type and set up writing tablets,
they scatter ink and apply vermilion.
Seeking the fine achievements of the literary grove,
they then join forces and plan together.
Some embrace the uncut jade of Jīng Mountain,
some boast the pearl of Suí Hóu,
some treasure the stone of Yān market,
some inflate the yu of Qí gate;
all harbor private aims and flatter themselves,
watching the master's finger and rushing towards it.
Since they take much and use broadly,
it is like storing provisions and gathering fodder.
They rely on great power to encompass preservation,
supplying the diligent learner's search and inquiry.
Establishing merit is indeed equal to establishing words,
how is it in any way inferior to the unique creations of specialists?
As for the evolution of the forms of the *Shī* and *Sāo*,
the Yuèfǔ takes the stage.
The titles of pieces like "*Zhū Lù*", "*Bēi Wēng*",
"*Shàng Yé*", "*Rú Zhāng*",
scholars find no evidence for their interpretation;
the sounds and beats of "Hū Xī", "Sè Èr",
"Cún Wú", "Jī Lìng",
musicians only remember their clanging and clinking.
Then there are those who deliberate and describe,
elaborate and expound.
The enthusiasts create explanations for them,
the heartbroken have their own unique sentiments.
Golden bridles and white horses,
wine shops and hairpin towers,
these are the joys of youth;
mountain passes with willows,
luggage and travel's mist,
these are the feelings of parting.
Lush grass and plump birds,
proud horses and swift bows,
these are the pleasures of hunting;
the Lǒng River's sobbing,
the frontier sun's dusky yellow,
these are the marches of campaign and garrison.
Some use indignation to voice the grievances of conscripted men,
some use melancholy to express the sorrow of a departing concubine;
some use broad-mindedness to expand the delights of travel and feasting,
some use ancient sentiments to entrust words of glamour and allure.
Since transmitters did not grasp their intent,
they then said "*Zǐ Yè*" was a woman's name,
"*Mù Lán*" was a self-narrated poem.
If they do not violate the analogies and stimulations of the Six Arts,
would the authors wish to selfishly claim the public Yuèfǔ with their personal names?
There is also the matter of writers altering texts,

somewhat imitating the historian's deletions and adaptations to form a text, or making slight alterations. Only historical writing has such principles and precedents. In poetry and prose collections, this practice originally does not exist. Occasionally, there are cases similar to this, but there is a great distinction between the miraculous and the rotten; one must discern carefully.
The phoenix trapped in the ruins of Jīng,
laments the bewildering sun in the southern land;
Zhuāngzǐ altered the "*Fèng Xī Gē*". "*Lù Míng*" in the duckweed-covered wilds,
recites the night "*Yǎ*" on "*Dōng Shān*" (Cáo Cāo used a *Xiǎo Yǎ* poem).
With maidenhair vine and clematis,
on the path they perform the words of the mountain ghost;
with fine silk and flowing yellow,
in the narrow lanes they adopt the old words of the "*Fù Yàn*" (the Yuèfǔ pieces "*Mò Shàng Sāng*" and "*Sān Fù Yàn*").
