Men of Liáng altered the song of "*Lǒng Tóu*" (they added to and subtracted from the ancient words to make it).
Hán Gōng deleted lines from "*Yuè Shí*" (he edited and altered Lú Tóng's poem).
Is it merely taking the meaning by breaking off the chapter?
It is no different from performing rhapsodies at a guest banquet (singing ancient poems to express one's own ideas).
So much so that where the river divides the mountain's form,
it connects with the green traces of spring grass;
(a Sòng dynasty poetic monk used Táng lines). Accumulated rain in the empty woods,
then enters the white egrets in the watery fields.
It is like an ancient prescription with modern effect,
the spirit adds and subtracts with the medicine spoon;
like Zhào's wall and Hàn's army,
changing banners according to the commander's orders.
The literary grove has its own elegant standards,
enumerating them in detail would be difficult to exhaust their number.
If it is not so,
imitation arises from excess.
Imitating the "*Tóng Gǔ*" seven songs (many poets after Sòng did this).
Modeling the "*Hé Jiān*" four autumns (Fù Xuán, Zhāng Zǎi still did this, quite astonishing).
Not issuing words from within the heart,
but like following a voice to aid the singing.
It is simply a toddler learning to speak,
truly something that the discerning would find shameful (the principle of altering texts).
There are also the different schools of poets,
their sentiments and aspirations differ.
They change the sounds of rhyme and cut the literary form,
model ancient events to convey private feelings.
The purport originates from the allegorical words of the various masters,
literati follow and transmit, forming a tradition;
later people do not know their source,
thus suspect forgery and attack each other.
For lamenting a lost homeland,

(Lǐ Líng's "*Reply to Sū Wǔ's Letter*", since Liú Zhījī, unanimous opinion has considered it a forgery. Reasoning it out, what would a forger gain from it? It should be that during the Northern and Southern Dynasties, there was a southerner detained in the north, whose circumstances resembled Lǐ Líng's, and who could not bear to speak openly, so he composed this letter to express his will). Ashes of ambition for fame and merit,
thus entrust the metaphor of the riverbank tree;

(the world transmits Guǐgǔzǐ's "*Letter to Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí*", speaking of a tree by the river, situated in the wrong place, thus inviting pruning, using metaphor to summon the two to retire in seclusion; it is suspected to also be the entrusted words of someone with great achievements who felt endangered). The reader uses his own mind to meet the author's intent,
it is no different from the Sāo poet's rhapsody (if it came from the original person, its meaning would be shallow; if it came from an imitation, its meaning is very deep, similar to the Sāo).
Afterwards, the literary examinations selected scholars,
using imitative writing as established precedent.
For solemnity, there were edicts, proclamations, memorials, and reports;
for fierceness, there were declarations and bulletins.
Composing eulogies followed the standard of Wáng Bāo,
writing treatises was modeled on Jiǎ Fù.
This then established the compass and square,
also following and treading in step.
Hoping that he has a mind and I can fathom it,
also sufficient to elucidate the obscure and subtle and mutually illuminate (the principle of imitative writing).
Again, like the hypothetical constructs of literati,
changing and transforming without constraint.
The *Shī* communicates through analogy and stimulation,
the *Yì* models images and beginnings.
Zhuāngzǐ entered Wū Xián's seat,
Qū Yuán visited Zhān Yǐn's hut.
The Chǔ crown prince ill,
a guest came from Wú.
Followers like Wū Yǒu and Zǐ Xū,
competed in discussing hunting comparisons;
categories like Píng Xū and Ān Chǔ,
lectured and debated about the capital.
Pieces like "*Jiě Cháo*", "*Kè Nán*", "*Bīn Xì*" extended this thread,
types like Jìng Jī, Xuán Wēi, Chōng Mò deepened this path.
This then is nine-tenths allegory,
with myriad different strange tales.
Yet they become famous because of events,
generate meaning based on people.
For example, wine adopts Dù Kāng's name,
money uses Dèng Tōng's character.
Empty locust tree, falling sparks,
Huán Wēn sighed over Zhòng Wén's transfer;
(borrowed by Yǔ Xìn in "*Kū Shù Fù*". Actually, Yīn Zhòngwén's transfer to Dōngyáng was long after Huán Wēn's death). Pale moon flowing across the sky,
Wáng Càn drew his brush upon Yìng and Liú's passing (borrowed by Xiè Zhuāng in "*Yuè Fù*". Actually, Wáng Càn died before Yìng and Liú).
Thus, one who is good at sorrow becomes Sòng Yù,
must it necessarily be the Chǔ court?
One naturally broad-minded is Liú Líng,
why discuss the Jìn era?
Being good at reading the books of the ancients,
especially values knowing the meaning in one's heart.
Fools argue with great concern,
the ancients would not find it strange (the principle of hypothetical constructs).
As for the examination essays of the classics scholars,
they elaborate on meanings to form texts;
although their source lies in exegesis,
their interpretation truly focuses on digesting the new.
They extract passages from the classics and histories as topics,
and the crafting of variations is up to the individual.
Long ones may stretch across chapters and sections,
short ones may be just a few words or a single phrase.
If a hair's breadth is added or subtracted,
it is like the shadow shifting with each step.
They speak for the sages and worthies,
or express the aspirations of the mediocre and foolish.
All seek to depict emotions and portray attitudes,
placing themselves in the situation.
Sometimes the words are complete but the meaning is half-formed,
sometimes the spirit arrives but the form is not yet present,
like clouds that have departed yet still linger,
like a horse that has leaped but not yet vanished.
They capture within a fleeting moment,
delineating at the brink of the infinitesimal.
Leveling water and measuring grain,
how can they compare to its fullness and pervasiveness?
Calendrical calculations and planetary conjunctions,
can hardly fathom its subtlety and profundity.
The strangeness of the *Yì*, the correctness of the *Shī*,
the restraint of the *Lǐ* and the harmony of the *Yuè*,
down to the exaggeration of the *Zuǒ* and the unrestrainedness of the *Zhuāng*,
the profundity of Qū and the purity of the *Shǐ*—their literary principles
are all-encompassing;
the nature of Heaven and humanity, destiny,
statecraft and broad learning,
as well as the contentiousness of the Ru, the frugality of the Mò,
the sharpness of the Names school and the depth of the Legalist school—their scholarship,
leaves nothing unprepared.
Only the regulations are issued by decree,
and their meaning is obtained through transmission from teachers.
They strictly adhere to the three affairs of the people's livelihood,
and constrain intelligence within rules and measures.
They uphold the shared principles and methods,
and elaborate the refined abilities each can fully exert.
Expressing through personal comprehension,
why should they be suspected of imitating the sages?
Establishing models based on one's mind,
must one necessarily follow one's own theories to achieve fame? The impartiality of regulated essays.
All these categories and classifications,
arranged in orderly sequence and comprehensive sections.
Delicate blossoms charm the spring,
plump fruits intoxicate the autumn.
They reach the extremes of shallow and deep in distinctive expressions,
marking the left and right divisions of the flow.
Their concealment is almost all-encompassing,
their contention is like enemies and foes.
Their agreement leads to mutual praise,
their difference leads to mutual correction.
Their accord brings self-satisfied delight,
their divergence brings anxious solitude and worry.
Who are the swans soaring high?
Who are the sparrows chirping below?
Who are the phoenix trees on the high ridge?
Who are the reeds and rushes on the flat isle?
The multitude considers themselves right and others wrong,
delighting in attacking differences and forming factions.
They brawl over drinking from the same well,
never knowing of the hidden spring flowing beneath.
Looking down upon the multitude of words from the great Way,
how can they be anything but the different sounds of shrieks, shouts, cries, calls, howls, roars, yelps, and chirps,
brewed in the different apertures of the nose, mouth, ears, beams, rings, mortars, hollows, and pools?
When the fierce wind ceases, all becomes empty;
know that what seems possessed and existing,
is but the sighing whistle of a single earthen bag.
The capable have nothing to compete for in fame,
the cunning have nothing to accomplish by plagiarism.
The scrutinizing have nothing to rely on in argument,
the boastful have nothing to contend for in display.
Understanding the subtle intent of the public nature of words,

one may nearly attain the wondrous essence of the Way. Some may doubt that scholarly writings should not be included under the category of poetic exposition (*cífù*), not knowing that the forms of scholarly writing originally had no such avoidance. Xún Qīng had his "Fu Chapters"; however, insubstantial poetic expositions naturally should not be confused with scholarly writings.

The Historian's Integrity
Talent, learning, and judgment: these three,
to possess one is not easy,
and to combine all three is especially difficult.
Throughout the ages, there have been many literary men but few good historians;
this is precisely the reason.
In the past, Liú Zǐxuán (Liú Zhījī)
seemed to consider this theory sufficient to exhaust the principle.
Nevertheless,
what history values is moral principle (*yì*),
what it relies on are the events (*shì*),
and what it depends on is the literary expression (*wén*).
Mèngzǐ said:
"The events are those of Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn,
the literary expression is that of the historian,
but the moral principle the Master said he privately appropriated."
Without judgment, one cannot determine its moral principle;
without talent, one cannot perfect its literary expression;
without learning, one cannot refine its events.
These three certainly each have their own affinities,
and among them are certainly some that appear similar but are not.
To consider memorization as learning,
literary embellishment as talent,
and arbitrary decision as judgment,
is not the talent, learning, and judgment of a good historian.
Even the talent, learning, and judgment spoken of by Liú
are still insufficient to exhaust the principle.
Now, Liú said that having learning without judgment
is like a foolish merchant holding gold,
not understanding trade and exchange.
Extending this argument to clarify Liú's point,
it merely aims, within the scope of memorization,
to know how to make selections,
in order to form coherent writing.
Therefore it is said:
The ancients' histories aimed to establish a school,
demoting recluses and promoting treacherous heroes,
rejecting those who died for principle and glossing over the faults of rulers,
also saying it was the natural way of their school.
This is still the judgment of a literary man,
not historical judgment.
One who can possess historical judgment
must understand the historian's integrity.
What is integrity?
It refers to the mental disposition of the author.
A vile history vilifies its author;
a slanderous book slanders its author.
If one's usual conduct is shameful to others,
how can one's literary compositions be valued?
Wèi Shōu's distortion and falsehood,
Shěn Yuē's hidden wickedness—
those who read their books
first distrust the men themselves.
Their harm has not reached the extreme.
What is to be feared in mental disposition
is when one has the mind of a gentleman,
but one's cultivation has not reached purity.
To have the mind of a gentleman
but cultivation not yet pure
is unavoidable for anyone below the great worthies.
If even this is considered a problem of mental disposition,
then unless it is the Master's *Chūnqiū*,
nothing would suffice.
To demand this of others,
is it not too difficult?
This is also not so.
For one who wishes to be a good historian,
should carefully distinguish between Heaven and man,
exhausting Heaven's principle and not adding to it with human will.
To exhaust Heaven's principle and not add to it with human will—
although one may not achieve it,
if one truly understands it,
it is sufficient to be called the mental disposition of a writer.
Yet the Confucians of literature and history
compete in discussing talent, learning, and judgment,
and do not know to distinguish mental disposition when discussing the historian's integrity.
How can this be acceptable?
Someone asks: Is there a different meaning between the term "shǐ" (scribe) in "fǔ shǐ" (clerks) from the Rites of Zhōu
and the term "shǐ" in Nèishǐ (Inner Scribe), Wàishǐ (Outer Scribe), Tàishǐ (Grand Scribe), Xiǎoshǐ (Junior Scribe), and Yùshǐ (Imperial Scribe)?
The reply is:
There is no different meaning.
The "shǐ" in "fǔ shǐ"
refers to commoners in government service performing clerical duties,
which are what are now called "shūlì" (clerks).
The Five Shǐ,
however, are filled by qīng (high ministers), dàfū (grandees), and shì (officers).
They are in charge of matters concerning documents, records, edicts, and legal statutes,
which are now the functions of bodies like the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat), the Liù Kē (Six Offices of Scrutiny), and the Hànlín (Hanlin Academy) and Zhōngshū (Central Drafting) officials.
The distinction between official and functionary,
the gap between high and low,
and the separation of their streams
are as vast as heaven and earth.
Yet there is no different meaning,
because both are custodians of precedents and regulations,
preserving the Way of the former kings through these statutes.
If a Shǐ guards the precedents but does not know how to select among them,
it is like a storekeeper guarding the treasury without knowing how to manage accounts.
The former kings held that the Tàizǎi (Grand Steward), who regulated the state's expenditures,
and the Sīkuài (Comptroller), who verified the annual accounts,
both embodied the principle of adjusting surplus and deficit and maintaining balanced order.
Such roles could not be entrusted
to anyone
but those of weighty status like qīng and dàfū.
As for the storekeepers,
they dared not act on their own authority in disbursements and receipts;
commoners in government service
were sufficient for such tasks without causing shortage.
Yet when qīng and dàfū
deliberated on state planning,
they grasped its broad and long-term aspects.
If asked about the minute details of the treasury stores,
they would certainly say, "That is the fǔ's (storehouse) affair."
The relationship of the Five Shǐ to documents
is like that of the Tàizǎi and Sīkuài to goods and wealth.
The Diǎn (Canons), Mó (Councils), Xùn (Instructions), and Gào (Announcements)
—Zēng Shì (Master Zeng) said of them: "In the flourishing eras of Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties,
those who wielded the brush to record
were also disciples of the sages."
His insight can be called profound.
The Five Shǐ, selected from among qīng and dàfū,
deliberated on subtle and refined principles;
the (fǔ) shǐ merely guarded the documents, archives, regulations, and precedents,
not daring to act on their own authority.
Yet if asked about the intricate details of precedents,
one would certainly say, "That is the shǐ's affair."
The Master said:
"The people may be made to follow it,
but they may not be made to understand it."
The Way and the statutes of the former kings
are not two separate things.
The qīng and dàfū could discuss the Way,
while the fǔ shǐ merely guarded the statutes.
Human knowledge and capability
can be such that some can be enabled and others cannot.
It is not that beyond what the fǔ shǐ guarded,
there existed a separate Way of the former kings.
The Master said:
"As for matters of sacrificial vessels,
I have heard about them."
Master Zēng then said:
"There are three things regarding the Way that the noble person values.
As for matters of sacrificial baskets and stands,
there are officers in charge of them."
This is not because Master Zēng's words differed from the Master's.
The Master extended the principle,
while Master Zēng feared people would become mired in the statutes.
Zǐgòng said:
"The Way of Wén and Wǔ
has not yet fallen to the ground;
it resides in people.
Is there anything our Master does not learn?
And why should he have a constant teacher?"
"When he entered the Grand Temple,
he asked about everything."
Thus, the lowly functionaries,
the shamans, invocators, and various artisans
were all teachers from whom our Master learned.
Asking about rituals and asking about offices—
was this not learning from precedents?
Therefore, the Way cannot be expounded emptily,
and writing cannot be composed emptily.
Before the Three Dynasties, they had not yet named teachings "the Way,"
yet the Way was ever-present,
for there was no empty principle.
Before the Three Dynasties, they had not yet regarded writing as "literary composition,"
yet their writing is unsurpassed by later ages,
for there was no empty speech.
It was only after the separation of official duties and instructional governance
that writing began to include private compositions.
Thereupon, literary writing and scholarship
parted ways with the precedents and regulations of the offices,
and those who established teachings could then discuss the substance of the Way apart from the statutes.
The Yì (Book of Changes) says:
"If it is not the right person,
the Way does not proceed emptily."
Scholars revere the Six Classics,
believing that the sages set down words to hand down teachings.
They do not realize that in the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties,
each guarded the precedents of his specific office,
and the sages did not intentionally compose literary works.
The Zhuàn (Commentary) says:
"In rituals,
timeliness is of greatest importance."
It also says:
"The writing should be uniform."
This speaks of valuing the institutions of the contemporary king.
Scholars merely recite the遗留 words of former sages
without comprehending the institutions of the contemporary king.
Thus, they treat writing as an ornament for embroidery and adornment,
and scholarship as a resource for contending in novelty and guesswork,
no longer considering its practical use.
Hence, the Way becomes hidden and difficult to know,
and the scholarship and literary compositions of the shì dàfū
may not suffice for the needs of the state.
The statutes are evident and easy to uphold.
The precedents preserved by the clerks
are in fact where the institutions of the state reside,
and also the actual traces
of the adaptations, additions, and subtractions since the time of Yáo and Shùn.
Therefore, if one has no aspiration for learning, so be it.
But if a noble person does aspire to learn,
he must seek the statutes and regulations of the present age,
so that they are relevant to human relations and daily use;
he must seek the precedents of the offices,
and through them penetrate the subtleties of classical scholarship.
Then learning becomes a matter of actual affairs,
and writing is not empty speech.
This is what is called: where there is substance, there must be function.
To discuss antiquity without knowing the present age,
to discuss classical scholarship without understanding precedents—
then the ornamented writing
and guesswork scholarship,
no matter how refined and capable,
are clearly of no practical use.
Mèngzǐ said:
"His strength is sufficient to lift a hundred jūn,
yet it is insufficient to lift one feather.
His eyesight is sharp enough to examine the tip of an autumn hair,
yet he does not see a cartload of firewood."
Making difficult what is easy,
and making easy what is difficult
is called losing the proper measure.
Scholars, ignorant of the present yet broad in antiquity,
neglectful of precedents yet versed in classical scholarship,
are capable of mastering what was difficult for the qīng and shì of the Zhōu offices,
yet do not know to seek what was easy for the fǔ shǐ.
Therefore, to discard the instruments and seek the Way,
to discard the present and seek antiquity,
to discard human relations and daily use and seek the subtleties of scholarship—
all are due to not understanding that the "shǐ" of the fǔ shǐ connects with the meaning of the Five Shǐ.
To take officials as teachers
was the old method of the Three Dynasties.
The way the Qín people violated antiquity
was in prohibiting the Shī (Book of Songs) and Shū (Book of Documents) and taking only the laws as teachers.
In the flourishing age of the Three Dynasties,
all learning under heaven
took officials as teachers without exception.
The three hundred sixty offices of the Zhōu
contained the complete learning of heaven and man.
Those who maintained their offices and fulfilled their duties,
without neglecting the work of heaven,
were all teachers and models for the world.
After the Eastern Zhōu,
the ruler's instruction and governmental teaching were no longer united.
Thereupon, human scholarship
did not entirely derive from the custodianship of the offices.
The Qín people, by taking officials as teachers,
began to restore the ancient system.
Yet people, accustomed to their own practices,
then regarded the Qín people as wrong.
The Qín people violated antiquity in many ways,
but one thing that accorded with antiquity
was taking officials as teachers.
Confucius said:
"Those who live in the present age
but revert to the ways of antiquity
will bring calamity upon themselves."
Lǐ Sī requested the banning of the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
arguing that Confucian scholars praised antiquity and criticized the present.
His words may seem similar,
but their meaning is greatly contradictory.
Later gentlemen
must not fail to examine this.
The Three Kings did not follow identical rites,
the Five Emperors did not adhere to the same music.
Not understanding that rites must accord with their time,
yet readily speaking of loving antiquity—
such persons are certainly not those who truly understand ancient institutions.
They are disorderly people who do not uphold the law,
hence the Master despised them.
As for the Yīn dynasty building upon Xià rites,
a hundred generations could be known.
Though additions and subtractions are said to follow the times,
there has never been one who disparaged Yáo and Shùn,
and vilified Yǔ, Tāng, King Wén, King Wǔ, and the Duke of Zhōu, yet could achieve good governance.
Lǐ Sī's request to ban the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*
is considered by gentlemen to be the height of folly.
Later generations are even more distant
from the times of Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties.
Yet the essential institutions of any dynasty,
those that can be passed down through generations and bring about an era of peace and order,
none have failed to approximate,
the Way of the ancient sage-kings.
Therefore, the statutes and regulations of a dynasty,
the precedents and practices held by its officials,
none are incompatible with what is transmitted in the *Book of Songs*, *Book of Documents*, and the Six Arts.
But scholars, ignorant of understanding their times,
often pride themselves on broad knowledge of antiquity.
It is like investigating the sericulture of Xīlíng,
or lecturing on Shénnóng's methods of planting,
thinking one can ward off hunger and cold without needing food and clothing.
Historical Commentary
In the past, when the Master composed the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
after the writing and editing were complete,
he further, through subtle words and profound meanings,
orally instructed his disciples.
The composition of the Three Commentaries
thus allowed each to rely on what they had heard and seen,
to elucidate and expand the meaning of the classic,
whereby the *Spring and Autumn Annals* became clear.
The various masters and hundred schools,
having established their doctrines,
also had disciples who upheld them together,
and only then did their doctrines become prominent in the world.
As for historical matters,
the ancients made it a hereditary family profession.
Scholars went to their families to transmit the profession—Confucius, inquiring about rites, necessarily went to the Archivist under the Pillar.
For within the realm's three great matters,
it was not that preparation was made by a single hand,
nor achievement accomplished within the forest of writing.
Sīmǎ Qiān wrote one hundred and thirty chapters; the *Hàn Shū* called it *Tàishǐ Gōng*; the *Suí Zhì* first called it *Shǐjì*.
He said:
"I shall hide it in a famous mountain,
and transmit it to the right person."
Later, his grandson Yáng Yùn
first disseminated his book.
Bān Gù's *Hàn Shū*,
after Gù's death,
for a time scholars
could not fully comprehend it.
Mǎ Róng then prostrated himself beneath the pavilion,
receiving instruction from his [Bān Gù's] younger sister,
and only then did that learning become prominent.
The books of Mǎ [Sīmǎ Qiān] and Bān [Gù]
are seen in their entirety by people today,
yet in their time, transmission necessarily relied on specific persons,
and receiving instruction necessarily had its source—
the specialized learning of the ancients
necessarily involved transmitting the mind beyond the method,
what the work of writing and editing could not reach,
was then orally instructed to disciples,
who together transmitted and practiced that profession,
to pass it down permanently.
Qiān's work, since Péi Yīn made commentaries,
and Gù's work, since Yìng Shào provided explanations,
and thereafter those who made commentaries for them,
still several families,
all were elucidating their family learning.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
writings have proliferated,
with no teacher inheritance from before,
and no followers to learn from after.
Moreover, their literary style,
the form being already diffuse and sprawling,
utterly lacks the rigorous meaning of the ancients' writing and editing;
their purport is again shallow and obvious,
also lacking the ancients' subtle and difficult-to-grasp reasons;
naturally they could follow their own attainments,
and circulate alone in the world.
As for the stewardship of historical records,
each age had its people,
but ancient learning was lost,
only the form of history remained.
Merely in the arrangement of documents and official files,
the sequence of daily and monthly records and annotations,
there was endless confusion,
and the writing also became verbose and repetitive,
completely losing the old style of Qiān and Gù.
Was this entirely because the authors' talent and strength were inadequate,
or because history lacked rules for annotation,
the situation inevitably tended daily toward complexity and abundance?
For the ancients, one book
was transmitted by several schools.
For later generations, several people
jointly completed one book.
When transmitters are broad,
the method of simplicity exhausting the subtle remains.
When authors are many,
the flaw of contradiction and repetition emerges.
Further, flowing onward, daily forgetting the source,
how can ancient learning be restored,
and how can historical records be simplified?
Thus the *Táng Shū* doubled the Hàn,
the *Sòng Shǐ* doubled the Táng,
those who consult them are overwhelmed by the labor,
the profession of transmission and learning,
how can it not perish?
Those hearing the same but narrating differently
see a fork and take separate paths.
The source being correct but streams diverging
over time loses authenticity.
The Nine Masters' *Yì*,
the Four Schools' *Shī*,
masters and Confucians standing like a forest,
their transmissions were already overwhelmingly numerous.
Scholars born after the Three Antiquity periods,
able to attain understanding from the ancients by themselves,
and carve out a work of their own school,
moreover wavering between the two,
isolated without disciples,
and wishing to hold this meager learning,
awaiting its explication by Zǐcháng's [Sīmǎ Qiān's] grandson,
or Mèngjiān's [Bān Gù's] younger sister,
is certainly an impossible expectation.
The Grand Historian's composition of the "Autobiographical Postface",
was it the beginning of self-annotation?
Clarifying the original intent of the composition,
showing the basis for inclusions and exclusions,
already seemed to fear later people not understanding what he said,
and specially wrote to mark it.
The so-called "not departing from ancient texts",
"thus verifying the Six Arts" and such statements,
are all the guiding principles of the one hundred and thirty chapters,
sometimes placed at the end of the scroll,
sometimes at the beginning of the chapter,
never failing to repeatedly clarify themselves.
In Bān's *Shū*, the ten chronological tables,
and the two treatises on *Geography* and *Arts and Letters* all have self-annotation,
which are again the rules for outline and details.
As for the two histories of Chén [Shòu] and Fàn [Yè],
there were still Sōng Zhī and Zhānghuái to annotate them.
Down to Xí Huìmíng's annotation of *Records of Qín*,
and Liú Xiàobiāo's annotation of *A New Account of the Tales of the World*,
these miscellaneous histories and offshoots
still had sub-commentaries,
which is one proof that the historiographical family methods of the Six Dynasties were not yet lost.
Afterward, the authority of history being already dispersed,
annals and biographies vast and numerous,
only Xú's *Annotations to the History of the Five Dynasties*,
though also already brief,
still preserved a thread of the sacrificial lamb.
But the various masters of Táng and Sòng,
were utterly unaware of its boundaries.
Sòng Fàn Chōng, revising the *Veritable Records of Shénzōng*,
separately made five chapters of *Textual Criticism*,
to elucidate its meaning.
This shows knowing there was no one later to replace him,
he explained it himself.
This should be, together with works like *Outline of the Comprehensive Mirror* and *Textual Criticism*,
considered good methods of recent times.
Liú's *Generalities on History*,
delineated the forms of supplementary annotation into three categories.
What he called minor works recording figures like *Decisive Records of the Three Capital Regions* and *Eminent Men and Women of Huáyáng*,
and what he called histories self-edited by historians like *The Monasteries of Luòyáng* and *Customs East of the Pass*,
though named as two types,
are actually one category.
These are what recent discussants of history must urgently restore.
Only what he called "seeking to broaden with different accounts" like Sōng Zhī's *Three Kingdoms* and Liú Zhāo's *Later Hàn*—this one category
is the old method of historians,
and those like *Suǒyǐn* and *Zhèngyì*
are largely similar with minor differences.
The texts of literature and history
daily grow more numerous.
Once a compilation is published,
the books from which materials were gathered
within a few decades
often lose five or six out of ten.
The established practices of compiling histories in the Song and Yuan dynasties
can be examined for verification.
If the practice of self-annotation were adopted,
then through the references made,
one could preserve the general state of ancient collections,
and thereby correct the merits and flaws in bibliographic records.
This would also be an aid to historical methodology.
Moreover, human hearts grow increasingly shallow,
and customs change daily.
The principle of leaving gaps for missing texts is no longer heard of,
while the habit of forced interpretations
becomes ever more refined.
In officially compiled books,
the sole aim is to fulfill obligations;
in private writings,
the goal is to embellish empty reputations.
Some plagiarize existing works,
others take shortcuts due to ignorance or laziness.
If their methods are slightly cunning,
they can deceive the eyes and ears of their time,
and the way of true authorship declines further.
If self-annotation were truly used to indicate selections and omissions,
then the breadth of one's knowledge,
the depth of one's effort,
and the sincerity or falsity of one's intent
would become clearly visible upon opening the book,
and customs could gradually return to the simplicity of antiquity.
This would be an even greater benefit.
Thus, examining past eras,
the family traditions were as described;
considering later generations,
the importance is again as stated.
When writing is more concise than before,
yet its effectiveness surpasses the old,
what could be better than self-annotation?
Biography
The genre of biographical writings
has existed for a long time,
emerging around the same period as the Six Classics.
Ancient writers did not adhere to fixed literary forms,
and there was no strict division between classics and history.
The three commentaries on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
each recording what was heard,
and deriving meaning from the classic,
could also be called "records."
The *Records* compiled by the two Dài from the *Classic of Rites*,
each transmitting their interpretations,
attached to the classic,
could also be called "commentaries."
Later, they branched into various schools.
By recent times,
it became customary to classify writings about people
as "biographies";
and narratives of events
as "records."
This was likely due to the proliferation of collected works,
leading people to make distinctions naturally,
without knowing why,
until it seemed as unchangeable as natural law.
There are many such cases.
Scholars born in later times
may follow the majority,
as long as it does not harm principle.
However, works like Yú Yù's *Record of Jealousy* and *Records of the Elders of Xiāngyáng*
narrate people—why are they not called "records"?
Chapters like "Turtle and Milfoil" and "Western Regions" in biographies
narrate events—why are they not called "biographies"?
Generally, works that became canons or classics
were created by those with virtue and position,
who established norms for human relations.
The present Six Classics are such works.
Confucius had virtue but no position,
so he transmitted rather than created.
Thus, the *Analects* and the *Classic of Filial Piety*
are commentaries, not classics.
Even the "Appended Phrases" of the *Book of Changes* is only called the "Great Commentary."
Later, they were all classified as classics,
as Confucian scholars revered Confucius's writings,
distinguishing them from later commentaries and biographies.
Confucian scholars from the late Zhou
to early Han
all knew that in writing,
one should not presume to establish canons,
lest one fall into reckless creation.
They also believed that establishing theories
should be based on sacred classics as authority.
Thus, they recorded what they saw and heard
in books as commentaries and biographies.
Examples include the various records of the two *Rites*, and the commentaries on the *Book of Songs*, *Book of Documents*, *Book of Changes*, and *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
These derived meaning from the classics,
but each was an independent work,
unlike later annotations and commentaries.
Later, specialized studies declined,
and collected works flourished.
Writings about people and events
appeared as scattered pieces,
also adopting the names "biography" or "record,"
aligning with the ancient specialized meaning of these terms.
Since the Jiājìng era of the Ming dynasty,
literary discussions split into factions.
Some who enjoyed lofty arguments
claimed that writing biographies was the duty of historians,
and unless one was an official historian,
how could one write biographies for others?
Those without sound judgment but eager to show understanding
echoed this view,
claiming it was unheard of in antiquity.
Yet many later literary forms
did not exist in ancient times,
but people followed one another in creating them.
The proliferation of collected works
is largely such a case.
As for biographies, they were not originally created by historians.
Before Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,

such writings already existed. When Mencius answered questions about King Tāng and King Wǔ, he said, "In the commentaries, there are records." At that time, there were no biographical histories—were these then the writings of official historians?
Now, if one insists that without holding the position of historian,
one should not write biographies,
then what distinguishes a biography from a record?
If one is not a master of the classics,
should one then write records?
Records are not frowned upon,
yet biographies are strictly forbidden—
this elevates history above the classics.
The purpose of literature
and the form of writing
are called principles and meanings.
Many contemporary writers
are ignorant and fail to examine this.
Only in such unquestionable matters
do they impose unreasonable restrictions.
It is like village witches
recklessly speaking of taboos,
making it difficult for ignorant people to act.
People of the late Ming
thought without studying,
and their absurd theories
are truly despicable.
Today's literary critics
study without thinking,
repeating those old theories
to boast of their insight,
thus being fooled by antiquity.
Arguments about official duties
are especially unreasonable.
If common biographies
can be written by anyone,
then there is no question of being a master of the classics or an official historian.
If only formal historical biographies
qualify as biographies,
then even if one holds the position of historian,
unless specifically compiling a history,
how could one write private biographies?
If writing biographies upon request
is no different
from what ordinary people do,
and only others not holding the position
are barred from doing so,
while one in the position
may do it freely—
this is like official documents requiring seals;
it reduces historians to clerks,
and turns writing biographies on request
into a tool for wielding power through official status.
This argument is especially untenable.
Those who spread hearsay
claim these words come from Mr. Zhū of Dàxīng.
They do not know this was a distorted argument of the late Ming,
used by factions to attack Wáng and Lǐ.
Mr. Zhū once said:
"One should not write biographies
for living persons."
This is indeed correct in principle.
But observing the ancients,
this was not always the case.
The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* mentions Páng Yù's mother, Zhào É,
who killed to avenge her father.
A note quotes Huángfǔ's *Biographies of Exemplary Women*:
"The late Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Liáng Kuān of Āndìng, wrote her biography."
Thus, for living persons,
the ancients did write biographies.
Lǐ Áo wrote *Biography of the Valiant Woman Yáng*,
while Yáng was still alive.
I fear there were many such cases among the ancients.
To cover a whole life in a biography
is the style of *Records of the Grand Historian* and *Book of Han* biographies.
To write a biography focusing on a single event
is the style of *Zuǒ's Commentary* on the classics.
Mr. Zhū's statement
specifically refers to the formal biographical style.
Shào Niànlǔ once debated with my late father Shǐ Zhān about the composition of private biographies by ancient people, saying:
"Have you not heard of Dèng Yǔ's biography?
Does the Fàn family not have its own basis?"
According to this, it is not only the Fàn family;
Chén Shòu's Records of the Three Kingdoms,
with annotations by Péi Sōngzhī, cites private biographies from various families of the Eastern Han, Wei, and Jin dynasties as evidence,
amounting to dozens of families.
Even those recorded in the Sui and Tang bibliographies, such as the Classic of Books and the Treatise on Arts and Literature,
like the Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò and the Biography of Master Lù,
are too numerous to list individually.
The matter itself requires no debate.
Those who cling to shallow knowledge,
having only seen the Wen Xuan by Zhāo Míng and the works of the Eight Masters of the Tang and Song dynasties, which rarely include this genre,
hastily conclude that all books in the world
cannot be cross-referenced.
In the past, when I was commissioned to compile the Húběi General Gazetteer,
relying on the deep understanding of the governor,
I employed distinctive insights and original approaches,
establishing the study of three schools.
For the section on notable figures,
I fully adopted the format of official historical biographies,
compiling them into chapters.
For figures before the Sui and Tang dynasties,
whose historical biographies are already clear and detailed,
leaving no room for additions or revisions,
I simply listed their names
in the Table of Notable Figures, as detailed in the preface and examples of this chapter.
Their original biographies from various histories
were all included in the Literary Selections,
to serve as references. This is what is meant by the study of three schools, with the Literary Selections modeled after the Wen Xuan.
In terms of the principles and examples of compilation,
it was precise and appropriate.
At the time, there was a petty person,
struggling in his official career due to incompetence,
who asked me to recommend him to the editorial bureau.
He contributed nothing but shamelessly accepted the stipend.
When the governor was demoted,
this petty person, driven by greed, slandered me,
stirring up a swarm of accusations.
The authorities were misled by this,
and ordered him to oversee corrections.
I had trusted him because I had recommended him,
but never expected him to betray my kindness and turn against me,
abandoning the principles he had once upheld
and resorting to deceit to mislead his superiors. There is a separate chapter discussing this example.
He claimed that the Literary Selections followed the examples of the Wen Xuan and the Wényuàn,
and that the Wen Xuan and the Wényuàn originally did not include biographies.
He cited biographies such as those of Hé Fān, Lǐ Chì, Máo Yǐng, and Sòng Qīng,
which were written as playful or dedicatory pieces,
and argued they should not be included in formal biographies.
The superior official praised him for his knowledge,
while secretly supporting his argument,
hiding it from me. Alas!
The Wényuàn Yīnghuá includes five volumes of biographies,
specifically from volumes 792 to 796,
among which are formal biographies,
such as those of high officials like Minister of War Liáng Gōng Lǐ Xiàn,
military governors like Lú Tǎn of Dōngchuān, both written by Lǐ Huá,
literary figures like Chén Zǐ'áng, written by Lú Cángyòng,
virtuous individuals like Lǐ Shēn, written by Shěn Yàzhī,
and chaste heroines like Yáng Fù, written by Lǐ Áo, and Dòu Nǚ, written by Dù Mù.
Those conforming to the standards of formal historical biographies
number over ten pieces. To claim that the Wényuàn lacks formal biographies
is truly heartless!
The compilation of the Wényuàn by Song dynasty scholars
may have its shortcomings in categorization,
but this is beyond the understanding of petty individuals.
As for the biographies included,
some are ornate like stele inscriptions, such as Yǔ Xìn's Biography of Qiū Nǎifū Dūn Chóng,
some are self-narratives and not formal biographies, such as the Autobiography of Lù Wénxué,
some convey allegorical messages, such as the Biography of Wáng Chéngfú,
some use names for satire, such as the Biography of Sòng Qīng,
some are dedicatory pieces resembling prefaces, such as the Biography of Qiáng Jūshì,
and some are playful and humorous, such as the Biography of Máo Yǐng.
These were also placed among the formal biographies,
unlike Lǐ Hàn's compilation of Hán Yù's works,
which categorized the Biography of Hé Fān under miscellaneous writings
and the Biography of Máo Yǐng under miscellaneous essays,
making the principles and examples clear.
How do debates arise?
They arise from the sense of right and wrong.
How does the sense of right and wrong arise?
It arises from ambiguous and doubtful situations.
Where does it reach its limit?
It reaches its limit in affirming Yáo and condemning Jié.
If the world had no need to distinguish between Yáo and Jié,
it would be like having no need to distinguish between the height of heaven and the depth of earth.
Eyesight limited to the finest details,
hearing confined to the sounds of ants in their holes—
being able to see Mount Tài does not make one sharp-eyed,
being able to hear thunder does not make one keen-eared.
Thus, Yáo and Jié are names for right and wrong,
not the means to distinguish right and wrong.
Ambiguous and doubtful situations
are not as clear-cut as the distinction between Yáo and Jié.
Extending them until they become as clear as the distinction between Yáo and Jié
begins with subtle distinctions of right and wrong
and culminates in the refinement of debate.
Therefore, Yáo and Jié represent the ultimate goal of debate,
while right and wrong originate from subtle and hidden distinctions.
Subtle and original insights
are prized and treasured by debaters.
If they cannot be extended to the level of Yáo and Jié,
there is no value in originality.
If they can be extended to the level of Yáo and Jié,
people will accept them as the established notions of Yáo and Jié.
Thus, original distinctions of right and wrong
ultimately become indistinguishable from conventional ones.
Yáo and Jié require no further extension.
The established notions of Yáo and Jié accepted throughout history
are the result of extending subtle and original insights accumulated over time.
Those who accept these extended distinctions of right and wrong
do not truly understand where right and wrong lie.
Not understanding where right and wrong lie
does not mean completely forgetting right and wrong,
but rather assuming them as given and not worth pondering.
When encountering similar situations and reflecting on them,
one may perceive what seems true,
condemning what is condemned and affirming what is affirmed,
prizing it as a subtle and original insight.
Extending and comparing it,
aligning and equating it,
reaching its extreme,
it becomes the same established notions of Yáo and Jié accepted before.
Previously, one did not know the reason,
but now one knows the reason,
so what one sees differs from what was seen before,
yet what one says is no different from what was said before.
Therefore, those who do not reflect deeply on right and wrong
prize as original insights
what is ordinary and unremarkable.
A wine seller whose wine turns sour
posts a sign saying "sour wine, reduced price" on the door,
hoping to sell it quickly.
An illiterate person
drinks the sour wine
and thinks the owner is unaware.
After leaving, he forgets something,
and the owner chases after him to return it.
The illiterate person thinks the owner is treating him kindly.
He pulls the owner aside and says,
"Your wine is sour.
Why not reduce the price and sell it quickly?"
The owner hears this and laughs silently.
Thus, those who do not reflect deeply on right and wrong
prize as original insights
what is like telling the owner his wine is sour.
Yáo and Jié require no debate.
Yet, those who embody Yáo's benevolence
must approach a state
where they can hardly speak of Yáo—
these are the true followers of Yáo.
Those who encounter Jié's tyranny
must approach a state
where they can hardly enumerate Jié's faults—
these are the true opponents of Jié.
The established notions of Yáo and Jié throughout history
still trace back to this state
of being almost unable to speak or enumerate,
which then defines the established notions of Yáo and Jié.
Therefore, those who truly understand right and wrong
cannot hastily speak of right and wrong.
Those who truly understand affirming Yáo and condemning Jié
possess knowledge that precedes right and wrong,
not merely affirming Yáo and condemning Jié.
Affirming Yáo and condemning Jié,
valuing kingship over hegemony,
revering Zhōu Gōng and Confucius while rejecting heterodox teachings,
upholding Chéng Yí and Zhū Xī while criticizing Lù Jiǔyuān and Wáng Shǒurén—
I do not say this is wrong;
but those who habitually say such things easily
I know are not truly knowledgeable.
Zhū Xī and Lù Jiǔyuān
The principles of Heaven, human nature, and destiny are thoroughly expounded in the classics and their commentaries.
Although the classics and commentaries are not the words of a single person,
their fundamental tenets have never been inconsistent,
because their principles are manifested in concrete affairs and things,
and are not entrusted to empty words.
When teachers and Confucian scholars explain principles to instruct later learners,
only by grounding them in affairs and things
can disputes among schools be avoided. Principles are like water;
affairs and things are like vessels.
Vessels vary in size and depth,
yet water fills them according to their capacity,
without excess or deficiency.
Now, if one wishes to pour water into vessels but instead sets the vessels aside
to debate the drawing, pouring, fullness, or emptiness of the water,
along with theories of measuring emptiness and assessing substance,
arguing endlessly year after year without cease,
then the vessels will surely become useless.
When Zǐxià’s disciples asked Zǐzhāng about friendship,
the division in scholarly pursuits began, and teachers and Confucian scholars esteemed knowledge while valuing conduct.
Unless one is a sage like the Master,
it is inevitable that divisions will arise.
The distinct tendencies of the lofty and bright versus the deep and reserved are like cold and heat, day and night.
Those who understand their meaning can mutually benefit from them;
those who do not understand will mutually harm each other.
Among the Song Confucians, there were Zhū Xī and Lù Jiǔyuān,
whose differences have been irreconcilable for ages,
yet these differences are also indispensable through the ages.
Later, ignorant followers engaged in mutual slander and abuse,
while others strained to mediate or reconcile ambiguously—all are unnecessary troubles.
Yet it is said that Zhūzi emphasized the inquiry into knowledge,
so followers of Lùshì attacked the Zhū school for approaching fragmentation;
it is said that Lùshì emphasized honoring the virtuous nature,
so followers of the Zhū school attacked the Lù school for descending into emptiness.
Each, focusing on what they prioritized, contended for their school’s supremacy—this, too, is a common human sentiment.
However, if one claims to inherit the teachings of the Zhū school
and attacks Lù and Wáng,
one must be broadly learned and well-informed,
thoroughly versed in the classics and devoted to antiquity,
like the diligent achievements of masters such as Xīshān, Hèshān, Dōngfā, and Bóhòu.
Only then can one substantiate one’s views
and rightly deem the empty talk of virtuous nature as emptiness.
Now, those who attack the learning of Lù and Wáng
are not erudite Confucian scholars
but uncouth and unsubstantiated pedants.
Thus, what they attack
contradicts what they practice.
When asked why they do not pursue learning,
they say it is fragmented.
When questioned why they cling to narrow ignorance,
they say it is about nature and destiny.
Thus, those who attack Lù and Wáng
have not even approximated Zhū’s teachings
but instead use false Lù and Wáng to attack true Lù and Wáng.
This can indeed be called lacking self-awareness.
Xúnzǐ said:
“Disputes arise from inferior learning.”
Zhū and Lù were fundamentally different;
how much more so the clamor of later learners?
Yet once schools are divided,
those who wish to attack Zhū
must steal the semblance of Lù and Wáng;
those who wish to attack Lù and Wáng
must steal the semblance of Zhūzi.
The semblance of Zhū must be intricate and detailed;
the semblance of Lù and Wáng must be ethereal and intuitive—this is an inevitable principle.
And throughout history, inter-school attacks
have all been from those who stubbornly cling to fragments,
bind books unread,
and loftily discuss nature and Heaven.
Thus, those who claim to be Lù and Wáng followers to attack Zhū
are certainly false Lù and Wáng;
even those who claim to be Zhū followers to attack Lù and Wáng
are also false Lù and Wáng
and cannot be called false Zhū.
Within the same school,
Lù and Wáng have false followers,
but Zhū has none,
because empty talk is easy,
while substantial learning is difficult.
Huáng, Cài, Zhēn, and Wèi
all inherited Zhūzi’s teachings and devoted themselves to substantial learning;
thus, they naturally had no time for views on school differences,
nor would they follow trends of rise and fall.
This shows that the lineage of Zhūzi
is superior to that of Lù and Wáng.
However, even false Lù and Wáng followers who impersonate Zhū’s learning
are still regarded as comrades;
I fear that true followers of Zhū
would scold and reject them.
It is said that there are both beautiful ailments and medicinal stones.
The attacks by Lù and Wáng on Zhū
are sufficient to mutually achieve but not to mutually harm.
False Lù and Wáng followers who claim to learn from and revere Zhū
are the worry of Zhū’s learning.
For nature and destiny, practical achievements, learning, and literature
combined into one—this is Zhūzi’s learning.
Seeking unity through broad learning and recognition,
and restraining rituals through extensive culture—this is the comprehensive integration of root and branch.
Interpretations of the various classics cannot be free from merits and faults;
philological exegesis and textual criticism cannot be free from omissions and errors—
how do these harm the great principles?
Moreover, those who transmit his learning,
such as Huáng, Cài, Zhēn, and Wèi,
are all sincere scholars thoroughly versed in the classics and devoted to antiquity,
personally practicing and embodying their knowledge.
Even regarding Zhūzi’s errors,
they do not blindly follow or force agreements—
this is sufficient to establish teachings.
Yet there are those who exalt nature and destiny while belittling practical achievements,
abandoning all learning and literature,
clinging only to the tenets of a few annotated passages and collected commentaries,
and thus denouncing Lù and ridiculing Wáng,
with a hatred as if they cannot share the same sky,
claiming to have received Zhū’s transmission.
Thus, they reduce Zhūzi, who integrated ancient and modern and ordered the world,
to an ignorant, arrogant, and self-righteous village pedant.
Moreover, interpretations cannot be free from merits and faults,
and textual criticism cannot be free from omissions and errors—
since the cessation of writing after the capture of the lin,
none have been exempt from this.
Now, having encountered false Lù and Wáng,
those who claim to learn from Zhū say:
“Even knowing it is poisonous,
we must still adhere rigidly to Zhūzi.”
They also say:
“Zhūzi truly combines the strengths of Confucius, Yánzǐ, Zēngzǐ, and Mencius.”
Alas! The right or wrong of such words
need not be debated.
If Zhūzi knew of this,
how sorrowful would he be?
Gàozǐ said:
“If you fail to understand words, do not seek it in the mind;
if you fail to understand the mind, do not seek it in the vital force.”
To have an unmoved mind
without seeking what is right and proper—
this is the origin of rigid adherence through the ages.
The sense of right and wrong
is inherent in all people.
If one cannot expand it with principles
and does not accept others’ goodness,
this rigid adherence resembles Gàozǐ.
Yet borrowing others’ right and wrong as one’s own
is inferior to Gàozǐ’s self-attainment.
Borrowing others’ right and wrong as one’s own
is like hiring laborers to join a fight:
they know only to strive for victory
but not why they strive.
Thus, they attack others with all their might,
but when questioned about the merits and faults of what they uphold,
they cannot fully explain.
Hence it is said:
“Even knowing it is poisonous,
one cannot but take it.”
When the later generations lose the root,
the lineage of Master Zhū,
is considered superior to those of Lù and Wáng.
But then, those who inherit Master Zhū's sacrificial rites,
are they necessarily without fault? It is said:
How could they be without fault?
Those who nowadays belittle Master Zhū's teachings,
are precisely those who arose several generations after Master Zhū.
Their opposition to Master Zhū,
in learning is a hundredfold greater than the later followers of Lù and Wáng,
in thought is deeper than the disciples of the Zhū school,
carried to its extreme,
Master Zhū would not escape the sages' fear of the younger generation.
Yet examining their inherited learning,
it actually arose several generations after Master Zhū,
and these people themselves are unaware of it.
And those in the world known as erudite and accomplished scholars,
are almost lifting their robes to follow them.
Those with discernment observe this,
it is like the people of Qí fighting over drinking from the same well.
The theories on nature and destiny,
easily fall into emptiness and nothingness.
Master Zhū sought unity through extensive learning and understanding,
embedding restraint in rites within broad culture,
his affairs were complex and detailed,
his achievements solid yet difficult;
even what Master Zhū sought,
one dare not claim it was without fault.
Yet those who followed his teachings,
in the first generation became Miǎnzhāi and Jiǔfēng,
in the second generation became Xīshān, Hèshān, Dōngfā, and Hòuzhāi,
in the third generation became Rénshān and Báiyún,
in the fourth generation became Qiánxī and Yìwū,
in the fifth generation became Níngrén and Bǎishī,
all were devoted to antiquity and well-versed in the classics,
their learning sought what was correct,
and were not those who stubbornly clung to fragments,
or empty talkers of nature and destiny.
Beyond these,
in literature they entered into rhetoric and composition,
in learning they flowed into broad elegance,
seeking where their essential purpose lay,
some may not have been self-aware.
Living in the present age,
influenced by the style of Níngrén and Bǎishī,
tracing back to ancient and modern writings,
there are those who understand the meaning in their hearts,
this is the thread of being well-versed in classics and devoted to antiquity,
continuing their legacy.
Yet, these individuals' intelligence surpasses their discernment and their spirit is agitated by ambition,
instead they find fault with Master Zhū,
thus forgetting their own origins.
Substantive learning seeking truth,
is different in kind from empty talk of nature and heaven.
Investigating antiquity is prone to error,
interpreting classics is prone to mistakes,
like celestial phenomena being difficult to exhaust from one perspective.
The study of calendars and phenomena,
later generations must surpass earlier ones,
the trend makes it so.
Because later generations are more precise and disparage Xī and Hé,
they do not realize it is the legacy of Xī and Hé's methods.
Now inheriting several generations after Master Zhū,
their insights surpass the predecessors,
not knowing it is precisely the legacy of the predecessors,
this is like later calendar makers disparaging Xī and Hé.
What they see,
can surpass the predecessors,
is due to excess intelligence.
Or perhaps it is the wisdom of later generations that should be thus,
not knowing it is precisely the legacy of the predecessors,
is due to insufficient discernment.
Their initial intent may not have been so,
their words are enough to awe the erudite and accomplished scholars of an era,
and those who follow their well-fighting,
are agitated by spirit.
Later they then dwell in it without doubt,
ambition is stirred by spirit.
Those who attack Lù and Wáng,
emerge from false Lù and Wáng,
their learning is vulgar and shallow,
not enough to fault Lù and Wáng.
Those who disparage Zhū emerge precisely from Zhū's learning,
their strength is deep and profound,
not mutually questioning source and flow,
nor cross-examining words and deeds;
in the world there are those who love learning but lack true discernment,
few do not follow the wind and succumb.
What the ancients wrote on bamboo and silk,
were all words spoken by mouth and heard by ear.
Once words are formed, those who observe them,
have hundreds and thousands of meanings,
thus inevitably there is alignment and opposition.
Today's cunning ones are not so,
with their strengths,
they have ways to move the knowledgeable of the world.
Knowing their weaknesses,
they cannot deceive,
thus they seem disdainful.
Snakes moving from the marsh,
even the small ones are revered as spirit lords.
When they encounter those who can know but need not necessarily act as knowers,
they overlook their strengths,
thinking they cannot be spoken with;
and yet adorn their weaknesses,
as if there is nothing they cannot do.
Using thunder and lightning to deify themselves,
using ghosts and spirits to mystify,
using locked boxes to secure themselves,
using banners to market themselves,
thus before them there are no ancients,
and after them no future generations.
In the world, the truly knowledgeable are few,
and those who need not necessarily act as knowers are many;
the truly knowledgeable are fixed and unchanging,
while those who need not necessarily act as knowers change endlessly;
thus with the pen they convince the knowledgeable,
and with the tongue they fool those who need not deeply understand,
the world thus follows in submission.
Overlooking weaknesses and seizing strengths,
the legacy texts remain preserved,
more than half should be followed and not discarded.
The world follows in submission,
what is there to fear!
Not knowing their oral legacy is severe,
deeply entering the hearts of those who seem to know but do not truly know,
selecting and discarding the ancients,
following biased hearts and harming the Way.
As the saying goes:
"If the father kills in revenge,
the son will surely become a robber."
These people towards Master Zhū have drunk the water and forgotten the source;
when writing in books,
there are only subtle criticisms faintly visible,
not daring to openly reprimand him.
This is why they are not detested by the truly knowledgeable.
But those who need not deeply understand,
accustomed to hearing oral discussions,
recklessly criticize and slander without fear,
thinking if such a person says such things,
then Master Zhū truly must be reprimanded.
Thus those who follow this trend,
none do not consider attacking Zhū as their capability.
Not out of hatred for Zhū,
but fearing not to resemble such people,
thus not being considered erudite.
Master Zhū's vulnerabilities given to others,
mostly come from the "Recorded Sayings".
The "Recorded Sayings" come from disciples' miscellaneous notes,
not necessarily without losing the original intent.
Yet the main ideas truly correspond with his written works,
thus what Master Zhū wrote on bamboo and silk,
are the words he spoke by mouth and heard by ear.
This unity of outward and inward,
is the learning of the ancients.
Using this principle to demand of these people,
one can know they are far inferior to Master Zhū,
why then contend over trivialities of text and language.
【Appendix】
〈Postscript to the Essay on Zhū and Lù (according to Liú's engraved "Posthumous Works" volume two)〉
Master Dài's learning,
deeply grasped the fundamental principles of the ancients,
making him worthy of being called a great Confucian of his generation.
However, his inner disposition was not pure,
and he has become quite a problem for recent scholars.
Therefore, I wrote the chapter "Zhū and Lù" to correct this.
It has now been over ten years since Master Dài passed away.
The wildly abusive critics of his time
certainly do not diminish Master Dài's stature.
But those who revere him excessively,
even to the point of calling him the only one after Mèngzǐ,
are also inevitably being deceived by Dài.
Now that he is gone, both gratitude and resentment should have subsided,
and impartial judgment ought to prevail.
Yet to this day, no one has been able to definitively assess Master Dài's character,
which shows how few truly understand virtue.
All that Master Dài studied,
his profound mastery of exegesis,
his exhaustive investigation of terminology and institutions,
and his grasp of their underlying reasons,
were intended to illuminate the Way.
People of his time valued broad erudition and textual criticism;
seeing his work on exegesis and terminology
aligned with contemporary tastes,
they considered this the pinnacle of Dài's achievement.
When Dài wrote pieces like "On Human Nature" and "Origins of Goodness,"
which discussed the principles of Heaven and humanity, material force and vital energy,
he truly elucidated points previous scholars had not addressed.
People of his time, however, called it empty discourse on principles,
saying it might as well not have been written.
This shows they did not understand Dài's learning.
Seeing the understanding of his contemporaries was like this,
Dài then made his claims more eccentric, saying:
"My work in exegesis, phonology, astronomy, and geography
is like the servants carrying a palanquin.
The Way I illuminate
is the great man riding inside it.
Those hailed as erudite scholars today
are only fit to exchange pleasantries with my palanquin bearers."
While his words were not entirely without cause,
they ultimately violated refined principles.
Yet they were still provoked by having no true understanding in the world,
and thus he could not avoid going too far.
This still did not harm righteousness.
He esteemed his own field so highly
that he believed scholars who did not delve into it
had no means to apprehend the Way.
He did not realize that exegesis and terminology
are merely one aspect.
The ancients learned from literary composition,
sought principles and meanings,
without following his method.
To say that scholars like Hán, Ōu, Chéng, and Zhāng
ultimately cannot be considered to have apprehended the Way
is also excessive.
Yet this was still expressing his own views,
wanting others to follow only him,
and did not yet involve deception in his arguments.
Regarding the principles of historiography and the standards of ancient-style prose,
he truly had no understanding.
But having long traveled the rivers and lakes,
ashamed of appearing ignorant,
he often forced himself to explain matters,
responding to others' requests.
Furthermore, not content with established practices,
he presumptuously prided himself on independent judgment.
For example, when compiling the *Gazetteer of Fénzhōu Prefecture*,
he claimed that Buddhist clergy should not be listed among humans,
and therefore placed the famous monks from the old gazetteer into the "Ancient Sites" section.
He also said the essential task in compiling a gazetteer was investigating historical changes,
and everything else could be done arbitrarily.
Here, his understanding was gradually descending into mediocrity and presumption.
However, this was merely self-deception,
not yet an intent to deceive others.
I once met Master Dài at the Ningbo Circuit Commissioner's office.
Our host was Féng Tíngchéng from Dàizhōu.
Féng, being from a distinguished family,
had long held Dài in high esteem.
At that time, all the Féng brothers and cousins
were also respectful and diligent in their studies,
revering Master Dài's words
as if they were divine edicts.
Master Dài then deliberately spoke loftily,
soaring between heaven and the abyss,
making himself unfathomable.
When someone asked about the relative merits of the two Histories by Bān and Sīmǎ,
he entirely plagiarized Zhèng Qiáo's criticisms of Bān Gù,
presenting them as his own original insight.
When another requested instruction on ancient-style prose,
he said:
"Ancient-style prose can be mastered without study.
I never understood ancient-style prose in my life.
Later, I suddenly wanted to write it but did not know the method.
So I took the writings of the ancients,
pondered them over and over,
forgetting sleep and food for several days.
One evening, I suddenly gained enlightenment.
The next day,
I took up what I wanted to write,
wielded my brush and wrote,
completing it without conscious thought.
The result far surpassed the *Zuǒ Commentary*, *Discourses of the States*, *Records of the Grand Historian*, and *History of the Hàn*."
Although the Féngs had always respected and trusted him,
hearing this, they were quite skeptical.
The idea likely originated from hearing Master Zhū Dàxīng and others discuss how literary composition should not be pursued with deliberate striving for polish,
but in reality, he had never experienced its hardships and rewards.
Finding Master Zhū's words plain and unremarkable,
he then expressed them in a bizarre and exaggerated manner,
hoping to startle his listeners.
He did not realize his wild fabrication had reached this point.
Here we see him progressing from self-deception to deceiving others;
his mind had already become hardened.
Yet he had not yet offended against orthodox teachings.
Master Dài's scholarship
actually derived from Master Zhū Xī's path of inquiry and study.
Therefore, he warned people against constructing empty theories about principle,
and his arguments probed deeply into the fundamental origins,
which is unalterable.
However, because his exegetical and terminological work
occasionally surpassed what Master Zhū had achieved,
he then vilified and disparaged Master Zhū,
even condemning him as absurd and erroneous,
denouncing him as presumptuous.
Furthermore, he said:
"Since Dài appeared,
Master Zhū has fortuitously been revered by the world
for five hundred years;
his influence should also gradually decline."
This is utterly fallacious and presumptuous!
What Master Dài committed to writing,
his points of agreement and disagreement with Master Zhū,
were expressed in terms similar to Masters Gù Yánwǔ and Yán Ruòqú.
He did not dare to be satirical or critical,
adhering firmly to the family tradition of Zhū's learning.
Where he differed from Masters Gù, Yán, and others
was in occasionally having subtle criticisms of Master Zhū,
but he still did not dare to openly and explicitly oppose him.
Yet the fallacies in his spoken words
reached such an extreme,
harming righteousness and injuring teaching.
How could this be trivial?
Some may say words spoken leave no trace;
he is already deceased,
and his writings show no major contradictions.
Why must we pick them apart and injure generosity?
They do not realize that no one has yet been inspired by studying Dài's surviving writings,
but those who heard Dài's oral pronouncements and carried them to extremes
are numerous and unceasing.
To this day, in the region between Huīzhōu and Shèzhōu,
those who style themselves as masters of the classics and antiquity
consider it essential to belittle Master Zhū;
otherwise, they cannot be considered erudite.
Slandering sages and rejecting worthies,
utterly without scruple—
this trend is greatly to be feared.
Previously, in Yángzhōu,
I presented my view to Master Shěn Jìtáng, saying:
"How does Master Dài's personal conduct and self-cultivation
compare to Master Zhū's?
As for their learning and literary compositions,
their mutual contention remains unresolved.
Can we perhaps postpone a final judgment?"
These words seem crude but are actually precise,
seem shallow but are actually profound.
Dài Dōngyuán said:
"Often, a person who captivates an audience with their eloquence in conversation,
after their death, when their writings are transmitted,
may not compare to someone who stutters and cannot fully express themselves."
Although this statement is not entirely accurate,
it is something that must exist in reason and emotion.
However, since Dài knew this principle,
why did he spend his life seeking victory in debates,
sometimes leading to angry disputes that harmed elegance?
Is it because he understood the principle but could not uphold benevolence, which became a burden?
Generally, Dài's conversations in his lifetime
can be roughly divided into three types:
When dealing with prominent officials in the central court who held great prestige,
he mostly echoed their views,
occasionally expressing his own ideas,
but always gauging what the other person could understand,
revealing only a glimpse of his sharpness,
unwilling to fully articulate his thoughts.
When dealing with his disciples,
he imparted knowledge and resolved doubts,
truly providing substantial benefits;
when dealing with those who admired his reputation
but were not yet ready to receive his teachings,
he often spoke in vague and unfounded terms,
making things increasingly mysterious,
leaving people with nothing to grasp,
causing them to doubt heaven and fate,
and ultimately unable to reach a conclusion.
Therefore, after his death,
the esteemed and accomplished gentry all said:
"Master Dài shared the same views as I did,
and I once determined the content of his certain book or certain text."
Or they said:
"Master Dài consulted me on a certain matter,
and he agreed to follow my advice."
They did not realize that Master Dài at the time merely echoed their words,
and what he truly stood for
was not in this.
Among his disciples,
the most outstanding ones
often surpassed Dài.
When Dài saw them approaching his own level,
he instead did not fully approve of them,
yet Dài truly understood these individuals well.
Later scholars who admired him,
upon hearing his vague and mysterious words,
became doubtful and hesitant to make judgments,
and to this day, they have not been able to determine what kind of person Dài was.
Those who believed in him excessively
even claimed that he surpassed the Confucian scholars of the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng dynasties,
regarding him as the only one after Mèngzǐ,
but these people do not truly understand Dài.
Literary virtue
When discussing principles and meanings,
there are cases where earlier scholars were broad and later scholars refined them further,
which cannot but provoke deep thought.
When ancient people discussed literature,
they only discussed literary style.
When Liú Xié appeared,
he built upon Lù Jī's theory and promoted the discussion of the "literary mind";
when Sū Zhé appeared,
he built upon Hán Yù's theory and promoted the discussion of "literary spirit";
it can be said that the more they elaborated, the more refined it became.
However, no one has been seen discussing literary virtue,
which scholars should deeply reflect upon.
Confucius once said, "One who has virtue will surely have words,"
and also said, "In rhetoric, establish sincerity."
Mèngzǐ discussed "understanding words"
and "nourishing the spirit,"
which are rooted in accumulating righteousness.
Hán Yù also said,
"The path of benevolence and righteousness,"
"The source of the *Book of Songs* and the *Book of Documents*,"
all of which pertain to virtue.
Now, it is said that no one has discussed literary virtue,
because what the ancients said
encompassed both the fundamental and the incidental,
including both the internal and the external,
uniting morality and literature as one;
they never discussed within literary style
that one has talent,
learning,
insight,
and also the virtue of literature.
All those who engage in ancient-style prose
must be reverent and forgiving.
When approaching writing, one must be reverent,
but this does not refer to cultivating virtue.
When discussing antiquity, one must be forgiving,
but this does not refer to tolerance.
Reverence does not mean cultivating virtue;
it means restraining one's spirit without letting it run wild,
for if it runs wild, it will inevitably fail to be moderate.
Forgiveness does not mean tolerance;
it means being able to put oneself in the place of the ancients.
Alas!
Those who understand virtue are few,
but if one knows that reverence and forgiveness are indispensable when approaching writing,
then one understands literary virtue.
In the past, Chén Shòu's *Records of the Three Kingdoms*
treated Wèi as the main record and Wú and Shǔ as biographies,
while Xí Zàochǐ, in his *Chronicles of Hàn and Jìn*,
corrected this by establishing the legitimate succession.
Simǎ Guāng's *Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government* followed Chén's view,
and Zhū Xī's *Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror* arose to correct it again.
"The sense of right and wrong
is something everyone possesses."
It should not be that Chén was mistaken first,
and Simǎ was mistaken again afterward,
while Xí and Zhū Xī's insight and judgment
were uniquely superior.
Yet those throughout history who criticized *Records of the Three Kingdoms* and *Comprehensive Mirror*
almost resorted to unrestrained cursing,
not knowing that if the ancients were resurrected from the grave,
would they willingly accept such criticism?
Chén lived during the Western Jìn dynasty,
and Simǎ lived during the Northern Sòng dynasty.
If they had rejected Cáo Wèi's abdication of the throne,
where would they have placed their rulers and fathers?
As for Xí and Zhū Xī,
they were people who had crossed south of the Yangtze River,
fearing only that the Central Plains would contend for the legitimate succession. This point has been made by earlier scholars.
If these worthies had exchanged places, they would have done the same,
and their insight might not have been inferior to that of today's pedants.
Thus, if one does not understand the era of the ancients,
one should not recklessly discuss their literary works.
Even if one knows their era,
if one does not understand the personal circumstances of the ancients,
one should not hastily discuss their writings either.
The circumstances in which one finds oneself
inevitably involve disparities in honor and disgrace, obscurity and prominence, advancement and retreat, joy and sorrow.
When one speaks with a purpose,
even a disciple like Zǐyóu did not fully understand what Confucius meant,
let alone those born thousands of years later?
The Confucian school's discussion of forgiveness
is: "Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire."
This principle is profound.
Now, as for literary scholars,
when discussing antiquity, they must first put themselves in the ancients' place,
and this is the forgiveness of literary virtue.
Hán Yù, in discussing literature, said:
"Welcome it yet resist it,
examine it with a calm mind."
He compared spirit to water,
and words to floating objects.
Liǔ Zōngyuán, in discussing literature, said:
"Do not treat it lightly or carelessly,"
"do not let laziness alter it,"
"do not let arrogance create it,"
"do not let confusion produce it."
Although these worthies discussed the mind and spirit,
they did not fully capture the essence of Confucius and Mèngzǐ's teachings
regarding the subtleties of heaven, humanity, nature, and destiny.
Yet their discussions are extensive and cannot be dismissed,
and their words vary, each fitting its purpose.
In essence, the main idea is that when approaching writing, one must uphold reverence,
which can be summarized in one phrase.
Upholding reverence leads to a calm mind,
and the spirit becomes restrained,
naturally able to change and adapt with ease, conforming to measure.
Historians possess three strengths:
talent, learning, and insight.
If ancient-style prose does not stem from history,
it is like food and drink not originating from farming.
Insight arises from the mind,
talent emerges from the spirit.
Learning
involves concentrating the mind to nourish the spirit,
refining insight to cultivate talent.
The mind is empty and difficult to rely on,
the spirit is volatile and easily dissipated.
Upholding reverence means
constantly examining and restraining the mind and spirit,
and carefully guarding against the flaw of letting them run wild without restraint.
"Cultivating brightness and resting in reverence"
is how the sages achieve both beginning and end,
and its meaning is broad.
Now, when approaching writing,
examining one's mind and spirit
is the reverence of literary virtue.
I happened to see a transcribed copy of the Records of the Grand Historian on Liáng Yǔ’s desk,
and picked it up to look at it.
It turned out to be marked with five-colored circles and dots,
each section divided into paragraphs.
I examined it over and over,
