but could not understand what it meant.
When I asked Liáng Yǔ about it,
he laughed heartily,
saying that he too had grown tired of looking at it.
He said the book was attributed to Guī Zhènchuān of the former Míng dynasty,
with five-colored markings
each representing a different principle and pattern,
so they would not be confused.
Some indicated the overall structure of an entire piece,
some highlighted the brilliance of each paragraph,
some pointed to the depth of thought and rhetorical waves,
and some captured the spirit and vigor.
They were categorized by examples
to facilitate careful study and emulation,
and were hailed as a secret transmission of ancient prose.
Elder scholars of ancient prose
treasured and passed them down through instruction,
never lightly showing them to others.
He also said:
"This is like the Fifth Patriarch passing on the lamp,
or Língsù receiving the register.
Those who emerge from this tradition
are considered orthodox;
those who do not,
no matter how extraordinary their works,
are ridiculed by Buddhists as wild fox Zen."
"I studied this in my youth,
but when I traveled to the capital,
my knowledge and experience broadened,
and I realized that the way of writing
did not originally stem from this.
However, I thought there might be one or two valuable insights in it,
so I did not hastily discard it—
not because I treasured it."
I said:
"The way of writing,
from before the Yuán dynasty onward,
had declined and grown sickly,
but it had not yet perished.
In the early Míng, people inherited what remained from the Sòng and Yuán,
roughly preserving the rules.
But by the Jiājìng and Lóngqìng eras,
it became obscure, stifled, and blocked,
and writing nearly died out.
Guī Zhènchuān lived during this time.
Though his strength could not rival that of Wáng and Lǐ and their followers,
he knew in his heart they were wrong,
so he denounced Fèngzhōu as mediocre and presumptuous.
He said they created a false style imitating Qín and Hàn,
even changing official titles and place names
to ancient terms,
making it impossible to understand what they were saying.
Thus, he directly accused them of being illogical in their writing—
and this was no baseless claim.
However, Guī's writing,
though clear in spirit and form,
when examined for its substance,
also cannot be forced to yield profound insights.
Thus, I once wrote a note at the end of his work,
saying that what allowed the gentleman to stand firm against the current
was merely his clear and fluent writing,
which did not drown in vulgar trends.
But as for what the ancients called 'breadth within and expansiveness without,'
using words to give voice to what the mind has attained,
he had not yet heard of it.
Nevertheless, he must still be called a hero of his time.
Moreover, in the realm of examination essays, Guī
is like Zǐcháng of the Hàn
or Tuìzhī of the Táng—
a great master whose lineage will never be discontinued.
Thus, modern writers of examination essays who discuss ancient prose
mostly revere Guī.
The selection of the Eight Masters of Táng and Sòng
has come to be almost as revered as the Five Classics and Four Books.
Only the collections of Guī and Táng
take the Records of the Grand Historian as their model in argumentative writing.
But the way they drew strength from the Records
is rather strangely unlike it.
The style of the Records is inherently robust and unadorned,
but Sīmǎ Qiān’s talent was vast,
so he wielded it with lightness and agility.
What Guī and Táng call 'spacious, resonant, halting, and forceful'
lacks substance within,
and thus cannot avoid being superficial and slick,
opening the door for later generations to adopt shallow and crude habits of imitation.
Thus, I suspect that Guī, Táng, and others
drew from the Records
only its surface aspects,
and never glimpsed the profound depths of the ancients.
Now, looking at the five-color annotated editions passed down by these gentlemen,
I finally understand why Guī could not reach the level of the ancients—
it is precisely because of this.
The essence of establishing words
lies in having substance.
When the ancients wrote their works,
they all based them on what they had perceived within,
not because they sought flashy brilliance,
like weavers and embroiderers boasting about their colors.
A wealthy young nobleman,
even in drunken dreams,
cannot speak the words of a destitute beggar;
a person in pain, suffering, or hardship,
even placed in a setting of music and lavish banquets,
cannot swap their groans for laughter.
This is why the voice reflects the heart,
and why writing cannot be exchanged between one and another—
each forms its own school.
Now, to abandon what one seeks oneself
and imitate the outward form of the ancients
is like the wife of Qǐ Liáng,
who wept skillfully for her husband,
and the elderly woman next door
also learning to wail in sorrow;
or like Qū Yuán drowning himself in the Mìluó River,
and the ministers of a court united in virtue
also ought to compose Chǔ-style laments.
Is this not absurd?
As for literary expression,
the ancients certainly did not neglect the pursuit of refinement.
Mencius said:
'Hold fast to your will,
and do not abuse your vital energy.'
Scholarship is the master of establishing words,
just as the will is;
writing is the tool for illuminating the Way,
just as vital energy is.
Seeking self-attainment in scholarship
is indeed the root of writing;
seeking flawlessness in writing
is also the expression of scholarship.
Thus, Sòng Confucians honored morality and belittled literary style.
Master Yīchuān said that refined writing harms the Way,
and Master Míngdào said that memorization is trifling with things and losing one’s will.
Though these remarks were directed at those who forgot the root and chased the branches,
inferring the intent of these two masters,
holding fast to one’s will
does not necessarily mean not abusing one’s vital energy.
And if staying far from vulgarity and presumption in one’s speech and energy,
and seeking clarity in expression,
were things Confucius and Zēngzǐ had never heard of in the Way.
But the excellence of writing
truly lies in the reader’s own attainment.
Just as with delicious food
or light, warm clothing,
the one who eats and wears them
knows the experience personally,
yet finds it hard to convey to others.
If you wish to tell someone about the way of food and clothing,
you should point to the roasted meat and let them taste it themselves—
then they can know its deliciousness;
point to the fox and raccoon furs and let them wear them themselves—
then they can know their lightness and warmth.
This is the way.
If you must spit out what you have tasted to feed others and impart sweetness,
or hug others and place them in your embrace to impart warmth,
there is no such principle.
Hán Tuìzhī said:
"Those who record events must grasp their essentials;
those who compile words must probe their profundities."
As for the books he referred to that probe profundities and grasp essentials,
not only have later generations been unable to hear of them,
but even among his contemporaries like Zhāng Jí and Huángfǔ Shí,
none have been heard to have seen them.
What indeed were they?
They were likely nothing more than gathering passages and selecting phrases,
to serve as aids in composing writings.
Such notes and records
must certainly have existed among the ancients.
For example, Zuǒ Sī spent ten years composing his "Rhapsody on the Three Capitals,"
with paper and brush placed everywhere in his courtyard, gates, and fences,
so that whenever an idea came,
he could immediately write it down.
Now, looking at his rhapsody,
it contains no extraordinary thoughts or marvelous ideas
that startle the heart and stir the soul;
it must have been achieved through ten years of bitter thought and strenuous searching.
What he called "writing it down immediately"
must also have involved noting books and recording meanings,
first gathering the essence of the ancients,
and only then having enough material to employ.
However, gaining insights from reading books
depends on the individual,
and each person's experience is unrelated to others.
Therefore, when the ancients discussed literature,
they often spoke of the effort of reading to cultivate one's vital force,
the essentials of being well-versed in antiquity and mastering the classics,
the benefits of drawing close to teachers and friends,
and the methods of gathering material and seeking assistance—
these constitute the Way.
As for discussing the skill or clumsiness of literary expression,
they would give one example to infer the rest,
comparing according to circumstances and categorizing by analogy,
such as in Lù Jī's "Rhapsody on Literature,"
Liú Xié's "The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons,"
and Zhōng Róng's "Gradations of Poets."
Sometimes they would occasionally cite precise characters or excellent lines,
sometimes evaluate the merits and flaws of entire works,
enabling readers to grasp the meaning within the text
and comprehend what lies beyond the words.
In this, they have already grasped more than half of what pertains to literary expression and thought.
As for being compelled to excerpt and record them in books,
marking and categorizing them,
this is merely what the mind happens to grasp at a given moment,
and not necessarily what emerges from the inherent nature of the books themselves.
For example, one who longs for someone sees the moon and thinks of them—
does the moon necessarily govern distant longing?
A long-time traveler hears the rain and feels sorrow—
does the rain necessarily contain melancholy circumstances?
Yet the longing under the moon,
the feelings in the rain—
are they not the most sublime writing of heaven and earth?
But if one wishes to take these feelings and this longing,
treasure them as secrets,
or perhaps wish to bestow favor on later learners,
saying that whenever facing the bright moon or listening to the continuous rain,
one must use this sorrow and feeling
to truly appreciate it,
then surely when a good friend is suddenly met,
or newlyweds in their joyful bliss,
they would certainly not believe it.
Therefore, in the matter of learning literature,
what can be imparted are the rules and forms;
what cannot be imparted is the mind's conception and creation.
As for books that compile categories and compare excerpts,
volumes that mark and comment,
these are fundamentally the lesser tasks of writing,
not to be displayed and told to others,
but only to be used for one's own records.
A father cannot give them to his son,
a teacher cannot transmit them to his disciple.
For it is feared that with the ancients' boundless books,
one would be constrained by the limited mind and hand of a single era.
Regulated verse should understand level and oblique tones;
ancient-style poetry should understand rhythm.
But level and oblique tones are obvious and easy to know,
while rhythm is subtle and difficult to discern;
if one becomes well-versed in ancient-style poetry,
one will naturally attain it.
To take ancient-style poetry and fix people's rhythm,
then the variations of rhythm
are certainly not something a single, fixed poem can limit.
Zhào Zhòngfú took ancient poems and made a "Manual of Tones and Rhythms";
learned men ridiculed him,
and I cannot explain it for Mr. Zhào.
However, for those who do not understand rhythm,
it is not that it cannot inspire their enlightenment;
only it should not be presented as a model for all under heaven.
Contemporary prose should understand rules and measures;
ancient-style prose should also understand that there are rules and measures.
The rules and measures of contemporary prose are obvious and easy to discuss,
while the rules and measures of ancient-style prose are subtle and difficult to explain;
if one becomes well-versed in ancient-style prose,
one will naturally attain them.
To take ancient-style prose and show people its rules and measures,
then the transformations of literary composition
are not something a single, fixed text can limit.
Guī Zhènchuān took writings from the "Records of the Grand Historian"
and marked them with five colors,
to demonstrate their principles and methods;
today's learned men,
if they heard of this matter, would surely secretly laugh at it,
and I cannot explain it for Mr. Guī.
However, for those who do not understand rules and measures,
it is not that it cannot aid their comprehension;
only it is insufficient to rely on as a secret transmission.
To rely on it as a secret transmission
is like the man of Yǐng treasuring a Yān stone.
Now, books are difficult to exhaust from a single perspective;
the benevolent see benevolence,
the wise see wisdom.
The rhythm of poetry,
the rules and measures of prose—
the gentleman considers them something one can achieve without learning,
like the restraint and release in crying and laughing,
the suppression and elevation in singing and weeping;
if one must display and show them to others,
people instead become constrained and cannot attain the utmost sincerity of singing, weeping, crying, and laughing.
Yet if one's own insights
do not involve forced interpretations or excessive demands,
but come from casual browsing,
and something resonates in the heart,
one writes it down to record it,
for self-reflection and recognition,
this can indeed aid in refining one's expression.
But to take one's own insights
and say that all people under heaven
should model their minds and hands after mine—
later people may follow me,
but if we raise the ancients and ask them,
they would say:
"What I intended
was not this!"
Would that not be an injustice?
Collected Works
The rise of anthologies,
did it not occur at the juncture of the rise and fall of literary works?
In ancient times, the court had its canons and plans,
officials preserved laws and decrees,
folk songs were collected from the villages,
memorials and petitions were presented in the ancestral temples and courts,
but there was no one who wrote books for themselves,

nor households that preserved a single doctrine. When Liú Xiàng collated books, he compiled records of the various masters and hundred schools, all stating that they originated from the duties of certain ancient officials or clans. This is evidence that in antiquity there was no private authorship. For further details, see the Outer Chapters.
Since the division of governance and learning into separate paths,
the hundred schools arose like the wind,
and the learning of the Zhōu and Qín masters
became overwhelmingly diverse;
discerning individuals already lamented the fragmentation of the Way and its arts.
However, the specialized teachings transmitted within families
were not intended to gain literary fame;
if they were sufficient to manifest their craft

and could be transmitted to their disciples (The various masters all had disciples for transmission. Books like Guǎnzi and Yànzǐ contain many records of events after their deaths; Zhuāngzǐ also records words spoken near death; the end of Hán Fēi's "Preserving Hán" includes Lǐ Sī's refutation—none were written by the original authors. It was likely their followers who supplemented them based on what they heard and saw.),
then their doctrines stopped there,
and there were no writings of inconsistency or杂乱庞杂.
During the two Hàn dynasties, literary works gradually flourished,
marking the beginning of the decline of original authorship.
However, Jiǎ Yí's memorials and discussions
were compiled into the Xīn Shū;
that is, the Jiǎzǐ Shū. The Táng dynasty's Jíxián Shūmù first gave it the name Xīn Shū. Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's rhapsodies and poems
only recorded their titles:

In the "Yìwén Zhì," Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's twenty-nine fu are listed after Qū Yuán's twenty-five fu, and the summary record states, "The Poetry and Fu section contains one hundred and one schools, totaling one thousand three hundred and eighteen pieces." Each formed a distinct school of thought, similar to Lí Sāo. All established their own schools of thought,
not far removed from the various masters,
and initially there was no compilation of various genres
gathered together as literary anthologies.
From the Eastern Hàn onward,
up to the Jiàn'ān and Huángchū periods,
literary works became abundant.
However, the "Wényuàn Zhuàn" in the histories of Fàn and Chén began with the Hòu Hàn Shū.
The biographies of literary scholars recorded therein,
noting their literary works,
all state how many poems, fu, stele inscriptions, admonitions, eulogies, and elegies they wrote,
but do not mention how many volumes of anthologies they had.
Thus, the substance of anthologies already existed,
but the name "anthology" had not yet been established (The Suí Zhì states: "The name 'biéjí' was created in the Eastern Hàn." This likely lacks thorough investigation.).
Since Zhì Yú created the Wénzhāng Liúbié,
scholars found it convenient,
and thus began to separately gather the works of ancient people,
labeling them as biéjí (individual anthologies);
then the name "anthology"

actually originated in the Jìn dynasty. Chén Shòu compiled the Zhūgě Liàng Jí in twenty-four chapters, originally called Zhūgě Liàng Gùshì. Its chapter titles are recorded in the Sānguó Zhì, still in the style of masters' works. Yet the Chén Shòu biography in the Jìn Shū states he compiled the Zhūgě Jí. Chén Shòu, in the catalog title, also called it the Zhūgěshì Jí, likely a common error.
Thereafter, works of social obligation and forced composition,
examination-oriented and frivolous writings,
also overflowed and spread chaotically,
vying to attach themselves to the name of biéjí.
These truly could not be included in Liú Xiàng's catalog,
nor attached to Bān Gù's "Treatise."
And the writings produced
were also pretentious and artificially adorned,
contradictory and inconsistent,
no longer the exclusive language of specialized masters without divergence.
The division of governance and learning led to the emergence of the various masters,
marking the intersection of public and private.
The divergence of words and actions gave rise to anthologies,
distinguishing sincerity from falsity.
As trends changed repeatedly, they declined repeatedly;
as writings became more numerous, they grew more chaotic.
If there were scholars who loved learning and deep thought,
using writings to seek the substance of established doctrines,
using dispersion to seek the convergence of unity,
then after three transformations, ancient learning could be revived.
Alas, those following the current forget the source,
and those obsessed with names lose the substance.
Even two fǒu jars can confuse a zhōng measure,
let alone an endless, torrential flow.
In the past,
the classification by the father and son Liú Xiàng and Liú Xīn,
was it not the legacy of the Zhōu Guān?
Gathering ancient and modern writings and distinguishing their schools,
uniting all-under-heaven's learning and preserving it under official control—
if not for a fixed system transmitted through generations,
then by the end of the Western Hàn,

there would have been no way to trace directly back to the sources of Zhōu and Qín (The "Yìwén Zhì" includes records without books, also classifying them accordingly. Thus, there must have been transmission before Liú Xiàng. Moreover, the division of the Qī Lüè into schools lacks definitive evidence; it is likely the Liú family lost the transmission.).
After Bān Gù's "Treatise,"
those who compiled catalogs one after another
sometimes combined, sometimes separated,
not knowing the essential principles.
Since their books were not fully transmitted,
the merits and faults of their classification,
the quality of their summaries and records,
also cannot be fully examined.
Xún Xù's Zhōng Jīng had four divisions,
placing poetry, fu, illustrations, and eulogies,
along with the books from the Jízhǒng tomb, into the Dīng division.
Wáng Jiǎn's Qī Zhì,
placed poetry and fu in the "Wénhàn Zhì,"
positioned between the masters and military books.
Thus, the gradual opening of the anthology division
had not yet firmly established a dedicated category.
When Ruǎn Xiàoxù compiled the Qī Lù,
only techniques, Buddhism, and Daoism were divided into three categories,
while the four records of classics, histories, masters and military, and literary collections
already fully foreshadowed the Táng dynasty's classics, histories, masters, and collections;
thus, the cataloging of the anthology division
actually began in Xiāo Liáng,
and the origins and flow of ancient learning
underwent a transformation here,
also due to the circumstances of the time.
Alas!
As original authorship declined, anthologies arose;
as classical precedents were exhausted, encyclopedias appeared.
Scholars grew fond of the ease of consulting them,
unaware of the decline of substantive learning;
accustomed to easily achieved names,
unaware of the dispersal of the great Way.
The rivers flow daily downward;
heroic individuals,
after the raging waves have already overturned,
wishing to dam all streams to flow eastward—
how could they avoid being ridiculed by the whole world,
pointed at and implicated in discussions,
what hope is there?
Moreover, names
are the guests of substance.
Categories
arise from precedents.
In ancient times, there was specialized learning,
and then there were specialized books;
with specialized books,
then there was specialized transmission and reception (Zhèng Qiáo once said something similar.).
Seeking books by category,
tracing the source from the flow,
if the method of classification is clear,
even the Three Mounds and Five Canons
could be obtained while sitting.
Since the art of collation was lost,
and the learning of anthologies and encyclopedias (as books),
within a single compilation,
first became unbearably杂乱庞杂;
how could later scholars
thereby glimpse the grand essence of the ancients?
The Chǔ Cí
is the book of a single school, that of Qū Yuán.
Since the Qī Lù first included it in the anthology division,
the Suí Zhì specially listed a Chǔ Cí category,
thus grouping general anthologies, individual anthologies, and it into three categories,
which became the established method for catalogers.
Extending this principle,
then Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's fu,
the five-character poems of Sū Wǔ and Lǐ Líng,
Méi Chéng's "Seven Stimuli,"
should also each have a separate category label,
becoming the fu category, five-character poem category, and "Seven Stimuli" category.
How can the designations "general anthology" and "individual anthology"
adequately match them?
The source of this泛滥
truly began with ci and fu not being listed as specialized schools,
and literary figures having individual anthologies.
The Wénxīn Diāolóng,
is Liú Xié's specialized book.
Since the Jíxián Shūmù included it as a general anthology (The Suí Zhì already did so.),
the Táng Zhì then grouped it with Shǐ Tōng, Wénzhāng Guījiàn, and Shǐ Hàn Yìyì into one category;

thus becoming the general rule for catalogs like Zhèng's Lüè and Mǎ's Kǎo (The Zhèng Zhì places Shǐ Tōng in the general history category and Diāolóng in the anthology category. Even Yú Zhòng's collation, with the most refined principles, contains such errors, showing how long vulgar learning has been transmitted.).
Extending this principle,
then Wèi Wén's Diǎn Lùn,
Gé Hóng's Shǐ Chāo,
Zhāng Zhì's Wénshì Zhuàn (Diǎn Lùn's "Discourse on Literature" is like Diāolóng; Shǐ Chāo is like Shǐ Hàn Yìyì; Wénshì Zhuàn is like Wénzhāng Guījiàn—all are similar in category.),
should also be mixed together and entered as general anthologies.
How then can the categories of history and masters be separated?

Diǎn Lùn belongs to the masters category. Shǐ Chāo and Wénshì Zhuàn belong to the history category. The confusion in classification truly arises from the difficulty of defining anthologies as specialized,
and the similar can confuse with the genuine.
Since cataloging lacks origins and flows,
authors' titles
thus have no fixed method.
Láng Wèizhī's Zhūzhōu Tújīng Jí
is a geography work in the history division but has an anthology name (collected in the Suí Zhì).
Wáng Fāngqìng's Bǎozhāng Jí
is a philology work in the classics division but has an anthology name (collected in the Táng Zhì).
Xuán Jué's Yǒngjiā Jí
is a Buddhist work in the masters division but has an anthology name (collected in the Táng Zhì).
The末流 of the hundred schools and miscellaneous arts,
with shallow understanding and mediocre insight,
and writings that are vulgar and crude,
sometimes copying from ancients,
sometimes explicating minor techniques,
are fundamentally not of the anthology category,
yet numerous claim the name "collection"—
how can they all be recounted?
Even works like Zēng's Lóngpíng Jí follow vulgar custom and should be changed to biographies or records to be appropriate. Thus, once the three types of anthologies arose,
the nine streams inevitably mixed,
and the confusion of scholarship—
is it not merely like the ghost of Líqiū,
or losing sheep at a fork in the road?
Chapters and volumes.
The Book of Changes says:
"Restraining the jaws,
words are orderly."
The Book of Songs says:
"Uttered words have pattern."
For the ancients regarding speech,
they sought only that it have pattern and order.
When recorded in writing,
there were bamboo slips.
Marking their beginning and end,
this is called chapters and sections.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Regarding the 'Wǔ Chéng,'
I take only two or three bundles."
This is evidence that connecting bundles forms a chapter.
The "Great Treatise" of the Book of Changes says:
"The bundles of the two parts,
number ten thousand one thousand five hundred twenty."
This is evidence that the whole from start to finish is a chapter.
When Zuǒshì quotes the Book of Songs,
he cites the chapter name,
and then quotes in sequence,
saying such-and-such section states thus.
This is evidence that the chapter is the complete whole,
and the section is a divided stanza.
The essential point is that writing fulfills speech,
forming sections with order,
taking what can travel far and reach.
Chapters, sections, bamboo slips,
are not what is considered.
In later ages, texts became numerous,
hence there arose the study of collation.
And when Liú Xiàng and Liú Xīn compiled records,
they mostly counted by chapters and scrolls.
Generally, chapters derived from bamboo slips,
scrolls derived from silk,
naming based on the material,
with no other meaning.
And silk as writing material,
came after bamboo slips,
hence Zhōu and Qín spoke of chapters,
entering Hàn, scrolls began to appear.
But at that time bamboo and silk were used concurrently,
and naming chapters necessarily had beginning and end;
scrolls had no designation of beginning and end,
often following chapters to form scrolls;
hence the Hàn Shū records so many chapters,
which became so many scrolls in later times,
this is the general situation.
However, the Shījīng has three hundred chapters,
but only twenty-eight scrolls;
the Shàngshū and Lǐjīng,
also all have fewer scrolls than chapters,
then we further know that at that time texts on silk,
were also called chapters.
The term chapter,
specifically denotes the beginning and end of textual meaning,
while scroll relates to the length of joined silk,
this has no other meaning,
probably taking the name chapter for books,
is older than scroll.
Thus different chapters can be in the same scroll,
but dividing scrolls is not heard to mark beginning and end.
As for Bān Gù's "Wǔ Xíng" zhì
and "Yuán Hòu" zhuàn,
chapters long, scrolls short,
then divided into sub-scrolls.
This shows chapters cannot be changed,
but scrolls can be divided or combined.
From then on,
until Suí and Táng,
books counted by scrolls were many,
counted by chapters few.
Various authors,
what they called one scroll,
often was what the ancients called one chapter;
thus affairs change with time,
people also act without self-awareness.
Only Sīmǎ Biāo's Xù Hòu Hàn Zhì,
an eight-chapter work,
divided into thirty scrolls,
splitting chapters to conform to scrolls,
greatly changed Bān Gù's method of sub-scrolls,
initiating Táng and Sòng historical biographies,
losing the ancients' meaning.
As for those with minor name differences but no real difference,
Dàoist texts call juàn,
which is another name for scroll,
Yuán people's Shuō Fú used it.
Kuǎi Tōng's Juàn Yǒng calls shǒu,
which is another name for section,
Liáng people's Wén Xuǎn used it.
This is establishing novelty and difference,
names and reality thus unharmed.
From Táng and Sòng onward,
scroll-bound books,
again changed to paper volumes;
then completing books became easy,
compared to the ancients,
not just several times over.
What the ancients called bamboo slips heavy and numerous,
cannot be combined into one chapter, dividing into upper, middle, lower etc.
Now even doubling the book,
is not difficult to bind in the same volume.
Therefore before Táng,
scroll division was very short.
Liùcháo and Táng literary collections,
what were ten scrolls,
nowadays are only three or four volumes.
From Sòng onward,
scroll division became long.
Because ancients' scrolls followed scroll rods,
naturally could not be too long;
later people used paper volumes for books,
only preserving the name scroll,
then following their intentions,
not difficult to have huge volumes.
Using paper volumes but preserving silk's scroll name,
is like Hàn people using silk but preserving bamboo's chapter name,
principle is the same.
But since chapters are used to count textual beginning and end,
this is eternally unchangeable,
even if said not deriving meaning from bamboo slips, it is acceptable.
Scrolls are limited by rod length,
and have no fixed rule of beginning and end.
Now since we don't use silk but paper volumes,
naturally should consider paper volume capacity and set boundaries.
Those loving antiquity and marking scroll names,
or following substance and marking volume names,
are both acceptable;
should not again take scroll numbers and volume copies,
deliberately making discrepancies,
making people follow scrolls to seek chapters,
and again making people hold volumes to seek scrolls,
only causing confusion.
Now textual complexity, brevity, beginning and end,
cannot be rigidly fixed;
and bamboo tablets' weight,
now also not used;
ancients' solitary short works could also be independent books, circulating alone.
Chapters naturally cannot stand isolated,
must rely on scrolls for connection,
this is the tendency.
Scrolls are not fixed and unchangeable,
wanting to encompass chapters to combine them,
yet wanting to break volumes to divide them,
making people search additionally beyond combination and division,
and unrelated to principles and examples,
isn't this confusing and troublesome?
Therefore writing books should only discuss chapters,
not count scrolls.
If must count scrolls,
let them consider volume length,
and allocate accordingly.
Not considering the volumes contained,
but meticulously dividing scrolls,
for beautiful labeling and cataloging appearance,
all are those clinging to antiquity and forgetting reality.
Chóng Wén and Sòng catalogues,
sometimes record volumes without detailing scrolls.
Míng's Wén Yuān Gé catalog,
then only counts volumes without scrolls.
Though this is a deficiency in cataloging,
if scrolls and volumes had no discrepancies,
how would this flaw arise?
Heaven
Heaven is vast and nameless.
Three Enclosures, Seven Luminaries, Twenty-eight Mansions, Twelve Stations, Three hundred sixty-five degrees, Yellow Path, Red Path—
calendricists forcibly name them to record numbers.
From ancient to modern times,
combined as cultural substance increase and decrease,
divided as learning, enterprise, achievement,
literature, nature, life.
At the beginning,
there was only seeing what should be,
and doing what must be done,
vast without fixed names.
Dividing into categories,
naming culture, naming substance,
naming learning, enterprise, achievement,
literature, nature, life,
and cannot be combined—
all because of correcting biases and remedying flaws,
having something to raise and instruct people,
forced to establish names,
determining direction.
Later people not examining the reason but following the names,
thinking this can self-designate their school,
and numerous become partisan.
Hàn learning and Sòng learning mocking each other,
philology and literary composition disparaging each other,
moral nature and knowledge disputing—
The purpose of scholarship is to govern the world.
It is like those who study calendrical systems:
they exhaust human effort in order to seek harmony with the movements of Heaven,
and from the outset do not insist on their own preconceptions.
What earlier people omitted, later people elaborate;
what earlier people lacked, later people create;
what earlier people practiced, later people change.
For example, the culminating stars in the Monthly Ordinances cannot be the same as those in the Canon of Yáo;
the calendrical methods of the Tàichū era cannot be the same as those in the Monthly Ordinances.
What is essential is that they are appropriate and suitable.
The Duke of Zhōu, succeeding King Wén and King Wǔ,
and serving as Chief Minister,
thus established rituals and music,
creating the established institutions for his generation.
Confucius was born in an age of decline,
possessing virtue but no position,
thus he transmitted and did not create,
in order to illuminate the great Way of the former kings.
Mèngzǐ lived in a time when common scholars held reckless debates,
thus he vigorously opposed Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí,
in order to honor the transmission of Confucius.
Hán Yù lived when Buddhism and Daoism were flourishing,
thus he elucidated the Way of the Sages,
in order to rectify the learning of the world.
The Chéng brothers and Zhū Xī lived at a time when later learning had forgotten its roots,
thus they clarified nature and principle,
in order to挽救 the hearts and minds of the common customs.
Their affairs and achievements
were not inherited from one another,
yet all spoke to governing the world.
Therefore, scholarship
is what opens up trends.
When trends have not yet opened,
scholarship has the means to open them.
When trends have already become corrupt,
scholarship has the means to挽救 them.
The hearts and minds and customs of people
cannot endure for long without becoming corrupt,
just as the methods of Xīhé and the Bǎozhāng officials
cannot endure for long without error.
Applying remedies according to their corruption
is like calendrical experts discussing changes according to their errors.
The errors in calendrical methods
are either excessive or deficient.
The corruption in trends
is either overly heavy or overly light.
The bias of heaviness, lightness, excess, or deficiency,
unless one reverses it according to its extreme,
cannot attain the appropriateness of centrality and correctness.
Scholars fond of fame
are precisely those who chase trends in their scholarship,
which is using fire to save fire,
and water to save water.
Heaven's decree overcomes man,
but man's determination can also overcome Heaven.
The twenty-eight lunar mansions,
the twelve stations,
with their encircling heavenly degrees,
exhaust the cities and capitals of the Central States during the Spring and Autumn period.
Now, the Central States are within the great earth,
merely one corner in the southeast.
Yet the star degrees encompassing Heaven,
belonging to divination and verification,
have never failed to correspond.
This perhaps cannot be reasoned and inferred,
for it is man's determination overcoming Heaven.
Moreover, like Zǐpíng's推算 of a person's year, month, day, and hour,
all use the sixty jiǎzǐ cycles,
assigning the mutual production and conquest of the Five Phases.
Now, year, month, and hour
are not recorded using jiǎzǐ cycles;
the ancients never had such words.
Yet later people, having established this method,
then also推算 good and bad fortune without fail to correspond,
is this not man's determination overcoming Heaven?
The Yì says, "Preceding Heaven, and Heaven does not oppose,"
it is precisely this.
In learning too, there is the principle of man's determination overcoming Heaven.
Principle divides into the Ultimateless and the Supreme Ultimate;
number divides into the Prior Heaven and the Posterior Heaven;
diagrams include the River Chart and the Luo Writing;
nature divides into moral principle and physical endowment.
The sage's meaning,
later worthies揣測 it with their own meaning,
then it seems as if the sage might不妨 be thus interpreted.
Following their theories,
one can also aspire to sagehood,
one can also aspire to Heaven.
Is this not man's determination overcoming Heaven?
Revering and believing too much,
thinking one truly grasps the sage's meaning is certainly wrong;
yet disputing and refuting too much,
considering it the various Confucians' slander,
how could that be appropriate?
On Teachers
Hán Tuìzhī said:
"A teacher
is one who transmits the Way, imparts learning, and resolves doubts."
He also said:
"A teacher need not be more worthy than his disciples,
disciples need not be不如 their teacher."
"Where the Way exists,
there the teacher exists."
He also said:
"Shamans, physicians, and the various artisans
are not ashamed to learn from each other."
And thus he wondered at the people of his time,
who considered learning from each other shameful,
and were even不如 shamans, physicians, and the various artisans.
Hán氏 spoke thus for the corrupt customs of his time,
and did not reach the ultimate truth about teachers.
The Record says:
"In people's lives there are three,
served as one:
ruler, parent, and teacher."
This is said regarding transmitting the Way.
Imparting learning and resolving doubts
then have different grades.
Learning has refinement and coarseness,
doubts also have greatness and smallness.
That those who impart and resolve are teachers
is固然 so;
yet there is a difference from transmitting the Way.
Shamans, physicians, and the various artisans learning from each other
also cannot be viewed一概.
For there are teachers who can be changed,
and teachers who cannot be changed.
The distance between them
cannot be spoken of in the same day.
Those who understand the theory of teachers,
do they understand Heaven?
For all people obey the command of Heaven.
Heaven has no sound or smell,
yet appoints the ruler to govern them.
All people are born by Heaven,
yet Heaven does not give birth to each thing individually,
and the parent gives them birth.
All people learn from Heaven,
yet Heaven does not instruct谆谆,
and the teacher teaches them.
Thus, if the noble person thinks of serving Heaven,
it lies simply in carefully serving these three.
If a person loses the Way,
they lose what makes them human,
just as without their body,
they would have no means to live.
Thus, parents give birth, and teachers provide instruction—
their underlying principles are fundamentally no different.
This is why the seventy disciples served Confucius,
willing to die for him,
willing to live for him,
going east, west, south, or north,
not daring to claim their own bodies as their own—
not out of personal affection,
but because principle and circumstance made it so.
As for imparting knowledge and resolving doubts,
there are varying degrees.
Classical masters transmitting teachings,
explaining chapters, sentences, and glosses;
the origins of historical studies,
the principles of editing and commentary—
all are encompassed within the substance of the Way.
The ancients said, "Writing cannot fully express speech,
and speech cannot fully convey meaning."
Beyond bamboo and silk texts,
there exists a transmission of the mind,
passed down orally and aurally,
whose origins must be clearly understood,
no less than the lineage of a clan's genealogy, which must not be confused.
This must be received from the right person,
for if it is not from that person,
then one receives nothing at all—
this is the teacher who cannot be replaced.
Specialized knowledge,
literature that governs the world—
the swiftness and slowness, the sweetness and bitterness within them—
can be grasped intuitively,
but cannot be conveyed in words.
This, too, is where the ultimate Way resides,
and must be received from the right person;
if not from that person,
then one receives nothing at all—
this is the teacher who cannot be replaced.
If this is the case,
then in life, one serves diligently,
attending without fixed methods;
after death, one offers sacrifices and rituals,
as the seventy disciples did for Confucius.
As for lecturing on classics and commentaries,
where the meaning requires no independent judgment;
or polishing literary compositions,
where the principles show no originality—
what is commonly known and commonly done,
which someone happens to impart to me—
if one does not finish learning from A,
it is permissible to leave and turn to B;
if A does not tell me,
B can also be consulted.
This does not touch upon the Way,
and thus the teacher can be replaced.
Even specialized knowledge and literary skill
are but minor arts.
What one learns from them
is no different from a carpenter's carving and polishing,
or a seamstress's embroidery techniques.
To regard them as having a slight advantage,
to bow and show respect,
to follow and sit respectfully—
this is acceptable, with love and reverence added.
But if one insists on strictly observing the threefold rites of service
and equating it with the duty owed to one's parents,
then the one demanding it is deluded,
and the one offering it does so insincerely.
The teachers of shamans, physicians, and various craftsmen
certainly cannot be compared to the Way of the gentleman,
yet there is something to be said.
The refinement of technical skills,
specialized and mastered by the ancients,
also had subtle and unique insights,
transmitted only to the right person,
and not to others—
this, too, is a teacher who cannot be replaced,
and should be served diligently in life,
and offered sacrifices after death.
The ancients, when eating and drinking,
would always offer sacrifices to the first person who provided food and drink,
not forgetting their origins.
How much more so for those who complete my moral, artistic, and technical skills,
when I have no other source from which to receive them?
As for disciples not necessarily being inferior to their teachers,
and teachers not necessarily being superior to their disciples—
this depends on what is gained.
What matters is the contention over the Way;
as for the strengths of skills and minor arts,
why cling to comparisons of superiority or inferiority?
Alas!
The tradition of the teacher has been lost for a long time.
Those with aspirations
search throughout the world
but find no teacher who cannot be replaced.
Yet, looking across past and present,
among them are those whose hearts stir,
unconsciously breaking into a smile,
feeling a sudden urge to weep without knowing why—
this, too, is my teacher.
Without seeing the person,
yet receiving a hidden transmission from them—
like an orphan seeing his deceased father in a portrait,
even if no one tells him,
in dreams he will surely be awakened.
Yet some say that the actions of the ancients
are not entirely worthy of emulation,
and one need not offer sacrifices to them.
Now, Yǔ certainly offered sacrifices to Gǔn,
honoring his origin.
Soldiers offer sacrifices to Chīyóu,
revering the founder of their craft.
If one must select a person to revere,
then even Zhōu Gōng and Confucius would have no regrets.
When a child serves their parents,
do they evaluate merit and virtue,
and then replace their father with their grandfather?
In the "Discussion on Extending Years,"
a guest discussing learning
argued that books have multiplied in later ages,
while human lifespan has not increased compared to antiquity,
so talent today is not as great as in ancient times.
If one could live for five hundred years with today's books,
then scholars would have no regrets.
In a thousand years,
books will surely multiply several times over,
and one would need a lifespan of a thousand years to match them—
some have passed this down as a famous saying.
I say this is the talk of a fool who does not understand learning.
If what he says were true,
even if the Creator granted him five thousand years,
he would still not attain it.
Learning is to the mind and body
as hunger and cold are to food and clothing.
Not to be content with satiety and warmth for a lifetime,
but to wish for extended years to exhaust all the food and clothing in the world—
this is either foolish or delusional.
The tradition says:
"If one can fully realize one's nature through utmost sincerity,
then one can fully realize the nature of others;
if one can fully realize the nature of others,
then one can fully realize the nature of all things."
What distinguishes humans from things
is the essence of benevolence, righteousness, morality, and virtue,
the tools for understanding things and discerning human relations,
and the ability to participate in heaven and assist earth—
these are not fully possessed by things.
As for perception, movement,
the mind's knowledge, and the vitality endowed by heaven—
are these any different from what things possess?
Those with great substance cannot be used for small purposes;
those with small substance do not rely on others for resources—
each thing has its limit.
Humans are also one kind of thing.
The lifespan of the Kūnpéng is billions of years;
even a thousand years is but infancy to it.
The cicada does not know spring and autumn;
a month is old age for it.
Humans, between heaven and earth,
are beings with a lifespan of a hundred years.
The mind's knowledge and vitality
are sufficient to meet the needs and desires of a hundred years,
and cannot be forced beyond that.
The Master set his heart upon learning at fifteen,
"and at seventy he could follow the desires of his heart without overstepping the bounds of what is right."
The sage is the ultimate embodiment of the human way.
For those who study to become sages,
there is only the effort of tenfold or a hundredfold,
never heard of waiting for tenfold or a hundredfold in years.
Even a single acquired skill or a particular expertise
has its beginning in the determination to learn
and its ultimate realization in not overstepping the bounds.
The reason one cannot attain sagehood
lies in the limitations of one's innate nature,
not in the brevity of years.
Yánzǐ died at thirty,
and the Master said:
"Alas!
I have seen him advance;
I have never seen him stop."
This expresses grief that he could not fully realize the ultimate within a hundred years.
He also said:
"The young are to be held in awe.
If by forty or fifty one has not yet made a name,
then one is not worthy of awe."
Though there are those who live to eighty, ninety, or a hundred years,
here, without waiting for the end of one's natural lifespan,
by forty or fifty,
one is deemed unworthy of awe.
This too is measured against the span of a hundred years of life,
gauging the use of one's mind and vital energy,
which can indeed be estimated by reasoning.
If one has not made a name by fifty,
even if granted a thousand more years,
it would still be the same.
The tales of immortals and eternal life
are truly vague and elusive.
That beings of the same kind possess different abilities
is also within the realm of reason;
thus, among the stories of transcendent immortals and spiritual grottoes,
perhaps one in a thousand may hold a fraction of truth,
not entirely false.
However, a thousand-year immortal
has never been heard to surpass a hundred-year erudite Confucian scholar;
this is clear evidence that borrowed years do not suffice to enhance learning.
Yǔ cherished every moment,
and Confucius "so devoted himself to study as to forget food,
found joy in it and forgot sorrow,
not realizing that old age was approaching."
He also said:
"If some years were added to my life,
I would study the Yì at fifty."
This expresses fear of not being able to fully accomplish what is possible within a hundred years,
believing that if there is something within human power to achieve,
and I fail to reach it,
then I have betrayed my life.
Even if the ephemeral cicada were granted the lifespan of the giant kūn and péng birds,
it could only produce its chirping song.
For years may be borrowed,
but innate nature cannot be changed;
thus, sages and worthies cherish their days and efforts,
yet do not regret the brevity of a hundred years,
which is why it is called fulfilling one's nature.
There are those in the world who show early brilliance in childhood,
reciting and reading several times more than others and still not stopping;
they should be vastly different from ordinary people.
Yet when they reach maturity,
compared to the hundredfold additional effort of the dull and weak,
they do not suddenly surpass them.
Thus, though sharpness and dullness differ,
both are ultimately confined to what can be accomplished in a hundred years,
and the mind and vital energy
can be reasonably estimated—clear evidence of this.
Now, not knowing to cultivate oneself,
but pursuing breadth to dazzle others—
the knowledge and sights of the world are inexhaustible,
and people's preferences cannot be the same.
With a finite life,
to chase infinite knowledge and sights;
with a single person's body,
to pursue endless preferences—
even Yáo and Shùn could not do this.
Mèngzǐ said:
"The wisdom of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to all things.
The benevolence of Yáo and Shùn
did not extend to loving all people."
Now, with ordinary and mediocre endowments,
to seek to exhaust what even Yáo and Shùn could not encompass,
and even wish to borrow five hundred years of natural lifespan—
fortunately, it is impossible.
If it were possible,
it would be nothing but monstrosity.
My clansman Tíng Fēng said:
"Whenever Uncle sees scholars
complain that they have poor memory,
that they forget books as soon as they read them,
and thus excuse themselves from studying,
Uncle always says:
'You simply do not know how to study properly.
If you truly studied well,
there is absolutely no reason for memory to be insufficient.
Books are as vast as the sea;
even sages cannot exhaust them all.
The reason the ancients valued breadth
is precisely because one must first specialize in an art,
and only then can one speak of breadth.
For specialization leads to mastery,
and mastery establishes oneself.
Among the phenomena and names of the universe,
those relevant to oneself,
even the slightest should not be overlooked.
Those irrelevant to oneself,
even as massive as Tài Shān should be ignored.
With such an approach,
even the dullest aptitude
will surely be able to remember.
Not knowing to specialize and establish mastery,
but vaguely seeking what even sages cannot exhaust—
this is the wisdom of the Foolish Old Man who moved mountains,
yet with the perspective of a peck and a pint.'"
This essay was written with a purpose,
also as an admonition to those who boast of abundance and compete in extravagance.
Thus its language is both solemn and humorous,
prompting deep reflection in the reader,
and together with previous discussions,
it sufficiently corroborates what scholars should know.
Reflections on Encounters
In ancient times, the roles of official, teacher, governance, and education were unified.
Outstanding individuals who did not cultivate their hundred acres of land
would receive support from the schools,
for without a constant profession, one cannot speak of scholarly learning.
There must be a constant livelihood,
so that nothing is left idle or neglected.
With the decline of the Zhōu dynasty, official positions were lost,
and the Way was practiced privately by teachers and Confucian scholars.
Thus began the emergence of scholars who had lost their positions,
those whom Mencius referred to as "those who uphold their aspirations."
Advancing, they could not receive official salary and enjoy their constant profession;
retreating, they could not farm and harvest their constant livelihood.
Living in isolation and peril,

this is the origin of the distinction between scholars and the nobility. Both scholars and high officials held ranks and positions, but there were none among those who neither farmed nor excelled who could be called "those who uphold their aspirations." What Mencius spoke of precisely referred to the separation of official duties and teaching roles, which gave rise to such categories.
When sages and worthies aspired to serve the world,
there were opportunities for official service through recommendation and public support,
with the principle of three approaches and three withdrawals.
The circumstances of meeting and aligning with rulers
were indeed difficult to speak of.
When the Master intended to go to Jīng,
he first sent Zǐxià,
and then followed with Rǎnyǒu.
Xiè Liǔ and Shēn Xiáng
had no one at Duke Mù's side,
and thus could not secure their positions.
When Mencius left Qí,
Shízǐ conveyed words of respect and admiration,
and a guest proposed to persuade him to stay.
The urgency of mutual need
and the rarity of actual encounters
led to introductions and indirect connections,
maintenance and mediation,
circumstances arising from unavoidable necessity.
Sages and worthies advanced according to ritual,
and withdrew according to righteousness.
Unaffected by external pressures,
they preserved their inner integrity.
Scholars without constant livelihood
pursued learning, for official salary lay within it.
It was not that they feared starvation from farming,
but that circumstances left them no leisure for it.
Nevertheless,
if three months passed without serving a ruler,
they would have no temple sacrifices after death,
and no banquets or music in life.
Frost and dew would grieve their hearts,
and desolation would accompany their solitude.
How could sages and worthies be far removed from human emotions?
The noble person remains steadfast in poverty.
To bend a foot in order to straighten a yard
is shameful, akin to deceitful flattery.
It is not a matter of contending over ritual propriety,
but rather the fear of being unable to preserve one's inner integrity.
In ancient times, those who did not meet with opportunity
lived in seclusion in humble positions.
In later ages, humble positions
could not be easily attained.
In ancient times, those who did not become officials
personally farmed and delighted in the Way.
In later ages, farmland
could not be easily obtained.
The realm of integrity and withdrawal that the ancients achieved,
later generations, exhausting methods of greed and opportunism to seek it,
still could not attain.
Therefore, when evaluating ancient noble persons,
one only expects them to understand the principles of advancement and withdrawal,
and not to covet glory and profit recklessly.
When evaluating later noble persons,
one must require them to possess the resolve of a determined scholar to face ditches and graves, and the courage to sacrifice their lives—only then is it acceptable.
For sages in dealing with circumstances,
there is certainly no distinction between difficulty and ease.
For those below great worthies,
one must fully demand their readiness to sacrifice their lives and face ditches and graves—only then is it acceptable.
This, too, is a difficult aspect of human nature.
Shāng Yāng expounded the Way of Emperors to test [the ruler],
Jiǎ Yǐ provided detailed responses concerning ghosts and spirits,
one eliciting weariness through indirect suggestions,
the other meeting with the ruler leaning forward on his mat.
Each had their own intentions.
Yet one met with opportunity, the other did not.
Shāng aligned with what Duke Xiào desired,
while Jiǎ confronted what Emperor Wén found difficult.
Hán Fēi expressed lament in "The Difficulties of Persuasion,"
Mànqiàn entrusted his words to humor and indirect speech.
They understood that the difficulty lay not in learning itself,
but in the means to express and apply that learning.
Yet Hán Fēi ultimately died because of his persuasion,
while Mànqiàn still preserved himself through jesting.
Why?
One exposed his sharpness and incurred jealousy,
the other concealed his edge and fortunately survived.
Thus, for the noble person, it is not difficult to use scholarship to serve the world,
but difficult to master the art of using that scholarship.
Ancient and modern times differ in circumstances and conditions,
and this must be discerned.
Ancient scholarship was simple and easy,
asking only whether it was appropriate or not.
Later scholarship is intricate and difficult.
Even if the scholarship is appropriate,
it may still not be employed.
There must be an art to employing that scholarship,
and within that art, there are levels of skill and clumsiness.
In one's life experiences,
appropriateness is not the first requirement;
skillfulness is demanded first.
If scholarship is appropriate but one's maneuvering is unskillful,
one is rejected by contemporaries.
If skillful in encountering opportunity but one's principles are inappropriate,
one is ridiculed by later generations.
The threat of ditches and graves presses from the front,
and the consequences of skill and clumsiness drive from behind.
Alas!
For scholars who cultivate and clarify scholarship,
seeking to minimize faults
and fully preserve their inner integrity,
is it not difficult indeed!
Moreover, prominence and obscurity depend on the times,
adversity and success depend on fate.
Talent bestowed by Heaven has its uniqueness,
and learning achieved through human effort has its excellence.
The urgent needs of a particular time
and the prevailing trends of an era
do not necessarily coincide,
and this too is a matter of circumstance.
Liú Xīn, master of classical scholarship, did not meet with Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Lǐ Guǎng, the Flying General, did not meet with Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
For millennia, this has been regarded as a pity.
The people of Zhōu learned martial arts,
but their rulers esteemed civil arts.
They changed to learn civil arts,
and the rulers again emphasized martial arts.
When young, the ruler preferred to employ the old;
when old, the ruler preferred to employ the young.
Weeping on the road with white hair
is indeed fitting.
As for what is possessed below,
being precisely what is sought above,
mutual need is extremely urgent,
yet actual encounters remain rare—
such cases are too numerous to recount.
Emperor Wén of Hàn patted his thigh, longing for Lián Pō and Lǐ Mù,
yet Wèi Shǎng could not avoid penal servitude.
Emperor Lǐ of Sòng sat upright and honored Chéng and Zhū,
yet Zhēn and Wèi could not avoid being kept at a distance.
Thus, the difficulty lies not in scholarship itself,
but in the art of employing that scholarship.
Truly, how difficult it is!
One who gazes at distant mountains
finds their lofty beauty captivating,
but upon entering them, remains unaware.
One who recalls past events
experiences unbounded sorrow and joy,
yet while in the midst of them, remains unknowing.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn read Simǎ Xiàngrú's rhapsodies,
admiring their soaring, cloud-reaching quality,
and regretted not being able to live in the same era.
Yet when he finally met Simǎ Xiàngrú,
he did not place him above the various attendants and courtiers of the time.
There are indeed those who love a person without knowing their scholarship,
and those who love their writings without knowing the person.
In the Táng, there were the factions of Niú and Lǐ.
Those who hated Bái Jūyì
sealed away his works,
saying that seeing them would make one feel affection,
fearing it would change their original intent.
Thus, toward one person's writings and conduct, they held contrasting love and hatred.
The daughter of Zhèng Tián
recited and chanted Luó Yǐn's poems,
to the point of wishing to devote herself to him.
Later, seeing Luó Yǐn's plain appearance,
she consequently stopped speaking of him entirely.
Thus, regarding one person's talent and appearance, she differentiated acceptance and rejection.
Contrasting love and hatred toward writings and conduct
arises from factional bias.
Differentiating acceptance and rejection based on talent and appearance
is the perspective of women and girls.
Yet the world esteems scholarship,
and reading the books of the ancients,
one often sighs at not being born in the same era.
If by chance one meets [such a person],
then one is constrained by views of factional support and differences,
or even imitates the daughter of Zhèng Tián in selecting based on appearance.
Then for scholars who cultivate and clarify scholarship,
seeking to minimize faults
and fully preserve their inner integrity,
is it not difficult indeed?
Chúnyú Liàng drank at the Dòu Shí,
Wúguǐ discussed physiognomy with dogs and horses,
which is what is meant by composing the "Guān Jū" to evoke thoughts of the virtuous maiden,
or chanting the "Lù Míng" to express the intent of welcoming esteemed guests.
Having something to rely on to stir inspiration,
one aims to enter the profound through the shallow,
not only reflecting the subtle and gentle style of poets,
but also embodying the quality of scholars presenting gifts of lambs and geese.
Those who wish to advance their learning
must gauge what contemporaries understand and gradually guide them in.
However, those who observe others in the world,
upon hearing the "Guān Jū," seek the river isles,
and upon speaking of the "Lù Míng," search for the wilds of duckweed,
while discarding and ignoring the virtuous maiden and esteemed guests.
The nature of ordinary people
is to prefer ease and fear difficulty,
to delight in similarity and detest difference.
Those who listen to words without examining what they truly mean
are often eight or nine out of ten.
There are petty men
who know how difficult it is to find such encounters and matches,
so they abandon their strengths
and force themselves in their weaknesses,
striving to follow trends,
without necessarily seeking inner satisfaction.
Are trends entirely without merit?
Those who initiate them
often have a purpose;
but those who follow them
merely imitate their falseness.
Elegant music is not destroyed by rustic songs
but by the music of Zhèng,
for the music of Zhèng is skillful.
Good seedlings are not ruined by weeds
but by darnel,
for darnel resembles them.
Scholarship is not lost to vulgar customs
but to false learning,
for false learning is cunning.
When the world does not understand scholarship,
it still maintains an open mind in anticipation.
Once false learning emerges,
the world no longer knows the true learning of self-attainment.
This is why Confucius detested the village hypocrite,
and why Mencius deeply loathed what seems right but is wrong.
Yet those who engage in such falseness
claim they are merely applying their scholarship.
In the past, the Master did not refrain from hunting competitions,
yet the method of correcting records was never abandoned;
when omens were insufficient to act upon, he then departed.
Thus, the scholarship used to apply scholarship
is not discarded by sages and worthies.
If scholarship cannot adapt to changes in trends,
then it need not be the way of sages and worthies;
even carpenters and wheelwrights
are the same in this regard.
Therefore, the noble person uses omens to advance learning,
leaving success or failure to heaven.
In the past, Yáng Zǐyún was early recommended for his ornate writings,
but in his later years, he composed the "Xuán" in solitude;
Liú Zhījī first gained fame for his poetry and prose,
but later his reputation diminished due to his historical writings.
Truly knowing what cannot be helped,
they accepted it as fate.
Discerning Similarities
People conceal their hearts,
making them impossible to measure.
Speech is the voice of the heart;
those skilled at observing others
need only observe what they say.
People are not necessarily all good,
yet what they say never fails to profess goodness.
Those skilled at observing others
examine the reasons behind their professed goodness.
The Master said:
"At first, in my dealings with people,
I listened to their words and believed their actions;
now, in my dealings with people,
I listen to their words and observe their actions."
Fearing that their words do not stem from sincere intent.
When words do not come from the heart,
like a lawsuit without genuine feeling,
when arguments are exhausted, the truth is easily revealed—
this is not what the noble person worries about.
The peril of scholarship
lies not so much in the words of noble persons,
nor in words spoken with purpose,
but in seeking the intent behind the words:
within a short distance,
there can be a gap as vast as heaven and earth,
seeming alike yet not.
The words of the world
are fundamentally not many. Words may change in myriad ways, but their essential principles can be encompassed by a few key points, hence it is said that words are fundamentally not many.
People, however, are endlessly varied and inconsistent.
With endlessly varied and inconsistent people
producing words that are not many,
it is natural that their traces differ while their words cannot but be similar.
For example, a city has only four gates;
the people inside number in the thousands.
When they go out through the gates to their destinations,
their paths are certainly more than four,
yet the gates they exit from
are only four.
Thus, although their directions differ,
when they set out, they cannot but start from the same gates.
It is not intentional imitation,
nor is it pretending to go east while actually heading west;
circumstances make it so.
Cultivating the five grains
is for the purpose of providing food for the people.
Yí Dí said:
"The five grains must ripen."
When asked why he prayed for ripening,
he said:
"Without ripening, there would be nothing to make wine."
Teaching people sericulture
is for the purpose of providing silk clothing for the elderly.
Chīyóu said:
"Mulberries must be planted."
When questioned why he wanted to plant them,
he said:
"Without planting, there would be nothing to make banners."
Now, did Yí Dí and Chīyóu
not genuinely need grain and silk?
Yet with such identical needs for food and clothing,
they cannot be relied upon.
The "Yì" says:
"The unfathomability of yīn and yáng is called spirit."
It also says:
"Spirit
is what is spoken of as marvelously acting upon all things."
Mencius said:
"Great and transformative is called sage;
sage and unknowable is called spirit."
This is the origin of the discourse on spirit, transformation, and marvel.
The unfathomability of yīn and yáng
does not depart from yīn and yáng.
Marvelously acting upon all things in speech
does not depart from all things.
The unknowability of the sage
does not depart from fullness and brilliance.
Yet speaking of sage, spirit, and marvel
is to prevent people from stagnating in traces,
using what is known and seen to envision what cannot be known or seen.
Scholarship and literature
have realms of spirit and marvel.
Superficial learners with shallow understanding
cling to traces in their pursuit;
those with true knowledge
believe there is spirit and marvel within,
which can be grasped by intuition but cannot be conveyed in words.
The unlearned and ignorant,
blocked in mind with no way in,
exhausted in argument with no way out,
also say it can be intuited but not conveyed in words.
Therefore, the noble person detests what seems right but is wrong.
Bó Hūn Màorén said to Liè Yùkòu:
"People will protect you,
not because you can make them protect you,
but because you cannot make them not protect you."
Thus, not being able to make people protect you is inferior;
being able to make people not protect you is superior;
the middle is being protected by others.
Therefore, in the world, only the middle realm is easy to distinguish;
what is above the middle and what is below the middle
often appear similar.
At the beginning of learning,
one may not yet be able to memorize;
after broad and deep study,
one will transcend memorization.
Thus, memorization
is the boat and carriage of learning.
When people go somewhere,
they must rely on boats and carriages;
upon reaching their destination,
they leave the boats and carriages behind.
Those who do not take a single step
also do not use boats and carriages.
Those who do not use boats and carriages
then claim kinship with those who leave boats and carriages behind.

Therefore, the noble person detests what seems right but is wrong. Chéngzǐ, seeing that Xiè Shàngcài was well-versed in classics and commentaries, said he was indulging in trivialities and losing his will—after all, this is not similar to the Confucian "one thread running through it all."
When first encountering a principle,
regardless of one's intelligence, wisdom, or character,
the understanding is not too far off.
Upon reconsidering it,
it becomes vague and unreliable.
After pondering it a third time,
one becomes confused as if it has been snatched away.
It is not that the effort of repeated contemplation
is inferior to the initial encounter.
The first encounter stands outside the matter,
thus the spirit remains whole;
repeated contemplation enters into its midst,
and one's self becomes entangled in its twists and turns.
Only by fully navigating these twists and turns
can one return to the supreme state of the initial encounter.
Therefore, in scholarly pursuit, one must not fear complexity.
However, while navigating these twists and turns,
the spirit lacks the wholeness of the initial encounter;
one must constantly recall that first insight
as a guide through the vagueness and confusion,
so that one may perhaps return to the beginning.
I observe that among today's diligent learners,
initially they act without true insight,
and later they have no expectation of reaching the ultimate.
They exert themselves in arduous study,
merely thinking that their learning can surpass others.
Like a boat adrift without a tether,
though it may travel a thousand li daily,
what use is it?
Yet they say, "Scholarly pursuit must not fear complexity."
Thus, the noble person detests what appears similar but is not.
Words are used to clarify principles,
and literary expression is the vessel that carries them.
An empty carriage, merely adorned,
with its owner unheard of—
thus, those drowned in literary embellishment
are not worth discussing literature with.
The *Yì* says:
"Things intermingle,
hence it is called pattern."
It also says:
"Its meaning is far-reaching,
its words are patterned."
The *Shū* says:
"Governance values constancy,
words esteem substance and essentials."
The *Shī* says:
"When words are harmonious,
the people are in accord."
The *Lǐjì* says:
"Do not plagiarize others' words,
do not echo mindlessly,
follow the ancients,
and praise the former kings."
The tradition says:
"Words need only convey the meaning."
Zēngzǐ said:
"In uttering words and tone,
one thereby stays far from vulgarity and error."
The words of the classics, traditions, sages, and worthies
have never failed to value literary expression.
For literature indeed carries principle;
if the literary form is inadequate,
then the principle remains unclear.
Moreover, literature also has its own inherent principle.
Beauty and ugliness,
when seen by people,
elicit shared feelings without prior agreement,
unrelated to the principle being conveyed—
this is the principle of literature itself.
Therefore, in the highest literature,
literary embellishment is not what is emphasized,
but it is not without literary expression.
Yet ignorant Confucians, lacking learning,
crudely claim that "skillful writing harms the Way."
Thus, the noble person detests what appears similar but is not.
Lù Jī said:
"Though I weave from my own heart,
I fear others precede me;
if it injures integrity and violates righteousness,
however beloved, it must be discarded."
This means that writers,
drawing from the depths of their minds,
often fear that the ancients have already spoken such words before them.
If indeed their words coincide with the ancients',
it constitutes injury to integrity and violation of righteousness;
however cherished,
they must cut it away.
Hán Yù said:
"Only in ancient writing must words be one's own;
those who cannot achieve this resort to plagiarism."
This conveys the same idea.
Those who establish doctrines
take meaning as their foundation,
which differs from the category of literary stylists.
People share this mind;
minds share this principle.
The cosmos is vast,
ancient texts are numerous and interwoven—
how can one ensure that what one says has never been said by the ancients?
This is the first point of no harm.
Human minds also differ,
just as their faces do.
If coincidence occurs without intent,
then the nuances, weight, and emphasis
will inevitably not be entirely identical;
people can discern this themselves.
This is the second point of no harm.
The central tenets of a written work are few;
its words may be countless and unending.
Occasional coincidence with the ancients
amounts to only one or two points;
the points of difference
are sufficient to overshadow the occasional similarities.
This is the third point of no harm.
I observe that among today's writers,
some have no real central tenet at all.
They quote ancient words and elaborate on them,
but the meaning of their elaboration
is already fully present in the ancients.
Nevertheless,
this is the work of the less talented;
people recognize it at a glance,
and it ultimately ends up covering pickle jars—
truly causing no harm.
Then there are the cunning ones
who alter the appearance of ancient words
but plagiarize their meaning.
When contemporaries propose original theories,
they elaborate on the ideas while concealing their source.
Or, hearing of someone's insights
not yet written down,
they hastily steal the ideas as their own;
later, when that person writes their own book,
they surprisingly appear afterward.
Moreover, their petty cleverness
is sufficient to patch over the gaps,
leaving people bewildered, unable to discern the truth.
Unless the one robbed confronts them face-to-face
and exhaustively probes what they have not reached,
their deceit is not easily exposed.
Alternatively, those sharing the same path
may also carefully study and repeatedly examine
the beginning and end of the matter,
only then can the hidden truth be attacked.
Yet stealing fame and deceiving the world
is no one-day evil.
And people of the time
may even say, "So-and-so's learning
is not inferior to such-and-such,"
or "So-and-so's achievement
surpasses such-and-such."
Thus, the noble person detests what appears similar but is not.
The one trusted by ten thousand generations
is the Master alone.
The Master's words are not of one kind;
the worthy each grasp his strengths,
the unworthy each err by what seems similar.
"Instructing others untiringly"
is not indiscriminate teaching.
"I wish to say nothing"
is not abandoning instruction.
"Loving the ancients and diligently seeking"
is not pursuing breadth alone.
"One thread runs through it all"
is not neglecting things.
For no single saying can encompass everything;
even with the Master's sageliness,
he could not achieve this.
Grasping one of his sayings,
not seeking what is right but seeking similarity—
whether one is worthy or unworthy
depends on the person;
this is something the Master could do nothing about.
Mèngzǐ was good at learning from Confucius.
The Master spoke of benevolence and wisdom,
while Mèngzǐ spoke of benevolence and righteousness;
the Master aimed to restore the Eastern Zhōu,
while Mèngzǐ advocated kingship for Qí and Liáng;
the Master "believed in and loved antiquity,"
yet Mèngzǐ said:
"To believe all in the *Shū*
would be better to have no *Shū* at all."
Yet those seeking Confucius
must start from Mèngzǐ.
Therefore, those who grasp what is right
do not seek mere similarity.
Those who seek similarity
certainly do not grasp what is right.
Yet those in the world who err by what seems similar
all say, "I have grasped what is right."

Shuō Lín
The Way is public;
learning is private.
The noble person learns in order to attain the Way,
aiming to fully realize the human and reach the heavenly.
What is the human?
Intelligence, talent, and strength,
divided by the private aspects of form and vital energy.
What is the heavenly?
Centrality, correctness, balance, and uprightness,
rooted in the public nature of spontaneity.
Therefore it is said: the Way is public, learning is private.
Those whose Way is the same but methods differ:
Hán Fēi had the books "Explaining the Lǎozi" and "Illustrating the Lǎozi,"
the Lièzǐ contains the chapter "Yáng Zhū,"
the Mohists recorded the affairs of Yàn Yīng;
their functions and applications differ,
yet their principles have points of interconnection.
Those whose methods are the same but inclinations differ:
Zǐzhāng challenged Zǐxià's teachings on friendship,
Xún Qing criticized Mèngzǐ's doctrines,
Zhāng Yí undermined Sū Qín's vertical alliance strategy;
their essential purposes are not different,
yet what they uphold mutually differs.
A steed from the Wòwā marshes
can bear a hundred jūn and travel a thousand lǐ;
combining the strength of two Wòwā steeds
ultimately cannot achieve two thousand lǐ.
This speaks of mastering learning through solitary attainment,
the unique arrival of innate intelligence;
even if there are biases and deficiencies,
they cannot be assisted by others.
Two Wòwā steeds
cannot achieve two thousand lǐ;
combining the strength of two Wòwā steeds
is not inherently incapable of bearing two hundred jūn and each traveling a thousand lǐ.
This speaks of grand achievements and peerless undertakings,
each contributing their own strengths;
even if there are contradictions,
they cannot be privately monopolized by anyone.
Literary composition was not highly valued by the ancients;
drafting, discussing,
revising, and polishing
indeed already combined the efforts of many to produce the writing.
They aimed for utmost excellence,
not for flaunting private skill.
Dīng Jìnglǐ had Cáo Zǐjiàn polish his writing,
saying, "Who in later generations will know who finalized my text?"
This was an intention to deceive the world.
Preserving the text while also preserving records of whether the revisions were good or not
enables later generations reading one person's writing
to gain the benefit of two excellences;
is the supplementation not great?
Sīmǎ Qiān incorporated texts from the Shàngshū, Zuǒzhuàn, and Guóyǔ;
this was not due to fondness for conformity,
but the inevitable logic and circumstance.
Sīmǎ Qiān edited and altered texts from the Shàngshū, Zuǒzhuàn, and Guóyǔ;
Bān Gù edited and altered Sīmǎ Qiān's texts;
this was not due to fondness for novelty,
but the inevitable logic and circumstance.
When engaged in a task,
inquiring about its beginning and end from others—
must one necessarily demand they personally heard and saw it?
Zhāng Jiǎ relates what he heard from Lǐ Yǐ—
is this plagiarism?
Human minds differ
as their faces differ.
Zhāng Jiǎ relates Lǐ Yǐ's words,
yet the voice, appearance, smile, and manner
cannot fully become Lǐ Yǐ's—
is this affectation of difference?
Confucius learned from the Duke of Zhōu,
the Duke of Zhōu observed the two dynasties (Xià and Shāng),
the two dynasties were based on Táng (Yáo) and Yú (Shùn),
Táng and Yú modeled themselves on earlier antiquity.
Therefore it is said:
"The great origin of the Way comes from Heaven."
For one may observe the spring emerging from the mountain foot:
sand and stones now hidden, now visible,
the flow winding or straight,
from subtlety gradually becoming manifest,
and thereby know the primordial state of rivers, lakes, boats, and oars.
Observe the babbling of an infant:
having sound but no words,
forms guessed, meanings sought,
and thereby know the very beginning of literary writing and composition.
There is the history of an era,
the history of a state,
the history of a family,
the history of an individual.
The principles of organizing past records and specialized family learning are not clearly explained (detailed in "Shì Tōng" and "Dá Kè Wèn").
Thus, the history of an era
is rarely understood.
