The principles of local gazetteers of districts and counties and the historical records of feudal states are not clearly explained (detailed in the "Fāngzhì" chapter).
Thus, the history of a state
is rarely understood.
Genealogical records do not follow the established methods of official historians (detailed in the "Jiāshǐ" chapter).
Thus, the history of a family
is rarely understood.
The stylistic conventions of the various masters are unclear;
collected writings are privately composed by individuals.
Thus, the history of an individual
is rarely understood.
Zhǎn Xǐ received instructions from Zhǎn Qín;
thus, the words that repelled Qí
may be said to come from Zhǎn Qín,
or may be said to come from Zhǎn Xǐ.
Disciples inherit their master's teachings and write books;
friends establish interpretations based on consultation;
later people draw on ancient meanings and elaborate in speech—
there is no need to conceal their sources,
nor would they feel ashamed in establishing their words.
Zǐjiàn liked people criticizing his writing;
when there were unsatisfactory parts,
he would revise them promptly.
The critical words may be preserved,
the revised text may also be preserved.
Those with outstanding ideas but stumbling diction:
polish them with a marvelous brush like painting.
Those with abundant diction but shallow learning:
The essential point is having enduring substance;
drawing on resources is nothing to conceal.
Chén Lín wrote a letter for Cáo Hóng to the Crown Prince of Wèi,
discussing the advantages and disadvantages of defeating the rebels.
This idea truly originated with Cáo Hóng;
openly adopting Chén Lín's wording
and including it in Cáo Hóng's collection is acceptable.
But now it says:
"I wished to have Chén Lín write the letter,
but Lín was recently occupied with many matters,
so I exhausted this old man's thoughts."
It also says:
"I am surprised you slight my family's hill,
saying it was done by a hired hand."
This is the ugliness of covering up;
it should not be included in Cáo Hóng's collection.
Compare them to birds:
ambition and understanding are their body,
literary composition is their wings.
Only with the body of a great roc spanning a thousand lǐ
can one wield wings that hang from the sky.
If a sparrow borrows the wings of a carving or fish hawk,
it will stumble before even attempting to rise,
let alone roc's wings.
Therefore, in refining language, one need not avoid temporary borrowing,
but values the ambition and understanding that carry the language,
and one's own ability to bear it. Alas!
This is difficult to discuss with those drowned in the trivialities of literary composition.
The various masters, with the unifying purpose of one school,
have a rigorous and concise literary style,
yet can incorporate the words of others.
Collected writings are a comprehensive collection of miscellaneous compositions,
encompassing various forms and styles,
yet dare not include writings by others.
What is the reason?
It is not that their literary elegance and diction
are inferior to the various masters;
but their ambition and understanding, though outstanding,
possess that which stands independently of words and establishes immortality—
they dare not aspire to the level of the various masters.
If there truly is a collected work that remarkably establishes its own school,
even if it includes words spoken on behalf of others,
what harm is there?
Disputing whether Zhuāng Zhōu's chapters like "Ràng Wáng" and "Yú Fù" are genuine or forged;
arguing whether Qu Yuán's fu "Zhāo Hún" and "Dà Zhāo" are jade or stone—
how rigid!
The perspective of literary scholars.
Sweet spring water is water that resembles sweet wine.
Under heaven, none fail to drink sweet wine,
yet they alone regret not being able to drink sweet spring water.
How extreme!
The world's valuing of that which seems so but is not.
In the style of original composition,
when citing ancient meanings
or adopting established texts,
it is not necessary to indicate the source.
This is not to plagiarize,
but because the form and momentum of the work leave no room for such details.
It is also essential that the author’s intent and insight are sufficient to stand on their own,
without relying on the weight of the cited words;
moreover, the cited material
should be universally recognized,
so that its reappearance does not cause concern.
Only then can one speak of the art of original composition.
In the style of textual criticism,
even a single character or fragment
must have its source indicated.
If the source text
is not unique but appears in multiple works,
the earliest source must be cited—for example, if both Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù record it, cite Sīmǎ Qiān rather than Bān Gù.
If the earliest text is lost,

then the source from which it is quoted must be indicated—for example, since Liú Xiàng’s Qī Lüè is lost, but its classification appears in the “Yìwén Zhì” of the Hànshū, and Ruǎn Xiàoxù’s Qī Lù is lost, but its missing entries appear in the annotations of the “Jīngjí Zhì” of the Suíshū, then when quoting from Qī Lüè or Qī Lù, one must state “Hànzhì” or “Suízhù.”
This is the established method for careful discourse.
If a text appears in multiple sources
but the earliest is not acknowledged,
it is crude.
Citing lost texts without indicating the source—making it seem as if the lost text still exists—
is deceptive.
Using the style of textual criticism
to improperly invoke the principles of original composition,
thereby concealing one’s plagiarism,
is erroneous.
Literary expression
is like an army;
intent and insight
are its generals.
When Lǐ Guǎng entered Chéng Bùshí’s camp,
the banners and fortifications were renewed,
yet not every object was changed,
nor every matter altered.
Those who understand this principle
may adopt established texts
without necessarily originating them themselves.
Literary expression
is like a boat or cart;
intent and insight
are its passengers.
Wheels should be sturdy,
sails should be swift—
all who use boats or carts
desire this.
But east, west, south, or north
depends on the passenger.
Those who understand this principle
can use literature for their own purposes,
rather than being enslaved by it.
Literary expression
is like goods;
intent and insight
are the craftsmen.
Oranges, tangerines, hawthorns, and plums—
a chef obtains them
to select sweet and crisp ones for offerings;
a physician takes them
to prepare medicines to cure illnesses.
Those who understand this principle
can take different meanings from the same text
or use the same meaning for different purposes,
without being confined by its traces. (Ancient texts are often interpreted out of context for various uses; rigid scholars fail to grasp this and argue stubbornly.)
Literary expression
is like metal and stone;
intent and insight
are the furnace and hammer.
The miraculous can transform into the rotten,
and the rotten can transform into the miraculous.
Those who understand this principle
need not cling to fixed doctrines. (What is gained is miraculous; what is not gained is rotten.)
Literary expression
is like wealth and goods;
intent and insight
are the shrewd merchant.
What others discard, I take;
what others seek, I give—
then the art of trade reaches divine clarity.
Those who understand this principle
can weigh trends and establish their discourse. (When trends lean to extremes, it is valuable to have discerning individuals uphold balance.)
Literary expression
is like medicine or poison;
intent and insight
are the physician.
To treat cold, use heat;
but excessive heat becomes more severe than cold.
To treat heat, use cold;
but excessive cold becomes more severe than heat.
A good physician, when excess is extreme,
worries about reversal into deficiency,
thus treating imbalances without agitation,
so that no residual harm remains.
Those who understand this principle
can rescue from flaws and maintain centrality.
To turn the mechanism of a well-sweep,
one must move it fully up, down, front, and back.
Pushing up and pulling down
are within one’s strength.
Directly forward or directly backward
are beyond one’s strength.
Doubling the push
causes forward to feel like falling;
doubling the pull
causes backward to feel like leaping.
Doubling the strength within reach
creates a realm beyond reach.
Human intelligence and knowledge
inevitably have limits,
so one must know what to double to create such a realm.
The blending of the five flavors,
the harmony of the eight tones—
their value lies in simultaneous use.
Tasting them sequentially,
listening to them sequentially—
they do not form flavor or sound.
The delivery of postal relays,
the regularity of water clocks—
their value lies in continuity.
Running together and stopping together,
operating together and resting together—
they do not form postal or clock systems.
Some books are completed by several people:
they may become more refined through successive transmissions,
or grow more disjointed despite simultaneous assistance.
Succession lacks competitiveness,
while simultaneity harbors rivalry;
succession allows instruction,
while simultaneity makes mutual understanding difficult;
succession permits补救,
while simultaneity rarely allows full composure.
Humans have abilities and inabilities—
whether commoner or sage,
none are exempt.
Exchanging what one can do for what one cannot
allows one to obtain
all that is sought.
Those who emphasize principles are clumsy with literary style;
those skilled in literary style are lax with evidence;
the three criticize each other endlessly.
Principles reside in insight,
literary style in talent,
evidence in learning—
this is why Liú Zīxuán argued that the three are rarely combined.
If one person cannot combine them,
consulting others can achieve merit.
It is not seen that the great achievements of the ancients cannot be revived.
If selfishness takes hold,
fearing that fame may not be claimed by oneself,
then the three do not aid each other
but instead harm each other.
So-called lovers of antiquity
do not claim that antiquity necessarily surpasses the present,
but precisely because the present is not different from antiquity,
they seek balance
in continuity, change, similarity, and difference.
The dregs of antiquity
can become the essence of the present.
It is not that dregs are valued as essence,
but because the preservation of dregs

allows us to imagine the essence that emerged from them. (For example, reference books have little profound meaning; ancient reference books are even less detailed than later ones, but they cite ancient texts unavailable to later generations, preserving them through this means, which is also valuable.)
The flaws of antiquity
can become models for later ages.
It is not that flaws are taken as models,
but because the preservation of flaws
allows us to imagine where the models lie. (For example, Lùn Héng is highly biased and inconsistent, yet what it discusses includes things lost to later generations, preserved through it.)
Thus, the value of learning in textual criticism
is to clarify principles.
In expressing words and tone,
one should distance oneself from vulgarity and error.
Error is the sinner of rhetoric,
but why must vulgarity be distanced?
Without refinement, there is no expression;
if expression cannot be preserved,
even that which expresses will be lost.
Among the various schools of thought,
some that err in principle have been transmitted,
but none vulgar in expression have survived.
If principle is not erroneous but expression is vulgar,
strength cannot prevail;
if expression is not vulgar but principle is erroneous,
it is like the saying, “If the five grains do not ripen,
they are不如荑稗.”
Principle is weighty, expression light—
this is a universal truth across time and space.
Yet vulgar expression cannot overcome erroneous principle,
for the public mind discerning beauty and ugliness, likes and dislikes,
also emerges from principle.
Waves are the wind of water;
wind is the waves of air;
dreams are the blossoms of the mind;
literature is the private aspect of the Way.
Still water has no waves;
calm air has no wind;
the perfected person has no dreams;
the ultimate literature has no privacy.
Those who perform vocal mimicry
can simultaneously produce myriad sounds and forms of humans and animals, water and fire, men and women, old and young.
This does not mean a single mouth can truly produce myriad forms.
Myriad sounds and forms
converge in the human ear;
inevitably, there must be a point of focus.
Taking what converges in the ear as the point of focus,
thus the technique is simple yet yields many sounds.
Those skilled in painting
can on a single scroll simultaneously depict myriad shapes of distance and proximity, shallowness and depth, front and side, interweaving and overlapping.
This does not mean a single scroll can truly contain myriad forms.
Myriad shapes converge in the human eye;
inevitably, there is also a point of focus.
Taking what converges in the eye as the point of focus,
thus the brushstrokes are simple yet depict many forms.
Now, sounds and sights converge in the ears and eyes,
and principles and meanings converge in the human mind;
they are alike.
If one truly grasps the convergence of principles and meanings,
and uses this as the focus for literary expression,
then one may discuss writing.
In the world, there are things that can be done halfway
but cannot be done in full.
Medicine for hemiplegia
can treat hemiplegia;
but doubling the medicine for hemiplegia
cannot revive the dead. This argument is seen in the *Lǚshì Chūnqiū*.
In the world, there are things that can be done in full
but cannot be done halfway.
A woodcutter carrying two *jūn* of firewood
walks briskly;
but if half is removed, he cannot walk.
It is not that his strength is insufficient,
but the situation is not convenient.
Trends of the times
inevitably have their flaws.
The gentleman establishes his words to remedy these flaws,
merely returning to the mean.
Fearing that his words are insufficient to change the trends of the times,
and overcorrecting them,
is like doubling the medicine for hemiplegia and hoping to revive the dead.
If one only seeks to remedy flaws
without elucidating the full scope of this Way,
that is like removing half the firewood from the load
and wanting to spare the woodcutter's strength.
Ten *cùn* make one *chǐ*,
eight *chǐ* make one *xún*.
Measuring eighty *chǐ* yields ten *xún*,
but measuring eight hundred *cùn* does not yield ten *xún*;
accumulating small units easily leads to error.
The strength of one man
can plow one hundred *mǔ*;
combining the strength of eight men can plow nine hundred *mǔ*;
pooling strengths easily achieves results.
In matters of learning,
being able to pool strengths
without being bogged down in minor details
is excellent.
Where the trends of the times tend,
even mediocre people can strive to follow;
where the trends of the times depart,
even heroes cannot revive them.
The Hàn court valued classical scholarship;
even clerks could master the six scripts,
and when officials and commoners submitted writings,
errors were immediately reported and censured.
In later generations, among literary scholars,
many are not familiar with the principles of the six scripts. Wáng Xīzhī's vulgar script was mocked by Hán Yù, who also said: "One should have some knowledge of characters when writing."
Could it be that the intelligence and ability of later literary scholars
are inferior to the clerks of the Hàn court?
It is the trends of the times that make it so.
People from Yuè boast of speaking the Yān dialect;
those who can speak the Yān dialect
must have traveled extensively in the capital,
gained much experience,
and have tongues more agile than others.
But when they arrive in Yān,
even lowly servants and maids,
young girls and boys,
all speak the Yān dialect.
To boast of speaking Yuè dialect as a man of Yuè—
is that a reasonable argument?
In the school of Confucius,
even a child of five *chǐ* would be ashamed to speak of the Five Hegemons.
To say that a child of five *chǐ*
has greater talent and insight than worthies like Guǎn Zhòng, Hú, and Zhào—
the Master would not allow it.
The five grains compared to weeds—
their noble and base qualities
are fixed.
Yet unripe five grains
are still inferior to fruitful weeds.
Those who rely on the trends of the times
boastfully pride themselves on their path,
thinking they have gained an inch of wood
and truly surpass others' towering buildings—

they can only be called unenlightened. Respecting Hàn learning and revering Zhèng Xuán and Xǔ Shèn is the current trend. This is studying antiquity, not being ancient learning itself. They actually spurn everything, as if secretly relying on something.
The servants of lords and princes
are not necessarily nobler than the attendants of scholar-officials.
Yet such servants,
coming and going through vermilion gates and grand mansions,
boastfully act superior and look down on scholar-officials, saying:
"My master's house is great."
They do not know that scholar-officials can indeed scold and bind them,
to request punishment from the lords and princes,
who will certainly whip and punish them,
to apologize for the lack of discipline in their households.
In learning, not seeking true attainment
but boasting of what one relies on to appear lofty—
is like the servants of lords and princes.
"In mourning, one desires to quickly become poor;
in death, one desires to quickly decay"—
Yǒuzǐ said these are not the words of a gentleman.
Thus, words spoken for a purpose
differ from orthodox meanings;
even the sage cannot avoid this.
Those today who rigidly adhere to literary expressions,
without examining what the words are meant to convey,
and hastily judge their right or wrong—
this is wanting to demand that people surpass Confucius.
*The Spring and Autumn Annals* criticizes flatterers (*Gōngyáng Zhuàn*).
The Master once said:
"I detest glib tongues that overturn states and families."
Thus, *nìng* is a name for wickedness.
Someone said, "Yōng is benevolent but not *nìng*."
However foolish that person may be,
how could he regret that a benevolent person cannot be wicked?
Moreover, the ancients humbly referred to themselves as *bù nìng*;
would they use inability to be wicked as humility?
Thus, *nìng* is also a general term for intelligence, talent, and eloquence.
Xúnzǐ wrote "Xìng È" (Human Nature Is Evil),
saying that the sage "transforms nature and raises artifice."
*Wěi* (artifice) in the six scripts
is the correct term for what is human-made.
Xúnzǐ's meaning
is that natural endowment cannot be relied upon,
and learning must rely on human effort;
it does not mean deceitful falsehood.
Yet those who blame Xúnzǐ
say he slandered the sage as deceitful—
this is not examining what the ancients meant,
and hastily judging right or wrong.
In ancient times, characters were few;
mutual explanation and interchangeable use
often combined meanings.
The various masters wrote books,
using characters
each with their own principles,
like military orders,
official regulations,
their own laws and precedents.
The interpretations they established
need not be mutually consistent.
Qū Yuán's *língxiū*,
Zhuāng Zhōu's *yīnshì*,
Hán Fēi's *cānwǔ*,
Guǐgǔ's *bǎihé*,
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí's *zònghéng*—
all, if moved to others' books, would be incomprehensible. Buddhist terms like *gēn*, *chén*, *fǎ*, *xiàng*, and legal terms like *yǐ*, *zhǔn*, *jiē*, *gè*, *jí*, *qí*, *jí*, *ruò* are all like this.
Féng Xuān asked Mèngcháng Jūn,
after collecting debts and reporting back,
what to buy on the return?
He said:
"Look at what my household lacks."
Learning that serves the world,
writings that instruct posterity—
like a physician's medicines for hemiplegia—
also look at what the world lacks.
Using learning and writing
to follow what the world values—
is like offering fine grain and meat when already full,
or adding fox and raccoon fur when already warm.
Not excelling in something
yet forcing oneself to follow it—
is like offering chaff when already full of fine grain and meat,
or offering coarse cloth when already wrapped in fox and raccoon fur.
As for those who seek fur in summer and hemp in winter—
I have rarely seen such.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Those in the world who practice specialized arts
all believe that what they possess cannot be surpassed."
Now, "the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose
each have their own clarity,
yet they cannot communicate with each other."
And all take what they themselves master
as unsurpassable—
this is the fault of lacking self-awareness.
Few in the world are self-aware,
hence those who truly understand each other are rare. All who defend their past actions and refuse to acknowledge others' excellence are largely those lacking self-awareness.
It is traditionally said that Xiāo Yǐngshì could recognize Lǐ Huá's "Essay on the Ancient Battlefield,"
which was considered a true appreciation of literature.
Now, words are rooted in the heart,
and their differences are like faces.
Yǐngshì could not determine at a glance that it was Huá's work,
but vaguely said that Huá was capable of such writing—
this cannot be called true understanding.
And in the world, those who possess Xiāo's discernment
are already fewer than one in ten thousand;
as for people's learning and achievements,
there are certainly those who surpass Lǐ Huá—
what then can the world rely upon?
All who receive form at birth
cannot avoid having distinct inclinations.
All endowed with blood and qi
cannot be without a contentious heart.
With distinct inclinations,
then the弊病 of favoring one's own school while disparaging others,
of allying with those who agree and attacking those who differ, arises.
With a contentious heart,
then, fearing exposure of one's flaws,
the door to jealousy, envy, slander, and defamation opens.
Huìzǐ said:
"Those who flee run east,
those who pursue also run east;
though both run east,
their hearts in running east differ."
Now, many run together—
can they know the hearts of those running alongside?
Seemingly reliable,
seemingly unreliable;
seemingly knowable,
seemingly unknowable—
this is why understanding among those sharing the same path is difficult to articulate.
Ōuyáng Xiū once lamented the "Seven Summaries" and fourfold classification,
that the titles remain but the books are lost,
considering it the misfortune of those authors.
He grieved that writings cannot be relied upon.
Yet since the capture of the unicorn,
in the enterprise of writing,
few have achieved the prominence of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Qiān hid his work in famous mountains,
to be transmitted to the right people;
Gù had his younger sister complete his work,
and Mǎ Róng prostrated outside the pavilion to receive his book—
their works still shine like the sun and moon today.
Yet reading the "Records of the Grand Historian" and "Book of Hàn,"
and examining the annotations by scholars like Xú Guǎng, Péi Yīn, Fú Qián, Yīng Shào,
among them, failing to grasp Qiān and Gù's intent
occurs in three or four out of ten instances.
Even with specialized study and mastery,
they still did not comprehend the ancients' subtleties;
how much more so for casual browsing,
where likes and dislikes are subjective?
For those not transmitted,
there is the lament of empty catalog entries;
for those transmitted,
there are the faults of misinterpreting the original intent,
and the variance of personal preferences.
Seemingly reliable,
seemingly unreliable;
seemingly knowable,
seemingly unknowable—
this is why posthumous understanding is difficult to articulate.
What distinguishes humans from wood and stone
is emotion.
What makes emotion precious
is mutual delight in understanding.
The worthy, unable to attain their aims, still join others to pursue their aspirations;
even in hardship, they find joy in their path with companions;
unable to gain recognition and grand encounters in their time,
they still hope for understanding from posterity after death.
Yet having the principle
does not guarantee the event;
connecting through traces
does not mean connecting through hearts.
Seemingly reliable,
seemingly unreliable;
seemingly knowable,
seemingly unknowable.
Future generations viewing the present
is just like the present viewing the past.
Alas!
This is why Bóyá broke his strings and ceased to play,
and why Biàn Hé clasped his jade and wept in sorrow.
Now, sparrows and magpies chirp,
and many join in harmony.
Reeds, yellow and white,
are trampled by many.
The phoenix soars high at a thousand ren,
the paulownia grows alone at a hundred xún;
knowing they have few harmonizers and no match,
yet unable to bend and follow the crowd—
this too is circumstance.
Therefore, the nobleman works with such zeal that he forgets to eat,
cultivating himself in obscurity,
unaware that old age approaches,
all to fulfill his own task.
How can one, with a finite life,
chase infinite praise and blame?
Explaining "Comprehensiveness"
The "Yì" says:
"Only the nobleman can comprehend the aspirations of the world."
Commentators say the nobleman takes cultured clarity as his virtue;
in times of uniting people,
he can reach the aspirations of the world.
The "Shū" says:
"Then he ordered Zhòng and Lí
to sever the connection between earth and heaven."
Commentators say humans and spirits were not disturbed,
each keeping to their proper order.
The ancient kings, fearing people might conceal their aspirations,
thus used cultured clarity to govern,
comprehending and clarifying human relations,
and broadening the capacity to unite people.
The ancient kings, fearing disorder in governance,
thus divided duties among human offices,
severed connections where inappropriate,
and strictly guarded against encroachments.
Since the six ministers divided the canons,
and the five historians managed writings (Inner Historian, Outer Historian, Grand Historian, Lesser Historian, Imperial Historian),
learning followed specialized teachers,
officials upheld their laws—
this is the meaning of severing earth and heaven.
Numbers converge at nine,
writings essentialize to six,
assorting things and describing virtues,
sharing script and standards—
this is the meaning of reaching the world's aspirations.
After the Master passed away, subtle words ceased;
after the seventy disciples were lost, the great meanings diverged.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
the "Spring and Autumn Annals" split into five,
the "Odes" split into four;
yet those studying the "Gōngyáng"
did not debate the "Zuǒ" or "Gǔliáng";
those mastering Hán's "Odes"
did not mix with Qí or Lǔ traditions—
specialized scholarship
was then at its peak.
Later, master-disciple transmission declined,
scholars' intelligence overflowed broadly,
and divergent theories arose in confusion.
Then, men of deep insight and broad vision,
fearing that the "Ěryǎ" glossary chapters
were insufficient to fully capture ancient, disconnected terms,
and different names for the same reality,
and that compiling scholars
had no way to converge their essential meanings;
thus they summarized the essentials of the "Five Classics,"
distinguished the texts of the six arts,
and works like the Stone Canal "Miscellaneous Discussions" (Bān Gù's "Treatise on Literature and Art," "Miscellaneous Discussions on the Five Classics" in eighteen chapters)
began to separate from the classics and become independent books—
hence the concept of "comprehensiveness" was modeled.
Liú Xiàng collated the "Five Classics" overall,
compiled and recorded the three rites,
and for the various records of the Dài family,
he categorized and titled them,
grouping them by class,
though their meanings were not unified.
Chapters like "Tángōng" and "Lǐyùn"
were all titled "General Discussions"—

thus the fixed name "comprehensiveness" became established (The "Suí Treatise" lists "General Meanings of the Five Classics" in eight scrolls, noting that Liáng had nine scrolls, author unknown. The "Táng Treatise" has Liú Xiàng's "General Meanings of the Five Classics" in nine scrolls. However, before Táng, historical records lack verification).
Bān Gù, following the imperial edict of the Jiànchū era,

composed the "White Tiger Hall Comprehensive Discussions." The "Rúlin Biography" refers to it as "Comprehensive Discussions," while his main biography calls it "Comprehensive Virtue Treatise." Later generations removed the character "yì" (discussions) and called it "White Tiger Hall Comprehensive," which is incorrect.
Yìng Shào, lamenting the failings of the contemporary trends,
wrote the "Comprehensive Discussions on Customs."
Indeed, the detailed exegesis and glosses
gradually lost their essence in later developments,
and the interpretations and discussions of the classics
emerged to remedy this.
These two authors produced works
that became the precursors for later generations to designate as "comprehensive."
From then on, basing their arguments on the classics,
there appeared "Collected Explanations" such as Dù Yù's "Zuǒzhuàn," Fàn Níng's "Gǔliáng," and Hé Yàn's "Lúnyǔ."

"Collected Commentaries" such as Xún Shuǎng's "Nine Schools' Yì," Cuī Líng'ēn's "Máoshī," and Kǒng Lún and Péi Sōngzhī's "Sāngfú Jīngzhuàn." "Differences and Similarities" such as Xǔ Shèn's "Different Meanings of the Five Classics" and Hè Yáng's "Critique of Differences and Similarities in the Five Classics." "Affirmations and Negations" such as Hé Xiū's "Mòshǒu of the Gōngyáng," Zhèng Xuán's "Refutations," and Qiáo Zhōu's "Treatise on Affirmations and Negations of the Five Classics." These various titles;
separating from the classics to write books,
there were works like "Six Arts" (Zhèng Xuán's treatise),
"Sacred Evidence" (Wáng Sù's treatise),
"Correcting Errors" (Táng Yán Shīgǔ's "Correcting Errors and Rectifying Customs"),
"Comprehensive Clarifications" (Sòng Qiū Guāngtíng's "Comprehensive Clarifications Book"). These various categories.
Although these works do not explicitly label themselves as "comprehensive,"
their structure indeed embodies the meaning of comprehensiveness.
The distinctions within the Classics section
must be clearly discerned.
As for the canons of Yáo and Shùn,
they were collectively named the "Book of Xià";

the "Zuǒzhuàn" refers to the "Book of Yú" as the "Book of Xià." Mǎ Róng, Zhèng Xuán, and Wáng Sù all titled the first chapter "Book of Yú and Xià." Fú Shēng's "Great Commentary" also titles its first chapter "Commentary on Yú and Xià."
The "Guóyǔ" and "Guócè"
do not follow the records of Zhōu;
the one hundred and thirty chapters of the "Grand Historian"
constitute a work of its own school;
originally named "The Book of the Grand Historian," it was not called "Shǐjì." Bān Gù's "Treatise on the Five Phases" and "Treatise on Geography"
trace back to Xià and Zhōu ("Geography" begins with the "Tribute of Yǔ," and "Five Phases" integrates with the "Spring and Autumn Annals"),
supplementing the omissions in Sīmǎ Qiān's work, without necessarily limiting it to the Hàn dynasty.
The writings of the ancients, belonging to their own schools,
established their forms upon completion,
their organization and arrangement
were solely based on principle.
They never separately created titles
to divide them into sections.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, considering the works from Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward
to be dynastic histories,
compiled a single work titled "Comprehensive History,"
covering from the Three Sovereigns
down to the Liáng dynasty,
intending to encompass all.
The designation of "comprehensive" in historical records
originated from this.
Thereafter,
the sources and streams gradually diverged.
Synthesizing the scholarship of ancient and modern times,
and modeling the annals and biographies entirely on Sīmǎ Qiān,

Zhèng Qiáo's "Comprehensive Records" was produced. (The essence of "Comprehensive Records" lies in its principles and examples. It represents the scholarship of a single school, the learning of the various masters, embodied within the framework of histories, and was not originally intended to excel in textual criticism. Later critics who fault it for being superficial and crude are mistaken.)
Unifying the treatises of previous histories,
and adopting the official rituals as a model for composition,
Dù Yòu's "Comprehensive Canons" was produced. ("Comprehensive Canons" was based on Liú Zhì's "Political Canons.")
Combining the intertextual elements of annals and biographies (the texts of annals and biographies complement each other in detail and brevity),

and compiling and summarizing based on Xún Yuè and Yuán Hóng (Xún Yuè's "Annals of Hàn" in 30 chapters and Yuán Hóng's "Annals of Later Hàn" in 30 chapters both transformed annals and biographies into chronicles),
Sīmǎ Guāng's "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" was produced.
Collecting both public and private writings,

and compiling them somewhat following the examples of Kǒng Huàn and Xiāo Tǒng (Kǒng Huàn's "Literary Garden" in 100 chapters and Crown Prince Zhāomíng Xiāo Tǒng's "Literary Selections" in 30 chapters),
Péi Jìng's "Comprehensive Selections of Tàihé" was produced.
These four authors
either preserved the format of standard histories ("Comprehensive Records" is an example. Since the "Suíshū·Jīngjízhì," annals and biographies have been classified as standard histories.),
or established the correct form of chronicles ("Comprehensive Mirror"),
or used institutions and precedents as the framework ("Comprehensive Canons"),
or preserved literary documents through belles-lettres ("Comprehensive Selections").
The comprehensive works in the History section

reached their peak here. (Large compilations and general anthologies intended to preserve institutions and precedents should belong to the History section and are not of the same category as literary criticism.)
As for works like Gāo's "Minor History" (Táng, Yuánhé period, Gāo Jùn and his son Gāo Jiǒng) and Yáo's "Comprehensive History" (Táng, Yáo Kāngfù),
they condensed verbose texts
into concise summaries.
Works like Luó's "Lùshǐ" (Sòng, Luó Mì) and Dèng's "Encompassing History" (Míng, Dèng Yuánxī)
possessed their own distinctive judgment

and formed the theories of their own schools. (Works like Qiáo Zhōu's "Examination of Ancient History," Sū Zhé's "Ancient History," and Mǎ Sù's "Expository History" all compile texts from the classics and commentaries and differ from comprehensive histories.)
Fàn's "Comprehensive Records of the Five Dynasties" (Sòng, Fàn Zhì used the chronicle format to record the events of Liáng, Táng, Jìn, Hàn, and Zhōu)

and Xióng's "Comprehensive Summary of Nine Courts" (Sòng, Xióng Kè combined Lǚ Yíjiǎn's "History of Three Courts," Wáng Guī's "History of Two Courts," and Lǐ Tāo and Hóng Mài's "History of Four Courts" to create a chronicle of nine courts)
are labeled as comprehensive but limited to dynasties. (A change in surname constitutes a "dynasty"; a continuous line constitutes a "court.")
Lǐ's "Histories of the Southern and Northern Dynasties" (Lǐ Yánshòu)
and Xuē and Ōu's "Histories of the Five Dynasties" (both Xuē Jūzhèng and Ōuyáng Xiū wrote "Histories of the Five Dynasties")

are dynastic histories that still employ comprehensive methods. (The two categories above, although covering several eras, ultimately have limits and divisions, unlike Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's "Comprehensive History," which integrates ancient and modern times.)
The remaining streams of annals, biographies, and historical accounts,
as well as compilations and edited records,
emerged in profusion and variety.
Although they cannot be uniformly measured,
they generally imitate the concept of Xiāo Liáng's "Comprehensive History"
for the convenience of readers.
The distinctions within the History section
must be understood.
When the methods of the masters were lost,
people became hesitant to return to antiquity.
As the later developments gradually lost the essence,
scholars became confined by their own knowledge and experience.
Glosses evolved into classical exegesis,
first transforming into the Confucian school of the Masters section (like Yìng Shào's "Comprehensive Discussions on Customs" and Cài Yōng's "Independent Judgments"),

then transforming into the recorded sayings of vulgar Confucians (the recorded sayings of Chéng and Zhū; where the recorders lacked discrimination, and by the time of further transmission, the essence was gradually lost, hence called vulgar Confucians),
and thirdly transforming into the lecture notes of mediocre teachers (like the "Méngcún Qiǎndá" category, which are more fragmented and verbose than recorded sayings).
Those unaware grow accustomed and comfortable with them,
while those who know despise and reject them,
not realizing they originate from the comprehensiveness of classical exegesis
but have lost their original intent.
Historical writing converged into comprehensive histories,

first transforming into historical extracts (like "Minor History" and "Comprehensive History," which merely abridge standard histories without distinctive judgment; they should belong to historical extracts. Previous catalogues incorrectly placed them under comprehensive histories. The History section's category of historical extracts began with the "Sòngshǐ."),

then transforming into the categorized summaries of examination candidates (like "Comprehensive Examination of Literary Documents," which, though modeled on "Comprehensive Canons," with its analysis and arrangement, is actually the learning of encyclopedias. The work lacks distinctive insight and comprehensive judgment, making it convenient for examination answers and expositions.),
and thirdly transforming into the excerpted comparisons of elementary primers (like "Combined Compilation of Outline Mirrors" and "Summaries of Current Affairs Policies").
Those unaware grow accustomed and comfortable with them,
while those who know despise and reject them,
not realizing they originate from the comprehensiveness of the History section
but have lost their fundamental source.
Moreover, the "Seven Summaries" evolved into the Four Sections,
with clear classification examples,
no longer deeply seeking the methods of the ancient schools.
However, with the mixing of recorded sayings and lecture notes,
the Classics cease to be Classics,
and the Masters cease to be Masters.
With the confusion of policy summaries and categorized excerpts,
Histories cease to be Histories,
and Collections cease to be Collections.
The Four Sections cannot contain them,
the Nine Schools cannot distinguish them.
They emerge in chaotic profusion,
presumptuously attempting to attach themselves to comprehensive works.
Their distinctions must be strictly discerned.
The ancients, in writing books,
based themselves on existing texts
but created their own systems,
thus achieving specialized scholarship.
Later generations combined and simplified general outlines
for the convenience of consultation,
thus falling into the shallowness of rote memorization.
Classical masters merely differed in their detailed exegesis

and thus established their own schools. (Fèi Zhí's "Yì" and Shēn Péi's "Shī"; the "Rúlin Biography" states they had no other writings or glosses, yet the "Yìwénzhì" lists "Fèi's Explanations" and "Shēngōng's Lǔshī," which likely refer to orally transmitted detailed exegesis.)
Historical books, following and inheriting from each other,

could coexist without hindrance. (For example, Sīmǎ Qiān based his work on the "Spring and Autumn Annals," "Strategies of the Warring States," and other texts; the "Hànshū" was based on Sīmǎ Qiān's records and Liú Xīn's writings. At the time, both works coexisted without concern for inheritance.)
Specialized scholarship
possessed its own ingenuity,
unconcerned with superficial resemblance.
Plagiarized lecture notes,
through long-term habitual use, lost their original intent. (Míng scholars compiling the "Great Compendium" altered the established theories of earlier Confucians to suit their own ideas.)
Excerpted and compared institutions and precedents,
with the original texts available, errors could not be concealed.
The shallowness of rote memorization,
utterly lacking the methods of a school,
easily led to plagiarism.
The compilation of comprehensive histories has six conveniences:
first, avoiding repetition;
second, standardizing categories and examples;
third, facilitating arrangement and allocation;
fourth, balancing judgments of right and wrong;
fifth, eliminating contradictions;
sixth, detailing neighboring affairs.
It has two strengths:
first, possessing skillful editing;
second, establishing a distinctive methodology.
It has three drawbacks:
first, lacking in strengths and weaknesses;
second, retaining original titles;
third, neglecting clear headings.
What is meant by avoiding repetition?
During periods of dynastic change,
figures and events
often appear simultaneously.
The defeated state leaves no records,
while the new king heralds auspicious signs—
this is one and the same event.
The rebels of the former dynasty
become the vanguards of the new ruler—
this is one and the same person.
Dǒng Zhuó and Lǚ Bù
are each given separate biographies by Fàn and Chén;
the edicts of abdication and enthronement
are recorded in full in both the histories of Liáng and Chén—
this is what is called repetition.
The *Tōngzhì* consolidates these into a single work,
where events can be cross-referenced
and the text is not duplicated—
is this not excellent?
What is meant by standardizing categories and examples?
Sīmǎ Qiān established the "Tiānguān" [celestial officials] section,
Bān Gù created the "Dìlǐ" [geography] section;
the "Tiānwén" [astronomy] section of the *Qízhì*
does not include calculations of celestial movements;
the "Yìwén" [bibliography] section of the *Tángshū* does not trace origins.
Since ancient times,
such inconsistencies have existed.
Zhèng Qiáo wrote the *Lüè*,
and although he altered the conventions of historical records,
he established his own methodology.
However, the six scripts and seven sounds
are not originally matters of historical evolution;
insects, plants, and trees—
why must they be carried over unchanged across dynasties?
Only by connecting past and present to form a unified work
can principles arise from meaning,
naturally achieving conciseness.
The historical records of the five dynasties in the *Suíshū* (Liáng, Chén, Běi Qí, Zhōu, Suí)
are ultimately superior to the works of Shěn, Xiāo, and Wèi (Shěn Yuē's *Sòngzhì*, Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's *Nán Qízhì*, Wèi Shōu's *Wèizhì*, all of which are inconsistent).
What is meant by facilitating arrangement and allocation?
Encompassing various histories,
systems and institutions remain consistent.
Only the emergence of figures
varies with the times.
From empresses and imperial clans,
the headings indicate their dynasties;
as for officials,
they are roughly arranged in chronological order,
grouped accordingly (*Nánshǐ* and *Běishǐ* place imperial clans above officials for distinction; Ōuyáng Xiū's *Wǔdàishǐ* begins to clearly mark dynasties).
Thus, descendants are attached to their ancestors,
and noble families gather their lineages (the biographies of Wáng and Xiè in *Nánshǐ* and *Běishǐ* are not strictly divided by dynasty).
A single lineage's bloodline succession
and the rise and fall of eras
can also be observed through this.
Even Qū Yuán of Chǔ
is placed in the same biography as Jiǎ Yí of Hàn;
the Grand Historian of Zhōu
is grouped with the prince of Hán.
The ancients had profound intent in this:
mutual illumination through association,
with judgments made independently.
Superficial scholars of later times—
how could they rashly criticize this?
What is meant by balancing judgments of right and wrong?
Matters of right and wrong
are settled after dynastic change.
Yet the history of Jìn must ultimately recognize Wèi as legitimate,
while the history of Zhōu does not include Hán Tōng among its officials.
Although the authors are outstanding,
sensitivity to state matters demands caution—
this is simply unavoidable.
Only when events are separated by several generations
and evaluation is utterly impartial
can editing be fair
and balanced judgments be established.
What is meant by eliminating contradictions?
Histories divided by dynasty
each have their own editorial standards;
differences in detail and selection
are not mutually obstructive.
Only when beginnings and ends overlap,
with mutual inconsistencies,
do contradictions arise.
The matter of regency
is treated differently by Bān and Fàn;
the accounts of Liú Biǎo and Liú Yān
differ between Fàn and Chén.
Consolidating them into a single compilation
may avoid this.
What is meant by detailing neighboring affairs?
Usurping states' records
and foreign tribes
cannot share the same beginning and end as a single dynasty.
Yet orthodox histories and biographies,
divided by dynasty,
result in the central dynasty's records being complete
while those of tributary states are only half included.
Only in comprehensive histories like *Nánběishǐ*
do Hòu Liáng and Dōng Wèi find their beginnings,
and in compiled histories like *Wǔdàishǐ*,
do Wúyuè, Jīng, and Tán find their conclusions.
These six points
are what are called conveniences.
What is meant by possessing skillful editing?
Combining various histories
is not merely about summarizing their general principles;
it should also supplement omissions,
cut redundant language,
and smooth out inconsistencies,
thereby conforming to a single standard.
For example, Lǐ's *Nánshǐ* and *Běishǐ*
are more concise than previous works
yet richer in detail—
hence they are called excellent histories.
Living in later times,
what one hears and sees
naturally supplements earlier accounts.
This is called the advantage of relying on existing resources,
making the task easier.
What is meant by establishing a distinctive methodology?
Existing works are all available—
why value recompilation?
Specialized scholarship
naturally possesses its own essence.
For instance, Zhèng's *Tōngzhì*
demonstrates exceptional insight and reasoning,
with unique perspectives and editorial judgment.
The ancients could not anticipate its innovations,
and later generations cannot surpass its framework.
Although the facts are no different from old records,
its clarification of names and realities,
embedding the ideas of various philosophers
into historical form,
makes it an immortal achievement.
These two points
are what are called strengths.
What is meant by lacking in strengths and weaknesses?
Compiled works
merely arrange materials in order,
with no additions or deletions,
only changing headings.
This is what Liú Zhījī called: "Scholars would rather study the original texts
than bother with new compilations."
What is meant by retaining original titles?
Different histories have varying classifications;
if the author does not revise them
to fit the new framework,
issues arise. For example, *Nánshǐ* has "Xiàoyì" [filial piety and righteousness] but not "Liènǚ" [exemplary women] (see the "Liènǚ" chapter);

*Tōngzhì* uses *Shǐjì* to indicate periods (*Tōngzhì* labels Hàn and Wèi figures by dynasty, not by historical work, but figures from *Shǐjì* are labeled by the work rather than period—a case of mistakenly retaining the original).
From one example, infer others—
there are many instances of inappropriate selection.
What is meant by neglecting clear headings?
Emperors, empresses, imperial clans, and noble families
have headings indicating their dynasties,
making distinctions easy to see.
Biographies of officials
naturally relate to contemporary events;
though not explicitly labeled,
their era can be discerned from the narrative.
However, chapters like "Dúxíng" [unique conduct], "Fāngjì" [special skills], "Wényuàn" [literati], and "Liènǚ" [exemplary women]
feature individuals not deeply involved in worldly affairs.
If compiled uniformly,
as with figures like Wú Kuí and Hán Língmǐn in *Nánshǐ*,
how can readers avoid not knowing their historical context?
These three points
are what are called drawbacks.
The Shuōwén defines "tōng" (comprehensive) as "dá" (penetrating),
meaning to go from here to there.
"Tōng" (comprehensive)
is that which connects what is unconnected in the world.
Reading the Yì (Book of Changes) as if the Shū (Book of Documents) did not exist,
reading the Shū as if the Shī (Book of Songs) did not exist.
The Ěryǎ manages glosses and explanations,
the "Lesser Learning" clarifies the six scripts,
this is what is meant by "tōng" (comprehensive).
When the ancients compiled works by separating and combining,
it was understood without being stated.
The Han people used "tōng" as a category heading,
the Liang dynasty incorporated "tōng" into historical genres.
Thus, their forms and conventions
were clearly distinct and could not be mixed.
Dù Yòu considered Liú Zhì's "Zhèngdiǎn" (Political Compendium) incomplete,
and extended it upwards to the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
hence the name "Diǎn" (Compendium) was called "Tōng" (Comprehensive).
Why then did Wèi Liǎowēng take the administrative precedents of the Zhào Sòng dynasty,
and also label it "Guócháo Tōngdiǎn" (Comprehensive Compendium of the Imperial Dynasty)?
Since it is called "Imperial Dynasty",
delimited by the dynasty's period,
what comprehensiveness is there?
This is also following the name without considering its meaning.
The six ministers jointly managing affairs,
books on official posts,
also have the meaning of "tōng" (comprehensive).
Why then did Pān Dí take the duties of the Censorate in the Yuán dynasty,
and also name his book "Xiàntái Tōngjì" (Comprehensive Records of the Censorate)?
Furthermore, the study of geography
has its own specialization.
Gazetteers of prefectures and commanderies
should belong to the Outer Histories (see detailed discussion in the Outer Chapter: "Discussion on the Bózhōu Gazetteer").
The early Míng dynasty changed the Yuán dynasty's provincial system to thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions,
the subordinate prefectures, subprefectures, counties, and garrisons
each had their own local gazetteers.
Since the jurisdiction of the Provincial Administration Commissions was vast,
and the various prefectures and counties within it
feared that each writing their own books
would lack uniformity,
therefore they compiled and combined their subordinate areas,
creating separate comprehensive gazetteers.
"Tōng" (comprehensive)
is that which connects the prefectures, subprefectures, counties, and garrisons that are otherwise unconnected.
Why then do those compiling comprehensive gazetteers
take prefectures, subprefectures, counties, mountains, rivers, people, and things,
classify and compile them,
using prefectures to lead counties,
using counties to lead factual records and human affairs,
extracting and dividing them under separate headings,
without interconnecting them?
If a book is made like this,
then readers might as well just consult the original prefectural and county gazetteers,
so what need is there for a "comprehensive" one?
Now, comprehensive histories and human affairs,
spanning a thousand years up and down,
yet where principles and conventions connect,
compiling across dynasties is not considered objectionable.
The areas governed by a Provincial Administration Commission
are only a few dozen subprefectures and counties,
yet they meticulously demarcate boundaries,
fearing only to overstep them,
truly because they lack the insight of comprehensive talent,
thus making their books no different from those of petty clerks.
Horizontal Comprehensiveness
The name "tōngrén" (comprehensive scholar)
cannot be applied indiscriminately.
Some have the depth of specialization,
others have the breadth of wide learning.
Each has its own unchangeable aspect;
changing it would prevent excellence.
Each has its own sphere that does not interfere with the other;
interfering would not be beneficial.
However, the term "tōng" (comprehensive)
is likely an analogy taken from roads,
intersecting from four sides and reaching eight directions,
there is nowhere it cannot reach,
hence it is called "tōng".
It also refers to what the mind comprehends;
although there are differences in level, bias/completeness, size, and breadth/narrowness,
all can reach the great Way,
therefore it is called "tōng".
Yet there are also those that cannot intersect from four sides and reach eight directions,
cannot reach the great Way,
but still must be called "tōng",
this is called "héngtōng" (horizontal comprehensiveness).
The relationship between "héngtōng" and "tōngrén"
is both similar and different,
close yet distant,
connected yet separate.
Old merchants skilled at selling books,
old families rich in book collections,
enthusiasts courageous in printing books—
all are those with whom the erudite and elegant mingle and enter the groves of learning.
When rituals are lost, seek them in the countryside;
their knowledge and experience can also somewhat supplement what the erudite and elegant lack,
thus they are certainly people the gentleman must visit.
However, such individuals are merely lute craftsmen and stele engravers,
whose skills happen to connect with refinement and elegance.
Since they interact with many famous scholars,
and are accustomed to hearing refined discourses and famous arguments,
yet lack pearls of wisdom in their own minds,
then their hearsay and roadside talk,
the shallowness of their foundation,
is not difficult to perceive.
Academician Zhōu Chángfā
called such people "héngtōng",
his words are unusual yet accurate.
Therefore, the gentleman takes their strengths
and overlooks their weaknesses,
just as lute craftsmen and stele engravers are sufficient to be of use.
It is not that scholars are limited in knowledge and experience;
upon encountering the arguments of "héngtōng",
it is already like a sudden thunderclap splitting a mountain,
thus causing fish eyes to be mixed with pearls,
and clear streams to have no distinction.
And such people then arrogantly consider themselves,
unaware that their comprehensiveness stems from the "horizontal".
Waving the duster in the rivers and lakes,
opening a different style of lute craftsmen and stele engravers' tradition—
this is where the gentleman should be careful about intellectual lineages.
Xú Shēng was skilled in ritual demeanor,
Zhì Shì understood the sounds of bells and chimes;
when the Hàn court discussed rituals and music,
even veteran Confucian scholars and aged experts
were not as good as Xú Shēng and Zhì Shì in some aspects.
Those discussing rituals and music,
how could they not interact with them?
However, the discussions in the Shíqú and Tiānlù pavilions
were not something Xú Shēng and Zhì Shì could participate in.
These are also examples of "horizontal comprehensiveness" in rituals and music.
Can "héngtōng" people be dispensed with?
They cannot be dispensed with.
Using their "horizontal" comprehensiveness
to assist the gentleman's "vertical" [comprehensiveness].
The gentleman also does not obscure the resources provided by their "horizontal" [aspect].
Then, like Xú Shēng's ritual demeanor,
Zhì Shì's knowledge of bells and chimes,
their contribution to rituals and music—
is it really small?
It is not that they themselves are unaware of their "horizontal" nature,
nor that the gentleman fails to recognize their "horizontal" nature.
Thus, if rituals have jade and silk,
then weavers and jade carvers
could participate in the high hall's discussions;
if music has bells and drums,
then metal casters and leather workers
could discuss the records of Héjiān.
Therefore, the gentleman must understand intellectual lineages,
and "héngtōng" must not forcibly attach themselves to the clear stream,
then there will be no harm.
Evaluating women's poetry and prose,
often involves indulgence;
writing prefaces and postfaces for "héngtōng",
often involves praise;
one pities their beauty,
the other utilizes their usefulness.
If, like in examinations, names were concealed and handwriting changed,
and someone with a slight sense of discernment
were to analyze them in detail,
they could not be deceived.
Even so,
women's poetry and prose
are merely about wind, clouds, moon, and dew,
their vulgarity is easily seen.
Prefaces and postfaces for "héngtōng",
however, praise scholarship;
a single word can be wise or unwise.
The gentleman in this matter
should indeed be cautious.
People of "héngtōng"
all love fame.
Those who love fame
are shallow in understanding true meaning.
Those they attach themselves to
are certainly not of the first rank.
If they had the keen hearing of Shī Kuàng,
whose discernment reached even ghosts and spirits,
that would be detestable.
Therefore, in the gentleman's association with "héngtōng",
he does not exhaust their joy,
nor does he exhaust his loyalty.
For tested praise,
leaving words unexhausted,
is also sufficient for mutual interaction.
Prolixity.
I have read the Zuǒzhuàn,
and found it troublesome that the way it records people's names
does not follow established rules.
In childhood, one has a given name;
upon capping, one receives a courtesy name;
at fifty, one is referred to by a style (like Bó or Zhòng);
and after death, one receives a posthumous title—
this is the way of the Zhōu.
These are terms used in ritual texts,
not the conventions for historical writing in narrating events.
The Zuǒzhuàn, however, mixes them arbitrarily
without consistent principles.
Moreover, beyond names, courtesy names, posthumous titles, and styles,
it also includes official titles, ranks, and fiefs.
Within a single chapter,
these appear interchangeably.
Were it not for the transmitted commentaries,
handed down through instruction,
we would no longer recognize who these people were.
Thus, later historical writings
all revere the Zuǒzhuàn,
yet in this matter alone,
they do not follow its example.
Sīmǎ Qiān created the biographical style,
and the term "biography" (lièzhuàn)
means arranging individuals from beginning to end,
thus distinguishing it from the chronological annals.
However, the way he lists names
is also inconsistent:
sometimes by title, like "Marquis of Huáiyīn,"
sometimes by office, like "General Lǐ,"
and sometimes directly by given name.
Though not as jumbled as in the Zuǒzhuàn,
it still lacks pure principles.
Some say:
"Qiān had subtle intentions."
Recording events directly,
letting good and evil reveal themselves—
this is the meaning of the Chūnqiū.
If one must use labels to show praise or blame,
why wonder that works like those of Shěn Yuē and Wèi Shōu
treat headings as mere playthings!
Moreover, among the seventy biographies,
those referring to official titles
are occasional exceptions;
the rest directly use given names,
and these are not cases where the principle demands criticism.
Thus, in Sīmǎ Qiān's pioneering work,
there were inevitably flaws.
To insist on justifying them
would harm the Way.
The customs of the late Táng and Five Dynasties were bizarre:
people were referred to without surname or given name,
often using playful, cryptic allegories.
Readers glancing at such texts
would not know who was being discussed.
For instance, Lǐ might be called "Lǒngxī,"
and Wáng labeled "Lángyá"—
though somewhat improper,
this still indicated their ancestral commanderies.
But referring to the surname Zhuāng as "Lacquer Garden"
or the surname Niú as "Grand Sacrifice"
was mere jest and farce,
no longer conforming to literary principles.
All such practices
began with ornate parallel prose,
gradually spread to letters and fiction,
and then ignorant literati
used them to record events.
No wonder examination essays
degenerated into obscure jargon,
and the art of writing fell into chaos.
Since Ōuyáng Xiū and Zēng Gǒng
purged the bizarre eccentricities of the late Táng and Five Dynasties,
over the several hundred years of Sòng and Yuán,
though literary quality varied,
the style and substance all valued clarity and purity—
this is praiseworthy.
Yet Sòng people also opened the door to petty artifice:
everyone had a sobriquet,
and not just one,
but three or more.
In ancient simplicity,
people only had given names.
The Zhōu valued refinement,
hence childhood names and capping names.
Thus, juniors addressing superiors
often avoided the given name and used the courtesy name.
Hence it is said: "The courtesy name expresses virtue."
If this was insufficient and sobriquets were added,
what explanation is there?
By recent times,
customs grew increasingly decadent:
first, given names were dropped for courtesy names,
then courtesy names were dropped for sobriquets.
Thus, juniors addressing superiors
not only avoided the given name
but also the courtesy name,
considering it offensive—
is this not flattery and profanity?
Confucius said:
"If names are not correct,
speech will not be in accord."
Using sobriquets and avoiding courtesy names—
is this not the epitome of incorrectness and discord?
The origin of sobriquets
did not begin with the Sòng.
In the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods,
signs of it already appeared.
Táo Zhū and Chīyí Zǐpí
were names assumed to escape notice.
Figures like Hèguàn and Guǐgǔ
concealed their true names,
and people gave them sobriquets based on their attire or dwellings.
None were without reason.
During the Táng's Kāiyuán era,
when Daoism was revered,
there were titles like "Perfected One," such as Nánhuá and Chōngxū,
or "Dharma Master," like Yèjìng Fǎshī,
or female Daoist titles, like Tàizhēn Yùfēi,
or monastic titles, like Sānzàng Fǎshī. (Sānzàng was in Tàizōng's time, not Kāiyuán, but is mentioned here as an example.)
These were labels used by Daoist and Buddhist followers,
later extended to recluses like Chén Tuán and Lín Bū.
Gradually, this spread among scholars.
Yet those bestowed by the court,
though not canonical,
were still not self-chosen.
Considering the intent of such honors,
for the deceased, it was like a posthumous title;
for the living, like an official title—
mere empty praise.
The proliferation of self-chosen sobriquets
imitated ancestral commanderies,
and degenerated in later excesses.
Since the Six Dynasties, families competed in flaunting ancestral commanderies:
when referring to someone,
they did not use their actual birthplace
but only the illustrious commandery of their clan,
placing it before the name.
This is why Liú Zǐxuán was ridiculed by historians.
Over time,
using commanderies became mere literary ornament.
Once such ornamentation sought novelty,
people vied in oddity and artifice,
creating names according to their whims,
for self-promotion.
Thus, early sobriquets
often derived from mountains, springs, woods, or marshes,
showing they were variations of commanderies,
based on one's dwelling place.
Gradually, these shifted to halls, studios, pavilions, or gardens,
reflecting a change from dwelling places
to imagined buildings.
At first, they were tied to actual locations,
but later, locations became unnecessary—
private, imagined landscapes emerged.
At first, they might have actual buildings,
but later, buildings became unnecessary—
airborne towers and pavilions were constructed.
The discerning see only people's fondness for artifice,
not realizing it began with the abuse of commanderies.
Thus, the gentleman detests the originator.
Peaks, springs, streams, bridges,
towers, pavilions, studios, halls—
these became tiresomely repetitive.
Then arose sobriquets from puns and hidden meanings,
which Sòng and Yuán people had not yet pioneered,
but which flourished in the Míng and recent times. (Some took homophones for sobriquets, others split or combined characters.)
Bandits create sobriquets
to confuse the masses. (Examples like Chìméi and Huángjīn are numerous.)
Courtesans and actors create sobriquets
to charm patrons. (Examples like Yàn, Yīng, Juān, Sù are numerous.)
Yet scholars and officials, uneasy with their own names,
eagerly adopt sobriquets—
this is simply thoughtless.
Escaped prisoners often change names
for fear of recognition.
Maidservants sold off change names
for new masters.
Thus, frequently escaped prisoners
and resold maidservants
have many names—
this is unavoidable.
If literati, having established sobriquets,
must convey some meaning,
it is understandable,
and one is enough.
Yet one is insufficient,
and they have three or even five. Alas!
This can only be called undaunted by trouble.
When the ancients wrote books,
they often did not indicate chapter titles.
Later scholars, in collating and editing,
would then name the chapters using the opening words or phrases.
If the book title was not indicated,
later collators and editors,
would name the book after its author.
This shows that the ancients had no intention of self-promotion.
Those that had chapter or book titles
were all clear and easy to understand,
never intentionally obscure or paradoxical.
However, when a single book had two names,
with earlier and later versions varying in simplicity or elaboration,
and no fixed standard,
it was all due to collators and editors
changing titles for cataloging purposes,
followed uncritically over time,
thus giving rise to discrepancies.
It was never the case that the original authors
themselves sought novelty
or aimed for paradox.
There are cases where the original name was plain but the cataloged name adopted an elaborate one,
cases where the original name was elaborate but the cataloged name adopted a plain one,
cases where the book was originally complete but was partially cited by others,
and cases where the book was originally partial but was fully cited by others.
Scholars must be aware of this.
Examples of original names being plain but cataloged names adopting elaborate ones include:
The Lǎozǐ originally had no sutra title,
but the book was honored as the Dàodé Jīng;
the Zhuāngzǐ was originally named after its author,
but the book was recorded as the Nánhuá Zhēnjīng,

which is indeed the case. In the Hàn dynasty, it was called Zhuāngzǐ. In the Táng dynasty, it was officially honored as the Nánhuá Zhēnjīng. By the Kāiyuán era, the Suíshū Yìwénzhì already listed the title Nánhuá.
Examples of original names being elaborate but cataloged names adopting plain ones include:
the book by Liú Ān,
originally titled Hóngliè Jiě,
but the Hànshū Yìwénzhì only records it as Huáinán Nèiwài;
the book by Kuǎi Tōng,
originally titled Juànyǒng,
but the Hànshū Yìwénzhì only records it as Kuǎi Tōng, using the original name,
which is indeed the case. Juànyǒng had eighty-one sections, as seen in his biography, which does not match the record in the Yìwénzhì.
Examples of book titles originally being complete but partially cited by others include:
the Lǚshì Chūnqiū, which has twelve annals, eight surveys, and six discourses,
but later people sometimes referred to it as Lǚlǎn;
the twenty-five pieces by Qū Yuán,
with Lísāo specifically being the first piece,
but later generations ended up calling it Sāofù, which is an example. Liú Xiàng named it Chǔcí, and later generations made it a distinct category.
Examples of book titles originally being partial but fully cited by others include:
Shǐjì being the general name for historical records,
but later people specifically named it Tàishǐgōng Shū;
Sūn Wǔ’s more than eighty pieces,
with diagrams and texts,
but later people referred to the thirteen chapters as Sūnzǐ,
which is indeed the case.
These are all matters that collators and catalogers should pay attention to, as detailed in the Jiàochóu Tōngyì.
Although there are shifts between simplicity and elaboration,
and the times may have their reasons,
if catalogers
do not clarify these distinctions,
then the resulting flaws
are no different from the paradox of using alternative names or titles.
For works in the categories of masters and histories,
the similarities and differences in names and realities
are indeed unavoidable in transmission.
The rise of collected works
all came from later compilations by others,
so they were named after individuals
to indicate distinction;
from the Eastern Hàn to the early Táng,
there were no other variations.
By the mid-Táng, literati
began compiling their own collected works,
often marking them with collection names,
such as Huìchāng Yīpǐn, Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì’s Chángqìng collections,
which were also excessive.
However, naming them after eras
was still acceptable.
Some used place names, like Dù Mù’s Fánchuān Collection, Dúgū Jí’s Pílíng Collection.
Some used official titles, like Hán Wò’s Hànlín Collection.
These still had some basis.
As for humorous or mocking works,
arbitrarily labeled with names,
such as Jǐn Náng by Lǐ Sōng, Wàng Quán by Yáng Huáiyù, Pī Shā by Lǐ Xiányòng, Tú Lóng by Xióng Jiǎo, Áo Shū by Shěn Yán, Màn Biān by Yuán Jié,
with numerous such titles,
the elegance of great refinement
could no longer be restored.
For works in the categories of masters and histories,
their names were established based on their substance,
out of necessity.
Collected works, however, are scattered writings compiled into collections.
Since the pieces are scattered,
they each arise from specific occasions,
with their own titles,
so there was never a problem of unclear intent.
Therefore, when collecting poems or prose,
since they are scattered but grouped as the words of one person,
naming the collection after the person
is sufficient for identification.
The best cases are where
the writings, though scattered, share a unified intent,
which indeed follows the legacy of masters and histories specialists.
The next best cases are where
the literary quality is excellent,
and they are gathered together,
which is also an achievement in literary craftsmanship.
Since the prose and poems
already have their own titles,
there is no need to take the collected poems and prose and give them another name.
Human nature loves novelty,
and competing to create titles
is already excessive.
When one name is not enough,
they divide into earlier and later compilations,
split chapters and pieces,
or take official ranks,
or travel routes,
flaunting wealth and glory if prosperous,
or hinting at hardship if humble,
ingeniously creating names,
arbitrarily dividing labels;
thus, for one person’s poems and prose,
there are countless collection names,
the records of titles
proliferate beyond the writings themselves,
chapters and volumes cannot be standardized,
cataloging cannot be simplified;
and when asked about their intent,
examining their literary quality,
they are like barren reeds,
with no distinction whatsoever;
such works should all be consigned to the flames,
how could they be allowed to clutter the shelves?
Rectifying Errors
Prefaces to books
are meant to clarify the author’s intent,
not for aesthetic display.
Preface to a chapter
is meant to clarify the intent of that chapter.
As for the sequence of chapters,
their order and arrangement,
the ancients sometimes followed principles of meaning and structure,
and sometimes did not,
summarizing the book’s intent accordingly,
without forcing anything.
The two chapters of Xù Guà in the Zhōuyì,
explain the sequence and interrelation of the sixty-four hexagrams,
from Qián, Kūn, Zhūn, Méng onward,
each transition has its explanation.
Although the meaning of the Yì is not exhausted here,
this is also inherent to the Yì’s meaning,
and not forcibly imposed.
Observing later people’s prefaces to books,
I find them incomprehensible.
The original intent of the book
had no inherent sequence of chapters,
yet inspired by the ancients,
they also write chapter prefaces.
Filling them with trivial phrases,
forcing rhyming words,
claiming “thus making such-and-such chapter first,”
“thus discussing such-and-such chapter second.”
Thinking themselves like Huáinán, Grand Historian, Bān Gù, Yáng Xióng,
how deluded!
As for “making” and “discussing,”
I have indeed heard the terms.
But “thus first,” “thus second,”
what is the basis for such claims?
Take, for example, the Xù Guà: Zhūn follows Qián and Kūn,
which must have its meaning.
Heaven and earth are filled with all things,
that is the meaning of Zhūn following Qián and Kūn.
Thus, “it is received by Zhūn”
means it cannot be received by Xū, Sòng, or other hexagrams,
but must be received by Zhūn for that reason.
For Méng, Xū, and onward,
it is the same.
This is why the Xù Guà discusses sequence.
Later people’s chapter prefaces
merely state that such a chapter must be written.
Forcing connections between earlier and later chapters,
linking them into text,
how can there be no possibility of interchangeability,
as with the sequence of Zhūn and Méng?
Thus, those who emulate the Yì’s prefaces
would do better to follow the prefaces to the Shī and Shū.
The chapter order of the Shī and Shū,
is it entirely without principles of meaning and structure?
But there is no such thing as one chapter necessarily following another in a specific way.
The Six Classics transmit teachings,
their principle is one.
Why favor the Yì’s prefaces
and slight those of the Shī and Shū?
As for books that are composed based on images and numbers,
their chapters and sections can be sought through images and numbers.
If a book originally has no connection to images and numbers,
yet one insists on seeking images and numbers to substantiate it,
then it becomes forced and artificial.
The *Yì* (Book of Changes) has the Two Forms and Four Images,
eight times eight generating each other,
its hexagrams number sixty-four,
all emerging naturally from the principles of heaven.
The *Tàixuán* (Supreme Mystery) has nine times nine as eighty-one,
the *Qiánxū* (Hidden Emptiness) has five times five as twenty-five.
Books that imitate the *Yì*
have their numbers predetermined,
and only then are the texts composed.
Therefore, their chapters and sections
are akin to the formations and ranks in military strategy,
which can be succinctly calculated.
Sīmǎ Qiān wrote one hundred and thirty chapters,
claiming to continue the renowned works and succeed the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals).
Truly,
it is a masterpiece unparalleled since the Three Dynasties.
However, his own imitation
also contains excesses.
The twelve Basic Annals
secretly emulate the twelve dukes of the *Chūnqiū*.
The "Qín Jì" (Annals of Qin) separates the period before Zhuāngxiāng,
making it a separate scroll,
and, not concluding with the era of Hàn Wǔdì,
he composed the "Jīnshàng Běnjì" (Basic Annals of the Present Emperor),
clearly intending to allocate space
to fulfill the number twelve.
The Master's *Chūnqiū*,
with its text completed and rules established,
has twelve reign periods,
which happened to fit the times;
it was not originally that thirteen would have been excessive
and twelve insufficient.
Hàn dynasty scholars seeking antiquity
were often constrained by superficial traces;
even one as discerning as Historian Qiān
could not avoid this,
as seen in such cases.
Yet this pertains only to the Basic Annals;
other chapters may not all have such intent.
But scholars studying Qiān's work eagerly and repeatedly force connections,
saying the twelve Basic Annals
represent the twelve months;
the eight Treatises represent the eight winds;
the ten Tables represent the ten heavenly stems;
the thirty Hereditary Houses represent the thirty days of a month;
the seventy Biographies represent the seventy-two pentads;
the one hundred and thirty chapters represent a year plus an intercalary month.
This is fragmented and difficult to comprehend.
Even if we accept their argument,
then the Tables representing the ten stems,
the Annals should represent the twelve earthly branches.
How could the emperors' annals instead use earthly numbers,
while the kings and marquises use heavenly numbers?
The years do not reach three,
how can they symbolize an intercalary month?
The seventy-two pentads,
why are two missing?
Examining the names and demanding the reality,
contradictions are encountered everywhere.
Nevertheless, various masters of the philosophical and historical schools
often follow this theory,
some taking yīn-yáng and odd-even numbers,
some taking the generation of the five phases,
with few numbers combined into three or five,
or many matched up to a hundred or ten,
preferring to shorten the duck and lengthen the crane,
insisting that images and numbers must correspond.
Mèngzǐ's seven chapters
must correspond to the seven governors;
Qū Yuán's "Jiǔ Gē" (Nine Songs),
hardly matches the nine sections;
recently, like Dèng's *Hánshǐ* (Comprehensive History) with its old yáng and young yáng,
or the *Jǐngyuè Quánshū* (Complete Works of Jǐngyuè) with its eight directions and eight formations,
then how close are these to being child's play?
When the ancients wrote books and named chapters,
they aimed to distinguish them by order,
not with profound meaning.
The texts of the Six Arts,
are fully recognizable today.
There are fixed names
and unfixed names,
but all essentially serve to distinguish order,
not with profound meaning.
Fixed names

are like Diǎn (Canon), Mó (Counsel), Gòng (Tribute), Fàn (Model) and such (e.g., *Dì Diǎn* [Canon of Emperor Yáo], *Gāoyáo Mó* [Counsel of Gāoyáo], *Yǔ Gòng* [Tribute of Yǔ], *Hóng Fàn* [Great Plan] are all ancient classic fixed names. Others like *Duōfāng* [Many Regions], *Duōshì* [Many Officers], *Zǐcái* [Timber of Rottlera] are not fixed names.).
Unfixed names,
are like the *Fēng* (Airs), *Yǎ* (Odes), *Sòng* (Hymns) of the *Shī* (Book of Songs) (all take the first two characters of the chapter as the name.).
The books of the various philosophers and historical records
also have both fixed and unfixed names,
following the text to establish examples,
too numerous to list;
their purpose to distinguish order,
without profound meaning,
is largely the same (books of images and numbers are not in this category.).
After the Master passed away, subtle words ceased;
the twenty chapters of the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects)
are indeed the profound repository of the Six Arts.
However, chapter titles like "Xué Ér" (To Learn) and "Wéi Zhèng" (Governing)
all take the opening words or phrases as labels,
with no other meaning.
The seven chapters of the *Mèngzǐ*,
some say were recorded by disciples like Wàn Zhāng,
some say were written by Mèngzǐ himself,
but in essence, it is also a book reciting and emulating the *Lúnyǔ*.
Chapter names like "Liáng Huìwáng" and "Gōngsūn Chǒu"
are likewise the opening words or phrases,
taken to label the chapters,
how could there be any other reason?
Commentators not seeking the principles within the chapters,
but excessively seeking meaning in the external titles,
then their interpretation becomes forced.
Questions and answers between teacher and disciple
are naturally common occurrences;
if they happen to be at the chapter's beginning and are taken to name the chapter,
what is so strange about that?
Commentators think that Wèi Línggōng and Jì Shì
were the feudal lords and ministers of that time,
and Confucius' virtue made him a teacher fit for kings,
hence they were taken to name chapters,
while chapters like "Gōngyě" and "Yōng Yě"
are placed among the disciples.
Chapter names in the *Mèngzǐ* include "Liáng Huìwáng" and "Téng Wéngōng",
both feudal lords of the time,
yet they are listed alongside chapters like "Wàn Zhāng" and "Gōngsūn Chǒu",
following the same pattern.
This can indeed be called far-fetched and unreasonable.
Even if we accept their argument,
then the *Lúnyǔ* has the chapter "Tàibó",
an ancient sage.
"Yáo Yuē",
an ancient sage emperor.
Would they then push the Master to be the teacher of Yáo and Tàibó?
"Wēizǐ",
was Confucius' ancestor.
Using "Wēizǐ" as a chapter title,
would that make an ancestor a disciple?
Moreover, among the feudal lords,
such as Qí Huán and Jìn Wén,
were they not more worthy than Wèi Líng?
Disciples are naturally considered among contemporaries; then Lǔ Āi and Qí Jǐng were also more worthy than Wèi Líng, so he should not have chosen this. Yàn Yīng and Qú Yuàn,
were they not more worthy than Jì Shì?
They appear in the same chapter;
why not elevate them to the chapter beginning,
but instead discard them and choose this?
Mèngzǐ's treatment of Gàozi,
was to belittle him as not worth mentioning.
Yet to place him alongside Gōngsūn and Wàn Zhāng
in the same rank,
