shows no sense of right and wrong.
Holding to this principle to interpret books,
no wonder later generations writing books,
recklessly imitating the ancients without grasping their intent,
continue endlessly.
Some say:
attaching chapter titles,
forcing labels and banners,
is likely the work of Han Confucian scholars interpreting the classics,
who, in seeking explanations, inevitably went too far.
Yet did these Han scholars act thus
without any insight whatsoever,
rashly asserting their own whims?
I say:
I fear that lowly scholars of the late Zhou
had already initiated this trend.
The flourishing of book-writing
reached its peak during the Warring States period;
using book-writing as a means to secure a livelihood and official salary
also began in the Warring States.
Thus, when Qu Píng’s draft manuscripts
were coveted by Shàngguān,
and the *Strategies of the Warring States* often records petitions written for others,
then literature gained importance,
and book-writing opened the door to borrowing and fabrication.
When the King of Qín saw the chapters “Five Vermin” and “Solitary Indignation,”
he regretted
not being born in the same era as their author,
so subordinates used this to seek advancement,
and superiors also used it to select talent.
As seekers multiplied,
boasting and self-promotion arose,
and the practice of embellishment and pretense began.
I perused the *Bibliographic Treatise of the Hàn*,
and among the Confucian school,
there are texts titled *Lord Wén of Wèi* and *Lord Píngyuán*.
Readers, failing to examine closely,
wonder why feudal lords and noble scions of the Warring States
are included among Confucian works.
They do not realize that the authors,
claiming to be Confucians,
narrated how these lords and scions sought instruction and posed questions,
thus naming the chapters after those inquired of.
The books are lost,
and later generations, misled by the chapter titles,
mistakenly believed they were written by Lord Wén and Lord Píngyuán themselves.
Could those who wrote books to follow trends of the time
possess such virtue as to be teachers,
with feudal lords and high ministers
making indiscriminate choices,
all following them to seek instruction?
Surely there were cases where no such events occurred,
and authors falsely claimed associations with the noble and prominent to deceive the world.
The *Strategies of the Warring States*,
largely recording the schemes of strategists of the time,
also occasionally includes clever plots and cunning plans
that went unused at the time.
Yet the writers,
unable to part with them,
fabricated dialogues between rulers and ministers to satisfy their inclinations,
as seen in Master Sū’s dealings with Lord Xuē and the Crown Prince of Chǔ—
clear evidence of this.
Thus, the poor and lowly claiming conversations with the eminent,
the foolish and ignorant aligning with the wise and noble,
the boastful and deceitful ways of strategists,
coupled with an era of rhetorical ostentation,
had long swept the world.
And scholars interpreting the classics, witnessing such contemporary practices,
came to believe that the lofty virtue of sages and worthies
must have relied on feudal lords and high ministers honoring them as teachers,
thereby rising above their age.
Alas!
This was being confined by the prevailing customs of the time.
Did the use of fabricated dialogues in writing exist in antiquity? I say:
There are cases moving from reality to fiction,
such as the allegories in *Zhuāngzǐ* and *Lièzǐ*,
which recount dialogues between Yáo, Shùn, Confucius, and Yán Huí—
recognizable at a glance as allegorical.
There are cases moving from fiction to reality,
such as the fisherman and Zhān Yǐn mentioned in *The Songs of Chǔ*,
who originally did not exist,
but are presented as speaking with Qu Yuán—
these are absent in reality but inherent to Qu Yuán’s work,
also recognizable as allegorical.
There are cases of literary fabrication,
such as the Crown Prince of Chǔ and the guest from Wú,
or Mr. Wūyǒu and Zǐxū.
There are cases of substantive fabrication,
such as the *Gōngyáng* and *Gǔliáng* commentaries on the classics,
which pose questions and challenges
without naming individuals—
this is an example.
Later scholars, wielding ornate language,
often resorted to deceptive fabrications,
knowing readers would not cling to literal details.
But in examining doubts and difficulties,
true names must be known.
If the person is unknown,
one may infer based on intent,
then refer to “someone asked,”
lest fabricated words
mislead later generations.
Regarding recent literary works,
I cannot help but have doubts.
For easily understood principles,
it is unnecessary to speak.
If one must speak,
writing directly in the book
is also acceptable.
If an author insists on posing questions,
that is already pedantic.
If one must pose questions,
using pseudonyms like “A” and “B,”
or referring to “someone asked,”
are all permissible.
But insisting on naming real persons to substantiate them—
what is the reasoning?
Moreover, those named
must be contemporaries with some association,
and possess a degree of reputation—
otherwise, they are insufficient for promotion.
To take someone’s writings
and then pose questions back to them,
when that person initially knows nothing of it—
is that not slanderous?
Furthermore, in the format of questions and answers,
the questioner must be shallow,
and the answerer must be profound;
the questioner must be wrong,
and the answerer must be right.
Now, fabricating dialogues
means always attributing depth and correctness to oneself,
while attributing shallowness and error to others—
is that not mean-spirited?
In their writings,
if it suffices to clarify their meaning
and adjudicate right and wrong,
even if there truly were such a person,
a gentleman would still conceal the name to preserve kindness.
How much more so when there was originally no such statement, yet forcibly attributing it to someone?
Slandering others to gain fame
is no different from
robbing others for profit.
Moreover, literary composition has its ebbs and flows,
often borrowing the format of questions and answers for rhetorical effect.
This is a matter of literary momentum,
not originally related to hidden meanings.
If one must still pose questions here,
it must be due to extreme foolishness and ignorance.
Now, to accuse others of foolishness and ignorance
to serve the ebbs and flows of one’s own writing—
is like borrowing an official’s title for rhyme.
Once, a low-ranking official composed a poem slandering his superior.
Summoned by the superior,
he happened to appear together with a certain deputy official.
Questioned by the superior,
he again recited a poem to explain himself,
ending with the line,
“Ask such-and-such deputy official.”
The deputy official, knowing nothing of it,
was terrified and unable to defend himself.
Afterward, he demanded why he had been slandered.
The answer was:
“No particular reason—
I just borrowed your title for the rhyme.”
The form of questioning and refutation
must inevitably humble the questioner while elevating the respondent.
Therefore, unless the principles and reasoning are of utmost importance,
a gentleman does not wish to record the names of those who are humbled.
When Mencius rejected the teachings of Yáng and Mò,
he necessarily took the doctrines of Yáng and Mò and refuted them,
thus focusing not on the individuals but on their learning.
Hence, when citing the words of Yáng and Mò,
he only clarified the school of thought of Yáng and Mò,
without necessarily specifically pointing to the individuals Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí.
This shows the depth of his rejection,
desiring to thoroughly eradicate their offshoots.
For it is a matter of mutual exclusivity,
and without doing so,
he could not sufficiently illuminate the great Way of the ancient kings.
How could the heterodox schools view our Confucians any differently?
When Hán Fēi studied the doctrines of Legalism and Logicians,
both Confucians and Mohists were rejected.
Mohist writings were few,
while the Confucians had the *Book of Songs*, *Book of Documents*, and the Six Arts,
all praised and cited by Confucians.
Therefore, when Hán Fēi repeatedly slandered the deeds of Yáo, Shùn, King Wén, and the Duke of Zhōu,
he necessarily relied on Confucian sayings to argue against them.
Thus, in his various chapters of refutation,
he often targeted Confucians,
using them as targets for archery practice.
This was inevitable from his perspective,
something a gentleman would disdain to contend with.
However, his writing is ornate and argumentative,
his ideas sharp and profound,
so later generations of literary scholars
often enjoy reading them.
If one appreciates only the writing and not the person,
then there is no harm in drawing references from it.
Wáng Chōng’s *Lùnhéng*
imitates the style of these refutation chapters.
Imitating the style
does not mean adopting the learning,
yet he also targeted Confucians for questioning and refutation.
Moreover, what he questioned
was a jumble of historical records and biographies,
not all of which originated from Confucians.
Forcibly attributing them to Confucian doctrines
and using them as targets for archery practice—
what grudge did Wáng Chōng hold against Confucians?
Furthermore, in his chapters such as "Questioning Confucius" and "Criticizing Mencius,"
he argued against what he considered errors in Confucian doctrines,
and his writing resembles that of Hán Fēi.
Hán Fēi rejected Confucianism
to promote Legalism and Logicians.
What did Wáng Chōng intend
to promote?
Observing his severe criticism of Hán Fēi’s analogy of deer and horses to honor Confucianism,
and his own preface,
where he distinguishes popular fallacies
to rectify human hearts and customs—
this aligns with the aims of Confucianism.
So, did Wáng Chōng, as a Confucian, reject Confucianism?
Hán Fēi’s aims
were indeed clear.
The brilliance of his writing
does not lie in his rejection of Confucianism.
Wáng Chōng, fixated on his writing style,
thought that without rejecting Confucianism,
his writing would not be brilliant?
When people quarrel,
they often retort with the other’s words—
this is human nature.
If one insults by naming names,
the one retorting will likely change the names—
this is the natural tendency.
Now, Wáng Chōng’s rejection of Confucianism
is like retorting an insult
while still using his own name.
Innate Nature
The "Hóng Fàn" speaks of the three virtues:
uprightness, harmony, and centrality,
with firmness and gentleness balancing each other
to correct excess and deficiency.
This encompasses all human hearts, knowledge, vitality,
intelligence, and talents
within these three.
When Confucius taught his disciples,
if they could not attain the Mean,
he considered the bold and the restrained—
this also draws from the three virtues.
However, the hypocrites,
who appear to follow the Mean while mocking the bold and restrained,
cannot be constrained by the three virtues.
Confucius and Mencius despised them as thieves of virtue,
for they, along with the Mean, the bold, and the restrained,
create confusion, making four.
As human hearts are no longer ancient,
and customs decline,
not only do false followers of the Mean
confuse three into four,
but also false bold and false restrained types
further confuse four into six.
Not only is the Mean unattainable,
but even seeking genuine bold or restrained individuals—
how can they be found?
Mencius’s discussion of understanding words
holds that arising thoughts and issuing policies
harm the affairs.
I have deeply sought the reasons
among various writers.
Those who ramble in their writings,
lacking any purpose in their words,
need not be discussed.
But there are those who claim to establish their own school,
and examining their aims,
they are not entirely meaningless.
Yet measured against the substance of the three virtues,
they lose their innate nature
and miss the essential Way of the ancients—
what is called seeming but not being.
If scholars seek great principles from the ancients
but do not distinguish this,
then starting with confusing three into six,
they may end up losing the three virtues due to three falsities.
Alas!
The discussion of innate nature—
how could it be avoided?
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Words should have substance, and actions should have constancy."
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Poetry expresses intent."
I observe the gentlemen who establish words
and the poets who sing—
how numerous and confused they are!
Seeking substance but finding none,
probing intent but finding emptiness,
yet all say:
"I establish words,"
"I compose poetry."
No words yet having words,
no poetry yet having poetry—
this is what they call substance and intent.
And thus, confusion multiplies.
Those with intent
cherish their hearts,
express their thoughts,
thinking they do not speak recklessly.
Learning must be rooted in nature and heaven,
aims must align with benevolence and righteousness,
citations must return to the *Book of Songs* and *Book of Documents*,
achievements must benefit the people and things,
praising Yáo and Shùn while condemning Jié and Zhòu,
honoring Confucius and Mencius while rejecting Yáng and Mò.
What they say—
even if sages were reborn—
could not be changed.
But seeking the purpose behind their words,
their aims are empty.
For example, "Red Bow" and "Heavy Dew,"
performed at guest banquets,
listeners think they are part of the repertoire.
Some say:
"Perhaps they are blameless."
Yet Zǐ Mò adhered to the Mean in this,
and hypocrites found nothing to criticize.
Huìzǐ said:
"Those fleeing run east,
those chasing also run east.
Though both run east,
their reasons for running east differ."
Observing what these people say,
are they fleeing east
or chasing east?
This is unknowable.
And thus, confusion multiplies again.
When a person of exceptional talent emerges,
they claim that they do not speak without purpose,
but indeed have a genuine aspiration,
for when things are unjust, they cry out.
Observing how they name and classify things,
sometimes like the poets using metaphors and allegories,
sometimes like the rhetoricians employing humor and subtlety,
using the small to illustrate the great,
lamenting the past while grieving the present,
their laughter and mockery sharper than glaring eyes,
their mournful songs capable of substituting tears,
it is truly because they cannot help but speak.
They say that when a virtuous person fails to realize their aspirations in their time,
they vent their frustrations through writing to express themselves.
The essence of their intent
does not stray beyond the spirit of the *Sāo*.
I have read the words of the *Sāo* poets:
"Abundant are the inner virtues I possess,
augmented further by cultivated abilities."
The Grand Historian Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"When I read the *Lísāo*,
I grieve for its author's aspirations."
He also said:
"It elucidates the breadth and loftiness of morality,
and the systematic coherence of order and chaos.
Its aspirations are pure,
its conduct is upright,
unsullied even when immersed in filth,
worthy of vying in brilliance with the sun and moon."
This is why Jiǎ Yí lamented over Qū Yuán,
and why Sīmǎ Qiān composed a biography for Jiǎ Yí;
these were all outstanding figures of the Three Dynasties.
As for those who claim affiliation with the *Sāo* to elevate themselves,
seeking the reasons for their grievances leaves one bewildered.
They bemoan poverty and lament old age,
resenting others' wealth and honor while they themselves remain poor and lowly,
envious of others' high ranks while they themselves are cast aside,
seeking patronage from the powerful only to meet with rejection,
vying for power and profit only to be overthrown and crushed.
Because of such failures to realize their aspirations,
they wish to entrust their writings to the traditions of the *Sāo* and the *Yǎ*,
claiming these represent the aspirations of the ancients;
unaware that those of middling or lower ability
are merely what is described as "sharing the same heart and desires,
harboring intentions yet unexpressed."
Now,
when the imperial examinations select a hundred or so top candidates,
there must be thousands of Jiǎ Yís,
weeping bitterly to lament by the Xiāng River,
yet the river remains unmoved.
When the Ministry of Personnel appoints hundreds or thousands to official posts,
there must be tens of thousands of Qū Yuáns,
scratching their heads to compose verses like "Tiānwèn,"
yet Heaven grows weary of them.
Mèngzǐ said:
"With the aspirations of Yī Yǐn, it is permissible;
without the aspirations of Yī Yǐn, it is usurpation."
I say of those who voice grievances:
with the aspirations of Qū Yuán and Jiǎ Yí, it is permissible;
without the aspirations of Qū Yuán and Jiǎ Yí, it is contemptible.
Yet those who claim affiliation with the *Sāo*
are numerous indeed.
There are those with broad perspectives
who offer explanations, saying:
"Why should this trouble you?
I have something to say,
and I say it to suit my own inclinations.
If others agree with me,
I am not pleased;
if others disagree with me,
I am not angered.
The rights and wrongs of past and present,
I do not wish to see too clearly;
the opinions of others and myself,
I do not wish to hold too firmly.
If one must insist on being trusted in the present,
what purpose does it serve?

My clansman Tíng Fēng said:
"To discuss historical talent and historical learning,
but not discuss historical virtue,
to discuss literary sentiment and literary heart,
but not discuss literary nature,
previous scholars naturally had a deficiency in meaning.
This piece, together with the chapter 'Historical Virtue',
is sufficient to uncover what previous scholars overlooked."
The cunning and shallow
gather rushes from Dǒngzé,
inherit the examination from the 'Cháng Yáng',
boast of the gatekeeper's understanding,
record the diviner's shop's responses,
people call them cunning;
they are not cunning,
they are shallow.
Name is the guest of substance,
to pursue name and forget substance,
is to lose even the name one sought;
when substance departs, literary form cannot exist alone.
The highest forgets name,
knowing only what must be done,
not caring what others say of me.
The next considers name and reflects on its meaning.
Under heaven there is no place that carelessly establishes a reputation for me;
because of where the name lies,
one reflects on why it is so,
then knows what must be done and can strive accordingly.
The next fears name and does not act recklessly.
Exhausts what one knows and can do,
without forcing what one does not know or cannot do.
The cunning view them,
as seemingly clumsy;
they are not clumsy,
but mutually achieving merit.
The lowest pursue name and forget substance.
Gathering rushes from Dǒngzé—
what does this mean?
Those who discuss literature revere the 'Zuǒ Zhuàn' and 'Shǐjì'.
The 'Zuǒ Zhuàn' and 'Shǐjì' in relation to literature,
are like the editing and compiling of the Six Classics.
The 'Zuǒ Zhuàn' relied on the precious books of a hundred states;
the 'Shǐjì' relied on the 'Shàngshū', 'Guóyǔ', and records such as 'Shìběn', 'Guócè', 'Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū',
what they themselves composed was one-tenth,
what was preserved through editing and compiling was nine-tenths.
The gentleman does not consider this wrong.
The purpose of their writing,
was fundamentally to take editing and compiling as their skill,
thereby continuing the 'Chūnqiū' and establishing a school of thought,
thus they were diligent and cautious,
with narrative and wording secondary.
The ancients did not boast privately of literary style,
historical writing moreover cannot be fabricated from emptiness;
and what they based themselves on,
was all suspended between heaven and earth,
observing the literary style that entered their editing and compiling,
still each had its excellence;
this is also like molding and refining being equal to creation.
I observe the collected works of recent times,
and cannot be without doubt.
Biographical writing,
the ancients made it into books forming their own school,
not placing it in collected works;
later scholars scattered writings to include in collected works,
is a change in literature.
Since it is biography within a collection,
it is no longer the book of an expert editor and compiler;
recording what one has heard and seen,
to prepare for later scholars' editing and compiling,
may be appropriate.
Those cunning in loving fame and shallow in understanding meaning,
observing the learning and literature of the present age,
cannot remain unmoved,
gauging their own talent and strength,
insufficient to achieve it;
thus seeing the reliance of historians on predecessors,
they cunningly arrange their writings as biography,
intending to make their collection profound and vast,
not knowing it is not so.
The calendrical calculations of the Méi family of Xuānchéng,
every household has their books.
Collecting and recording calendrical discussions,
filling two volumes with writing,
making it a biography and placing it in a collected works,
for what purpose?
Stepping back to examine their private affairs,
one has not heard they have any understanding of harmonics and calculation.
The medical principles of Master Zhū of Dānxī,
people transmit his learning.
Excerpting and copying medical case records,
writing accumulating ten thousand words,
making it a biography and placing it in a collected works,
for what purpose?
Advancing to seek their theories,
one has not heard they have any discernment regarding prescriptions and techniques.
Bān Gù, following the tradition of the 'Hóng Fàn', composed the 'Wǔ Xíng';
following the books of the 'Qī Lüè', narrated the 'Yì Wén'.
Bān did not necessarily deeply understand portents and auspices,
nor was he expert in textual criticism,
yet gentlemen consider Bān's editing and compiling,
his merit supplements Sīmǎ Qiān;
and praise Bān's editing and compiling,
as good at relying on others and not being self-reliant.
Because the 'Hànshū' is like the imperial temple,
the various schools of learning,
are comparable to the arrangement of great bells and drums.
Those now writing biographies for Méi and Zhū,
seem to envy the beauty and richness of the ancestral temple's hundred officials,
and steal courtyard torches and returned wine vessels,
to adorn their thatched hut doors.
Even so,
they can also be called clumsy.
Classical masters' transmission,
masters' specialized techniques,
were the lifelong work of the ancients.
If one could hunt for the essence,
to enrich one's own writing,
then the Four Treasuries' canonical texts,
are still like the rushes of Dǒngzé,
why then be so fixated on this?
Inheriting the examination from the 'Cháng Yáng'—
what does this mean?
Attributing goodness to one's parents,
taking faults upon oneself,
this is the conduct of a filial son,
and also the style of literature.
What the 'Shī' and 'Shū' recount,
is ancient.
After the Three Dynasties,
Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù both had generations of historians,
and the work of Tán and Biāo,
is also briefly seen in the narratives of Qiān and Gù.
Later people then say Gù stole his father's writings,
while Qiān praised his father's excellence.
Viewing it today,
why must it be so?
Tán's concluding discourse,
only shows the essential tenets of the six schools,
as for lingering south of the Zhōu,
father and son holding hands sighing,
transmitting history,
only recorded in empty words,
without actual traces.
As for Biāo writing the 'Hòu Zhuàn',
the origin and sequence fully exist,
and the three annals' discussions and judgments,
clearly record Biāo's views,
showing the transmission of family learning;
how could it be as later people say,
leading to Zhèng Qiāo's suspicion falsely accusing Bān of plagiarism?
However, Sīmǎ Qiān's narrative of Tán,
was not intentionally brief;
and Bān Gù's account of Biāo,
was not fond of being detailed;
a filial son deeply loves his parent,
taking his parent's conduct and writing it in a book,
must resemble his parent's usual self,
and not involve the circumstances of his own life.
I observe the collected works of recent times,
and cannot be without doubt.
If their parent has nothing worthy of recounting?
Omit it, that is acceptable.
If their parent only has minor goodness?
Record it according to its measure,
one cannot be brief to the point of omission,
nor excessive to the point of falsehood, that is acceptable.
Those cunning in loving fame and shallow in understanding meaning,
extravagantly display their own achievements,
writing volumes without cease,
and at the song's end play the elegant refrain,
then say it is my ancestor's teaching.
Even more, elaborating on their own glorious encounters,
relishing the flavor of their words,
and the ode concludes with disorder,
then say it is the reward of my ancestor's virtue.
Autobiographical writing,
overly boastful,
Liú Zhījī still criticized it for speaking of ambition without humility,
rashly becoming an object of ridicule.
Moreover, recounting one's parent,
is it for the purpose of self-praise?
Zhāng Tāng had descendants,
the historian's minister encouraged recommending the worthy;
coming from Ānshì's mouth,
would be perverse.
Bóqǐ's generational virtue,
the historian's minister considered it fortunate for the pure and loyal;
appearing in Bǐng and Cì's writings,
would be erroneous.
Former people said the 'Cháng Yáng', 'Shàng Lín' and other rhapsodies,
extravagantly described tours and observations,
and ended with implied admonitions,
considered to satirize one and encourage a hundred.
This person's writing,
is probably self-praise a hundred,
and praising his parent one?
What does it mean to take pride in the access of the petitioner?
What is meant by this?
The official historians compiled the *Book of Songs*,
clarifying the Six Arts.
Since poetry does not convey fixed meanings,
the intentions of the authors,
if not explained by prefaces,
then their compositions,
how can one discern what they mean?
As for the current *Preface to the Book of Songs*,
if one says that its transmission has lost its original meaning,
that is acceptable;
but to claim that prefaces are unnecessary,
is unacceptable.
The *Book of Documents* has prefaces,
perhaps because the external historians were in charge of the books of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
and there must have been chapter titles?
The current *Preface to the Book of Documents*,
likely consists of the words passed down by classical scholars,
modeled after the *Preface to the Book of Songs*?
Readers, upon finishing the entire text,
will naturally understand the principles and events;
thus, even if the *Book of Documents* lacked prefaces,
its meaning would not be hindered.
Moreover, the *Book of Documents* originally had prefaces;
in the admonitions and proclamations, the entire text records speeches,
so the events must be noted at the beginning of the bamboo slips,
to show the reason for the admonitions and proclamations.
Thus, historical records do not require prefaces,
while records of speeches inherently have prefaces.
From this perspective,
the presence or absence of prefaces,
depends on the clarity or obscurity of the text,
can also be seen.
I observe the collected works of recent times,
and cannot help but feel perplexed.
Essays that establish principles,
may reiterate what predecessors have already said,
or their right and wrong may be easily discerned;
the authors are surely aware of this,
yet they insist on writing treatises,
perhaps because there are subtle intentions within,
or because they wish to convey something through allegory,
or because they are moved by feelings to express themselves;
since they do not explicitly state the reasons,
they should preface their treatises with the era in which they were written,
and a general account of what they saw and heard,
so that later generations can cross-reference and verify,
and understand the purpose behind the treatise.
This is also a legacy of the prefaces to the admonitions and proclamations in the *Book of Documents*.
Yet, looking at treatises and essays,
those that discuss what need not be discussed,
account for seven out of ten;
among these, are there not one or two that arise from purposeful words?
However, like the *Airs of the States* without prefaces,
how can one know their subtle meanings?
Moreover, if discussions were accompanied by prefaces,
then empty words resembling the stereotyped essays of examination candidates,
could be somewhat eliminated,
yet people are accustomed to this and do not notice it.
As for narrative essays,
the ancients wrote them according to the events.
Yet, looking at the collected works of later generations,
when writing biographies or epitaphs upon request,
they often preface them with the person who made the request,
and detail the words of the request.
If done occasionally,
it is certainly harmless;
but when it becomes a common practice,
it becomes a preface to the preface.
Even so,
it is still tolerable.
Those who are cunning in seeking fame but shallow in understanding meaning,
when preluding the words of the petitioner,
deliberately exaggerate and flatter themselves.
On one hand, they say:
"Your virtue and morality are profound,
your words are a model for the world;
without your writing,
the deceased would not rest in peace."
On the other hand, they say:
"Your literary and scholarly achievements,
are revered by contemporaries;
if we could have a word from you,
it would serve as evidence for later generations."
They themselves repeatedly decline,
while others insistently beg.
All such things,
are included in the literary composition,
yet they contribute nothing to the matter at hand,
and using others to boast about oneself—
how utterly shameless is this?
Moreover, if the writing does not deserve such praise,
it deceives the dead;
if the petitioner never said such things,
it deceives the living.
If one argues that the origin of the matter
must be detailed,
then the petitioner should have been announced by the gatekeeper,
presented their card first,
exchanged greetings upon entering,
and offered gifts afterward.
These are also part of the origin,
so why not record them in detail as well?
And are the words of praise in a request for writing
any different from this?
What is meant by the response of the divination stall?
When writings decline and become literary collections,
there is the operation of heaven’s will,
and there are the affairs of men.
If one does not cultivate virtue,
learning has no means to stand on its own;
when the roots are damaged, the branches and leaves wither—
this is the inevitable decline in human affairs.
As worldly affairs change, literary substance transforms;
human interactions,
rituals and institutions,
things that existed in antiquity but not today—
all are manifested in literary works.
Thus, only if one remains secluded in the deep mountains without emerging is it acceptable;
but once one steps into human society,
then one must respond to demands and fulfill needs,
the uses of literature multiply and literary genres divide,
and division inevitably leads to the emergence of literary collections.
Those with profound virtue
and refined learning
use literary collections as their writings,
which is what is called establishing words according to circumstances.
Yet they cannot avoid mixing in matters of social interaction
and the utility of fulfilling demands.
If one cannot become a specialist in the masters’ works or histories,
one’s words will not broadly encompass all.
Those who mistakenly regard writings for social interaction and fulfilling demands as standing on their own and hastily label them as collections—
how many such cases are there, one wonders?
This is due to the workings of fate,
not entirely related to human affairs.
I observe the literary collections of recent times
and cannot help but feel perplexed.
When historiography declines,
biographies become numerous and mixed,
such as after the Eastern Hàn,
the various biographies like “Xiánxián” and “Qíjiù,”
and records like “Shíyí” and “Sōushén”—
all are examples of this.
When historiography is abandoned,
biographies enter literary collections,
such as since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the epitaphs and inscriptions of Hán Yù and Liǔ Zōngyuán,
the prefaces and accounts of Ōuyáng Xiū and Zēng Gǒng—
all are examples of this.
Those endowed with historical talent cannot personally undertake the responsibility of writing history
to fully exercise their abilities;
they should also gather what they have seen and heard,
verify right and wrong,
and compose their own works
to align with the specialists in biography.
When compelled by necessity,
and at the request of others,
they compose styles such as steles, inscriptions, prefaces, and accounts—
they cannot avoid writing words for social interaction and fulfilling demands,
mixing them with the intent of their writings.
This is what Hán Yù, Liǔ Zōngyuán, Ōuyáng Xiū, and Zēng Gǒng called having no alternative.
Those cunning in their love of fame but shallow in understanding,
judging that their literary flair is insufficient to move people
and their learning insufficient to stand on its own,
then think of relying on something to attach themselves to an immortal enterprise.
They see the figures and achievements of the contemporary world
being widely praised and boasted about,
and thus believe they can borrow from them.
Borrowing, it seems similar;
but they do not understand that the specialized writings of biographies
do not surpass the literary collections of Hán and Ōuyáng in insight.
They believe that without steles and inscriptions, it cannot be done.
Steles and inscriptions must be requested by descendants,
but when no one’s descendants have requested them,
they fabricate steles and inscriptions to include in their collections,
as if requested by descendants,
and consider themselves nearly on par with Hán and Ōuyáng.
Hán and Ōuyáng wrote at the request of others,
out of necessity;
thus, Ōuyáng Xiū took pride in his history of the Five Dynasties,
and Hán Yù wished to condemn traitors and flatterers after their deaths,
reveal the hidden virtue’s faint glow,
and compose a classic for the Táng,
still regretting that it was entrusted to empty words.
Now, taking what others produced out of necessity
and looking up with envy,
even imitating it like Yōumèng—
this is like drafting imperial edicts for the literary examination,
not originating from silk ribbons;
or the questions and answers of the “Qī Lín,”
which need not have been spoken.
How then can they serve as evidence for metal and stone
or illuminate for future generations?
Abandoning the direct expression of biographies
to imitate the indirect communication of steles and inscriptions—
is it to resemble Hán and Ōuyáng?
Then it is like the frown of the ugly woman.
Is it to gain literary reputation by responding to others’ requests?
Then it is like a divination stall.
In the past, Xīshī frowned due to heartache,
and the ugly woman of Lǐ,
thinking it beautiful, imitated her;
the rich shut their doors and did not emerge,
while the poor took their wives and children and left.
A lowly craftsman selling divination in the city market,
with no one passing by to inquire,
would say:
“A certain nobleman treated me generously,
a certain high official considered my art divine.”
Such is the vulgar trend.
The difficulty of writing in engaging with the world lies in the multitude of vulgar taboos.
Hán Tuìzhī (Hán Yù) suffered slander from Lǐ Sù because his "Stele Inscription for the Pacification of Huáixī" did not fully detail Lǐ Sù’s achievements.
Ōuyáng Xiū defended the epitaph for Shī Lǔ (Yǐn Shīlǔ),
yet since ancient times, those who truly understand have been few.
I once studied ancient-style prose with Master Zhū.
Master Zhū composed the "Epitaph for Jǔrén Lǚ."
Lǚ had long struggled without passing the examinations,
and studied diligently every night.
A neighboring woman said to her husband:
"Lǚ Shēng’s reading voice is loud,
yet the rhythm is mournful and sorrowful.
Could it be that he is discontent within?"
Her husband relayed this to Lǚ.
Lǚ wept uncontrollably and said:
"That lady understands me.
If only the chief examiner possessed her discernment,
would I have remained unsuccessful for so long?"
From then on, each time he read, he would bow three times toward the neighbor’s wall.
The text deeply expressed Lǚ Jūn’s sorrow over his lack of recognition;
yet at the time, it was considered frivolous and improper,
with no regard for the distinction between men and women,
so people gathered to criticize it.
He also composed an epitaph for a certain lady.
Her husband was teaching his nephew, but the boy was disobedient,
so he beat him until he bled.
The grandmother, protecting her grandson, became angry
and refused to eat.
The lady knelt and urged her to take food.
The grandmother, still angry,
slapped her face.
The lady maintained a pleasant expression even more so,
and ultimately won her mother-in-law’s favor.
The text originally contained nothing discordant regarding familial affection, filial piety, and harmony;
yet at the time, it was said that a daughter-in-law being struck by her mother-in-law was a shame that should be concealed,
and that beating the nephew and striking the daughter-in-law both violated kindness and love,
so these parts were excised.
I once composed the "Stele Inscription for Repairing the City Walls of Qiān'ān County,"
which described how the walls had long been dilapidated,
and at the time, there were more urgent projects,
so senior officials classified it as a deferred project;
now, with even more time passed,
the collapse and damage had worsened,
making further delay intolerable.
This was written based on facts,
and should have been uncontroversial.
Yet readers at the time said that since the stele argued for the necessity of repairing the walls,
it should not mention the officials who deferred the project, as it would highlight their shortcomings.
At first, I suspected they were overly cautious,
but later, when I consulted those renowned for understanding literature,
they all held this view,
unanimously.
I also once wrote a "Biography of a Chaste Widow" for someone,
describing how she lived in poverty,
with no support from relatives or clan,
yet managed through hard work to support herself
and raise her orphaned child to adulthood.
But her son said:
"At that time, not all relatives were impoverished;
they simply showed no pity for us mother and son.
Now, if we write it thus,
I fear they will feel ashamed,
and it may create resentment.
Please only describe my mother’s hardships,
and do not mention the lack of support from relatives."

There are many such rigid constraints, too numerous to count. Occasionally, situations are too pressing, making it truly difficult to write according to rules, not entirely due to rigidity. Also, when composing "Inscription for a Birthday Banner" for Master Zhū, I wrote:
"Since returning from resigning as Education Commissioner in the Guǐsì year,
the disciples following and studying with him have reached their peak."
Yet among his peers,
some who had followed him before the Guǐsì year
angrily retorted:
"Must it only be prosperous after that?
Are we, then, not worthy of esteem?"
Also, when collating and annotating "Chronological Biography of Liáng Wéndìng," I wrote:
"He, mindful that his sister-in-law was widowed young,
respected her as a mother for life.
Whenever she was displeased,
he would invariably accommodate her to win her favor."
Yet someone said:
"A sister-in-law should naturally be respected.
Now, saying he respected her because she was widowed young implies he was guarding against her not maintaining her chastity,
not showing genuine respect."
Other trivial matters
that people picked apart and criticized
cannot all be discussed here;
I merely summarize the main points.
This shows how difficult it truly is for writing to engage with the world.
Now, the function of writing:
if internally it is not rooted in learning,
and externally it is unrelated to societal instruction,
it has already lost the essence of writing.
And if one harbors a biased mind,
defaming others,
even attacking and exposing private matters,
falsely tarnishing the innocent—
such a person is a sinner within the moral order,
and even if they luckily escape punishment,
heavenly retribution will surely reach them.
As for where right and wrong lie,
writing may have its emphases;
in comparisons,
there are naturally principal and secondary elements;
what is substantial must be said not to be meager,
what is pure must be said to be flawless—
it is almost like composing poetry, which must follow tonal patterns
to achieve harmony;
phrasing must employ particles
to achieve clarity.
Now, if when praising purity and substance,
one fears being suspected of flaws and meagerness;
if in prose one must eliminate particles like yān, zāi, hū, yě,
and in poetry one must use all level or all oblique tones—
even if the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius were reborn,
they could not produce a single phrase deemed perfect.
Alas!
Works that manage worldly affairs
cannot serve as writings that engage with the world.
Unexpected praise,
perfection-seeking criticism—
this has been so since ancient times.
Reading ancient Yuèfǔ poems,
describing the hardships of the Shǔ roads,
the twists and turns of Tàiháng—
one thinks they depict narrow paths,
metaphors for the impasse of the Way;
not knowing that the path of writing
is also rugged like this.
Thus, those with deep insight remain silent and wordless.
They engrave their works for the mountains,
awaiting understanding readers to uncover them—
how could they contend over sweetness and bitterness with those who seek to please?
Needle fame
Fame is the guest of substance.
When substance arrives, fame follows—
this is the natural principle,
not an inevitable occurrence.
The noble person follows the natural principle,
not seeking the inevitable occurrence.
The learning of the noble person
knows only what is appropriate to attend to;
not knowing so-called fame,
how can one perceive its substance?
Those who crave fame,
pursue fame and forget substance,
and thus see what is not forgotten as substance.
Discerning people find this problematic
and wish to make others prioritize substance over fame.
However,
they still have not forgotten the notions of fame and substance.
The noble person is not like this.
The noble person’s actions and retirements
should accord with reputation and righteousness.
The way the ancient kings enlightened the world and guided the people
lay not beyond reputation and teaching.
Since antiquity,
there has never been governance that could abandon reputation.
Why does craving fame lead to forgetting substance? I say:
Righteousness originally has no name;
because we wish those who do not know righteousness to follow it,
we call it reputation-righteousness.
Teaching originally has no name;
because we wish those who do not know teaching to adhere to it,
we call it reputation-teaching.
To proclaim it as reputation
is to seek substance.
It is like people not knowing food,
so we proclaim the name of cultivation to encourage farming;
people not knowing clothing,
so we proclaim the name of reeling silk to encourage sericulture;
those who are warmly clothed and well-fed
do not seek the names of farming and sericulture.
Now, if one does not inquire into farming and sericulture,
but only boasts of being well-fed and warmly clothed,
there will surely be those who abandon plowing and weaving, endure hunger and cold,
borrow chaff to fill their bellies,
and hide in tattered cotton to feign warmth—
this is the harm of craving fame.
Therefore, the reputation in reputation-teaching and reputation-righteousness
is like farming and sericulture.
The fame craved by fame-seekers
is like being well-fed and warmly clothed.
If one insists on chasing the fame of being well-fed and warmly clothed,
none can avoid forcibly enduring hunger and cold.
Yet to say that those who crave fame will lose it
is a principle of nature.
It is not an inevitable occurrence.
In ancient times, Jiè Zhītuī did not speak of rewards,
and rewards did not reach him either.
When substance is achieved, fame follows;
yet fame may not necessarily arrive immediately.
The fame of the world
is determined by those with true understanding,
and is bolstered by those who seem to understand but in truth do not deeply comprehend.
Those with true understanding
must first know themselves.
Few in the world are self-aware,
so those who truly understand others are not many.
Those who seem to understand but in truth do not deeply comprehend are numerous.
Because they seem to understand,
they can collaborate to build reputations.
Because they do not deeply comprehend,
those who crave fame can succeed in their deceptions.
Moreover, with clever strategies and manipulative tactics,
exhausting the thoughts and efforts of a lifetime,
how can one say they have not achieved a single success in this?
Thus, those who crave fame often gain temporary fame,
just as those who crave profit may not lack temporary gains.
Furthermore, those who crave fame
act with certain benefits in mind.
Like merchants profiting from the market,
merchants must bring out their accumulated goods
before they can reap profits;
those who crave fame
must also dilute their substance
to pursue temporary fame.
For human hearts differ as much as their faces,
so those who focus on substance
cannot please everyone.
Those who crave fame,
however, strive to gauge what is common in human sentiments,
without necessarily acting from genuine sincerity within.
Moreover, those who crave fame
must chase the trends of the time.
Trends cycle and change,
like spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums alternating,
without repeating.
Living within these cycles,
one's innate talents and qualities
may not necessarily align with them.
Those who crave fame,
however, must bend and conform to them,
so their inner motives are often questionable.
When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold;
when Lǔ's wine is thin, Hándān is besieged.
This speaks of tendencies that inevitably arise,
and principles that are inherently so.
The way of learning
holds no envy or jealousy toward others,
yet where fame is concerned,
envy and jealousy are bound to arise.
The way of learning
requires no artifice or affectation toward the world,
yet where fame resides,
artifice and affectation are inevitable.
Thus, those who crave fame
are thieves of virtue.
As for those with true understanding,
they know themselves with certainty,
and do not seek the world's recognition.
They disdain to walk the same path
as those who seem to understand but in truth do not deeply comprehend.
Perhaps across a hundred generations,
one person may be found
who laments their solitude without a peer,
and has always awaited someone like me as a later ally.
Perhaps a thousand miles away,
one person may be found
who regrets the distance that keeps us from meeting,
and has always been a harmonious neighbor to me in spirit.
To seek understanding in the present age with this mindset,
is to find but few,
yet the noble person does not consider this a cause for concern.
When superficial trends cease,
and prevailing customs calm,
in this vast world,
how can there be no one with true understanding?
By then, the tricks of those who crave fame
will also reach their limit.
Therefore, it is said:
When substance is achieved, fame follows;
those who crave fame will lose it.
These are both principles of nature,
not inevitable occurrences.
Yet in the end, occurrences do not transcend principles.
To admonish the aberrant.
The ancients in their learning sought what was right,
never seeking to be different from others.
When learning reaches its utmost,
others look up to it but cannot attain it,
and thus perceive it as different—
not that it intentionally sets itself apart.
The Master said:
"In frugality,
I follow the multitude.
In matters of dignity,
though it goes against the multitude,
I follow what is proper."
Even the sage sought to align with others.
If at times he differed from the multitude,
it was the sage's不得已 (unavoidable necessity).
Under heaven there is a public rightness,
formed from the multitude unknowingly yet naturally,
which even the sage cannot alter.
The wise and intelligent,
deeply probing its reasons,
believe it to be so.
The平庸 (mediocre) and愚昧 (ignorant), though lacking understanding,
also accept it as such.
But those who pride themselves on their talent,
ashamed to share the same views as the平庸 (mediocre) and愚昧 (ignorant),
deliberately twist their arguments to claim otherwise.
For example, a skilled cook
creates flavors that all enjoy,
and even those with no palate
never fail to call them delicious.
Now, if one is ashamed to share the same tastes as those without a palate,
they must drink dregs and discard fine wine,
abandon delicacies for coarse野菜 (wild greens),
only then can they differ from the庸俗 (common).
As the saying goes:
"If later ages were not fair,
there would be no sages or worthies until now."
The one trusted by all generations
is the Master alone.
That the Master can be trusted
is determined by whom?
Public rightness tolerates no violation.
The Master discussed many
ancient神圣 (divine sages) and贤人 (worthies).
Bóyí sought benevolence and attained it,
Tàibó yielded the empire—
without the Master illuminating their hidden virtues,
people would have no way of knowing them.
Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōugōng—
even without the Master's praise,
would people not know of them?
With the Master's sageliness,
he praised Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and Zhōugōng,
yet never heard to differ from the multitude in his judgments—
thus under heaven truly has no one who seeks to be different.
The sense of right and wrong
is possessed by all.
As for sounds, colors, flavors, and smells,
the ears, eyes, mouths, and noses of all under heaven
are alike.
What the mind finds alike
is principle
and righteousness.
Yet the divergent paths under heaven
all arise from contending over principle and righteousness,
and the sense of right and wrong
thereby changes easily.
Is it that the mind's shared understanding
is less than the ears, eyes, mouth, and nose?
Sounds, colors, flavors, and smells have tangible basis, while principle and righteousness are formless.
Having tangible basis, even the平庸 (mediocre) and愚昧 (ignorant) know to follow;
being formless, even the wise and intelligent cannot avoid self-assertion.
Thus, those who seek to differ from others
invariably arise from self-assertion.
To remedy the弊病 (flaw) of self-assertion,
nothing is better than using tangible learning
to substantiate formless principle and righteousness,
so that one's path does not diverge.
When inner substance is weighty, outward show becomes light;
when reality is attained, fame is forgotten.
All who seek to differ from others
do so due to inner insufficiency.
Knowing one's own insufficiency,
yet unable to overcome the desire for fame,
they then seek to differ so as to surpass others,
but others ultimately remain unsurpassed.
Inner insufficiency
compels outward pretense;
lack of substance
drives pursuit of fame—
this is大抵 (generally) the nature of human sentiment.
Since human sentiment is大抵 (generally) thus,
those seeking to differ cannot avoid this path,
so how are they different from others?
Only different from the坦荡 (open-hearted)君子 (gentleman).
Take horses:
their manes and coats are alike,
they chew grass and drink water,
feed on fodder and grain,
and are saddled and bridled—
all alike.
Yet some run a hundred lǐ in a day,
others a thousand lǐ;
within similarity lies unique difference—
this is how sages, worthies, and heroes
differ from ordinary people.
Not following what the multitude shares,
but first seeking difference,
is like a horse biting the bit or shaking off the bridle,
kicking and biting,
unfit for riding.
To critique俗 (vulgar) practices:
Literary scholars speak of birthday screens and funeral banners
as almost equal to market-stall frameworks,
unworthy of entering the halls of learning.
Yet this is often the case.
In society, one cannot avoid customary social exchanges,
and祝贺 (congratulatory) clichés,
哀挽 (mourning) platitudes
also lack personal expression—
yet to fuss over these,
debating skill or clumsiness,
how is it different from dreaming within a dream?
Writing conveys intent;
if intent has no means of self-expression,
and one merely follows convention,
then the ancients did not compose special texts—
like祝福 (blessings) for capping a youth,
or injunctions for a maiden's醮 (coming-of-age ceremony),
they simply used existing documents.
The habit of valuing form over substance
insists on composing texts,
and in doing so, can there be no merit?
Thus, people become pretentious and deliberate,
striving to imitate and admire,
until a trickle becomes a river,
impossible to dam.
Writing arises from substance;
the first creators
did not grasp change,
so their methods were easily exhausted.
Those who follow and copy them have no good path.
Facing an unstoppable river,
one should survey and channel it,
use it for irrigation,
and navigate it with boats—
only then is its divine and enduring function seen.
In the way of writing,
all that did not exist in antiquity but exists now
is natural.
Birthday tributes were unseen in antiquity,
yet narrating a life
uses the method of记录 (recording);
to make the person immortal
is the writing of historical records.
挽祭 (Mourning and sacrificial) texts originate from literary compositions,
yet tracing deeds
uses the intent of诔谥 (eulogies and posthumous titles);
to mark the person's end
is the writing of金石 (metal and stone) inscriptions.
Writing arises from substance;
apply one's writing according to the substance—
this can still benefit worldly teaching.
Why doubt market-stall frameworks,
and why should scholars disdain to speak of them?
During life there are congratulatory addresses,
and after death there are sacrificial elegies;
these are the rituals of recent times that have lost the essence of ritual.
Rituals should adapt to circumstances,
and practices should follow customs.
As long as they do not contradict the Way of the ancients,
the gentleman does not discard them.
Among literary families,
congratulatory and elegiac writings are looked down upon,
not realizing that if the method is made divine and enlightened,
the flaws would certainly reach this point.
The more extreme among them
preserve sacrificial elegies but are ashamed to record congratulatory addresses.
Recent literati,
when compiling their own collected works,
if they cannot bear to discard them and occasionally include such pieces,
they must also separate them into distinct volumes,

as if elegant and vulgar cannot be mentioned in the same breath. Wāng Dùnwēng prided himself on classical prose, often reproaching others. In truth, he had talent but lacked discernment, fond of making unnecessary taboos and restrictions, yet boasting of his own discernment. Most cases are like this.
This can be said to know ten but be ignorant of two times five.
They merely see that the collected works of earlier writers contain lamentations and elegies but no congratulatory addresses,
thinking that lamentations and elegies can be traced to antiquity,
while congratulatory and blessing texts
were nonexistent in ancient times.
They do not realize that tomb inscriptions began in the Six Dynasties,
and stele texts flourished in the Eastern Hàn,
neither having existed in antiquity.
The stele inscriptions of Cài Yōng,
and the tomb records and inscriptions of Hán Yù,
are highly praised by scholars.
Now, looking at the collected works of Cài and Hán,
among them are praises without virtue,
preserving only rhetorical elegance.
Are those with whom they associated and interacted
any different from the congratulatory addresses of recent times?
Lenient in judging antiquity,
but harsh in measuring the present,
the gentleman considers this as having ears but no eyes.
If it is insisted that genres like inscriptions and records
indeed originated in antiquity,
then congratulatory and blessing texts
also originated from the "Zhōu Guān" (Offices of Zhōu),
with the six blessings' texts
used to pray for good fortune.
Because literati composed them later,
they are thus distinguished by category and precedent.
How can this be spoken of as understanding the changes of the times?
Writing arises from substance.
Congratulatory blessings and mournful elegies
apply writing according to the substance of the person.
Thus, transformations are boundless;
what later people create
can surpass that of earlier people.
That which depends on the person:
the person changes myriad ways, and the writing also changes myriad ways.
That which depends on the event:
the event does not change, and the writing also does not change.
The toasts for the maiden's libation,
the praises for the youth's capping ceremony,
all use established texts and classical precedents.
The ancients did not compose separate texts;
recorded in biographies and histories,
there are also many such cases.
The ceremonial rituals of bowing and yielding,
the rhythms of drumming and piping,
are not discarded by ritual and music.
However, if their substance is not preserved,
even if divinely and sagely created,
there is no need for ceremonial rituals and rhythms
to be considered uniquely remarkable.
Later people follow the flow without discerning the source,
then indiscriminately compose texts,
resulting in wasted words.
The steles for inscribed names of jìnshì,
must have records;
the flaws of the Míng people, now no longer exist. The records of offerings for the imperial examinations,
must have prefaces;
these still exist today. It seems possible to request using a fixed format, like the example of congratulatory memorials. Since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
autumn preliminary exams and spring assemblies,
jìnshì passing the examinations,
are equivalent to grain transport and annual reports,
not extraordinary or uniquely creative events.
Inscribed names and presented records,
are customary practices.
Even if Lǐ Sī engraved stones (referring to inscribed name steles),
Liú Xiàng presented writings (referring to presented records),
how could they, beyond ordinary lines and ink,
compose additional texts?
Yet the capable boast,
the inept feel ashamed,
valuing only the writing and not the event,
which is called delusion.
Completing a house and raising the beam,
must have a text;
marriage and betrothal exchanges,
must have letters;
the same hall construction,
the same man and woman,
even if Lǔ Bān gave the command,
Gāoméi introduced the guests,
how could they, beyond ordinary lines and ink,
compose additional texts?
Yet the capable boast,
the inept feel ashamed,
valuing only the writing and not the event,
which is called delusion.
Yet contemporary literati,
still consider the former inferior and the latter superior.
Why?
National statutes and ordinances,
suburban and ancestral temple blessing plaques,
annually performed regular affairs,
have fixed formats,
with no alterations.
Extending grace following precedents,
official edicts and patents for ministers,
with identical official ranks,
have fixed formats,
with no alterations.
Imperial birthday celebrations,
auspicious occasions and festivals,
congratulatory memorials from ministers,
all have fixed formats,
with no alterations.
The sages' creations,
established as ritual classics,
appropriate in substance and form,
must suit what is fitting.
Writing depends on events;
events change myriad ways, and writing also changes myriad ways;
events do not change, and writing also does not change.
Even if created by the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
how could it be different?
The ceremonial rituals of bowing and yielding,
the rhythms of drumming and piping,
what ordinary people cannot diminish,
the divine and sagely cannot increase.
Yet literati, following accumulated habits,
must desire to boast of abundance and contend in extravagance.
No wonder collected works are so numerous and disorderly.
The "Lǐ Jì" says:
"The gentleman, before burial, reads the mourning rituals;
after burial, reads the sacrificial rituals;
when mourning returns to normal, reads the music chapters."
Mourning rituals differ for near and distant,
and substance and form are distinguished,
because they are based on utmost sincerity.
Recent literati,
however, have sacrificial texts for donning mourning garments upon a parent's death,
sacrificial texts for hall offerings when burying a parent,
and biographical accounts distributed to condolence guests.
The tradition says:
"When a filial son mourns a parent,
his weeping is not rhythmic,
his rituals have no formal demeanor,
his speech is not ornate.
Amidst the desolation of the mourning hut and mat,
he can rise only with a staff,
weeping morning and evening without fixed times."
How could there still be someone
capable of wielding the brush to compose ornate writings,
to record on bamboo and silk,
different from the man of Cāngwú yielding his wife,
or Minister Huá praising his ancestor?
Some say:
Perhaps the text is not composed by oneself,
but is a substitute speech by the funeral assistant.
Writing arises from substance.
Substitute speeches
must be such that the person could have uttered these words.
The owl, already in a precarious swaying nest,
does not produce pleasant and clear beautiful notes;
the crucian carp, stuck in a dried rut,
cannot avoid showing an indignant expression.
Even speaking on behalf of birds and fish,
one must also match their feelings.
How can it be said that because it is a substitute speech,
one forgets the situation of the filial son?
Some say that when composing drafts on behalf of others,
if one has parents,
one should not write about the deceased parents of others.
Yán Zhītuī, in his family instructions,
likely meant that a filial son should avoid suspicion,
listening without sound and seeing without form,
to the point of being earnest and meticulous.
However,
this fails to understand the essence of writing on behalf of others.
The greatest suspicion
lies in the relationship between ruler and minister;
when the Duke of Zhōu issued edicts to the officials and people on behalf of King Chéng,
he did not avoid suspicion despite his position facing south.
The gravest suspicion
lies in the relationship between men and women;
when Gǔ Yǒng replied to Empress Xǔ on behalf of Emperor Yuán,
he did not avoid suspicion despite being an in-law.
Since ancient times, renowned ministers
drafted imperial edicts and proclamations,
posthumously honoring previous dynasties,
establishing empresses and crown princes,
and even instructing officials,
all of which involved speaking on behalf of the emperor.
How could there be any suspicion?
If one insists on avoiding suspicion in worldly affairs,
and not taking on official duties,
then the "Orphan" poem in the Music Bureau,
must it have been written by a mourning son in plain attire?
The laments of widows in ancient times,
were they not composed by bearded men?
If a scholar writes about his parents,
he must be an orphan to do so;
then if a husband writes about his wife,
must he be a eunuch to do so?
Rituals that are not rituals,
righteousness that is not righteousness,
are not practiced by the noble person,
and this is precisely why.

In Defense of Zhèng
Since Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù are no more,
the specialized study of history has declined.
From Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè onward,
some succeeded, some failed,
barely earning reputations as masters.
By the Táng dynasty, with the establishment of official history bureaus,
they compiled the histories of Jìn and Suí,
and also called their works "histories";
yet scholars mistakenly followed these traditions,
failing to distinguish their proper forms,
so the original intent of ancient historians
became obscured and unclear.
As for literary scholars embellishing their prose,
and memorization experts refining their textual research,
their contributions to historiography
seem minor;
but following the stream while forgetting the source,
ignoring the broader principles,
the more diligent their efforts,
the further their understanding
strays from antiquity and becomes increasingly irrelevant.
Zhèng Qiáo, born a thousand years later,
profoundly understood the origins of ancient writings,
and knew that the author's intent
was not merely to display literary elegance,
nor to rely solely on textual research.
Thus, he sought to correct Sīmǎ Qiān,
enhancing with erudition,
criticizing Bān Gù,
mocking his lack of originality,
and uniquely drew upon
three thousand years of historical texts,
applying his distinctive insight and judgment,
upholding the tradition of comprehensive histories,
and weaving his own framework,
establishing a school of thought.
Scholars, seeing little and marveling much,
failed to examine his principles and examples,
his profound insights and broad discussions,
which synthesized various viewpoints,
as essential to historiography;
instead, they merely pointed out his occasional oversights in citations,
or the unfinished nature of his compilations,
and attacked him vehemently,
as if he were an irreconcilable enemy.
If the ancients were to return,
would they not consider such criticisms as trivial as a puff of air?
As for the twenty treatises,
particularly "Six Scripts," "Seven Tones," and "Insects and Plants,"
these are said to use history to support the classics,
not being limited to a single dynasty,
and can be continued endlessly,
truly representing specialized and unparalleled achievements,
which Hàn and Táng Confucian scholars
could not have imagined.
Establishing principles and examples,
creating monumental works,
he clarified his scholarly tradition through categories and meanings.
His work inevitably relied on the materials of his time,
roughly organized and summarized,
and was never intended
to compete with specialized philological works
in terms of detail;
nor did he wish for later generations
to rigidly adhere to his conclusions
without any adaptation.
Zhèng focused on grand principles,
while petty scholars nitpicked
over minor details.
Is this not like criticizing famed generals like Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè
for not being as refined as scholars from Zōu and Lǔ;
or blaming great Confucians like Fú Shēng and Kǒng Ānguó
for not excelling in trivial literary arts?
Sīmǎ Qiān's unparalleled scholarship,
after the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
stands alone.
What encompassed antiquity and synthesized hundreds of schools
was his establishment of principles and examples,
his exceptional insight and judgment,
which aligned with the origins of ancient authors,
and embodied the tradition of the "Spring and Autumn Annals."
As for factual inaccuracies,
inappropriate selections,
or unrefined discussions,
had he lived after the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
without the judgments of ancients;
or if the archives of stone chambers and golden cabinets,
and works like "Shìběn," "Diéjì," and "Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū,"
had not been lost;
later scholars obsessed with literary style and textual research
would have nitpicked every detail,
measuring with rigid standards,
and who knows how harshly they would have criticized him.
Are today's critics of Zhèng Qiáo any different?
How do they differ?
When Confucius composed the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
he said the events were those of Duke Huán of Qí and Duke Wén of Jìn,
the prose was historical,
but the meaning was what Confucius himself deemed worthy.
The events are what later textual researchers emphasize,
the prose is what later literary scholars value,
yet what Confucius valued
was not these but the meaning.
Then, in historical writing,
should one not seek the underlying meaning?
Since Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
historians lacked distinctive insight and judgment,
focusing only on events and prose.
Only Zhèng Qiáo somewhat aimed to seek meaning,
yet pedantic scholars
noisily rose to dispute him.
If their arguments were followed,
then all examination essays
and clerks' records,
being clear and flawless,
factual and reliable,
would seem far superior to Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
However,
Zhèng was not without faults.
Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù inherited their family profession,
serving as historians for life,
which is beyond comparison.
Sīmǎ Guāng's "Zīzhì Tōngjiàn,"
took nineteen years to complete,
with a dedicated bureau,
and his own staff;
those he discussed with
were all renowned scholars of the time;
thus, he could achieve unparalleled work,
becoming a master for generations.
Zhèng, alone and humble,
living in obscurity and poverty,
dared to do what none since Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù had attempted,
setting lofty and profound arguments,
though his fame exceeded his actual achievements.
Unfortunately, he was compared with Mǎ Duānlín's "Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo,"
and while both were celebrated in their time,
the superficiality and flaws of "Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo"
were not as severe as his.
Superficial scholars,
lacking firm judgment,
exaggeratedly praised or criticized,
making reckless comparisons,
thus equating his work
with mere compilation,
and in weighing strengths and weaknesses,
made it seem as if a towering peak were no match for a tiny piece of wood.
Is this not a great injustice?
Reply to a Guest's Questions, Part One
On the guǐsì day in Hángzhōu,
I heard that during a conversation between Dài Zhēnjūn Zhèn and Wú Chǔshì Yǐngfāng,
they vehemently criticized Zhèng Jūn’s *General Treatises*,
their words utterly bizarre and laughable.
I considered it not worth deep refutation,
and set it aside without discussion.
Later scholars,
however, often disparaged it.
Therefore, borrowing a certain gentleman’s preface and explanation,
I clarified the origins and development of the work.
I myself believed that the prevailing superficial criticisms
were largely dismantled and cleared away by my efforts.
Yet my writing traced back to Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and distinguished the *General Investigation*,
all being essential principles of historiography,
not entirely focused on the *General Treatises*.
Those who did not understand raised further objections,
so I composed three essays titled *Responses to a Guest*.
A guest who had seen my *Postscript to the Preface of the Continued General Treatises*
asked me:
"That the *General Treatises* should not be lightly criticized,
I have already heard your instruction.
However, your refutation,
though elaborate and exhaustive,
in its inferences
evaluates the ancients,
often differing from contemporary discussions.
Is this deliberate praise and blame
to support your argument?
Or do you have another explanation?"
Scholars all speak of the Twenty-Two Histories,
and bibliographers
take from Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward
up to the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
classifying them under the category of Standard Histories.
Now you alone say that the Táng people systematized the records of the Jìn and Suí,
also naming their works as histories,
and that scholars mistakenly accepted their classification,
without further correcting their form.
Could it be that from the Jìn and Suí onward,
they cannot be called histories?
Observing their established forms of tables and treatises,
and fixed styles of annals and biographies,
they are no different
from the histories of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
Establishing bureaus and appointing supervisors,
gathering crowds to compile books,
was also due to the circumstances of the times.
Seeking their essence,
they are of the same category.
Now you say scholars mistakenly accepted their classification;
I dare ask, from the Jìn and Suí onward,
what distinguishes them so clearly
from Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè and earlier?
I replied:
The great origin of history
lies in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The meaning of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
is manifest in its recording and deletion.
The principle of recording and deletion
is not merely about presenting events from beginning to end
and writing according to established norms.
Viewing it from the Master’s intention of "appropriating the meaning,"
it surely aimed to order the world
and elucidate the great Way.
To comprehend the changes of past and present
and form the words of a single school,
one must elaborate what others omit,
differentiate what others treat as the same,
emphasize what others neglect,
and overlook what others carefully attend to.
It must not be constrained by rigid rules,
nor bound by fixed categories.
Only then, in subtle and minute details,
can one make independent judgments with a single mind.
When such a work is completed,
it naturally can stand alongside heaven and earth and face spirits and ghosts,
accord with past sages and await future worthies.
This is why the learning of a school is precious.
From Chén Shòu and Fàn Yè onward,
measured by the meaning of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
one cannot say there were no faults.
Yet their unique insights and judgments,
the learning of their schools, remain.
Even if criticized,
such as saying Sīmǎ Qiān’s work demotes recluses and promotes villains,
or Bān Gù’s work suppresses loyalty and embellishes rulers’ faults,
the essence of their integration and transformation,
their meaning without deviation,
sufficiently establishes their school’s learning and aligns with the classical intent.
They are not at all like the later compilations,
which imitate Zǐ Mò’s rigid moderation,
seek the faultlessness of the village worthy,
and boastfully claim to surpass Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù.
As for the deeds of rulers and ministers,
the regulations of offices,
the change of dynasties and reception of the mandate,
reviewing previous eras,
compiling and comparing,
to preserve the old institutions of a dynasty—
this is what is called the work of systematizing records.
Establishing bureaus and appointing supervisors,
gathering crowds to compile books,
should precisely follow their principles and norms,
adhere to their rules,
awaiting later generations’ judgment.
How can this be spoken of in the same breath as specialized authorship?
The *Book of Changes* says:
"If it is not the right person,
the Way does not proceed emptily."
Historical talent does not appear in every age,
and the changes of the times are not constant.
Timely compiling what is seen and heard,
without urgently distinguishing school learning or making decisive selections—
is this not true of the histories of the Jìn and Suí?
Before Bān Gù,
there were the *Historical Records* of Liú Xiàng, Liú Xīn, Yáng Xióng, and Jiǎ Kuí;
before Fàn Yè,
there were the *Records of the Hàn* of Liú Zhēn, Lǐ Yóu, Cài Yōng, Lú Zhí, and Yáng Biāo.
Did these works not follow the established forms of tables and treatises,
and employ the fixed styles of annals and biographies?
Yet the records preserved for posterity
and the specialized works with independent judgment through recording and deletion
have functions that can complement each other,
but their classifications cannot be confused.
This is clear.
Tracing further back,
the treasured books of the hundred states relative to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the *Genealogical Records* and *Strategies of the Warring States* relative to the *Records of the Grand Historian*,
their meaning is likewise.
After the Táng, historiography declined,
and there were no specialized authors.
Later generations did not understand the school learning of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
and crudely grouped the officially compiled records
with the works of Sīmǎ Qiān, Bān Gù, Chén Shòu, and Fàn Yè,
classifying them together as Standard Histories.
Thus historical writing became like examination essays,
or clerks’ documents,
with no room for flexibility.
Occasionally, a thoughtful and learned scholar,
able to take the ancients as his teachers,
proposing principles beyond convention,
expressing unique personal judgment,
would face the world’s collective strange looks and curses,
pointed fingers and tangled criticisms,
like a monkey seeing ceremonial robes—
unless it bites, tears, and destroys them,
it will not stop.
Zhèng’s *General Treatises* being slandered
is entirely due to this.
Alas!
The Way has long been unclear.
The *Six Classics* are all history.
What is above form is called the Way;
what is within form is called the vessel.
In composing the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
Confucius said:
"I wish to express it in empty words,
but it is not as profound and clear as showing it in actual events."
Thus, institutions and facts
are not neglected by the author,
for they illuminate the Way through the vessel.
If a book sufficiently clarifies the Way,
matters of ritual vessels
are left to the officials.
A gentleman does not consider these trivial.
When the Way is unclear, contention focuses on the vessel;
when substance is lacking, competition centers on style.
The flaw of this
and winning with empty words,
or flowery rhetoric harming principle,
differs by less than an inch.
Yet those immersed in it do not discern this.
The Grand Historian said:
"Be fond of learning and deep in thought,
and know the meaning in your mind."
In the present age,
where can one find those who know the meaning
to discuss the purpose of writing?
The guest said:
Confucius described himself as:
"Transmitting rather than creating,
trusting in and loving antiquity."
He also said:
"Loving antiquity, I diligently seek it."
Regarding the rituals of the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
the Master could speak of them,
yet without evidence, they cannot be trusted,
lamenting the insufficiency of documents and traditions.
Now, sir, you say that authors have their underlying principles,
while the number of ritual vessels such as biāndòu
is not considered trivial.
Is this not contrary to the Master's teaching?
The comprehensiveness and detail of Mǎ Duānlín's Tōng Kǎo,
and the errors and omissions in Zhèng Qiáo's Tōng Zhì,
are known even to a child.
Yet you, sir, only value their underlying principles,
without holding them accountable for practical utility,
and thus wish to elevate Zhèng and diminish Mǎ.
Is your argument not somewhat biased?
Master Zhāng said:
All statements in the world
have their proper place;
the words of the Classics and commentaries
are also like this.
When reading the books of the ancients,
if one cannot grasp their overall meaning,
but merely clings to ambiguous interpretations
to argue for superiority in a narrow aspect,
then such narrow arguments
are of little use.
In the world, there are works of compilation,
there is the learning of independent judgment,
and there is the effort of investigation and inquiry.
These three each have their own focus,
and cannot be interchanged.
The Six Classics in relation to other texts
are like the sun and moon in the sky.
Reading the Shū without the Shī,
or reading the Yì without the Chūnqiū,
even with the sages' texts,
one cannot, within a single book,
encompass the inquiries of multiple schools.
The Yì says, "One cannot hold to fixed rules,"
while the Shū emphasizes that "words should embody the essential."
Reading the Shī, one should not let the words obscure the intent,
while the Chūnqiū uses a single word to determine right and wrong.
If one were to take the imagery of dragon's blood and ghost chariots
and seek evidence in phrases like "yuè ruò jī gǔ,"
or use dreams of bears, snakes, fish, and banners
to record the ordinances of "the king's first month of spring,"
then the sages' work would be neglected,
and the purpose of studying the Classics would be perverted.
As for loving antiquity and diligent seeking,
and verifying through documents and traditions,
I do not say that past deeds and ancient words can be treated carelessly.
One should hear much and make selections,
study broadly yet focus on the essential.
What one selects must have its own justification,
and cannot be constrained entirely by established theories.
When the great Way was hidden,
the various masters contended,
each grasping one aspect of the former kings' teachings,
as Zhuāngzǐ said, "Eyes, ears, mouth, and nose
each have their clarity,
but cannot interchange their functions."
