The eyes can discern the finest hair,
but cannot see thunder and lightning.
The ears can distinguish the five tones,
but cannot perceive Mount Tài.
To say that the eyes and ears have their capabilities and limitations
is permissible;
but to say that what the ears hear and eyes see are insufficient for understanding thunder, lightning, mountains, and peaks—
is that acceptable?
Since the Hàn dynasty,
scholars have expressed their insights
through writings to make themselves known,
and there have been many such cases.
The brilliant often excel in independent judgment,
the profound emphasize investigation and inquiry.
The world of scholarship
inevitably encompasses these two paths.
They are like day and night,
summer and winter:
for succession and completion of the yearly cycle,
they benefit from mutual need;
but for self-confinement and establishing boundaries,
they suffer the harm of mutual injury.
Thus, Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù are ancestors of history,
while Fú Shēng and Zhèng Xuán are masters of the Classics.
Change their domains and they cannot excel,
yet they proceed along their own paths without contradicting each other.
If Fú and Zhèng were to comment on the same classic,
there would inevitably be contradictions.
If Sīmǎ and Bān were to compile the same history,
there would surely be conflicts.
From this we know that specialized learning
always follows its own intent independently.
Even if peers dispute it, it remains unshaken;
even if the whole world condemns it, it remains undeterred.
This is why Sīmǎ Qiān insisted on transmitting his work to the right person,
and why Bān Gù had to wait for Mǎ Róng to study under his sister
before his learning became prominent.
Sīmǎ's work was transmitted by scholars like Xú Guǎng and Péi Yīn,
Bān's work by scholars like Fú Qián and Yīng Shào.
Specialized learning,
passed down orally and mentally,
is no different from the masters of the Classics having their commentaries.
Thus, the intent of the Chūnqiū to order the world
must contain elements that cannot be fully detailed in writing,
nor measured by fixed standards.
Yet scholars today,
whenever they encounter works of independent judgment by the ancients,
if they find the meaning unsatisfactory,
noisily rise up to attack them.
This shows they enjoy debate but do not seek genuine achievement.
As for compiled works,
they are like the catalogs of clerks and archivists,
the established formats of records and registers.
Their origin lies in the collections under the pillars,
and their use is limited to facilitating reference and selection.
There is nothing extraordinary about them initially.
Yet learning of independent judgment
cannot select material without them;
the effort of investigation and inquiry
cannot rely on evidence without them.
Just as fine wine cannot be separated from its dregs,
and good grain cannot be separated from manure,
so books of official duties, precedents, documents, charts, and maps
should not be lightly criticized.
However, the learning of independent judgment
and the effort of investigation and inquiry require wisdom,
while compiled works require simplicity.
Just as wine can fill ritual vessels,
but dregs cannot fill ritual vessels;
grain can be placed in sacrificial containers,
but manure cannot be placed in sacrificial containers—
the principle is perfectly clear.
The ancients said:
"If words are not refined,
they will not travel far."
"If writing is not elegant and proper,
gentlemen will find it difficult to speak of."
Because works on official duties, precedents, documents, charts, and maps are difficult to compile and transmit widely,
the method of compilation was established.
They do not establish a school of thought,
nor present unique interpretations.
They organize past records
and await later generations' judgment.
This is the effect of keeping compiled works simple.
To elevate them to the hall of authorship,
and claim them as one's own school of thought—
how easy is that?
Moreover, Bān Gù's talent
can be said to be supreme.
Yet when he, along with Chén Zōng, Yǐn Mǐn, and others,
compiled the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shìzǔ"
and the biographies of Xīnshì, Pínglín, and others,
these could not stand alongside the Hàn Shū,
and Fàn Yè's work became the orthodox version.
This shows that compiling official historical records
and the independent judgment of historical composition
are clearly not connected.
Since then,
the proper tradition has been lost.
Zhèng Qiáo lacked the effort of investigation and inquiry,
yet his Tōng Zhì sufficiently demonstrates the learning of independent judgment.
Gentlemen find value in this.
Mǎ Duānlín lacked the learning of independent judgment,
and his Tōng Kǎo is insufficient as a work of compilation.
One can say his wisdom is not commendable,
and his approach to simplicity
is also incomplete.
Moreover, he divided the Tōng Diǎn into many categories
merely for convenience of reference.
He collected discussions from historical records
to facilitate balanced judgment.
This is like the examination cribs of classical scholars—
daring not to express a single original view,
nor to propose an idea beyond convention,
but obscurely flattering the world as a hypocrite.
As for the underlying principles of ancient authors,
they cannot be heard.
Vulgar learning finds his classification easy to follow,
appreciates his discussions as moderate and safe,
and unanimously praises him,
not realizing how unlike the true tradition of authorship this is.
This is why crude and discordant tunes
can attract countless followers.
Reply to the Guest, Part Two
The guest said:
Regarding the learning of independent judgment
and the effort of investigation and inquiry,
I have heard your explanation.
May I ask about compiled works?
You, sir, compare them to dregs and manure—
what does this mean?
Zhāngzǐ said:
This is not a derogatory statement.
Only when there is uncarved jade can carving be applied;
only when there is raw material can the axe be wielded.
In the distinction between what comes first and what comes later, what is light and what is heavy,
the principle is easily understood.
The Shī and Shū before the Master edited them,
and the Yì, Lǐ, and Chūnqiū before they were finalized,
were all the old classics of the former kings.
Yet without the Master’s judgment and determination,
they could not have been transmitted to scholars.
Lǐ Tāo said, “Zuǒshì intended to transmit the Chūnqiū,
so he first gathered the historical records of various states,
arranged them by state as narratives,
to serve as material for the compilation of the ‘Inner Biography.’”
Although this is speculative,
the ancients, in writing books,
never had absolutely no basis at all.
From this, we know that the work of compilation and arrangement
cannot be left unexamined.
The methods of compilation and arrangement
generally fall into three categories:
There is the timely collection and compilation
to await the judgment and determination of later generations,
such as the Shǐjì by Liú Xīn and Yáng Xióng,
and the Hànjì by Bān Gù and Chén Zōng.
There is the intentional composition of works,
first gathering numerous books
as fuel for the fire,
such as Wáng’s Yùhǎi,
and Sīmǎ’s Chángbiān.
There is the refining of specialized knowledge
to compile great works,
such as Sīmǎ Qiān recording the techniques of Cāngōng,
and Bān Gù editing Liú Xiàng’s “Wǔxíng.”
As for timely compilation awaiting judgment,
the key lies in the details of what to include or omit,
and precision in organization.
Gathering numerous books as fuel for the fire
requires distinguishing similarities and examining differences,
and caution in verification.
Refining specialized knowledge to compile great works
involves extracting the essence and summarizing key points,
and grasping the overall framework.
Since the work of compilation and arrangement
differs in these ways,
the author’s intent
also varies accordingly.
Yet scholars today
believe that the way of the world
lies solely in comparing the similarities and differences of names and numbers,
and determining the correctness of phonetic glosses.
Is this not like observing the sky from the bottom of a well
or measuring the water in a puddle,
and then claiming to fully comprehend the movements of the universe
or gauge the waves of the four seas?
The ages of the Hàn emperors
are recorded in the Biélù;
Fúshēng and Wénwēng’s names
are verified by stone inscriptions.
Gāozǔ’s construction of Xīnfēng
is detailed in Liú’s records;
the Xījīng Zájì records Xiàowǔ’s fondness for incognito travels,
as noted in the outer biographies;
the Hànwǔ Gùshì, yet the works of Qiān and Gù
do not include these,
showing that the abundance of compiled materials
does not hinder the author’s selectivity.
Cáo Pī’s memorial of abdication
is detailed in the Xiàndì Zhuàn;
the virtuous conduct of Empress Zhēn
is highly praised in the Wèishū;
the account of Āiláo
is verified by census officials;
as seen in the Lùnhéng, the list of earlier worthies
is recorded in the Huángchū era;
yet the histories by Chén and Fàn
do not include these,
showing that the private nature of compiled materials
awaits the impartial judgment of the author.
However, scholars of the classics, in their studies,
compile canonical forests,
while literary writers, in their compositions,
collect rhyming phrases.
The shallow habits of recent times
prioritize convenience and reference,
each creating their own private handbooks,
to serve the needs of mediocre learning.
In such cases, even if the work of compilation
were like dregs or dung,
hoping to transform decay into wonder,
how could it be achieved?
Since village books and vulgar learning
lack good material,
the work of compilation
faces its first difficulty in reliance.
The historical facts cited
are often not from the original texts,
and there is a tendency to alter words and sentences,
diluting their essence,
so that scholars prefer to study the original works
and are reluctant to consult new compilations.
This is the second difficulty in reliance.
Grouping similar things together
is not inherently a work of authorship,
yet compiling old texts
without citing their sources,
as if they were one’s own discoveries,
makes it impossible for others to verify.
This is the third difficulty in reliance.
Different accounts of hearsay
and varying records
are not collected and included together
for the author’s judgment,
but are privately selected
based on one’s own cleverness.
This is the fourth difficulty in reliance.
The study of illustrations and paintings
is not included in historical works,
and inscriptions on bronze and stone
are only listed in catalogs,
making it impossible for later scholars
to verify and rely on them.
This is the fifth difficulty in reliance.
Specialized books
that have become great works
are not included in compilations,
generally to prevent loss,
yet allowing them to circulate alone
gradually leads to their disappearance.
This is the sixth difficulty in reliance.
Constrained by classifications and examples,
compiling just enough to form a book,
without seeking materials beyond the rules
to prepare for the author’s judgment,
is like a net with only one eye—
it will never catch a bird.
This is the seventh difficulty in reliance.
All these issues
were not fully addressed by the ancients,
and later scholars are even less aware of them.
If one is concerned about gathering provisions for three months,
how can one not prepare for study and practice?
Yet scholars of the age,
not knowing to assess their own virtue and strength,
all clamor to proclaim themselves authors,
unwilling to engage in the foundational work of tools and guides.
As Liú Xīn said, “They harbor the selfish fear of being exposed as flawed,
and lack the public-mindedness to follow goodness and accept righteousness.”
How can their methods and works be proper?
And how can the way of authorship
be corrected?
Someone asked:
Can the literary compositions of predecessors
be altered and adapted as one's own work?
The answer:
Why not?
In ancient times, writing was considered a public instrument;
if the expressions of predecessors were already exhaustive,
later people could transmit them without necessarily creating anew.
Quoting poetry by extracting sections,
it is no different than if the words came from one's own mouth.
What matters is the intent behind the literary expression,
not the expression itself.
If one grasps the underlying meaning,
there is no need for alteration,
and the predecessor's literary expression becomes no different from one's own.
Without that intent yet seeking to match the literary expression,
even if not a single word or phrase is directly copied,
but one secretly imitates what the predecessor said,
a noble person would scorn it as plagiarism.
Someone said:
Chén Lín drafted a report for Cáo Hóng to the Crown Prince of Wèi,
yet it was discreetly said that Chén Lín composed the text.
Dīng Jìnglǐ asked Cáo Zǐjiàn to polish his writing,
and then said, "Who in later generations will know who finalized my text?"
Hán Yù of the Táng dynasty said:
"Only in antiquity was writing necessarily one's own creation;
later, when unable, one resorted to plagiarism."
The ancients certainly desired their literary expressions to be their own mastery;
how could it be said they valued only the meaning?
The answer:
The writing of literary men
and the writing of scholarly works
cannot be spoken of in the same breath.
Scholarly works must have something established prior to the literary expression,
borrowing literary expression merely to convey it.
For example, in ceremonial rites at the imperial temple,
brocade sashes and jade pendants must be used.
Those performing the rites
do not inquire about the making of the sashes and pendants.
Such is the writing of scholarly works.
Brocade weavers and jade craftsmen
have never studied the rites;
they rely solely on weaving brocade and carving jade to demonstrate their skill.
If they claim the work of other craftsmen as their own,
everyone would consider it theft.
Such is the writing of literary men.
Therefore, to judge the literary expression of scholarly works
from the perspective of literary men
is like having brocade weavers and jade craftsmen
discuss the ceremonial codes of the imperial temple.
Someone said:
In ancient times, diplomatic documents were drafted
and then revised and polished;
in later ages, poetry and prose
also had the "teacher of a single character."
If what is valued is the meaning,
and the expression is not considered,
for example, in ceremonial rites at the imperial temple,
even if one does not consider the sashes and pendants,
if the sashes and pendants are worn and torn,
not conforming to regulation,
could the rites still proceed?
The answer:
This is discussing writing in terms of writing itself,
a separate category altogether.
Discussing writing in terms of writing,
the former master had the instruction that "expression should convey meaning,"
Zēngzǐ warned against crude and perverse speech,
the sage's school established disciplines,
with literature and speech both preserved.
Persuasive speech also values those skilled in its use;
the literary expressions of the ancients
certainly sought refinement.
But this is not about drawing boundaries
and contending that writing must be one's own creation
to boast of private skill.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the discussion of writing has also had its specialists.
The Yuèfǔ adapted old poems for their sonorous quality;
the *Wénxuǎn* trimmed the works of predecessors;
both focused on sound, emotion, and color,
not the same as the category of scholarly works.
The preface to the *Huìchāng Imperial Edict Collection*,
where Zhèng Yà trimmed Lǐ Shāngyǐn's lushness;
the "Song of the Yuèshí Eclipse" from the Yuánhé era,
where Hán Yù elevated Lú Tóng's eccentricity;
sometimes preserving the original attribution to return it to its author,
sometimes changing the title to include it in one's own collection—
though these are minor skills in discussing writing,
there are those who excel in them.
Having attained deep understanding,
they no longer haggle over trivial details of words and phrases between self and other.
Someone said:
In the past, Yuè Guǎng was skilled in speech,
and Zhì Yú had marvelous brushwork;
Yuè's discussions, Zhì could not seal;
Zhì's brushwork, Yuè could not replicate.
Each person has their own partial strengths.
Then, for those who can speak but cannot write,
is it permissible to borrow another to wield the brush?
The answer:
Pān Yuè also drafted a declining memorial for Yuè Guǎng;
he had to grasp Yuè's intended meaning and phrasing,
and then compose it into a renowned piece.
History has also praised both.
After the two Hàn dynasties,
few people possessed multiple strengths:
some excelled in learning but were deficient in expression;
some were skilled in writing but negligent in recording.
Even within scholarship,
there are partial specialties;
within the realm of literary expression,
there are specialized skills.
These could mutually assist and achieve merit,
yet the world often exchanges ridicule and mutual disparagement,
so the great Way ultimately cannot be seen.
Literary expression is a minor matter;
if one removes boundaries and gathers specialized strengths,
there can still be outstanding, imperishable achievement,
let alone progressing from scholarship to seek the greater substance of the ancients?
Yet from ancient times to the present,
there has been no such person—
this is simply unavoidable.
Someone said:
If it is truly as you say,
that literary writing and scholarship
can be mutually entrusted,
then if there is a cunning person
with no real strength,
who falsely claims public-mindedness
to mingle among them like the untalented musician in the ensemble,
how can this be discerned?
The answer:
A tripod weighing a thousand jūn,
if two people lift it
who cannot bear five hundred jūn each,
will stumble and fall.
When Lǐ Guǎng entered Chéng Bùshí's army,
the banners and fortifications
were renewed.
If his talent and wisdom were inferior to Chéng's,
the whole army would be in chaos.
A wealthy man traveling far,
carrying not a single coin,
needs something and seeks a loan—
people vie to lend to him.
Why can others not do this?
Only because he is rich in money
can he later borrow others' money.
Therefore, if literature is dedicated to the public good,
those without substance
cannot pretend.
Someone said:
The writings of predecessors
are not all perfect;
later people then revise and amend them to demonstrate method.
Can this also be done?
The answer:
This is difficult to say.
In scholarly works, altering predecessors
has a different, specific purpose,
so it is not harmful.
In discussing writing, altering predecessors—
the literary mind differs
just as human faces do;
one cannot, based on one's own view,
hastily claim superiority over predecessors.
Liú Zhījī's *Shǐtōng*
includes the chapter "Diǎn Fán" (Pointing Out Redundancies).
From Zuǒ Qiūmíng and Sīmǎ Qiān onward,
there have been deletions and alterations;
some have criticized him for knowing history but not literature.
Yet Liú acted with a purpose,
so merits and faults can both be seen.
As for those specializing solely in discussing writing,
they should be cautious.
The intelligence and wisdom of past and present
are themselves difficult to exhaust;
modern people's insights
are not necessarily all inferior to the ancients'.
Generally, unintentional, chance correspondences
may achieve the success of turning base metal into gold;
intentional alterations
often invite the ridicule of painting on already finished plaster.
For discussing writing values the natural revelation of innate talent,
not wanting human effort to be forced and contrived.
Someone asked:
In recent times, figures like Fāng Bāo
have edited and altered the works of the great masters of the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
Was there any benefit to this?
Now, Fāng was merely a man of letters;
his understanding was not particularly profound to begin with.
Moreover, he was further burdened by personal bias and a contentious spirit.
Not only did this fail to benefit literature,
but it actually initiated a trend of recklessness among later generations of young scholars.
Clever tricks and petty wisdom,
a smattering of knowledge and half-understood ideas—
these are not necessarily incapable of finding fault in the ancients' writings
or picking up what they left behind.
Discussing this in terms of scholarship,
one could classify it under the example of "the less worthy noting the minor details,"
preserving such theories for later generations to consider and select from—that is acceptable.
But if we are discussing literary style,
since these matters do not concern the greater meaning,
they can all be set aside and not discussed.
This is just like the saying, "People's minds differ as their faces do";
there is no need to force uniformity.
However, if regarding matters of right and wrong, gain and loss,
later generations indeed have their own insights,
they naturally cannot remain silent.
If one must express them, it should be as if compelled by necessity,
carefully deliberating again and again before acting.
It is like the state deliberating on old regulations,
or famous ministers strategizing on advantages and disadvantages:
unless there is a clear disparity of ten or a hundredfold,
it is better to preserve the old and not recklessly make changes.
If one does not deeply understand this principle
and lightly criticizes the ancients,
this is the height of mediocrity and presumption.
Even if there might be some small gain,
it would not be enough to compensate for the great loss.
In Fāng's editing and altering of the great masters,
was there any compelling necessity?
Was there any clear right or wrong, gain or loss,
with a disparity as obvious as ten or a hundredfold?
Was there anything like the state deliberating on old regulations,
or famous ministers strategizing on advantages and disadvantages,
with the original intent being to preserve the old and not recklessly make changes?
Even Fāng himself would not dare claim this was so.
Thus, personal bias and a contentious spirit,
seeking to surpass the ancients—
this is why Fāng ultimately never reached the level of the ancients.
Generally, those who can achieve transformation through the ancients
must first strictly adhere to the ancients' rules and measures, not daring to overstep them.
For if one does not believe in them wholeheartedly and uphold them steadfastly,
then one's entry into antiquity will not be deep;
if not deep, one cannot achieve transformation.
It is like with friends:
to fully embody the righteousness of Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shūyá sharing wealth,
one must first be strictly disciplined in the minutiae of giving and receiving.
Otherwise, it is certainly impossible.
Therefore, studying the ancients yet not daring to rigidly adhere to them
is actually the utmost reverence and strictness in serving the ancients,
not a disregard for them.
Fāng did not understand the intentions of the ancients
and was only concerned with literary style.
Moreover, what he grasped of literary style
was not particularly profound to begin with.
His petty wisdom and clever tricks
were just sufficient to glimpse what the ancients took for granted,
without understanding that it was not always entirely so.
No wonder he found it so easy to boldly take up his brush and alter their works.
The standard forms of ancient prose
and the origins and evolution of ancient prose styles—
these are what beginners
should first distinguish.
Sū Zǐzhān's "Stele of the Temple of Manifest Loyalty"
fully transcribes Zhào Biàn's memorial,
without adding or subtracting a word from the text.
Right after it, he attached the inscription poem.
This was actually a common convention of Hàn dynasty steles,
seen in various books on bronze and stone inscriptions—
too numerous to record.
Even among the prose of the Eight Masters of the Táng and Sòng,
such as Liǔ Zǐhòu's "Stele of the Filial Gate in Ānfēng, Shòu Prefecture,"
he also used this convention,
which is not strange at all.
Wáng Jièfǔ expressed surprise, saying it imitated the "Hereditary Houses" and "Yearly Tables" of the *Records of the Grand Historian*—
truly the words of a pedant.
Lǐ Qíqīng said its style imitated the *Book of Hàn*,
which is also completely inexplicable.
This is an extremely common matter within ordinary experience;
why did these gentlemen make it out to be so bizarre and strange,
treating it like an antique curio?
Moreover, even in recent times, in marketplaces and villages,
if there are advantages and disadvantages, gains and losses,
and public discussion leads to prohibitions,
requesting officials to establish laws,
and erecting a stele to endure for ages,
that stele simply carves the original text of the official document or proclamation,
with no need to add or subtract words or phrases—
this too is an ancient method.
Could it be that Wáng Jièfǔ and the others
had never seen such steles and inscriptions?
The criticisms and shocked exclamations from Wáng's disciples at the time
are not even worth a laugh.
Speaking in terms of literary style,
Zhào Qīngxiàn's original memorial requesting the repair of the Temple of Manifest Loyalty
was likely not as elegantly archaic as Sū's stele text.
Historians recording events and speeches,
adopting existing texts,
originally had methods of editing and altering.
Sū's stele,
though it seems like a copied and transcribed text,
actually required considerable effort in arrangement and composition.
However, while the wording can be edited,
the form must follow the conventions of the time.
In this stele, the three characters at the beginning,
"Chén Biàn yán" ("Your servant Biàn says"),
and the three characters at the end,
"Zhì yuē kě" ("The decree says: Approved"),
are likely not the style for submitting memorials and issuing imperial decrees in the Sòng dynasty.
But in Sū's mind,
he was too familiar with phrases from the "Basic Annals of Qín" like
"Chéngxiàng chén Sī mèisǐ yán" ("The Chancellor, your servant Sī, dares to speak at the risk of death")
and "Zhì yuē kě" ("The decree says: Approved").
Thus, he could not avoid what Liú Zhījī criticized:
similar in appearance but different in essence.
I once compiled the *Gazetteer of Hézhōu*,
which included the "Biographies of the Righteous and Heroic of Yǐhài,"
specifically recording events from the eighth year of the Chóngzhēn reign of the late Míng,
when the rebel army of Lǐ Zìchéng
captured Hézhōu,
and officials, gentry, commoners, men and women died as martyrs.
Using the style of chronicling events from beginning to end,
I took events as the warp
and people as the weft,
recording everything in detail.
But disputes erupted within the prefecture.
This was because the rebel army of Lǐ Zìchéng,
enraged by the resistance, slaughtered the city.
The descendants of those slaughtered
blamed those who had proposed defending the city,
accusing them of endangering the entire city's population.
There were also essays criticizing the defenders for improper deployment,
leading to the city's fall.
Some even falsely accused those who proposed the defense
of trying to escape by being lowered from the city walls,
only to be captured and killed by the rebels—
claiming they were not true martyrs.
I searched and found the memorial by Zhū Dàdiǎn, Grand Coordinator of Fèngyáng,
reporting the fall of Hézhōu
and the circumstances of the officials and gentry dying as martyrs.
It was based on reports from the Hézhōu Assistant Prefect of River Defense,
which in turn relied on eyewitness accounts from refugees who escaped the besieged city.
The loyalty and heroism of the officials and gentry
could not be falsely denied.
Therefore, I fully transcribed the memorial report
to serve as the preface to that section.
Within the text, there were edits and alterations
that had some excellent points.
However, the beginning necessarily stated:
"On such-and-such day of the second month in the ninth year of Chóngzhēn,
Zhū Dàdiǎn, Your Servant, Grand Coordinator of Fèngyáng, Commander of Military Affairs, and Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Right of the Censorate, respectfully memorializes:
Regarding the fall of Hé City to the rebels,
and the pitiable martyrdom of officials and gentry,
I beg to bestow honors and recognition
to manifest their righteousness and heroism."
The end stated:
"By Imperial Decree:
Having read the memorial with compassion,
let the relevant ministry investigate the precedents and implement accordingly."
This was indeed the format for memorials and imperial responses at that time.
Some said that since the memorial text in the middle
had already been edited to be elegantly archaic,
the beginning and end could similarly be polished.
I argued that the wording of memorials
does not have a fixed stylistic form,
so they can be edited to be elegantly archaic
without hindering the matter or principle.
But the beginning and end were the standard formulas of the time;
how can one dress a Míng dynasty figure
in Qín or Hàn dynasty attire?
Regarding Sū's "Stele of the Temple of Manifest Loyalty,"
previous scholars did not understand it
and expressed shock and surprise—
this was naturally due to their lack of learning.
Sū's text itself
is not open to criticism.
As for people becoming accustomed to it and not finding it strange,
what is actually untenable
is solely the six characters at the beginning and end that do not follow the standard formula.
If one does not examine the principles and conventions of literary style
but only pursues archaic elegance,
then why not use the three characters "Yuè yuē yú" ("The Chief Minister said: Oh!")
instead of "Chén Biàn yán" ("Your servant Biàn says")—
wouldn't that be even more archaic?
And why not use the three characters "Dì yuē yú" ("The Emperor said: Yes")
instead of "Zhì yuē kě" ("The decree says: Approved")—
wouldn't that be even more archaic?
Abandoning the models of Táng and Yú to imitate Qín and Hàn—
I have yet to see that this constitutes a genuine love for antiquity.
Wāng Dùnwēng composed the "Preface to the Commendation of the Gate for the Chaste Woman of Suīzhōu, Madame Tāng,"
beginning with the report submitted by the Investigating Censor,
which is a common practice,
not to be criticized,
nor is it particularly commendable.
However, Mr. Wāng did not understand that while literary style may follow ancient methods,
official documents must adhere to contemporary regulations.
The format of reports from the Qín and Hàn dynasties
cannot be used to modify modern documents.
At the beginning of the piece, he wrote, "The Investigating Censor, Your Servant Cuìrán, states,"
which is likely due to his overfamiliarity with the three characters "Your Servant Biàn states" from the "Stele of the Temple of Loyalty,"
without realizing that Sū Shì's usage was already improper.
In modern memorials,
the official title at the beginning
always includes the surname,
as per official regulations.
What was Cuìrán's surname?
How could Mr. Wāng omit it in his attempt to emulate antiquity?
Moreover, in modern memorials,
below the official title and name,
it is customary to write "respectfully submits,"
not "states."
A mere four-character phrase,
yet it violates official regulations in two ways.
How can this be considered proper classical prose?
For women, those with names are referred to by name,
those without names are referred to by surname,
such as Zhāng or Lǐ.
In modern official documents
and popular petitions,
it is common to omit the surname and simply refer to them as "Madame,"
or even "the said Madame,"
which is indeed vulgar and improper.
However, as there are no explicit prohibitions,
if clerks have any sense,
they will still refer to them as Zhāng or Lǐ,
which is not forbidden by officials,
and thus remains a flexible practice.
Mr. Wāng, when faced with unchangeable official regulations,
deliberately altered them to the ancient style of Qín and Hàn,
which is already a case of superficial similarity but fundamental difference.
As for commonly accepted forms of address,
he instead abandoned the proper form and followed the vulgar one.
How could he be so contradictory?
The concluding sentence also states, "Your Servant respectfully dares to risk death to report,"
which is also not in accordance with modern regulations.
Mr. Wāng usually prides himself on his classical prose,
yet he is so mediocre and ignorant.
Why is this?
In Wāng's preface,
after the phrase "Your Servant Cuìrán states,"
he directly begins with: "Zhào, wife of a scholar of Suīzhōu named Tāng,
during the turmoil of Lǐ Zìchéng's rebellion at the end of the Míng dynasty..."
and so on,
which is also not well done.
It should have been: "Zhào, wife of a scholar of the former Míng dynasty named Tāng of Suīzhōu,
during the turmoil of Lǐ Zìchéng's rebellion..."
This would have been more appropriate in wording.
The abrupt mention makes it seem like a present-day person,
and the following sentence adds "during the turmoil of Lǐ Zìchéng at the end of the Míng dynasty,"
making the flow of the text somewhat awkward.
Those who study literature
should pay attention to such distinctions.
Ten Common Faults in Classical Prose
I have discussed the principles and examples of classical prose,
in letters to friends who share my interests,
totaling several dozen.
Written as treatises,
there are also works such as "Literary Virtue," "Literary Principles," "Innate Nature," "Craftiness and Ignorance," "Vulgar Taboos," and "Common Avoidances,"
which elaborate on these matters in detail.
However, most of these discussions concern ancient times,
with little mention of recent eras.
Observing contemporary authors,
their statements and writings
often leave me uneasy.
Therefore, I have selected the most straightforward examples,
organizing them into ten points,
hoping to discuss and clarify them with like-minded friends.
I will not repeat what has already been covered in other works;
readers may refer to them for further insight.
This does not exhaust all the subtleties of writing,
but by inferring from one example to others,
one may come close to understanding.
First,
those who write classical prose
must first understand the fundamental principles of the ancients,
with the elegance of the prose being secondary.
Without understanding these principles,
one's judgment cannot be relied upon,
and what one composes
may not align with reason.
Even when the reasoning itself is sound,
one may mistakenly perceive flaws and attempt to remedy them,
thereby leading the world astray in matters of benevolence and righteousness.
A renowned scholar submitted an account of his mother's conduct,
requesting Mr. Zhū of Dàxīng to compose an epitaph.
In describing his mother's chastity and filial piety,
he mentioned that her grandfather, in his old age, was bedridden due to illness,
with no control over his bodily functions,
and there were no other males in the household.
His mother, undeterred by the filth,
personally attended to the washing and cleaning.
This act was already commendable.
Yet he added that the grandfather felt uneasy at the time,
and his mother solemnly replied:
"I am fifty years old,
now serving an eighty-year-old man.
What suspicion or doubt could there be?"
Alas!
The mother's conduct is praiseworthy,
but the son's writing is highly improper.
There was originally no issue,
so why raise suspicions?
A chaste woman who understood great righteousness
would certainly never have uttered such words.
This gentleman unnecessarily created suspicion,
adding annotations to justify the situation,
thinking it appropriate,
unaware that it was like carving sores onto flawless skin,
only making the flaws more apparent with each attempt to wash them away.
If one does not understand literary expression,
when encountering such situations,
one should simply record the facts directly,
without arbitrarily adding embellishments.
Arbitrarily adding embellishments
is called "carving flesh into sores,"
a common fault among writers.
Second,
The Spring and Autumn Annals records minor faults within the state without concealment.
Only in harsh winter does one realize the pine and cypress remain evergreen.
Thus, to praise the steadfastness of the pine and cypress,
one must clarify the severity of the frost and snow,
as this is the natural course of things.
In an age full of taboos and suspicions,
when praising the pine and cypress,
one fears the frost and snow may feel ashamed,
making everything one touches thorny.
However, while major faults are concealed,
minor faults are not,
as the Spring and Autumn Annals' recording of internal affairs
follows its own principles.
An old family in Jiāngnán compiled a clan genealogy.
One of their ancestors had arranged a marriage for his son with a certain family's daughter,
but due to the distance and poverty,
they could not afford the wedding.
Fearing the marriage would be delayed,
they falsely reported the son's death,
allowing the girl to marry another.
The girl then starved herself to death,
unaware that the son was still alive.
In this situation, neither chastity nor martyrdom applied.
Yet the girl's actions
were truly worthy of chastity and martyrdom,
and should not be forgotten.
Recording the facts directly
would undoubtedly reflect poorly on the old man.
However, according to the Rites of Zhōu, matchmakers are prohibited from arranging marriages for the deceased,
meaning the girl had no obligation to die.
In the "Questions of Zēngzǐ,"
if the wedding date is set
and the parents of the groom die,
a messenger is sent to inform the bride's family.
The commentary explains this is to avoid missing the auspicious time for marriage.
Thus, in ancient times, there was a ritual for canceling marriages.
According to current regulations,
if the groom travels far away
and is unheard from for three years,
the woman may petition the authorities to remarry.
Thus, the law includes provisions for annulling marriages due to prolonged absence.
Therefore, the old man's false report of his son's death,
when considered in context and with understanding,
is not a major fault that must be concealed.
Yet his clansmen, with grave expressions, insisted
that it could not be recorded directly,
so they obscured the wording, saying:
"They reported the death of a young son,
and the girl's family mistakenly thought it was the groom."
Why would anyone, from thousands of miles away,
report the death of a young son for no reason,
without mentioning the wedding date?
Anyone with sense would know this makes no logic.
This is a flaw in the writing.
No one is a sage;
how can one be without faults?
When ancient writers narrated a person's deeds,
they did not shy away from mentioning both strengths and weaknesses.
Nowadays, when narrating a person's story,
one must consider everyone around them—above, below, left, right, front, and back—
ensuring none have even minor flaws,
which is nearly impossible.
This is called "seeking perfection from all sides,"
another common fault among writers.
The sixth point:
Once historical writing became a specialized field,
texts preserved cross-references,
as seen in the example of the "Biographies of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng,"
where their achievements are detailed in the "Hereditary House of Qí";
Zhāng Ěr is treated separately,
yet his deeds are summarized in the "Biography of Chén Yú."
This is not only due to differences in intent,
but also because the style of detail and brevity demands it.
As for collections of literary works,
which contain standalone biographies,
whenever related matters are involved,
there are no cross-referenced chapters,
so it becomes necessary to elaborate in detail—
this is also reasonable.
However, one must weigh the circumstances and principles,
ensuring they are sufficient to match the person,
so as not to suffer from excessive verbosity.
For instance, in the Táng dynasty's pacification of Huáixī,
the "Hán Stele" attributed the credit to Péi Dù,
which can be considered appropriate.
Later, due to slander and defamation,
the task was reassigned to Duàn Wénchāng,
and for ages, people lamented this.
However, Wénchāng yielded to Lǐ Sù,
and Sù's contributions should not be overlooked—
thus, the error was not too severe.
But if some unknown minor officer,
unrelated to the outcome,
had his tomb inscription posthumously
extravagantly detailing achievements in Huáixī,
that would be unreasonable.
Master Zhū once composed an epitaph for the late compiler, Master Jiǎng,
which included a summary of the state's successive pacifications of Zhǔn and Huí.
This was because Master Jiǎng oversaw the compilation of the strategic records,
laboring diligently alone,
and died upon completing the work,
yet received no recognition for his merit.
The epitaph was elegant and robust,
admired by scholars.
Later, when a certain secretarial courtier died,
someone wrote a family biography for him,
entirely plagiarizing the text of Master Jiǎng's epitaph,
merely because the man had served as a compiler for a few months,
and by convention, his name could be listed among the contributors.
In reality, he had never even glanced at the work.
How is this different from an unknown minor officer
claiming credit for the Huáixī campaign?
And how could it be any different?
Yet literary men delight in gathering such matters,
almost akin to military officers seizing credit—
how can this be exemplary?
This is called "the funeral banner of a fellow villager."
In the past, there was a boastful man
who never held an official post in his lifetime,
yet loved to adopt titles.
As he was dying,
he summoned all his acquaintances
to discuss the inscription for his funeral banner.
Some, indulging his wishes,
falsely added titles like "Honorary Posthumous Appointments" or "Administrative Ranks,"
but he shook his head in displeasure.
Finally, a witty person
took the most illustrious noble from his hometown
and inscribed in large characters: "The coffin of So-and-so, fellow villager of the Duke of Such-and-such, with honors, titles, and positions in the imperial court, ministry, and region."
People spread this as a joke.
Thus, anyone who attaches themselves without cause
is called "the funeral banner of a fellow villager."
It is lamentable that literary men also imitate this—
this is yet another common flaw among literati.
The seventh point:
Chén Píng assisted the Hàn dynasty,
and his ambition was revealed in the division of sacrificial meat;
Lǐ Sī contributed to the fall of Qín,
and the omen began with a rat in the latrine.
Inferring the significant from the trivial
is indeed the subtle art of physiognomists;
searching for details to convey spirit
is also the wonderful skill of writers.
But one must grasp the essence of the spirit,
like a master painter
adding fine hairs to a cheek to capture likeness.
If one merely admires the elegance of earlier writings
and forcibly seeks trivial details
to mimic them,
it is like gaining insight upon seeing peach blossoms
and then trying to cook rice with peach blossoms—
what spiritual wonder remains in that?
Moreover, recent scholars
enjoy seeking concrete evidence,
often coming across broken steles and fragmented stones,
with remaining texts and leftover characters
unrelated to the main meaning.
They frequently use these to investigate ancient institutions
and supplement historical gaps,
which is indeed commendable.
But in writing,
driven by greed for quantity and acquisition,
they knowingly include superfluous and non-essential details,
believing it benefits later generations,
and spare no effort in elaboration.
This not only lacks stylistic essence in writing,
but also fails to consider that trying to prepare everything for future investigation in the present age
is like gathering materials for arrows at Dǒngzé—
how can it ever be sufficient?
In writing biographies, the style should match the person;
in narrating events, the style should match the events—
that is enough.
If there are matters relevant to investigation,
they must inherently belong to the subject's essence.
Even if incidental details emerge,
they should serve to convey the spirit vividly.
Failing to focus on this
and merely seeking to add more, like haggling over vegetables,
is called "drawing a snake and adding feet"—
yet another common flaw among literati.
The eighth point:
Literary men are certainly skilled in writing,
but the people they write about
are not necessarily all skilled in writing.
Narrative writing
consists of the author's words.
Whether refined or plain,
it is as the author wishes,
aiming only to match the events.
However, writing that records speech
is not the author's words;
whether refined or plain,
it must precisely match the person's speech,
and is not something the author can freely control.
Chaste and heroic women
who are well-versed in poetry and rituals
certainly exist.
But there are those without learning,
perhaps from rural alleys,
or even servant women and maids,
whose chastity, filial piety, and righteousness
stem from innate excellence.
While their character is worthy of the ancients,
their speech cannot be expected to be refined and elegant.
Often, in biographies of such individuals,
their recorded speech
is based on the *Analects* and the *Classic of Filial Piety*,
drawing from the *Máo Odes* and the *Inner Regulations*,
Liú Xiàng's *Biographies*,
and Cáo Zhāo's *Admonitions*,
as if spoken from their own mouths—
this may be considered refined writing.
But consider: must a woman skilled in assisting her husband
necessarily know about "deer carts" and "wild goose tables"?
Must a woman skilled in educating her children
always be familiar with "drawing in the sand" or "pill-making bears"?
Because literary men have preconceived notions,
they render women's cultivation
as uniform as printed boards.
Rather than refined writing that loses truth,
why not use plain language to convey authenticity?
Extending this further,
famous generals arise from the ranks,
righteous knights may emerge from the alleys—
their speech need not be that of classical scholars,
but recording it should vividly resemble them.
Yet many writers
do not reflect on this,
which is called "actors performing a play."
For in actors' songs,
even peasants and servants
spontaneously follow musical tones—
that is why it is called theater.
But if biographical writing
imitates this,
it becomes yet another common flaw among literati.
The ninth point:
In ancient times, when literary works were completed and methods established,
there was never a fixed pattern.
Portraying people should fit them exactly as they are,
narrating events should fit them exactly as they occur.
Within the absence of fixity,
there exists a certain constancy.
Those who understand this principle
may encounter it at any time.
Those who do not understand this principle,
merely imitating the external form,
will fail to capture the spirit.
Previously, when I wrote the biography of Chéng Xìng, the former Reminder of the Left from Hézhōu,
Xìng was renowned for his remonstrances,
so I included his memorials.
However, Xìng suffered displacement in his youth due to turmoil,
with his entire family killed,
and whenever he expressed mourning for his ancestors in writing,
it was always through literary compositions.
Among these, the piece "Měng Xǐng" is particularly profound and poignant,
capable of teaching filial piety,
so I included the full text at the end.
A well-known scholar from his hometown praised my work, saying:
"If the earlier section contained so many memorials
without the inclusion of 'Měng Xǐng,'
it would be like sailing a ship
with the prow too heavy and the stern too light.
Now, with this piece as the conclusion,
it can be said that the composition is well-planned."
I jokingly retorted:
"If Mr. Chéng had not written this piece,
would the ship never have sailed?"
Generally, when tutors explain the meanings of the Four Books,
referred to as contemporary prose,
there must be rules to conform to the format.
Since rules are difficult to explain in abstract terms,
they often use analogies to instruct beginners.
Comparing it to a house,
there is what is called the framework and structure;
comparing it to the human body,
there is what is called the eyebrows, eyes, sinews, and joints;
comparing it to painting,
there is what is called adding the finishing touch;
comparing it to geomancy,
there is what is called the dragon's approach and the focal point.
Analogies are drawn as needed.
However, for instructing beginners in methods,
this is inevitably necessary,
and there is no need to criticize it.
It is only when the habits of contemporary prose
become deeply ingrained
that when approaching all ancient books and prose,
they are viewed through the lens of contemporary prose,
and one frequently applies the tutor's elementary discussions,
which is like using a chessboard for Go stones—
it simply does not fit.
This is what is called viewing the sky from the bottom of a well,
another common flaw among literati.
The tenth point:
Contemporary prose can be selected and evaluated,
but ancient prose, as a vehicle for statecraft,
cannot be selected and evaluated.
If predecessors have already selected and evaluated it,
then one can discuss the prose based on the text alone.
However, those who select and evaluate
are often not deeply knowledgeable about ancient prose.
The books of the ancients
are not all extant today;
their writings appear in historical records,
and those who select and evaluate
mostly extract them from these records.
Yet the convention of historical records
often involves abridging the original text
to achieve conciseness,
so the full stylistic features of the text
are not entirely preserved.
Those who select and evaluate,
unaware of this fact,
mistakenly believe the original text was like this,
and then elaborate on it further.
Regarding texts that lack a proper beginning
and start abruptly in the middle,
they praise them as remarkably unconventional openings;
regarding texts where extraneous content is cut
and the main narrative begins abruptly,
they marvel at them as strikingly abrupt conclusions.
Thus, those who are curious but lack discernment
admire and praise them in turn,
deliberately imitating them,
almost as Zuǒ Qiūmíng said:
"Not seeking the child,
but looking for the rushes."
Since the mid-Míng dynasty,
a type of so-called ancient prose, unreasonable and illogical,
appears without a clear origin,
ends without a clear destination,
relying solely on such bewildering elements
to boast of their peculiarity,
thus turning broad and open paths
into thorny brambles.
The transformations in literature are as unpredictable as ghosts and spirits,
suddenly arriving,
abruptly stopping—
has there never been such imagery?
Has it never been peculiar?
But like the steep cliffs of mountains
or the waves of water,
they accumulate energy and momentum,
emerging naturally;
if one insists on forcing them into being,
it is unreasonable.
Literati, curious by nature,
are easily misled—
this is what is called mistakenly learning from Hándān,
another common flaw among literati.
The Academic Tradition of Zhèdōng
The learning of Zhèdōng,
though originating from Wùyuán,
since scholars like the three Yuáns,
has largely followed the Lù school of Jiāngxī,
yet it emphasizes mastering the classics and revering antiquity,
absolutely avoiding empty talk about moral nature,
thus not contradicting Master Zhū's teachings.
By the time of Master Wáng Yángmíng,
who championed Mencius's innate knowledge,
it again conflicted with Master Zhū's teachings.
Liú Zōngzhōu of Jíshān,
building on innate knowledge and elucidating vigilance in solitude,
differed from Master Zhū
but did not engage in denigration either.
Huáng Zōngxī of Lízhōu,
a disciple of Liú Zōngzhōu of Jíshān,
initiated the Wàn brothers' studies of classics and history;
down to Quán Zǔwàng,
his intent was still preserved,
adhering to Lù without contradicting Zhū.
Only Máo Xīhé of the West River,
who expounded the learning of innate knowledge,
achieved considerable insights;
yet due to sectarian biases,
he attacked others excessively,
so even people from Zhèdōng did not entirely approve.
The world regards Gù Tínglín as the founding Confucian patriarch,
but his tradition belongs to Zhèxī.
People are unaware that contemporaneously, Huáng Lízhōu,
from Zhèdōng,
though standing shoulder to shoulder with Gù,
traced his lineage upward to Wáng and Liú,
and downward initiated the two Wàns,
compared to Gù,
his source is deeper and his influence longer.
Gù followed Zhū,
while Huáng followed Lù.
Since they were not specialized scholars
holding sectarian views,
they respected each other
without mutual denigration.
Scholars must have a guiding principle,
but must not have sectarian biases;
thus, Zhèdōng and Zhèxī
pursue their paths in parallel without conflict.
Zhèdōng values specialization,
Zhèxī emphasizes broad erudition,
each following its own practices.
The study of heaven, human nature, and destiny
cannot be discussed through empty words.
Thus, Sīmǎ Qiān, based on Dǒng Zhòngshū's theories of heaven, human nature, and destiny,
wrote works on statecraft.
If Confucians wish to exalt moral nature
but rely on empty discussions of principles as achievement,
this is why Sòng learning is criticized by the refined.
The Master said:
"I would rather not rely on empty words,
but demonstrate through actions, which is more profound and clear."
This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals serve statecraft.
Even a sage like Confucius,
whose words were the bell of heaven,
did not rely on empty words to prevail,
let alone others?
Thus, those who excel in discussing heaven, human nature, and destiny
always relate them to human affairs.
In the learning of the Three Dynasties,
history was known, but the classics were not,
as they focused on human affairs.
Later generations valued classical studies
because they were the history of the Three Dynasties.
Recent Confucians discussing the classics
seem to treat principles
as separate from human affairs.
The learning of Zhèdōng,
when discussing human nature and destiny, always delves into history,
which is why it is outstanding.
The differences and similarities between Zhū Xī and Lù Jiǔyuān,
the conflicts among schools,
have been for millennia a prison of shackles,
and also for millennia a forest of thorns.
Examining the reasons for their disputes,
it is only because they elevated empty words without being relevant to human affairs.
Understanding that historiography is rooted in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and understanding that the *Spring and Autumn Annals* was intended to govern the world,
then one understands that human nature and destiny cannot be discussed with empty words,
and those who expound learning must be engaged in practical affairs.
Not only is there no school to uphold,
but there is also nothing with which to uphold a school.
The learning of Eastern Zhèjiāng,
although its origins and flow are not different,
encountered different circumstances.
Therefore, as manifested in the world,
Wáng Yángmíng obtained it as achievements in governance,
Liú Zōngzhōu obtained it as integrity and righteousness,
Huáng Zōngxī obtained it as reclusion and withdrawal,
and the Wàn brothers obtained it as classical scholarship and historical judgment.
Although their transmission and reception came from the same source,
their appearances are vastly different,
because each had their own practical affairs.
Those who do not engage in their proper affairs,
but only speak emptily of moral nature,
or speak emptily of inquiry and learning,
are like yellow reeds and white rushes,
extremely similar in appearance,
and thus cannot but differentiate into schools,
in order to have their own ground to stand on.
Therefore, only ignorant Confucians contend over schools.
Some may ask: Can achievements in governance and moral integrity truly be placed on equal footing with literary compositions? The answer is:
Historiography is what records the ages,
and is certainly not empty words or compositions.
Moreover, consider the Six Classics:
all originated from Confucius,
and earlier scholars considered that none had greater merit than the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
precisely because it closely corresponded to the human affairs of its time.
Later those who speak of literary compositions,
abandon the present to seek the ancient,
abandon human affairs to speak of nature and heaven,
—this I cannot comprehend.
Scholars who do not understand this principle
are not qualified to speak of historiography. Compiling and arranging is called historical compilation; comparing and investigating is called historical examination; neither is historiography.
Women's Learning
The *Zhōu Guān* records female invocators and female scribes,
the Hàn system had inner court daily records,
women's relation to writing,
in antiquity indeed had its uses.
The term "women's learning,"
appears in the inner duties of the *Tiān Guān*,
virtue, speech, appearance, and work—
what it encompasses is broad,
unlike later ages where only literary arts were considered learning.
Yet the *Yì* instructs "correct position within the inner quarters,"
the *Lǐ* assigns women's work of silk and hemp,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* commentary speaks of assigning tasks and presenting achievements,
the *Xiǎo Yǎ* poems discuss deliberating on wine and food,
thus women's occupations

can roughly be known. Men bear bows and arrows, women bear girdle ornaments—there is a natural distinction. As for ritual texts and literary compositions, both men and women practiced them. Consorts, wives, inner ladies, and titled women all had ritual texts for hosting guests, sacrifices, and mourning—these could not be managed without learning.
The categories of women's learning:
virtue, speech, appearance, and work.
Zhèng's commentary:
"Speech refers to diplomatic language."
Unless one is well-versed in classical rituals,
and practiced in literary compositions,
one cannot be considered learned.
Thus we know that reciting the *Shī* and practicing the *Lǐ*—
the women's learning of antiquity—
was slightly inferior to that of men.
The literary works of women in later ages,
although somewhat biased toward ornate elegance,
considering the origins of their tradition,
should be understood as having been received.
Women's learning was managed by the nine concubines,
its teaching methods practiced within the palace;
internally among the ministers' consorts,
externally extending to feudal lords,
though the six codes do not detail it,
it can be inferred by analogy.
The *Gé Tán* poem's instructress,
recorded in the *Airs*—women's learning among feudal lords.
Gentle and compliant, the matron's teaching,
preserved in the *Nèi Zé*—women's learning among ministers and grandees.
Surveying the various commentaries of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
the wives of feudal lords,
the inner ladies of grandees,
all could discuss literature and relate ancient matters,
with elegant and patterned writing.
As for the omen of fullness,
Dèng Màn meticulously deduced from the way of heaven;
the meaning of "beneficial and steadfast,"
Mù Jiāng precisely interpreted the origin of qián;
the virtuous wife of Lǔ Mù Bó,
whose exemplary words passed down instruction;
the inner mistress of the Qí minister of works,
who was enfeoffed for her ritual propriety;
the commandant who died peacefully by the window,
whose wife composed a eulogy;
the souls of the state's martyrs returning from the battlefield,
whose widows declined suburban mourning.
Down to the bubbling flow of the spring,
gracefully composing verses of longing for return;
the swallows flying up and down,
sorrowfully sending off poems of accompanying brides.
All these classical rituals, canonical laws,
literary elegance and refined grace—
how do they differ from famous ministers and grandees?
Yet all are incidentally recorded
because they were connected to events,
not specially highlighted.
If they appeared in later ages,
history would certainly devote chapters to them,
categorically collecting exemplary women,
like the stories of Bān Zhāo and Cài Yǎn,
their splendor and brilliance
would be ten times that of the books of Liú Xiàng and Fàn Yè.
Thus we know that women's learning was also lost in transmission after antiquity.
In the flourishing of the Three Dynasties,
together with men's ritual texts,
it all followed established precedents,

and was not originally considered extraordinary. Unlearned people, taking poems like "Zhēn and Wěi" as self-narratives by the licentious, claim that ancient women and girls could compose verses effortlessly, surpassing later literati. They do not realize this is utterly unreasonable. I will discuss this in detail later; here there is no leisure to debate it. But women's learning did indeed exist in antiquity, practiced only among ministers and grandees, not among common women.
After the Spring and Autumn period,
officials and teachers divided their duties,
learning was no longer confined to official responsibilities,
and writing flowed into private compositions. In antiquity there was no private composition; this is discussed in detail in the *General Principles of Collation*.
The outstanding among men,
all according to their natural inclinations,

became famous masters through their writings. This refers to the various philosophical schools of the Warring States and pre-Qin periods, as well as the specialized studies of classics and history from the Western Hàn onward.
As for descending to belles-lettres,
it was also due to their superior talent,
that they displayed literary elegance. This refers to poetry and literary collections from after the Yuán and Chéng periods of the Western Hàn, and onward through the Eastern Hàn.
And women of extraordinary intelligence and exceptional ability,
endowed with rare qi,
also thereby achieved distinction through literary compositions,
and were praised through the ages—
this too was due to the circumstances of the times.
Yet the flourishing of Confucian scholarship in the Hàn court,
Bān Gù attributed to the path of profit and rank.
For what the official decrees honored,
the worthy and talented strove for,
the scholarly pursuits of gentlemen,
were like farmers tending their fields—
this is indeed the principle.
Literary writing for women,
was not their occupation;
occasionally there were those who excelled,
due to their innate superiority,
not because they contended in trends,

or sought fame. The habit of seeking fame arose among mid to late period literati; although the ancients had the flaw of loving fame, they did not fuss over it in literary arts. For a man to seek literary fame is already despised by the discerning; for a woman to chase reputation is unfeminine.
The "Fáng Zhōng" songs of Tángshān,
the "Cháng Xìn" rhapsody of Bān Jī,
the orthodox and changed forms of the *Airs* and *Odes*—the *Odes* refers to "Fáng Zhōng," the *Airs* refers to "Cháng Xìn"—
originated within the palace,
concerned matters of state,
and were recorded in historical annals.
Other compositions are few,
and those transmitted are scarce;
what the "Treatise on Arts and Letters" records
can roughly be observed.
As for Yuèfǔ ballads that circulated,
imitated in song-poetry,
"Mùlán" on expedition and garrison,
"Kǒngquè" on separation,
and the "Mò Shàng" piece on picking mulberry leaves,
the "Shān Xià" poem on líwú herbs,
the four-season "Bái Zhù" songs,
"Zǐ Yè" with its fragrance,
their sounds are expansive and slow,
their rhythm soft and delicate—
then from the ancient lyrics of the two Hàn, all anonymous,
to the miscellaneous imitations of the Six Dynasties,
all are compositions by poets,
thoughts of people expressing their sentiments,
though the emotions are entrusted to boys and girls,
the meaning is truly rooted in the airs of the people.
Therefore their diction is often flowing and unrestrained,

not avoiding the exchange between men and women. Like "Mò Shàng Sāng," "Yǔ Lín Láng," and such—although they profess chastity, how could secluded women chatter and argue with reckless men? Being imitative compositions, they are fine.
As for boudoir compositions,
occasionally some are transmitted;
regardless of whether the person is chaste or licentious,
their phrasing all has restraint.
Zhūo Wénjūn
was a licentious eloper,
yet "White Head" only satirized Sīmǎ Xiàngrú.
Cài Yǎn
was a woman who lost her chastity,
yet her copying of texts earnestly declined ten clerks.
Others who lived in peace and顺应,
and those renowned for chastity,
whenever they had compositions,
were all as calm as still water,
as solemn as a clear breeze.
Although their literary talent came from natural grace,
their thoughts did not transgress beyond the inner quarters.
This shows that although women's learning differed from antiquity,
it also did not contradict moral instruction.
The male-female lyrics in the "Guó Fēng" section
were all composed by poets;
as evidenced by the works of the Hàn, Wèi, and Six Dynasties periods,

there is no further doubt. The principle is the same across ancient and modern times; it should not be that the children of the ancients could effortlessly produce elegant verses, while later scholars, despite striving, could never match them.
It is like a male actor
playing a gentle maiden on stage—
he can never truly resemble the refined simplicity of a lady in her boudoir.
Those ignorant of this principle
mistakenly believe that even the children of the ancients
could effortlessly compose verses,
and thus argue that women are naturally suited to elegance and refinement.
This is akin to seeing actors on stage performing the deeds of the ancients

and foolishly suspecting that the ancients must have sung songs before every action. Actors performing stories of the ancients—the lyrics of their songs are like the inserted commentaries in historical biographies. They contain words intended in the heart, certainly not spoken aloud, as well as observations from bystanders, definitely not from the person themselves. The lyrics of the songs do not shy away from these. Thus, a gentleman may sometimes engage in self-praise, while a petty person may sometimes mock themselves, allowing the audience to feel as if they are reading a historical biography while also enjoying the sentiment of poetic recitation. This is how the form should be, and it is not considered inappropriate. If such words truly came from the mouths of gentlemen or petty people, it would be unreasonable. The male-female lyrics in the "Guó Fēng" section and the lyrics composed by the ancients imitating male-female voices should be viewed in this way. If one insists they truly came from the mouths of men and women, not only would the licentious never expose themselves so blatantly, but even the chaste would never debase themselves in such a manner.
In the past, Bān Gù’s "Hàn Shū"
was left unfinished at his death,
and an imperial decree ordered his younger sister, Cáo Zhāo,
to personally go to the Dōng Guān library
to complete it.
Thus, high-ranking ministers and officials
brought gifts to seek instruction from the great Confucian scholar Mǎ Róng, who studied the punctuation and reading of the "Hàn Shū" under her guidance.
This can be said to be unprecedented in history.
However, specialized and profound learning
often runs in families,
and the books do not convey everything;
unless one is the right person, they cannot receive such knowledge.
Also, when the Fú-Qín state first established schools,
it widely appointed erudites and classical teachers.
While the "Five Classics" were roughly complete,
the "Zhōu Guān" was lost.
The erudites submitted a memorial,
stating that the mother of Wéi Chěng, the Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Sòng Shì,
had a family tradition of the pronunciation and meaning of the "Zhōu Guān."
An imperial decree ordered a lecture hall to be set up in her home,
where 120 students were enrolled.
They studied behind a crimson curtain,
and Sòng Shì was granted the noble title of Xuān Wén Jūn.
This, too, was unprecedented in history.
However, at that time, literary and cultural heritage
flourished south of the Yangtze River,
while the Fú clan occupied Shāndōng.
The surviving classics and rare knowledge
were preserved only in the families of learned women,
and were not something even renowned officials could forcibly access.
These two mothers
both acted in the capacity of men.
For transmitting classics and narrating history
pertains to the principles of heaven, humanity, and law.
Fearing that these might be lost or forgotten,
rulers had no choice but to break conventions and honor them with rituals.
It was not because their talents dazzled
or astonished the common folk.
Similarly, there were figures like Lady Xiān of Qiáo Xǐ, who pacified the borders,
and Princess Píng Yáng of Chái, who assisted in establishing a dynasty.
These, too, were rare in history.
One was granted a special military headquarters,
with the authority to appoint officials;
the other was honored with feather canopies, drums, and pipes,
as well as tiger-warrior guards and ceremonial swords.
To say that the rulers of the Suí and Táng dynasties acted inappropriately
is certainly not acceptable;
but to insist that women of all times should emulate them
is not only unacceptable
but also unreasonable.
The people of the Jìn dynasty revered metaphysical discussions,
indulging in unrestrained expressions and unconventional behavior.
Men treated the Six Arts as dregs,
while women also admired refined conversation.
Discussions to resolve sieges behind screens,
and games where a bride participated in military affairs—
although major principles were not entirely lost,
the norms of propriety were utterly disregarded.
Commentators attribute the division of the Sixteen Kingdoms
and the suffering of the people
to the metaphysical discussions that undermined ritual teachings—
a truly insightful observation.
The great families of Wáng and Xiè,
though they transgressed ritual norms,
their refined conversations and profound principles
reached far into the depths of understanding.
They were versed in Confucian traditions
and also well-versed in metaphysical ideas.
Compared to scholarly learning,
they were like those who lost their way in moderation
and became wild and simplistic—close to heterodoxy, not close to actors or courtesans.
They were not merely capable of composing five- or seven-character verses
and boasting of surpassing the Four Virtues and Three Obediences.
As for those who indulged in romantic scenes,
exchanged pleasantries and greetings,
depicted delicate sentiments,
and portrayed superficial resemblances,
enhancing their charm with cosmetics,
and embellishing their empty reputations with praise—
even the people of the Jìn dynasty, known for their frivolity,
if they had witnessed this,

would have fled with their wives and children. The great families of Wáng and Xiè, though they transgressed ritual norms, were truly learned and knowledgeable, so their thoughts were profound and far-reaching. They were not like those talented scholars and beauties who were merely shallow, vulgar, and fame-seeking.
From the Táng and Sòng dynasties onward,
the literary talents visible among women
were mostly limited to spring boudoir laments and autumn sorrows,
the blooming and withering of flowers and plants,
short pieces and minor compositions,
through which their elegance and excellence were transmitted.
Occasionally, there were other works,
such as Sòng Shàng Gōng’s "Nǚ Lún Yǔ"
and Hóu Zhèng Shì’s "Nǚ Xiào Jīng."

Although their talent and knowledge were inevitably pedantic and shallow—they wished to write instructions for women but did not know to follow the rituals of Cáo Dà Jiā’s "Nǚ Jiè," instead presumptuously imitating the classics, equating them to the "Qī Lín" rhetorical questions, which are mere fabrications—
their inclinations were still close to elegance and correctness.
The literary world spoke of them,
forgiving them because their intentions were commendable. This was all because the ancient women’s learning was lost, so those with aspirations could achieve no more than this.
Lǐ Yì'ān’s compilation of inscriptions on bronzes and stones,
and Guǎn Dào Shēng’s exquisite calligraphy and painting—
later generations also rarely had their equals.
However, the inscriptions and markings on precious objects
were only used for verification in Húzhōu;
the skill in brush and ink
also relied on observation and emulation under imperial decree.
It was unheard of for the wife of a prime minister’s son
to engage in literary discussions with scholars of the Imperial Academy. Lǐ Yì'ān and Zhào Míng Chéng compiled the "Jīn Shí Lù." Míng Chéng was then at the Imperial Academy, hence the reference.
Nor could a Hanlin Academy scholar’s wife
join high officials in wielding a whisk for scholarly debate.
Although literature is said to be a public instrument,
the distinction between men and women is indeed a great boundary through the ages.
The stern principles of reputation, righteousness, and social order—
how can they be disregarded?
From the Táng and Sòng dynasties up to the previous Míng dynasty,
the state system never abolished female entertainers.
When high officials attended court duties,
there were green-sleeved maidens tending incense burners;
when official banquets were held,
red-skirted women were often seen urging guests to drink.
By the golden well under the parasol tree,
there were autumn sentiments at postal stations;
amid the fragrance of orchids and musk,
spring vows were made at the Qǔ Jiāng river.
These are recorded in detail
in historical accounts.
Moreover, under the oppressive policies of the previous dynasty,
when officials were implicated and their properties confiscated,
their wives and children were also affected,
causing many families of poetry and propriety
to fall into the pleasure quarters.
Those among them who possessed both beauty and talent,
excelling in poetry and song,
were sought after by scholars and officials of the capital
for poetic exchanges.
Generally, their emotions were as lingering as spring grass,
their thoughts as distant as autumn maples.
Their poetic exchanges resembled friendships,
and their affections conveyed intimacy.
The sentiments in their poetry were broad and unrestrained,
without regard for suspicion or taboo.
The verses from the boudoir
resounded beyond the women’s quarters—
such was the natural way of things.
Moreover, during the golden age of poetry in the Táng dynasty,
few works by women have been passed down.
Counting across the entire dynasty,
the most prolific poets
were Lǐ Yě, Xuē Tāo, and Yú Xuán Jī—
no others could compare.
This shows that female Daoist priests and courtesans
often produced many literary works due to frequent social interactions,
while women from families of propriety and reputation
naturally avoided writing verses that might violate norms.
This is clear evidence.
Those renowned courtesans who captivate cities,
frequently mingled with celebrated literati,
exchanging poetic compositions in response.
In their intended meanings,
they encompassed the sentiments of both husband and wife as well as friends,
which can be said to skillfully employ language.
Yet when the ancients longed for their sovereign or missed their friends,
they often entrusted these feelings to the earnest affections between men and women.
As for poets satirizing depravity and licentiousness,
their writings served as substitutes for the self-expressions of wanton and unrestrained individuals.
Distinguishing among these three types,
their paths are somewhat similar.
When evaluating poetic works,
one must not be unaware of the distinctions.
For loyal ministers and righteous friends,
their sincerity and earnestness are subtly conveyed;
when satirizing evil and detesting depravity,
a sense of sorrow and concern is revealed beyond the words.
As for self-narratives expressing abandonment and neglect,
the merits and flaws of the poetry vary greatly.
If the original intent is unclear,

the refinement or crudeness of the language will differ vastly. If "Lísāo" seeking women is taken as genuine emotion, then the language becomes incoherent; if "Guófēng" poems like "Zhēn, Wěi" are considered self-narratives, they too become straightforward and insipid. When composed as imitations or entrustments, the literary sentiment naturally deepens.
Therefore, poems about nameless men and women
perhaps grasp the principle of the Supreme Ultimate and yin-yang,
existing between heaven and earth,
where the wise perceive wisdom,
and the benevolent perceive benevolence.
Renowned courtesans skilled in poetry
also understood ancient principles,
thus transforming the reality of mutual admiration between men and women
into the gentle and sincere words of poets.
Hence, their遗留 words
are elegant and principled,
genuine yet not vulgar,
流传 for a thousand years,
shining in the annals of literature,
and cannot be dismissed because of the person.
However, there is a proper form for expressing oneself,
and women differ from men.
For example, although "Xièlù" is skillfully composed,
it is only fitting when performed by mourning singers;
even if boat songs are exquisite,
they are more appropriate when sung by boat women.
Their赠 poems to Lǐ and Zhāng
were appropriate given their circumstances.
For respectable women in inner chambers,
even their private words should not be heard outside,
so how could singing and exchanging poems beyond the gate
ever reach them?
Although the pleasure quarters and song lanes
were not part of the ancient kings' legal systems,
they were indeed customs passed down from previous dynasties.
Unless one is among the likes of Lián and Luò,
what harm is there in minor moral deviations?
Thus, those who assisted in achieving merit and fame,
those loyal and righteous with strong principles,
Confucian scholars of literature and virtue,
and noble recluses and hermits
often found places for their leisurely sentiments
in written records.
Even under strict prohibitions,
these did not heavily burden their great virtue.
However, while literature may follow antiquity,
institutions must adapt to the times.
The rites and teachings of our dynasty are precise and strict,
with careful distinctions to avoid suspicion.
Since the Three Dynasties,
there has never been such solemnity.
Since the palace abolished female musicians
and officials no longer established pleasure quarters,
there has been no pretext
for interactions between men and women under heaven.
Those who are wandering prostitutes or顿 courtesans,
seeking lust and selling treachery,
all violate strict laws,
and even杖 punishment cannot redeem them. Officials, students, and监生 alike are considered to have flawed conduct and are never reappointed.
Although some major offenders may slip through the net,
not all are recorded in legal documents;
but a noble man is mindful of punishment,
how could he willingly subject himself to judicial scrutiny?
Often when seeing celebrated literati,
with their poetry manuscripts carved on blocks,
before glimpsing the complete collection,
one first reads the titles.
Some record romantic affairs with beauties,
others describe singing exchanges in pleasure quarters,
considering themselves风流 and倜傥,
believing the ancients did the same.
They do not realize that living in this era,
as people of today,
if they are unfamiliar with prohibitions and decrees,
how can they even discuss literary matters?
The Duke of Zhōu established rites,
forbidding marriage between those of the same surname.
Suppose someone born after the Zhōu dynasty
claimed that in ancient times men and women had no distinctions,
thus混乱 human relations,
behaving like beasts,
and said the ancients did so,
would that be acceptable?
Talent requires learning,
and learning values discernment.
Talent without learning
is mere cleverness.
Cleverness without discernment
is incompetence.
Incompetent and clever individuals
