will stop at nothing.

Those who consider frivolity and轻浮 as风雅—elegance means correctness, opposite to vulgarity. Habits influenced by prevailing trends are called俗; frivolity and鄙俚 are both vulgar. Vulgar鄙俚 does not harm societal morals and人心, but frivolous vulgarity makes one an offender against风雅.
Those who create appearances and boast for reputation—no one who seeks fame is not vulgar.
Flaunting before the younger generation,
recklessly among scholars and women,
人心 and customs
suffer流弊 beyond description.
Frivolity出自于 students,
existed among the ancients;
but ostentation flowing into women,
was unheard of in previous eras.
This is because lacking substance, they争骛 after fame;
not being true men, they rely on others for importance.
Men with aspirations
would all be ashamed of such behavior.
Even to the extent of severing bonds of affection,
violating rites of giving and receiving,
they often entrust emotionally ornate works
to the connection of refined literary spirits,
thus listening to rankings in传 announcements,
seeking evaluations in monthly critiques.
This occurred often in pleasure quarters and勾曲 in previous dynasties;
but for modest maidens and闺姝,
since天地 began,
such rites have never been heard of.
The ancient learning for women,
such as女史,女祝,女巫,
each studied according to their profession,
somewhat like men specializing in arts and holding official posts.
As for comprehensive learning,
it emphasized virtue, speech, appearance, and work.
Virtue is隐 and hard to name—only sages like Rén and Sì could embody its entirety.
Work like sericulture was common among both scholars and commoners.
Among studies接近 literature,
speech and appearance were most important.
From家庭内则
to the Son of Heaven, feudal lords, ministers, officials, and scholars,
all were practiced in ritual demeanor.
During朝聘,丧祭,
后妃,夫人,内子,命妇
all had their duties.
If not studied平日,
how could they perform appropriately临事?
Hàn dynasty经师
often explained rites through章句,
yet still relied on Xú Shēng,
skilled in demeanor,
because威严仪容 and进退举止
could not be fully conveyed by mere recitation.
Thus, women's appearance must be practiced in rites—
later great Confucians

might not even hear of this. Observing敬姜's recorded words, strictly adhering to礼法, how could later经师 or great Confucians match them? As for妇言 focusing on辞命, ancient times内言 did not leave the闺;所谓辞命 also necessarily followed礼文. Confucius said: "Without studying the 'Shī,' one has no means to speak."
Those skilled in辞命
were all deeply versed in the Shī. Observing春秋 women's辞命, graceful and meaningful.
Thus, ancient妇学
necessarily proceeded from rites to understand poetry—without rites, one does not know appearance; without poetry, one does not know speech.
Mastery of the六艺 might be combined by some, like穆姜 discussing the "Yì."
Later妇学 was lost.
Those秀颖 and literate
considered themselves combining women's and men's studies,
showing pride in their faces.
They did not realize women originally had their own learning,
which must be based on rites.
Abandoning their本业 and recklessly entrusting themselves to poetry,
and poetry not being what the ancients called practicing辞命 and excelling in妇言—
thus, even in terms of learning,
it is like farmers abandoning their fields,
or scholars losing their出疆 gifts.
How could this represent妇学?
Alas!
Ancient妇学
necessarily proceeded from rites to understand poetry;
modern妇学
instead uses poetry to破坏 rites.
Once礼防 collapses,
人心 and customs become unspeakable.
This is truly due to unscrupulous文人
promoting邪说 to mislead them.
Those who truly understand妇学
view unscrupulous文人
as粪土. Unscrupulous文人 have shallow learning; those truly knowledgeable are not easily deceived.
How could they be迷惑 by them?
Adorning the fashionable among mediocre talents,
they become the transcendent beings of the women's quarters.
Those who borrow their names to critique and praise either overstate their merits or embellish their writings,
merely out of pity for their beauty.
Unprincipled literati—
their hearts cannot be questioned.
Alas!
While they themselves flaunt their talents,
others pity them for their beauty.
Not knowing this yet pursuing them—
how foolish!
Vaguely aware of the reason
and still pursuing them—
the height of foolishness!
The laudable title for a woman
is "the gentlewoman,"
for gentleness approaches learning.
How agitated are those today who call themselves talented women!
How exceedingly turbulent!
Ah!
Postscript to "The Essay on Women's Learning"
The essay on women's learning
aims to rescue decadent customs,
uphold worldly teachings,
rectify ethical principles,
and distinguish humans from beasts—
it was written out of necessity,
not out of a fondness for argument.
Critics say its interpretation of the *Book of Songs* differs from Zhū Xī's,
contravening official standards.
They do not realize that drawing on ancient meanings from the classics
is not contrary to official standards.
Speaking from reason and sentiment,
how could rustic men and women
compose verses spontaneously,
far surpassing later literati?
The disparity between ancient and modern times should not be so vast.
Moreover, the distance between the Hàn dynasty and the Spring and Autumn period
is akin to today's distance from the Hàn.
Hàn dynasty poetry and prose
preserved to this day
are all lofty, ancient, and unadorned;
thus people suspect Hàn-era talent
far exceeded later generations.
Yet examining collections of inscriptions on metal and stone,
the writings of Hàn people
not recorded on bamboo or silk
but transmitted through metal and stone to later ages
contain much that is verbose and mediocre,
not vastly different
from the works of modern people who lack literary skill.
This shows that not all Hàn people were skilled writers;
only the best were transmitted.
The writings passed down from the Three Dynasties
likely followed the same pattern.
To claim that the spontaneous songs of women of that era
were all worthy of becoming canonical teachings—
is that reasonable?
Zhū Xī's interpretation
initially merely presented one viewpoint;
it seemed harmless enough.
Yet nowadays, unlearned individuals
cite it to mislead ignorant men and women,
breaching boundaries and disregarding restraints,
blurring the line between human and beast.
Thus, the error in interpreting the *Book of Songs*
is no different from misinterpreting the "Jīn Téng" chapter to justify regency,
or misinterpreting the *Zhōu Lǐ* to justify the Green Sprouts policy.
How could Zhū Xī have known the resulting calamity would reach such extremes?
Even those who debated Zhū Xī in his time
did not foresee the calamity reaching this point.
Since ancient times, poetry has valued elegance.
Even in Táng and Sòng dynasty poetry critiques,
though discussions were shallow,
they merely compared skill and clumsiness
or matched phrases and lines—
things the ancients disdained to discuss.
Those unlearned individuals
groundlessly label this as "charm and interest,"
entirely dismissing distinctions of uprightness and depravity, right and wrong, gain and loss,
and urging people to seek only charm and interest.
They even argue that poems about picking orchids and presenting peonies
have no relevance, yet the Master recorded them
to support the notion of charm and interest.
Ignorant men and women
suddenly forget modesty and restraint,
succumbing to the trend and becoming decadent.
Thus, the Six Classics become tools to incite desire and promote licentiousness—
this is impious and lawless.
Some say:
"The Preface to the *Book of Songs* should not be entirely discarded.
But to claim ancient commoners
could not compose poetry—
what of the laborers' ballads
and the charioteers' prayers,
all from commoners,
whose words are still recited today?
Are historical records false?"
The reply:
"These were proverbs of the time,
not refined language.
As earlier scholars said of the Yīn dynasty's Pán inscriptions and Zhōu dynasty's Gào declarations,
they were constrained by local customs.
Over long ages,
they became archaic and abstruse,
hence their unusual and rugged style.
They are not like the gentle, dignified, and elegant Airs of the States,
which came from literary scholars,
just as the writings of the Canons and Counsels,
though ancient, are not difficult to recite and understand.
The gentleness and elegance of the Airs
are utterly different
from folk ballads and proverbs.
This further shows that the male-female verses in the Airs of the States
were composed by poets for satire,
not by rustic men and women.
Thus, the theory of charm and interest
collapses without attack
and condemns itself without reproof.
As for women's learning in ancient times,
though different from men's,
in the cultivation through rites and music,
from princes, consorts, and queens above
to outstanding commoners below,
both men and women practiced it diligently.
Among the Four Virtues,
without rites, one cannot cultivate demeanor;
without poetry, one cannot cultivate speech.
Poetic education thus connects with music;
hence, the transformation from "Guān Jū" began in the inner chambers,
and all husbands and wives under heaven were well-ordered.
After the Three Dynasties,
elementary learning declined,
and Confucian teachings became fragmented;
women's learning declined,
and scholars seldom achieved harmony in their households;
with fragmented teachings,
heterodox doctrines disrupted education—
a longstanding ailment.
As for the decline of women's learning,
people say household management suffered somewhat.
Who knew that a millennium later,
unlearned individuals
would invent the theory of charm and interest,
causing women to neglect their proper roles,
coveting the fame-seeking of base scholars?
The calamity is fiercer than floods and wild beasts.
Gentlemen who uphold righteousness and reputation—
can they not worry about the state of the world?
In the past, Ōuyáng Xiū lamented the spread of Buddhism
and sought to restore the governance of ancient kings
to strengthen the fundamental vitality—
hence his writing of "The Fundamental Discourse."
Now, unlearned individuals
delude women with heterodox doctrines,
precisely because women's learning is neglected,
making women easily misled.
Though women are cautioned against improper conduct,
adhering to rites and understanding poetry
are like daily food and drink—
they cannot be dispensed with even briefly.
Some say women's duties lie in weaving, cooking, and managing the household,
and literary composition should not be prioritized—
this is also mistaken.
Intelligence and brilliance
are endowed by Heaven without distinction between men and women,
like the blossoms of plants,
or the pearls and jade of mountains and rivers—
even sages treasure them.
How can they be suppressed?
They should be properly nurtured.
Thus, if a woman is born simple and unadorned,
she need only grasp the basics of inner teachings
and avoid errors.
If she is intelligent and well-read,
build on her understanding,
clarify the origins of poetry and rites,
and elevate her to the grand principles of the ancients—
why must Bān Jí and Wéi Mǔ
be distant ideals?
Taking Bān Jí and Wéi Mǔ as teachers,
compared to unlearned individuals,
the latter are mere fools.
Poetry critiques
The origin of poetic criticism
lies in Zhōng Róng's "The Grading of Poets."
However, examining the classics and commentaries,
such as the saying:
"The one who made this poem,
must have known the Way, right?"
And also:
"If one does not think of it,
how can it be far away?"
This is discussing poetry while touching upon matters.
Again, such as "Jǐfǔ composed a song,
harmonious as a clear breeze;
his poem is very grand,
its style is excellent,"
this is discussing poetry while touching upon diction.
Matters have right and wrong,
diction has skill and clumsiness;
touching upon one category and extending to others,
the enlightenment is indeed great.
Great rivers begin from a tiny source.
The words of later poetic critics,
though said to originate from Zhōng Róng,
in essence, their branches and streams proliferated,
and cannot be fully encompassed by a single approach.
"The Grading of Poets" in discussing poetry,
compared to "The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons" in discussing literature,
both are specialized works by renowned masters,
and are the founding ancestors of books compiled into complete works.
"The Literary Mind" is grand in structure and thorough in consideration,
"The Grading of Poets" is deep in thought and far-reaching in meaning;
for "The Literary Mind" encompasses all kinds of discourse,

while "The Grading of Poets" deeply traces the branches and streams from the Six Arts, such as saying that someone's poetry originates from a certain school, which is the most well-grounded learning. Its method comes from Liú Xiàng and his son.
Discussing poetry and literature,
and knowing to trace branches and streams,
then one can explore the sources in the classics,
and advance to glimpse the purity of heaven and earth,
and the general substance of the ancients.

This meaning is not something later poetic critics could comprehend. The branches and streams that Master Zhōng traced also have some points that are not very clear. This is because many ancient books are lost, making it difficult to find evidence. But he was already able to perceive the general idea, which is truly beyond what later poetry critics achieved.
Tang dynasty poetic criticism,
originally focused on discussing poetry,
but after Mèng Qǐ's "Original Stories of Poems" appeared, which also follows "The Minor Prefaces to the Poetry,"
it made people understand the intention of the state historians in narrating poetry;
and enthusiasts followed and expanded it,
so poetic criticism became connected with biographies in the historical section.
Occasionally explaining names and objects,
then poetic criticism became connected with philology in the classical section. This belongs to the category of exegesis like the "Ěryǎ."
Or broadly recounting what is heard and seen,
then poetic criticism became connected with the miscellaneous schools in the philosophical section. These two aspects became more common after the Song dynasty.
Although the purposes of these books are not uniform,
their general scope does not go beyond discussing diction and matters,
inferring the author's intent,
hoping only to be beneficial to the teaching of poetry.
"The Grading of Poets" and "The Literary Mind,"
being specialized writings,
naturally are not easy to produce without abundant learning and superior talent,
hence they declined into poetic criticism.
Following the stream and forgetting the source,
those who write poetic criticism
no longer know the original intent of scholarly writing.
Just as exegesis and the specialized studies of philosophy and history—philosophy refers to the miscellaneous schools mentioned above, history refers to the biographies mentioned above—
are not easy to produce,
hence they declined into anecdotal writings.
Following the stream and forgetting the source,
those who write anecdotal works
no longer know the original intent of specialized studies.
The degenerate forms of poetic criticism and anecdotal writings,
become entangled and cannot be clearly distinguished;
when scholarship is not clear,
human minds and customs may consequently suffer harm.
Song dynasty Confucian scholars lecturing on learning,
personally practicing and applying it,
was not easy to do.
Following the trend of the times,
compiling recorded sayings to champion or oppose Zhū Xī or Lù Jiǔyuān,
then anyone could do it.
Discussing literature and examining arts,
their origins and branches,
are not easy to know.
With the habit of seeking fame,
writing poetic criticism to form factions and attack differences,
then anyone could do it.
Taking learning that cannot establish a school—if it could establish a school, it would already be independent writing—
entering into the trend of following fashions and seeking fame,
wielding a pen that anyone can wield,
writing whatever words one desires,
is worrisome,
is dangerous!
The harmful tendencies of anecdotal writings,
go as far as slandering the good and forming cliques with the wicked,
using false names and assuming identities.
What previous people discussed,
such as "Records of Lóngchéng," "Bìyún Huá," and the like,
are also too numerous to count,
which is why historians have methods for selecting from unofficial histories.
Events have records that can mutually verify,
but with writing, it is only according to one's will to give or take;
poetic criticism being unreliable
may be even worse than anecdotal writings.
The faults of previous poetic criticism,
were merely losing fairness in judging right and wrong, likes and dislikes.
The faults of contemporary poetic criticism,
even become harmful to the way of the world and human minds.
Losing fairness in right and wrong, likes and dislikes,
is merely the habit of literati belittling each other;
public judgment will stabilize over time,
its harm is not enough to worry about.
Harm to the way of the world and human minds,
then will intoxicate the world's intelligence and talent,
and ensnare people into the realm of beasts.
Its mechanism is very deep,
its methods are very cunning,
and its calamities will be too numerous to describe;
gentlemen who care about reputation and righteousness
must not fail to strengthen their defenses and make strict distinctions.
Fiction originates from unofficial historians,
alleyway rumors and trivialities,
which even the ancients did not discard.
However, vulgar and crude tales are mostly unreliable;
generally they mix matters with ghosts and spirits,
and retribution involving gratitude and grudges.
Works like "Dòngmíng," "Shíyí,"
"Sōushén," "Língyì,"
from the Six Dynasties onward,
each family wrote its own book.
In the Tang dynasty, there appeared individual tales,
separately forming the category of "chuánqí," focusing on the beginning and end of a single story, no longer compiling by categories into books.
Generally focusing on the passions between men and women,
not beyond separation and reunion, sorrow and joy.
Hóngfú leaving Yáng,
Embroidered Jacket repaying Zhèng,
Hán and Lǐ's connection through fallen leaves,
Cuī and Zhāng's feelings guided by the lute's heart,
and also Bright Pearl returning alive,
Xiǎoyù repaying in death,
all such types,
either attaching to doubtful resemblances,
or outright fabricating from nothing,
though emotions and situations are infinitely varied,
their general outlines are somewhat similar.
Initially, they were merely licentious thoughts with ancient sentiments,
writers expressing their feelings,
like the ancient amorous pieces in the Music Bureau poetry of the poets.
From the Song and Yuan dynasties onward,
they were broadly adapted into popular stories,
set to lyrics and tunes,
so that blind historians sang them with string accompaniment,
actors performed them on stage,
regardless of refined or vulgar, men or women,
all indulged their senses of sound and sight.
Since unofficial historians appeared in the "History of the Hàn Dynasty,"
through three transformations they completely lost the origins and streams of the ancients.
Fiction, songs, tales, and popular stories,
in narrating men and women,
the men are inevitably frivolous and fickle,
yet praised as talented scholars and romantic;
the women are inevitably seductive and passionate,
yet praised as peerless beauties.
Men in the world with petty cleverness but no learning,
and women who understand writing but are ignorant of ritual teachings,
all take the talented scholars and beauties of tales
as people of ancient times,
people of ancient times.
Those who now write poetic criticism
are precisely those with petty cleverness but no learning.
Having petty cleverness but no learning,
aided by a devious and wicked heart,
then they become petty men without fear or shame!
What will they not do?

Discussion on Establishing Three Books in Local Gazetteers
Generally, to manage the literary documents of a region,
it is necessary to establish three schools of learning,
and then one can comprehend the legacy of the ancients.
Imitating the style of standard histories with annals and biographies to make the gazetteer,
imitating the style of laws, decrees, statutes, and precedents to make the administrative records,
imitating the style of "Literary Selections" and "Literary Gardens" to make the literary collection.
These three books complement each other and are used together,
missing one is not acceptable;
combining them into one
is especially unacceptable.
Fearing that people might think I intentionally seek novelty,
I therefore borrow a hypothetical dialogue to fully express the meaning.
Someone asked:
The origin of local gazetteers is long-standing,
yet there has never been a division into three types of books.
Now you suddenly divide them into three,
why is that? I replied:
To clarify historiography.
Jiǎzǐ once said that the ancients governed the world
with the utmost detail and analysis.
I examined this in the Zhōu Guān,
and realized that the ancients’ approach to historical matters
was indeed characterized by meticulous detail and analysis.
The Outer Historian was in charge of the records of the four regions,
with annotations stating:
"Such as Jìn’s Shèng, Lǔ’s Chūnqiū, Chǔ’s Táowù, and the like,"
which constitute the complete history of a state.
Moreover, the Messengers presented five types of documents,
and the Grand Master presented folk songs (for details, see the "Discussion on the Gazetteer Section"; here, only those relevant to the three books are cited).
Thus, when the royal court collected from the feudal states,
the evidence from documents and traditions
was certainly not limited to a single source.
If one could be omitted,
then the ancients should not have established such an office;
if they could be combined into one,
then the ancients would have already created a unified book.
Someone asked:
With the abolition of feudalism and the establishment of commanderies and counties,
modern local gazetteers
cannot be compared to the ancient state histories. I replied:
In today’s world,
the moral principles and natural order of things
have not changed much from ancient times.
If local gazetteers cannot be compared to state histories,
it is because the officials such as prefects and magistrates
are all appointed by the Ministry of Personnel.
Since they do not inherit their positions hereditarily,
they cannot, like feudal lords, record their origins in their own books.
But as for the documents and traditions submitted to the court for collection,
how could they be any different?
People see the autonomy of the states in the Spring and Autumn period
and assume that the feudal lords each had their own systems,
somewhat like the state histories of later separatist regimes,
and thus think this cannot be applied to local gazetteers.
They do not realize that the system of the Zhōu Guān
was part of the prosperous rule of unified writing and standardized tracks,
where feudal lords followed the royal regulations
no differently from the commanderies and counties of later times.
In antiquity, there were no private writings;
the Six Classics are all history.
What later generations inherited and never abandoned
were only the three traditions derived from the Chūnqiū, the Shī, and the Lǐ.
The standard histories in annals-biographies form
are derived from the Chūnqiū tradition;
the records of institutions and essential regulations
are derived from the official Lǐ tradition;
the literary collections and anthologies
are derived from the folk Shī tradition.
Since the capture of the unicorn marked the end of the Chūnqiū,
later scholars have rarely fully understood the grand framework of the ancients,
and it took a long accumulation of time before gradual deductions became clear.
Since Sīmǎ Qiān’s Shǐjì and Bān Gù’s Hànshū,
the thread of the Chūnqiū has been extended.
Liú Zhì’s Zhèngdiǎn
and Dù Yòu’s Tōngdiǎn
began to extend the thread of the official Lǐ tradition.
Lǚ Zǔqiān’s Wénjiàn
and Sū Shì’s Wénlèi
began to extend the thread of the folk Shī tradition.
These all encompass entire eras in their books,
mutually supporting and verifying each other,
with no empty words.
Someone asked:
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
"The sage’s historical accounts are three:
the Shū, the Shī, and the Chūnqiū."
Now you discuss three histories,
but replace the Shū with the Lǐ.
Does this differ from Wénzhōngzǐ’s point? I replied:
The Shū and the Chūnqiū
originally belong to the same school of learning.
Although the Zhúshū cannot be fully trusted,
annalistic history likely existed in antiquity.
The chapters of the Shū are a distinct form of historical writing.
The ancients, being simple and质朴,
did not combine annals and biographies into a single compilation.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng used commentaries to support the classic,
thus merging them into one.
The diplomatic discourses within
are remnants of the instructions and proclamations;
the cited institutions and facts
are akin to the tributes and models.
Therefore, the Zhōushū ends with King Píng’s Qínshì, which is appended as a feudal state’s document.
And the Chūnqiū begins with King Píng,
clearly showing their continuity.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng combined them, and Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù followed suit,
thus establishing a fixed rule for historians,
much like the Yangtze and Han rivers separating at their sources but merging in their flow,
without anyone knowing why it happened so.
Later generations did not understand this
and regarded the Shàngshū and Chūnqiū as separately recording speeches and events,
showing their ignorance of the traditions of the Six Arts.
As for the indispensability of the official Lǐ,
this has already been explained earlier.
Someone asked:
With the loss of the Yuè, the Shū merged with the Chūnqiū,
leaving only four of the Six Arts.
Since you say the Six Classics are all history,
why have later histories not developed a tradition derived from the Yì? I replied:
Ancient governance emphasized heavenly principles but was brief on human affairs,
while later times emphasized human affairs but were brief on heavenly principles.
This is due to the circumstances of the times,
which even sages could not force to change.
In high antiquity, officials were named after clouds and birds,
appointed according to heavenly seasons.
Only in the times of Táng and Yú did appointments begin to be based on human affairs.
The Yáodiǎn details the appointments of Xī and Hé,
while in the Zhōu Guān, the Bǎozhāng official
is merely a mid-ranking officer under the Ministry of Spring.
This illustrates the general shift in emphasis from detail to brevity.
The Yì as a book
reveals things and accomplishes tasks;
the sages used divine principles to establish teachings,
creating it as a sacred object
to guide the people’s use beforehand.
Xī, Nóng, and Huángdì did not follow one another’s systems,
nor did Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties continue each other’s ways.
This is similar to establishing calendars and clarifying seasons,
both being innovative institutions of a dynasty,
refreshing the eyes and ears of the multitude.
Later generations only regarded issuing calendars and appointing times as governmental regulations,
while divination for seasons and days became the duty of officials in charge of heavenly matters.
As the saying goes, heavenly principles are distant, and human affairs are near—
a circumstance of the times that could not be otherwise.
Thus, among later historians,
only Sīmǎ Qiān still held the office of celestial official,
but from Bān Gù onward,
heavenly matters were no longer discussed.
Someone asked:
The Six Classics evolved into the three histories,
which are also monumental institutions of a dynasty.
A local region is but a tiny place;
a single gazetteer should suffice to cover it.
Why insist on including all things? I replied:
Categories and examples cannot be combined into one.
In antiquity, the Son of Heaven’s robe
had twelve emblems;
for dukes, marquises, ministers, grand masters, and scholars, the number decreased step by step,
down to a single black lower garment—
this was the minimum.
Yet if we consider it lowly
and try to combine it with caps and shoes into one object,
it is certainly impossible.
Previous scholars have written gazetteers for the six ministries and high offices.
However, the Ministry of Personnel knew nothing of military affairs,
and the Ministry of Revenue did not encroach on rites.
Although they encompassed the entire realm,
in reality, each focused on the partial duties of one office,
and one cannot demand that they include all things.
A local region, though small,
implements and administers all matters
pertaining to personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice, and works—
nothing is omitted.
Thus, it can be said to possess all essentials in miniature.
The state history draws materials from this,
much like the Chūnqiū relying on the precious books of the hundred states.
How can this be overlooked?
Someone asked:
Since the existence of local gazetteers,
we have never heard of the state history using them as evidence.
Why do you now say the state history draws materials from local gazetteers? I replied:
The tradition of local gazetteers has long been lost.
What are called local gazetteers today
are not true local gazetteers.
The elegant ones
are merely literary diversions,
short notes and brief writings,
refined talk and collected anecdotes.
The vulgar ones
are official documents and case files,
wandering beggars’ tales,
or mere conventional social exchanges.
Gentlemen and scholars often find them difficult to discuss.
The state history, having no alternative,
resorts to using family genealogies, biographical accounts,
literary collections, and personal records—
the so-called "when rites are lost, seek them among the common people."
However, private writings
may lack accuracy,
and without local gazetteers to corroborate them,
the labor of verification becomes overwhelming,
and the risk of mistaken belief
is likely unavoidable.
Thus, with the loss of local gazetteers, the state history has long suffered.
Since local gazetteers are not relied upon by the state history,
they become虚设 and fail to serve their purpose—
like a gu that is not a gu.
Can these be called local gazetteers?
Someone asks:
Now that three books are established side by side,
will they divide and analyze everything that was previously contained in local gazetteers?
Or will they add what local gazetteers lacked, forming a tripartite division? I say:
There is some division,
and also some addition.
However, the underlying principles are difficult to fully express in a single statement.
The way of history is such that
the elegant words of literary scholars,
and the documents and records of petty officials,
are both unusable;
yet if one discards these two,
then there is nothing with which to make history.
Mèngzǐ said:
The events,
the literary form,
the underlying principles—
these are what the *Spring and Autumn Annals* drew upon.
That is, to take the matters from official documents and refine them with elegant literary language,
and to judge them according to principle.
Both state histories and local gazetteers
are branches flowing from the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Using the human body as an analogy,
the events are its bones,
the literary form is its skin,
and the underlying principles are its spirit.
To judge them according to principle
is how a book begins to form its own school.
A book must form its own school,
and only then can it have its canons and methods,
be worthy of recitation and understanding,
and thereby be transmitted through the ages and travel far.
Therefore it is said:
"Zhì" means to record,
desiring it to endure long and be memorable.
Someone asks:
Since the gazetteer already takes official documents as its bones,
why then edit the official documents to create the "Administrative Precedents"? I say:
The explanation is detailed in the "Discussion of Examples" for the *Bózhōu Administrative Precedents*,
but I will now briefly summarize it again.
The eight treatises of Sīmǎ Qiān
all synthesize and examine statutes and regulations,
elucidating their main purposes.
The example for his "Treatise on Rites" states:
"Matters concerning sacrificial vessels
are the responsibility of the relevant officials."
This is the general rule for treatises in historical works.
What Sīmǎ Qiān referred to as the responsibility of officials,
such as Shūsūn Tōng's court rituals,
Hán Xìn's military laws,
Xiāo Hé's legal statutes,
each had its own official custodians who preserved the administrative precedents;
historical writing could not encompass them all.
It is regrettable that there were no figures like Liú Zhì or Dù Yòu
to separately compile administrative precedents and edit them into essential compendiums.
Therefore, those seeking Han dynasty statutes
have only Bān Gù's *History*,
and the details of regulations and numbers cannot be as comprehensive as those of the Táng dynasty;
the effect is easily seen.
Thus, separately compiling administrative precedents to supplement the gazetteer
is like the *History of the Táng Dynasty* having the *Táng Huìyào*,
the *History of the Sòng Dynasty* having the *Sòng Huìyào*,
the *History of the Yuán Dynasty* having the *Yuán Diǎnzhāng*,
and the *History of the Míng Dynasty* having the *Míng Huìdiǎn*.
Someone asks:
In present-day local gazetteers,
what is called the "Arts and Letters" section,
sets aside bibliographies and selects many poems and prose pieces,
seemingly aiming for mutual verification between events and words,
having found a flexible approach.
Now you insist on separately compiling a book as a "Literary Collection";
is the intention not the same? I say:
The explanation is detailed in the preface and examples of the *Yǒngqīng Literary Collection*,
but I will now briefly summarize it again.
Since the gazetteer imitates the style of history in its compilation,
then poems and prose pieces relevant to historical composition
should be included within the annals and biographies,
as with the edicts, memorials, and other texts recorded in the biographies and treatises of Bān Gù's *History*,
which is acceptable.
To use the method of literary anthologies for the "Arts and Letters" treatise
would mean the *Sòng Wénjiàn* could be merged with the *History of the Sòng Dynasty* into one book,
and the *Yuán Wénlèi* could be merged with the *History of the Yuán Dynasty* into one book.
How then would they be distinguished from the writings contained in the annals and biographies?
Someone asks:
The practice of literary selection began with the Liáng dynasty of the Xiāo family,
followed by the *Wényuàn Yīnghuá* and the *Táng Wéncuì*;
it has a long history.
Now you cite the *Wénjiàn* and *Wénlèi*,
which began to extend the tradition of the *Airs of the States*,
why is that? I say:
Works like the *Wénxuǎn* and *Wényuàn* aimed at literary elegance,
not at verifying actual events.
The *Wénjiàn* first showed an intention towards governance,
and the *Wénlèi* then showed an intention towards historical precedents.
This is because later generations practiced this over time,
and their insights surpassed those of the ancients.
Someone asks:
The writings of a local region are not numerous.
Having already taken the essential canonical pieces for inclusion in the annals and biographies,
and then compiling poems and prose that can mutually verify with the gazetteer
into a separate book,
I fear the number of pieces will be very few. I say:
Since it is already a separate book,
the principles and categories can naturally be slightly broader.
Even with the *Wénjiàn* and *Wénlèi*,
whose main purpose is to verify history,
one cannot apply a single rigid standard to every piece.
Famous writings and excellent compositions
are appreciated by all.
Even if they do not fully meet the criteria for verifying history,
there is no reason not to include them as well.
For each book naturally has its own style and principles;
the teaching of the *Book of Songs* naturally follows a different path from that of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
As for the "Arts and Letters" sections in modern local gazetteers,
the vulgar and excessive ones
need not be discussed.
Even those with some discernment
know to select what is useful,
and are cautious, selecting not too many.
They do not realize that judged by the principles of historical treatises,
even this already constitutes excessive inclusion.
If one wishes to show the flourishing of a region's culture,
even doubling the "Arts and Letters" section
would still seem inadequate.
Without compiling a dedicated collection to clarify the learning of the three schools,
one would lack a basis for both inclusion and exclusion.
Someone asks:
The *Wénxuǎn* encompasses all literary forms;
why now classify it under the branch of the *Airs of the States*?
What does this mean? I say:
The explanation is detailed in the chapter "The Teaching of Poetry",
but I will now briefly summarize it again.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"Poetry expresses intent."
In antiquity, there were no private writings;
the Classics, the Masters, and the various histories
all originated from the official duties of the ancients.
Poetry alone could express whatever the mind desired to say.
Before the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
there were no discursive writings within literary collections.
Writings that were not exegetical works on the Classics, biographical histories, or discourses belonging to the Masters' schools—
these the ancients began to call "wén" (literature).
Those that were exegetical, biographical, or discursive in form
the ancients called "shū" (books),
not "wén".
Xiāo Tǒng's *Wénxuǎn*,
combining poetry and prose and calling them all "wén",
shows that literary collections and poetry
belong to the same branch.
Now, imitating the anthology model to create a "Literary Collection",
the writings selected for inclusion,
though not uniform in type,
are essentially those that speak according to the author's own intent.
Therefore, they are attached to the tradition of the *Airs of the States*.
Someone asks:
Kǒng Yǎn had the *Hàn Wèi Shàngshū*,
and Wáng Tōng also had the *Xù Shū*,
both collecting edicts, proclamations, memorials, and submissions
into a single collection,
which is also a branch of the *Wénxuǎn*.
Yet they classified these to extend the *Book of Documents* school,
and did not place them in the poetry section.
Why is that? I say:
The learning of the *Book of Documents*, since Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
merged with the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Followers like Kǒng Yǎn and Wáng Tōng,
not understanding this principle, forced the issue,
and thus their way ultimately could not prevail.
It is like later times,
when the Jì River had already joined the Huáng Hé,
yet those clinging to the *Tribute of Yǔ*
still wanted to dredge the old course at Xíngzé and Táoqiū.
Someone asked:
Besides the three types of books,
there are also those that have been continued and not abandoned,
such as the chronological style of the Comprehensive Mirror,
and the event-based narratives of the "Outline and Details" format.
These have been passed down since then,
and should be like ancestral sacrifices that are never removed.
In relation to the Six Arts,
how do they derive their different streams?
The reply is: These are all branches of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
For the historical style of annals and biographies
originally developed from the Spring and Autumn school of learning,
and the Comprehensive Mirror derives from the texts of the basic annals,
combining the treatises and biographies into one.
As for the "Outline and Details" format,
its source lies in the Book of Documents;
but the Book of Documents branched off and entered the Spring and Autumn Annals,
so it is also a branch of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
From Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward,
each generation developed the Spring and Autumn Annals through annals and biographies.
The Comprehensive Mirror took the divisions of annals and biographies
and combined them into a chronological format.
The "Outline and Details" format then took the combined approach of the Comprehensive Mirror
and divided it according to event categories;
and by composing chapters based on events,
not adhering to fixed conventions,
it actually recaptured the lost methods of the Book of Documents.
This is what is meant by events undergoing repeated changes yet returning to their origin,
like the hexagram Bì receiving from Bō,
and Bō at its extremity receiving from Fù.
It is like cinnabar being refined into mercury,
and the mercury being refined again,
returning to cinnabar—
this is the principle.
This theory is discussed in a separate dedicated essay,
and will not be detailed here. This is a supplementary discussion, not about local gazetteers.
Someone asked:
You are compiling a local gazetteer,
and beyond the three types of books,
why is there an additional book called Collected Discussions?
The reply is: This is the leftover material gathered.
The ancients, in writing books to establish a school of thought,
did not boast of quantity or seek exhaustiveness.
However, without broad study,
there is no basis for selective extraction.
Once selective extraction is done,
the leftover material from broad study,
if included, would be inappropriate;
if discarded, it would be a pity.
Therefore, following the tradition of unofficial histories and anecdotal collections,
Collected Discussions is compiled,
akin to alternative interpretations of the Classics,
unofficial biographies of history,
and supplementary chapters of the Masters.
Why is it not included under the three types of books but called the fourth?
Because
the three types of books are all essential to the Classics,
while Collected Discussions is not an indispensable book.
Previous compilers of gazetteers
often attached such material at the end of the gazetteer,
calling it "Supplementary Compilation"
or "Miscellaneous Records."
They did not see the principles and meanings of the book
as achieving a distinctive school of thought,
so attaching it at the end
was not harmful.
Now that the three schools of learning are established,
and the three types of books are written,
there is no reason to regret discarding material,
so it is better to compile a separate volume for proper placement.
As the "Treatise on Literature" in the Book of Hàn says, the category of minor tales
originated from low-ranking officials,
street gossip and alley talk,
which were also not discarded in collecting folk customs.
Proposal for Establishing Gazetteer Offices in Prefectures and Counties
I, a humble person, grew up in poverty,
earning a living by writing for others,
and was frequently invited to compile gazetteers,
thus gaining much experience in gazetteer matters.
In evaluating the rights and wrongs of ancient people
and deliberating on the general principles of later gazetteers,
I have indeed spoken in great detail.
The essence is to match substance with literary form,
and establish structure according to the style.
As for establishing methods to pioneer,
and setting good rules to prevent future issues,
since it was not within my professional duties,
I hesitated to offer presumptuous advice.
Occasionally, during leisurely conversations,
such thoughts were often dismissed like clay oxen entering the sea.
Fine gazetteers were not achieved,
and my heart felt lacking.
However, since established methods are not for one time only,
why not propose theories for later consideration?
Therefore, I wish to speak fully,
awaiting the selection of the knowledgeable.
According to the Zhou Rituals, under the Ministry of Rites,
the Outer Historian was in charge of the records of the four regions,
noted as works like the Jìn Shèng and Chǔ Táowù,
which were the completed books of the feudal lords.
Could completed books have no basis?
I have examined the Zhou system
and learned that the ancients' handling of historical matters
was indeed extremely meticulous.
The Controller not only kept duplicates of contracts, registers, and maps in the suburbs, counties, and capitals;
the Party Leader "gathered the people to read the laws,
recording their virtues, conduct, skills, and arts";
the Village Head compared the masses,
"recording their respect, diligence, responsibility, and compassion";
the Recitation Instructor "was in charge of explaining local records,
to inform about affairs,
and explaining local taboos,
to inform about avoidances,
thus understanding local customs";
the Minor Historian "was in charge of the records of the states,
establishing genealogies,
and distinguishing the order of ancestors";
the Instruction Officer "was in charge of guiding the administrative affairs of the four regions,
and the records of their upper and lower levels,
reciting the transmitted ways of the four regions";
the Territorial Officer "was in charge of the territories of the states,
and correcting their boundaries";
the Mountain and River Officers "each were in charge of the names of mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
distinguishing their products and benefits or harms";
the Plain Officer "was in charge of the place names of the four regions,
distinguishing the names of hills, mounds, plains, and wetlands";
thus, within the villages, settlements, and outlying areas,
mountains, rivers, and customs,
products, and human relations,
were already recorded without omission, great or small.
As for the Messengers presenting the five books,
the Regional Officers collecting maps and records,
and the Grand Masters presenting folk songs,
these were what was reported upward.
For systems were established from above downward,
while collection was done from below upward.
Only when collection was thorough
could the systems become more refined—
this was the excellent method of the Three Dynasties.
In later historical matters,
the upper levels were detailed, but the lower levels were not.
Prefectures and counties differed from the feudal system,
and local gazetteers no longer served as ancient state histories
but fell into the category of geographical writings,
so their content became biased and incomplete.
Moreover, these books lacked official systems and responsibilities,
and were left to individuals to compile as they pleased,
so their principles became inconsistent and could not serve as canonical standards—
a situation dictated by circumstances.
Literature is to be judged by governance and administration alone.
After the Three Dynasties, literature
could exist without the inherited institutions of the Three Dynasties;
but governance and administration after the Three Dynasties
could not fail to follow the inherited principles of the Three Dynasties.
If in governance and law we also preserved the inherited institutions of the literature of the Three Dynasties,
then why worry that literature would not achieve the beauty and completeness of the Three Dynasties?
The governance and administration of the realm
begin in the districts and counties,
and reach up to the imperial court,
just as in the Three Dynasties, the bǐ, lǘ, zú, and dǎng units
ascended to the Six Ministers;
in the feudal states,
they proceeded from the leaders, commanders, and administrators
to communicate with the Son of Heaven.
What the Six Ministries of the court administer
is the consolidation of the archival records of the six departments of clerks in all the districts and counties to establish governance.
Their progression from the bottom upward
also resembles the inherited system of the bǐ, lǘ, zú, dǎng units and the leaders, commanders, and administrators of the Three Dynasties.
The Six Ministries must consolidate the archival records of the realm for governance to exist;
the official historians must consolidate the records of the realm for the registers to be complete.
Yet the archival records of districts and counties
are named according to affairs,
and the clerks who carry out duties
often add annotations beyond the six departments.
As for the records of districts and counties,
there is no dedicated official to preserve them,
and the great principles are lacking.
Occasionally, there are those with good intentions
who compile local gazetteers,
but they generally rely on temporary investigations,
the people involved are often mediocre and vulgar,
and the examples are rarely complete;
some even harbor private biases, deceive falsely,
and engage in bribery through writing.
Thus, when it comes to local gazetteers,
gentlemen and scholars often find them difficult to discuss.
When official historians gather information from below,
if the local gazetteers of districts and counties are like this,
what will they rely on as material for editing and revising?
Moreover, there is the history of the realm,
the history of a state,
the history of a family,
and the history of an individual.
Biographies, accounts, epitaphs, and narratives
are the history of an individual;
family records and genealogies
are the history of a family;
the gazetteers of provinces, prefectures, and counties
are the history of a state;
comprehensive records of a dynasty
are the history of the realm.
From individuals, families are formed;
from families, states are formed;
from states, the realm is formed.
Only when the parts are extremely detailed
can the whole select the good without regret.
Genealogies are scattered and difficult to verify;
biographies and epitaphs are private and often flattering;
when the court compiles history,
it must draw material from local gazetteers.
And among local gazetteers,
the provincial gazetteers draw from the prefectures,
and the prefectural gazetteers draw from the districts and counties,
which is also the principle of progressing from the bottom upward.
Thus, the gazetteers of districts and counties
serve below to balance genealogies, biographies, and epitaphs,
and above to provide reliable evidence for provinces and prefectures,
making them essential abridgments for the court's history.
Meetings, projects,
taxes, lawsuits,
—districts and counties rely on clerks and archival records
to meet the demands of the Six Ministries;
but when it comes to examining documents and gathering literature,
districts and counties only have crude and lawless gazetteers—
how can these suffice for the selection of official historians?
Since the essential records of districts and counties
are not worth examining,
it is no wonder that the court's historians prefer to seek material from genealogies, biographies, and epitaphs below
and no longer inquire of the districts and counties.
But if meetings, projects,
taxes, lawsuits,
were handled by the Six Ministries not through districts and counties
but by directly inquiring among the people,
would that be appropriate?
Then, is it not difficult
to compile historical records after the Three Dynasties?
Literature is to be judged by governance and administration alone.
Without the official duties and典籍 of the Three Dynasties,
there would be no literature of the Three Dynasties;
without the literature of the Three Dynasties,
even if there were the achievements of the Three Dynasties,
they could not shine as brightly as the sun and moon.
The documents and records of clerks
are disdained by literary scholars.
Yet governance and administration
cannot proceed without them.
Later generations placed the responsibility for historical records solely on literary scholars,
while the archival records of officials
were not prepared with the legal institutions for historians.
This is why, after the Three Dynasties,
when substance was separated from literary expression,
historical records became difficult to discuss.
Now, since the grand administration of the realm
begins in the districts and counties,
the responsibility for historical records
should also begin with the gazetteers of districts and counties.
Districts and counties may have crude and unverifiable gazetteers,
but they do not have crude and unverifiable documents and records of clerks.
Gazetteers have principles, examples, and literary expressions that depend on the praise or blame of individuals and their skill or clumsiness;
documents and records have no principles, examples, or literary expressions that depend on the praise or blame of individuals or their skill or clumsiness;
for their entries follow fixed methods,
and their preservation is entrusted to fixed personnel—
this is what is called following the inherited principles of the Three Dynasties.
Therefore, the gazetteers of districts and counties
cannot be compiled in a short time;
ordinarily, among the various clerks,
a special "Gazetteer Section" should be established,
and clerks with some understanding of literary methods
should be selected to fill its ranks.
Moreover, established regulations should be set,
so that records are kept according to the rules,
somewhat like the formulas in documents and records,
to avoid the flaw of arbitrary cleverness.
After accumulating records for several decades,
seek those skilled in literature and versed in historical editing
to revise and compile them into a finished book—
this is what is called waiting for the right person to act.
Proceeding in this way, accumulating and then revising,
the effort is not laborious,
yet the effectiveness surpasses what literary historians can achieve—
this is what is called preserving in governance and law the inherited institutions of the literature of the Three Dynasties.
Then, how should we establish a complete system?
For the documents of the six departments,
we can extract the main points
and record and store copies.
For officials and scholars,
upon leaving office,
we can record their conduct, whether good or bad, based on concrete evidence,
and document the entire course of events.
Within the jurisdiction,
each family should compile its genealogy,
and individuals should write biographies, epitaphs, or accounts,
which must be submitted in duplicate;
the scholars and teachers in schools
should gather public opinion,
verify and correct them, and store them in the archival department.
For local scholars,
if they have compiled works on classics or history,
poetry, essays, or other writings,
once finalized and compiled,
they must submit copies,
to be stored in the archival department,
along with a catalog of the contents.
For the construction or repair of government offices, city walls,
schools, temples, and shrines,
dikes, dams, and bridges,
the details must be reported to the department,
and the full account submitted.
For inscriptions on metal or stone,
recording events or composing texts,
rubbings must be made
and stored in the department.
For ceremonies such as honoring scholars or village banquets,
reading laws or lecturing on books,
whenever such events are held,
the names and ranks of the officials and participants at the time must be recorded,
along with what was seen and heard.
A storage room should be established,
protected from fire and water.
Locked cabinets should be provided,
categorized by department and type,
sealed and stored by date,
and not opened without reason.
Following the idea of village schools or charitable schools,
each of the four districts should appoint an investigator,
selected from among the fair-minded gentry with public trust,
to search for lost texts and anecdotes,
and submit them periodically.
The scholars and teachers in schools
should carefully select experienced individuals
to impartially verify all submissions.
For rituals, music, and governance,
they are interrelated.
When scholars discuss rituals and music,
they must inquire about ceremonial vessels from the ritual officers,
and examine musical rhythms from the musicians,
so that their writings are not empty words.
The documents of clerks and officials
are the basis for ministers discussing state affairs,
just as rituals rely on ceremonial vessels,
and music relies on rhythms.
If one discusses governance but despises official documents,
or determines rituals and music but scorns ceremonial vessels and rhythms,
then such writings lack substance
and are useless.
As for the work of historians,
if no proper system is established to avoid flaws,
can it be said that entrusting it to literary scholars alone is sufficient?
Some may say:
Once archival departments are established in prefectures and counties,
there is no need to worry about the loss of documents.
But from prefectures and counties to the official historians,
the distance is great and there is no unified oversight.
Should the prefectural and provincial administrations not be involved? I say:
If prefectures and counties do not implement this properly,
the provincial administrations must inspect them according to regulations.
As for the archival departments,
since they summarize the key points of the six departments’ documents
to preserve records,
the prefectural offices should summarize the key points of the county archival departments
to compile the prefectural records;
the provincial offices should summarize the key points of the prefectural departments
to compile the provincial records.
Not only will the prefectural and provincial records have material to draw from,
but by collecting and comparing them,
the accuracy of the county archival departments can be verified.
As for high-ranking officials in the provincial administration,
upon leaving office,
the provincial archival department should, like the county departments do for their officials and scholars,
record their conduct, whether good or bad, based on concrete evidence,
detail the course of events,
and store it in the department.
For prefectural officials,
the prefectural archival department should also record them upon leaving office,
as the counties do.
Thus, the prefectural archival clerks
not only combine the county records and store copies,
and the provincial archival clerks
not only combine the prefectural records and store copies,
but also handle matters specific to their own prefecture or province,
which cannot be neglected.
Some may say:
This is indeed beneficial for historical work.
But is it also useful for governance? I say:
Literature and governance
are always interrelated.
Official documents are the basis of governance.
Unexpected events may cause loss by fire or water;
poor storage may lead to damage by dampness or insects;
corrupt clerks may tamper or alter them.
If key points are recorded and copies stored in the archival department,
these problems can be avoided.
This greatly benefits governance.
Genealogies are not managed by the government,
which differs from ancient practices,
as the numerous clans in the country cannot all be verified by the capital offices.
But disputes arise over ancestral rites and succession;
over property and inheritance;
over false claims to surnames or registration,
or returning to one’s original clan;
over marriages violating laws;
over hidden households or tax evasion.
If genealogical records are lost
or forged by deceitful individuals,
confusion arises and problems multiply.
If all genealogies are submitted in duplicate to the archival department,
these problems can be avoided.
This also greatly benefits governance.
In ancient times, there were no private writings,
but since the Warring States period,
this cannot be constrained by old methods.
However, if writings are not overseen by officials,
people will indulge in selfish biases.
When the teachings of the sages decline, reckless arguments disrupt them;
when official historians fail, unofficial histories spread private views.
The excessive and chaotic collections of recent times,
the confusion in unofficial records,
distort historical accounts
and mislead public opinion,
to an extent that cannot be fully addressed.
If all finalized writings
must be submitted in duplicate to the archival department,
and school scholars discuss them impartially,
then proximity allows for verification of facts,
and recent events cannot be attributed to mere hearsay,
avoiding these problems.
This benefits governance immeasurably.
Thus, literature and governance are always interrelated.
Regarding provincial gazetteers,
Hóng Liàngjí, a compiler from Yánghú,
once compiled the *Qiánlóng Prefectural, Subprefectural, and County Gazetteer*,
using the administrative divisions of the *Unified Gazetteer*,
with provinces overseeing prefectures, subprefectures, and counties.
Ten years ago,
I visited Hóng at his home
and said that for the current system, it should be called “ministries and courts,”
not rigidly adhere to the old term “provincial administration commissions.”
I explained how the current divisions differ from the original system
to clarify the principles.
Hóng did not agree.
Recently, I saw his published *Juǎnshī Gé Collected Works*,
which includes *A Letter to Jìnshì Zhāng*,
with extensive references
strongly refuting the division system.
I still cannot agree.
Moreover, his arguments
mostly repeat what I have already addressed,
and need not be reiterated.
My original intent
seems not well remembered by Hóng.
Therefore, I clarify my views separately,
to leave for my disciples,
showing what I believe,
not claiming my view is necessarily correct.
The system of administrative divisions,
in the era of feudalism,
had regional overlords.
In the era of commanderies and counties,
starting from the Han dynasty, thirteen regional inspectorates were established;
during the Six Dynasties, the systems of provinces and commanderies
underwent repeated changes,
and the officials overseeing the divisions,
although bearing titles such as military governor and general administrator,
did not have fixed administrative seats,
so when the Tang people compiled the geographical records of the Five Dynasties,
namely the *Suíshū* (History of the Sui Dynasty),
they could not establish a clear concept of administrative divisions,
resorting instead to the nine provinces of the *Yǔgòng* (Tribute of Yu),
to delineate commanderies and counties,
which was a flawed approach.
The Tang people divided the land into circuits,
and the Song people divided it into routes,
although the official system and jurisdiction were not constant,
the names of the circuits and routes remained unchanged;
thus, those compiling geographical records
could simply refer to the circuits and routes to clarify the divisions.
The Yuan system also divided the land into routes,
but each route was governed by a chief administrator of the Branch Secretariat,
hence it was also called the Branch Secretariat.
The Ming dynasty changed the Branch Secretariat to thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions,
and the officials governing the territory
were called Provincial Administration Commissioners.
The Provincial Administration Commission
is the name of the division,
while the Provincial Administration Commissioner
is the official overseeing the division,
and the two should not be confused.
However, the term "Provincial Administration Commission"
consists of four characters,
while "Branch Secretariat" could be abbreviated as "Province,"
and people naturally prefer simplicity,
so even though the system changed,
the common practice at the time
was still to refer to it as a province.
As this practice persisted over time,
it often appeared in memorials and official documents,
gradually becoming entrenched.
In our dynasty, the Provincial Administration Commissions
followed the old Ming system;
and the customary use of "province"
also continued from the Ming dynasty.
This is similar to the Han system, where sons and brothers were enfeoffed as kingdoms,
granted the title of king,
yet in imperial edicts, proclamations, and memorials,
they were referred to as feudal lords and kings;
at the time, they were not actually feudal lords,
but the name was retained in deference to antiquity.
However, since the initial system closely followed the Ming model,
the proper name should indeed be Provincial Administration Commission.
Over the past hundred years,
adapting to the times,
although the names have followed the Ming precedent,
the actual structure has gradually diverged from that of the Ming.
Now, since Mr. Hóng's book is titled Qiánlóng,
then, holding the name to account for the reality,
it must refer to the Ministry and Censorate rather than the Administration Commission.
For in the early system, the Xúnfǔ had no fixed territory;
in the former Míng dynasty, the two capitals had no Administration Commissions,
yet Xúnfǔ were established between Shùntiān and Yìngtiān;
outside Shùntiān,
there was also Zhèngdìng,
and outside Yìngtiān,
there were the various Xúnfǔ such as Fèngyáng.
They were not like today's Xúnfǔ, who govern an entire province,
each having their own fixed territory.
This is the first reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
In the early system, the Xúnfǔ had no fixed official rank.
Thus, before the Kāngxī period,
Xúnfǔ had varying ranks of second, third, and fourth grade,
those concurrently holding the title of Shìláng were second grade,
those concurrently holding the title of Deputy Censor-in-Chief were third grade,
and those concurrently holding the title of Assistant Censor-in-Chief were fourth grade;
now, however, they all concurrently hold the titles of Vice Minister of War and Right Deputy Censor-in-Chief.
Their unified system
no longer follows the irregular precedent of imperial commissioners.
This is the second reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
Education commissioners and customs officials
all hold capital appointments;
if their capital appointments are removed,
they lose their official positions.
Now, when a new Xúnfǔ is appointed,
the Ministry of Personnel must inquire whether they should concurrently hold the titles of the Ministry of War and the Censorate.
Although it has become customary,
there is no case of not holding concurrent titles;
but since there is an inquiry about whether it should be done,
there is also the possibility of not holding concurrent titles.
According to books such as the Collected Statutes and the Ranks and Grades Examination,
the Xúnfǔ is already listed as second grade junior,
with a note stating:
"When the title of Shìláng is added, it becomes second grade senior."
Thus, even if the Xúnfǔ does not hold concurrent capital titles,
they already have a fixed rank,
just like the capital officials of the Sòng dynasty,
who served as prefects or county magistrates;
although they held capital titles,
one cannot say that the prefectures and counties were not part of the territorial administration.
This is the third reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
The great affairs of the state
lie in sacrifices and warfare.
Now, military affairs are the exclusive responsibility of the Zǒngdū,
but the Xúnfǔ also commands troops,
so there is no need to discuss this further.
As for sacrifices at altars and temples,
which were formerly presided over by the Administration Commissioner,
they are now presided over by the Xúnfǔ.
This is the fourth reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
The grand ceremony of provincial examinations,
which formerly used the seal of the Administration Commissioner to stamp the lists,
now uses the official seal of the Xúnfǔ.
This is the fifth reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
In the early system, the Administration Commission had left and right commissioners,
who separately handled affairs of personnel, revenue, rites, and works.
The Regional Military Commission managed military affairs,
and the Surveillance Commission handled judicial matters.
Thus, the two Administration Commissioners
internally corresponded to the Six Ministries;
while the one Surveillance Commissioner
internally corresponded to the Censorate.
Now, the two commissioners have been merged into one,
and the responsibility for postal stations has been transferred to the Surveillance Commissioner,
while the Regional Military Commission has been abolished, and military authority has been transferred to the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ.
Their duties and responsibilities differ from before.
Therefore, from imperial edicts above
to memorials and official documents below,
all refer to the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ as frontier officials,
and not as commissioners;
all refer to the Administration Commission as the general treasury for revenue,
and the Surveillance Commission as the general office for judicial matters,
and do not regard the Administration Commissioner as a frontier official.
This especially shows that, in accordance with the times and the establishment of the system,
they must be called the Ministry and Censorate. This is the sixth reason.
Although both Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ are called frontier officials,
the title of Zǒngdū is referred to as Ministry Hall;
for the head of the Ministry of War,
although concurrently holding the title of Right Censor-in-Chief,
still primarily focuses on military affairs.
The title of Xúnfǔ is referred to as Ministry and Censorate;
for the head of the Censorate,
although concurrently holding the title of Vice Minister of War,
still primarily focuses on overseeing officials.
Therefore, under the current system, except for the secondary capital,
there are prefectures, subprefectures, and counties not subordinate to a Zǒngdū,
but there are certainly none not subordinate to a Xúnfǔ.
For example, Hénán, Shāndōng, and Shānxī
have Xúnfǔ but no Zǒngdū.
The Xúnfǔ need not concurrently hold the title of Zǒngdū.
Zhílì, Sìchuān, and Gānsù
have Zǒngdū but no Xúnfǔ,
so the Zǒngdū must concurrently hold the title of Xúnfǔ.
The authority of Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ is equal;
why is it that where there is a Zǒngdū but no Xúnfǔ,
the Zǒngdū must concurrently hold the title of Xúnfǔ?
Precisely because the Xúnfǔ, as the Ministry and Censorate,
unifies the territorial administrative system,
and it is not without reason that this concurrent title is added.
This especially shows that, living in the present time,
one should understand the current system,
and they must be called the Ministry and Censorate. This is the seventh reason.
Now, there are nineteen Administration Commissions in the empire,
but the Collected Statutes and regulations,
as well as documents from the Six Ministries,
such as the triennial evaluations by the Ministry of Personnel,
the revenue reports by the Ministry of Revenue,
the metropolitan examinations by the Ministry of Rites,
and the autumn assizes by the Ministry of Justice,
all only recognize eighteen provinces,
and do not recognize nineteen Administration Commissions;
this is because there are only eighteen Ministries and Censorates for Xúnfǔ (in reality, there are only fifteen Xúnfǔ, with three concurrently held by Zǒngdū).
Thus, the Ministry and Censorate of Jiāngsū
has long been conventionally called the province of Jiāngsū.
The Sūsōng Administration Commission
and the Jiānghuái Administration Commission
separately administer eight prefectures and three subprefectures,
yet no public or private documents
refer to Sūsōng Province or Jiānghuái Province.
This especially shows that in the division of territorial administration,
it is absolutely inappropriate today to refer to them as Commissions,
and they must be called the Ministry and Censorate. This is the eighth reason.
Mr. Hóng argues that because the Xúnfǔ uses an official seal,
unlike the regular seal of the Administration Commission,
it cannot be considered the proper authority of the locality.
This can be said to know ten but forget that it is two times five.
According to Mr. Hóng's argument,
then his references to prefectures, subprefectures, and counties
are also inappropriate.
Prefectures and counties indeed have their own seals,
but subprefectures are directly administered assistant prefects,
who only have official seals and no regular seals.
Assistant prefects issue documents under the prefect's seal,
yet their official seals can represent territorial administration;
the Xúnfǔ shares the seal of the Censorate,
yet his official seal cannot represent territorial administration?
How can one be clear on small matters but confused on major ones?
This is the ninth reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
Mr. Hóng also says that the current system of Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ
should be like the Hàn dynasty's use of the Chancellor's Chief Clerk to inspect provinces,
where although the province governed commanderies,
the Hàn Records still focused on commanderies and kingdoms,
not listing the Inspector among them.
This analogy is not very apt.
In the current system, only the one Ministry and Censorate of Jiāngsū
has two Administration Commissions;
in other places, the area administered by the Commission
is the same as that administered by the Ministry and Censorate,
unlike the Hàn system where one province necessarily governed several commanderies.
However, even according to Mr. Hóng's statement,
then Guàn's Records of the Thirteen Provinces
is a specialized work in itself,
so why would it not record provincial inspectors as part of territorial administration?
This is the tenth reason why they should be called the Ministry and Censorate.
Now, when systems are changed,
there must be explicit documentation.
In the early Míng dynasty, when Xúnfǔ were first dispatched alongside the three Commission officials,
their relationship was like that of host and guest.
The slightly more respected ones
were merely like royal ministers placed above the feudal lords.
Later, the authority of the Censorate gradually increased,
and the three Commissions carried out the Censorate's orders.
However, the system was not changed,
and all evaluation ceremonies, revenue reports,
provincial examinations, and sacrifices
were exclusively managed by the Administration Commissioner.
Therefore, they were considered the chief officials of the unified province,
and their title could not be changed due to diminished authority.
In our dynasty, over the past hundred years,
official duties and systems
have gradually changed.
Today, the Administration Commissioner and the Surveillance Commissioner
separately handle revenue and judicial matters,
both being subordinate officials of the Ministry and Censorate,
somewhat like the Administrative Assistants and Counselors in the provincial system of the Yuán dynasty.
All major administrative affairs and ceremonies
that have been taken from the Administration Commissioner and given to the Ministry and Censorate
have been documented in explicit regulations,
which is known to both the court and the public.
Yet, whether the unified province should be called a Commission
or changed to Ministry and Censorate
has no explicit documentation.
Why is this?
Because both official and private documents
have conventionally used the convenient term "province,"
not only has the Ministry and Censorate not adopted a new name,
but even the Commission has not retained the old name.
Laws, statutes, regulations,
edicts, and official documents
all use the term "province";
only the Comprehensive Geography still follows the old practice,
referring to the Administration Commission,
which has not been corrected by chance.
Since Mr. Hóng's book is titled Qiánlóng,
how could he not know the affairs of the sixty years of the Qiánlóng period?
Some may say:
The Comprehensive Gazetteer is a work of the imperial library,
compiled by Hóng Jūnzūn according to established regulations and precedents;
how can it be criticized?
I contend that the initial precedents of the Comprehensive Gazetteer were already fixed,
and later compilers followed them without making changes. The original precedent should have been based on the Commissioner’s Office.
The change in regulations from Commissioner’s Office to Ministry or Academy
occurred gradually,
not as a sudden innovation;
thus the imperial library did not update it.
Private works,
establishing precedents based on principle,
should precisely reflect the current regulations.
Moreover, my critique
is not solely directed at Hóng Jūnzūn’s work.
Those who write in classical prose today,
when referring to the unified administrative divisions,
also speak of “the various provinces,”
or “such-and-such province.”
Abandoning the current administrative system
to borrow the terminology of the Yuán people—
this is unheard of in antiquity.
Before the Yōngzhèng and Kāngxī reigns,
classical prose also did not use the term “Commissioner’s Office”;
at that time, it was proper to refer to Commissioner’s Office. The Míng people, for brevity,
continued the Yuán system,
and this has long been a flaw in classical prose.
Therefore, in my classical prose,
when it is appropriate to refer to the unified division,
where common usage says “such-and-such province,”
I always say “such-and-such Ministry or Academy,”
or abbreviate it as “such-and-such Ministry”;
where common usage says “the various provinces” or “such-and-such and such-and-such provinces,”
I always say “the various Ministries or Academies” or “such-and-such and such-and-such Ministries or Academies,”
abbreviated as “the various Ministries” or “such-and-such and such-and-such Ministries”;
so that names are correct and speech follows accordingly.
If it were not the current system,
one should say “Commissioner’s Office,”
or abbreviate it as “Office”;
that would be acceptable,
but using “province” is not permissible.
Some may ask:
Why do imperial edicts, memorials, and official documents
still use these terms?
I reply:
This is permissible as rhetorical usage,
but not as precedent in classical prose.
Moreover, in edicts, memorials, and documents,
the Administration Commissioner is called “fān,”
the Surveillance Commissioner “niè,”
and the prefect, subprefect, and magistrate “shǒu,” “mù,” “lìng”;
this is harmless as rhetoric,
but historical texts do not follow this precedent.
Preface and Principles for the Imperial Edicts Chronicle of the Hézhōu Gazetteer
The Rites of Zhōu states
that the Outer Historian “oversees the records of the four regions,”
and “when sent on missions to the four regions,
he records their orders.”
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary on “records of the four regions”
refers to “Lǔ’s Spring and Autumn Annals,
Jìn’s Shèng,
and Chǔ’s Táowù.”
This is correct.
“Records their orders”
means “records the king’s commands to be given to the envoys.”
This is correct.
The District Grand Master, “on the first auspicious day of the first month,
receives the instructional regulations from the Minister of Education,
and returns to promulgate them to the local officials.”
Kǒng Yǐngdá’s subcommentary says, “This refers to the twelve instructions and below in the duties of the Grand Minister of Education.”
This is correct.
Within the royal domain, the six districts
were governed directly by the Son of Heaven,
so they received regulations from the Minister of Education;
outside the royal domain, the feudal lords
governed their own states,
and each compiled its own Spring and Autumn Annals—the histories of the various states were collectively called Spring and Autumn Annals.
However, the records of the four regions
were necessarily subordinate to the Outer Historian;
the orders issued
were upheld as statutes.
Thus, in antiquity, each state had its own history,
and what was recorded on bamboo slips
gave first importance to the king’s commands—
this can indeed be verified.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals always began the year with the king’s calendar,
and when Hán Xuānzǐ visited Lǔ,
he saw the Changes and the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and said that the Zhōu rituals were preserved there.
For records from the four regions
were brought in and corrected by the Outer Historian;
and commands issued by the royal court
were also promulgated by the Outer Historian.
Thus, affairs had specialized officials,
and records had fixed regulations,
ensuring uniformity in writing throughout the realm.
I suspect that under the Zhōu governance,
the historical records of the various states
must have followed established rules,
received from the royal court,
like the District Grand Master receiving instructional regulations,
