so that the written language
showed no irregularities.
As for the histories of Jìn and Chǔ,
which used Shèng and Táowù as their titles—
was this due to the decline of Zhōu and loss of official functions,
allowing the states to act on their own?
Sīmǎ Qiān, in his Hereditary Houses of the feudal states,
preserved the principle of each state having its own history,
and in his chapter on Emperor Wǔ’s Three Kings,
he recorded imperial edicts in detail,
placing them at the beginning.
The king’s words, like fine silk threads,
were valued by historians—
this has its origins.
Later local gazetteers
were compiled without proper order,
lacking essential principles,
and imperial edicts and proclamations
were sometimes placed in the arts and literature section,
or mentioned in the introductory chronicle,
or included in the historical evolution section.
Moreover, some remote prefectures and counties
never received special imperial pronouncements,
so that the court’s historical precedents
scattered in local gazetteers
were missing and could not be examined.
This is due to the decline of the compilation tradition
over time;
but also because since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
the specialized office of Outer Historian
has not been recognized.
In the feudal era,
each state had its own history,
yet the beginning still emphasized the king’s calendar.
Under the commandery-county system,
prefects and magistrates received and implemented imperial edicts,
just like the district and village administration within the royal domain in antiquity;
yet the historical precedents of the Outer Historian
were never established as a separate category.
The Sòng, Yuán, and Míng dynasty prefectural and county gazetteers
that survive today
all follow the same pattern—
how greatly they neglect the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals!
Now I gather all that exists in the prefecture,
and respectfully compile it into one Imperial Edicts Chronicle,
arranged chronologically,
placed gloriously at the beginning,
to record the source of our reverent reception.
Preface and Principles for the Officials Table of the Hézhōu Gazetteer
The Rites of Zhōu states
that the Censor “assists in recording and
enumerates those in government service.”
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary says, “This includes both those currently serving and vacant positions.”
This was to assist the Grand Steward in establishing the six codes and overseeing the state’s governance precedents.
Officials have seniority,
administrations have successes and failures;
the Grand Steward preserved the framework,
and the Censor enumerated the individuals to assist him,
so all officials were ordered and achievements flourished.
Later works on official ceremonies,
and regulations for examination and selection—Hàn Official Ceremonies, Táng Six Codes, Liáng Selection Register, Suí Official Records—
were produced in each era,
but the names and titles of officials
were too numerous to record comprehensively;
this meant having the Grand Steward’s framework
but lacking the Censor’s enumeration of those in service.
Bān Gù’s Table of Hundred Officials and Ministers
still preserved the ancient intent:
the beginning describes the offices,
which is the legacy of the Grand Steward’s six codes;
the later table listing officials’ names
is the legacy of the Censor’s enumeration.
After Fàn Yè and Chén Shòu,
this tradition faded.
As for the Táng History and Sòng History,
they have Yearly Tables of Chief Ministers,
but lack the capacity to cover all ministers and officials;
not only were the historians’ considerations incomplete,
but also historical records became voluminous,
making it difficult to cover everything comprehensively.
As for scholars with a passion for antiquity,
they compiled lists of officials,
connected names,
and wrote books on official positions and historical precedents.
Since the Six Dynasties,
such works have flourished.
However, records of the central court's precedents
did not extend to regional administrations,
and trivial compilations
could hardly be included in historical annals;
this was due to a lack of proper methods in recording,
and disorganized compilation,
for which earlier historians cannot escape blame.
The various officials and ministers
were recorded by the central court;
regional governors and magistrates
were documented by local historians.
The "Zhōu Guān" states that the royal historian counted officials in service,
so the records of the four regions under the charge of local historians
were not limited to mountains, rivers, and local customs;
all matters of official duties and responsibilities
must have been recorded in books
and stored in the archives,
as can be inferred.
Tang dynasty literary collections
often included records of names inscribed on office walls,
which also followed the idea of listing officials.
However, while the texts survive, the names cannot be verified.
Unless one searches through metal and stone inscriptions,
examines steles and tablets in detail,
it is impossible to know them,
which is because they were never compiled into dedicated books.
From the Song and Yuan dynasties onward,
up to recent times, regional records
often noted the names of officeholders;
but they were trivial and lacking in literary refinement,
like reviewing a county magistrate's roster of clerks,
and did not follow the method of arranging by year and month as in Bān Gù's history.
Some compiled them into tables,
but the prefaces and records were not detailed,
and official ranks were not in order;
some were limited by space,
so when there were many official ranks,
or changes in systems,
they would separate civil and military officials,
or record prefectures and counties separately,
for the sake of simplicity.
This shows a lack of understanding of Bān Gù's method of dividing thirty-four offices
into fourteen grades.
Moreover, the surnames and names of earlier people
could not be fully known,
yet surviving records exist,
and other accounts provide mutual references.
Without broadly collecting and searching,
and merely relying on the principle of leaving gaps for missing information,
this cannot be considered an achievement in studying antiquity.
Now, synthesizing various schools,
examining and arranging them chronologically,
starting from the Hàn dynasty,
up to the present,
I compile them into a single table,
leaving gaps for doubtful cases.
May later readers
examine it in detail.
Hézhōu Zhì, Preface and Examples for the Table of Officials
In the "Zhōu Guān,"
the village chief "every three years conducted a grand review,
selected the worthy and capable of the village,
and presented a document to the king.
The king bowed twice to receive it,
and stored it in the imperial archives,"
a grand ceremony indeed.
Under the Hàn system,
the recommendations of Filial and Incorrupt, Eminent Talent, Diligent Farmer, and Worthy and Good
followed the ancient tradition of village and community selection.
At that time, records of worthy individuals and classics,
precedents of recruitment,
were not compiled into dedicated books;
because regulations were numerous,
and the rise and fall of talented people
were scattered in annals and biographies;
scholars who delved deeply
could examine and learn from them.
During the Six Dynasties south of the Yangtze,
prefectures and counties were relocated,
scholars were not settled,
learning was not specialized,
and village recommendations and local selections
gradually became difficult to implement.
By the Suí dynasty,
solely based on literary and poetic talent,
the imperial examination system was created.
Since the Táng dynasty,
this flourished greatly.
As selection became specialized,
qualifications became more important,
regulations grew detailed and complex,
and precedents were passed down.
Thus, literary scholars
collected statutes and regulations,
gathered hearsay and observations,
recording both major and minor matters,
and compiled them into books.
Biographies and historical accounts,
mixed with anecdotes and humor,
made books on selection
as abundant as those stored in the archives.
As writings proliferated,
their organization and principles
were not uniform.
Examining their purposes,
they can be roughly divided into three categories:
Works like Cháo Jiǒng's "Imperial Examination Regulations"
and Lù Shēn's "Examination Hall Regulations"
are books of laws and regulations;
Yáo Kāng and Lè Shǐ's "Records of Examination Success" (Yáo Kāng in 16 volumes, Lè Shǐ in 10 volumes),
Lǐ Yì and Hóng Kuò's "Registers of Successful Candidates" (Lǐ Yì in 2 volumes, lost; Hóng Kuò in 15 volumes),
are records of names and biographies;
Wáng Dìngbǎo's "Táng Gathering Tales,"
Qián Míngyì's "Splendid Affairs of Sòng Officialdom,"
are miscellaneous anecdotal records.
Historians collected precedents,
compiled them into historical treatises,
selected personnel matters,
and arranged them into biographies;
given the vastness of an era,
and strict principles of compilation,
the leftover materials
were like discarded soil or fruit pits.
Yet trivial old compilations,
miscellaneous records lacking refinement,
short notes and brief writings,
could not be transmitted widely or endure;
thus, the top candidates and talented individuals,
whom the "Zhōu Guān" described as being presented to the king and stored in the archives,
were incompletely recorded.
This is why regional records
did not follow the village chief's system of carefully documenting worthy individuals,
resulting in disorganized records
and unclear principles.
In recent times, some have compiled regional studies,
such as Lè Shǐ's "Jiāngnán Records of Examination Success,"
Zhāng Cháoruì's "Southern Worthy Records,"
and Chén Rǔyuán's "Míng Dynasty Zhèjiāng Examination Success Study,"
which gathered regional precedents,
but unfortunately were not circulated nationwide.
As for prefectural and county records,
they compiled examination categories,
listed successful candidates and tribute scholars in tables,
a practice that has existed since the Míng dynasty,
and compared to Sòng and Yuán regional records,
can be said to have their strengths.
However, their formats were not pure,
and their records were disorganized;
not following the method of arranging by year and event (some used tables, but entries for successful candidates, appointed clerks, and hereditary titles often conflicted),
they became messy compilations;
some even appended biographical details,
blurring the line between tables and biographies,
a practice that became customary,
with too many errors to list in detail (discussed in the general remarks of the first biography in the "Discussions on Poetry").
Now, drawing from historical records,
I first detail the systems,
then list the names,
arranged chronologically,
starting from the Táng dynasty,
up to the present,
to create the "Table of Successful Candidates."
Hereditary titles, appointments, and recommendations
that cannot be arranged by year
are appended at the end.
Hézhōu Zhì, Preface and Examples for the Table of Clans, Part 1
The "Offices of Zhōu" states,
the minor historian "establishes the genealogies and
distinguishes the order of generations."
The management of genealogical records
had dedicated officials in antiquity.
Sīmǎ Qiān, using the "Genealogies of the Five Emperors" and the generational records collected in the "Shàngshū,"
compiled the "Genealogical Table of the Three Dynasties."
The origins of clans and lineages
thus have a long history.
From Bān Gù onward,
genealogical records were no longer included.
However, Wáng Fú's chapter on "Clans and Surnames" (the thirty-fifth chapter of "Qiánfū Lùn")
and Dù Yù's "Genealogy of Generational Clans" (the second chapter of "Explanations of the Spring and Autumn Annals")
demonstrate that in studying the classics and composing treatises,
they possessed distinct expertise,
exhausting the meaning and stopping there,
without further pursuing genealogical studies.
From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onward,
through the Six Dynasties,
the prestige of clans gradually rose.
Scholars and officials
often followed the legacy of the Grand Historian's hereditary houses,
compiling their own family biographies.
The variations in their titles,
such as "Wáng Sù's Family Biography," Yú Lǎn's "Family Records," Fàn Wāng's "Generational Biographies," Míng Càn's "Generational Records," Lù Xǔ's "Family History" (in fifteen volumes), and the like,
were all, apart from genealogical records,
compiled into dedicated books,
awaiting collection and recording.

As for works like Zhì Yú's "Record of Generational Order," Wáng Jiǎn's "Register of a Hundred Families," as well as Hé's "Garden of Surnames," Jiǎ's "Essential Forms" (Jiǎ Xījiàn's "Essential Forms of Clans and Lineages" in fifteen volumes), and other compilations,
they aggregated various lineages,
organizing and classifying them.
The superior ones could supplement historical records,
while the inferior might degenerate into encyclopedias.
The distinctions among them are vast,
and they must be discerned.
As clan affiliations became stricter,
the prestige of commandery origins grew more significant.
For instance, the Liú clan of Pèiguó,
the Lǐ clan of Lǒngxī,
the Wáng clan of Tàiyuán,
and the Xiè clan of Chénjùn,
though their descendants scattered,
or they did not originally reside together,
when discussing clan prestige,
they always traced back to their origins.
When the Later Wèi dynasty moved its capital to Luòyáng,
there were eight clans, ten surnames, thirty-six lineages, and ninety-two surnames,
all residing in Hénán and Luòyáng.
Meanwhile, the gentry of the Central Plains
each ranked their family status,
categorizing them into great surnames of the realm, provincial surnames, commandery surnames, and county surnames,
and compiled genealogical records.
Between the Qí and Liáng dynasties,
this practice flourished even more,
with commandery genealogies and provincial records
all compiled into dedicated books.

For example, the works recorded by Wáng Jiǎn and Wáng Sēngrú (Wáng Jiǎn's "Genealogies of Various Provinces" in twelve volumes; Wáng Sēngrú's "Genealogies of Eighteen Provinces" in seven hundred volumes),
and works like "Clans and Lineages of Jìzhōu" and "Extracts from Yángzhōu Genealogies,"
are too numerous to record,
all linking clans to their provincial or commandery origins.
Táng dynasty historian Liú Zhījī, in discussing historical records,
argued that genealogical books
should indeed be included in history.
Later, Ōuyáng Xiū's "History of the Táng Dynasty"
compiled the "Genealogical Tables of Chancellors";
however, distinguished and prominent clans
that did not produce chancellors
were sometimes omitted.
By the time of Zhèng Qiáo's "General History,"
he first composed the "Brief on Clans and Lineages."
In his introductory remarks,
he elucidated the importance of genealogical studies,
tracing the reasons why historiography lacked proper transmission,
and expressed profound sentiments on the matter.
Yet later historians,
not following his method,
left this as a gap in historical records.
In antiquity,
blind musicians recited poetry
and also recited genealogies
to admonish and advise rulers.
As stated in the "Discourses of the States": "Teach them their lineage,
so as to make their virtuous deeds illustrious."
This is indeed the case.
Thus, the establishment of genealogies,
managed by minor historians
and recited by blind musicians,
was valued by the ancient kings;
it was to honor human relations and trace origins.
At that time, the leaders of districts, neighborhoods, clans, and associations
gathered the people to read the laws;
the district grand masters, during the triennial great review,
examined virtue and skills and presented records to the king;
thus, their genealogical records
must have been compiled in fixed numbers,
collected and submitted to the minor historians,
as can be inferred.
Where there are people, there are families;
where there are families, there is a state;
where there is a state, there is the realm.
If family genealogies are not maintained,
then on what basis can the state's historical records
be verified and trusted?
The "Book of Changes" states:
"Heaven and fire form the image of Fellowship.
The superior man distinguishes things by grouping them according to their kinds."
Among all things,
none is greater than humanity.
Within humanity,
nothing is more important than clans.
Some historical records
even include insects and fish;
geographical works
necessarily document local products;
yet regarding the ancient kings' granting of lands and distinguishing surnames,
which emphasized human relations and clarified ethical order,
there is a lack of records,
which does not elucidate the principle of great unity.
Moreover, genealogical books,
kept within families,
are easily scattered and lost;
if fully incorporated into state history,
there is fear of excessive volume;
thus, local gazetteers,
compiled and verified,
can summarize the records of various families
and serve as essential extracts for state history,
which is also a task that historians must understand and undertake.
Preface and Guidelines to the Clan Tables of the Hézhōu Gazetteer.
The responsibility for establishing genealogical records lies with the minor historian,
just as the responsibility for population records lies with the minister of education;
their principles are the same.
Dù Zǐchūn said:
"Establishing genealogical records refers to the imperial lineage, the genealogies of feudal lords, ministers, and grandees, and the like."
Thus, it is evident that
the genealogical registers of the common people,
organized in groups of five households,
are not under the jurisdiction of the minor historian.
The district grandee annually records the number of households and individuals,
and every three years, through a great review, promotes the worthy and capable in the district.
The number of households and individuals
corresponds to the population records reported to the grand minister of education,
and the worthy and capable are selected for positions as ministers and grandees,
which is also evident.
The common people are of low status,
so only the numbers of households and individuals are recorded;
ministers and grandees are of high status,
so their genealogical records are detailed—this is the natural order of things.
In later historical records,
population figures are recorded in detail,
but the compilation of genealogies is unheard of,
which means there are records of common people but not of ministers and grandees.
The *Book of Documents* says:
"When the nine clans are harmonious,
the hundred surnames are distinguished and made illustrious."
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states:
"The hundred surnames
refer to the fathers, sons, and brothers of the officials."
See the commentary in Sīmǎ Qiān's "Annals of the Five Emperors." "Distinguished and made illustrious"
means to differentiate and clarify them,
which is the origin of the minor historian's responsibility to establish genealogies in the *Rites of Zhōu*.
Mèngzǐ said:
"What is meant by an old state
is not that it has tall trees,
but that it has ministers whose families have served for generations."
In recent times, local gazetteers
linger over ancient sites
and attach undue importance to native places;
as for genealogical records,
they are omitted and not discussed,
which means valuing tall trees over families of long-standing service.
Moreover, if state histories do not record them
and local gazetteers do not include them,
and the method of compiling genealogies
is not managed by the government,
then each family will compile its own records,
and each person will offer their own interpretations.
Descendants may overpraise their ancestors,
and judgments may deviate significantly from state histories.
Among the unworthy,
some may falsely claim descent from sages,
or privately sell clan genealogies,
mixing falsehood with truth,
leading to absurdities and confusion
beyond description.
Among distinguished families of noble descent,
they boast of their lineage
and privately adopt prestigious names.
For example, families like Wáng and Xiè south of the Yangtze,
as long as they held official titles or honors,
were listed in biographies,
leaving historians at a loss,
unable to make judgments.
Thus, Lǐs are invariably from Lǒngxī,
Liús from Pèiguó,
seeking only prestige and reputation,
without inquiring into their origins.
In such cases, having genealogies
is worse than having none.
The omissions in historical records
are also the fault of earlier generations.
If provinces and prefectures oversee districts and counties,
districts and counties oversee prominent families,
and prominent families lead the common people,
then the great affairs of the state
can be managed with ease.
In the three hundred years of the Táng dynasty, genealogies
only recorded chancellors,
due to the overwhelming volume of records
and the lack of a better method.
Local gazetteers,
recording those who passed the imperial examinations or held office,
follow the practice of the Zhōu district grandees in recording the worthy and capable.
Now, following the spirit of the *Rites of Zhōu*,
I specifically highlight clan lineages,
which offers ten advantages.
First, the authority of history is not dispersed;
private records
can be evaluated against an official standard,
which is the first advantage.
Second, genealogical methods are standardized;
private genealogies often lack consistent rules,
which can be referenced and improved,
which is the second advantage.
Third, the pure and impure are distinguished;
those not of the lineage
cannot falsely claim descent,
ensuring clear social distinctions,
which is the third advantage.
Fourth, once registrations are fixed,
selecting scholars through examinations
can be verified by lineage;
those not registered
can be easily identified,
which is the fourth advantage.
Fifth, the order of seniority and closeness of relations
is clearly arranged;
disputes over succession,
such as appointing heirs for deceased worthies
or for families without descendants,
can be easily resolved,
which is the fifth advantage.
Sixth, ancestral lines are clearly defined;
whether families migrated from other regions
or later moved elsewhere,
their generational tables compiled in local gazetteers
can help other districts and counties
where genealogies are lost
to verify information,
which is the sixth advantage.
Seventh, changes in surnames
and the reasons for such changes
are clearly recorded,
helping to distinguish marital connections;
moreover, those studying genealogy
can trace their origins,
which is the seventh advantage.
Eighth, for families with continuous lineages,
especially prominent and noble ones,
if members passed examinations or held office
but their genealogies are recorded
while their virtues and achievements
are not included in biographies,
they remain unrecognized after death,
which is a disgrace to scholars;
thus, without altering the text,
the principle of encouraging virtue and discouraging vice is upheld,
which is the eighth advantage.
Ninth, the importance of regional prestige is emphasized;
landmarks like arches and neighborhoods
are not merely decorative,
which is the ninth advantage.
Tenth, for collecting documents and examining records,
when archives and libraries request materials,
they can be easily found by consulting the gazetteer,
as easily as pointing to one's palm,
which is the tenth advantage.
Thus, by compiling and clarifying these,
the practice can be extended to all prefectures, districts, and counties,
not limited to a single district's gazetteer.
Hézhōu Gazetteer, Clan Tables, Introduction and Examples, Part Two
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Things cannot be exhausted,
therefore it is followed by *Wèi Jì* (Incomplete)."
Gathering scattered and lost records
presupposes that there are scattered and lost records
to be gathered.
Highlighting what is hidden or obscure
presupposes that there are hidden or obscure things
to be highlighted.
Chén Shòu's "History of Shǔ" concludes its biographies
with Yáng Xì's eulogies;
Cháng Qú's "Huáyáng Gazetteer"
generally preserves the names of notable men and women.
These two understood that historical records are sometimes incomplete,
so they used eulogies and prefaces to record names,
preserving the general outline
and clearly stating the necessity of preserving only what remains.
This follows the old tradition of historians leaving gaps when information is lacking.
Hézhōu was a prominent prefecture during the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
but evidence of its cultural heritage
is scarce.
As for family genealogies and lineage records,
very few are known.
Inquiring of the elders,
they say that during the turmoil of the Yǐhài year in the late Míng dynasty,
documents were destroyed in the war.
The current residents of the prefecture
are the great- or great-great-grandchildren of those who barely survived.
What is heard and passed down
extends only five or seven generations at most,
with no ability to trace further back.
Since the generations are not distant,
and descendants are not numerous,
genealogical practices are largely neglected.
Examining what remains,
they consist of private notes and memoranda,
lacking standardized formats,
and are difficult to use as authoritative sources.
Some cannot even trace the origins of their surnames.
I sigh deeply over this.
As for family genealogies, their volumes are
lighter than prefectural gazetteers;
after the ravages of war,
family genealogies were not preserved.
Yet the prefectural gazetteers compiled by Prefect Yì Luán during the Jiājìng era of the Ming dynasty and by Prefect Kāng Gào during the Wànlì era,
being of even older times,
are still fully extant today;
this is clear evidence that official records are easily preserved,
while private households struggle to maintain them.
If we do not urgently take measures now,
then even these modest works
will later have nothing to rely upon for verification.
Moreover, I observe in the "Tables of the Hereditary Houses of Chancellors" in the *History of the Tang*,
which list their ancestors,
some reach back to the Liáng and Chén dynasties,
and some to the Northern Wèi and Later Zhōu,
but they do not further trace back through successive generations;
thus, gaps in the genealogical records
are not the result of a single day or night.
Therefore, recording what can be verified
and omitting what cannot be known
avoids the reproach of writing without knowledge.
For each surname, tracing its origins
provides material for investigating antiquity.
Detailing the generations of registration
establishes the prefectural summary.
Taking imperial degrees and official positions as headings,
with tribute students, imperial college students, and those granted honorary titles,
as well as those who purchased empty ranks, all included,
follows their categories.
For those without imperial degrees or official positions,
but only with student status or purchased empty ranks,
no separate table is created,
determining the balance between primary and secondary, heavy and light.
For clans with imperial degrees and official positions,
their collateral branches, being commoners,
are recorded only up to the branching individuals.
Not listing their sons or grandsons further
is because the influence of a gentleman
lasts only five generations.
If all were listed,
it would be no different from household registers.
Even with imperial degrees and official positions,
those without genealogies are omitted,
strictly guarding against errors and excesses.
Regular tribute students are also considered as having imperial degrees,
minor ranks are also considered as official positions,
without further distinguishing their grades,
due to the lack of documentary evidence.
Rather than err by omission,
it is better to err by inclusion;
this is the principle of *Wèijì* (the hexagram of Incompletion).
Preface and Guidelines for the Maps of Hézhōu Gazetteer
The study of charts and illustrations
had its own specialized tradition in antiquity,
as Zhèng Qiáo discussed in detail.
When Sīmǎ Qiān wrote history,
he only adopted the legacy of horizontal and diagonal tables,
creating ten tables;
but did not adopt the practice of displaying laws on gate towers,
to create various maps.
Thus, later historians followed suit,
tables and treatises multiplied,
while illustrated classics gradually disappeared.
Antiquarian scholars,
examining ancient texts,
recite the words orally,
yet are confused by the images,
which is a common flaw in historical writing,
a missing canon in literature.
Zhèng Qiáo, born a thousand years later,
earnestly aspired to the legacy of the Three Dynasties,
and in his chapter "Charts and Illustrations,"
clarified their utility;
he also traced the reasons later generations lost their basis,
attributing it to Bān Gù including books but omitting maps,
and expressed this with deep feeling.
However, Zhèng's intention
was only that cataloguers
did not establish a separate category for charts and illustrations,
so he wished to create a separate catalogue
to supplement the shortcomings of the *Seven Summaries* and Four Categories.
In fact, he did not deeply investigate;
the loss of cartographic learning
was due to Sīmǎ Qiān having tables but no maps,
thus causing later historians
not to know to collect and record them;
therefore, even in his own *Comprehensive Records*, with annals, biographies, genealogies, and summaries,
though various forms were complete,
for topography and notable figures,
he also did not create maps.
With this, to criticize Bān Gù,
is this not the so-called "Chǔ was wrong,
but Qí was not right either"?
The use of charts and illustrations
complements each other with tables.
The Zhōu genealogies have long been lost,
yet the generational sequences of the Three Dynasties,
and the years and months of the feudal lords,
can still be examined today,
because Sīmǎ Qiān collected them to make tables.
Since the collections of laws on gate towers were lost,
the forms, names, and institutions,
the square, round, straight, and curved,
cannot be known today,
because Sīmǎ Qiān did not include them as maps.
Thus, the preservation or loss of writings
depends on the historian's pen,
is clear.
As for ancient maps,
let us not discuss them in detail.
Since the *Plans of the Three Capital Regions* and *Plans of the Luòyáng Palaces*,
records of capitals and cities
have been compiled in every era,
yet later collections
preserve not one in a hundred.
Zhèng alone showed originality,
establishing a separate catalogue,
believing that if something is raised up,
it will not be neglected.
However, examining what Zhèng collected today,
their loss and dispersal
compared to earlier compilations
is not fundamentally different;
thus, the preservation or loss of writings
depends even more on the historian's pen,
while dependence on cataloguing categories is less significant,
which is also clear.
Even minor items like wine vessels,
may rely on broad knowledge,
and things like imperial processional guards,
may display majestic ceremonies;
earlier people had both illustrations and texts,
which were indeed abundant.
Historians recognized their essential points,
but lacked time to fully incorporate them;
Zhèng listed them in a separate catalogue,
so that they could be consulted;
one need only seek the original works.
As for the topography of regions and prefectures,
matters of great importance to the realm,
if not included as a separate section among tables and treatises,
then readers of such works
would be like walking in darkness and groping,
how can that be acceptable?
Those who study the *Yì* must understand its images,
those who study the *Spring and Autumn Annals* must master its genealogies;
images and charts, genealogies and records,
are the great foundations of the *Yì* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
The *Yì* says:
"Appended statements to exhaust the words."
The *Record* says:
"Comparing events and connecting statements,
is the teaching of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*."
Calling them appended and connected statements
clarifies that the literary expressions follow from them.
Thus, images and charts are history without words,
genealogies and records are books without text;
they complement each other,
and one cannot be omitted.
How much more so for prefectural and commandery maps and classics,
which were especially valued by earlier people?
Some say:
Scholars also know that the use of images and maps is great.
However, texts can be transmitted and studied,
while maps cannot be recited or read aloud.
Thus, even though the books remain intact,
the maps cannot be examined.
This is the inevitable situation.
Nevertheless,
this is not a perceptive statement.
If maps cannot be recited,
then tables also lack literary expressions.
Tables are recorded in histories,
while maps are not included in compilations.
This is why they are lost.
Moreover, there are two reasons why maps cannot be transmitted:
First, they compete in the skill of painting.
The ancients specialized in artistic endeavors,
establishing themselves as masters,
but these were not truly aligned with the great classics and principles.
For example, Guō Pú's "Illustrated Eulogies to the Classic of Mountains and Seas,"
the eulogies survive, but the illustrations are lost.
Now, examining the eulogies,
they resemble the craftsmanship of carving dragons,
so we know that the illustrations
were likely just the skill of painting tigers.
Second, they are treated as trivial as hairpins and caps.
In recent times, local gazetteers
include illustrations and maps,
placed between prefaces and examples,
without establishing a specialized category.
They merely append famous sites,
serving as decorative markers for a book,
but they do not align with the ancient study of maps and charts.
Competing in painting skills
means art is irrelevant to historical judgment;
and treating them as trivial as hairpins and caps
means bookshops hastily create labels,
using them as a means for trade.
Neither can be spoken of in terms of the profundity of historiography.
The ancients had specialized studies,
and thus specialized books;
with specialized books,
came specialized formats.
Horizontal and diagonal lines,
with annotations branching off,
are the format of genealogical charts.
Calculating distances in squares,
mapping mountains and rivers,
are the format of geographical maps.
When maps are not detailed, they are supplemented with explanations;
when explanations are unclear, they are substantiated with maps.
This is the principle of mutual reinforcement.
Texts are concise yet nothing is obscured;
forms are clear and words have their place.
This is the rule for writing.
Errors like "亥" and "豕" cannot confuse their transmission;
editing cannot damage their essence.
This is a long-lasting endeavor.
The goal is that even those who have not visited the place
or are not deeply versed in literature
can consult the maps
and see as clearly as observing fire.
This is also the way of broad understanding.
With maps of celestial officials and river channels,
the "Eight Treatises" could be reduced to six;
with maps of geography and irrigation canals,
the "Ten Treatises" could be reduced to eight.
Yet today, seeking the celestial phenomena of the Tàichū era
or verifying the territories of the Western Hàn,
might not be so utterly obscure.
Moreover, local gazetteers,
which verify names and distinguish objects,
should especially be detailed and comprehensive,
approaching the work of a specialized school.
Instead, they linger on scenery,
forcing connections to famous sites,
treating them as mere visual arts.
Is this not neglecting the ancient principle of "left map, right history"?
Maps cannot but be accompanied by explanations,
and detailed explanations
are equivalent to books.
Are the names of maps not then redundant? I say:
They are not redundant.
Formats have their specialties,
and meanings have their emphases.
The ancients had books with specialized names
and chapters with specialized meanings.
The wording's variations were not their concern;
rather, in the relationship between name and reality, host and guest,
the authors sought to capture the essence.
Moreover, I have seen in historical texts
tables that resemble treatises (e.g., the "Table of Officials and Nobles" in the Book of Hàn, which begins with a narrative of official systems),
not necessarily all in horizontal or diagonal lines.
There are treatises that resemble tables (e.g., the "Treatise on Pitch and Calendar" in the Book of Hàn, which arranges the three systems and the sexagenary cycle),
not necessarily all following the example of comparing events and connecting texts.
The "Three Capital Regions Yellow Map,"
now lost,
is quoted in other texts,
and those are its words.
The "Dùnjiǎ Tōngtǒng Map,"
its explanations survive today,
just as "Huá Shǔ" and "Yóu Gēng" have their meanings.
Even a one-foot map
can be accompanied by explanations eight or ten feet long.
Since it is called a map,
it can uniformly be termed a map.
Maps are also arranged by category.
Is this not excessive? I say:
It is not excessive.
The categorization of maps
is like the chapter names in books.
Attaching maps to books
obscures their meaning;
separating maps and accompanying them with explanations
makes the meaning clear.
For example, the "Treatise on Pitch and Calendar" in the current dynasty's History of Míng,
includes illustrations for instruments and calculations,
something unprecedented among earlier scholars.
The historians of that time
did not establish separate maps,
so they did not create a specialized category.
Each matter has its appropriate place.
Now, the local gazetteer divides maps into four categories:
first, geography;
second, establishments;
third, military posts;
fourth, water conservancy.
All are selected for their relevance to key principles
and necessity for understanding shapes and layouts.
Detailed explanations accompany them,
and they are placed after the annals and tables,
to serve as a comprehensive study of one school,
with the examples set forth in the opening section.
Preface and Examples for the Book on Land Taxes in the Hézhōu Gazetteer.
Since the demarcation of territories and establishment of tribute systems,
first created in the Xia documents,
with the allocation of land based on soil quality, appointment of officials, and the duties of the land overseer in managing land affairs and assigning land responsibilities,
detailed in the Rites of Zhōu;
and the records of land taxes,
the specialized administration of such matters,
have had their origins.
Bān Gù condensed the eight governmental affairs from the "Hóng Fàn"
to compile the chapter on "Food and Currency,"
which later historians followed,
establishing it as a standard.
However, the agricultural records and maps,
the accounting ledgers and registers,
piled up in archives,
are too numerous to exhaust;
thus, a selection was made from within each dynasty,
to serve as fixed regulations.
The general principles of continuity and change,
the overall calculations of surplus and deficit,
are briefly preserved in the essential abridgments of historians,
and the memorials of fiscal officials;
so that readers may understand the books on their own,
which is also the natural tendency.
As for the registers of state finances by Lǐ Jífǔ and Wéi Chùhòu (Lǐ Jífǔ's Yuánhé Guójì Bù in ten volumes, Wéi Chùhòu's Tàihé Guójì in twenty volumes),
and the accounting records by Dīng Wèi and Tián Kuàng (Dīng Wèi's Jǐngdé Kuàijì Lù in six volumes, Tián Kuàng's Huángyòu Kuàijì Lù in six volumes),
they followed the system of the Zhōu official Sīkuài's duplicates,
and the regulations of written contracts and maps.
Dù Yòu and Sòng Bái's Tōngdiǎn,
Wáng Pǔ and Zhāng Déxiàng's Huìyào,
are compilations of precedents;
among them, food and currency are given primary importance,
with the aim of comprehensive verification,
covering matters ancient and modern;
down to the minutiae of hemp threads,
the trivialities of small weights,
no further exhaustive details are sought.
Zhào Guò's proposal for equal land distribution,
Lǐ Áo's book on equitable taxation,
are official documents and private discussions,
each expressing their views;
only addressing the immediate benefits and drawbacks,
seeking a balanced compromise,
no longer adhering to the historian's method of recording facts.
The clerks' registers and records,
trivial and lacking literary refinement,
cannot be transmitted through the ages or spread afar;
the literary compilations of precedents,
broadly synthesizing the main points,
cannot deeply discern hidden subtleties;
this is why land taxes are difficult to clarify,
and why comprehensive books on the subject are hard to come by.
In ancient times, fiscal matters,
were levied by the Minister of Education (the land overseer was under the Grand Minister of Education),
and accounted by the Grand Steward (the accountant was under the Grand Steward).
The Grand Steward established thirty years as a cycle for the nine expenditures,
balancing the nine taxes,
from major items like sacrifices and guests,
down to minor ones like fodder and distributions,
all had fixed amounts,
based on what was produced,
measured against what was collected;
even if one wished to take more from the people,
beyond the fixed standards,
there was no way to do so.
This is why fiscal matters value the method of proper accounting.
Since the Táng dynasty changed the zu-yōng-diào system to the two-tax system,
and the Míng dynasty further changed the two-tax system to the single-whip method,
the trend was toward simplicity and convenience,
ensuring no oppressive disturbances,
also assessing the times and weighing the circumstances,
it could be said to have achieved expediency.
However, expenses for retained supplies and provisions,
items like local tribute and regional products,
funds for conscripted or hired transport,
were all combined and paid in full,
convenient for the people,
ensuring no confusion or disturbance.
Official documents,
clerks' registers,
should naturally record the old categories in full,
clearly stating the reasons for consolidation and simplification according to the laws,
then adjusting them according to the current legal standards;
so that the fiscal officials' duties,
and the registered common households,
all clearly understand that the system has changed,
but the amounts have not increased or decreased.
Official correspondence increasingly tends toward simplification,
but archival records over time lack evidence,
only preserving the total combined figures of the time,
without listing the various categories separately,
then when legal restrictions slacken slightly,
officials not adhering to the law,
may add or embellish names,
imposing uniform levies,
claiming it aligns with the ancient principle of proper tribute,
who then can dispute that it is not according to regulation?
Reforming laws is meant to benefit the people,
but officials sometimes exploit the laws for corruption,
the function of documents,
may not be fully preserved,
which is why maps and records serve as the classics for governing the state.
However, the vast complexity of a dynasty,
the records of historians,
cannot fully encompass it;
only local gazetteers of prefectures and counties,
with their limited scope,
can separately list various categories,
leaving no triviality omitted,
thus supplementing what the state histories cannot provide.
Since the Míng dynasty,
records in local gazetteers,
have generally been crude and lacking method;
as for land tax matters,
deeming clerks' registers,
entirely unworthy of grand literary elegance,
they thus based them on current archives,
uniformly compiling them,
no longer investigating past and present,
deeply seeking origins and details;
like a jade cup without a bottom,
who can appreciate its beauty?
The Míng dynasty's single-whip method,
was established in the Jiājìng era,
and the old gazetteer of Hézhōu,
still available for examination today,
also ends with Yì Luán's Prefectural Gazetteer from the mid-Jiājìng era.
At that time, just as the regulations were first changed,
the prefectural gazetteer adopted the new method,
completely eliminating the old provisions,
thus making it impossible to trace the evolution since the Táng dynasty's two-tax system,
a pity!
Moreover, private discussions,
official documents,
related to the benefits and drawbacks of land taxes,
should naturally be incorporated into this book;
like Bān Gù's inclusion of Cháo Cuò's memorial on "Valuing Grain" in the "Treatise on Food and Currency,"
and Jiǎ Ràng's strategy for "Managing the River" in the "Treatise on Canals,"
so that matters are clearly presented,
and learning serves practical use.
Otherwise, include them in the individual's biography,
facilitating cross-referencing and study,
as in the established method of Zhào Chōngguó's discussions on "Military Agricultural Colonies."
Modern gazetteer compilers generally cut off the literary texts,
separately compiling them into a treatise on arts and letters;
while the actual facts of the subject,
and the individual's conduct,
are left barren and lacking material.
How can a gazetteer's headings prominently label specialized topics,
specially marking principles and examples,
accumulating into volumes,
only to hang like a bitter gourd,
looked up to but not eaten?
Kāng Gào's old gazetteer,
glimpsed this approach.
Later writers wielding the brush,
resolutely deleted them,
once and then again,
beyond recovery,
truly lamentable!
Now, before Yì's Gazetteer,
what has been lost,
cannot be recovered;
after Yì's Gazetteer,
the complete beginning and end is recorded,
compiled into a book.
Kāng Gào's discussion on "Equal Land Distribution,"
truly pertains to the benefits and drawbacks of land taxes;
others like documents in the prefecture related to land taxes,
are all collected and recorded,
placed after the various provisions;
some may also be included in biographies,
mutually illuminating,
doubts left unaddressed.
Future readers,
may find value in this.
Hézhōu Gazetteer: Preface and Examples to the Treatise on Arts and Letters
The Book of Changes states:
"In ancient times, governance was achieved through knotted cords.
Later, sages replaced them with written records,
so that officials could govern,
and the myriad people could be examined."
The origin of writing
was what the ancients used as a method of governance.
During the flourishing eras of the Three Dynasties,
laws were recorded in writing,
and writing was preserved by officials.
All the arts and professions of the world
originated from the precedents held by official teachers.
Here, the Way and skills were harmonized,
and virtue and conduct were understood.
This is why the world was governed through a unified script.
The six chapters of the Zhou Guan
are all records of how the ancients preserved official duties and upheld the methods of teachers.
What was not preserved by official teachers and professions
was considered unlawful.
Even when Confucius spoke of rituals,
he necessarily consulted the archives stored under the pillars.
After the Three Dynasties,
writing was no longer subordinate to official duties,
leading to a division between
the regulations of the government and
the studies of teachers and scholars.
This resulted in
each person writing their own books
and each family promoting their own theories.
Thus, writings overflowed beyond the precedents of the hundred offices.
Once books were scattered across the world,
with no unifying authority,
methods of cataloging and classification
emerged to manage them,
a situation that inevitably arose.
However, since the advent of cataloging,
scholars have regarded it merely as record-keeping,
rarely seeking to explore how unified writing served governance
or to preserve the legacy of the six codes and official duties.
Only the works of Liú Xiàng and Liú Xīn, such as the Qī Lüè and Bié Lù, achieved this.
Thus, when they categorized the nine schools
and arranged the various masters,
they always stated that each originated from the duties of a certain ancient office,
how it evolved into a particular school of thought,
and how it degenerated into certain flaws.
They elucidated thoroughly,
leaving nothing unaddressed.
If scholars could trace the flow back to its source,
even minor arts and trivial techniques,
biased words and heretical doctrines,
could be returned and connected to the great Way.
And those who study these theories
could also discern the extent of their own efforts.
If there is something to uphold,
it will not drift away;
if there is a direction to follow,
it will not go astray.
Speech and writing
would all return to their proper duties,
the methods of teachers could be restored,
and ancient learning could flourish.
Would this not be magnificent?
Hán Yù said:
"Distinguishing the authenticity of ancient books
is as clear as separating black from white."
Mencius said:
"With biased words, know what they obscure;
with excessive words, know where they sink;
with heretical words, know where they deviate;
with evasive words, know where they are exhausted."
Confucius said:
"Listen widely,
and choose the good to follow."
To distinguish the authenticity of ancient books,
to approach understanding words,
and to listen widely and choose the good,
one must deeply understand the duties of officials and teachers,
then fully grasp the origins of various schools,
and ultimately recognize the flaws of later developments.
Thus, the cataloging by the Liú family
serves as a crucial link for the continuation of scholarship.
Without understanding the duties of officials and teachers,
one cannot elucidate the origins of various schools,
and thus will not recognize the flaws of later developments.
Then, the scholarship of the world
will have no guiding authority.
"Giving rise to misguided thoughts and policies,
enacting harmful governance and causing trouble"—
Mencius spoke of this
with absolute certainty.
Yet, superficial scholars
still flaunt their broad and comprehensive talents;
those engaged in obscure inquiries
still pride themselves on their narrow views.
They think that mere cataloging
and textual collation
can benefit literary endeavors. Alas!
How mistaken they are.
When the Six Codes were lost and replaced by the Seven Summaries,
it was because officials had lost their charge.
When the Seven Summaries were lost and replaced by the Four Categories,
it was because masters had lost their transmission.
The records of the Zhōuguān were abundant;
the Bǎozhāng handled astronomy,
the Zhífāng handled geography,
the Yúhéng managed natural resources,
the Wūzhù communicated with spirits,
each holding established texts to promulgate governance methods,
and each mastering their profession to transmit learning and techniques,
not only the Six Arts—the texts of the Shī and Shū—as referred to by the Shīshì and Bǎoshì.
When the Sikōng chapter was lost,
Liú Xīn took the Kǎogōng Jì to supplement it.
It was not a supplementation;
the Kǎogōng should have been an official subordinate of the Sikōng,
and its so-called record
was precisely the canonical texts of the Winter Office;
just as the seventeen chapters of the Yílǐ
were the canonical texts of the Spring Office;
the one hundred and fifty chapters of the Sīmǎ Fǎ
were the canonical texts of the Summer Office,
all fortunately transmitted to later ages.
At that time, the canonical texts were fully preserved,
and the three hundred and sixty chapters
were arranged according to official ranks,
so how could writings become scattered?
After the decline of the Zhōu,
the official system ceased to function,
and books were scattered and lost,
with only one-tenth
remaining out of a thousand or a hundred.
With only this one-tenth preserved,
and attempting to restore the arrangement of the three hundred and sixty chapters,
would result in either forced or incomplete classification,
making it difficult to implement,

已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不得已不
