I have heard of using classification to organize books,
but never of letting books disrupt classification.
In the early Han dynasty, the various schools of thought and hundred schools
were vast and lacked systematic organization,
and the essence of the official "Rites" was lost.
Liú Xiàng and his son inherited the shortcomings of the Western Han,
yet were able to investigate the ancient principle of the unity of officials and teachers,
establishing a systematic framework
to trace its origins,
thus their organization was indeed meticulous.
During the Wèi and Jìn periods,
literary collections and encyclopedic compilations

lacked any systematic structure (Emperor Wén of Wèi compiled the writings of Xú, Chén, Yīng, and Liú into a single collection, marking the beginning of collections; Zhì Yú composed the "Wénzhāng Liúbié Jí," also a beginning of collections; Emperor Wén of Wèi created the "Huánglǎn," marking the beginning of encyclopedic compilations),
and the tradition of specialized transmission declined.
Scholars like Xún and Lǐ (Xún Xù, Lǐ Chōng)
failed to investigate the origins and development of the "Seven Summaries";
as for scholars like Wáng and Ruǎn (Wáng Jiǎn, Ruǎn Xiàoxù),
they strayed even further.
Subsequently, works on techniques and military strategy
were merged into the Masters category,
while literary collections became a separate specialty,
and encyclopedic compilations were classified under the various schools of thought.

The Táng dynasty's Four Categories system (the Four Categories originated with Xún Xù, but its structure differed from later Four Categories systems, hence it is said to have begun in the Táng dynasty)
became the unchanging standard for later cataloging,
yet the world of scholarship
grew increasingly chaotic and lost all discipline.
The "Seven Summaries" inherited the flaws of the Six Canons
but understood to preserve their legacy;
the Four Categories inherited the flaws of the "Seven Summaries"
but failed to preserve its legacy.
Thus, the "Seven Summaries" could use classification to organize books,
while the Four Categories inevitably let books disrupt classification.
Moreover, the Four Categories' excuse for not restoring the "Seven Summaries" is twofold:
First, the abundance of historical works
cannot be subsumed under the "Spring and Autumn" school.
Organizing the Twenty-One Histories
is not difficult;
however, works on official duties and precedents,
genealogies and biographies,
may originate from official rites and institutions,
or involve Confucian or eclectic teachings,
and are not necessarily all historical in form.
Now, to encompass all these forms
and rigidly classify them as History
results in ritual manuals being separated from the Classics of Rites,
official duties disconnected from the Six Canons,
proclamations and edicts isolated from the "Shūjīng,"
and historical criticism diverging from the various schools of thought (historical criticism is a legacy of the various schools; placing it in the History category is incorrect).
To distort the original intent of ancient writings and disrupt established classification for the sake of simplicity—
how can this be acceptable?
Second, literary collections proliferate daily,
and without a dedicated category,
they lack systematic organization.
The various schools of thought and hundred schools
did not originate from official duties,
yet Liú Xiàng and his son traced them to official lineages;
then literary collections, though not part of the various schools,
why cannot cataloging principles
apply the discernment used for the various schools to organize them?
Though the forms of collections are complex,
one must first identify the authors.
A person's disposition inevitably leans toward certain tendencies;
grasping their fundamental disposition and interests,
then the themes expressed in their poetry and rhapsodies,
the analogies cited in their discourses,
the traditions revered in their narratives—
capturing the main ideas,
omitting the trivial details,
one can discern what the ancients called a "distinctive school of thought."
Within categories like Confucianism, Mohism, Dialecticians, and Legalism,
there must be those whose lineage can be identified (e.g., Hán Yù as Confucian, Liǔ Zōngyuán as Dialectician, Sū Shì as Political Strategist, Wáng Ānshí as Ritualist).
Preserving the original titles of their collections,
discussing the origins of their lineage,
appending their catalog to the classification system of Liú Xiàng and his son,
and distinguishing between what aligns and what does not,
to provide guidance for later scholars—
then random, unfounded words will have no place to cling,
and the flaws of literary collections
may gradually diminish.
Perhaps then words will have substance and actions constancy,
allowing us to move from the specialized approach of the "Seven Summaries"
to glimpse the legacy of the Six Canons?
Once specialized traditions are established,
the rootless and eclectic,
such as categorized excerpts and selected critiques,
can be managed without much effort.
Thus, the principles of cataloging
are connected to educational methods;
how can one lightly speak of compilation
merely in terms of numerical categories and headings?
But if scholars do not first glimpse the purity of heaven and earth,
understand the grand principles of the ancients,
and hastily seek to classify various writings,
distinguish and clarify lineages,
they will hope for even a single correct statement and find it unattainable.
Therefore, those engaged in cataloging
prefer to speak of the Four Categories
and dread hearing of the "Seven Summaries."
The method of categorizing and classifying that historians speak of,
was fully developed by Bān Gù,
but was actually modeled after Sīmǎ Qiān.
Sīmǎ Qiān did not establish a complete method,
and Bān Gù inherited Liú Xīn's scholarship but not its essence.
Thus, to speak of the subtleties of cataloging,
one must thoroughly study the work of the Liú family.
To study the work of the Liú family,
one should start from the books of Bān Gù—
this is known to people;
but to study the work of the Liú family,
one should also incorporate the methods of Sīmǎ Qiān—
this is not known to people.
Now, what Sīmǎ Qiān called "ordering the six schools,"
distinguishing the similarities and differences in scholarship,
and investigating their strengths and weaknesses,
originated from his family's scholarship: Sīmǎ Tán discussed Yīnyáng, Rú, Mò, Míng, Fǎ, and Dàodé, considering them the six schools.
This is indeed profound.
The annals begin by tracing their origins to the *Shàngshū* (as seen in the "Eulogy of the Five Emperors' Basic Annals").
The tables begin by tracing their origins to the *Chūnqiū* (as seen in the "Preface to the Generational Table of the Three Dynasties").
The biographies begin by tracing their origins to the gaps in the *Shī* and *Shū*,
down to the writings of Yú and Xià (as seen in the "Biography of Bó Yí").
All these reveal the origins and inspirations of cataloging.
After the Six Arts,
the various masters of the Zhōu and Qín periods,
such as the biographies of Mèng, Xún, the three Zōus, Lǎo, Zhuāng, Shēn, Hán, Guǎn, Yàn, Qū Yuán, Yú Qīng, and Lǚ Bùwéi,
discuss and arrange their writings,
summarize their main ideas,
elaborate or simplify their language,
and evaluate their quality;
through praise and criticism,
their meanings are not confined to narrow views.
For people, these are biographies;
for books, these are catalog prefaces.
The ancients intended meaning and titled chapters—
how can vulgar scholarship restrict them with rigid rules?
The work of the Liú family,
its method of categorization,
is based on the official *Lǐ*;
as for the text of the catalog prefaces,
it subtly adopts the style of the Grand Historian's biographies.
For distinguishing origins and lineages,
managing the chaos of the hundred schools,
and seeking to connect them with the Great Way—
this is the fundamental purpose.
As for the order of volumes and categories,
the sequence of chapters and classifications,
although they follow a set order,
and are orderly and不乱,
they actually interconnect official duties and affairs,
complementing each other to achieve results.
For example, *Guǎnzǐ* is listed under the Dàoist school,
but when discussing the lineage of minor learning,
its chapter "Dìzǐ Zhí" is taken
and appended after the *Ěryǎ*;
thus, it is known that the words of one school's book,
if valuable,
can be separately extracted as a rule.
*Yī Yǐn* and *Tàigōng*,
the ancestors of the Dàoist school, have their books placed under Dàoism.
*Sūzǐ* and *Kuǎi Tōng*,
belonging to the School of Diplomacy,
because their military strategies are revered,
are re-recorded in the military strategy section,
placed above Sūn and Wú's schools.
Thus, it is known that Dàodé and military strategy,
wherever their main ideas converge,
can cross-reference each other as a rule.
Now, if chapters can be separately extracted,
then the origins and lineages of scholarship
will not suffer from gaps or incompleteness.
If categories can cross-reference,
then dividing main outlines and subcategories
will not suffer from ambiguity or contradiction.
When the origins and lineages of scholarship
have no gaps or incompleteness,
and dividing main outlines and subcategories
has no ambiguity or contradiction,
then the intent of the six ministers of the *Zhōu Guān* working together is preserved,

and the purpose of the Grand Historian's biographies cross-referencing details is revealed (e.g., the "Biographies of the Money-makers" mentions Zǐ Gòng without involving the "Biographies of the Disciples"; the "Biographies of the Rú Scholars" mentions Dǒng Zhòngshū and Wáng Jí, who have separate biographies).
The method of managing books,
the ancients had their own teachings—
how can it be ignored?
Since Bān Gù删除了 the *Jí Lüè*,
the introductory discussions of the Liú family have not been transmitted;
the *Jí Lüè* was a general discussion of the main ideas of all books. By simplifying the categories,
the essential methods of the Liú family are not clearly presented;
Bān Gù merged the duplicate entries in the Liú family's work into one. Thus, scholars do not know the method of cataloging,
which is to distinguish and clarify the hundred schools
and connect them with the Great Way (the chapter "Tiānxià" in *Zhuāngzǐ* also expresses this idea).
Instead, they merely see it as a need for numbering classifications;
no wonder scholarship lacks specialization,
and books are not preserved across generations,
turning不如 the spells and talismans of shamans or the secret formulas of physicians,
which still have methods passed down through teachers without loss.
Zhèng Qiáo's *Jiàochóu* outline
strongly criticizes the errors in the categorization of the *Chóngfāng*,
and from Bān Gù onward,
all are ridiculed.
However, Zhèng did not clarify the origins and lineages of cataloging,
which should trace back to the official *Lǐ*,
and merely nitpicked about which book should be in category A but was mistakenly placed in B,
or which book should be in category C but was erroneously placed in D.
Now, errors in categorization,
although due to the loss of family methods,
the容易混淆 of the Rú and Miscellaneous schools,
and the ambiguities in official duties and historical accounts,
mean that some books are in a borderline situation,
and were not originally cataloging errors.
If the Liú family's methods of separate extraction and cross-referencing
are not understood by later generations,
even if the Grand Historian were reborn,
or Yáng Xióng reappeared,
they would still be茫然 and unable to systematize the method of categorization.
Zhèng was able to criticize the inappropriateness of Bān's *Zhì* appending categories,
but could not correct its improper merging and simplification—
this can be said to know ten but not two fives.
Moreover, I observe that later catalogers
have separately extracted *Xiǎo Ěryǎ* to归入 the *Lúnyǔ* (originally a chapter title in *Kǒng Cóngzǐ*; the *Suí·Jīngjí Zhì* separately extracts it to归入 the *Lúnyǔ*).
Some have separately extracted *Xià Xiǎozhèng* to归入 seasonal ordinances (originally a chapter title in *Dàdài Lǐ*; the *Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo* separately extracts it to归入 seasonal ordinances).
Do they truly understand the ancients' method of separate extraction?
They merely forget the original book,
and lose their basis by appending categories.
*Jiāruì Jì* is placed in the Five Elements category,
and also cross-referenced in miscellaneous biographies (*Suíshū·Jīngjí Zhì*).
*Xījīng Zájì* is placed in historical accounts,
and also cross-referenced in geography (*Tángshū·Yìwén Zhì*).
Do they truly understand the ancients' method of cross-referencing?
They merely forget that it has already been recorded,
leading to repetition and errors.
Now, the fragmentation of末学,
to the point of appending categories without basis,
and重复 errors,
can be said to have reached an extreme.
Investigating the reasons for these errors,
it is because the principles inherently cause doubts,
and the situation inevitably leads to this.
Merely adhering to the established rules of classification,
without analyzing the subtleties of why the ancients separately extracted or cross-referenced,
results in茫然 and lack of定识,
and弊端 inevitably reach this point.
However, if those in the field of校雠
are not deeply knowledgeable about the origins and lineages of scholarship,
and merely engage in cutting chapters for separate extraction,
or断 categories for cross-referencing,
it will lead to fragmentation and chaos,
with no more rules or章程,
thus curing one弊 only to滋生 another.
Therefore, the师法 of校雠
must be transmitted,
and the expertise in cataloging
must be established.
The literary sections in the gazetteers of prefectures and counties
must be thoroughly deliberated.
In ancient times, envoys collected writings,
and the Grand Historian managed the classics;
literary works and records
were all held by the court.
Thus, beyond what the officials guarded,
there were no ancient texts.
In later ages, people wrote their own books,
and each family distinguished its doctrines.
Even when encountering eras that esteemed literature
and periods of collecting classics,
those that could enter the imperial library
and be overseen by the historians
were fewer than seven or eight out of ten;
such was the natural tendency.
With literary works scattered throughout the realm
and historians lacking exclusive responsibility,
the governance of a unified script
could only be taught and studied by school instructors,
while prefectural and county gazetteers could classify and arrange them,
establishing fixed regulations
and preserving them in local regions,
thereby preparing for the imperial envoys to gather folk customs
and awaiting the imperial library’s definitive judgments.
Even unusual and unorthodox doctrines
could be examined based on what was heard and seen,
collating and correcting them;
thus, literary works and classics
would have their unifying principles,
and scholarship and human minds
would find their norms.
In the past, Cài Yōng corrected and established the Stone Classics,
stating that scholars from all regions
even went so far as to bribe officials to alter the lacquer texts of the Lántái
to match private writings.
This clearly demonstrates that at that time,
the teachings transmitted in commanderies and kingdoms
did not align with the central archives.
Even the strokes and dots of characters,
the work of philology,
had variations in transmission across regions;
how much more so for recorded accounts and hearsay,
private writings and separate records?
If schools do not transmit their teachings,
and gazetteers do not manage their classification,
then literary works will be scattered and recorded haphazardly,
with ambiguities and confusions,
and what will later generations rely on for verification and determination?
Zhèng Qiáo discussed methods for seeking books,
saying to seek them by location
and to seek them by person.
Thus, the classification of literary works by local regions
is indeed meant to serve as an essential compilation based on location and person.
In previous eras, when searching for books and charts,
if heavy rewards were not offered,
rare books and secret strategies
could not be gathered;
but if heavy rewards were offered,
forged ancient lost texts
would falsely hope to match them.
The “Yì” of the Sānfén
and the “Shū” in ancient script
are clear evidence of this.
If local regions had classified books,
correcting private collections below
and borrowing from the central archives above,
then all writings in the realm
would be recorded in registers.
Even if one wished to hoard them privately, it would be impossible;
even if one wished to forge them, it would be unfeasible.
This is a natural outcome.
The growth of population
is still recorded in household registers;
the products of water and land
are still listed in geographical records.
How much more so for literary works and classics,
which are the sources of scholarly traditions
and the transmissions of governance and achievements?
If they are not classified and categorized
in prefectural and county gazetteers,
and their essentials compiled,
how can the literary heritage of a region be preserved without loss?
Preface and Guidelines to the “Administrative Summaries” of the Hézhōu Gazetteer
The gazetteers of prefectures and counties
are comparable to the historical records of ancient states,
which is a long-standing practice.
The feudal lords of ancient states founded and inherited their domains,
with elevated status and distinct authority;
historical records compiled them into hereditary houses,
placing them above ministers and commoners,
which was indeed appropriate.
The chief officials of prefectures and counties,
however, are merely selections akin to ancient district magistrates.
They do not reside in their posts for long,
nor do they hold hereditary salaries.
If they leave behind benevolent legacies
and exemplary conduct worthy of emulation,
compiling them into biographies
and placing them among literary and administrative affairs
is also fitting.
What past records contained
is now unknown.
For example, the “Biographies of Dānyáng Administrators” by Emperor Yuán of Liáng (see Suíshū·Jīngjízhì, in ten volumes),
and the “Biographies of Virtuous Governors” by Sūn Zhòng (see Tángshū·Yìwénzhì, in fifteen volumes),
were specialized compilations
largely following old conventions.
The “Biographies of Upright Officials” by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
remain essentially unchallenged.
As for comprehensive prefectural and county gazetteers,
categorizing and ranking individuals
by using “Famous Officials” as a heading,
alongside “Local Worthies,” “Exemplary Women,” “Immortals and Buddhists,” and “Sojourners,”
merely results in a reference book of extracts
or a miscellaneous compilation by literati.
Although loosely imitating the categories appended in Lè Shǐ’s “Tàipíng Huányǔ Jì,”
it essentially serves as a precursor to the haphazard collection of literary phrases in commonplace books.
To emulate the family learning of the “Chūnqiū”
and the historical records kept by external historians,
individuals should be compiled into biographies,
with events presented from beginning to end.
If officials and commoners are recorded together
without distinction in format,
it would be like Dé Cáo visiting Péng Gōng’s home,
where host and guest are indistinguishable in one room.
I believe that Shǔ Commandery’s admiration for Wén Wēng
and Nányáng’s remembrance of Shào Fù
stem from their ability to benefit their regions
by promoting advantages and abolishing弊端.
Though these individuals have departed,
their benevolent legacy remains among the people,
and this is precisely why.
Even Bóyí’s purity
and Liǔxià Huì’s benevolence
are not considered incompatible in the same category.
If, before taking office,
local evaluation was unfavorable,
or after leaving office,
their later conduct was not consistent,
yet they were upright and capable for a time,
how does that harm the good governance of the region?
Emphasizing administrative achievements
over other aspects of conduct
differs from assessing local figures
by examining their entire lives,
evaluating their flaws and virtues,
and distinguishing them like plants and trees,
categorizing and arranging them in sections.
The principles are inherently different.
Thus, separately titling this section
as “Administrative Summaries”
is indeed appropriate.
The term “summary” (lüè)
denotes a grand framework
and a majestic designation for compilation.
Works like Huáng Shí’s and Huáinánzǐ’s bear such titles (e.g., “Huángshí Sān Lüè,” “Huáinánzǐ Yàolüè”).
Figures like Zhāng Wēn and Yú Huàn divided their records accordingly (e.g., Zhāng Wēn’s “Sānshǐ Lüè,” Yú Huàn’s “Diǎnlüè”).
This draws from the legacy of strategic planning,
not solely from Zhèng Qiáo’s twenty summaries (referring to Zhèng Qiáo’s “Tōngzhì” twenty summaries).
Using it to compare administrative affairs
and compile achievements
sufficiently guides the local people
and crowns the biographies.
Considering historical records,
the format is indeed appropriate,
unlike Péi Zǐyě’s abridgment of the “Sòng Lüè,”
which merely aimed at condensing the text.
General Discussion on Biographies in the Hézhōu Gazetteer
The Records state:
The literary form of biographies and records
had no fixed style in antiquity.
The texts such as "Military Records" and "Zhōu Records" quoted in the Zuǒzhuàn
are actually biographies.
Mencius's responses to questions about the parks and gardens of Tāng and Wǔ
all said, "In the records, there is mention of this,"
which refers to records.
The Six Classics are considered canonical texts,
so works like the Analects and the Book of Rites are called commentaries.
The hexagrams and lines are the canonical texts,
so the Tuàn, Xiàng, and Wényán are called commentaries.
Since the Zuǒzhuàn Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals derived its meaning from the classics,
it also incorporated historical judgment.
Sīmǎ Qiān's seventy biographies
slightly followed this example;
and Bān Gù, with his twelve basic annals,
privately compared them to the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Separating individuals into distinct chapters,
categorizing and arranging them in sequence,
when examined against the Zuǒzhuàn,
appears somewhat rigid and strict,
yet their unique insights and creative minds
somewhat resemble the various masters.
Considering the origins of their naming,
the biographies that followed the Spring and Autumn Annals
were merely like the records based on classical rituals,
determining style based on names,
with no profound literary intent.
Even Qu Yuán of Chǔ
was combined in a biography with Jiǎ Yí of Hàn;
Zōu Yǎn, who discoursed on heaven,
was appended to the chapters on the great Confucians Mèng and Xún;
classifying individuals by their characteristics,
evaluating without fixed standards,
with passionate sighs and激昂tones,

this also reflects the legacy of the Six Discourses of the Lǚshì (The Annals of Lü Buwei) (The Twelve Chronicles of the Lǚshì seem to be the model for the basic annals, the Eight Observations for the eight treatises, and the Six Discourses for the biographies).
In the History of the Hàn Dynasty by Bān Gù, within a single scroll,
individuals are divided into beginning and end,
and once the names of biographies were established,
the structure became extremely meticulous.
However, figures like the Four Hermits of Yìmín
were subordinate to Wáng and Gòng.
Individuals like Wáng Jí and Wéi Xián
were distinct branches of the Forest of Confucian Scholars.
Subordinates, like Zhuānyú依附于Lǔ,
are not recorded by name;
distinct branches, like Tián and Chén residing in Qí,
are重新labeled with titles;
in literary compositions, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú extravagantly displayed his poetry and rhapsodies;
in discerning customs, Dōngfāng Shuò did not avoid humorous words;
indeed, profound insight and grand structure
cannot be measured by a single standard.
Fàn Yè's work on the Eastern Hàn
had fragmented and trivial titles,
resembling rice and salt;
the names listed in the biographies
were always annotated at the beginning of each chapter.
Thus, the style of biographies
became like annotated official documents,
first tracing ancestral lineage,
ending with descendants,
arranged chronologically,
fearing any omission.
Seeking works like Chén Shòu's Records of the State of Shǔ,
which drew broadly from Supplementary Ministers of the Late Hàn,
or Shěn Yuē's biography of Xiè Língyùn,
which comprehensively discussed the literature and history of the Six Dynasties,
unconstrained by rigid rules,
subtly preserving the author's intent,
are as rare as the sound of footsteps in an empty valley.
Yet, though master craftsmen no longer exist,
their rules and standards remain.
Compiling and editing into volumes,
awaiting capable individuals;
harmonizing without taking the lead,
seems feasible;
however, with numerous fields of writing,
versatile talents and broad knowledge
should not be confined to trivial details.
Beyond the official histories,
there are miscellaneous records,
such as Gāozǔ and Xiàowén,
discussing policies and edicts,
all referred to as biographies (The Hàn·Yìwénzhì lists "Biography of Gāozǔ" in thirteen chapters and "Biography of Xiàowén" in eleven chapters).
These are the origins of historical anecdotes.
The Biography of King Mù and The Inner Biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
belong to the category of fiction.
Liú Xiàng's Biographies of Exemplary Women,
Jī Kāng's Biographies of Noble Scholars,
are specialized records.
Wáng Sù's Family Biography,
Wáng Póu's Generational Biography,
are records of individual families.
The Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò and The Biography of Master Lù
are accounts of individual lives.
As for local gazetteers,
from the Eastern Capital onward,
until the Six Dynasties and beyond,
such as The Biographies of Elderly Worthies of Chénliú,
The Biographies of Former Worthies of Kuàijī, and the like;
those not explicitly called biographies,
such as The Records of Elderly Worthies of Xiāngyáng and The Later Compilation of the Records of Yùzhāng;
the writing is voluminous and detailed,
too numerous to count.
Gathering lost materials,
compiling earlier accounts,
is like streams converging into a valley,
accepting both large and small;
like metals in a furnace,
both sharp and dull are cast.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"The words of the hundred schools are not elegant and refined,
and gentlemen find them difficult to discuss."
He also said:
"Those that do not deviate from ancient texts are close to the truth."
And also:
"Select those words that are particularly elegant."
With vast records,
one must judge by the Six Classics.
"Although the Odes and Documents are incomplete,
the times of Yú and Xià can be known."
Thus, by extensive inference and evidence,
correlating what is heard and seen,
revealing the subtle and elucidating the obscure,
judging with utmost fairness,
the goal is to establish literary form and rules;
how can one be拘拘bound to a single path?
Combining sweet and spicy to create flavor,
interweaving threads to form patterns,
adjusting to the times,
evaluating scholarly customs,
is the study of historical periods.
Comparing virtues of contemporaries,
appending them equally in compilation,
is the method of categorization.
Emotions may be stirred yet appear calm,
intentions may seem satirical but are truly惋惜,
this is the power of judgment.
Sometimes using反证for comparison,
sometimes drawing distant parallels as inspiration;
one event detailed differently in various accounts,
different writings suddenly compiled together,
this is the principle of classification and moderation.
If words lack elegance,
they will not travel far.
Gathering both public and private records,
comparing the strengths and weaknesses of the hundred schools,
if one cannot exercise independent judgment,
but is斤斤meticulous about being mere clerks of documents,
how can one inspire readers
and hope to publish works that endure不朽?
Moreover, national histories draw from local records,
and local records draw from family genealogies;
the sources must be broad,
so that selective extraction can be comprehensive.
Today's local records
do not distinguish between annals and biographies,
often confusing names and realities;
they label figures and exemplary women as specialized categories,
and separate literary circles and local worthies into fixed ranks;
abridging historical biographies,
omitting facts,
appending notes条目by条目,
resembling the format of encyclopedic摘比,
no longer reflecting the ancient art of传记;
attempting to compile by state,
or divide by region for records,
is this not difficult?
Furthermore, their listings of imperial examination graduates and officials
sometimes detail election regulations;
biographical accounts and epitaphs
are included among literary works.
The affairs of a single individual
appear repeatedly,
with notes like "detailed in biography, volume X,"
or "see event in条目X";
this resembles annotating medicinal herbs in本草,
where roots and fruits are listed separately;
or rhyme books explaining sounds,
where level and oblique tones are marked for usage.
If the writing is not elegant and refined,
scholars find it difficult to discuss.
Now, using the comprehensive style of official histories,
specifically highlighting biographies,
drawing广泛parallels and mutual evidence,
compiling them into specialized works,
to supplement the遗留writings of ancient history above,
and provide material for后人采录below;
hopefully, future authors
may examine and seek from them.
If this is deemed incorrect,
I await the judgment of future sages.
Preface and Guidelines to the Biographies of Missing Records in the Hézhōu Gazetteer
Confucius said:
"I can still see the gaps in the historical records."
He also said:
"Listen widely, set aside what is doubtful,
and speak cautiously about the rest."
Now, in gathering scattered and lost materials,
organizing and interpreting ancient texts,
what one sees and hears
often yields doubtful or ambiguous information.
This does not mean it is noble to leave gaps unaddressed.
Take, for example, "Guō Gōng" and "Xià Wǔ"—
originally, there were no profound texts about them;
tools like the plow and fishing nets
also have preserved discussions.
Yet the *Spring and Autumn Annals* retained their original headings,
and the *Book of Documents* begins with the "Canon of Yáo";
doubtful matters were left unresolved,
and gaps were preserved without deletion—
this is the essence of caution.
Sīmǎ Qiān said:
"There are gaps in the records,
but their missing parts occasionally appear in other accounts."
Now, traces of doubt and ambiguity
may not lack other accounts for reference,
yet ancient texts are valued for their classical origins,
and the various schools select what is elegant and refined.
Understanding the underlying intent
is why we admire those who are diligent in learning and deep in thought.
In Bān Gù's *Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò*,
he noted that many strange and bizarre sayings
had been attached to it,
so he meticulously recorded the trivial talks of riddles and divination games
to show that Shuò was truly only this,
which is the historian's method of resolving doubts.
In Chén Shòu's *Records of Shǔ*,
because Zhūgě Liàng did not establish official historians,
the affairs of Shǔ were difficult to investigate,
he thus recorded Yáng Xì's eulogies for the famous ministers of the late Hàn,
briefly preserving their names,
to convey his intent.

This is the traditional practice of leaving gaps in historical records. Chén Shòu separately compiled the *Biographies of the Elderly of Yì Province* in ten volumes, showing he did not neglect Shǔ. The *Biographies of the Elderly of Yì Province* was not included in the *Records of Shǔ*, as each has its appropriate style. Some criticize Shòu for this, but they are mistaken.
Since the tradition of historiography was lost,
mediocre historians failed to grasp the meaning of leaving gaps.
Those fond of elaborate language
sometimes mixed in strange and astonishing tales;
those favoring conciseness
often deleted essential words from the classics.
The *Book of Jìn* delighted in collecting anecdotes, while the *Book of Táng* frequently omitted memorials. They did not follow the principle of listening widely,
and misunderstood the admonition to speak cautiously.
If something appears doubtful,
or events are connected by forced associations,
and one hesitates to make a judgment,
with old records difficult to verify,
some argue that such chapters should be deleted
to align with the idea of leaving gaps.
But this is merely eliminating what is doubtful—
how can there be any gaps left?
Zhèng Qiāo, in his *Outline of Textual Criticism*,
stated that when the imperial library collected books,
there was traditionally a catalog of missing works;
all who examine texts
must record their classifications
and seek them throughout the land.
His argument is indeed insightful.
I believe that just as with texts,
so it is with human affairs.
All historians
should, after compiling their accounts,
note cases where a person is mentioned but details are lacking,
or where biographies differ and accounts are inconsistent,
as well as those who are prominently listed
but whose facts are unverified.
For instance, Bóyí and Shūqí are praised for their purity,
yet the story of gathering ferns on Mount Xīshān is omitted;
Yán Huí and Zēng Shēn are renowned for their learning,
but their achievements in the eastern states are not recorded.
From one example, infer three others—
such cases are numerous.
Some result from errors in recording or deletion,
others from collecting unsubstantiated reputations.
It is difficult to rely on conjecture,
so they should be left as doubtful.
When biographies are nearly complete,
a separate section titled "Missing Inquiries" should be compiled
to adhere to the admonition of speaking cautiously.
Later readers
can then investigate further.
Take, for example, Chén Shòu's eulogies for the famous ministers of the late Hàn (see above),
or Cháng Qú's *Men and Women of Huáyáng* in the *Records of Huáyáng*, which lists only names, stating that their deeds are unknown.
Is this not excellent?
As for local gazetteers,
their style should be more detailed than that of histories.
Yet, traditionally compiled gazetteers
regulate entries on figures
within limited space,
selecting and comparing facts,
adding brief annotations,
and classifying local products and specialties
in a roughly similar manner.
As for the annotated facts,
they often resemble official evaluations,
legal case documents,
with parallel prose,
abrupt and lacking narrative.
Scholars are described as filial, friendly, upright, and proper,
kind, benevolent, and harmonious;
officials are praised as honest, capable, pure, cautious,
loyal, trustworthy, benevolent, and good;
learning is attributed entirely to Confucian scholars,
and chastity to women like Jiāng.
A thousand pieces share the same pattern,
vague as reeds in the mist—
what is there to observe?
Now, adopting the general style of historians,
we specifically highlight biographies.
We strive to select those with commendable deeds
and verifiable facts worthy of recording;
what previous gazetteers omitted
has been largely searched and gathered.
Others, like those with only names and brief notes,
whose facts are hard to verify,
lost to distant ages and eroded by time,
impossible to investigate—
keeping them would leave them without proper attribution,
but deleting them would obscure their hidden virtues.
All such cases
are compiled into the *Biographies of Missing Inquiries*,
awaiting the discernment of later generations.
Hézhōu Gazetteer: Preface to the Biographies Section of Previous Gazetteers, Part One.
The Records states:
"To be broad-minded and knowledgeable of distant matters—
this is the teaching of the Documents.
To arrange events and compose writings—
this is the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals."
This means that although the methods of narration and composition differ,
their influence and teachings are distinct.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To recite their poems,
to read their books,
is it acceptable not to know the person?"
This means that although ancient texts are preserved,
the author's intent
must be discerned.
In ancient times, historians each had established methods;
their language was refined and their meaning far-reaching,
depending on the individual.
What Mèngzǐ called "their writings are historical,"
and what Confucius meant by "I have privately taken their righteousness,"
clarifies that the historian's methods and standards cannot be altered,
while the meaning and intent are uniquely determined by the sage.
Thus, a good historian and fine writings
must also follow principles.
The official historians of ancient times cannot be examined,
but the good historians of the Spring and Autumn states,
such as Dǒng Hú and Nánshǐ's straightforward recording,
and Zuǒshǐ Yǐxiāng's erudition and elegance,
represent the general standard.
I suspect that figures like Nánshǐ, Dǒng Hú, and Zuǒshǐ
must have had teachers and transmitted methods in their time.
However, due to the specialized nature of their work,
and the remoteness of events, transmission was lost,
so we cannot fully investigate it today.
Sīmǎ Qiān gathered scattered and lost materials,
collected old accounts,
and compiled them into one hundred and thirty chapters,
to continue the work of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Regarding the Spring and Autumn school writings from the declining Zhōu and Warring States periods,

such as those by Yàn Yīng, Yú Qīng, Lǚ Bùwéi—Yànzǐ Spring and Autumn Annals, Yúshì Spring and Autumn Annals, Lǚshì Spring and Autumn Annals—all employed the method of arranging events and composing writings. That is, the Spring and Autumn school writings of that time each had their own factions and were not solely confined to the "Spring King First Month" style. ,
he recorded the general outlines of their writings,
compiling and arranging them;
this was to demonstrate his broad collection from various schools,
harmonizing the Six Arts,
and detailing their origins and branches,

necessitating a clear account of their sources Sīmǎ Qiān's "Autobiographical Postface" continues the work of the Spring and Autumn Annals, tracing its factional origins, which is not an arrogant claim. .
After Sīmǎ's death,
Bān Gù arose,
compiling the historical events of the Western Hàn,
fully transcribing the "Grand Historian's Autobiographical Postface,"
extending its principles and examples,
likely placing it in the same category as the biographies of Xiàngrú and Yáng Xióng.
Fàn Yèzōng's Book of the Later Hàn's account of Bān Gù
followed established practice,
adhering strictly to old methods,
without overstepping boundaries;
though lacking independent judgment,
it still preserved the ritual forms, like the ceremonial offering of a sheep at the new moon,
where the ritual is abandoned but the text remains.
As for the Book of Sòng's biography of Fàn Yèzōng,
and the Book of Jìn's biography of Chén Shòu,
they were either mixed among literary figures,
or haphazardly compiled alongside contemporaries,
with no regard for the origins of historiography,
or the methods of composition and transmission,
showing no attention to these matters;
this reflects the gradual loss of historical methodology.
By the time of the Táng compilation of the Books of Jìn and Suí,
they relied solely on collective effort.
Talents were dispersed,
and collaborators
could not all be known;
some were appended to others' biographies,
or mentioned incidentally in literary discussions,
with no separate records,
causing the Spring and Autumn school learning
to lose its path of transmission,
and the master-disciple tradition of historians
to become as obscure as the Milky Way.
It is like a clan without someone to gather its members,
where family records become disordered;
or like Buddhist monks scattered,
leaving temples to fall into ruin;
such outcomes are inevitable,
and logically natural.
Now, Sīmǎ and Bān's historical writings
are akin to Fúshēng and Kǒng Ānguó's transmission of the classics.
Their profound meanings and subtle words
were transmitted orally and mentally;
some wished to hide them in famous mountains,
to be passed on to the right person;
others had great scholars kneel at the pavilion,
receiving instruction from their younger sisters.
How could this compare to later dynastic histories,
where meaning is exhausted within the pages,
and writing resembles that of petty clerks,
constrained by conventions,
leaving nothing to the imagination?
Yet Sīmǎ and Bān's "Forest of Scholars" chapters
could use the Six Arts as a framework,
with masters and scholars transmitting teachings.
Threaded together like pearls,
they formed their own warp and weft;
this was to clarify the succession of master-disciple methods,

and trace unbroken origins The "Forest of Scholars" biography style uses the classics as the warp and people as the weft, unlike ordinary biographies that detail an individual's life. From the Book of the Later Hàn onward, this transmission was lost. .
If later official historians' biographies
could thoroughly study the ancient masters' methods,
somewhat imitating the example of classical masters' transmissions,
using history as the framework,
and thereby weaving together the branches of composition and transmission,
mutually forming warp and weft.
Take Sīmǎ and Bān as examples:
their prior sources and foundations,
such as Shìběn and Strategies of the Warring States for Sīmǎ's Historical Records,
and Yáng Xióng and Liú Xīn for the Book of Hàn.
Later extensions of their transmission,
such as Yáng Yùn disseminating Sīmǎ's Historical Records,
and Mǎ Róng receiving the Book of Hàn.
Separate commentaries and annotations,
such as Xú Guǎng and Péi Yīn for Sīmǎ's Historical Records,
and Fú Qián and Yīng Shào for the Book of Hàn.
All such cases
should be compiled according to category,
clarifying the family learning,
with the text as the main focus,
no longer using a single individual's life as the chapter title.
Then the Spring and Autumn's governance of the world,
could be said to survive to this day.
As for histories of the Later Hàn,
the works of Liú Zhēn and Yuán Hóng,
the books of Huá Qiáo, Xiè Chéng, and Sīmǎ Biāo,
all coexisted alongside Fàn's work.
For Jìn history,
from Wáng Yǐn, Yú Yù, Hé Fǎshèng, Gān Bǎo, Lù Jī, Xiè Língyùn, and others,
there were eighteen authors in total,
truly a flourishing era.
Yet later historians,
unable to distinguish the styles of these various schools,
or evaluate the merits and flaws of their books,
lumped them together in a single chapter.
It is like the Yǐng craftsman's skill at carving—
if the material is lost, what can be sought?
Or like being able to speak of Xià rituals—
without evidence, there is no credibility.
Moreover, when gathering crowds to compile books,
establishing supervisors and editors,
it is especially important to examine and fix the chapters,
review the text,
noting which book records what,
who compiled which work,
which tables or biographies
were written by whom.
This would allow readers to discern good and bad,
and determine right and wrong;
so even if the waters of Jīng and Wèi mix,
those of Zī and Shéng can be distinguished;
the evils of later trends
could still rely on dikes for defense.
Yet Táng and Sòng historians
ultimately lacked specialized records,
allowing classical students' exam cramming
and literary embellishments
to chirp in the halls of Bān and Sīmǎ,
and boldly intrude into the task of writing history.
Preface to the Biographies of Former Records in the Hézhōu Gazetteer.
Jìn Zhì Yú created the "Wénzhāng Zhì" (Record of Literary Works),
narrating the lives of literary scholars,
and discussing the origins and development of literary compositions;
this is what Fàn Yè's "Wényuàn Lièzhuàn" (Biographies of the Literary Garden) in the History of the Later Han followed.
Since then, biographies of literary scholars
have been compiled in every era,
and the inclusion of literary gardens in histories
has thus been established as a fixed rule.
As for the different schools of historiography,
there has been no discussion heard,
and the merits and faults of historians
have thus been placed beyond consideration.
How extreme it is
that the world finds it easy to speak of literature but fears to speak of history!
The works of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
did not establish a "Literary Garden" section,
not because there was no literature;
figures such as Lǎozi, Zhuāngzi, Shēn Bùhài, Hán Fēi, Guǎn Zhòng, Yàn Yīng, Mèngzǐ, Xúnzǐ, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Yáng Xióng, Méi Chéng, and Zōu Yáng,
for whom biographies were written,
all had achievements in writing,
and were not without repeated emphasis.
Not labeling them as a "Literary Garden"
was to discuss and arrange them according to their specialized learning.
Having a "Literary Garden" section in biographies
is likely due to the lack of specialized learning,
which is a decline in literary writing.
However, when historians record,
they extravagantly speak of the literary garden,
but for the family learning of the "Chūnqiū" (Spring and Autumn Annals),
its schools and origins,
they have never paid the slightest attention.
I do not know what they intend their histories to be regarded as?
The tradition of "Wénzhāng Zhì"
after Zhì Yú,
with people like Shěn Yuē, Fù Liàng, and Zhāng Zhì

compiling records one after another Fù Liàng's "Xù Wénzhāng Zhì" (Sequel to the Record of Literary Works), Shěn Yuē's "Sòng Shì Wénzhāng Zhì" (Record of Literary Works of the Song Dynasty), Zhāng Zhì's "Wénshì Zhuàn" (Biographies of Literary Scholars). ,
are too numerous to count.
However, the historians' selection and compilation,
preserving the general outline,
and the recorded books,
are now all lost.
Thus, the origins and development of historiography,
and the traces of compilation,
at the time when they were edited into books,
whether in official documents or private papers,
were not necessarily without evidence for reference.
Yet earlier histories did not establish special topics,
and later scholars do not know the essential principles,
so even if there were traces,
they have essentially been lost and no longer exist.
Thus, what the ancients called officials guarding their books,
and families passing down their professions,
turns out to be inferior to literary talent and compositions,
which still managed to be listed among Cháng Bǎodǐng's "Wénxuǎn Zhùzuò Rénmíng" (Names of Authors in the Literary Selections) Cháng's work is in three volumes. .
Táng Lǐ Zhào wrote "Jīngshǐ Shìtí" (Explanations of Classics and Histories),
and Zōng Qiàn annotated the "Shísāndài Shǐmù" (Catalogue of Histories of Thirteen Dynasties).
Their books were classified under catalogues,
but did not comprehend the grand style of biographies.
In the Sòng dynasty, Kǒng Píngzhòng
once wrote "Liángshǐ Shìjī" (Deeds of Good Historians),
which is also now lost,
and the recorded version is only one volume,
so it is crude and not worth viewing or adopting.
Historians creating precedents
each have their basis;
the "Liènǚ" (Biographies of Exemplary Women) section originated from Liú Xiàng,
"Xiàoyì" (Filial Piety and Righteousness) from Xiāo Guǎngjì a Jìn dynasty person, who wrote "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn" (Biographies of Filial Sons). ,
"Zhōngyì" (Loyalty and Righteousness) from Liáng Yuándì's "Zhōngchén Zhuàn" (Biographies of Loyal Ministers) in thirty volumes. ,
"Yǐnyì" (Recluses) from Huángfǔ Mì's "Yìshì Zhuàn" (Biographies of Recluses) and "Gāoshì Zhuàn" (Biographies of Eminent Scholars). ,
all are grand styles of earlier histories,
adapted according to the times to establish righteousness.
The "Rúlín" (Forest of Scholars) biographies of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
were based on the professions of erudites;
it is a pity they did not take the duties of historians
and compile them into a specialized book.
Later people's knowledge and understanding
do not match those of earlier people,
so they have not inherited
and are unable to serve.
Hàn dynasty Confucians transmitted the classics,
but the teacher's methods were lost.
Later histories' "Rúlín" chapters
could not follow their method of tracing origins and developments,
yet they still took contemporary teachers and Confucians,
based on their professions,
to record the learning of an era.
Thus, when Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù wrote histories,
the family methods were already lost;
the tasks of later historians,
even if they could not align with their principles and examples,
why could they not, based on the general compilation of their time,
the people above and below,
arrange and compose biographies,
to complete a history?
The "Rúlín" deals with classics,
and the "Wényuàn" discusses arts,
the profession of historians
lies between them,
and it is also something that compilers must know their duties in.
Some use the classification of arts and literature,
listing their volumes,
with postscripts in the narratives,
briefly indicating the authors' intentions,
thinking that the essential purpose of the history section
has already been generally seen.
They do not realize that the commentaries of classical teachers
and the compositions of literary scholars,
the arts and literature section does not fail to record their classifications;
but the chapters on "Rúlín" and "Wényuàn",
examining lives in detail,
separately evaluating them,
comparing and mutually verifying,
how can they be neglected?
If there are too many deeds,
and separate special biographies are marked,
unable to be combined into one chapter,
then within the historians' chapters,
the names should still be recorded,
with a note that they have separate biographies elsewhere.
The examples of Dǒng Zhòngshū, Wáng Jí, and Wéi Xián,
already have old precedents Dǒng Zhòngshū studied the "Chūnqiū", Wáng Jí studied the "Máoshī", Wéi Xián studied the "Lǔshī", all appear in the "Rúlín" but also have separate biographies. ,
with no mutual hindrance.
Xúnzǐ wrote discussions on "Lǐ" (Rites) and "Yuè" (Music),
and also the book criticizing twelve philosophers;
Zhuāng Zhōu indulged in absurd words,
yet still narrated various philosophers like Qín and Mò,
wishing to establish his own school of thought,
but without clearly analyzing
the earlier discussions and writings,
tracing origins and developments,
and achieving a balanced and appropriate judgment;
even if one wishes to contribute to earlier people
and benefit future learners,
it is like walking backward to seek progress—
none can achieve the ultimate.
Hézhōu Zhì, Preface to the Biographies of Former Records, Part Two
For local county histories,
discussing and arranging earlier people's writings,
and specially compiling biographies,
is indeed an innovative precedent.
Extending this to all directions,
so that the "Chūnqiū" governing the world
and the family methods of historians
shine brightly under heaven,
then once external records are well managed,
and books have unified comprehension,
the essential abridgments of national histories
can be discussed with ease.
However,
there are three difficulties in narration,
and three that must be narrated;
those who record with the brush
must carefully consider this discussion.
What are the three difficulties in compilation?
First, the writings lack scholarly tradition,
the prose is not worth reading,
and they are easily scattered and lost.
After the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the methods of historiography were lost,
especially regarding the specialized work of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
which could no longer be revived.
As for the established rules of annals and tables,
the old conventions of treatises and biographies,
they remained unchanged for a long time,
equivalent to examination regulations,
official decrees and statutes.
Even mediocre historians,
could strive to adhere to the standards,
roughly achieving conformity;
thus, although the quality of the writings varied,
with strengths and weaknesses intermingled,
readers could still apply established criteria to evaluate the editing.
Local gazetteers, however, completely lacked such standards,
with no fixed form or style,
excerpts resembling reference books,
annotations like account ledgers,
plain language akin to clerks’ documents,
and literary expressions like personal letters;
readers were left bewildered,
unable to grasp their main purpose.
Literary scholars
disdained and ignored them;
once new editions were completed,
old gazetteers quickly vanished.
Like changing clothes with the seasons,
or travelers passing through a lodging,
to hope for their preservation,
is that not difficult?
Second, the compilers and editors,
their conduct and achievements are unclear,
making it difficult to write their biographies.
The historians recruited by the imperial court,
were generally literary scholars,
officials with court ranks,
among whom were even renowned ministers.
Their writings might appear in bibliographies,
their conduct detailed in biographies,
cross-referencing and investigation
could still be relatively easy.
County and prefecture gazetteers, however,
were often compiled by temporary officials,
casually passing through;
the compilation and completion,
did not exceed a year or so,
discussions and deliberations,
were confined within the local area.
Some of these individuals might have hidden virtues unrecorded,
or fine accomplishments not yet known;
their travels unknown in regularity,
their pursuits unclear in profession,
like the gathering of duckweed traces,
or the fleeting marks of wild geese;
even if one wished to emulate the collected works of literary figures,
or imitate the biographies of Confucian scholars,
how could it be done?
Third, prefaces and postscripts are verbose and excessive,
the essence of form long lost,
making it difficult to establish compilation standards.
The biographies by Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
all included their own prefaces.
For their life conduct and achievements,
as well as the general principles of their editing,
were already clarified in their own prefaces;
based on the original text, written directly,
incorporated into the biographies;
if readers could comprehend them,
they would grasp more than half of the work.
The origin of writing prefaces and records,
though rooted in the "Xì Cí" of the Yìjīng and the poems of the Shījīng,
the essential editing by historians,
actually began with the collators,
who particularly valued this form.
What Liú Xiàng called organizing the chapters,
summarizing the main ideas,
and presenting them in memorials to the throne,
were generally clear and concise,
providing genuine insights
into both the work and the person.
Prefatory remarks at the beginning,
benefited later learners,
precisely for this reason.
Later generations, lacking formal essence,
and not tasked with collation,
could all rashly take up the brush;
whenever there was a compilation,
they would attach a preface,
words issued by officialdom,
principles all vague and general.
Covering the contents,
reading the preface hastily,
one would not know whom it referred to,
or what matters it addressed.
Yet literary habits persisted,
unable to self-correct,
is this not also perplexing?
In compiling county and prefecture gazetteers,
having many prefaces was especially seen as an honor,
with cursive script praised,
and ornate style competing.
Shade of pear trees, flowers in bloom,
first became eulogies for virtuous officials;
torrential waters, towering mountains,
then turned into praises for cultural achievements.
A thousand books, one same pattern,
leaving readers bored;
they could be swapped with others,
or assigned arbitrarily.
How could one still gather old gazetteer prefaces,
record previous compilation guidelines,
use them as material for biographies,
or as a coherent framework for a book?
All these three points
are the reasons for the difficulty in compilation.
What are the three reasons that make it necessary to provide an account?
First, if the earlier gazetteer is inappropriate,
and the later gazetteer revises it,
it is proper to preserve both for mutual verification.
The world's eyes and ears are boundless,
while the wisdom of one person is limited.
The account of Mínshān in the "Tribute of Yǔ" is ancient,
but upon obtaining the "Miǎnzhì,"
the source of the river was detailed as the Jīnshā.
Zhèng Xuán's theory of the suōzūn is ancient,
but with Wáng Sù,
the casting of metal and carving on the back of the sacrificial ox became clear.
The endeavor to exhaust the classics
may later surpass the earlier;
how could the talent for compiling gazetteers
remain unchanged once established?
However, when later scholars compile new editions,
they may not necessarily preserve the old records;
if the earlier gazetteer lacks an account,
how can one understand the painstaking effort behind the revisions,
or recognize the utmost appropriateness of the discernment and editing?
Thus, arranging and recording the earlier accounts
not only preserves the names of the old gazetteers,
but also clarifies the distinctive editing of the new gazetteer.
Second, if the earlier gazetteer has evidence,
and the later gazetteer mistakenly revises it,
it should be prepared for selection.
People's minds differ,
just as their faces do,
and so too with writing.
Historians have a long-standing habit
of preferring to alter old texts,
finding it easier to conform to general rules,
not out of intentional harshness.
However, with Huáiyín wearing a sword,
it is unclear who it refers to;

Sīmǎ Qiān's "Biography of Hán Xìn" says: The youth of Huáiyín insulted Xìn, saying, "Though you are tall, your heart is timid." Bān Gù removed the word "ruò" (you), and the meaning became obscure. The Grand Commandant brought his head,
who would dare to borrow it?

Earlier scholars discussed the "New Táng History: Biography of Duàn Xiùshí": Liǔ Zōngyuán's account states the Grand Commandant said, "I have brought my own head." The text is clear. The "New Táng History" changed it to: "I have brought the head." Whose head is it? If the original text of the time is not preserved,
then after three rounds of editing,
not only will there be errors like "hài" and "shǐ,"
but it may even change the form of insects and fish.
Third, gazetteers should be successively continued,
not repeatedly revised;
it is proper to adhere to general rules.
Sīmǎ Qiān's work drew from the "Shìběn" and "Strategies of the Warring States,"
compiling the chronicles of the "Shàngshū,"
and the "History of the Southern and Northern Dynasties" compiled the works of eight scholars including Shěn, Xiāo, Yáo, and Lǐ.
It has never been heard that when a new compilation was completed,
the old books were immediately discarded.
How much more so for the humble gazetteers of prefectures and counties?
Since they lack distinctive insight and original editing,
they should narrate without creating. Yet recent writers,
striving to show off their strengths,
without even glimpsing the threshold of the Dragon Gate,
first learn the tricks of the monkey trainer,
shifting three and changing four,
repeating and relying on each other,
which is truly self-inflicted trouble.
Thirty years constitute a generation,
allowing for the supplementation of lost texts
and the collection of historical anecdotes.
After another thirty years,
leave it to later worthies,
so that the first compilation and the second record
continuously succeed each other,
somewhat like Bān continuing Sīmǎ,
and Fàn succeeding Bān.
Would that not be good?
If the earlier book's principles and examples are incomplete,
and its categories are lacking,
later scholars initiating
to supplement missing texts
should also act as when Sīmǎ lacked geography,
and Bān's "Treatise" directly traced back to the "Xiàshū";
when Liáng and Chén lacked treatises,
the "Suí History" connected to the Five Dynasties;
Liáng, Chén, Northern Qí, Later Zhōu, and Suí—the Five Dynasties. Examples are derived from principles,
how could it be otherwise?
Yet some rashly change the categories,
and fully copy old texts;
catching the fish but forgetting the trap,
akin to plagiarism.
How can this be acceptable?
However, if the qín and sè are out of tune,
they must be restrung and adjusted.
Now, in creating this book,
we cannot be bound by the rule of successive continuation;
even if it seems contradictory,
I do not shy away;
may later comers
understand my sincere intentions.
By recounting the earlier gazetteers,
preserving their framework,
it also shows that creating new examples and compilations
was initially unavoidable.
These three points
are what is called不得不敘 (must be accounted for).
Preface and Examples to the Hézhōu Literary Collection
In the thirty-ninth year of the Qiánlóng reign (1774),
I compiled the "Hézhōu Gazetteer" in forty-two chapters.
After the compilation was completed,
I gathered writings from the prefecture that contributed to historical records,
such as elegant literary compositions that enhance grandeur,
and compiled them into two volumes of memorials,
three volumes of narratives,
one volume of discourses,
and two volumes of poetry,
totaling eight volumes of the "Literary Collection,"
comprising a certain number of pieces.
Having categorized them,
I explain the reasons for their selection and compilation,
and provide this preface.
The preface states:
Ancient scholars wrote works,
each establishing their own school,
and there was no practice of gathering various people's writings
into a single collection.
After specialized studies declined,
the trend of individual collections flourished,
their styles varied,
and their words occasionally had merit,
leading to the rise of anthologies.
As for historical collections,
the Hàn Dynasty was still close to antiquity.
Even though Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Yáng Xióng, Méi Chéng, and Zōu Yáng
were selected only for their ornate rhetoric and beautiful phrases,
and compiled into biographies;
the original intention of the historians
was not only to preserve the elegance of the time,
but also because people's qualities differ,
and the importance of literary works
could indeed be passed down alongside their achievements;
unlike later generations, constrained by literary meanings,
where biographies only record deeds.
However, the customs of the Western Capital were simple and质朴,
and both Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù wrote their own distinctive works,
thus allowing the use of their principles and examples.
Later literary works,
like a trickle becoming a river,
if not categorized and collected separately,
would fill rooms with records,
becoming unmanageable.
Táng Dynasty historian Liú Zhījī once worried about the abundance of words in historical biographies,
and proposed taking imperial edicts
and ministers' memorials,
following the example of specialized treatises,
to create a separate category.
Classifying them within annals and biographies,
his idea was commendable.
However, since annals and biographies cannot entirely omit literary compositions,
and if literary compositions are specially compiled into history,
it may become too vast to exhaust,
which is why later generations kept the idea
but never implemented it.
The works of historians
encompass broad principles and categories.
The forms of the *Book of Songs* and the *Book of Documents*
differ from those of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
For instance, the twelve sections of the *Discourses of the States*
and the fifteen sections of the *Airs of the States*
represent canonical instructions, folk songs, and ballads,
each serving its appropriate purpose.
Therefore, the Grand Master presented the poems,
and the Outer Historian was in charge of the records from the four quarters;
it was never heard that one relied solely on a single category of books.
Since Kǒng Dào's *Literary Garden* and Xiāo Tǒng's *Selections of Refined Literature*,
the Táng dynasty had the *Quintessence of Literature*,
and the Sòng dynasty had the *Mirror of Literature*,
all of which compiled writings from their eras,
broadly collecting various genres.
However, their underlying intentions and established principles
still did not escape the habit of men of letters discussing literature
and the style of Confucian scholars preparing for examinations;
regarding historical matters,
they were not very closely related.
As for the Yuán dynasty's *Classified Collection of Literature*,
through long practice, its shortcomings gradually became apparent;
therefore, in compiling literary works,
it often preserved a historical intent,
and its preface and principles explicitly stated this.
However, its classifications were not clearly divided,
and regarding the origins and development of literature,
it offered little discussion or arrangement.
Furthermore, the ancients said:
"Recite his poems,
read his books,
but can one do so without knowing the man?"
The major life events of the authors,
along with the titles of their works,
should perhaps follow the example of Lǐ Shàn's annotations to the *Selections of Refined Literature*,
providing some explanatory notes.
As for proposals and discussions,
they are often brilliantly written,
inspiring readers,
yet by the end, one feels frustrated,
not knowing the full context of the matter.
This is like dreaming of an ancient person and suddenly waking up,
or listening to a marvelous tune that is not finished,
inevitably leaving one unsettled.
All such cases
are sufficient in discussing literature
but inadequate in verifying history,
something later historians examining history
must carefully consider.
As for regional literary selections,
the concepts of the *Discourses of the States* and *Airs of the States* are long past.
Works like the modern collections *Zhōngzhōu* and *Héfén*,
and pieces such as *Liángyuán* and *Jīnlíng*,
all delineate boundaries in discussing literature,
slightly embodying the intention of gathering and presenting materials,
which is acceptable.
However, why do compilers of local gazetteers, when arranging arts and literature,
not understand the formats of various historical works,
but instead fully imitate the model of literary anthologies
by including poems, songs, rhapsodies, records, biographies, and miscellaneous writings,
placing them among the bibliographic sections?
This can be said to lack understanding of proper classification.
Therefore, in my spare time from compiling the gazetteer,
I have gathered various genres,
drafted regulations,
roughly grouping them by category,
to record the development and distinctions of their streams,
hoping that those who continue this work
may build upon it and enhance its splendor.
First: Memorials and Proposals
Placing memorials and proposals at the beginning of literary collections
is like placing annals at the start of a gazetteer.
Since Xiāo Tǒng selected literary works,
he placed rhapsodies at the forefront,
yet chronologically, Bān Gù came after Qū Yuán,
and in terms of genre, rhapsodies are a derivative of poetry.
Can such principles and categories
still be considered authoritative?
Yet later compilers of literary anthologies
have revered this as an unchangeable model for generations.
This is indeed strange.
Now, I place memorials and proposals at the beginning,
with official documents appended.
Memorials and proposals correspond to annals,
while official documents correspond to administrative summaries,
both being repositories of precedents.
Second: Biographical Accounts and Records
Biographical accounts and records
include biographies, prefaces, narratives, epitaphs, inscriptions, and similar genres.
Their content and the biographies and records in historical works
complement each other in detail and brevity.
As historiography became scattered and books were no longer specialized,
within the collected works of literati,
writings preserved for social occasions
often include biographical and other genres
that can supplement historical matters.
At the time of Xiāo Tǒng's literary selections,
this did not yet exist.
Later, literary collections incorporated historical genres,
and compilers of historical biographies often drew from them.
Thus, the writings of biographical accounts and records
are indeed essential.
Third: Discourses and Treatises
Discourses and treatises
carry on the legacy of the various philosophers,
serving as a means to entrust words to antiquity and achieve immortality;
their origin lies here.
Liú Xié said that the naming of "discourses"
began with the *Analects*,
which is correct.
Cháo Gōngwù's *Record of Books Read*
cites "discussing the Way and governing the state,"
from the *Book of Documents*,
thereby criticizing Liú Xié for being粗略.
However, the "Offices of Zhōu" chapter comes from the forged ancient text,
which Cháo failed to examine,
showing his confusion.
As the style of the various philosophers declined,
the collected works of literati came to include discourses, explanations, and disputations.
Genres like letters and colophons
also establish words based on events,
representing branches of discourses and treatises.
Fourth: Poetry and Rhapsodies
Poetry and rhapsodies
are the legacy of the Six Principles.
The genre of the *Airs of the States*
is indeed close to the literary collections of prefectures and counties.
"Sweet Springs" and "Shanglin"
were recorded by Bān Gù in biographies,
which was acceptable for his time.
Later generations produced abundant writings,
so they should naturally be compiled into separate books.
However, poets and rhapsodists,
up to recent times,
have become obsessed with ornate language,
losing the original intent of the state historians' prefaces to the *Songs*;
they foolishly contend over the craftsmanship of words,
making them unfit to discuss literary collections.
Here, I select earlier rhapsodies and poems,
arranging them in order,
to preserve the legacy of the *Airs* and *Elegantiae*;
works by contemporaries
are generally placed in appendices,
awaiting the selection of later generations.

Preface and Principles for the Imperial Edicts Annals of the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The annals in history
originated from the "Twelve Monthly Records" in *The Spring and Autumn Annals of Mr. Lü*.
Sīmǎ Qiān used them to record the actions of emperors and kings,
placing them at the beginning of his 130 chapters,
following the old method of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Subsequently, the twenty-one standard histories
successively followed this tradition,
with strict format and rigorous principles,
like laws and decrees.
However, local gazetteers
are often misled by the format of geographical reference books,
showing no adherence to these principles;
this is like shaking clothes without holding the collar,
detailing the items without lifting the net,
inevitably resulting in disorganization
and losing the essential editing principles of state history.
In ancient times, during the feudal era,
each state had its own historical records;
yet the first month must be associated with the Zhōu king,
and the Lǔ history must refer to Zhōu classics. When Hán Xuānzǐ saw the *Changes* and *Spring and Autumn Annals*, he said that the *Zhōu Rituals* were all preserved in Lǔ.
This shows the origin of acknowledging authority.
In later times, with the commandery and county system,
even places ten thousand *li* away
were governed like the ancient capital region,
yet their classification and arrangement
lacked any rules or regulations.
How could this align with the principles of the Outer Historian in the *Zhōu Rituals*?

The Outer Historian in the *Zhōu Rituals* was in charge of the records of the four quarters and responsible for communicating book titles to the four quarters. This shows that the books of the various states could not be independently produced but had to follow the established principles of the Outer Historian. This is the error of gazetteer compilers
who do not understand historiography.
The Lǚshì's "Twelve Monthly Ordinances,"
were merely called "Records";
whereas figures like Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
termed them "Basic Annals."
Examining the rationale behind the term "basic,"
Sīmǎ Qiān's intent was to inherit the methods of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*;
however, the specialists Zuǒ, Gōng, and Gǔ,
each composed their own commentaries for it;
whereas Qiān's work was a single author's book,
which further included treatises, tables, and biographies as its weft,
thus he added "basic" to "annals,"
to clarify that his annals served as the warp. His naming actually followed the old designation from the *Shìběn*.
Bān Gù, not grasping his meaning,
consequently also titled the ten treatises as "Basic Treatises."
However, the reason tables and biographies did not receive the "basic" designation
is specifically because tables were called "chronological tables,"
and biographies were called "arrayed biographies,"
both, like "basic annals," used two-character names for fixation,
only the treatises had a single-character name,
so he forcibly matched the count,

unaware that it harmed the meaning of warp-annals and weft-biographies. The ancients often matched characters for double or single terms, such as the *Qī Lüè* calling methods "classic methods," or the *Huáinánzǐ* calling discussions "book discussions," and so on, too numerous to list. Only when it did no harm to the meaning could it be done.
As for establishing precedents based on principle,
local gazetteers composing annals,
considering them the warp of a book,
is appropriate.
If they also followed the histories and called them "basic annals,"
then name and substance would be confused,
which is not the way to honor the principle of the state history.
Moreover, like the poems and prose later literati wrote,
if they concerned the actions of contemporary rulers,
their texts were not originally in the annals style,
yet they were also called "respectful records" to show reverence,
which in principle does no harm.
But if they were called "basic annals,"
that would be unreasonable.
Thus, what local gazetteers call "annals,"
compared to the tables and biographies within the same book,
is stylistically lighter;
contrasted with the "basic annals" of the state history,
they again serve as the weft.
Therefore, in composing annals, they cannot be called "basic."
From Qiān and Gù onward,
although "basic annals" followed the methods of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
they included edicts, proclamations, and commands within,
mixing in the style of the *Shàngshū*.
By the time Ōuyáng Xiū compiled the *New Book of Táng*,
he began using the method of grand writing,
his pen excising with strict care,
surpassing even Qiān and Gù,
this can indeed be called excelling in learning from the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
As for local gazetteers composing annals,
their purpose is to supply material for the external historians' gleanings,
preserving the reverence of a region,
what is called measuring the sun's illumination by the hall pillars,
glimpsing the passage of heavenly light through a window crack,
aiming for careful compilation and detailed recording,
not adopting the *Spring and Autumn Annals*' manner of recording events.
Therefore, respectfully recording the imperial words,
placing them at the beginning of the volume;
with the historians' precedents,
they mutually form warp and weft,
one cannot rigidly adhere to a single precedent.
Great indeed are the king's words,
originating from the *Shàngshū*;
"The king's words are like silk,"
originating from the *Lǐjì*.
In the Three Dynasties, the Son of Heaven was called "king,"
hence the Son of Heaven's words were called "king's words."
Later ages continued using "king's words,"
citing it as an established典故.
But they did not realize that after the Three Dynasties,
"king" also became a noble title for ministers;
yet all edicts and proclamations of the Son of Heaven were still called "king's words,"
this is being constrained by rigid antiquarianism,
failing to adapt to the times.
The text of the *Shàngshū*,
where ministers and sons refer to themselves as "zhèn,"
and their statements can also be called "gào."
In later ages, honorific terms
were fixed uniformly,
thus literary expressions must correspond to name and substance,
how can one cling to ancient precedents,
unaware of the need for change?
Therefore, changing the old term "king's words,"
to the grand designation "imperial words,"
hopefully aligns the matter with its substance,
and name and substance are not confused.
The song "Chì Tiān,"
is recorded in the canonical counsels;
yet later historical basic annals,
only record edicts and proclamations.
For poetry expresses emotion and nature,
while edicts and proclamations are applied to governance,
thus what the history section collects,
each has its proper place.
As for the style of local gazetteers,
the principle lies in venerating the respected,
by precedent should not make selective distinctions.
The former Governor-General Lǐ Wèi, in compiling the *Jīfǔ General Gazetteer*,
placed the two categories "Imperial Edicts" and "Imperial Writings" at the beginning,
which in principle is more appropriate.
As for Yǒngqīng County,
close to the southern capital region,
certainly had no specially issued imperial edicts.
If involving various prefectures, departments, and counties,
or encompassing the entire Zhílì region,
then they should be recorded in the general gazetteer,
and one cannot, just because Yǒngqīng is also included,
presumptuously record them into this book.
If there were imperial grants of tax exemptions, debt relief, or famine relief,
then the facts would be respectfully entered in the "Record of Imperial Favors,"
but the scope covered by imperial edicts is broad,
thus one also dare not overstep boundaries to record them.
Only the extensive grace and benevolent favors,
honorary awards and extended titles,
are indeed the glory of family records,
and the crowning part of local writings,
therefore they are compiled and recorded.
The imperially composed poem,
there is only the piece "Ice Cellar,"
which cannot form a separate volume,
is respectfully recorded after the imperial edicts,
to mark the splendor of the celestial river's light.
Preface and Guidelines for the "Record of Imperial Favors" in the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
In ancient times, the left historian recorded words,
the right historian recorded events,
Master Zhū believed words belonged to the category of the *Shàngshū*,
events to the category of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
his theory seems plausible.
However, the precedent of the *Shàngshū*,
is not entirely recording words;
and the so-called method of recording events,
is also not fully contained in the "Spring, the king's first month" style alone.
The methods of the five historians in the *Zhōuguān*,
are detailed and comprehensive;
but the books of records and annotations,
later generations cannot fully know in detail.
Besides the *Shū* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
what can be referenced,
the *Jí Zhǒng Zhōushū* resembles the *Shàngshū*,
and the *Bamboo Annals* resembles the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, that is all.
Yet the *Chronicle of King Mù*,
uniquely approximates the annotations of the daily records.
Although its contents may not be entirely credible,
still it represents the ancient methods of recording,
with warp and weft, surface and interior,
each having its focus;
initially not confined to the two styles of the *Shàngshū* and *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and to say the methods were fully present there,
can thus be understood.
After the Three Dynasties,
on a smaller scale were palace histories,
like the *Han Wǔ Forbidden Palace Daily Records*,
Empress Mǎ's *Xiǎnzōng Daily Records*,
are examples.
On a larger scale were records of current governance,
like the Táng *Zhēnguàn Essentials of Governance*,
the Later Zhōu *Xiǎndé Daily Calendar*,
are examples.
Recording by time,
the daily records of successive reigns,
are examples.
Compiling complete books,
the veritable records from Liáng Tàiqīng onward,
are examples.
For the virtue of the ruler is like heaven,
measuring by sundial and tracking celestial paths,
