gauging with armillary sphere and gnomon,
the system of laws must be comprehensive,
then nothing will be lacking or omitted.
Therefore, in establishing the statutes of the *Zhōuguān*,
one cannot but detail their principles,
and the *Rites* speaking of the duties of left and right historians,
truly, neither can be dispensed with.
The distinction between annals (jì) and biographies (zhuàn) by the ancients was meant to differentiate between warp and weft,
and was never originally intended to distinguish between high and low status.
Therefore, in Sima Qiān’s Shǐjì, there are annals without chronological years,
which Liú Zhīxuán was the first to criticize.
In the autobiographical preface of Bān Gù’s Hànshū,
he refers to the twelve annals as “Chūnqiū examination annals,”
the meaning of which is clear.
Since the time of Bān and Simǎ,
successive histories have followed this tradition,
all using “annals” as an honorific title,
while “biographies” became exclusively assigned to ministers and subordinates.
This, however, cannot explain the existence of The Biography of King Mù of Zhōu,
or the biographies of Gāozǔ and Xiàowén.
Now, let us discuss the flaw in successive histories where emperors have annals but no biographies.
For instance, the deeds of rulers are not as detailed as those of their ministers.
The beginning of an annals entry narrates their divine signs,
and the end summarizes their general achievements.
The rest, arranged by year and month,
only records governmental affairs,
serving as an outline for the treatises and biographies.
The literary structure cannot extend further,
because the warp and weft, by their nature, cannot be combined.
If judged by the essential principles of the Chūnqiū,
then the basic annals need only record the first year of accession to the throne
and the major laws and institutions,
which suffice as a record of events
and satisfy the principles of righteousness.
The deeds of rulers should incorporate the style of biographies,
recording their lives in detail
and placing them above the biographies of empresses and consorts.
This is similar to how Zuǒ’s commentary,
with a few lines about Huìgōng’s principal consort,
begins the narrative before the classic text,
which then belongs to the commentary under Duke Yǐn’s entry—
a point that can be mutually verified.
However, the distinction between the high status of annals and the low status of biographies
has long been established.
Treating rulers and ministers alike
would be logically problematic.
Thus, it would be best to follow the annals of an emperor
immediately with that emperor’s biography.
This is like the example in Zhèng Xuán’s version of the Yìjīng,
where the “Xiàng Zhuàn” and “Tuàn Cí”
are appended after the original hexagram.
Moreover, elevating the title to “Great Biography”
and not mixing it with ordinary biographies
would align name with reality
and seem a balanced approach.
As for local gazetteers,
they differentiate between events and narratives,
all under the general name “annals.”
This is to provide material for the correction by external historians
and originally did not follow the principles and examples of the Chūnqiū.
Therefore, there is no need to propose changes.
Preface and Examples for the Table of Officials in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The sections on officials and civil service examinations in local gazetteers
are both in the form of tables.
Yet those who compile gazetteers today say,
“Histories have treatises on officials and examinations,
so we follow ancient models
and establish grand titles,
compiling them all as treatises.”
This is pedantic and inappropriate.
The treatises in standard histories
detail the systems of official posts
and clarify the regulations of examinations.
Their style may imitate the classics of the Zhōuguān
or blend the forms of records and commentaries.
Compiling them as treatises is indeed fitting.
However, what local gazetteers record
are the tenures of successive officials
and the years of examination degrees.
Arranged with years as the warp and events as the weft,
they provide clear overviews
and serve for reference.
Checking against the grid is sufficient for the purpose.
Now, adopting the style of treatises for books,
categorizing magistrates, deputy magistrates, instructors, and assistant instructors together,
results in a Qiánlóng magistrate
being placed before a Shùnzhì deputy magistrate,
or a Kāngxī assistant instructor
coming after a Yōngzhèng instructor.
When one needs to check chronological order
or examine colleagues who served together,
it requires tedious searching,
making it hard to ascertain details,
wasting space,
and lacking proper organization.
I cannot understand why they insist on creating such trouble for themselves!
Compiling biographies of individuals
is a grand form in historical works,
yet local gazetteers show no evidence of following such models.
As for officials and examinations,
though different in substance, they share the same name,
and some cleverly try to attach themselves to this.
This is like the case of the Yǒngzhōu iron furnace,
which has been lamented for ages.
In the Zhōuguān, the御史 (yùshǐ) is in charge of recording documents
and counting those in government service.
Zhèng’s commentary says, “counting the current official positions.”
Thus, records of official posts and names
existed in ancient times.
For the 360 official positions,
recording those in service in a register
must have followed certain methods.
The general principles of warp and weft in Zhōu genealogies

were likely not solely for calendrical and astronomical use. (Liú Xiàng grouped genealogies and calendars together under arts and numerology, but Simǎ Qiān’s reference to Zhōu genealogies suggests they were not works of numerology. It is suspected that the ancients often used the genealogical form for cumulative recording methods.)
Bān Gù’s “Table of Officials and Ministers”
is entirely in the style of a treatise in its narrative examples,
yet it is not called a treatise
because he understood that recording successive officials requires the genealogical method.
Taking the style of the Zhōuguān as the warp
and the method of Hàn tables as the weft,
the ancients’ establishment of systems
was broad and comprehensive yet not lax,
as can generally be seen.
From the Eastern Hàn onward,
only official registers existed,
while the histories of the Táng and Sòng
came to include tables of chancellors and ministers,
which also indicates that the multitude of officials and ministers could not all be recorded.
As for specialized works,
records of official ceremonies and registers,
since the two Hàn dynasties onward,
each era had its compilations,
and arranging them in tables and chronicles
became more common in the Sòng dynasty;
such as Sīmǎ Guāng's *Tables of the Hundred Officials and Ministers* in 150 volumes. It is also seen that books recording the numbers of officials over time
often lacked literary quality and thus easily perished.
As for local records,
the names inscribed on the walls of Táng and Sòng government offices,
vanished with time,
and the ancient regulations in geographical treatises
no longer categorized officials,
was this not a deficiency in the records?
From the Yuán and Míng onward,
the gazetteers of prefectures and counties
often preserved the names of successive officeholders,
but due to the lack of method in recording,
they easily became confused,
which is something that must be rectified.
Some say that tabulating officials
is only suitable for the Three Dukes and chancellors,
and for prefectural and county gazetteers;
the former because the format is dignified and the rules strict,
the latter because the number of officials is small and easy to manage.
As for the gazetteers of provinces and prefectures,
the number of official positions is vast,
and limited space makes it difficult to complete,
if all are tabulated,

it is feared that it would be easy to arrange by year but difficult to arrange by office (the vertical axis is years, the horizontal axis is official ranks; with many officials, there is no room to lay out the grid).
If the principles are not precise,
and one merely struggles with the difficulty of managing the records,
this is why, after Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
the books became voluminous yet events were omitted.
The table of officials in Bān Gù's *History*,
though not extensive in length,
recorded details down to the Nine Ministers;
the tables of chancellors and ministers in the Táng and Sòng,
though twice as long,
only recorded up to the assistants and ministers.
This is not because ancient books were concise in recording events,
and later histories had complex formats,
but because the method of categorizing by class and appending
was not applied within the framework of years as the warp and events as the weft,
hence it was prone to inconsistencies,
making it difficult to manage complexity with simplicity.
Examining Bān Gù's *History*,
the table lists thirty-four offices,
with only fourteen rows;
some are grouped by evolution,
with notes in the first section on titles like Xiàngguó, Chéngxiàng, Fèngcháng, Tàicháng, etc.
some are grouped by official association,
sharing the same row;
such as Dàxínglìng and Dàhónglú sharing a row, Zuǒpíngyì and Jīngzhàoyǐn sharing a row, etc. The text is concise and easy to grasp,
events are grouped and thus clear,
so it enables readers
to consult it without missing anything.
If tabulating for a province,
then the Governor-General, Governor, Provincial Commander, and Garrison Commander, etc.,
can share one row.
The Provincial Administration Commissioner, Surveillance Commissioner, Circuit Intendant, etc.,
can share one row.
The rest can be divided by prefecture and subprefecture,
with officials under the prefecture
grouped in the same row,
which is certainly not harmful.
When compiling prefectural gazetteers,
each county can occupy a row,
and nothing will be omitted.
Thus, tabulating officials over time
is certainly not hindered by the lack of applicable rules,
especially since county gazetteers can certainly assign one row per official?
Below the name,
note the native place and examination rank,
since not all individuals are included in the political summaries,
noting their origins
also serves to save space in biographies.
If unavailable, leave it blank.
As for records from inscriptions,
if there is other evidence,
and they are supplemented in the gazetteer,
use the date from the inscription as the heading,
without further detailing the year of initial appointment
or the month of departure from office,
this is also a situation where nothing more can be done.
As for those whose dates cannot be verified but only their names are known,
then at the end of the chronological table,
list them horizontally to preserve the record,
which is also the intent of leaving doubts for later.
Preface and Principles for the Table of Examination Graduates in the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
The table of examination graduates
is a legacy of the ancients' records of the worthy.
In ancient times, selecting scholars
did not have specialized categories;
promoting the worthy to become leaders,
promoting the capable to govern;
recommending talent was equivalent to employing them,
employing people was equivalent to putting them to work.
The worthies, filial, and talented of the two Hàn,
as well as the appointments in prefectures and commanderies,
events are also seen in the annals and biographies,
so there is no need to seek separate records of examinations.
From the Suí and Táng onward,
examinations became specialized,
and qualifications became more important.
Regulations became numerous and detailed,
precedents were passed down,
books on examinations
piled up filling the shelves.
Thus, those recommended were not necessarily all employed,
and those employed were not necessarily all recorded in events.
Old regulations and precedents
could not be found in the annals and biographies,
so records of examinations
became a specialized section in historical gazetteers.
Gazetteer compilers recording examinations
do not understand the method of years as warp and events as weft,
generally dividing them into categories like jìnshì, jǔrén, gòngshēng, and military selections,
each in separate sections,
and placing jìnshì first,
with jǔrén and gòngshēng following in order.
Thus, for someone who advanced from gòngshēng to jǔrén and then to jìnshì,
one first sees the jìnshì examination year,
then searches for the provincial examination period,
and only at the end of the text learns the year of becoming a gòngshēng.
This is reversing the order of events,
and is the text not redundant?
Occasionally, some create tables with warp and weft,
but within the horizontal and vertical grid,
they annotate the facts.
Using the style of biographies to create chronological tables
is a flawed method from the Yuán compilers of the *Liáo* and *Jīn Histories*,
wasting space,
and confusing the layout,
I do not see what merit this has.
Tables in histories
are the index to the biographies.
Names listed in the table
but without a biography
are those without virtue worth mentioning,
and events are recorded briefly.
Those with biographies but not listed in the table
are those with events worth recording,
using the principle of special recording.
Now, gazetteer compilers,
under the sections for examinations and officials,
often mix in one or two facts;
as for the major deeds of the person's life,
they use a general summary,
compiled under the section for notable figures and officials;
then they take the full biography
and include it in the literature section;
here it says "see details under such-and-such,"
there it says "already listed under such-and-such,"
one person's affairs
appear repeatedly.
Even those who can make tables
cannot avoid annotating under the name in the table
that there is a biography,
how chaotic and imprecise this is!
Some tables have warp and weft,
others cannot have warp and weft.
For example, the annual gòngshēng of Yǒngqīng,
before the Jiājìng era,
seventy-seven people whose examination years cannot be verified,
if included, there is no row to place them,
if deleted, it is not satisfactory in principle,
so list their names before the Jiājìng examination records,
placed after the Zhèngdé examination records,
this is the *Spring and Autumn Annals* principle of placing leftovers at the end,
and the *Book of Changes* principle of ending with the hexagram *Wèijì*.
Sīmǎ Qiān's *Chronological Table of the Three Dynasties*,
from Xià Xiè onward,
having no warp and weft,
lists them without arranging horizontally and vertically,
this is also an ancient method that can be applied.
Preface and Principles for the Table of Gentry Families in the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
The recording of prominent clans in local gazetteers
is actually rooted in ancient practices,
not an innovation.
The Minor Scribe in the *Zhōu Guān*
"established genealogies and lineages,
distinguishing the order of ancestors and descendants."
Dù Zǐchūn's commentary states:
"Genealogies and lineages refer to records such as the lineage origins of feudal lords, ministers, and grand masters."
This is indeed the case.
The *Shū* says:
"To harmonize and distinguish the hundred surnames."
Zhèng Kāngchéng explained:
"The hundred surnames refer to the fathers, sons, brothers of the ministers."
To harmonize and distinguish means to differentiate and clarify them.
The ancient kings granted lands and divided surnames,
and the means to honor governance and clarify ethical order
all stemmed from this.
Therefore, to harmonize the myriad states,
one must first harmonize and distinguish the hundred surnames.
This institution is of utmost importance.
Scholars are also common people,
yet detailing scholar clans while neglecting common surnames
is still following the ancient way.
The *Zhōu Guān* states that the District Grand Master "annually registers the numbers of households and individuals,"
and every three years, through a great comparison, promotes the worthy and capable of the district.
Commoners are lowly, while scholars are esteemed;
thus, for households and individuals,
only their numbers are recorded;
but for the worthy and capable who become ministers and grand masters,
their genealogical records are detailed.
This shows that genealogical records
are more important than household registers,
a clear evidence indeed.
Modern local gazetteers
invariably record households and populations in detail,
yet records of genealogies
are silent and unheard of,
which also loses the principle of distinguishing importance from triviality.
People combine to form families,
families combine to form states,
and states combine to form the world.
The vastness of the world
begins with combining people into families.
Families cannot all be enumerated,
hence the importance of prominent clans.
Using prominent clans to lead the common people,
using prefectures and counties to oversee prominent clans,
using departments and offices to oversee prefectures and counties,
and using ministries and courts to oversee departments and offices—
then by grasping the simple to control the complex,
the world can be managed as if in the palm of one's hand.
Mèngzǐ said:
"When we speak of an old state,
we do not mean that it has tall trees,
but that it has ministers from old families."
If the records of prefectures and counties
can systematically arrange prominent clans,
thereby reaching departments, offices, ministries, and courts,
then ethical order will have connections,
and governance and transformation will have direction.
Today, those compiling gazetteers
often linger on old sites,
and force connections to their hometowns,
while the compilation of genealogies is neglected.
This is what is called valuing tall trees over old families.
If genealogies are managed by officials,
then affairs will have centralized control,
people will have registered records,
and the overall situation of the world can be balanced.
Now, south of the great river,
culture and scholarship are flourishing,
but customs tend toward superficiality.
Private family genealogies
often falsely claim connections to famous worthies,
extravagantly displaying virtues and achievements—
their fault is deception.
North of the great river,
customs are simple and unadorned,
and the people are mostly rustic and unrefined.
The study of genealogies
is lacking and incomplete;
often, descendants do not record the names of their great-grandfathers and grandfathers.
Occasionally, there are records,
but they are crude and difficult to verify—
their fault is crudeness.
Is there any place without people,
or any person without ancestors?
Yet such extreme biases toward deception and crudeness,
with abuses reaching such severity,
are due to genealogies not being managed by officials,
and historical authority lacking centralization.
Some say the ancients valued old families,
but later abuses
led to contention over social status.
After the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the Wáng, Xiè, Cuī, and Lú clans often clashed over pedigree;
and regarding family prestige,
even the worthy could not avoid bias.
How can this serve as a model?
This is not so.
The selection criteria of the Ministry of Personnel,
and the impartial judges in prefectures and commanderies,
should not determine appointments based solely on family status—
this is correct.
As for genealogies,
if managed by officials and clerks,
it is precisely to prevent loss and forgery,
and initially, there are no abuses.
Moreover, if clerks manage genealogies,
and the Ministry of Personnel registers the talented and virtuous,
then prominent families and great clans
without worthy members to lead,
or capable members to govern,
will be spurred to strive and distinguish themselves.
This is also a way to encourage talent.
Sīmǎ Qiān's genealogical tables
only recorded the origins of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors;
and the clan records in the *Chūnqiū*
only survive in Dù Yù's genealogical tables.
Thus, historians lost knowledge of clans.
Ōuyáng Xiū's *Genealogical Tables of Chancellors*
seems inspired by Liú Zhījī's allegorical suggestion;
the "Treatises" chapter of *Shǐ Tōng* proposed establishing clan records, but the intent was deliberative, not Liú's original purpose. However, the Hán clan of Dèngzhōu,
though not producing chancellors,
was included due to Hán Yù's fame,
showing an impure innovation in practice.
This is also an innovation that is not pure.
Wèi Shōu's *Official Clans* and Zhèng Qiáo's *Clans*
only record the origins of surnames,
without detailing branch lineages.
Thus, genealogical tables by historians
are only seen in Ōuyáng,
and later generations did not follow this method,
perhaps due to recognizing the impurity of Ōuyáng's example?
I humbly believe that compiling records of an era,
with vast and numerous documents,
values grasping the overall picture,
and clear judgment to decide inclusion or exclusion,
to create an enduring classic.
Genealogies need not be limited to chancellors;
prominent clans of a dynasty,
whose prestige endures alongside the state,
compiled into tables,
would not be overly voluminous.
If titled simply as "Prominent Clans,"
how could it be impure in practice?
Liú Xīn said:
"Rather than err by omission,
it is better to err by inclusion."
This applies here.
Official histories preserve the overall picture,
while gazetteers of ministries, offices, prefectures, and counties
gradually add detail.
As the saying goes: to go far, start from nearby;
to climb high, start from below.
Extensive collection by prefectures and counties
serves to provide material for the concise selection of official histories.
Some say:
Prefectures and counties vary in size,
and humble towns may not all have complete genealogies.
Yet within a single county,
there are already scholars and commoners.
Commoners can be counted by household,
while scholars naturally have lineages.
Others say:
Those above government students
are all called scholars.
In culturally rich regions,
there is fear of overwhelming numbers.
Then, adjust leniency or strictness
based on the region's prosperity.
Some may use provincial graduates as the standard,
others may use metropolitan graduates as the standard.
As for ministry and office gazetteers,
they may use officials of the fifth rank or third rank as the standard,
and there should be no fear of excessive detail.
The recording of events in gazetteers
is like a mirror reflecting an image.
A mirror of small diameter
shows the whole in miniature;
a mirror over a foot in size
shows the form more expansively.
There is no case where it is so limited that it cannot reflect an image.
If prefectural and county gazetteers
fully engrave genealogies,
then ancestral origins for official appointments and selections can be verified;
disputes over succession can be fairly adjudicated;
unofficial and unorthodox records can be corrected;
errors in official genealogies can be collated (collating official genealogies with private ones, or with genealogies from other counties, is possible).
Distinctions between pure and impure lineages can be made;
marital harmony, filial piety, and fraternal love can be encouraged.
All that aids governance and benefits scholars and commoners
can find its essentials here.
The ancient kings bestowed lands and divided surnames,
using the land to establish people,
how could they ever use people to establish the land?
When the feudal system was abolished,
people no longer had fixed residences.
Yet during the Six Dynasties, the commandery origins of clans,
when asking about the Xiè clan, one knew they were from Yángxià,
when asking about the Cuī clan, one knew they were from Qīnghé,
this shows that households were determined by their registers,
and the wards, markers, districts, and neighborhoods
were not empty designations.
As for places like Méilǐ and Zhèngxiāng,
they were esteemed for their human relations,
and the prominence of the locality depended on the people.
Therefore, in the tables of clans and lineages,
they are arranged according to the villages and neighborhoods where they resided.
First, within the city walls,
the main area governed by the county.
Next, the eastern region,
then the southern region,
and afterward the western countryside,
while the northern region is omitted as it had none,
recording the actual situation.
Within the city, north streets come before south streets,
as the方位 is north above and south below,
the方位 within the city walls is fixed.
For the four countryside regions, east and south come before west and north,
following the order in the "Tribute of Yǔ," which lists Qīng and Yǎn first,
then Yáng and Jīng,
and ends with Liáng and Yōng.
However, this is not an inflexible rule;
it can be adapted to the topography of a county,
and there is no issue with that.
All who served as scholars
are eligible to be listed in the tables,
while those without genealogical records are omitted.
Descendants who did not become scholars are not included,
but brothers, even if not scholars, are recorded,
to establish their order of seniority.
Those who became heirs to another line
are recorded under the line they succeeded,
without detailing their biological origins;
the records are kept brief,
as family genealogies can provide details.
Even if only a few individuals,
they are included in the genealogy;
if earlier generations are unverifiable,
they are still noted in the text;
for private records are easily lost,
while official genealogies are more likely preserved,
so it is urgent to record them,
so that later generations may verify and finalize them,
this is what is meant by establishing a preliminary example.
Private genealogies often list official ranks and honors granted,
but contain many errors.
For instance, assistant prefects and vice prefects are called "fēn fǔ,"
garrison commanders are called "shǒu fǔ,"
following vulgar custom.
For a "brocade-clad" chiliarch,
they are called "crown-belt general,"
or "imperial guard general,"
or "jīn wú,"
which is extremely crude and absurd,
making it unclear what official position they actually held.
Now, all such titles are compared, clarified, and corrected.
Also, many genealogies mention "provincial sacrifice officials,"
but it is unclear what title this refers to,
so it is retained as is,
but not included in the total count of officials.
Preface and Examples to the Maps of the Geography Section of the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The essential principles of historical works,
take the basic annals as the warp,
and the other forms as the weft.
Those with textual content
are called treatises and biographies;
those without textual content
are called tables and maps;
the substantial and the schematic complement each other,
detail and brevity are mutually illuminating,
so that there may be no omissions.
In the past, Sīmǎ Qiān established the one hundred and thirty chapters,
but only knew to base the tables on the Zhōu dynasty genealogies,
not realizing he could trace back to the Xià dynasty tripods for maps;
thus, the generations, sequences, and years of the ancients
could be deduced,
but the forms, features, names, and images of earlier times
left no trace;
this shows he learned the genealogical and chronological principles from the Spring and Autumn Annals,
but did not trace back to the "Images of the Changes" to understand the comprehensive nature of maps and charts.
The need for tables to bring order to the biographies
is like the need for maps to make the treatises clear.
Earlier scholars said that without tables, the biographies inevitably become冗长,
but they failed to realize that without maps, the treatises inevitably become冗长.
Alas!
From Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward,
for two thousand years,
no one has创立 this practice,
this is tracing matters to their source and following them to their end,
deeply regrettable for the one hundred and thirty chapters.
Zhèng Qiáo's "Brief on Maps and Charts,"
claimed to be a unique scholarly achievement;
but this is merely a method for cataloging book titles,
highlighting classification and arrangement.
In fact, the grand format of historical works,
should broadly collect and include,
preserving various scholarly traditions,
to guard against遗忘,
but Zhèng Qiáo failed to see this.
Moreover, in works like the Comprehensive Records,
the annals and biographies all follow the ancients.
Changing tables to genealogies,
renaming treatises as briefs,
the format could be considered complete.
Why only know to collect catalogs of maps and charts,
and not create a map format oneself,
to supplement what previous histories lacked;
to boast of this as something Hàn and Táng scholars had not heard of,
should one not feel ashamed?
Also, Zhèng Qiáo's cataloging of maps and charts,
claimed that centralized classification makes preservation easy,
while分散 classification leads to loss,
his argument seems reasonable.
But now, examining Zhèng Qiáo's classifications,
and checking the maps of previous dynasties against them,
their loss and dispersal
is not much different from before.
Thus, specialized scholarship
must be incorporated into the grand compilations of history,
not merely recorded in minor catalogs,
to ensure its preservation.
Sīmǎ Qiān created tables,
and the methods of the Zhōu genealogies
survive to this day;
Rén Hóng recorded maps (Zhèng Qiáo said: Rén Hóng collated military texts, which included both texts and maps; his method can be considered excellent.)
but the ceremonial institutions of the Hàn dynasty
were already不可考 by the Wèi and Jìn periods;
this shows that the achievement of cataloging is minor,
while the achievement of establishing a historical format is major,
the道理 is clear.
If history lacks tables,
the generations, sequences, and years
can still be pieced together from the text;
but if history lacks maps,
the forms, features, names, and images
cannot be sought from文字 alone.
This is why耳治 and目治 differ,
and why the essential importance of maps
surpasses that of tables.
The oral-aural learning of the ancients,
contained elements文字 could not capture,
valued for mental grasp and spiritual comprehension.
As for the study of images and maps,
it cannot be conveyed orally or aurally,
but is valued for direct visual observation and the presence of the道 within.
With the scholarship of Zhèng Kāngchéng,
relying on文字 to seek understanding,
the "suō zūn" vessel was interpreted as a "phoenix dance";
but once the ox-shaped vessel with the hollow back appeared,
Wáng Sù's interpretation prevailed.
With the scholarship of Kǒng Yǐngdá,
relying on textual meaning for explanation,
the Jiāng River's source was said to be from the Mín Mountains;
but once the course through the Jīnshā River was understood,
the distant flow recorded in the "Miǎn志" became known.
There is no other reason,
one was hindered by the loss of maps from the Three Dynasties,
the other was hindered by Bān Gù's "Treatise on Geography" lacking cartographic learning (The "Treatise on Geography" began with Bān Gù, hence the specific criticism).
Even for the diligent and深思 scholar,
reading history without seeing its maps
is like walking in darkness and groping the ground.
The gazetteers of the Tang and Song dynasties
were often titled "Illustrated Classics,"
while comprehensive geographical maps
originated from Xiāo Hé's collection of maps and records.
As for maps preserved from antiquity,
each era had its own works,
but because the Historiography Section did not include them,
they lacked the strength to survive independently through the ages.
Moreover, in terms of their form,
they contained no literary prose that could be memorized and studied,
nor could they be concisely compiled through editing;
their content belonged to specialized scholarship,
a field beyond the capabilities of literary scholars.
Since the Historiography Section did not engage in their compilation,
they were lost after being transmitted only once or twice.
For example, works like the "Sānfǔ Huángtú"
and "Yuánhé Túzhì"
now survive only as texts without their maps.
How could this have happened overnight?
In ancient times, there was no woodblock printing,
making it difficult to reproduce maps through copying;
moreover, the cumbersome nature of bamboo and silk scrolls
made it hard for every household to possess a copy.
Specialized scholars like Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
did not establish a standardized format for them,
and later generations, tracing the stream while forgetting the source,
naturally followed suit and neglected them.
Errors in interpreting the classics abound,
and reading history becomes bewildering,
all due to this.
Modern local gazetteers
often include maps,
yet they are rarely regarded as authoritative models.
The reasons for this are twofold:
First, they focus excessively on scenery,
with landscapes meticulously painted,
emphasizing artistic skill,
which is irrelevant to historical methodology.
Second, they are relegated to prefaces, tables of contents, or explanatory notes,
treated as trivial adornments,
without systematic explanations or titles,
or careful arrangement of sections,
thus failing to establish a proper form.
Tables have warp and weft but no explanatory text,
while maps have images but no warp and weft.
Both are essential summaries for treatises and biographies in historical works;
yet, following vulgar conventions,
they are treated merely as tools to please the eye.
Over time,
hoping to find surviving texts like the "Sānfǔ Huángtú" or "Yuánhé Túzhì"
becomes impossible,
let alone supplementing what Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù omitted
to achieve a grand spectacle in historiography!
Maps inherently lack warp and weft,
but geographical maps should roughly incorporate them.
Mèngzǐ said:
"To practice benevolent governance,
one must begin with defining boundaries."
The "Shìmíng" explains:
"North-south lines are the warp,
east-west lines are the weft."
Thus, the pursuit of warp and weft in geography is paramount.
Modern county and prefecture maps
often adjust the map's scale
based on the paper's dimensions;
this is an old habit from painting traditions
and should not be adopted in historical methodology.
Now, using grid squares to calculate distances as the warp
and marking counties, townships, villages, and hamlets as the weft
allows later readers
to consult the map grid by grid,
without the slightest error.
This is the true meaning of an "Illustrated Classic."
Preface and Guidelines for the Maps of Establishments in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The methods of the Xiàngwěi in the "Zhōuguān"
are no longer verifiable.
Later works like the "Sānfǔ Huángtú" and maps of Luòyáng palaces
served as models for capital cities and palaces.
The Jiànzhāng Palace had thousands of gates and doors,
yet Zhāng Huá could name them all;
Zhèng Qiáo attributed this to the effectiveness of studying maps
rather than reading texts.
Thus, maps of architectural layouts
are of great importance, are they not?
Zhūzǐ once wrote the "Yílǐ Shìgōng,"
arguing that without understanding the layout,
ritual procedures and measurements
would have no basis.
As ancient and modern palaces differ in design,
scholars relying solely on texts
may fail to comprehend them,
leading to the neglect of both maps and texts.
Future generations viewing our era
will be like us viewing antiquity.
City walls, government offices,
altars, temples, and shrines,
along with institutions and regulations,
are vital to the state and its people.
Without carefully documenting them in maps,
later readers of gazetteers
will have no guidance.
Since the time of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
historical works have lacked maps of establishments;
this is why, after the Yuán and Chéng eras,
discussions of the Míngtáng and ancestral temples
have been fraught with conflicting theories.
Shào Yōng said:
"The Way of Heaven appears in the south
and lies hidden in the north;
thus, people know what is before them
but are ignorant of what lies behind."
Most things in nature
turn their backs to the north and face south.
Therefore, when drawing maps,
one must orient them with south at the bottom and north at the top.
For mountains, rivers, and their orientations,
as well as the expanse of geography,
depicting them on maps
with north at the bottom and south at the top
still loses the proper sense of orientation.
For the layouts of temples, shrines, and government offices,
if north is placed at the bottom and south at the top,
eaves, plaques, gates, and doors
would no longer be correctly positioned.
Huáng Zhījùn of Huátíng,
referring to the Bāguà diagram,
with Qián (south) placed above
and Kūn (north) below,
argued that all maps should have south at the top.
He failed to realize that the Hétú, Luòshū, and "Xiāntiān/Hòutiān" diagrams
were only elaborated in the Song dynasty,
mistaking them for ancient artifacts.
Moreover, the essence of cosmological principles
establishes symbolic forms from the formless,
and should precisely correspond to their inherent positions.
Mountains, rivers, palaces,
and all tangible objects
are depicted in maps based on their forms,
and must be viewed as if facing them to be accurate.
For instance, when a person observes a Bāguà diagram,
if the person is seated facing south,
the observer should face north.
Thus, the Bāguà diagram
must have south at the bottom and north at the top.
This aligns with the natural order of things.
Formless principles,
like sunlight shining on eaves,
allow no deviation.
Tangible objects,
like reflections in a mirror,
are reversed when viewed face-to-face.
This is an inevitable aspect of map-making.
Those who blindly advocate antiquity
without considering rational coherence
are unqualified to discuss scholarly works.
Records of establishments document laws and institutions.
What falls outside institutional frameworks
should not be included in such records.
Modern local gazetteers
sometimes include ancient sites,
but ancient sites were not established by design.
Sometimes they include temples and monasteries,
but these do not qualify as institutional establishments.
Old gazetteer maps
lacked detailed institutional layouts
but featured illustrations of "Eight Scenes,"
with titles such as:
Autumn Waters at the Southern Bridge,
Spring Rainbows over the Three Pagodas,
Hánchéng's Lingering Horn,
Western Winds at the Hàn Temple,
Layered Verdure of the Western Hills,
Bell Tolls from Tōngzhèn,
Rhythmic Drums of Língquán,
and Goose Pass's Echoing Calls.
The names are vulgar and crude,
the concepts forced and contrived,
with no substantive value.
Therefore, all such content has been removed from this gazetteer,
including any related poems or inscriptions,
to uphold the rigor of historical form.
Moreover, elements like wind and moonlight are natural phenomena,
and spring and autumn are inevitable seasons.
Forcing them into scenic descriptions
with far-fetched and disjointed associations
can lead to absurdities.
Even within a single room,
dawn glow or evening sunlight,
morning sun or clear breeze,
from east, west, south, or north,
can be named based on association,
but what value does this hold?
Yet, those who enjoy composing such poems
and competing for contemporary fame,
with daily and monthly novelties,
chasing folly unawares,
should cease such practices.
Preface and Guidelines for the Watercourse Maps in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
Simǎ Qiān wrote the "Treatise on Rivers and Canals,"
and Bān Gù wrote the "Treatise on Ditches and Channels."
This is because geography serves as the warp,
and waterways as the weft.
Geography is fixed,
while water constantly shifts and changes.
This is why Bān Gù separated the "Treatise on Ditches and Channels" from the "Treatise on Geography."
However, rivers are naturally formed,
while canals are man-made.
Simǎ Qiān titled his work "Rivers and Canals"
to encompass both natural barriers and human efforts.
Bān Gù, on the other hand, named his work "Ditches and Channels,"
which refers to the methods of surveying land for water management,
such as the irrigation systems of the well-field system,
specifically under the purview of craftsmen.
But is it appropriate to equate the four-foot-wide channels and
the eight-foot-wide ditches
with the breaching of the Hùzǐ River or the flow into the sea at Jiéshí?
Thus, the titles of various historical works
follow Simǎ Qiān rather than Bān Gù,
and not without reason.
"Hé" is the name of one of the great rivers,
alongside the Jiāng, Hàn, Huái, and Jì.
Simǎ Qiān titled his work "Rivers and Canals"
because the methods of river management in the Hàn dynasty
were combined with the construction of canals like Zhèng and Bái,
without including rivers such as the Jiāng, Huái, Wèn, and Sì.
Hence, it was uniquely named after the Hé River.
The histories of the Sòng and Yuán dynasties
broadly covered water conservancy projects across the land,
such as the embankments and sluices of the Biàn, Luò, Zhāng, Cài, Jiāng, and Huái rivers,
preserving their systems,
yet their titles were also "Treatise on Rivers and Canals."
Moreover, they took the northern waterways
and uniformly named them as rivers—calling the Biàn not just Biàn but Biàn Hé, the Luò not just Luò but Luò Hé, and so on,
which is almost like drinking water and forgetting its source. (The "Classic of Waterways" refers to various waters without using "Hé" as a generic term.)
Using the name of one great river
to encompass all man-made canal systems,
including reservoirs and sluices,
may follow ancient naming conventions,
but it lacks adaptability.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Yǔ's management of water
followed the way of water."
If "waterways" were used as a general term,
with the methods embedded in the systems,
and titled as such in the treatises,
calling it "Waterways,"
would that not be better?
The name Yǒngdìng Hé
was bestowed by the Sacred Ancestor;
Hún Hé and Lúgōu
have been known since ancient times.
Titling it "Rivers and Canals"
is indeed appropriate;
however, waters like Jiǎnshuǐ and Yǎba
do not all flow into a single river.
Thus, labeling it "Waterways"
allows all the waters of the entire county
to be encompassed.
Geographical writings
generally fall into three categories:
historical changes, topography, and water conservancy.
Historical changes are best presented in tables,
while topography and water conservancy are best illustrated with maps,
neither of which can be fully conveyed through text alone.
Since Simǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
only written treatises have been produced,
without accompanying maps,
forcing readers to memorize
for examination purposes.
The overall layout of the land
must be clear to the eye
before it can be fully grasped in the mind.
If a discussion is clear in theory
but impossible to follow in practice,
is this not the fault of prioritizing literary form over practical utility?
The historical changes of place names
can be managed with tables,
but the historical changes of water conservancy
cannot be managed with tables.
Tables are for standardizing names,
not for standardizing forms.
Maps can capture forms,
but the historical changes of forms
cannot be fully conveyed by maps alone.
Therefore, maps should be created
according to the historical changes of forms,
so that viewers can understand at a glance.
The "Tribute of Yǔ" records geography
using mountains and rivers as markers,
with the boundaries of the nine provinces
determined accordingly.
Later scholars argued that mountains and rivers are fixed,
while boundaries change,
but this is a generalization.
The course of the Yǒngdìng Hé frequently shifts,
often changing its form
within a few years.
Using it to define boundaries
is unclear.
Now, using villages as the warp
and calculating distances with grid squares,
a fixed method is established.
Changes in the river's course
are recorded in the grid squares of villages,
following the ancient principle of mutual verification.
This treatise is written for a single county,
yet waters not belonging to Yǒngqīng
are also included in the maps.
What is the reason for this?
To clarify the sources and courses of the waters
and show the systematic efforts of water management.
Bān Gù's history only records events of the Western Hàn,
but his "Treatise on Geography"
traces back to the "Tribute of Yǔ" and "Offices of Zhōu."
This also shows the origins and development.
However, the method of grid squares and distance calculation
and the reasons for historical changes
are detailed only for Yǒngqīng,
without covering the entire river's topography,
reflecting the principle of prioritizing the main over the secondary.
Counties along the river
can follow this example,
and the historical records of managing the Yǒngdìng Hé
will thus be well-organized.
Discussion on the Six Treatises of the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The genre of historical treatises
is a legacy of ancient official rituals.
The Zhōu rituals were preserved in Lǔ,
and the "Zuǒzhuàn"
records institutions brilliantly,
though it cannot cover all offices.
Instead, it follows the classics in chronological order,
appearing intermittently as events unfold,
a necessity of its format.
Since Simǎ Qiān's eight treatises
and Bān Gù's ten treatises,
authors have acted on their own judgment,
unaware of the texts of the six canons,
making it difficult to systematize
the grand institutions of a dynasty.
Later historians followed this,
with arbitrary decisions on details and omissions,
lacking a balanced approach.
The origin of these flaws
dates back long ago.
Zhèng Qiáo once said that the origin of historical treatises
lies in the "Ěryǎ."
He specifically wrote about the "Six Scripts," "Seven Sounds," "Insects, Plants, and Trees," etc.,
hoping to intertwine classics and history.
This can be considered his own scholarly view.
But in terms of institutional creation,
it is fully covered in official rituals.
What he called the "Six Scripts" and "Seven Sounds,"
along with the explanation of terms and objects,
all originate from offices like the Minister of Education,
such as the masters and guardians,
whose duties these were.
As for the great principles and laws
that systematize the natural and human realms and propagate the kingly way,
how can the meaning of the "Ěryǎ"
fully encompass them?
The meaning of official rituals
is broad, and historical treatises
cannot be tied solely to the "Ěryǎ."
This道理 is easily seen.
Yǔwén modeled his work on the "Offices of Zhōu,"
and the Táng people compiled the "Six Canons."
Though not entirely conforming to antiquity,
they represent the regulations of their time.
Yet scholars like Niú Hóng and Liú Xù
failed to grasp the overarching principles
to systematically record the institutions of their era,
causing works like "Assembled Essentials" and "Assembled Canons"
to remain separate from historical treatises.
This is something worth deep reflection.
Throughout history, records and documents
are easily preserved when unified,
but difficult to rely upon when fragmented.
If one argues that institutional precedents are fully covered in works like *Huìyào* and *Huìdiǎn*,
and that the treatises in historical works
may thus focus on what the author deems important;
then the *Hànshū* treatises did not use Hàn official titles as their framework,
and Yìng Shào’s rituals
remain incomplete and fragmentary;
the *Jìnshū* treatises did not adopt Jìn official titles as their framework,
and Xú Xuānyú’s *Jìn Guānpǐn* (Xú’s *Rankings of Jìn Officials*)
has been lost and does not survive,
with many of the major principles and laws
consequently impossible to grasp in their entirety.
Moreover, focusing on what one deems important
is merely a private opinion of one school,
hardly suitable as a canonical standard.
If literature originates from institutions,
and institutions reside within official responsibilities;
extending this to its ultimate conclusion,
then establishing offices and institutions
is something even the sages did not treat as their private possession;
how then can historians
decide on details based solely on their own opinions?
The style of treatises should be uniform,
yet historians have erred through inconsistency.
The style of biographies is inherently varied,
yet historians have erred through imposing uniformity.
Statutes and institutions
fundamentally derive from the official *Rites*,
and their formats are originally distinct.
Yet some histories include an *Astronomical Treatise* but lack a *Geographical Treatise*,
or separate *Rites* and *Music* but combine *Military* and *Punishments*,
failing to use the contemporary official system as their framework,
resulting in the error of dispersion.
Biographies are based on the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
originally without fixed form,
structured by Sīmǎ Qiān,
who roughly indicated distinctions.
Praise and criticism, lament and admiration,
inclusion, exclusion, division, and combination—
within these lies the straightforward recording of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
as well as the subtle refinement of the poets,
difficult to constrain by a single standard.
Later historians categorized by type,
整齐ized order,
rigidly adhered to official ranks,
计较ed every minor detail,
daring not to deviate slightly,
resulting in the error of rigidity.
Dispersion and rigidity
are not the comprehensive approach of true authorship.
The compilation of local gazetteers for prefectures and counties
resembles the records of feudal states in antiquity.
Matters of administration, population, military, and justice
are present in miniature.
Today, while the official titles may not exist, the clerks remain,
and these are indeed where responsibilities lie,
where institutional precedents are most complete,
and where methods of governance are most fully embodied.
Moreover, the numbers of minor officials and clerks
were recorded in the *Zhōuguān*,
and their systems preserved in the *Huìdiǎn*,
while their duties encompass the statutes of an entire county,
truly comprehensive and capable of serving as a framework;
only because these individuals are lowly and not discussed by the gentry
have compilers of gazetteers not used them for material.
Yet when one enters a region and inquires about its affairs,
without this there is no way to grasp the essentials.
Thus, clerks are called lìngshǐ,
and the leading official is called diǎnshǐ.
Understanding that the "shǐ" in lìngshǐ and diǎnshǐ
is the same "shǐ" as in records and institutional precedents
allows one to grasp the essential principle of compiling gazetteers.
Today’s prefectures and counties
vary in complexity and circumstances,
and the institutional precedents and clerks
are established according to affairs,
not all corresponding to the six bureaus of administration, population, military, justice, rites, and works.
Yet when recording the affairs of a single county,
one should use that county’s institutions to structure the book,
and by presenting its general categories,
one can better reveal the county’s actual situation.
Official documents and registers lack literary elegance,
yet the literary expressions of a county
must trace their origins here,
though ordinary people use them daily without realizing it.
Now, by clarifying their framework,
revising and illuminating these records,
enabling people to follow the laws through the books,
and understand their duties through the laws,
then their work can be refined and transmitted to suitable individuals.
This is what the ancients meant by "when records are clear, all officials are well-governed,"
and it is this very principle.
Some say that books of institutional precedents
are each kept by specialized officials,
piled up layer upon layer,
and cannot be fully encompassed by the treatise style,
hence they are preserved in works like *Huìdiǎn* and *Huìyào*,
while historical treatises adopt a different approach.
This cannot be considered insightful.
The *Zhōuguān* outlines the grand framework of an era,
yet the three thousand rituals
are not said to be fully included under the Ministry of Rites;
the six chapters of the *Sīmǎ Fǎ*
are not said to be fully included under the Ministry of War;
yet by preserving the duties of the Minister of Rites and the Minister of War,
the essential principles of rites and military affairs
can be discussed with ease.
Moreover, just as Sīmǎ Qiān wrote the *Astronomical Treatise*,
yet the calendrical systems of the Tàichū period
are not fully seen in his writings.
Bān Gù composed the *Treatise on Literature*;
yet Liú Xīn’s *Seven Summaries*
are not fully preserved in his discussions.
Historians selectively adopt institutional precedents
to provide scholars with essential extracts;
compared to specialized books,
they cannot be expected to be equally detailed—
this is also due to circumstance.
Since they are not seeking detail,
and yet lack a framework to organize them,
then they become scattered and without method.
Using scattered and methodless writing
to categorize the statutes of an era—
no wonder it is difficult!
Some say that seeking institutional precedents from clerks
and using the six bureaus as a framework
would mean that the styles of annals, tables, maps, and books
could no longer be separated.
For example, tables on official selection
would belong to the Bureau of Administration,
maps on waterways
would belong to the Bureau of Works;
extending this to its limit,
a gazetteer would only contain six books—
why then separate different styles?
This also cannot be considered insightful.
The ancients wrote books,
each with its own principles and categories;
once principles and categories are distinguished,
they should not be forcibly combined.
Sīmǎ Qiān based his tables on ancient genealogies,
yet genealogical and calendrical books
were kept by the Grand Historian,
and the tabular format with horizontal and diagonal lines
is not said to be mixed into the six codes.
For charts and genealogies each have their specialized books,
while the treatise style
specifically emphasizes statutes and institutions,
and should naturally use the official system of an era as its framework.
This does not mean that specialized works with distinct formats
should all be混杂ed within it
to be considered comprehensive.
Moreover, just as the Six Arts were all managed by Zhōu officials,
yet the *Changes* is not recorded under the Grand Diviner,
and the *Songs* is not recorded under the Grand Master;
however, the names of the three *Changes*
are indeed seen under the Grand Diviner,
and the categories of the four *Songs*
are indeed recorded under the Grand Master—
this illustrates the principle.
The six ministers coordinated affairs,
interacting to achieve results,
which is why earlier scholars suspected that the Winter Offices were scattered among the other five.
Prefectures and counties adapt measures to local conditions,
especially without fixed methods.
For example, population registers are managed by the Bureau of Population,
yet household registration records
belong to the Bureau of Justice;
because registration records are not for tax purposes,
but intended for investigating wrongdoing.
Military students and military examination candidates are under the Ministry of War,
yet their management falls to the Bureau of Rites;
because students, whether civil or military,
are all within the schools,
and schools are connected to the examination system.
In the distinctions, combinations, details, and omissions,
seeking the reasons behind them and examining them—
is this not all scholarship?
Preface and Guidelines for the Administrative Summaries of the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
Modern gazetteer compilers,
take notable figures as the main framework,
with categories such as distinguished officials, local worthies, and sojourners,
listed as subheadings.
This practice originated from the unified gazetteers of the Yuán and Míng dynasties.
However, when compiling separate books for provinces, prefectures, and counties,
they also adopted the method of categorizing and compiling used in unified gazetteers,
which can be said to have lost the proper form.
The inappropriateness of categorizing and compiling notable figures
is explained in detail in the first chapter on exemplary biographies;
as for the inappropriateness of including distinguished officials among notable figures,
it stems from a lack of understanding of the genre of historical writing,
and thus a failure to grasp the principles of balance and judgment.
In ancient times, feudal lords governed their territories for generations,
and each state had its own chronicles, such as Yángshé Xī’s *Jìn Chūnqiū* and the *Yān Chūnqiū* cited by Mòzǐ.
Thus, when a ruler governed within his fief,
the first year of his reign simply followed the royal calendar.
After the abolition of feudalism and the establishment of commanderies and counties,
prefects and magistrates carried out imperial decrees,
even in remote regions thousands of miles away,
much like the local officials within the capital region.
The odes praising Zhào Gōng under the sweet pear tree,
and the songs of the Zhèng people for Zǐchǎn,
as well as the biographies of “Exemplary Officials” in the histories of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
all reflect how their reputations rose and fell with the times.
Apart from the official histories,
there were specialized works on prefectures and regions,
authored in ancient times,
whose principles and examples are not without merit.
Emperor Yuán of Liáng compiled the *Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn* (ten volumes, recorded in the *Suíshū*).
Hè’s work included the *Kuàijī Tàishǒu Zàn* (two volumes, recorded in the *Tángshū*).
Táng dynasty authors wrote the *Chéngdū Mùfǔ Jì* (two volumes, covering the period from Zhēnyuán to Xiántōng, recorded in the *Tángshū*).
These works selected individuals who served in those regions
and recorded their deeds and achievements.
These books were compiled separately,

and were not originally mixed with works like the *Guǎnglíng Lièshì Zhuàn* (by Huá Gé, recorded in the *Suíshū*), the *Kuàijī Xiānxián Zhuàn* (by Xiè Chéng, recorded in the *Suíshū*), or the *Yìbù Qíjiù Zhuàn* (by Chén Shòu, recorded in the *Suíshū*).
Thus, the virtuous local officials
and the distinguished local figures
were not originally grouped together like clouds following dragons;
indeed, their matters were as unrelated as wind and horses.
When arranging the accounts of distinguished officials,
they should not be placed in the same category as local worthies,
not only because guests and hosts differ in form,
but also because the details and brevity of their accounts vary in style.
Officials who served in a region
are selected for their contributions to that area,
promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
leaving a legacy of virtue among the people,
and thus deserve to be honored and remembered.
Otherwise, even if their learning resembled that of Yán Huí or Zēng Shēn,
or their conduct matched that of Lián Pō or Huì Shī,
if they brought no benefit to the county,
the gazetteer’s brush cannot overstep its bounds to record them,
as this is the principle.
If before taking office,
their local reputation was not favorable,
or after leaving office,
their later conduct was not consistent,
yet if they were temporarily exemplary officials,
their good governance in that region should still be recorded.
Wú Qǐ killed his wife,
yet achieved success in Xīhé;
the gazetteer should not dwell on past faults.
Huáng Bà became chancellor,
yet his reputation in Yǐngchuān diminished;
the gazetteer should not anticipate future outcomes.
Governance is paramount,
while other matters are secondary;
how can this be compared to compiling biographies
of local individuals,
tracing their entire lives,
in the same format?
Old gazetteers, under the section on officials,
fully recorded their administrative achievements,
while the section on distinguished officials was merely nominal,
with only a note under their names
stating, “details already recorded earlier.”
This not only inverts the roles of host and guest,
but also fails to distinguish between praise and criticism, selection and omission,
completely losing the *Chūnqiū* principle of recording events as they are.
The section on recommended officials serves as the framework for notable figures,
just as the section on officials serves as the framework for distinguished officials.
The inclusion of recommended officials and officials regardless of their virtue
is akin to including distinguished officials and notable figures regardless of their status,
though the examples differ, the principles are mutually supportive.
Having tables for recommended officials but no biographies for them,
or having tables for officials but no records of their governance,
allows readers to examine the sequence,
assess the reality based on the names,
with words devoid of praise or criticism yet conveying implicit judgment,
which can serve as encouragement for later generations.
The style of biographies is elaborate and literary,
while the style of governance summaries is straightforward and concise,
not because the writing differs in intent,
but because the nature of the matters dictates it.
Biographies encompass both major and minor details,
evaluating individuals,
grouping them like clans,
or dividing them like well-fields;
flexible and unrestrained,
they embody the imagery of the *Yì*;
expounding principles and strategies,
they reflect the substance of the *Shū*;
with praise and lament,
they capture the essence of the *Shī*;
intricate and detailed,
they follow the order of the *Lǐ*;
comparing events and composing narratives,
they adhere to the fundamental meaning of the *Chūnqiū*.
Possessing the discernment of human relationships,
exhausting the principles of things,
harboring aspirations spanning millennia,
extracting the essence of classics and commentaries,
and expressing them in writing,
they become unparalleled.
Thus, the talents of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
are not fully displayed in the basic annals, tables, and treatises,
but are fully manifested in the biographies.
As for the style of governance summaries,
the principle emphasizes rigor,
with the intent to remedy shortcomings,
constrained by chronological order,
focusing on the essentials of administration.
By refining and purifying the style,
it can guide the people of the region,
crown the biographies,
interweaving and organizing,
centered on key principles,
which is indeed difficult to convey to literary scholars.
Ancient works with warp but no weft
are generally termed “summaries.”
Péi Zǐyě took Shěn Yuē’s *Sòngshū*
and compiled it chronologically as a summary,
which is an example of this.
However, Liú Zhījī criticized Péi’s work for being called a summary
yet its text remaining verbose,
which shows a lack of understanding of the ancients’ intent.
The *Huángshí* and *Huáinán* (*Huángshígōng Sānlüè*, *Huáinánzǐ·Yàolüè*)
are chapters from the philosophical masters.
Zhāng Wēn and Yú Huàn (Zhāng Wēn’s *Sānshǐ Lüè*, Yú Huàn’s *Diǎnlüè*)
are texts from historical records.
Do they not also contain the idea of summarizing?
How can it be said that they all take brevity as their principle?
Recording the deeds of exemplary officials
is more challenging than recording local worthies.
Governance involves rewards and punishments,
which give rise to gratitude and resentment;
differing opinions among people
make it difficult to achieve consensus—this is the first challenge.
Affairs involve abolition and establishment,
which vary in difficulty;
perspectives from past and present differ—this is the second challenge.
Officials come and go,
unlike local descendants who remain;
thus, distant deeds are easily forgotten—this is the third challenge.
Exemplary officials are sincere and unadorned,
while cunning officials excel at embellishment;
commemorative stelae left behind
are often filled with exaggerated praise;
eulogies and blessings
are hard to verify with actual deeds—this is the fourth challenge.
When promoted to influential positions,
recorders dare not speak frankly;
when transferred to neighboring regions,
how can they avoid partiality?—this is the fifth challenge.
Worldly norms are full of taboos,
and people judge talent by success or failure;
occasional mistakes or impeachment
lead to labeling someone as unworthy—this is the sixth challenge.
Old gazetteers lack proper methods of recording,
and historical traces easily vanish;
even if general outlines can be provided,
specific dates and details remain unverifiable—this is the seventh challenge.
Knowing these difficulties,
one must still rely on what is heard and seen to preserve a rough outline,
doing one’s best under unavoidable circumstances,
and exercising even greater caution.
Biographies begin with the name,
followed by official background—
this is the fixed format of historical writing.
Governance summaries lead with the official title,
not only because the roles of guest and host dictate it,
but also to adhere to the principle of “understanding the meaning from the name,”
which should not be overlooked.
Old gazetteers categorized officials such as magistrates and assistant magistrates
without following the chronological order of their tenures,
which contradicts the intent of governance summaries,
and thus deserves no praise.
Preface and Examples for the Biographies in the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
A commentary is so called in relation to the classic,
as it serves to transmit and explain glosses,
elaborate on the meanings and implications,
and is only committed to writing when absolutely necessary.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng compiled and gathered precious documents,
providing a detailed account of the beginning and end of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
while Sīmǎ Qiān distinguished individuals into separate chapters,
labeling them as biographies and categorizing them,
which is how the name originated.
The classics are concise and rigorous in their intent,
while the commentaries are ornate and elegant in style.
As a result, literary figures followed the flow and forgot the source,
one after another composing commentaries without classics,
so that among the collected works of the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
there are numerous works in the form of biographies.
Some modern scholars argue that literary figures, not being official historians,
are not entitled to compose biographies.
Now, regarding the task of elucidating the classics,
if one pursues the trivial and neglects the essential,
and is judged by the standards of propriety,
they indeed have no defense.
Yet to invoke the role of official historians,
accusing them of overstepping their bounds,
would only provoke them to retort sarcastically,
asking how Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng, who were not official historians of Lǔ,
could also have composed commentaries.
Then such critics would have no way to justify themselves.
Moreover, even if one were an official historian,
without having compiled the basic annals,
how could they hastily proceed to write biographies?
This is why the principles of biography must be clearly understood.
Commentaries without classics
belong to the collected works of literary figures.
Classics without commentaries
are the gazetteers of local regions.
Collected works suffer from being overly ornate and unreliable,
while local gazetteers suffer from being brief and vulgar.
Since the conclusion of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
official historians have not understood the significance of the precious documents of the various states.
The records of prefectures and commanderies,
named "illustrated classics,"
over many generations,
lost their illustrations, leaving only the text isolated,
with the biographical form inadequately detailed,
causing these works to become hollow and ineffective.
Yuè Shǐ's "Huányǔ Jì,"
adopting the style of the "Yuánhé Zhì,"
only briefly preserved famous sites and historical traces
as embellishments.
Later, the Yuán and Míng "Yītǒng Zhì"
included categories such as figures, chaste women, distinguished officials, and sojourners,
alongside mountains, rivers, temples, and tombs,
arranged in classified order.
This is merely a specialized form of geography,
somewhat resembling a categorized compilation,
serving to supply literary figures with material for timely use,

and was never intended to carry significant weight. Yán Ruòqú wanted to remove the figures section from the "Yītǒng Zhì"; this view seems reasonable. In fact, such inclusions are harmless, and the ancients did not entirely reject them. After all, these matters are unrelated to the proper form of official history.
The gazetteers of prefectures and counties
originally possess the form of a state's history,
yet their compilers instead adopt the headings of the unified categorized compilations.
Can this be called extensive collection to prepare for the concise selection of the state history?
Biographies having titles
indicate that the emphasis is on events rather than individuals,
such as the chapters on "Rúlín" and "Xúnlì,"
which were not originally created for individuals like Shī, Mèng, Liángqiū, Gōng, Huáng, Zhuō, or Lǔ.
The differences among other categories of people
are not just ten or a hundredfold but thousands and tens of thousands.
If one insists on using two-character titles for all,
even Confucius said, "To compare men,
I have no leisure."
In Ōuyáng Xiū's "History of the Five Dynasties,"
everyone is labeled with their rank or category.
How can this be compared to the Spring and Autumn Annals' governance of the world,
where the sage discussed but did not pass judgment?
In local gazetteers,
events are excerpted and abridged,
classified and compiled by category,
leaving readers disinterested,
as if peering at a ledger of ghosts.
As for distinguished worthies and chaste women,
there are separate accounts, epitaphs, biographies, and inscriptions,
which are further fragmented into chapters
and placed under the "Yìwén" section.
Thus, with no alternative,
they merely add sub-notes,
saying here, "see details in such-and-such volume,"
and there, "already listed in such-and-such entry,"
resulting in repetition and overlap,
making it laborious for readers to peruse,
and one wonders why they trouble themselves so!
This is another aspect of biographical writing in gazetteers that requires deep and careful consideration.
Modern people,
based on what they have seen and heard,
compile biographies in sequence,
which is indeed appropriate.
As for ancient figures
already detailed in previous histories,
copying the original text of their historical biographies
without any alteration
also aligns with the principle of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù successively editing and narrating
without presuming to act on their own cleverness.
However,
in the writing of biographies in successive histories,
within a single work,
there is mutual detailing and abbreviation,
allowing readers to understand comprehensively through perusal.
Thus, in the biography of Chén Yú,
the deeds of Zhāng Ěr are also detailed,
and the administrative affairs of Guǎn Zhòng and Yàn Yīng
are fully covered in the chapter on Tàigōng.
This is clear evidence.
Now, having excerpted history to incorporate into gazetteers,
if one still retains the original text of the biographies
without adopting the cross-references in the historical texts,
how is this different from carving the mark of another boat
and seeking one's own lost sword?
If there are errors in the historical texts,
and the gazetteer compilers correct them,
they must explain the reasons for the corrections,
showing that their alterations
were not made lightly.
This is also due to the circumstances of the times,
hence Sīmǎ Guāng's "Tōngjiàn Kǎoyì"
cannot be equated with Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù's pioneering work.
As for the praise and criticism in historical texts,
since the Spring and Autumn Annals,
none have changed this practice.
Yet compilers of gazetteers
often adopt the strengths while concealing the shortcomings,
which is worse than not using the text at all,
as it would allow readers to remain unaware.
When gazetteer compilers select historical biographies to include in the "Yìwén" section,
they label them as "biography of so-and-so from such-and-such history."
But examining the biographical text, it does not reflect the intent of the history,
and seeking the reasons for the deletions and abridgments
yields no evidence.
Thus, attempting to conceal shortcomings
only ends up exposing them.
The order of historical biographies
generally follows chronological sequence;
otherwise, separate arrangements like Qū Yuán and Jiǎ Yì, or Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi, have specific intentions.
Comparing events and connecting narratives
is the teaching of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
where analogy and inspiration are preserved;
broad understanding and far-reaching insight
are the teaching of the Shàngshū,
where symbolism and transformation also converge.
To write biographies without understanding that the spirit resides in the people
is merely to compose self-reported age and status records for individuals.
Preface and Guidelines for the Biographies of Exemplary Women in the Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer
The biographies of exemplary women
record their fortune.
The biographies titled and categorized by historians—
such as Confucian scholars, literary figures, loyal and righteous individuals, upright officials,
and including the chapters on exemplary women—
are all arranged by category.
Since Fàn Yè and Wèi Shōu,
this practice has largely remained unchanged.
However, Confucian scholars and literary figures
have their own biographical traditions,
while loyal and righteous individuals and upright officials
are inscribed on metal and stone.
Moreover, such people are rare in any era,
and when they appear, it is not for a single reason.
Thus, the grand historian's collection
is easy to recognize.
But chaste women and virtuous wives
are often of humble status and obscure traces,
yet they uphold great righteousness
and exemplify human relationships.
No place lacks such people,
and no such person lacks stories.
However, they are distant and difficult to gather for the imperial envoys,
and public opinion takes them for granted.
Unfortunately, if they do not encounter the right time,
or if they encounter the right time but are entrusted to the wrong person,
even if they possess lofty conduct and extraordinary integrity,
they end up withering like grass and trees.
Is this not lamentable!
The old gazetteer of Yǒngqīng
listed only a few names of exemplary women;
upon reviewing the text,
the facts could not be verified,
which is the result of entrusting the task to the wrong person.
After the old gazetteer was compiled
and before the new edition was assembled,
for several decades in between,
there was almost nothing to record,
which is the result of not encountering the right time.
Now, through extensive collection and inquiry,
detailed accounts of their conduct and facts are prepared.
That they can be included in the biographies—
is this not their fortune?
To rejoice in their encounter
is to deeply mourn for those who did not encounter such fortune!
The term "Biographies of Women"
originated with Liú Xiàng,
but it does not refer solely to women of chastity.
If Cáo Zhāo, who valued her learning,
had been a man,
she would have been selected for the "Forest of Scholars."
If Cài Yǎn, who displayed her talent,
had been a man,
she would have been material for the "Garden of Literature."
Liú Zhījī criticized Fàn Yè's history for including a biography of Cài Yǎn,
but his argument is very mistaken;
yet later historians upheld it as a rule,
exclusively recording the category of chastity and fidelity.
If this principle were extended,
in historical records of men,
it would suffice to have only one section for loyal ministers;
this is called not understanding classification.
The biographies of women in Yǒngqīng
certainly do not include selections for the "Garden of Literature" or "Forest of Scholars,"
but if a woman's husband died before she was thirty,
and she lived past fifty,
the period of her widowhood in between
must also be a full thirty years;
if unfortunately she died young,
it must also be fifteen years later,
and if her husband was over forty,
the laws and regulations cannot but be thus.
The virtue of a woman's character
cannot be measured by years.
When Mù Bó died,
it was not necessarily before Jìng Jiāng was thirty;
when Qǐliáng's wife died,
it was not necessarily fifteen years after the battle of Jǔ.
Based on this reasoning,
we should only verify truth and falsehood,
and not be constrained by years.
The records of prefectures and counties,
being close at hand and easy to verify,
are not like laws and regulations which encompass many things,
and thus must maintain restrictions.
The histories of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù do not include "Biographies of Women,"
not because they omitted them;
Bā Qīng is mentioned in "Biographies of the Money-makers,"
Wén Jūn is attached to "Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,"
Tángshān is included in "Treatise on Literature,"
Tíyíng appears in "Treatise on Punishments,"
some for chastity, some for filial piety,
some for learning, some for literary talent,
standing out prominently;
not only Yáng Chǎng having a wise wife,
or Zhū Mǎichén having a foolish one.
The methods of Sīmǎ and Bān were concise,
still retaining the lingering style of the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and *Guóyǔ*,
not bothering to meticulously categorize;
just as the Four Haos and Jūn Píng are not labeled as recluses,
and Zōu, Méi, Yán, and Yuè are not designated as literary figures.
Lǐ Yánshòu's two histories, *Southern* and *Northern*,
came from the same author;
the *History of the Northern Dynasties* followed the titles of Wei and Sui,
specifically including "Biographies of Women";
the *History of the Southern Dynasties*, having no original title for biographies of women,
placed Xiāo Jiǎo's wife Yáng and others
mixed into the chapter on "Filial Piety and Righteousness";
thus causing men and women in one volume
to have no distinction,
and without any special meaning,
this is simply called confusion,
and cannot be falsely attributed to the examples of Sīmǎ and Bān.
As for chapters on categorized clans,
they also reflect the intent of hereditary houses,
such as the descendants and branches of the Wáng, Xiè, Cuī, and Lú families,
spanning generations in the same chapter;
Wáng, Xiè, Cuī, and Lú were originally separated by dynasty in their respective histories, but Lǐ combined them into one place. Also, Lǐ's work has its strengths,
and one flaw should not obscure its other merits.
Now, for the chapter "Biographies of Women,"
I establish my own principles.
Those who are included by association,
such as a mother-in-law advanced in years with virtuous conduct,
or a young daughter-in-law displaying exemplary behavior,

I follow Liú Xiàng's example Liú Xiàng's example: "Biographies of Women" lists women's conduct, not strictly limited to chastity and fidelity. Attaching mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law together also reflects the intent of hereditary houses.
and compile them together,
which is called taking what others discard.
Some matters relate to the three obediences,
and conduct detailed within a clan,
although they are the main text on chastity,
they are also placed in separate categories;
such as Liú's widow who maintained her chastity and was included in the biographies of the righteous gate. This ensures events are systematically connected,
and principles are not fragmented,
not rigidly bound by titles,
still adhering to the methods of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
which is called separating what others combine.
The style of biographies in Fàn's history,
with each person as a separate chapter,
and each chapter having its own commentary,
completely loses the combined biographies of Sīmǎ and Bān,

who followed the *Spring and Autumn Annals* in grouping events and composing narratives Sīmǎ and Bān's division and combination of chapters have deep meaning, unlike Fàn's history which merely fills volumes.
