Therefore, the *Book of Han*, in places with heavy content, prefers to divide into upper, middle, and lower parts while still being one chapter, rather than splitting the chapter into one, two, three.
As for the chapter "Biographies of Women,"
the preface clearly states it is not limited to one virtue The preface says: "Recording their outstanding qualities, not limited to one virtue."
yet they are mixed in compilation,

without separate commentaries for each In other biographies, often after one person's story ends, a judgment is made, breaking the style. Here, where division is appropriate, there is conversely no judgment.
How contradictory, each making its own error?
In the biographies in this gazetteer,
I dare not arbitrarily divide or combine,
breaking the style to add commentaries.
Only in this "Biographies of Women" chapter,
I reference Liú Xiàng's original intent Biographies are not limited to one virtue; each person is given a eulogy.
each is given commentary,
which also follows the poets' intent of praise.
For matters that are ordinary,
with no special principles,
I will not elaborate further.
The Grand Historian's titles,
were not bound by rigid rules At the beginning of biographies, he directly called them "Chief Commandant Zhāng," "General Lǐ," etc.
reflecting the legacy of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* and various philosophers in naming chapters according to intent.
By the time of Bān's biographies,
names were no longer borrowed.
Fàn's biographies
all use Bān's method;
but in the "Biographies of Women" chapter,
each section begins with the woman's native place and her husband's name,
since it is not a geographical record,
why put the place name first?
And since it is not about men,
why mention the husband's name first?

This already loses the meaning of titling the chapter "Biographies of Women" It should say "so-and-so, wife of so-and-so from such-and-such commandery," not "so-and-so commandery, so-and-so's wife so-and-so."
As for the two women Cáo É and Shūxiān Xióng,
they are additionally labeled "filial daughters"
above their names,
how could Fàn Yè be so unbothered by the trouble?
Since the chapter is titled "Biographies of Women,"
Cáo Zhāo is not labeled a virtuous mother,
Cài Yǎn is not labeled a talented woman,
Huángfǔ is not called a chaste widow,
Páng is not called a filial daughter-in-law,
so the embellishments for É and Xióng
do not align with the *Spring and Autumn Annals* principle of recording events directly,
letting good and evil reveal themselves.
In later ages, writing
even reached the point of narrating women's deeds
without recording their surnames,
but directly using "chaste woman" or "virtuous widow" in place of their names,
how is this different from imperial examination essays,
where in the opening the person is not named,
but called "sage," "great worthy," "worthy person," or "people of the time"?
This indeed stems from Fàn Yè.
Now, I begin each section with the woman's surname,
placing her husband's name and paternal clan below,
and detailing her village,
to serve as evidence for future divisions of townships and counties.
As for deeds of chastity, fidelity, and filial piety,
they are clear from the text,
and I will not forcibly create labels,

allowing readers to understand in detail Women are referred to by surname, Zhāng or Lǐ, which is acceptable. Nowadays, if not called "virtuous widow" or "chaste woman," they are called "so-and-so's wife"; the ancients did not have this practice. Calling them "virtuous widow" or "chaste woman" is like an essay opening. Calling them "so-and-so's wife" is like a legal document format.
The order roughly follows chronological sequence.
Those from the same clan
are grouped together;
for those whose era cannot be determined,
they are approximately attached.
If there are no events to narrate,
I still detail their marriage dates,
and their current age if living,
because what makes each person's face different
is only this small detail. Alas!
People may find this troublesome For those whose age is not recorded, it is because inquiry yielded no result.
Preface to the Biographies of Missing Persons in the *Gazetteer of Yǒngqīng County*
The principle of historians omitting uncertain texts
is fully embodied in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Since the two Hàn dynasties,
Fú Shēng and Zhèng Xuán transmitted the classics,
while Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù composed histories;
the classics adhered to the teachings of masters,
whereas histories were shaped by personal judgment.
Thus, the Six Classics contain passages with missing bamboo slips,

yet the Three Commentaries lack examples of preserving divergent accounts (The Gongyang and Guliang traditions record different accounts not found in the Zuozhuan; the Zuozhuan includes separate accounts not preserved in the Gongyang and Guliang).
Since the classics are revered and their commentaries distinguish their texts,
therefore, favoring one and rejecting another
does not hinder the simultaneous inclusion of both;
histories are straightforward, and their narratives are unified,
so through omissions, the brushwork is clarified,
and it is not permissible to preserve both accounts—
such is the natural tendency.
Sīmǎ Qiān initiated the method of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
creating the annals and biographies format.
In dealing with differing accounts from hearsay,
he weighed and selected them,
which can be said to be cautious.
However, the stone chambers and metal cabinets,
the ancient records left behind,
the famous mountains and great rivers,
all added to what was seen and heard.
The principle stated in his preface, "where there is doubt, omit it,"
along with discrepancies in ancient texts,
as well as gaps in the records,
and the scattered fragments occasionally seen in other accounts—
he only recorded what he selected,
without clarifying the reason for his selection;
he considered it an omission,
but did not preserve the reasoning behind the omission.
This is like standing on tiptoe and reaching down to the Yellow Springs—
beyond the space for one's feet,
everything else is discarded.
The Master said:
"Hear much and omit what is doubtful;
speak cautiously of the rest."
To hear much and preserve doubt as omission
is the height of caution.
From Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù onward,
preserving what is credible without recording the doubts for later inquiry
is simply what is called deleting what is doubtful,
so what omission remains?
There are three principles for omitting doubts:
First, when one event has two accounts and it is difficult to reconcile them,
as in the Spring and Autumn Annals recording the death of Marquis Bào of Chén,
preserving both the texts of Jiǎxū and Jǐchǒu.
Second, when an old text exists but its explanation is now lost,
as in the Spring and Autumn Annals recording "Xiàwǔ" and "Guōgōng."
Third, when cautiously recording what is heard or seen without offering an explanation,
as in the Spring and Autumn Annals recording "the fixed stars are not seen,"
without mentioning the falling of fixed stars.
Hán Fēi's "Chǔ Shuō,"
arranging events from the Spring and Autumn period,
whenever there were differences,
would add "some say" and so forth,
and note it below the main text—
this is the example of Jiǎxū and Jǐchǒu.
Mencius mentions Xiànzǐ's five friends,
but only records two—
this is the example of "Guōgōng" and "Xiàwǔ."
The "Tángōng" records "the horses were startled and the battle was lost,"
but does not record "the horses were hit by stray arrows"—
this is the example of "the fixed stars are not seen."
Since Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
there have been those who recorded what they heard or seen to convey meaning;
however,
recording one event in two ways,
or merely preserving the title of an event,
is unheard of.
If it is said that the classic texts are clarified through commentaries,
and historical writing is not suited to annotating and explaining itself,
then setting aside separate chapters
and clearly noting omissions and doubts for later inquiry
does not seem harmful to the format.
The absence of a chapter for omitted inquiries in histories
leads to ten drawbacks.
First, using one's own views
to reconcile various accounts,
if slightly biased,
leaves later generations no way to correct it—
this is the first drawback.
Second, talented scholars, intent on seeking novelty,
and literary men, reluctant to part with their favorites,
indiscriminately include materials in their writings,
harming the historical format;
if cut and not recorded,
the sentiment and literary quality are lost—
this is the second drawback.
Third, hearsay inevitably has differences,
and it is difficult to completely erase its traces;
if not broadly summarized and listed,
then unofficial accounts and miscellaneous sayings
will arise and cause confusion—
this is the third drawback.
Fourth, initially because facts were unclear,
they were temporarily set aside and not recorded;
later, the event titles were omitted,
akin to clay oxen entering the sea—
this is the fourth drawback.
Fifth, records are easily scattered and hard to gather;
if not preserved as evidence in outline,
then the writings of an era
will be lost along with their chapter titles,
and later generations, even if they wish to investigate,
will have no source to trace—
this is the fifth drawback.
Sixth, recording based on what is seen or heard at the time
is easy to preserve;
later generations, piecing together fragments,
waste words and labor,
and still find it hard to obtain the truth—
this is the sixth drawback.
Seventh, the Spring and Autumn Annals had oral transmissions,
and Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù had specialized learning;
the tradition of historiography has long been lost,
and it is hard to expect it from Sīmǎ Qiān's grandson-in-law
or Bān Gù's sister;
without preserving omitted inquiries,
the original intent becomes difficult to clarify—
this is the seventh drawback.
Eighth, the conception and titling of historical biographies,
such as "Lǎozhuāng" and "Qūjiǎ,"
or categorical narratives with titles,
such as "Xúnlì" and "Rúlín,"
all have fixed positions in historical methodology,
and there is certainly no room for appended side texts.
All events that are briefly mentioned or unclear,
or doubtful and hard to decide,
if not preserved in a chapter for omitted inquiries,
must be attached within the main text,
leading to unclear categorization,
and the writing难以称得上纯粹简洁—
this is the eighth drawback.
Ninth, when opening a bureau to compile a history,
disputes over right and wrong arise;
descendants wish to glorify their ancestors,
and factions each promote their private interests.
If there is no evidence from metal or stone inscriptions,
and hearsay is hard to believe,
without establishing omitted inquiries

to prevent endless petitions (if facts are still lacking, and what is said is as such, cautiously preserve the outline and allow for later investigation, then even biased individuals will have no grounds to start disputes),
there is no way to reject one-sided claims—
this is the ninth drawback.
Tenth, if history lacks independent judgment and conception,
it is like clerical records;
if it possesses independent judgment and conception,
but does not use omitted inquiries to provide补救,
then without the talent of the Uncrowned King,
the editing will surely be biased—
this is the tenth drawback.
Some say that history reached its peak with Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and they have never heard of such meticulousness.
Now, if we must take the distant example of the Spring and Autumn Annals
and the recent lineage of the Shǐjì and Hànshū,
have later historians also seen and addressed this?
The answer is:
Later histories all follow the Shǐjì and Hànshū.
Methods not established in the Shǐjì and Hànshū
were created by later generations according to their ideas,
mostly resembling categorized compilations,
which Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù rejected and did not adopt.
Even striving to follow Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
is still feared to be insufficient,
let alone creating new ideas to remedy their shortcomings?
However, there are those who glimpsed a thing or two
and subtly preserved the intent—
their contributions should not be entirely dismissed.
Chén Shòu's "Shǔzhì,"
because Zhūgě Liàng did not establish official historians,
and Shǔ affairs were difficult to search and inquire about,
thus at the end of the fifteen biographies,
uniquely included Yáng Xì's "Praise of the Ministers of Jì Hàn"
and the "Miscellaneous Records of the Elders of Yìbù" to supplement it.
Cháng Qú's "Huáyáng Guózhì,"
regarding the famous virtuous and chaste women of Hànzhōng,
passed down over time,
but with lost words and anecdotes
that could not be verified,
in the "Xùzhì" chapter,
listed their names
without any editing.
This seems to have grasped the intent of "hearing much and omitting doubts."
It is a pity that they did not establish general principles and examples,
nor specially create dedicated chapters;
later generations had no time to explore their underlying meanings,
thus allowing arbitrary scholarship
and categorized books
to follow one after another in the world,
and the essence of the Spring and Autumn Annals faded.
In modern prefectural and county gazetteers,
it is customary to compile a section on notable figures,
placing it among sections on mountains and rivers, temples and tombs, local products and native goods,
while the style of biographies in earlier histories
is no longer considered.
Those with great achievements and merits,
as well as those with hidden virtues and subtle brilliance,
are all constrained within brief summaries of a few inches,
arranged and compiled in sequence,
somewhat like encyclopedias;
the style is thus debased,
and the selection becomes indiscriminate and excessive.
The old gazetteers record
only a few figures,
and in their praise,
there is no distinction,
all scholars are likened to Fú Shēng and Zhèng Xuán,
all talents to Bān Gù and Yáng Xióng,
all officials to Gǒng Suì and Huáng Bà,
all conduct to Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Yú.
Moreover, the literary style
is particularly incomprehensible,
sometimes resembling superficial polite phrases,
sometimes like official documents and dispatches,
filled with empty parallel phrases,
intermixed with examination-style sentences,
so that matching names with realities
leaves one bewildered upon opening the book.
All such cases
may involve ordinary deeds of locals,
included through improper requests;
or famous figures of the time,
whose facts have been lost;
to omit them would be unjust to the deceased,
to include them would violate biographical conventions.
Again, some events have two accounts,
with discrepancies and similarities,
to favor one would create stark praise or blame,
to include both would leave evaluation indecisive,
seeking to avoid fault in name and reality,
placement is truly difficult.
As for modern individuals,
submitted accounts of their deeds
are all thoroughly inquired from beginning to end,
leaving no detail omitted,
fully compiled into biographies,
with no limitation of era;
among them are those with notable surnames,
but whose actual conduct is not distinguished,
included in miscellaneous records,
they may be concealed,
but to place them in the style of historical biographies
is hardly permissible.
Now, to separately compile a section for missing inquiries,
sharing the chapter of biographies,
each with its own heading,
can complement the formally included biographies,
mutually illuminating each other.
Thus, I explain its principles and examples,
so that later generations may know how to examine and determine.
Preface to the Biographies Section of the Former Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer.
When historians complete their works,
they must gather previous writings
and compile them together;
this is to distinguish the origins of scholarly traditions,
and clarify the sources of their judgments.
Sīmǎ Tán’s discussion of the six schools of thought
was still like Zhuāngzǐ’s accounts of Qín Gǔlí and Mò Dí,
or Xúnzǐ’s critiques of the twelve schools.
But in Sīmǎ Qiān’s “Preface to the Twelve Feudal Lords Table,”
he repeatedly elucidates the purposes behind the works on the *Spring and Autumn Annals* by Lǚ Bùwéi, Yú Qīng, Duó Jiāo, and Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
which are the sources
he repeatedly clarifies as the intent behind their writings,

and this is what the one hundred thirty chapters of the *Records of the Grand Historian* follow and elaborate upon. Sīmǎ Qiān’s continuation of the *Spring and Autumn Annals* follows the intentions of Yú, Lǚ, Duó, and Zuǒ; those who criticize him for overstepping are mistaken.
When Bān Gù wrote Sīmǎ Qiān’s biography,
and Fàn Yè wrote Bān Gù’s biography,
scholarly traditions were preserved.
But when Shěn Yuē wrote Fàn Yè’s biography,
and Yáo Chá wrote Shěn Yuē’s biography,
they did not emphasize the historical works as dedicated sections,
and thus historians no longer followed the method of tracing scholarly origins.
Now, in compiling this gazetteer,
if we do not write biographies for previous gazetteers,
it would be outright appropriating others’ work and erasing their names,
even worse than Shěn and Yáo not preserving scholarly traditions.
For the old gazetteers of prefectures and counties are easily lost,
unlike Fàn’s *History* and Shěn’s *Book*, which have the strength to endure.
The importance of recording for historians
is like the importance of classical masters in the *Forest of Scholars*,
or authors in the *Garden of Literature*.
The *Forest of Scholars Biographies* should clarify the dissemination of the great Way,
and the origins of master-disciple transmission;
the *Garden of Literature Biographies* should clarify the changes in literary trends,
and the different schools of writers;
this is what is meant by historical works,
not merely recording events,
but also elucidating principles.
If the *Forest of Scholars* and *Garden of Literature* cannot elucidate the essence of the Way,
but only narrate a few deeds of scholars and literati,
they have already lost the original intent of these chapters.
Moreover, the importance of historiography,
which traces back to the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
is such that later histories not having dedicated chapters
causes specialized scholarly works
to be obscured and unexamined,
is this not a grave oversight by historians?
With standard histories existing,
yet lacking dedicated biographies,
the flaws are already thus,
how much more for prefectural and county records,
which are minor and easily overlooked,
should they not have dedicated records?
When a work is unfinished,
it must draw from sources,
such as Sīmǎ Qiān’s reliance on the *Shìběn* and *Strategies of the Warring States*,
or Bān Gù’s reliance on Féng Shāng and Liú Xīn,
this is so.
When a work is completed,
it must have its transmission,
such as Yáng Yùn’s dissemination of Sīmǎ Qiān’s work,
or Mǎ Róng’s reception of Hàn history,
this is so.
When a work becomes established,
it must have those who study and critique it,
such as Xú Guǎng and Cuī Yīn annotating Sīmǎ,
or Fú Qián and Yīng Shào explicating Bān,
this is so.
This is why scholarly traditions and origins must be clarified through dedicated biographical chapters.
After Mǎ and Bān,
scholarly traditions gradually declined. Referring to family-transmitted scholarly traditions.
But outstanding individuals
established distinctive scholarly schools,
such as the various authors of the *History of the Later Han*: Sīmǎ Biāo, Huá Qiáo, Xiè Chéng, Fàn Yèzōng,
and the eighteen authors of the *History of the Jin* like Hé Fǎshèng,
this is so.
Recording the same dynasty’s history,
yet without historians holding dedicated offices,
each person compiles independently,
each family offers its own interpretation;
without narrating and discussing,
gathering them into a single chapter,
how can a balanced judgment be reached?
This is why the different schools must be clarified through dedicated biographical chapters.
After the Six Dynasties,
distinctive schools declined again. Father-son transmission constitutes family learning; individual exceptional compilation constitutes a distinctive school.
And the method of compiling works collectively arose,
such as the Táng compilation of the *History of the Jin*,
or the Yuán compilation of the three histories of *Sòng*, *Liáo*, and *Jīn*,
this is so.
Supervising ministers
have their names listed at the beginning,
but the compiling and editing officials
are variably visible or hidden.
Even if some are occasionally noted as participating in the historical work,
which annals or tables were compiled by whom,
which treatises or biographies were edited by whom,
who drafted the regulations,
who polished the literary style,
without systematically combining
and tracing each to its source,
inevitably within one work,
strengths and weaknesses appear mixed,
and contributions and faults are hard to discern.
This is why the efforts behind a work must be clarified through dedicated biographical chapters.
As for methods like daily records and court diaries,
collections in imperial libraries,
systems of submitting petitions and debating posthumous titles,
or gathering unofficial histories and anecdotes,
these can be detailed in the preface to a biography,
explaining the system clearly;
or discussed at the end of a biography,
elaborating on their origins,
any approach is feasible.
This is like the *Forest of Scholars Biographies* preface,
clarifying the educational system,
reflecting the original intent of establishing official academic posts.
If this idea is truly understood and applied to writing,
one need not worry that historiography will not flourish,
or that the principles of history will remain unclear,
such a thing has never been heard of.
Local gazetteers are the records of a county,
equivalent to the histories of ancient states,
yet people often neglect them;
this is because family learning is not established,
the transmission of scholarly traditions is lost,
the writing lacks elegance and refinement,
making it difficult to serve as enduring models.
When a new compilation is completed,
the old books are cast aside like discarded jar covers,
not necessarily because the new books are all superior,
or the old gazetteers entirely inferior.
What the old gazetteers contain,
the new ones redundantly record again,
whether the editing is good or bad,
is initially not examined;
but what the old gazetteers failed to include,
the new ones inevitably add,
which is the first reason old gazetteers are easily discarded.
Compilers and authors
love to flaunt their own strengths,
and later works
easily criticize earlier ones.
Often, those who compile gazetteers,
when establishing their guidelines,
either claim the old books are crude and shallow,
or say previous authors lacked evidence,
with later ones attacking the earlier,
imitating faults endlessly.
In reality, like the monkey trainer swapping three and four,
there is no great difference;
but since predecessors are gone,
there is no way to verify,
which is the second reason old gazetteers are easily discarded.
County and prefecture records
are mostly crude and shallow,
so literati and scholars
set them aside unread.
Those who specifically search and gather them,
drawing on auxiliary sources for verification,
merely use them to corroborate other materials,
not out of genuine delight in the books themselves.
When old and new editions
are placed side by side,
those who browse them
are like examination candidates
purchasing model essays,
or yīn-yáng practitioners
consulting almanacs:
they take the new and discard the old,
a natural tendency,
not due to any particular discernment,
which is the third reason old gazetteers are easily discarded.
Now, Suǒ Suǐ’s *Chūnqiū* (Suǒ Suǐ compiled the *Qián Liáng Chūnqiū*),
relied entirely on Biān Liú;
Liú, commissioned by Zhāng Jùn, collected internal and external affairs of Liáng. Cháng Qú’s *Guózhi* (the *Huáyáng Guózhi*),
half borrowed from Qiáo Zhōu (the *Huáyáng Guózhi* records the Lǐ clan’s history. Its accounts of the Liú clan largely draw from Qiáo Zhōu’s *Shǔ Běnjì*).
Thus, records of a region
cannot do without the historical accounts of that region,
yet gazetteer compilers do not preserve predecessors’ transmissions—
is this not “forgetting the trap once the fish is caught,”
a habit gone unnoticed?
Then why wonder that local gazetteers
are lost and hard to examine?
The officials in charge of compilation
and the writers recording events
compose texts
without distinguishing name and substance;
this is the first difficulty in transmitting earlier gazetteers.
Prefaces and postscripts are empty formalities,
offering no elucidation of the work;
this is the second difficulty in transmitting earlier gazetteers.
If there were elucidation, then like Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù including their own prefaces, they could serve as transmissions.
The compilers’
conduct and achievements are unclear;
this is the third difficulty in transmitting earlier gazetteers.
The sources from which the book draws
are not indicated;
this is the fourth difficulty in transmitting earlier gazetteers.
Gazetteers should be successively continued;
unless absolutely necessary,
they should not be repeatedly revised;
for repeatedly revised books
to be preserved together
is cumbersome and unsustainable;
this is the fifth difficulty in transmitting earlier gazetteers.
Amid these difficulties in transmission,
to create a transmission for them
is a不得已 measure to preserve them,
clarifying the reasons
to set an example for later generations.
Preface to the Literary Selections of the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*
Upon completion of the *Yǒngqīng County Gazetteer*,
it is divided into six formats: annals, tables, maps, documents, administrative summaries, and biographies,
comprising twenty-five chapters in total,
each with its own guidelines.
Additionally, the collected stories and writings gathered at the time,
selected for their relevance to Yǒngqīng but unsuitable for inclusion in the main gazetteer,
are further categorized by type
into memorials, factual records, discourses, and poetry,
each forming one volume,
totaling four volumes.
Each volume has a descriptive catalog as below,
with a general preface outlining the main intent
placed at the beginning of the compilation.
The preface states:
In ancient times, there were officials with specific duties,
hence there were specifically managed records;
there were specialized fields of learning,
hence there were expert writings;
there was no such practice as broadly collecting various authors
and compiling diverse genres
as in later literary anthologies like *Wénxuǎn*.
When official posts were lost and learning declined,
literary embellishment proliferated.
According to personal preferences,
selecting famous and elegant works,
such as Xiāo Tǒng’s *Wénxuǎn*
and Yáo Xuàn’s *Wéncuì*,
exemplifies this.
Tracing the flow back to its source,
extending it to principles of governance,
as in *Sòng Wénzhī Jiàn*,
is another approach.
Examining substance and unfolding style,
advancing to serve as a supplement to history,
as in *Yuán Wénzhī Lèi*,
is yet another.
The intentions of these compilers
can be said to be most earnest.
However, considering the ancient fifteen *Guófēng*, the eight states’ *Guóyǔ*,
as well as *Jìn Shèng*, *Chǔ Táowù*, and the purposes derived from various states’ *Chūnqiū*,
it is clear that the historical records of the states
and their proclamations and odes
complemented each other.
In the past, this was not without precedent.
Táng dynasty historian Liú Zhījī once lamented that historical formats made recording speeches cumbersome,
proposing to take edicts, proclamations, memorials, and the like,
categorize them,
and create a separate section
within annals and biographies.
This shows he did not recognize that the ancients each had their own completed works,
which complemented and illuminated each other.
Examining ancient texts,
the *Guóyǔ* records speeches
while necessarily narrating the beginning and end of events;
the *Chūnqiū*’s meaning is conveyed through the *Zuǒzhuàn*;
the *Shījīng* has prefaces by state historians;
thus, even though events are millennia past,
readers understand clearly without doubt.
Later compilers of literary selections,
extracting literary pieces,
no longer provide their full context:
memorials may be admirable,
but imperial responses are not included;
allusive words may carry meaning,
but the historical context is not stated;
poems may convey寓意,
but the occasions are not attached;
thus, readers cannot ascertain the facts,
and how can this benefit historical understanding?
*Wénxuǎn* and *Wéncuì*
certainly cannot be blamed;
but *Wénjiàn* and *Wénlèi*
failing to see this point—
is this not their shortcoming?
Recent compilers of gazetteers
do not list book titles in the “Arts and Letters” section,
instead indiscriminately including poetry and miscellaneous writings—
their error is obvious;
but it also stems from not recognizing, at the time of compilation,
that a gazetteer should follow the format of a state history.
With crude and miscellaneous contents
including everything indiscriminately,
what is there to wonder?
Now, we make slight corrections,
separately compiling *Wénzhēng* (Literary Selections),
and still provide brief contexts after poems and writings
for easier reading,
leaving doubtful points blank.
Through this preface and guidelines,
we clarify the intent.
Preface to Memorials
Memorials and proposals as a genre of writing
serve to manage affairs and synthesize matters,
expounding the principles of governance;
among the uses of literary composition,
none is more important than this.
Yet when Xiāo Tǒng compiled his selection of writings,
he placed the fu at the forefront;
later generations of compilers and editors,
taking this as an established rule,
also lost the proper sense of what is weighty and what is light.
If it is said that those were merely the works of literary stylists,
originally not fitting the standards of historical writing,
then the fu is but an offshoot of the Six Principles,
yet it is placed before poetry;
the sāo is the progenitor of the fu,
yet it is separately placed after poetry—
such arbitrary reversals
are again difficult to justify.
And works like Wényuàn and Wénjiàn,
following and honoring this arrangement,
what explanation can be offered?
Now, placing memorials and proposals at the forefront
is taken as the general principle for compiling writings,
privately comparing it to placing the basic annals at the beginning of historical records.
When historians incorporate memorials and proposals,
it is like the Shàngshū recording instructions and proclamations;
those concerning the institutions of an era
are included in the treatises and records;
those concerning the achievements of an individual
are compiled within the biographies.
However, the length of annals and biographies
each has its limits;
the memorials and documents of a dynasty
are numerous in text,
collecting them all would make the historical form inappropriate,
while omitting them would leave gaps in the writings.
Examining Bān Gù's Hànshū,
it details written memorials comprehensively,
yet reviewing the "Treatise on Literature" within,
categories like the Shíqú memorials and proposals,
and the discussions, edicts, and proclamations of Gāozǔ and Xiàowén,
it is clear that beyond the standard histories,
there were also separate specialized books.
Thus, the compilation of memorials and proposals
indeed complements the veritable records and daily chronicles.
Earlier generations compiled the Hàn Wèi Shàngshū,
and recent times compiled the Míngchén Zhāngzòu,
both rigorous in form and substantial in use,
unlike the selections made by literary scholars,
yet those unaware of this
often overlook it without examination,
truly regrettable.
Dù Yòu compiled the Tōngdiǎn,
in addition to the institutions of successive dynasties,
he separately included over twenty volumes of ritual discussions,
not necessarily whether the proposals were adopted or not,
but because the discussions were insightful,
preserving their principles and reasoning.
This reflects the independent judgment in writing
and the comprehensive approach in compilation;
its intent can be grasped intuitively,
yet its arguments cannot be rigidly traced or constrained.
However, specialized books
are self-contained in their compilation,
whether abridged or excerpted,
it is certainly permissible.
The form of historical treatises
each has its own scope and responsibility;
to supplement the gaps in treatises and records with collected writings,
then recording without narration
follows established practice.
Now, four memorials and proposals have been collected,
along with three advisory and report documents,
also appended here,
as they are official government documents,
similar to memorials and proposals,
thus categorized accordingly.
Their order follows chronology,
to provide the full context of events.
Records of Verification and Narrative Accounts
Writings of verification
are a branch of historical biographies.
In ancient times, historical methods were rigorous,
and the forms of recording
each had their specialists.
Thus, since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
literati generally had separate collections.
However, the biographies in various histories,
when recording their lifetime writings,
only mention categories like poetry, fu, admonitions, inscriptions, eulogies, and elegies,
totaling a certain number of pieces.
It is unheard of to record a certain number of accounts,
a certain number of biographies,
a certain number of records,
or a certain number of narratives.
From this, it can be seen
that the forms of accounts, biographies, records, and narratives
were each specialized books by the ancients,
originally not scattered within literary collections,
as is generally known.
Since the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the trend of literary collections has grown daily,
while specialized studies have faded.
Thus, within a single collection,
poetry and fu coexist with classical exegesis,
discourses and narratives are compiled together,
and books compiled into collections
begin to make it difficult to determine the focus of their scholarly tradition.
As for selected and compiled books,
Xiāo Tǒng's Wénxuǎn did not include biographies,
while Wényuàn and Wénjiàn gradually added more detail,
reflecting the trends of the time.
The collections of literati
can serve as historical material,
due to their learning not being specialized,
and matters often overlapping—
is this not indeed true?
The form of verification,
aside from recording events,
also includes writings that enumerate precedents,
a category for textual critics
to distinguish from narrative writings.
Using historical methods as a standard,
recording events is an extension of annals and biographies,
while enumerating precedents derives from treatises and records—
what is called sharing the same source but flowing differently.
The source of recording events
comes from the Chūnqiū,
while the source of enumerating precedents
stems from the official Lǐ,
these are the main points.
Writings that enumerate precedents
have also had specialists since ancient times;
after the Dàijì,
works like Bān Gù's Báihǔ Tōngyì,
Yìng Shào's Fēngsú Tōngyì,
and Cài Yōng's Dúduàn, among others,
are too numerous to count.
Yet their inclusion in literary collections
was rarely seen before the Suí and Táng dynasties.
This form was particularly absent.
As specialized studies declined,
literati occasionally based on their findings,
wrote textual critiques,
composed discussions and proposals,
insufficient to form a book,
yet too regrettable to discard,
thus having no alternative,
they compiled them into literary collections,
alongside poetry, fu, letters, and memorials,
occupying a distinct category—
this is why later selections of writings inevitably include them.
Writings of verification
are especially complementary to the historical narratives of this book,
mutually illuminating each other,
hence more are selected compared to other forms.
As for biographical writings,
those resembling the biographies in this historical record
serve to preserve both detailed and concise versions,
and to show the sources from which the biographies were compiled,
while the quality of their editing, whether good or poor, skillful or clumsy,
can be left for later generations to evaluate and determine,
not daring to claim them as private possessions.
As for inscriptions on steles,
sometimes not included in epigraphy,
their full texts are recorded here,
with emphasis on verifying facts accurately.
Still, the inscriptions and markings of the stone carvings are noted after the text,
to allow mutual reference with epigraphy.
Discourses and Narrative Accounts
Discursive and argumentative writings
originate from the *Analects*.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the *Book of Changes* states:
"When clouds gather and thunder rumbles,
the noble person engages in planning and ordering.
This refers to discussing, compiling, and establishing rituals,
music, governance, and affairs."
When such writings are put to use,
they become canons, counsels, instructions, and proclamations;
when not yet employed,
they take the form of discussions, compilations, discourses, and deliberations.
The works of the sages,
though their applications differ,
share a common origin.
The various masters of the Zhōu and Qín periods,
each adhered to their own specialized schools.
Although their doctrines vary in purity and their expressions in balance,
their underlying intent
was to record in writing
what they wished to implement but could not,
rather than to create writings of literary elegance for its own sake;
this is the fundamental nature of discursive writing.
Once learning ceased to be specialized
and literary style began to pursue ornate beauty,
the collections compiled by literati
became filled with numerous discourses and deliberations.
Among these, occasional insights
and accidentally fitting remarks
often align with the ancients;
yet with shallow foundations
and undistinguished purposes,
either various styles intermingle haphazardly,
or when viewed collectively,
they become repetitious and redundant.
This is why the discursive writings in literary collections
differ from the unified teachings of the various masters.
Mǎ Zǒng of the Táng compiled *Forest of Ideas*,
excerpting from the various masters
and highlighting their notable points,
which also embodies the principle of discarding the short and adopting the long.
In selecting writings now,
preserving those with fitting discussions
is likewise a general principle of compilation.
The various essays in the *Literary Selections*,
such as "Guò Qín" and "Biàn Wáng",
aim at modulation and lyrical lament,
their purpose not being critical exposition or development;
these belong to the category of historical critiques and eulogies,
their origin somewhat akin to the poetic tradition of analogy and evocative imagery,
and thus, though sharing the name, they differ in substance from the essays of the Táng and Sòng.
However, essays like "Yǎngshēng" and "Bóyì"
already possess their own intended themes;
this indeed marks the period when literary collections flourished
and the style of the masters declined.
Xiāo Tǒng, failing to discern this,
grouped them together in one category,
which does not reflect their true nature.
The various masters first transformed into the discourses of literary collections,
then further evolved into the jottings of anecdotal writings,
which was when Sòng scholars, aspiring to learning,
sought a return to simplicity and purity.
Yet with diverse inclinations,
they could neither rid themselves of literati habits
nor, due to the ease of composition,
achieve profound mastery and access to the source.
Surveying the authors broadly,
tracing their beginnings and ends,
most gathered the remnants of literary collections,
taking their occasional insights
that could not yet be formed into full compositions,
jotting them down in notes,
accumulating bit by bit into volumes.
Thus, while their arguments and principles are often commendable,
their central tenets ultimately remain difficult to ascertain.
The literary heritage of Yǒngqīng is sparse and neglected;
among discursive writings,
there is little worthy of selection.
Approximately one piece is preserved
merely to represent the genre,
not daring to claim it aligns with the ancients.
Preface to Poetry and Rhapsody
Poetry and rhapsody
are the resonant expressions of the Six Classics
and the regulated articulations of literature.
In ancient times, poetic songs were established for education,
their rhythms practiced by music officials,
their compositions recorded by the Grand Historian;
affairs were overseen by specialized officers,
traditions transmitted by scholars;
to understand the principles of sound,
or inquire about the implementation of moral instruction,
one consulted the archival records,
where origins and details were clearly preserved.
After poetry and music diverged in origin,
common musicians only practiced musical notation,
while literati merely pursued ornate descriptions of moon and dew;
thus, the way of poetic songs
ceased to connect with governance and affairs;
and the traditions once guarded by specialized officers
and preserved in archival records
became obscure and irrecoverable.
However, from Hàn and Wèi onward,
ballads and Music Bureau poems
narrated events and conveyed emotions;
from the best of these,
one can still examine their language
and verify the events of their time.
After Táng and Sòng,
though said to be the domain of literati,
authors emerged successively,
elucidating subtleties and obscurities,
expounding on governance and instruction;
selecting the finest among them,
they too can stand without shame before the ancients.
Therefore, in selecting writings down to poetry and rhapsody,
if one can avoid falling into the habit of literati ornate language,
that is nearly sufficient.
Liú Xiàng's *Seven Summaries*
classified ceremonial records of imperial sacrifices under *Classic of Rites*,
placed Qín official memorials and *Records of the Grand Historian* under *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
while *Poetry and Rhapsody* formed a separate summary,
not subordinated to the *Classic of Poetry*;
this was because the volumes were numerous,
necessitating separate categorization.
It is regrettable that its introductory principles
did not clarify the origins and development,
thus initiating the later confusion where poetry, rhapsody, and literary collections became blended without clear distinction.
As for the rhapsody, it is one of the Six Principles,
its form recited but not sung.
Yet the *Seven Summaries* collected rhapsodies
in numbers several times greater than poems,
thus placing rhapsodies first
and poems and miscellaneous forms
relegated to the rear,
leading later compilations like Xiāo Tǒng's *Selections*
to adopt this as a fixed model,
which can be said to have misplaced the relative importance.
Furthermore, it divided poetry and rhapsody into five categories;
for example, the miscellaneous rhapsody section
included works without specific attributed authors,
similar to how later anthologies differ from individual collections.
The poetry section
formed its own category;
though lacking explanatory principles,
readers could still discern by context
and understand the classifications.
As for the twenty authors from Qū Yuán downward,
the twenty-one from Lù Jiǎ downward,
and the twenty-five from Xúnzǐ downward,
since the categories were divided into three,
there must have been reasoning at the time;
yet the introductory principles are missing—unlike the summaries for the various masters, which clarify that such-and-such school originated from such-and-such ancient office, etc.—
and do not, like the books of the various masters,
explain origins and development;
this is why later generations,
wishing to study the surviving writings of the *Poetry and Rhapsody* summary,
cannot discern its guiding principles.
The collection of poetry and rhapsody in local gazetteers
follows the ancient intent of the *Airs of the States*.
The old gazetteer's poems on the "Eight Views"
were rather tainted by literati habits,
so they have all been deleted
to uphold historical standards strictly.
The lyrics of Wén Chéngxiàng and the "Sacrificial Ode to the Luò River"
are not poetry or rhapsody but are included nonetheless,
as rhymed writings like inscriptions, admonitions, eulogies, and elegies
are all legacies of ancient poetry.
Discussion on the Principles for the Biographical Tables in the Bózhōu Gazetteer, Part One
Bān Gù's "Table of Ancient and Modern Figures"
has long been criticized by the world.
From today's perspective,
for histories of a single dynasty,
such a table may be unnecessary;
but for comprehensive histories spanning antiquity,
a table of figures is indispensable.
Bān Gù compiled a dynastic history,
continuing Sīmǎ Qiān's work,
and supplemented all categories missing in Sīmǎ Qiān's history;
it was not merely a matter of confining the deeds of rulers and ministers recorded in the annals and biographies
to the boundaries of the Western Hàn.
Thus, his "Treatise on Geography" extended to the "Tribute of Yǔ" and the "Offices of Zhōu,"
and his "Treatise on the Five Phases" enumerated events from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods;
the principle of the "Table of Figures"
can be analogized accordingly.
The flaw of the "Table of Figures"
lies not in its creation,
but in its use of nine grades to categorize people,
forcing them into fixed positions,
and arbitrarily labeling them as sage, benevolent, wise, or foolish,
thus failing to capture the rigorous intent of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Furthermore, Liú Zhījī pointed out its inclusion of ancient figures to the exclusion of contemporary ones,
and the discrepancy between names and realities,
which is a valid criticism.
As for the myriad other criticisms of its inappropriateness,
they are insufficient to fault Bān Gù.
Had he removed the nine grades of high and low,
along with the labels of sage, benevolent, foolish, and wise,
and instead distinguished categories based on nobility and humility,
or used titles to differentiate by capital, state, or region,
arranging them horizontally as the warp,
and marking chronological order above as the weft;
and clearly stated in his explanation
that it was intended to supplement Sīmǎ Qiān's work,
serving as a reference for compiling biographies—
then the establishment of this principle
would have become a fixed rule for later compilers of comprehensive histories,
and how could it have instead become the target of criticism?
Alas,
an excellent method for the ages
has been drowned in a sea of censure,
with no historian of refined judgment
to remedy its flaws and put it to good use.
In recent times, Mǎ Suì's "Extended History"
seems to have employed this principle.
However, Mǎ's work
is fundamentally a compilation,
not an original composition.
Inferring his intent,
it was merely because the events of the Three Dynasties are far removed from today,
with materials scattered and emerging haphazardly,
lacking clear order,
that he created a table of figures
as a reference for names found in the classics and commentaries.
Moreover, he even disparaged Bān Gù's table,
failing to understand that it could fill gaps in Sīmǎ Qiān's work;
nor did he grasp that expanding its categories
could serve as a general framework for historiography;
instead, he regarded the "Table of Figures"
as if created solely for his "Extended History,"
which shows a lack of understanding of classification.
For comprehensive histories spanning antiquity,
the events recorded
mostly draw from ancient texts and historical accounts;
unlike contemporary records,
which rely on eyewitness accounts
where truth and falsehood can be cross-referenced.
Since it is an original work,
claiming expertise,
the selection of biographies
must involve unique judgment and personal conception,
forming a distinctive scholarly tradition;
it cannot possibly include all categories comprehensively,
akin to a mere compilation—

this is inevitable. For instance, events from the Zuǒzhuàn were incorporated into the Shǐjì, yet figures like Zǐchǎn and Shūxiàng could not all be included in biographies. How then can a "Table of Figures" be omitted?
As for the deeds of earlier figures,
scattered across biographies and records,
the prominence or obscurity of their names
inevitably leads to variations in detail and discrepancies.
If the remnants left after the selection of biographies
are not summarized in a table of figures,
then omissions invite criticism of negligence,
while detailed inclusions invite accusations of bias.
Even later readers of my work
would feel it lacks structure and discipline.
Thus, Bān Gù's "Table of Figures"
likely drew from ancient traditions,
and should not be lightly criticized.
In the Discussion on the Principles of the Table of Figures in the Bózhōu Gazetteer, Part I,
some say:
"The need for a table of figures in comprehensive histories
is indeed true.
But for dynastic histories,
you say such a table may be unnecessary—
'may' implies uncertainty.
If dynastic histories do not require tracing antiquity,
why should they have a table of figures at all?"
I reply:
"Dynastic histories are not uniform;
roughly speaking, they fall into three categories,
yet all require a table of figures.
Compared to comprehensive histories,
the need is somewhat less urgent;
but having one
is still preferable.
The presence of biographies in history
is like the Zuǒzhuàn to the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Zuǒzhuàn follows the classic, arranging events by year and month,
while biographies separate individuals under headings—
their forms differ slightly,
but their function
is to fully present the context of the classic (the Spring and Autumn Annals) and the annals.
Those studying the Zuǒzhuàn
have compiled genealogies of nobles from various states.
Those studying dynastic annals and biographies
have only Bān Gù's "Table of Figures,"
which was scarcely recorded before being overwhelmed by criticism—
who would dare again discuss the systematic arrangement of figures?
Genealogies such as the 'Nobles of the Spring and Autumn Period' and 'Posthumous Titles and Clans' (by Dù Yù, etc.),
and records of 'Variants in Names' (by Féng Jìxiān, etc.)—
those studying chronicle histories
are so meticulous.
Yet for histories with annals and biographies,
there is only a table of contents for biographies,
and the number of biographies is limited;
even chronological or genealogical tables
only include kings, nobles, generals, and ministers—
by nature, they cannot comprehensively cover all figures
or classify them into categories.
Thus, for scholars seeking to understand the times and the people,
and to examine the principles of selection in historical biographies,
it is generally vague and difficult to discern;
hence, the indispensability of a table of figures
is indeed true.
Gù Yánwǔ said:
'If a history lacks chronological tables,
then biographies must necessarily multiply;
if biographies multiply,
the text becomes冗长 and events are反而遗漏.'
He attributed this flaw to Chén Shòu,
and noted that Fàn, Shěn, Yáo, Lǐ, and others
were all deficient in this regard.
Gù's argument
can be said to know one but not the other.
Chronological tables are indeed indispensable;
but how much space do kings, dukes, generals, and ministers
occupy in the histories of Fàn, Shěn, Yáo, Lǐ, and others?
The histories of the Táng and Sòng dynasties
reinstated chronological tables,
yet their biographies were several times more numerous than those in the works of Fàn and Shěn—
how did chronological tables prevent the proliferation of biographies?
It is the absence of a table of figures
that leads to the multiplication of biographies;
chronological tables are of secondary importance.
Yet the table of figures is ridiculed and mocked by historians,
and none dare attempt it again.
No wonder biographies are compiled in great numbers,
like filling household registers,
making it difficult to decide
on inclusions and exclusions.
For comprehensive histories spanning antiquity,
the materials drawn from ancient records
are preserved in texts;
not having a table of figures
might be acceptable, as Sīmǎ Qiān's history could be supplemented later by Bān Gù—
it would not be too late.
But for dynastic histories,
which draw materials from official documents and records
or rely on eyewitness accounts,
it is inherently impossible to include all categories in writing,
yet one cannot guarantee the absence of events
that are interconnected.
Thus, compiling a comprehensive list of names
and categorizing them into a table
is sufficient to reveal the general principles
and strictly define the general framework for biographies.
How can we leave this to later generations?
Dynastic histories
range from the specialized expertise of Bān and Chén,
to the collective strengths of Jìn and Táng compilations,
down to the forced categorizations of Sòng and Yuán.
For histories of specialized expertise,
a table of figures is necessary to clarify their independent judgment and unique approach;
for histories drawing on collective strengths,
a table of figures is necessary to prevent discrepancies and inconsistencies;
for histories with forced categorizations,
a table of figures is necessary to curb冗长 and混乱.
Therefore, I say
dynastic histories,
roughly falling into three categories,
all require a table of figures.
Discussion on the Principles of the Table of Figures in the Bózhōu Gazetteer, Part II.
Why create tables of figures in local gazetteers?
I say:
It is to remedy the flaws of local gazetteers,
not necessarily to imitate the style of histories,
yet the form of historical writing is thereby preserved.
Those who compile local gazetteers today,
when recording figures,
leave nothing worth tabulating.
Moreover, the figures they record
resemble tables of figures instead,
with no proper biographies of figures to speak of,
and the tables themselves are not truly tables.
Indeed, the flaws of local gazetteers have long persisted!
Since Sīmǎ Qiān,
the format of biographies
has remained unchanged.
Local gazetteers serve as source material for national histories,
so when compiling biographies of figures,
they should be more detailed than those in national histories.
Yet today’s compilers of figures
omit facts,
summarize general ideas,
condense content,
and categorize arbitrarily.
Their prose is neither narrative nor exposition,
resembling both prose and parallel prose;
casual greetings from letters,
formulaic phrases from official documents—
all are indiscriminately included
without any editing.
As for their character, all are like Zēng Shēn or Shǐ Qiū,
their governance like Gāo Yáo or Huáng Dì,
their scholarship like Hàn Confucians,
their chastity like Jiāng Nǚ—
all with identical faces,
their true nature impossible to discern.
Such works are indeed not worth criticizing,
and may be left aside without discussion.
Even if there are one or two outstanding compilers
who favor distinctive styles,
they oversimplify their wording,
falsely claiming lofty antiquity;
some imitate the annotated style of the *Bamboo Annals*,
others emulate inscriptions on stone tablets.
Though free from vulgar and shallow words,
they lack comprehensive judgment and insight.
What is called “resembling a table but not a table,”
“resembling annotations but not annotations”—
this chronic flaw has long persisted.
Thus, national histories prefer family records
over local gazetteers,
precisely for this reason.
A gazetteer is meant to record.
Biographies of figures
must be crafted with discernment and originality,
following the rigor of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
and incorporating the metaphorical style of the *Book of Songs*.
Selection and arrangement
should form a distinctive scholarly work;
though called a local gazetteer,
it is a microcosm of national history.
Now, creating tables for figures
has three advantages.
Former emperors and their descendants,
whose hometowns still exist today—
gazetteers include them among figures,
which is inappropriate in principle;
yet omitting them entirely
seems like neglecting an important subject.
Thus, when local gazetteers encounter this,
disputes arise endlessly,
and those with biased, far-fetched views
often excerpt from imperial annals,
cleverly change titles,
rearrange positions,
yet never achieve appropriateness.
Now, by removing figures from biographies
and listing emperors in tables,
both inclusion and exclusion become appropriate,
establishing a lasting standard.
This is the first advantage.
Historical biographies of figures are originally detailed,
but gazetteers instead condense them into summaries.
This resembles excerpting from reference books,
not the comprehensive approach of historians.
Yet if events and writings are organized by their meaning,
then even if records contain names,
they cannot all be included indiscriminately,
as in categorized compilations.
For ancient figures recorded in historical texts,
if they do not meet the criteria for biographies,
listing them in tables of figures
ensures thoroughness without clutter,
and breadth without omission.
This is the second advantage.
Historians rely more on written records than oral accounts,
being lenient with the present and strict with the past—
a tendency dictated by circumstances.
As for local virtues,
small acts of goodness within families,
righteous deeds noted only by title,
moral integrity recorded only by year—
these are not included in historical methods,
but should be recorded in gazetteers.
If biographies lack substantial material,
the prose need not be verbose;
if tables highlight notable names,
the meaning is not compromised.
This is the third advantage.
All three address common flaws in modern gazetteers,
which compilers find difficult to articulate.
Thus I say:
Creating tables of figures in local gazetteers
is meant to remedy the flaws of local gazetteers.
Discussion on the Compilation of Precedents in the *Bózhōu Gazetteer*, Part One
The institutions of ancient kings
are preserved in the Six Classics;
understanding their principles
makes the world’s affairs clear as one’s palm.
The *Book of Documents* records governance,
with Canons, Counsels, Tributes, and Plans
serving as essential classics.
Yet the details of vessels and numbers in the *Rites of Zhōu*
are not included among the books of the Four Dynasties.
The rites of Xià and Shāng—
though Confucius could speak of them—
their texts no longer survive today.
Thus, major institutions of governance and instruction
form separate books;
while minor details of human affairs and material objects
are preserved in other records,
each serving its proper purpose.
Even with the efforts of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
they could not be combined into one.
Sīmǎ Qiān, following the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
composed twelve Basic Annals;
his chronological tables and biographies,
arranged in sequence,
sufficed to record the entirety of events.
As for institutions and regulations
that govern human relations
and uphold the world’s order,
he separately created eight treatises
to discuss them.
Bān Gù expanded these into ten treatises,
and later historians followed suit,
making additions and deletions,
establishing a fixed format for historians.
Long ago, Hán Xuānzǐ saw the *Changes* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
and said that the rites of Zhōu were preserved in Lǔ.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng, compiling the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
often cited the classics of rites.
The origin of historical treatises
lies in official rites.
The “Treatise on Astronomy” still reflects the “Offices of Heaven,”
the “Treatise on Food and Money” still reflects the “Equalization”—
traces of *Hànshū* terminology remain,
allowing us to imagine.
Yet Zhèng Qiáo said:
“The great origin of treatises
lies in the *Eryǎ*”—
this is not accurate.
However, the treatises of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
capture the essentials,
discussing general principles,
enabling readers to infer the outline of an era
and complement the annals and biographies—
this suffices.
As for names, objects, vessels, and numbers,
they believed separate specialized books existed,
so they did not seek completeness,
just as Zuǒ Qiūmíng cited典故 and texts
without detailing every minor aspect of the *Rites of Zhōu*.
At the end of Sīmǎ Qiān’s “Treatise on Rites,” it says:
“As for matters of sacrificial vessels,
there are officials in charge.”
The rest can be inferred.
Since Shěn Yuē and Fàn Yè onward,
the purpose of discussion has gradually diminished,
while the inclusion of instruments and numbers has gradually expanded.
By the time of Ōuyáng Xiū’s “Treatises” in the *New History of the Táng*,
with thirteen categories,
the resulting work reached fifty volumes,
featuring official registers and documents,
currency records and annotations,
classified and categorized,
with a fear of not being detailed enough.
The *History of the Sòng*, *History of the Jīn*, and *History of the Yuán* became even more verbose and cluttered,
piling up on desks and tables,
making it difficult to grasp their main points.
This seems to be an attempt to incorporate all the official duties of the *Zhōu Guān*,
the rituals and ceremonial forms,
into the *Chūnqiū*,
before considering it a complete work.
If so, then why would Master Kǒngzǐ have edited and compiled the *Lǐ*, *Yuè*, *Shī*, and *Shū*
without dividing the classics into six parts?
The treatises of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
at their inception,
preserved some remnants of the various philosophical schools.
Works such as the *Guǎnzǐ*, *Lǚshì Chūnqiū*, and *Huáinánzǐ*,
with their chapters on astronomy, geography, official charts, and musical systems,
gathered regulations and numbers,
applying their own judgment,
to establish their own scholarly traditions—
these were their models.
Did Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù not know that names, numbers, instruments, and objects
could not be ignored?
Rather, they believed that each had its own dedicated works,
and should not be exhaustively included in a single scholarly tradition,
lest they become overly detailed in pursuit of completeness.
If one seeks exhaustive detail,
the writing will inevitably become verbose and cluttered,
the examples will grow numerous and disordered,
and the subject matter may become obscured rather than clarified.
As for the compilations of examination candidates
and the summaries of encyclopedists,
these are not true works of scholarship;
they merely aim to cover all things,
for the sake of convenience in reference.
Such works are trivial and shallow, not worthy of criticism.
Historians, who organize and compile the words of many,
seeking to establish enduring works,
yet become fixated on instruments and numbers,
scrambling to collect them without respite—
this is to misunderstand that the intent of the *Chūnqiū* and official *Lǐ*
may be mutually sought,
but their forms should not be blended.
In the discussion of the rules for “Administrative Records” in the *Gazetteer of Bózhōu*,
it is noted that detailed registers and documents
should not be mixed with historical treatises.
Yet, the original records of the ancients
are no longer accessible to later generations.
If one wishes to investigate ancient institutions in detail,
how can this be achieved? The answer is:
The regulations of Shūsūn Tōng,
the military laws of Hán Xìn,
and the legal codes of Xiāo Hé
were all essential texts of the early Hàn,
akin to the six codes of the *Zhōu Guān*.
The treatises on rituals, music, and penal law in the *History of the Hàn*
could not preserve them in full,
because these texts were held by government offices,
and people could consult the relevant authorities to obtain them.
When the offices were lost and the texts perished,
it was due to their cumbersome nature,
which inherently prevented them from enduring.
This has been the case since ancient times,
not unique to the Hàn.
Ōuyáng Xiū and Sòng Qí, among others,
failing to understand this,
sought to rely on the power of history to transmit them.
Yet literary works are easily transmitted,
while measurements and numbers are difficult to preserve long-term.
Thus, more than half of the *Lǐ* has been lost,
and the *Yuèjīng* has vanished entirely.
If even the Six Classics met this fate,
how much more so historical writings?
Moreover, the *History of the Táng* is twice the size of the *History of the Hàn*,
and the *History of the Sòng* is twice the size of the *History of the Táng*,
already reaching an overwhelming scale.
All things in the world
have their limits.
If later generations again double the size of the *History of the Táng* and *History of the Sòng* to compile new works,
they will pile up like mountains,
not to mention that human capacity for perception will inevitably fall short,
and over time,
they will ultimately be lost.
Thus, due to the cumbersome nature of measurements and numbers,
the historical writings themselves may be lost alongside them.
How, then, can the power of history preserve measurements and numbers?
Should we, then, allow the regulations and precedents of earlier dynasties to be lost? The answer is:
The study of history declined after the Táng,
but the methods of history were also most fully developed in the Táng.
Before Ōuyáng Xiū’s *Treatises* in the *History of the Táng* appeared,
Táng scholars had already recognized that statutes and institutions
could not be exhaustively covered in historical treatises.
Liú Zhì produced the *Zhèngdiǎn*,
and Dù Yòu produced the *Tōngdiǎn*,
both modeled on the six codes of the *Zhōu Guān*,
encompassing statutes and institutions,
collecting both major and minor details,
filling over a hundred volumes.
They explicitly stated that the deeds of rulers and ministers
could be detailed in annals and biographies,
while institutions, names, and numbers
were difficult to cover exhaustively in treatises.
Thus, they compiled these works with great urgency.
By the early Sòng, Wáng Pǔ produced the *Táng Huìyào* and *Wǔdài Huìyào*,
and later Xú Tiānlín compiled the *Liǎng Hàn Huìyào*,
supplementing the records of antiquity
and summarizing entire dynasties in single works.
Although these differ in form from the compilations of Liú and Dù,
they share the same origin,
focusing on synthesizing and verifying statutes and institutions,
distinct from historical treatises.
Their principles and forms are clear
and should not be altered.
Since the compilations of the Táng and Sòng were as described,
later scholars compiling histories of the Táng and Sòng
should adopt their methods
to organize the institutions of those dynasties,
allowing them to complement the annals and biographies,
so that the *Chūnqiū* and *Zhōu Lǐ*
may trace their origins and development together.
If followed generation after generation,
would this not be excellent?
Why did Ōuyáng Xiū in compiling the *History of the Táng*
and Yuán scholars in compiling the *History of the Sòng*
instead include instruments and numbers not collected in earlier histories,
haphazardly listing them?
This shows a lack of consideration for the times.
Some may argue that works like the *Tōngdiǎn* and *Huìyào*
are merely more detailed than the treatises of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
and that they, too, fail to comprehensively cover instruments and numbers,
forcing those studying antiquity to consult other books.
This, however, is not a well-informed view.
If ancient objects survive to the present,
even household registers
or market currency ledgers
can serve as references for research.
But if everything is preserved without selection,
then even Mount Tài would be insufficient for storing books,
and the vast sea would not hold enough ink.
Thus, for the long-term strategy of historical study,
annals, tables, treatises, and biographies
should follow established forms.
Drawing further on the legacy of the *Zhōu* codes,
one may select from official registers and documents
the names, objects, instruments, and numbers,
organizing them with some coherence
to preserve the administrative records of the time,
complementing history without encroaching upon it.
This could serve as an unchanging rule for all generations.
In the discussion of the rules for “Administrative Records” in the *Gazetteer of Bózhōu*,
the origin of administrative records
lies in the official *Lǐ*.
With all offices represented at court,
only the treatises of the dynastic history
can extract their essentials,
while the state compilations of statutes and summaries
can fully record their objects and numbers.
Why should compilers of local gazetteers separate treatises from administrative records? The answer is:
The treatises of ministries and directorates
are administrative records.
Compared to the *Zhōu Guān*,
they are like the *Sīmǎ Fǎ* of the Ministry of War
or the *Kǎogōng Jì* of the Ministry of Works.
The gazetteers of provinces, prefectures, and counties
are branches of the dynastic history.
Compared to the Zhōu system,
they are like the *Jìn Shèng*, *Chǔ Táowù*, and *Lǔ Chūnqiū*.
Since commanderies and counties differ from the feudal system,
administrative records all derive from the institutions of the court.
The duties of the six ministries,
issued from above and implemented,
received from below and followed,
are, compared to the dynastic history,
specific yet limited in scope.
Treatises and administrative records
each have their immutable roles
and should not be confused.
The local gazetteers of today are
trivial, vulgar, and shallow.
If we seek in them the principles and standards of historical writing,
they seem like gazetteers yet are not,
seem like archival records yet are not;
truly, they are not worth criticizing.
However, official documents and records,
issued according to administrative decrees
and preserved by clerks and officials,
have their own fixed rules and regulations.
Even with exceptional talent,
one cannot add to them;
even with foolish clumsiness,
one cannot diminish them.
Famous and great regions
and remote, backward counties
are no different in this regard.
Therefore, if we seek in today's gazetteers,
we cannot see the historical judgment of the ancients;
but if we seek in today's official documents,
we can indeed thereby see the statutes and systems of the ancients.
Hence it is said:
"When ritual is lost, seek it in the countryside."
Those who study national history
should extend from national history to archival records,
for while historical methods are not lost,
the meaning of archival records is unclear,
Those who study local gazetteers,
on the other hand, should use archival records to correct the gazetteers;
for while the meaning of gazetteers has long been lost,
the preservation of archival records has not fallen into disuse.
By cultivating these archival records,
the meaning of gazetteers can in turn be clarified.
The Book of Changes says:
"When exhausted, it changes;
when changed, it becomes open;
when open, it endures."
The meaning of a gazetteer should be concise and clear,
yet events cannot be omitted.
Archival records should be orderly and systematic,
yet essentials cannot be left unselected.
To consider mere brevity as a gazetteer
is the shallow understanding of works like the Cháoyì and Wǔgōng gazetteers.
To think that mere detailed comprehensiveness constitutes archival records
is something even petty clerks can do well,
not realizing it is unworkable.
A gazetteer is a record.
Beyond its events and prose,
there lies its meaning.
This is what is meant by the method of grasping the essential.
Yet some mistakenly think that merging and reducing events
and deleting text
constitutes conciseness;
are they not far removed from the ancients?
The writings of renowned masters
always possess distinctive judgment in their intentions,
sometimes elaborating what others omit,
sometimes discarding what others select,
with no fixed rule from the start.
The key is that readers,
admiring and cherishing them, pass them on,
and suddenly perceive their meaning within the events and prose,
thus relating to moral instruction.
However, if archival records are not systematically organized
into separate specialized books,
then the gazetteer itself cannot manifest its intent.

First Letter in Reply to Xiùcai Zhēn on Compiling Gazetteers
The magistrate of Wén'ān has sent gifts to engage you to compile a gazetteer.
You have long been devoted to historical matters,
and now have a small opportunity to test your skills.
You should eagerly undertake this journey.
What knowledge do I possess
that you honor me with your inquiry?
Yet your generous intent cannot go unanswered,
so I dare to outline a few points based on what I usually pay attention to,
hoping for your discerning judgment!
If there are points that are not so,
please inform me in return.
First, prefectures and commanderies are all subordinate to the territorial administration,
and naturally cannot, like feudal states, have separate histories.
However, principles and standards must be clear.
For example, biographies and treatises are originally two distinct genres.
In compiling gazetteers today,
since both figures and institutions are generally called "treatises,"
then categories such as distinguished officials and local worthies
should not be separately classified as biographies.
If biographies are separately categorized,
then matters like rites, music, military, and punishments
should not still follow the general title of "treatise."
I consider that "treatise" is the overall name for the entire book.
Imperial favors and celebratory events
should be recorded as "outer annals";
appointments and removals of officials
should be delineated as "chronicles";
classics, statutes, and institutions
should be presented as "examinations" to elucidate them;
figures and distinguished officials
should be arranged as "biographies" to list them.
Changing the names and categories
avoids the suspicion of usurping history;
raising the key points and displaying the details
prevents the flaw of omissions.
Others can generally be appended by category.
As for matters that are not analogous,
standards can be established based on principles,
and new creations are permissible.
Trivial and fragmented details
unrelated to moral admonition
may be excised and not preserved.
Detailed, comprehensive, clear, and complete,
orderly and uniform—
only then can they provide material for national history;
otherwise, even if extremely brilliant,
they are merely a private tale,
and what benefit do they offer?
Second, those who compile treatises on arts and letters nowadays
often take the poems, rhapsodies, records, prefaces, and miscellaneous writings
by local officials and gentry,
and attach them by category;
even more, irrelevant pieces on wind, clouds, moon, and dew
that lack moral admonition,
and shrine inscriptions and eulogies
entirely without factual evidence,
are all included.
Leaving aside right or wrong,
even if the prose is all canonical and standard,
and the poetry necessarily elegant and refined,
yet compiling and classifying them by category,
striving to include all genres—
this is the method of selecting writings,
not the style of gazetteers and records.
Since it is a treatise on arts and letters,
it should follow the intent of the Sāntōng and Qīlüè,
taking the books and selected works by scholars of this region,
dividing them into sections and collections,
first listing the catalog,
then ordering the beginnings and ends,
removing the superfluous and selecting the excellent,
extracting the main ideas,
discussing their strengths and weaknesses,
comparing and classifying them to form a compilation—
only then will later generations have something to consult,
or it may provide material for imperial library collation,
thus not losing the style of gazetteers and records.
As for altar and temple inscriptions,
city wall and embankment accounts,
discourses on advantages and disadvantages,
and verses on local products,
they may be appended to examinations on products, land taxes, customs, geography, etc.,
to show the reasons for gains and losses,
the causes of continuity and change;
like the example of Bān Gù's History taking Yánnián's and Jiǎ Ràng's memorials into the "Treatise on Rivers and Canals,"
and Jiǎ Yì's and Cháo Cuò's memorials into the "Treatise on Food and Money,"
this is permissible.
Scholarly discourses
that can reveal their authors' lifelong aspirations
should be fully recorded in their biographies;
like the example of Bān Gù's History recording the "Three Responses on Heaven and Man" in the "Biography of Dǒng Zhòngshū,"
and recording the various memorials on "Public Security" in the "Biographies of Jiǎ Yì,"
this is permissible.
As for tomb inscriptions, biographical eulogies, and the like,
if verified as factual and not false,
already having established principles,
they may be taken directly as biographical text;
like the example of Bān Gù's History following the "Autobiographical Postface" of the Records of the Grand Historian for the "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān,"
and following Yáng Xióng's "Autobiographical Preface" for the "Biography of Yáng Xióng,"
this is permissible.
These are fixed standards,
leaving no room for doubt,
yet they remain unchanged through convention—
how difficult indeed is historical discernment!
1. When funds are raised to compile a gazetteer,
a bureau is established and scholars are invited,
yet genuine learning is seldom heard of,
and the guidelines are first broadened,
striving for novelty to impress,
hastily altering old books;
in reality, it is like the monkey trainer’s trick of颠倒狙公,
what true insight is there?
The establishment of gazetteers by prefectures and counties
began in the former Ming dynasty.
At that time, in the initial stages of drafting,
although the principles and structure were not very orderly,
the literary style still valued truthfulness,
and the editing mostly came from the authors themselves;
unlike the recent practice of following worn-out conventions,
where frivolous young men,
who have not even fully mastered historical characters,
can all boldly take up the brush and recklessly compile,
secretly receiving stipends and provisions.
Yet, not one in a hundred of their books survives.
This is all due to later generations replacing earlier ones,
where those compiling new gazetteers
plagiarize the records of old gazetteers,
while erasing the names of the authors.
Extending this principle,
would it mean that once Bān Gù’s Book of Hàn was published,
the Records of the Grand Historian should be handed over to the flames?
Or that after Ōu Yángxiū and Sòng Qí completed their book,
the Old Book of Táng could be used to cover jars?
I believe that those compiling gazetteers
should continue the records of their predecessors,
and not destroy the completed works of earlier authors.
Even if the principles and structure of the previous gazetteer are unclear,
and the literary style is flawed,
and I create a new system,
revising the completed work;
the old and new should still be allowed to coexist,
with each new version continuing from the last,
and none should be arbitrarily destroyed;
the merits and flaws of each
will be judged fairly by readers.
The volume titles and table of contents of the previous book,
along with the author’s name,
should be recorded in the “Bibliography” section of the new gazetteer,
to preserve what might otherwise be lost;
this would reflect a spirit of impartiality and selflessness,
and I, too, would avoid being destroyed by later generations.
2. The style of a gazetteer
should be more detailed than that of a history,
yet what is recorded in today’s gazetteers
is less than one percent.
This is for no other reason than that
the collection and compilation of materials
are difficult to complete thoroughly in a short time;
and the preservation of historical records
lacks dedicated oversight on a daily basis.
I have often proposed to those in charge
