that to ensure no omissions in the gazetteer,
a Gazetteer Compilation Office should be established routinely,
staffed by clerks with some literary skill.
All matters of governance and education,
official activities and facts,
and the documents of the six bureaus
should be required to be reported,
with catalogs and original records
compiled into volumes and stored in the archives.
When a bureau is later established for compilation,
the materials for selection would be abundant,
and although this cannot compare to the official historians of the feudal states,
it would still capture the essence of the local clerks’ historical role.
Since this is no longer feasible now,
it should be proposed as a method for the future.
3. A gazetteer is a form of history,
originally belonging to the public domain,
not like a family tomb inscription or birthday essay,
which can be filled with empty praise
to please people’s ears and eyes.
I have heard that in recent compilations,
bribery is often openly practiced,
with requests made to write biographies,
entirely lacking verification of facts.
Although this is done by unworthy and frivolous scholars,
the encouragement of good and punishment of evil
must not be abandoned.
Today’s gazetteers
never record anything unfavorable,
partly due to the habitual desire to praise the good,
and partly due to the fear of future repercussions.
I believe that criticism and censure are inherently unsuitable for the style of a gazetteer;
recording events truthfully,
the good and bad will naturally be apparent,
aligning with the principles of straightforwardness, leniency, and implicit revelation;
one should not focus solely on ornate language
or engage in empty praise.
4. Historical and gazetteer works
that contribute to moral education
originally rely on narrating loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness,
making them awe-inspiring and vivid,
full of sound and color,
so that even a hundred generations later,
the timid will feel courage,
and the greedy will become upright.
The Records of the Grand Historian favored chivalry,
often writing about assassins and unconventional figures,
yet it still inspires people to value life and bolster their spirit;
how much more so the great principles and righteousness of heaven and earth,
on which social order relies for support,
and worldly teachings depend for upholding?
I often see scholars compiling gazetteers,
where scenes and objects that linger in the mind,
allowing literary flair to shine,
or textual research and考证,
offering opportunities to boast of broad knowledge,
are all described in voluminous detail.
But when it comes to filial sons, loyal ministers,
righteous men, and chaste women,
only a few brushstrokes are given;
or even just the names are listed,
with no details of their deeds,
making readers feel as if they are looking at a county magistrate’s roster of clerks,
what value is there in that?
I believe that a county gazetteer’s collection spans only a few decades,
and its research covers only a hundred miles or so,
so what is seen and heard should be based on true evidence,
and extra effort should be made to collect and compile,
widely narrating their stories;
so that readers may feel inspired,
and beneath the autumn grass on ancient graves,
there will surely be those who weep in the autumn rain while honoring the red brush.
Special attention should be paid to remote and secluded places,
to extraordinary conduct and remarkable integrity,
where descendants are constrained by lack of means,
or hindered by established rules,
and cannot receive honors or awards.
Once their traces are verified,
efforts should be made to write their biographies,
for the observation of those who collect folk customs,
reflecting the desire to praise the good.
The above six points,
based on my observations,
I dare not claim are necessarily correct.
Yet among the gazetteers published in the world today,
there are indeed some that are not acceptable.
If a man is not born to be a historian,
he should still follow renowned officials and great ministers,
wielding the brush as a secretary,
and thus have the opportunity to discuss contemporary affairs,
using his literary talents to serve the times.
Compiling gazetteers
is one such endeavor.
What is called gazetteer compilation today,
where officials merely seek empty fame,
and authors lack learning and insight;
the higher-ups aim only to fulfill administrative duties,
while the lower ones seek nothing more than stipends and profits.
Worse still, local gentry use it to engage in competition,
and scholars take advantage to distort the truth;
hosts and guests each hold their own prejudices,
and conflicts may arise within the same bureau,
then as for the task of compiling gazetteers,
it might as well not be done.
But as for you, endowed with historical talent,
I have often regretted that you have not had the chance to试牛刀.
Previously, in our exchanges and discussions,
I glimpsed your depth of knowledge,
and you are surely not one to act carelessly.
Wén’ān Jūn is also able to listen with an open mind,
sending gifts and earnestly inviting,
so naturally, the old habits will be broken;
before the final version is even completed,
readers will be astonished,
considering it innovative and exceptional,
and it will not merely be a book for one county,
but truly a book for the world.
As for me, in this matter,
I am incapable of contributing,
but I am honored to be consulted,
and I offer my humble thoughts,
hoping to add a glow like that of fireflies and candles,
and perhaps you, my brother, have something to advance my understanding?
Recently, I respectfully offered some humble opinions,
which were shallow and lacking in depth,
and I had no firm views,
not hoping to contribute anything profound,
but merely to fulfill my duty.
Yet you honored me with a reply,
lavishing praise upon me,
setting lofty standards and drawing from distant sources,
with sincere and earnest words,
reading which I truly felt both ashamed and awed!
You possess the talent of a fine historian,
broad in knowledge and decisive in judgment,
looking down upon the ancients,
with an ambition that seeks to surpass Fàn and outdo Chén,
while this mere local gazetteer,
is nothing more than using a butcher's knife to kill a chicken.
Yet, with great talent and a humble heart,
you are not ashamed to inquire repeatedly.
Someone as shallow as I,
how can I match your open-mindedness?
In my previous letter, I roughly outlined the main points,
and you undeservedly praised me excessively,
even wishing to inquire about the details.
Although I am not the right person for this,
due to the depth of your sincere and earnest affection,
I dare not fail to offer a single word in reply,
and I hope you will consider and choose wisely.
First, the style should adhere to historical methods.
The gazetteers of prefectures and counties,
are mixed and disordered,
neither following the proper form,
nor dividing into annals and tables,
which also borders on presumption.
Therefore, in my previous letter, I proposed a balanced approach to establishing rules,
focusing on four forms: outer annals, chronicles, examinations, and biographies,
to avoid the suspicion of presumptuous history,
and to seek the reality of records.
However, while empty titles should avoid imitating national histories,
the substance should follow the ancients.
Forms such as outer annals and chronicles,
in today's gazetteers,
are seen in only one or two out of a hundred.
As for examinations and biographies,
although they are now collectively called gazetteer biographies,
in reality, the substance of both,
is not without records;
but the reason they do not conform to the good methods of ancient history is that,
the examination form often suffers from excessive detail and fragmentation,
while the biographical form often suffers from excessive uniformity.
The examination form,
is modeled after the treatises.
Sīmǎ Qiān's eight treatises,
Bān Gù's ten treatises,
comprehensively examined institutions and regulations,
covering a wide range.
Fàn Yè's history divided them into thirty treatises,
the "Táng Shū" expanded to fifty chapters,
which was already quite broad.
By the time the Yuán compiled the "Sòng Shǐ,"
the treatises were divided into over one hundred and sixty.
Critics mocked it as a clerk's ledger.
However, it only lacked proper editing,
resulting in diffuseness;
unlike today's prefectural and county gazetteers,
which divide into numerous topics,
vast and without coherence.
For example, astrological divisions, territorial boundaries, and historical changes,
mountains, rivers, and products,
all belong to the category of geographical treatises;
household registration, taxes, and labor services,
levies, trade, and grain purchases,
all belong to the category of economic examinations;
auspicious and inauspicious signs, songs, and ballads,
anomalies, floods, and droughts,
all belong to the category of treatises on the five phases;
court congratulations, altars, temples, and sacrificial ceremonies,
village banquets and guest receptions,
all belong to the category of treatises on rituals.
All matters, great and small,
can be analogized accordingly.
Begin each section with a general title,
then detail each item below,
compiling them into a volume;
not only is it easier to grasp the whole,
but it is also rigorous and appropriate.
Such items,
merely require a rearrangement.
Yet today's gazetteers are trivial and fragmented,
no different from a merchant's account book,
cluttered with rice and salt details,
what is there to see?
Some may say that long chapters,
like Bān Gù's "Shí Huò,"
or Sīmǎ Qiān's "Píng Zhǔn,"
are difficult to structure.
How would they know that if the literary style conforms to historical norms,
even if the wording is like arranging counting rods,
it will still be orderly and observable,
practical and useful.
There is no need to be overly concerned with the writing,
or to favor complexity.
Second, existing texts should credit their authors.
Bān Gù followed Sīmǎ Qiān's history,
for the period before Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
he mostly used the original text,
without making distinctions;
since both "Shǐ Jì" and "Hàn Shū" record the same events,
and Sīmǎ Qiān's history had long been circulated,
there was no issue.
As for edicts, letters, memorials, and the like,
since they narrate the person and events themselves,
there is also no issue with copying existing texts.
In the "Shǐ Jì," the praise of Qín,
fully uses Jiǎ Yí's three essays,
introduced with the phrase,
"How excellent is Jiǎ Yí's exposition!"
The "Hàn Shū" biography of Sīmǎ Qiān fully uses the "Shǐ Jì Autobiography,"
concluding with the phrase,
"as stated in Sīmǎ Qiān's autobiography."
Although using existing texts,
the distinction between host and guest is clear,
unlike plagiarizing others' merits.
Gazetteers are a form of history,
and they inevitably quote existing texts.
If they are like the vulgar literary anthologies,
the author's name
should naturally be listed under the title.
Now, if we omit the included literary texts
and categorize them into examinations, biographies, and other forms,
the author's name may be easily omitted,
so we should follow the example of "Shǐ Jì" and "Hàn Shū,"
and clearly mark it.
For texts that are lengthy
and require abridgment,
use the three characters "qí lüè yuē"
to introduce them,
as Bān Gù did when recording Jiǎ Yí's memorials,
which is acceptable.
When quoting old texts
to support one's own arguments,
follow the example of the "Bó Yí Liè Zhuàn,"
which includes a passage introduced by
"qí zhuàn yuē,"
which is acceptable.
As for prefacing with an introduction
or appending comments and evaluations,
many compilers today
use "yě shǐ shì yuē"
or "wài shǐ shì yuē."
Judging by principle,
neither is appropriate;
it would be better to directly follow the Eastern Hàn example,
and use "lùn yuē" or "xù yuē" for safety.
For repeated debates and corrections,
preserving doubts or appending differences,
adding "àn yuē" is also acceptable.
Otherwise, directly enter the main text,
without adding labels,
adjusting as needed,
all depending on tailoring the approach to the situation.
I. The format of biographies should be standardized.
The inclusion of biographies and conduct records in the treatises on arts and letters,
as previously discussed, has already been identified as inappropriate.
However, national histories draw material from local gazetteers,
and the section on personages is particularly crucial.
This is because statutes and regulations,
being part of the national compendium of institutions,
and official documents and archives,
flow from the top down,
and are thus uniform across the realm.
Even if there are occasional omissions,
there is no concern about a lack of sources for verification.
As for the category of personages,
unless they hold prominent positions and enjoy widespread renown,
receive posthumous titles from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
or have biographies composed by court historians,
their names would have no way of reaching the capital.
For reclusive scholars
and chaste women,
if they are fortunate enough to receive commendations and awards,
an examination of the relevant archives
reveals records that are little more than rosters of names.
Only when an imperial edict is issued to compile histories,
establishing bureaus and soliciting submissions,
can verification then take place.
Therefore, this process flows from the bottom up.
If local gazetteers are not detailed and comprehensive,
how can evidence be provided in the future?
Now, biographies are precisely the biographical format used in histories.
Categories such as "Confucian Scholars" and "Knights-errant"
were first established as general headings in Simǎ Qiān's *Records of the Grand Historian*;
"Men of Letters" and "Scholars of the Way"
were further delineated into three subcategories in the *History of the Sòng Dynasty*.
Earlier Confucians criticized this practice of creating categories as inciting contention,
but their criticism was solely directed at the lack of prudence in establishing these headings.
It was not like later generations' gazetteers, narratives, and stele inscriptions,
which were all lumped together under "Arts and Letters."
Moreover, when composing biographical accounts of personages,
they insisted on exclusively using specific labels,
such as loyal officials, filial sons, famous worthies, men of letters, and the like,
arranging them in sequence,
with each entry typically no more than eight or nine lines,
sometimes as few as one, two, or three lines,
and calling them "biographical sketches."
Now, gazetteers are meant to be detailed records from imperial commissioners,
and should be more detailed than histories.
Yet they are executed in this abbreviated form—
what is the reasoning behind this?
As for what cannot be encompassed by these labels,
or matters that belong to multiple categories,
if not placing Dǒng Xuān among the "Cruel Officials,"
then omitting Hán Tōng from the "Officials of the Zhōu."
Consider that in the *Records of the Grand Historian*, among its seventy biographies,
only nine, starting with "Exemplary Officials" and "Confucian Scholars,"
are given general headings.
In the *Book of Hàn*, seven chapters, up to "Imperial Relatives by Marriage" and "Flatterers and Favorites,"
are given general headings.
Jiāngdū submitted three memorials;
he need not be listed under "Confucian Scholars."
Dōngfāng Shuò was particularly fond of jesting;
he need not be listed under "Jesters."
Since the conventions for biographies are broad,
extraordinary conduct that falls outside standard norms can be recorded;
those with similar conduct
can be grouped together;
those with numerous literary works
can have them recorded and included.
One must only guard against mediocrity, excess, and favoritism,
and not be constrained by the length or brevity of the account.
This would be the best approach.
II. Judgments and critiques should adhere to strict caution.
In Simǎ Qiān's prefaces and concluding remarks, his judgments
are all introduced with "The Grand Historian remarks..."
This was to distinguish them from the narrative text,
not specifically to create a separate category.
Since Bān Gù composed "Eulogies,"
and Fàn Yè wrote "Discussions,"
there has already been some decline into excess.
The histories of the Southern Dynasties
then, at the end of biographies and treatises,
added discursive critiques in prose,
and also used rhymed verse,
imitating Bān Gù's style in his autobiographical postface to create "Eulogies,"
appending them after the discursive critiques—
building a house under a house,
this is mere verbosity.
Since then, the practice has continued,
with no uniform style.
When Emperor Tàizǔ of the Míng compiled the *History of the Yuán Dynasty*,
he instructed Sòng Lián and others to record events directly based on facts,
without adding judgments or eulogies.
Although this embodied the intention of strict caution,
it was not a truly fair and correct approach.
In my humble opinion, regarding judgments of right and wrong, praise and criticism,
the only desire is for them to be balanced.
There is no harm in appending judgments and eulogies;
but one must not intentionally show bias,
nor deliberately indulge in strange paradoxes.
For cases where right and wrong are obvious,
requiring no further discussion,
or where the biographical text already fully conveys praise or blame,
leaving no sentiment unexpressed,
there is no need to laboriously compose a conclusion
merely to fill out the format.
III. Statutes and institutions should be treated with thorough detail.
I stated that statutes and institutions, flowing from the top down,
can be treated somewhat more briefly than personages,
but this was said in the context of emphasizing that biographies should be even more detailed.
Matters such as schools and sacrifices,
all recorded in the compendium of institutions,
if they are regularly performed by prefectures and counties,
how can they be omitted?
The compendium of institutions is vast in its volumes,
and purchasing and reading it is not easy.
If its contents were dispersed among the various local gazetteers,
then everyone could read them—
would this not be a great thing?
Moreover, recording the institutions practiced by prefectures and counties
would only require a few more printing blocks.
Yet current gazetteers often delete and omit them;
I do not understand the reasoning.
IV. Self-annotations should be applied judiciously.
Bān Gù's history employs self-annotation extensively, especially in its ten treatises.
Subsequent historians
often used self-annotation in their writings.
When Sòng dynasty people printed the forged "Sū Shì's Commentary on Dù Fǔ's Poetry,"
for passages they could not forcefully explain,
they presumptuously added the three characters
"the Master's own note."
Later generations, realizing the forgery,
overcorrected by saying:
"The writings of the ancients
never contained self-annotations."
But then what about Sīmǎ Guāng's *Hidden Void*,
to which he himself added explanatory commentaries?
How does one explain that?
Since the gazetteer format values comprehensive detail,
and the writing style prizes conciseness,
applying the principle of compilation by category
to the writing of annals and biographies—
without adding self-annotations,
how can clarity and fluency be achieved?
However, self-annotation may be used
for factual matters in the text that require detailed examination of beginning and end.
As for self-annotation like that in the *Hidden Void*, which explains the meaning of the text itself,
that is not appropriate for the gazetteer format.
First, the literary anthology should complement the local gazetteer.
Poetry, prose, and miscellaneous genres are included in the "Treatise on Arts and Letters,"
which is certainly not an appropriate format.
Therefore, in my previous book, I intended to incorporate various genres into biographies and examinations.
However, the literary works of the Western Han dynasty are abundant,
yet beyond those collected in Ban Gu's *History of the Han*,
very few are seen.
This is because scholarly writings
must conform to historical conventions to be included,
while all poetry, prose, fu, and eulogies
lacked someone like Zhāomíng or Lǐ Fǎng
to compile and collect them beforehand.
Historical works are viewed vertically,
while treatises are viewed horizontally,
yet both serve the purpose of comprehensive compilation.
However, comprehensive compilation involves detailed events,
and thus extends to literature.
Literature related to local customs and human affairs
is quite numerous in its categories,
and history certainly cannot include it all.
For this reason, since the time of Zhāomíng,
anthologies spanning dynasties have been compiled:
the Tang dynasty had *Wényuàn*,
the Song dynasty had *Wénjiàn*,
the Yuan dynasty had *Wénlèi*,
and the Ming dynasty had *Wénxuǎn*.
These works extensively selected and arranged
both major and minor pieces,
serving to supplement what historical records missed,
and such examples are numerous.
Thus, when Zuǒ Qiūmíng compiled *Guóyǔ*,
he did not refrain from citing proverbs and folk songs;
and the fifteen *Guófēng*
were also compiled separately,
both under the jurisdiction of the Grand Historian.
This is clear evidence
that literary anthologies and local gazetteers mutually benefit each other.
Recently, the Governor of Chǔ, in addition to the *Húguǎng Tōngzhì*,
also compiled *Sānchǔ Wénxiàn Lù*.
Similarly, Governor Sòng of Jiāngsū, besides commissioning Shào Pílíng to compile the *Míng Wén Lù*,
also authored collections such as *Sānwú Wénxiàn Lù*,
to supplement the inadequacies of the *Jiāngnán Tōngzhì*.
I am shallow and poorly informed,
and do not know if other provinces have done the same.
However, from this one example,
we can infer the rest.
Why not slightly emulate the legacy of the *Guófēng*,
selecting pieces related to folk customs,
comparing and verifying them,
to serve as references for examination,
and categorize them into genres such as poetry, prose, records, and prefaces,
compiling them into a book for the county,
to complement the gazetteer?
This would certainly not be without benefit.
However, this is not something within your power to accomplish alone.
Why not take the opportunity to inform the authorities?
Second, the biographies of exemplary women should follow separate conventions.
The "Biographies of Exemplary Women"
was initiated by Liú Xiàng,
divided into seven sections,
with principles akin to those of philosophical works;
linking eulogies and odes,
its learning connects with the *Shījīng*,
and in narrating events and composing texts,
it is truly a work of historians.
However, the histories by Bān and Sīmǎ
both lacked this biography.
It was only in Fàn Yè's *History of the Later Han*
that the "Biographies of Exemplary Women" first appeared,
and later histories followed this,
making it a fixed rule.
However, what later historians called "exemplary women"
referred specifically to those of chastity and martyrdom,
while Liú Xiàng's compilation
referred to a broad array of women.
If "exemplary women" only meant those of chastity and martyrdom,
then chaste women and martyrs
would already be distinct;
furthermore, filial daughters and righteous wives
would not fit in,
and talented women in the inner chambers,
Daoist nuns, and female immortals
would never have a place in such biographies.
Now, in the way of women, aside from
chastity, martyrdom, filial piety, and righteousness,
other aspects may be slightly overlooked;
but could the great virtue of Bān Jī,
the historical talent of Cáo Zhāo,
or the literary prowess of Cài Yǎn
really be inferior to that of artisans or entertainers,
with no worthy deeds to record?
In Liú Xiàng's biographies,
aside from chastity, martyrdom, filial piety, and righteousness,
talented women like Qiè Jìng,
remarkable women like the woman of Lǔ,
were all included;
even down to Shī and Dàn,
they were attached as well.
The meaning of "array"
can indeed be broad.
Since the Eastern Han dynasty,
various histories mistakenly interpreted "array" as "martyrdom,"
equating "array" with "martyrdom,"
so beyond legal standards,
few could be included,
and even the inclusion of Cài Wénjī in history
drew criticism.
Now, we should establish a separate biography for chaste women,
to record those honored and awarded;
beyond the main entries,
if there are women of exceptional talent and sentiment,
or with different moral conduct,
or possessing remarkable literary elegance,
and excelling in a particular skill,
they may be included in the "Biographies of Exemplary Women,"
following the examples of biographies for artisans, literary circles, and recluses;
thus, women's virtues would not be limited to chastity and martyrdom,
and those with even one outstanding quality worth recording
would not be lamented as forgotten.
These are the reckless words of a blind man,
and I hope you will select from them wisely.
Written hastily while intoxicated,
I beg your pardon.
Letter to Xiùcai Zhēn on the Principles and Examples of Literary Anthologies (Part Two)
I am honored to receive your "Principles and Examples of Literary Anthologies,"
which is highly insightful.
Without deep familiarity with the intricacies of this field,
how could one produce such a work?
However, I have a few minor points for discussion.
Building upon predecessors' work and enhancing it
makes it easier for later generations;
compiling an anthology spanning dynasties
must be viewed through the lens of historical conventions.
Zhāomíng's pioneering work
is somewhat similar to Sīmǎ Qiān's.
From the perspective of the Six Dynasties looking back at the Two Han dynasties,
they are already summarized,
and the pre-Qin period is summarized even further.
For the Zhou dynasty, aside from Zǐxià's "Preface to the Shījīng"
and Qū Yuán's *Lísāo*,
nothing else is included.
This is akin to the perspective of the Han dynasty looking back at the pre-Qin period,
which is already summarized,
and the Zhou dynasty is summarized even further.
For the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns,
aside from brief records in the basic annals,
no further details are provided.
Zhāomíng covered eight dynasties,
while *Shǐjì* drew from three ancient eras,
and both were pioneering works,
so their examples are broad and their texts concise.
*Wényuàn* and *Wénjiàn*
both encompass a single dynasty;
*Hànshū* and *Tángshū*
each focus on one dynasty;
and by building upon earlier models,
their entries are detailed and their texts comprehensive.
*Wényuàn* supplements the Chen and Sui dynasties,
continuing what Zhāomíng left unfinished;
*Wénjiàn* includes examination essays,
expanding beyond Zhāomíng's scope.
This is similar to how Bān Gù's "Treatise on Geography" incorporated *Zhífāng* and *Yǔgòng*,
and how the treatises in *Suíshū* supplement the Liang, Chen, Northern Zhou, and Northern Qi dynasties.
Examples arise from principles,
and through careful consideration and adjustment,
there is certainly no issue.
The literary heritage of a dynasty
is not fully detailed in historical records,
relying entirely on comprehensive anthologies
to include various texts beyond legal statutes,
allowing for cross-referencing and examination,
and supplementing what the Twenty-One Histories missed.
This task is of great importance,
fundamentally different from the selective critiques of literary commentators,
and one should not nitpick over
the quality, complexity, or brevity of the texts.
Readers should focus on capturing the main ideas,
using them to deepen their understanding of antiquity,
which is truly beneficial.
Response to the Letter on the Principles and Examples of Literary Anthologies, Replied Again
Your letter states:
"Having received your discussion on the principles and categories of the *Wénxuǎn*,
I find myself strongly disagreeing.
The domain of literature
is extremely broad,
and history is but one category within it.
The categories established by anthologists
are numerous, extensive, and not always consistent;
the four divisions and nine schools of thought—
what do they not encompass?
Yet you seem intent on comparing them all to history.
Whether it's Sīmǎ Qiān or Bān Gù,
whether it's tables or treatises,
you meticulously try to fit them into the various anthologies of the Xiāo and Táng periods,
like cutting off toes to fit a shoe,
seeking points where they might correspond.
Is this not akin to Chén Dàshì, when first learning the eight-legged essay,
recasting all his family letters into that rigid format?
The literary works of the Western and Eastern Hàn,
selected for anthologies are exceedingly few,
yet the compilations and arrangements by Bān Gù and Fàn Yè
became the definitive versions.
Take only Lǐ Líng's letter from beyond the frontier—
Bān Gù's *History* does not include it,
and thus it seems closer to the trivial works of the Qí and Liáng periods.
Does this truly show that anthologies supplement what histories lack?
Or do histories supplement what anthologies lack?
For chronicles, we have the *Gāngmù*;
for biographies, we have the Twenty-One Histories;
the events of successive dynasties are already as clear as the sun and stars.
Yet you further consider matching them with the *Wénxuǎn*,
piling bed upon bed and building roof upon roof.
Can it be that ornate phrases about wind, clouds, moon, and dew
can supplement the collections stored beneath the pillars?
The practice of anthologizing began in the Six Dynasties,
and the form of historical writing also deteriorated at that time;
thus it is clear that anthologies are of no aid to history.
Examining and reflecting on past and present,
discussing and evaluating merits and faults—
these lie with outstanding individuals
who do not rigidly cling to chapters and sentences.
The songs of youths and the sighs of women
can all be observed and gathered,
but are they all to be equated with history?
People of old called Dù Fǔ's poetry 'poetic history,'
but Yáng Wànlǐ refuted this,
asking whether the *Book of Songs* could indeed encompass the *Book of Documents*.
Your reading of books has always been outstanding,
yet your current words still seem constrained by textual exegesis,
which privately displeases me.
If you disagree,
please quickly bestow your judgment and instruction!"
Your esteemed letter is quite eloquent and discerning;
what you have bestowed upon me
is certainly not shallow or insignificant.
However, it seems your understanding of my intent is still not entirely clear,
and I cannot let your generous sentiments go unanswered.
Therefore, I dare to reply by letter.
In the domain of literature,
forms and styles did not initially follow one another,
yet each had its own origin.
The writings of the ancients
initially emerged in profuse and varied forms,
used only as appropriate.
How could they have meticulously established a single category
and rigidly sought uniformity?
If one says literary matters are inherently broad,
and history merely occupies one category within it,
then the categories would become unbearably numerous.
Biographies like those of Bóyí and Qū Yuán
interweave narrative and discussion;
while works like those of Zhuāng Zhōu and Liè Zǐ
often employ narrative as a vehicle for their writing.
Since you hold that the categories of anthologies cannot be uniformly applied,
then how would you
draw the line for such writings?
The Classics, Histories, Masters, and Collections
have long been listed as the Four Treasuries;
their origins are not so distant.
Consider the beginning of the Six Arts:
originally, there was no such category as 'Classics.'
The great *Yì* (Book of Changes) was not revered because it was a sage's book—
it was merely a work of the Masters category.
The *Shū* (Book of Documents) and the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals)
were simply two historical records.
The three hundred poems of the *Shī* (Book of Songs)
were a collection of literary works.
The *Yílǐ* (Ceremonies and Rites) and *Zhōuguān* (Offices of Zhōu)
were books of statutes and regulations.
Apart from the *Yì* being stored with the Grand Diviner,
the other four
all belonged to the collections beneath the pillars (i.e., the archives).
Later generations took them to examine and verify the forest of successes and failures, past and present,
but I have not heard of anyone fastidiously selecting those resembling the *Gāngmù* or standard histories
to exclusively form a 'History' category,
while other forms, being broad and numerous,
were abruptly excluded from such selection.
After the *Shī* (Songs) declined, the *Chūnqiū* (Annals) was created.
The *Shī* category is like today's literary anthologies;
how is it then that it also shares a beginning and end with history?
Local customs differ,
human affairs rise and fall;
what standard biographies fail to detail,
what chronicles cannot record—
yet by cross-referencing and examining,
what corresponds to this is found within them,
such as "The Owl" in relation to the "Metal-Bound Coffer" chapter,
or "Riding in a Boat" in relation to the *Zuǒzhuàn*;
and what lies outside of this,
such as "The Seventh Month" recalling Zhōu ancestors,
or the "Shāng Odes" also touching upon different eras—
is this not precisely because literature and historical events
inherently share a beginning and end?
The literary works of the two Hàn capitals,
selected for anthologies are very few,
not matching what Bān Gù and Fàn Yè collected.
If in those years there had already been someone like the compiler of a *Wényuàn* (Literary Garden),
who edited them into a grand compendium,
then the events and traces of the two Hàn dynasties,
I believe, would be even more vividly clear as if from yesterday.
The form of historical writing deteriorated in the Six Dynasties;
from then on, the trend declined daily,
but this was unrelated to the *Wénxuǎn*.
What is regrettable is that Zhāomíng's selection was overly sparse.
That is the true pity.
You speak of not rigidly clinging to chapters and sentences,
of not necessarily placing literature within history;
yet you meticulously draw a line placing literature outside of history.
Can such a view still be called outstanding?
Yáng Wànlǐ did not understand the Grand Historian's intent of observing customs,
hence he refuted the theory of 'poetic history.'
That someone with your outstanding insight should be confused by this—
why is that?
Ten Proposals for Compiling Local Gazetteers (Presented to Magistrate Hú of Tiānmén)
There are two advantages to compiling gazetteers:
Proximity to the locality makes verification easy,
and proximity in time makes the traces authentic.
There are three essential qualities:
Discernment sufficient to determine the guiding principles,
Clarity sufficient to decide on inclusions and exclusions,
and Impartiality sufficient to reject all personal requests.
There are five difficulties:
Clarifying astronomical divisions is difficult,
Investigating and determining ancient boundaries is difficult,
Reconciling diverse opinions is difficult,
Widely collecting and consulting books is difficult,
and Preventing disputes in advance is difficult.
There are eight taboos:
Avoid confused organization,
Avoid inappropriate levels of detail,
Avoid undue emphasis on literary embellishment,
Avoid embellishing famous sites,
Avoid arbitrarily overturning old cases,
Avoid superficial recording of achievements,
Avoid inflexible adherence to antiquity,
and Avoid greedily including legends.
There are four forms:
Imperial favors and grand ceremonies should be recorded as Annals,
Officials, teachers, and examination graduates should be recorded as Registers,
Classics, documents, laws, and institutions should be recorded as Investigations,
and Famous officials and notable figures should be recorded as Biographies.
There are four essentials:
Be concise,
Be rigorous,
Be verifiable,
and Be elegant.
Now, I propose to utilize the two advantages,
fulfill the three qualities,
overcome the five difficulties,
eliminate the eight taboos,
establish the four forms,
and thereby achieve the four essentials.
Please allow me to briefly discuss the reasons for this in ten proposals.
First, I will present the practical matters,
then establish the guiding principles,
in hopes of achieving the idea of drawing the palace plan on the wall.
First,
Proposal on Duties and Responsibilities.
The Supervisor should focus exclusively on adjudicating right and wrong,
the Chief Editor should focus exclusively on editing and polishing the text,
those submitting documents should narrate without discussing,
and reviewers should discuss without making final decisions.
Thus, each will not encroach upon the others' roles,
and responsibilities will be clearly defined.
Second,
Discussion on Verification.
Although a county gazetteer is small in scale,
its format should be comprehensive in all aspects.
Examination and verification should be as meticulous and detailed as possible,
and synthesis must strive for perfection.
All necessary books,
in addition to gazetteers from the province, prefecture, and neighboring regions,

such as the "Twenty-Two Histories," "Records of the Three Chǔ Regions' Literature," "Comprehensive Gazetteer," the Kangxi Emperor's imperially compiled "Atlas of Routes and Distances," "Collected Statutes of the Great Qing," "Complete Book of Taxes and Corvée," and the like,
must all be diligently sought and consulted.
Other materials, such as unofficial histories, private records, literary compilations, anecdotal histories, family genealogies, maps, and registers compiled by local gentry,
anything that can aid in research,
should also be publicly solicited for collection,
examined broadly and selected judiciously.
As for the documents and records of the six government offices,
legal statutes and official correspondence,
those that pertain to governance, education, historical precedents, local customs, advantages, and disadvantages,
should all be copied into duplicates,
and uniformly sent to the compilation office,
to be carefully and prudently arranged and edited.
Only then can nothing be omitted, whether major or minor,
and a reliable history be passed down forever.
Third,
Discussion on Trustworthiness.
A county gazetteer places particular emphasis on biographies of individuals,
and the selection criteria must distinguish between truth and falsehood.
For biographies of individuals included in previous gazetteers,
the rule is to amend but not delete.
For new biographies of individuals,
they should be based entirely on memorials submitted by their descendants into the collection box,
verified for accuracy without falsehood,
and then sent to the compilation office for inclusion in biographies.
These are all matters beyond dispute.
However, the submitted biographical accounts
must contain verifiable facts worth recording,
listed in detail,
to be available for selection,
before they can be accepted for inclusion.
For example, when submitting information on distinguished officials,
it is essential to detail what positions they held,
what benefits they actually promoted,
what malpractices they actually eliminated,
and in what matters they genuinely contributed to the state's economy and people's livelihood;
only then does it meet the criteria.
If it merely states they were honest, diligent, cautious,
kind, benevolent, strict, and fair,
without any concrete evidence,
and reads like a routine evaluation or recommendation,
such submissions should not be accepted.
Similarly, for those of outstanding conduct, it must specify how their conduct was outstanding;
for those in the literary sphere, it must list what books they authored,
and how they were esteemed by scholarly circles;
for Confucian scholars, it must verify their contributions to which classics,
and what works they produced that are relevant to orthodox teachings;
for those known for filial piety and fraternal duty, it must clearly state in what matters they demonstrated these virtues.
Regardless of whether their character is ordinary, exceptional, biased, or well-rounded,
there must be genuine evidence,
to facilitate investigation.
Otherwise, if everyone's conduct is like that of Zēng Shēn and Shǐ Qiū,
their learning like that of Chéng Yí and Zhū Xī,
their writing like that of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù,
their character like that of Bó Yí and Liǔ Xià Huì,
all appearing identical and indistinguishable,
how can truth and falsehood be discerned?
As for individuals included in previous gazetteers,
if there are indeed omissions,
or if their major life events
are not recorded in sufficient detail,
they are also permitted, along with newly included individuals,
to submit detailed information uniformly,
for verification and supplementation.
Fourth,
Discussion on Soliciting Literary Works.
After individuals,
literature and arts are of great importance.
In recent times, those compiling sections on literature and arts in gazetteers
typically collect poems, essays, records, and prefaces,
making the format resemble a literary anthology;
while the catalog of works from the county,
and the origins and development of authors,
are left unexamined,
which is not in keeping with the purpose of a gazetteer.
Now it is proposed to revise the general rules,
following the examples of Bān Gù's "Treatise on Literature" and Liú Xiàng's "Seven Summaries";
categorizing by sections and collections,
removing the superfluous and selecting the excellent,
appending notes on their origins and development,
and compiling a separate critical examination,
which can serve as source material for future palace library collation,
thus benefiting literary heritage.
However, for literature and arts to be included in the gazetteer,
the rule is to evaluate only after the person's death;
living persons,
even if they have produced works,
are by rule not included.
This follows the established method of the Imperial Compilation Bureau for Continuing Examinations,
different from recent gazetteers,
which gather poems and essays,
including contemporary compositions and inscriptions,
and extensively publish even short pieces.
All scholars and writers from the current dynasty or previous eras,
who have indeed achieved distinction and established their own school,
with works that can endure不朽,
regardless of whether they are classics, histories, philosophies, or collections,
technical arts or miscellaneous schools,
Buddhist or Daoist canons,
paintings, genealogies, or registers,
examination essays or glossaries,
may all submit duplicate copies,
deposited in the collection box and sent to the compilation office,
for verification and compilation.
However, the submitted books
must be widely known and accessible;
even if not published,
they must at least be completed collections,
to be accepted for inclusion.
If they are merely draft manuscripts,
scattered pages,
or books without any preface, postscript, or definitive evaluation,
they should generally not be compiled,
in accordance with the principle of matching name with reality.
Only for works listed in previous gazetteers' catalogs,
but whose texts are now lost or scattered,
may they still be included in the gazetteer,
with the note "lost"
under the entry in the catalog
to distinguish them.
Fifth,
Discussion on Biographical Conventions.
The composition of historical biographies
follows the rule of evaluating after the person's death,
and not writing biographies for the living.
Reviewing practices since the two Hàn dynasties,
works like "Biography of Mr. Fēiyǒu" and "Biography of Lǐ Chì"
use biography as a form of literary play.
Works like "The Plasterer" and "The Camel"
use biography as a vehicle for discussion.
As for biographies like "Hé Fān" and "Fāngshān,"
they serve as prefaces for gifts or farewells.
By the time of the Sòng people,
it became common to write biographies for the living,
which is actually not in accordance with historical method.
Biographies in county gazetteers
should fully adopt historical conventions;
all living persons
are by rule not included in biographies.
Only for women who have maintained chastity,
and have already received imperial commendation;
or even if not yet commended,
but meet the age requirement,
and whose conduct is pure and unsullied,
may all be exceptionally included.
This is because a woman's duty to follow one husband until death,
leaves no other aspirations;
her lifelong responsibility is thus fulfilled,
and there is no need to wait for her death.
Moreover, such families of humble means
may not necessarily have connections among the gentry like those in literary circles or of outstanding conduct;
some may reside in remote villages or secluded areas,
with descendants lacking the means,
or occasionally failing to meet standard criteria;
if not commended now,
it is feared that in future gazetteer revisions,
they may be omitted,
hence the urgency in searching for them.
As for officials who have left their posts,
if their administrative achievements during their tenure are truly remarkable and worthy of record,
widely praised by public opinion,
with no dissent,
even though they have not yet passed away for final evaluation,
by rule they may also have biographies written.
This is because the gazetteer is compiled for this county,
and if an official contributed to this county,
then his legacy, like the sweet pear tree, may be preserved;
even if he was impeached for some reason,
or local opinion is not fully known,
how can his actual deeds be erased?
Moreover, since the person has already left,
there is no suspicion of flattery or praise,
and being separated by distance and jurisdiction,
there is also no precedent for remotely inquiring whether the person is still alive.
However, if the person currently resides in this county,
or has been promoted to a higher provincial office with authority over this county,
a biography should still not be written;
this is to avoid any suspicion of currying favor,
and to prevent disputes over right and wrong.
For those who by rule qualify for biographies,
when submitting biographical accounts,
they must focus on major life events consistent with historical conventions,
recorded in detail and with care;
trivial and fragmented details,
all that is superfluous writing,
should be edited out.
If the accounts involve the bizarre and fantastical,
with no moral lesson for warning;
or invoke spirits and ghosts,
or speak of strange dreams,
even if there is some basis,
they should not be included,
to avoid ridicule of tales like "ducks wearing shoes" or "sheep speaking."
Six,
On the Principles of Writing.
For institutions and precedents, create investigative records;
for individuals, compose biographies.
In selecting and discarding material for these two forms,
one must exercise judgment to achieve perfection,
ensuring they are both substantive and essential,
so that the work becomes an authoritative text
that can serve as a model for later generations.
For example, investigative records should focus on governance, education, rituals, and ceremonies,
local customs and folkways,
while exaggerated descriptions of scenic beauty
and forced associations with landscapes
should generally be omitted.
If there are ancient sites or notable scenery
that are reliably documented,
or inscriptions and poems by famous figures
that are truly worthy of record,
they may also follow the example of smaller texts with separate annotations,
and be appropriately appended under the main investigative record;
this is to rectify the form of historical writing
and distinguish it from unofficial records.
The form of a gazetteer can be compared to building a house:
the main halls and grand residences
may be called the main mansion.
But structures built against cliffs
or pavilions spanning water
may be called villas,
yet cannot be considered the main dwelling.
Jade hairpins and silk ribbons
may be called immortal attire,
but cannot be considered official robes and tablets.
This is the distinction between county and prefectural gazetteers
and compilations meant for armchair travel and leisurely enjoyment.
Biographies should also prioritize renowned officials, local worthies,
loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness,
as well as distinguished Confucian scholars.
Literary figures and specialists with notable achievements
come next.
If officials have no deeds worth recording,
or examination graduates have no accomplishments to highlight,
they should not, by principle, be given biographies.
For gazetteers belong to the category of reliable history,
unlike registers of officials
that merely list ranks and titles in order.
For those who do not merit biographies,
officials should have separate chronological records of their tenures,
and local gentry should have separate records of their examination successes.
Under these chronological frameworks,
only names should be noted,
with no superfluous words added.
Even if among them there are those who deserve biographies,
there is no need to note in the chronological record
that a biography exists,
so as to maintain uniformity.
If we follow the common practice of recent times,
then for recording officials,
there is already an "Officials" section
to record the dates of their appointments,
and a "Renowned Officials" section
to record their administrative achievements;
and for other matters found in shrine inscriptions, stele eulogies, or records of governance,
they are also included in the "Literature" section.
For recording local gentry,
there is already an "Examination Graduates" section,
and a "Personages" section,
also separating the year of passing the examination and their lifelong conduct into two sections;
and for their conduct found in epitaphs, biographies, or funeral orations,
they are again included in the "Literature" section.
Thus, matters concerning a single person
appear repeatedly across three or four categories,
leading to notes here saying "see biography in such volume,"
and notes there saying "see details in such section,"
resulting in chaotic annotations,
disordered facts,
and fragmented organization—
nothing is worse than this.
In compiling gazetteers today,
it is especially important to first rectify this
and break away from vulgar conventions.
Seven,
On Quotations.
Historical gazetteers quote existing texts
to clarify facts,
not to showcase literary elegance.
If it is relevant to the facts,
even documents from clerks
may be selected and recorded,
let alone texts of higher quality.
If it is irrelevant to the facts,
even the works of Bān Gù or Yáng Xióng
should not be included,
let alone texts of lower quality.
However, the literary works recorded in the "Literature" sections of old gazetteers
are now all dispersed under the relevant events or individuals,
resulting in uneven lengths and arrangements;
when incorporated into the investigative records or biographies,
it is inevitable to edit and polish them.
If there is concern about appearing to plagiarize,
then above the text,
still indicate the author's name
to show its source.
The method of titling
should follow the example of the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū*.
When the *Shǐjì* and *Hànshū* quote pre-Qin philosophers,
for ordinary deletions or alterations of words and sentences,
they do not mark them separately,
but directly use the phrase "the text says"
to introduce it.
Only when there are significant deletions or alterations,
and the original structure is not retained,
do they use the phrase "the gist says"
to distinguish it.
Such as the memorials of Jiǎ Yí.
All quotations now
should follow this example.
However, among various literary forms,
each has its appropriate place for quotation,
but the form of poetry and rhapsodies
has very few suitable applications.
Only within the geographical investigative records,
under the category of scenic spots,
in separate annotations,
a small amount may be included
to attest to the spiritual and outstanding nature of the place.
As for works expressing personal sentiments,
or describing wind, clouds, moon, and dew,
if they are truly excellent compositions,
they should naturally be kept in separate personal manuscripts
or included in anthologies dedicated to literary selection,
and should not be mixed into historical gazetteers—
this is the proper approach.
Moreover, since ancient times, the fifteen *Guófēng*
and the twelve *Guóyǔ*
have coexisted without conflict,
but it has never been heard that they could be combined into one book.
Thus, the excessive inclusion of poetry and lyrics in gazetteers
is also a vulgar convention that must be urgently reformed.
However, if in the section on customs,
there is a need to quote songs or ballads,
that is an exception.
This follows the principle of the *Zuǒzhuàn* and *Guóyǔ* quoting proverbs and ballads.
Discussion on Editing and Compilation.
All literary works that should be included in the Arts and Literature section
should be attributed to their respective authors and events,
leaving no room for debate.
However, regarding genres such as biographies, epitaphs, and accounts of conduct that should be included,
if they are all omitted now,
and their content is instead incorporated into the biographies section,
three difficulties arise:
First, some individuals who should not have biographies according to the rules,
or whose biographies should not be fully recorded,
may have had their epitaphs and accounts of conduct
overvalued due to their literary merit,
leading to indiscriminate inclusion.
Second, the biographies in local gazetteers
have limited space,
while the original accounts may be lengthy;
if the full original text is recorded,
it disrupts the balance between brevity and detail;
if events are omitted,
it invites criticism and resentment.
Third, incorporating existing texts
into the examinations or biographies sections
originally belongs to the practice of citation in writing,
so the author's name and the phrase "their words are as follows"
can be indicated
to adhere to the citation format.
But if old biographies are now taken
and edited into new ones,
they become part of a continuous narrative,
making it inconvenient to retain the author's name.
For example, when Bān Gù wrote the "Biography of Sīmǎ Qiān"
and fully used the "Autobiographical Postface of the Records of the Grand Historian,"
he used the phrase "Qiān's autobiographical postface states"
to clarify the distinction between host and guest.
This is because Sīmǎ Qiān's "Autobiographical Postface"
was originally not part of the biography,
so this phrase could be used to mark it.
As for the annals and biographies before Emperor Wǔ,
which fully use the text of the "Records of the Grand Historian,"
no such marking is applied;
this is because the annals are these annals,
the biographies are these biographies,
and the commentaries are these commentaries,
and their format does not allow for adding "Sīmǎ Qiān said."
If we hastily adopt this practice now,
it would be uncommon in recent times,
and would inevitably invite accusations of plagiarism and lack of originality.
For these three issues,
there is absolutely no other solution
except to adopt the method of main text with sub-commentaries,
which can achieve both goals.
That is, take the old biographies,
adapt them to the principles of the current gazetteer,
and edit them into new biographies,
while for content that should be omitted according to the rules
but cannot be hastily deleted,
include it as double-line small characters,
along with the author's name
and the reason for editing or omission,
all appended as notes below the main text.
This way, the factual content of the old gazetteers
is not entirely lost,
and the rigorous format of the new gazetteers
is not compromised.
For original texts that are not overly scattered
and still conform to the rigorous format,
they should be retained as they are
to show that changes are not made arbitrarily.
Discussion on Titles.
Recent local gazetteers
often lack proper selection and organization,
and are too cluttered and crude to be of value.
Not only is the writing lacking in substance,
but even their titles
fail to adhere to historical methods.
For example, when compiling examinations based on classical references,
broad categories such as astronomy, geography, rituals, and economy
should suffice to cover all specific subtopics.
Yet people nowadays often overanalyze,
dividing astronomy into star fields and divination as two separate sections,
and geography into territories, mountains, and rivers as multiple chapters,
resulting in lengthy volumes
divided into dozens of categories.
The examples of the eight treatises in the "Records of the Grand Historian" and the ten treatises in the "Book of Hàn" are still available;
why make things so fragmented and complicated?
When compiling biographies based on notable figures,
categories such as distinguished officials, local worthies, Confucian scholars, and exceptional conduct
are insufficient to cover all types of people throughout history.
Yet people nowadays often force mergers,
so when encountering an extraordinary talent,
instead of considering how outstanding their conduct and achievements are,
they first try to fit them into a predefined category;
when encountering a well-rounded talent,
instead of considering how comprehensive their learning and conduct are,
they first decide which category to prioritize;
this leads to contradictions and forced categorizations.
The examples of combined and individual biographies in historical records are still available;
why must categories be emphasized from the start?
The reason for this
is that texts such as classical references and evidence
are placed in the Arts and Literature section rather than in the examinations section,
so events lack context,
forcing them to be scattered
to hide the shame of oversimplification.
Texts such as accounts of conduct and epitaphs
are placed in the Arts and Literature section rather than in the biographies section,
so individuals lack complete biographies,
forcing them to be merged arbitrarily
to meet the required number of entries.
Thus, the format of gazetteers is ruined by titles that do not follow historical methods,
and titles are ruined because the Arts and Literature section does not adhere to historical principles.
The root cause of the Arts and Literature section not adhering to historical principles
lies in the initial compilation of prefectural and county gazetteers,
which mistakenly imitated the practice of famous mountain gazetteers in extensively including poetry and prose.
Gazetteers for prefectures and counties differ from those for famous mountains.
The latter focus on scenic landscapes and attractions,
emphasizing vivid descriptions,
and include inscriptions on cliffs,
records on walls,
traces of supernatural phenomena,
texts from caves and talismans,
as well as works by ancient and modern literati from visits and sightseeing,
leaving nothing out
to demonstrate depth and breadth,
as they originally do not employ historical methods.
As for prefectural and county gazetteers,
they are records of a region at a given time,
covering the people, society, governance, and classical references,
with broad applications;
how can they be treated the same?
Yet since the Míng dynasty,
this practice has persisted unchanged,
so although some prefectural and county gazetteers are better than others,
few have achieved independent judgment,
established historical principles,
or set exemplary standards.
Today, it is especially important to break away from old habits
and restore the format of official histories.
Discussion on Supplementary Compilations.
Among the Twenty-One Histories,
besides the four formats of annals, tables, treatises, and biographies,
the "Book of Jìn" includes records of states,
the "History of the Five Dynasties" includes appendices,
and the "History of Liáo" includes "Explanations of National Languages."
When compiling the "History of Míng" in our dynasty,
besides chronological tables,
illustrations and diagrams were also included.
Although their uses differ,
they are all created based on principles,
aiming to be neither excessive nor lacking.
County gazetteers are often cluttered and disorganized,
resembling unofficial histories and novels,
which is not the proper format.
Yet if they are treated with the strict simplicity of national histories,
it would contradict the intention of broad collection for selective use.
For matters that are trivial but cannot be omitted,
such as triple births,
centenarians,
traces of immortals,
and remarkable achievements in imperial examinations—
all novel and delightful accounts
that, while not central to historical format,
are difficult to omit entirely—
they should be recorded after the main biographies
in a miscellaneous style,
as scattered notes,
either titled "Supplementary Compilations"
or "Miscellaneous Records,"
forming a separate category.
This way, trivial and fragmented details
have a designated place,
helping to clarify the format of the main content.
Folksongs, proverbs,
street gossip, and rumors,
if they have value,
should all follow this rule.
In the late winter of the Jiǎshēn year,
Magistrate Hú of Tiānmén County proposed revising the county gazetteer,
and thus I composed this piece
to contribute to the discussion.
Its main arguments regarding the principles of editing and compilation
overlap with those in the two previous letters, "Reply to Xiùcai Zhēn."
However, the first five points of this proposal
concern preparatory matters
not covered in those letters.
As for the items listed in those letters,
not all are included in this proposal,
for this addresses specific issues as they arise,
while broader considerations beyond compilation
are not addressed here.
Regarding the constraints of conventional practices,
this discussion is more thorough than the previous letters;
and the section on arts and literature
is examined in particular detail.
Having investigated the origins of the flaws in common practices,
I found they all stem from this,
so I aimed to uproot the source of these issues
and decisively implement new principles.
This was not done out of a desire for change for its own sake.
Readers may compare the two texts,
and in the process of compilation,
hopefully find this of some small benefit. Postscript.
Preface to the Examination of Arts and Literature in the Tiānmén County Gazetteetteer (with appended discussion on arts and literature)
Alas!
The examination of arts and literature
not only records the flourishing of literature
but also laments its decline.
Scholars with aspirations,
bearing the extraordinary thoughts in their hearts,
often face conflicts and obstacles,
and reluctantly express them in writing—
how sorrowful!
Yet what they call literature
often results from decades of diligent study by lamplight and in harsh conditions,
amidst bitter rains and desolate winds,
refined through intense effort,
draining their heart's blood,
and presented with great care.
Yet within a few generations,
these works become scattered and obscure,
lingering among the living and the dead,
until, like dew chilled by wind,
they vanish entirely.
How lamentable!
Fortunately, when official historians record them,
they may be passed down to future generations.
Yet among those recorded in Han histories,
many are missing from the Suí Treatise;
and among those in the Suí Treatise,
many are fragmented or lost in the Táng History.
From the Chóngwén General Catalogue,
the Zhōngxīng Bibliography,
to the Wényuāngé Catalogue,
over a thousand years,
the situation is largely the same.
Is it that nature begrudges talent,
seeking to conceal its essence?
Or are the writings themselves
lacking in brilliance,
insufficient to endure?
Yet since the two Han dynasties,
countless schools have arisen,
mixing elegance with vulgarity,
and even trivial, crude discussions
have survived.
Thus, there is an element of fortune and misfortune in this.
The old Jǐnglíng gazetteer
did not include bibliographies in its arts and literature section,
so earlier works
were not fully collected;
and while biographies appended lists of lifetime writings,
few are seen today.
Thus, the works collected in this examination,
after another thirty or fifty years,
how much more scattered and lost
will they be compared to now?
This is why I deeply regret the fate of these authors.
Now, gathering from various sources,
I compile this examination,
categorized into four classes:
Classics,
Histories,
Masters,
and Collections.
There are three distinctions:
those transmitted through the ages,
those held in private collections,
both classified under the four divisions;
and those lost or missing,
treated as a separate category,
appended at the end.
Discussion:
Recent gazetteers' arts and literature sections
have departed from ancient methods,
grouping poetry and prose together
without listing bibliographies—
not without reason.
Compiling writings by category into volumes
benefits historical records:
events gain clarity through corroborating evidence,
and literature becomes comprehensive through inclusion.
Thus, after Zhāomíng,
the Táng had its Literary Garden,
the Sòng its Literary Mirror,
the Yuán its Literary Compendium,
each era producing comprehensive anthologies
mixing refined and popular works,
all to supplement official histories,
broaden knowledge,
and showcase literature.
But the fifteen Guófēng
and twelve Guóyǔ
should each form their own collections,
as mixing them is unreasonable.
Modern works often imitate Guóyǔ in compiling county gazetteers,
but none imitate Guófēng to gather a county's poetry and prose
into a dedicated collection.
This leads to reluctance to delete anything,
resulting in contradictions and inconsistencies,
altering the established methods for arts and literature.
Historical style values rigor,
while anthologies prize broad collection.
Incorporating poetry and prose into gazetteers
already feels excessive,
yet by anthology standards,
it seems insufficient.
Thus, the two should be separate works,
mutually supporting each other.
As for bibliographies of works,
they are of great importance
and should not be lightly omitted.
Therefore, I adhere to ancient methods
to align with historical standards.
Writings especially不忍删去不忍删除 are
temporarily placed in an appendix.
If future efforts enhance this,
gathering them into a separate book
to supplement the gazetteer's shortcomings—
Alas!
may there be those who follow this example and continue the compilation?
Preface to the Examination of the Five Agents in the Tiānmén County Gazetteetteer
Yáo faced floods, Tāng faced droughts—
even sage eras are not free from disasters.
Stars retrograde, fires reverse—
can external phenomena truly be anomalies?
Yet stone swallows are recorded,
locusts meticulously noted,
to guide human affairs
and respond to celestial changes.
Since the Yuánshén and Gōumìng texts,
with their absurd prophecies and omens,
rigor was lost.
The records of Bān and Fàn
followed Liú Xiàng's interpretation of the Hóngfàn,
drawing analogies and connections,
linking them to human affairs.
Though meant as warnings,
they inevitably involved forced correlations.
The relationship between heaven and humanity
is treated with caution by sages.
Over the 242 years of the Spring and Autumn period,
numerous portents and disasters
appeared variably;
the sages simply recorded them carefully
without meticulously matching
which event corresponded to what,
or which person.
Not that they couldn't,
but because the principles of cosmic response, constant and variable,
preserved in their general form,
are enough to warn people.
Forcing specific correlations
risks discrepancies,
leading some to doubt the seriousness of disasters,
thus undermining the intended caution.
Abnormalities in plants,
calamities from insects and beasts—
historians classify them under the five agents,
aligning them with five affairs.
I believe some anomalies occur for reasons,
but others may not,
making forced correlations difficult.
Thus, I record events directly,
without categorizing,
without noting correspondences,
solely in chronological order.
Related human affairs
appear scattered in other sections,
where readers may find them.
Preface to the Examination of Schools in the Tiānmén County Gazetteetteer
The ancestral home of Confucius has already compiled its family records,
and the Imperial Academy has collected its historical accounts.
Schools and academies,
share the same customs throughout the world.
Why compile extensive records and gather materials,
only to produce specialized studies?
However, since the two Han dynasties,
governance and education have each had their own emphases,
yet schools have flourished without decline.
Building halls by the water,
dusting off ritual vessels and wiping shoes,
when there are matters to discuss, they are explained and implemented here;
when there are no matters, the elders and the youth
come here to observe, wander, and cultivate themselves.
Rituals, laws, punishments, and governance,
the constant principles of human relations and the natural order,
all originate from this.
Thus, schools are inherently intertwined with the administration of officials.
The models and standards are all present,
yet the broken threads of tradition are lost in obscurity.
Stroking the bells and drums, one can imagine their harmonious sounds,
and be stirred to rise with vigor.
Discussing the Principles of Gazetteer Compilation with Magistrate Wáng of Shíshǒu
Gazetteers are a form of historical writing,
and the entire work must adhere to its own stylistic rules.
The language used in a gazetteer
is all related to historical methodology.
Thus, the choice of words and phrasing throughout the entire work
must also follow certain rules and standards,
which cannot be overlooked.
Stylistic rules are not fixed,
but they must ensure that the entire work is self-consistent,
without internal contradictions;
there is no need to alter them lightly
due to differences in personal opinions.
Even the originally established eight major categories,
subdivided into dozens of subcategories,
with slight adjustments,
can still form a distinctive system.
A table of contents has been prepared for your review.
However, those who write narratives and biographies
all come from the field of historiography.
If historiography is not properly studied,
then the narratives and biographical writings
will lack all methodological discipline.
As a result, the writings of local gazetteers
become habitual and unexamined,
not only lacking elegance and refinement in language,
but also harming the understanding of facts and principles.
Master Zēng said:
"In one's speech and tone,
one should keep far from vulgarity and error."
Vulgarity means the language is not elegant,
and error means it harms the understanding of facts.
Literary scholars, confined by habitual practices,
each take pride in their own preferences,
competing over intangible distinctions like plainness versus novelty or richness versus subtlety.
This is like people having different hearts,
and each having distinct faces.
How can one compete over this,
and why must one compete?
Only when it comes to methodological rules and principles,
if one does not know how to deliberate,
not only will the language lack elegance and refinement,
making it difficult to endure;
but it will also harm the understanding of facts and principles,
losing the very purpose of writing.
Now, corrections have been made following the text,
and discussions are attached.
Fearing that the reasons for these necessary changes are not fully understood,
a few points are briefly outlined here
to provide a general idea.
This will not only ensure the gazetteer's principles are clear and pure,
but also extend to narrative and biographical writings,
making them all clear, rigorous, and concise,
practical and useful,
without allowing empty rhetoric to harm factual accuracy.
For example, in the *Shíshǒu County Gazetteer*,
the text frequently refers to Shíshǒu as "Shíyì,"
which harms factual understanding.
A place name consists of two characters;
if one character is extracted,
then for other places with the same character,
how can they be distinguished?
For instance, referring to Shíshǒu as "Shí,"
among ancient county names,
the Hàn dynasty had Shíchéng,
the Qí dynasty had Shíqiū,
the Suí dynasty had Shínán,
the Táng dynasty had Shíyán,
today Sìchuān has Shízhù Subprefecture,
Yúnnán has Shípíng Department,
Shānxī has Shílóu County,
Jiāngnán has Shídài County,
Jiāngxī and Guǎngdōng both have Shíchéng County,
how will future readers
know it refers to present-day Shíshǒu?
As for using "yì" to refer to a county,
this is also habitual and unexamined in its actual meaning,
and cannot serve as a standard.
"Yì" is a general term for walled settlements,
from large capital cities, provincial capitals, and prefectural or departmental cities,
all can be called "yì."
The *Book of Songs* refers to the capital as "jīngyì,"
during the Spring and Autumn period, states in diplomatic exchanges
referred to themselves as "bìyì,"
was this specifically for modern county names?
Even small villages with fortifications,
settlements of ten households,
can all be called "yì,"
does this refer to county seats?
As for referring to the current county magistrate as "administrator of such-and-such county affairs,"
this is also inaccurate.
In the Sòng dynasty, capital officials were appointed to administer county affairs outside the capital,
their status was higher than that of county magistrates,
their titles still carried capital ranks,
hence they were called "such-and-such official administering such-and-such county affairs."
If we adopt this title today,
future generations will surely suspect our current system follows Sòng dynasty practices.
Terms like "yìhóu" or "yìdàfū"
are respectful forms of address used by subordinates;
they may be used in literary compositions,
but using them in narrative writing
is vulgar and erroneous.
"Yìzǎi" was an official title in the Spring and Autumn period,
although Hàn dynasty people used it in inscriptions,
it ultimately cannot serve as a standard.
"Lìngyǐn" is also an ancient official title,
and should not be used indiscriminately to confuse later generations.
Using ornate language instead of institutional titles for official positions
greatly harms factual understanding.
I recall someone referring to an ancestor as "Sīmǎ Gōng,"
and when I tried to investigate this ancestor,
I was confused for several days,
unable to find an explanation.
This is because common practice favors ornate language.
Using "Sīmǎ" from the *Zhōu Officials*
to refer to the modern Ministry of War;
however, ministers, vice ministers, and their subordinate officials
can all be generally called "Sīmǎ,"
making it already difficult to distinguish.
Moreover, prefectural vice administrators
are commonly called "Sīmǎ,"
and departmental vice administrators are also called "departmental Sīmǎ."
From the Minister of War down to a departmental vice administrator,
their official ranks are vastly different.
The three characters "Sīmǎ Gōng,"
even people today cannot discern what official rank they refer to,
let alone future generations?
Using ancient "Chéngjūn" to refer to modern National Academy students,
using ancient "xiángxù" to refer to modern stipendiary, supplementary, or attached students.
"Míngjīng" originally denoted a separate category from "jìnshì,"
but today it is a general term for tribute students.
However, the ten categories such as grace, selection, deputy, annual, excellence, merit, stipendiary, supplementary, attached, and purchased,
become indistinguishable if not specified.
For prominent and high-ranking officials,
posthumous titles often include "gōng," "wén," "yì," or "mǐn";
for scholars and literati,
literary names often include "fēng," "yán," "xī," or "quán."
Posthumous titles add "Gōng,"
literary names add "Xiānshēng" or "Chǔshì,"
sometimes resembling birthday congratulations,
other times like memorial prayers for the deceased.
One wonders where such styles originated.
Xiàng Jí said:
"Writing is sufficient to record names."
Now, reading such writings,
seeing the events described,
yet not knowing who the person is by name,
how can this be considered proper historical writing?
Another example is using only one character of a two-character personal name.
Ancient scholars have long criticized this fault.
For instance, referring to Dù Táiliǔ as "Qīng"
makes the expression incomplete,
while Xún Qīng and Yú Qīng
could both be referred to as "Qīng."
Referring to Ān Zhòngróng as "Róng"
makes the expression incomplete,
while Huán Róng and Kòu Róng
could both be referred to as "Róng."
As for referring to Qùjí as "Jí,"
Wújì as "Jì,"
and Bùhài as "Hài,"
these even contradict the original meaning of their names.
How can they still be considered accurate references to the individuals?
For women, those with given names should be referred to by their names,
while those without should be referred to by their surnames.
Since the time of the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* and *Shǐjì*,
this practice has never been altered.
Yet modern chroniclers omit surnames and refer to them by their clan names,
even going so far as to call them "the said clan,"
which is logically incoherent
and stylistically crude and awkward.
In contemporary writings about chaste and martyred women,
it is common not to mention their surnames,
but to refer to them directly as "chaste woman" or "martyred woman."
This is especially contrary to reason.
A woman preserving her chastity
is comparable to a man displaying loyalty.
If one were to write biographies of figures like Féng or Bǐ,
would it make sense not to use their names,
but to refer to them simply as "loyal ministers"?
Is there any logic in that?
When scholars of the classics compose examination essays,
they begin with two sentences to "break the topic."
In breaking the topic, it is customary not to write names:
the master is referred to as "the Sage,"
disciples as "the Worthy,"
and Yán, Zēng, or Mèngzǐ as "the Great Worthy."
This follows the practice of regulated verse,
starting abstractly before moving to the concrete,
as dictated by the conventions of examination poetry.
Now, applying this method to refer to chastity and filial piety
is truly what is called "acting out of habit without scrutiny."
Liǔ Zǐyuān said:
"Draw upon the Grand Historian to achieve clarity."
One cannot discuss historical writing without clarity.
How does writing achieve clarity?
By selecting words that are pure and unadulterated.
The ancients read the *Yìjīng* as if the *Shūjīng* did not exist—
this is what is meant by "unadulterated."
Though both are classics
and the words of sages,
if one were to mix imagery like "dragon's blood" and "ghost chariots"
with phrases like "Yáo examined antiquity,"
or pair dreams of bears, snakes, fish, and banners
with passages like "the first month of spring, the king's reign,"
then the work of the sages would be corrupted,
and the texts of the Six Classics would lose their purity.
Now, when writing biographies of chaste women,
instead of narrating their deeds,
they are often described as "vowing like the cypress boat,"
making the meaning of the text incomprehensible.
The "cypress boat"
is simply a boat made of cypress wood.
The poet used it to evoke an image,
not to imply that the cypress boat itself represents chastity.
The *Guān Jū* can evoke the image of a virtuous maiden,
but the osprey cannot be directly equated with the maiden.
The *Lù Míng* can evoke the image of esteemed guests,
but the calling deer cannot be directly equated with the guests.
The reasoning is quite clear.
Why then should narrative writing
be adulterated with the ornate language of poetry and rhapsodies?
The Master said:
"What is necessary is to rectify names."
Writing is the crystallization of names and speech.
"If names are not rectified, speech will not be fluent,"
and matters and principles will remain unclear.
Thus, documents have their forms,
