and writing has its rules—
these are the unavoidable constraints for the gentleman.
If following custom does not harm principle
or hinder affairs,
even if it was not practiced by the ancients,
one may invoke the principle of adapting to changing times,
and today we do not rigidly adhere to all past practices.
A Record of Discussing Chronicle Compilation with Dài Dōngyuán
In the summer of the thirty-eighth year of the Qiánlóng reign, guǐsì
I met Dài Dōngyuán at the Ningbo Circuit Office,
where Féng Jūnbì was serving as the Military Defense Circuit Intendant of Ningshàotái.
Dài was deeply versed in classical studies,
and his reputation was long established among high officials,
but he did not understand historiography.
Hearing me discuss historical matters,
he often responded with overbearing arrogance.
After reading my *Hézhōu Chronicle Guidelines*,
he said:
"In terms of style and structure,
this is quite elegant and classical,
but elegance and classicality are not the priorities in compiling chronicles.
In my compilation of the *Fénzhōu* and other chronicles,
I followed contemporary customs,
without differing from others,
and without fixed principles or structures—
only what was convenient.
Chronicles are for examining geography;
if one focuses solely on geographical changes over time,
the task of chronicling is complete.
Extravagant discussions of literature and documents—
are these so-called urgent matters?"
I replied:
"In matters of style and structure,
I seek what is correct,
not deliberately pursuing elegance and classicality.
However, what is correct
is never at odds with elegance and classicality.
If one says we must simply follow custom,
then anyone in the world could do it.
Why then select specific individuals for the task?
Local chronicles are like the histories of ancient states;
they are not specialized geographical works.
If you say only changes over time are important,
and literature and documents are not urgent,
then compiling a single essay on geographical changes would suffice.
Why gather people to establish offices,
collect funds amounting to thousands of taels,
use humble words and generous gifts,
invite you to travel from afar,
spend long days and months,
and produce volumes of books?
Moreover, changes over time, ancient and modern,
cannot be determined by my subjective conjectures.
Those studying changes over time
draw from historical records.
The records are there for all to see;
anyone can examine them.
Even if I make mistakes today,
later generations can still correct them.
But as for the literature and documents of a region,
if they are not collected in time,
or if they are compiled without proper methods,
or if inclusions and exclusions are inappropriate,
then in the future, they may be lost and difficult to verify,
vanishing without a trace.
The key to planning affairs
is to prioritize what later generations cannot correct or remedy,
and to pay special attention to it.
Thus, in my view,
examining antiquity should indeed be detailed and careful;
but when forced to choose between conflicting priorities,
it is better to emphasize literature and documents over changes over time."
Dài turned away and said to others:
"If changes over time are mistaken,
then the entire book is mistaken.
If it is called the chronicle of this prefecture or department,
but in reality, it is not about this prefecture or department—is that acceptable?"
I replied:
"When we say mistakes in changes over time
render the entire book mistaken,
this only applies to ancient events that can be verified through records.
If ancient events are mistaken,
they can still be corrected based on ancient books—
the issue is similar to that of changes over time.
But as for the scattered and emerging lost texts and documents
from the past two or three hundred years,
or those passed down orally,
which may not survive for later generations—
as well as the benefits and drawbacks of policies and initiatives
that are practically relevant to the region—
these can all be verified with facts.
They certainly will not be mistaken due to a lack of examination of changes over time,
nor will they fail to correspond to this prefecture or department."
Féng Jūn said:
"A local gazetteer should integrate ancient and modern times,
only then is it a complete book.
How could it be intended only for the last three or four hundred years?"
I said:
"Books in the historical category
are detailed about recent times and brief about distant ones;
this is typical of all schools,
not unique to local gazetteers.
The *Records of the Grand Historian* is detailed about the Han system;
in its accounts of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu,
there are also quite a few instances
that clearly contradict the Six Classics.
However, the Six Classics are all extant,
so people can rely on them to correct Simǎ Qiān's errors.
Thus, even if Simǎ Qiān's book contains mistakes,
it is still not harmful.
From the period between Qín and Chǔ
down to the Tiānhàn era,
a span of over a hundred years,
people will rely solely on Simǎ Qiān's book;
if Simǎ Qiān is not detailed about this period,
how will later generations examine its events?
Moreover, those who compile local gazetteers today,
insisting on integrating ancient and modern,
do so largely because previous compilers of such gazetteers
were generally vulgar and shallow,
with nothing worth adopting,
forcing them to establish principles and set examples
as if creating anew.
If the previous gazetteer had no shortcomings,
then one should merely continue what it contains;
if the previous gazetteer had omissions,
then one should merely supplement what it lacks.
The compilation of local gazetteers
should span at most a hundred years for distant periods,
and only thirty or forty years for recent ones.
Now, extending the scope to three or four hundred years
is because, although the work is done successively,
its purpose is akin to creation,
so we deliberately set a broad timeframe.
If the previous gazetteer is indeed worthy,
there is certainly no need for all local gazetteers to cover three or four hundred years.
The purpose of compiling gazetteers
is not to display beauty,
but to seek practical utility.
Times change and circumstances differ;
old gazetteers cannot encompass everything,
hence the need for revision
every hundred years or so for distant periods,
and every thirty or forty years for recent ones.
If one says that only examining historical evolution is important,
and nothing else matters,
then since historical evolution is clear,
there is no need for textual criticism,
and prefectures and counties would have no need to compile gazetteers."
Féng Jūn suddenly understood and said:
"Indeed."
Dài brushed his sleeves and left directly.
The next day, he showed me the *Fénzhōu Fǔ Gazetteer* and said:
"Beyond historical evolution,
I do have distinctive insights and outstanding views.
The old gazetteer's section on figures
began with famous monks.
I wanted to delete it,
but the recorded facts about them
are so outstanding,
they cannot be removed.
However, how can monks be considered people?
Other gazetteers placing them among the figures
shows great lack of discernment.
I thought that famous monks must reside in ancient temples,
and ancient temples should belong to ancient sites,
so I took the facts about famous monks
and placed them under ancient sites.
Mediocre historians do not understand this innovative approach."
I said:
"Ancient sites are not a major focus of gazetteers;
they should be attached to maps of the territory,
not made into a separate category.
Creating a separate category for ancient sites
is a practice of comprehensive gazetteers and classified compilations;
shallow Confucians imitate it
and introduce it into local gazetteers,
which is not a sound approach.
If you say monks cannot be considered people,
then since they are flesh and blood,
neither wood nor stone,
what exactly are they?
The principles of writing and editing are extremely strict,
reaching their peak in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*.
Its condemnations and criticisms
extend even to treacherous ministers and wicked sons.
Yet it only rectifies their names to condemn and criticize them;
I have never heard of not considering them human
and treating their writing style differently from that of round-headed, square-footed beings.
Moreover, the section on figures follows historical precedent.
History places treacherous ministers and rebels
alongside loyal and good officials in biographies;
I have never heard of not considering them human
and attaching them to geographical records.
Deleting monks' deeds and not recording them
is merely the view of a vulgar Confucian.
If you consider ancient sites as traces left by famous monks
and not classify them as figures,
then the *Kuàijī Gazetteer* has Yǔ's Cave,
but its figures section lacks Yǔ;
the *Yǎnshī Gazetteer* has Tāng's Tomb,
but its figures section lacks Tāng;
the *Qūfù Gazetteer* has Confucius's Forest,
but its figures section lacks Confucius.
How fortunate are those famous monks
to be honored equally with Yǔ, Tāng, and Confucius?
Lacking discernment yet forcing interpretations
is certainly worse than being mediocre and avoiding absurdity."
Reply to Magistrate Huáng of Guǎngjì on Compiling Gazetteers
I have received the draft gazetteer you sent,
its style concise and dignified,
its rules strict and rigorous.
Yet you earnestly deign to inquire of me,
fearing only to disappoint your generous intent.
Thus, I will merely offer one or two points
based on my humble opinions,
for your consideration,
though they may not necessarily be correct.
The flaws in local gazetteers have long existed;
vulgar and excessive books by popular custom
certainly need not be discussed.
But those with refined intent, polished and refined,
aiming to establish a school,
often exist.
Generally, there are books by literati,
books by scholars,
books by rhetoricians,
books by storytellers,
and books by historians;
only historians represent the orthodox tradition.
Among historians, there are those who write original histories
and those who compile and edit histories,
their approaches differing.
Original historical writing
has been rare
since the Sòng dynasty.
As for compiled and edited histories,
they focus on broad learning and elegance,
aiming for every word to have a basis,
interweaving and arranging materials,
refining and editing them,
which is considered excellent.
The draft you sent largely follows Zhū's *Old Accounts*,
which is a fine example of compilation and editing;
but its application seems inconsistent in style.
Previously, Zhōu Shūchāng and Lǐ Nánjiàn jointly compiled the *Lìchéng County Gazetteer*,
with not a single word lacking a source.
For ancient books and old gazetteers with clear references,
they noted the original book titles;
for newly collected events
with no book to cite,
if taken from official documents,
they noted the office and file number;
if taken from submitted biographies or statements,
they noted 'family biography' or 'submitted statement';
for information obtained orally,
they noted the person's name and 'oral account'.
This shows the entire book contains not a single word of their own,
truly imitating *Old Accounts* with consistency.
In your gazetteer, some entries note 'newly added',
while others lack notation,
which seems inconsistent with the principles.
Also, the chronicle section omits too much;
regarding local historical evolution found in historical records,
it has not yet been fully collected,
and the rest also seems lacking in organization;
this section does not yet seem usable.
As for schools in the city section,
recording musical pieces and the positions of former sages and Confucians,
these are common throughout the land,
promulgated by official codes,
and originally need not be included;
now they are included,
but not cited as from the *Collected Statutes*,
instead cited from old gazetteers,
which seems to lose the original source.
Also, including poetry and prose in gazetteers
should be done with discretion;
my humble opinion is to separate them into a literary collection.
Now, following the example of *Old Accounts*,
including them under respective sections,
the approach should also be consistent.
According to *Old Accounts*, whether poetry or prose,
all are indented and listed separately.
Now, only in the mountains and rivers section
are entire poems recorded,
while in other sections, prose that should be included in biographies, records, or narratives
is often abridged without presenting the full text.
I fear that while conciseness is achieved,
comprehensiveness is not attained.
Moreover, the form of tables,
with their vertical and horizontal lines,
is intended to make the content clear and easy to follow,
and to condense the text,
which is an excellent principle.
However, in the current tables for official positions and civil service examinations,
the entries are still scattered like a roster of names.
Although they are called tables,
they are not truly tables in practice.
The household registration tables are well done,
but it would suffice to note the surnames under the respective districts;
now there are annotations of personal names,
but it is unclear whom they refer to,
so it seems appropriate to verify and correct them.
As for the category of arts and literature,
the classics, histories, philosophers, and literary collections
should all be included.
The authors of these works
are not all from the literary circles.
Now, the biographies from the literary circles have been cut and placed under arts and literature,
claiming to follow the *Shūlù Jiětí*.
In fact, Liú Xiàng’s *Qīlüè Biélù*
did not fail to list the authors,
which is somewhat similar to the form of biographies.
However, when Bān Gù compiled the *Hànshū·Yìwénzhì*,
he wrote separate biographies for each,
and under the *Yìwén* category,
he simply noted “has a biography,”
which was the proper approach.
Now, it seems the roles have been reversed, and the guest has become the host.
Regarding the above points,
I am well aware that my views are like those of a blind man,
and may not be worth considering.
Moreover, I have overstepped my bounds
by offering unsolicited advice,
so I dare not trouble you with trivial matters;
however, since you have inquired,
I cannot help but present a general outline.
A Reply to Prefect Cuī Jīngzhōu
Last month, when I visited,
you were in the midst of pressing official duties,
yet you kindly provided me with gifts and a boat,
for which I feel deeply uneasy.
As a scholar with narrow perspectives,
I am unaware of the urgent matters in official circles,
and I have repeatedly written to trouble you,
for which I am utterly ashamed!
Now that winter is cold,
I respectfully hope that you are well.
Regarding the draft of the gazetteer you entrusted to me,
I departed in such haste
that I did not have time to open and examine it.
I had previously written to you,
saying I would reply after returning to the provincial capital;
but with nothing to do on the boat,
I briefly glanced through it,
and I marveled at your discernment,
which is unmatched by others.
When we met earlier in the provincial capital,
and I presented the draft to you,
you had little time to spare,
yet you immediately said:
“The gazetteer is quite precise;
if there are any errors,
they can easily be corrected.”
These few words were a definitive judgment.
Now, after the local gentry
have scrutinized it for over a month,
their annotations are as numerous as hemp fibers,
and they have even repeatedly resorted to ridicule and mockery,
completely lacking in refinement,
which has left me utterly ashamed!
However, upon closer examination,
the issues are only with the two tables of official positions and civil service examinations,
where the names are disordered and misplaced;
and with one volume of inscriptions and records in the literary collection,
where the chronology is not in order,
which indeed creates contradictions.
But proofreading should be meticulous,
and debates over rituals can lead to disputes;
having annotations and discussions during the compilation of a book
is a normal part of the process.
Otherwise, the ancients would not have established the study of textual criticism;
nor would modern compilers
need to list the names of proofreaders and reviewers.
Moreover, the two tables of official positions and civil service examinations
do indeed contain errors in their compilation;
and the submitted records
were incomplete to begin with.
As for the literary collection,
since it was compiled into volumes first,
and later additions were made,
the chronology became disordered.
Although these are errors,
they are not entirely without cause.
Yet, beyond pointing out these issues,
the gentry have harshly criticized and rebuked,
as if a tutor scolding a child,
or an official reprimanding a clerk,
which is excessive.
If their literary understanding were truly clear and their criticisms accurate,
I would have no difficulty treating them as strict teachers.
However, the very first annotation in the draft
concerns the original statement in the general principles: “Local gazetteers are essential abridgments of national history.”
The meaning is clear.
“Essential abridgment”
means “abridged for essential use.”
The phrase comes from the *Shǐjì*,
and is not particularly obscure.
Yet the annotation suggests changing it to “essential canon,”
which would imply that national history relies on local gazetteers for importance,
distorting the facts
and making the phrase difficult to understand.
In the literary collection’s “Record of the Two Sages Shrine,”
it says above, “stood and transformed before the statue,”
and below, “revived after a meal’s time.”
“Transformed” here means “died,”
which is why the character for “death” (死) is derived from half of the character for “transform” (化).
The text is also clear in itself.
Yet the annotation on the phrase “stood and transformed” says:
“There is an error, otherwise the revival below has no basis.”
From this, it is evident
that the annotator’s literary understanding is fundamentally unclear,
which explains why they arbitrarily criticize and scold,
unaware of the dignity of scholarly writing.
As for the tables of official positions and civil service examinations,
errors should indeed be corrected.
However, official positions include civil and military, principal and auxiliary,
and civil service examinations also include civil and military, first and second classes.
Since the seven counties under the jurisdiction are divided into seven columns,
and the official positions and examination results for each county
are further subdivided column by column,
the space on the page would be insufficient;
therefore, only seven columns are used,
with the various categories
annotated beneath the names.
This method is based on the *Hànshū·Bǎiguānbiǎo*,
where thirty-four official titles
are listed in fourteen columns,
with the categories still annotated within the table,
which is an excellent method for simplifying complexity.
Now, the annotation states:
“Mixing everything into one table makes it unclear.”
Moreover, the literary collection is organized by literary genres,
with a consistent format throughout.
If there are errors in the arrangement of inscriptions and records,
they should naturally be annotated and corrected.
Yet the annotation suddenly says:
“Records of schools should come first,
government offices next,
and temples and monasteries last.”
This would require further classification within a single genre;
classification is not inherently wrong,
but genres like memorials, prefaces, discussions, poems, and rhapsodies
are not classified,
nor are they annotated for changes,
making the principles of the book
self-contradictory.
From this, it is evident
that the annotator is unfamiliar with the conventions of book compilation,
and only knows how to rant and scold arbitrarily,
unaware that social interactions should be guided by propriety and righteousness.
There are many other instances where the annotations point out non-issues or criticize unnecessarily,
but I will mention one or two to represent the rest.
Thus, the annotations provided by the gentry
may not all be credible.
The section on customs in the *Jīngzhōu Gazetteer*
follows old texts,
claiming that the scholars uphold integrity and humility.
But judging from the annotations in this book,
which come from the gentry,
they neither understand the nuances of language in literary texts
nor the arrangement of categories in compilation conventions.
Instead, they indulge in unrestrained criticism and insults,
approaching the height of ignorance and arrogance,
making it difficult to discuss literary culture and scholarly practices with them.
Reflecting on how, in just a few days,
you assessed the strengths and weaknesses of the draft,
far surpassing the gentry who spent many days
pointing out countless issues,
I am filled with utmost admiration.
However, you are currently too busy to attend to this matter,
and I am pressed by my return deadline.
I will wait until next year to respond to the annotations
and await your further instructions.
Preface to the *Dàmíng County Gazetteer*, Written for Sima Zhāng Jífǔ
In the winter of the forty-sixth year of the Qiánlóng reign,
I was transferred from the position of magistrate of Féixiāng County to the more demanding post of Dàmíng.
Dàmíng, having been moved from its original location in Wèi to the prefectural seat,
was known as a crucial hub south of the capital region;
yet the county gazetteer had not yet been compiled into a complete book,
and the collection of historical documents
remained incomplete and inadequate.
I had the intention to gather materials,
but upon taking office,
I was initially too occupied to do so.
By the forty-ninth year,
I began to discuss and deliberate with the local gentry,
drawing from the old gazetteers of the two counties,
cross-referencing and verifying them,
supplementing them with what I had seen and heard thereafter,
and compiling them into a volume;
resulting in two chapters of maps and descriptions,
two chapters of tables,
seven chapters of records,
and five chapters of biographies,
totaling sixteen chapters in all.
The preface, guidelines, and table of contents placed at the beginning of the volume,
and the miscellaneous notes appended at the end,
were not included in this count.
In the first month of spring in the fiftieth year,
the book was completed.
At that time, I was promoted to assistant prefect of Héjiān Prefecture,
but soon after, I was dismissed from office due to a mistake,
and remained stranded in my former jurisdiction.
The successor in governance,
Mr. Wú of Xiūníng,
was transferred from Lóngpíng to administer this county.
Mr. Wú had long been renowned in the capital region for his virtuous governance,
and was also highly accomplished in literature,
his learning deeply rooted in tradition.
When we became acquainted,
we found ourselves in perfect harmony.
Thus, I entrusted the draft of the gazetteer to him for revision,
and had it sent to the printers.
I then recounted the reasons for compiling the gazetteer
and sought Mr. Wú's opinion.
He said:
"When I was in the official residence at Féixiāng,
my friend and fellow examination candidate Zhāng Xuéchéng of Kuàijī
discussed with me the matter of compiling gazetteers.
What Zhāng said
differed from the practices of modern gazetteer compilers.
I inquired about his views,
and Zhāng said:
'Local gazetteers of prefectures and counties
are the legacy of the historiographers of the feudal states in ancient times;
yet modern compilers of gazetteers
mistakenly imitate the maps and records of prefectures and counties from the Táng and Sòng dynasties, thereby losing their true essence.
The "Zhōu Guān" states that the external historian was in charge of the records of the four regions,
with annotations referring to works such as Jìn's "Shèng,"
Chǔ's "Táowù,"
and Lǔ's "Chūnqiū."
These are the histories of individual states,
recording everything without omission,
and thus can serve as sources for the histories of dynasties.
When Confucius composed the "Chūnqiū,"
he necessarily consulted the treasured documents of a hundred states,
which illustrates this principle.
As for the use of maps and records,
they belong specifically to the field of geography.
According to the "Tiān Guān," the records and maps managed by the accounting office note:
records refer to household registers,
maps refer to the shapes and features of the land,
and the extent of fields,
which later maps and records followed.
Thus, local gazetteers and maps and records
are fundamentally different in form;
yet later generations have long failed to distinguish between the two.'"
I said:
"Can maps and records from the past still be examined today?"
Zhāng said:
"Ancient maps and records
are no longer visible today.
Occasionally, the text survives but the maps are lost,
such as the 'Wújùn Tújīng' and 'Gāolí Tújīng';
or they are briefly mentioned in various books,
such as the 'Shuǐjīng' and geographical records,
but their complete form cannot be obtained.
Modern maps and records
are the maps of prefectures and counties,
along with the registers of the six administrative guidelines,
which exist as scattered documents.
Works like the Yuán and Míng dynasties' 'Yītǒngzhì'
are comprehensive compilations.
The scattered documents,
preserved in official records,
lack literary refinement
and are disdained by scholars.
The comprehensive works,
while specialized in geography,
include categories such as notable figures, visitors,
scenic spots, local products,
historical sites, and temples,
which are grouped together under geography
to supply material for literary compositions,
rather than serving the original purpose of such works.
Thus, descriptions of scenic spots are inevitably written in parallel prose,
notable figures are summarized briefly,
historical sites focus on lingering over scenery,
and temples are recorded for their appeal to tourists.
These are merely classified compilations within geography
and do not serve as a comprehensive collection of local historical documents,
which is quite evident."
I said:
"Then, is the format of comprehensive gazetteers incorrect?
Yán Ruòqú argued that comprehensive gazetteers
should not include notable figures.
Are his words truly worthy of emulation?"
Zhāng said:
"Comprehensive gazetteers originated in the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
their format based on those of the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
Their substance and style, with additions and omissions,
have their origins,
and cannot be deemed incorrect.
The 'Yuánhé Jùnxiànzhì'
begins each section with a map,
followed by the distances to the four directions and eight points.
Beyond the经纬 of mountains and rivers,
nothing else is appended;
this is the essence of maps and records.
The 'Tàipíng Huányǔjì'
includes notable figures and literary works,
representing an expansion upon earlier works.
The 'Jiāxī Fāngyú Shènglǎn'
extravagantly displays famous scenic spots and historical sites,
along with travelogues and poetic compositions,
representing a further drift into excess.
The format of comprehensive gazetteers
supplements what the 'Huányǔjì' omitted,
prunes the superfluous descriptions of scenic spots,
strikes a balance among earlier works,
and has its basis.
Yán Ruòqú's criticism of it is excessive.
However, their format inherently has its priorities,
and one must not adhere rigidly to classified compilations
to achieve a comprehensive collection of local historical documents,
which is quite clear."
I said:
"What were the principles and formats of ancient local gazetteers?"
Zhāng said:
"During the Three Dynasties of feudalism,
and the later periods of separatist rule,
each state largely had its own system,
and their formats naturally differed.
In the era of prefectures and counties,
works such as the Hàn dynasty's 'Rǔnán Xiānxiánzhuàn,' 'Xiāngyáng Qíjiùzhuàn,' and 'Guāndōng Fēngsúzhuàn'
were already partial and incomplete,
and what has been passed down is not their original texts.
What can be seen today
are over ten Sòng dynasty gazetteers.
Although they are not without flaws,
at that time, the practice of classified compilations in maps and records was not yet prevalent,
and the historiographical tradition was still preserved.
They are not like modern gazetteers, which directly adopt classified subheadings
to form the entire gazetteer,
as if this were an unchangeable, sacred principle."
I said:
"Among the over ten Sòng dynasty gazetteers,
what are their strengths and weaknesses?"
Zhāng said:
"Fàn's 'Wújùnzhì'
and Luó's 'Xīn'ānzhì'
are particularly outstanding.
Luó's gazetteer is verbose but not precise,
while Fàn's is concise but not detailed—
these are their shortcomings.
Luó's gazetteer aims at scholarly composition,
while Fàn's demonstrates editorial skill—
these are their strengths.
Few later generations have grasped the intent of scholarly composition.
Those who understand editing
often produce writing that is sparse and lacking in richness,
with narratives that are constrained and not fluid.
Their insights
do not extend beyond the habits of literary men
and cannot align with the grand framework of historiography.
Examples such as Kāng's 'Wǔgōngzhì'
and Hán's 'Cháoyìzhì'
are clear illustrations of this.
What are the habits of literary men?
Imitating Hán Tuìzhī's 'Huàjì' to describe mountains, rivers, and products,
without realizing that the format of the eight treatises and ten records
cannot be discarded.
Imitating Liǔ Zǐhòu's 'Xiānyǒujì' to record notable figures,
without remembering the example of the seventy biographies,
which cannot be forgotten.
Yet these are still the faults of literary men pursuing fame.
Those of lower caliber
need not even be discussed."
I said:
"As you have said,
how then should gazetteers be compiled?"
Zhāng Jūn said:
"A gazetteer is
a record.
Beyond its events and writings,
there must be meaning,
the subtle intent of the historian's composition.
The historical records of a region,
why should they rely on a single author's work?
Yet if not entrusted to a composition,
they cannot be transmitted through the ages and reach far.
Official documents and registers,
though not lacking in detail and clarity,
are particularly difficult to preserve long.
Therefore, specialists are valued.
The intent of specialists,
spiritual and illuminating,
lies within the person,
and cannot be conveyed in words.
What can be conveyed in words
are the rules and methods,
which must clarify the comprehensive framework of all history."
"How should one clarify the comprehensive framework of all history?"He said:
"Understand that local gazetteers are not specialized geographical books;
thus mountains, rivers, cities, villages, memorial arches, and scenic spots
should all be compiled into geography,
and should not occupy separate chapters,
losing the principle of guest and host.
Understand that local gazetteers provide material for national history;
thus biographies of figures should be more detailed than historical accounts,
and should not be abridged summaries;
literature and arts should fully list bibliographies,
and should not categorize selected poems and essays.
Understand that local gazetteers are essential abridgments of historical works;
thus clerks' documents
and literati's ornate words
are all useless,
and the form should follow historical methods.
These are what can be spoken of.
Families have genealogies,
prefectures and counties have gazetteers,
the state has history,
their principle is the same.
Yet if family genealogies are verifiable,
then county gazetteers draw from them.
If county gazetteers are verifiable,
then national history draws from them.
Now compiling the history of a dynasty,
there are those who draw from family genealogies.
I have not heard of drawing from county gazetteers.
This is because they are crude and unverifiable,
difficult for gentry and scholars to discuss.
Yet the reason
actually begins with mistakenly imitating the names of illustrated classics and compilations,
this must be clearly distinguished."
Alas!
Zhāng Jūn's words,
I have not been able to fully grasp.
Yet regarding gazetteer work,
I truly dare not treat it lightly.
Two maps encompass geography,
I dare not linger on scenic spots,
or elaborate on scenery.
Seven records separate categories,
I dare not cause disorder by improper attachments,
leading to dispersion.
Two tables analyze warp and weft,
I dare not use rosters of names,
leading to clutter.
Five biographies detail facts,
I dare not abridge or embellish,
losing credibility.
The local gentry did not consider my words extravagant,
diligently discussed,
and compiled this gazetteer,
hoping that the historical records of the region
would not end up as Zhāng Jūn said, mistaken in geographical bias.
If seeking this gazetteer
and wishing to attach it to specialist compositions,
then I decline, lacking such ability.
Written as the preface to the Chángdé Prefecture Gazetteer for Governor-General Bì Qiūfān
Chángdé is an ancient famous prefecture,
left embracing Dòngtíng Lake,
right controlling the Five Streams,
the land of Chángdé in the Warring States period,
when Qín and Chǔ contended for supremacy,
they had to obtain Chángdé as a key point;
so-called controlling the stream barbarians on the side,
connecting south to the mountain ranges,
from here benefits extend to the South Sea.
Later Hàn once moved the Jīngzhōu administration here,
for externally controlling the various barbarians,
then within the province,
a thousand lǐ were peaceful.
Since Suí and Táng times,
it increasingly became the key point of all Chǔ.
In the Five Dynasties, after the Mǎ clan annexed Lǎngzhōu,
they stood firm and looked proudly,
no other garrison dared oppose them.
For shielding Jīngzhǔ to the north,
facing Chángshā to the south,
remotely serving as gateway to Diān and Qián,
it truly is a controlling strategic area,
is it not so?
Our dynasty, generation after generation of peace,
barbarians submitting,
north and south of the great lake,
all become heartland.
In the twenty-second year of Kāngxī,
Mǎnzhōu generals garrisoned Jīngzhōu,
then moved the military governor's headquarters,
to control Chángdé.
Later though Húnán and Húběi were divided into two ministries,
the military system connected the two ministries,
breathing together,
so the responsibility of command
remained unified under one.
I temporarily filled the post in Liǎnghú,
once inspected Chángdé,
viewed its mountains, rivers, and terrain,
with emotion thought of since Qín and Hàn opened roads,
the mechanisms of order and chaos,
the pros and cons of administration,
and the way of thinking of order in peace,
transforming customs to suit the people,
then summoned the local officials,
to study and thoroughly discuss it.
Prefect Lǐ Jūn Dàyǔlóng of Sānyuán,
is a sincere and diligent official.
The six inspections,
have gradually been implemented.
The prefectural gazetteer was compiled in the ninth year of Kāngxī,
the old volume crude and deficient,
cannot be thoroughly examined;
over a hundred years of cultural records,
again distant without evidence;
thus he requested to undertake revision.
I said this shows he knows the greater matters.
Although,
local gazetteers are everywhere under heaven,
wise officials know governance has constancy,
yet those who wield the brush,
do not know writing should value essential form,
vulgar, crude, miscellaneous, excessive,
not worth criticizing.
Even those who rise above common trends,
consider themselves establishing a school,
either literati proud of literary grace,
scholars boasting of their collections,
yet regarding matters related to statecraft,
and writing derived from historical form,
they have not deliberated.
Zhāng Xuéchéng, a scholar from Kuàijī,
studied under my tutelage.
He often discussed historical matters with me,
and his insights resonated deeply with my own thoughts.
I appreciated Mr. Lǐ's intention,
and thus entrusted Xuéchéng
to compile and arrange it,
which was completed after one year.
The work comprises twenty-four chapters in total:
two are Annals,
using chronological compilation to synthesize the major events of the entire commandery;
ten are Investigations,
categorized to document the institutions and regulations of past and present;
four are Tables,
with years as the warp and events as the weft,
to record the names and surnames related to feudal enfeoffments, official posts, selections, and notable figures;
one is a Summary,
and seven are Biographies,
gathered from historical records and biographies,
combined with firsthand accounts and hearsay,
to document the deeds of distinguished officials, local worthies, and those exemplifying loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness.
Thus, the main principles are established, and the details are laid out accordingly;
the structure is set, and its application can be fully realized.
Local gazetteers often attach undue significance to ancient sites
or inscribe poems on the "Eight Scenes,"
which lack substance and are merely ornate prose;
all such content has been generally omitted.
As for records, prefaces, literary compositions,
songs, and poems
that suffice to verify facts
and embellish elegance,
gazetteers conventionally include them under "Arts and Letters";
now, "Arts and Letters" is dedicated solely to listing titles of works,
as poetry and prose should not be confused with historical composition.
A separate work, *Wénzhēng* in seven volumes,
has been compiled as an independent book,
to complement the gazetteer.
Furthermore, from the remaining collected materials,
scattered remarks and trivial anecdotes,
though not pertinent to statecraft,
yet useful for conversational reference,
have been compiled into an additional volume titled *Cóngtán*.
None of these are included in the main gazetteer chapters.
All these classifications and categorizations
serve to clarify the scope and duties
and adhere to the essential principles of style.
Thus, the historical典故 of Chángdé
can be easily pointed out and discussed.
For a gazetteer not only serves to document literature and records,
but also to assist governance and education.
Perusing the maps,
one can see Shàndé and Táoyuán as mountainous strongholds,
and the Yuán, Qián, and Cānglàng as rivers and marshes,
vividly recalling the noble demeanor of the ancients,
which can inspire and uplift decadent customs.
Seeking traces of the past,
there were figures like Mǎ Fúbō and Yìng Sīlì,
who subdued the Miáo and Mán barbarians during the Hàn dynasty;
and individuals such as Lǐ Xízhī and Wēn Jiǎnyú,
who developed water conservancy projects in the Táng era;
adapting measures to local conditions,
responding to changes as they arose,
all are exemplars for civil and military officials of later generations.
Studying antiquity serves to inform the present,
and daily discussions and deliberations
cannot be undertaken without preparation.
Indeed, the constancy of governance and the essential principles of rhetoric
are fundamentally not two separate matters,
though those ignorant of governance fail to discern this.
Therefore, I take this opportunity, inspired by Mr. Lǐ's understanding of priorities,
to elucidate the main principles,
so that those seeking to govern may take them as a model.
Preface to the *Jīngzhōu Fǔ Gazetteer*, Written for Governor-General Bì Qiūfān
Jīngzhōu is richly documented in the *Yǔgòng* and *Zhífāng*,
held strategic importance during the Three Kingdoms, Six Dynasties, and Five Dynasties periods,
and became a crucial and administratively complex area in the early Míng.
Nowadays, it administers only seven cities,
yet among the eleven prefectures and subprefectures within Húběi province,
it still holds significant prominence.
During the Three Dynasties, when provinces were demarcated,
the territory of Jīng extended for several thousand *lǐ*—
this goes without saying.
In the Hàn dynasty, Nánjùn was established,
under the jurisdiction of Jīngzhōu.
Kuǎi Yuè advised Liú Biǎo, saying:
"With Jīngzhōu holding Jiānglíng in the south
and guarding Xiāngyáng in the north,
the eight commanderies can be secured by proclamation."
Zhūgě Zhōngwǔ advised Zhāoliè, saying:
"Jīngzhōu controls the Hàn and Miǎn rivers in the north,
harnesses the advantages of the southern seas,
connects to Wú and Kuàijī in the east,
and communicates with Bā and Shǔ in the west—
it is a land for military prowess."
During the Six Dynasties, it was fiercely contested in the Liáng dynasty,
and in the Five Dynasties period, the Gāo family rose to power there.
Though many offered ingenious strategies and proposals at the time,
and numerous theories proliferated,
they largely did not exceed the few words of Kuǎi and Zhūgě.
However, at that time, Jīngzhōu
actually encompassed commanderies such as Wǔlíng and Guìyáng,
its territory covering the Húnán region.
By the Míng dynasty, when the Yuán's Zhōngxīng Circuit was changed to Jīngzhōu Prefecture,
it became the present-day territory of Jīngzhōu.
At that time, it was enfeoffed as a princely state,
flourishing into a major metropolis.
Our dynasty followed the Míng's former administrative setup,
initially stationing a Regional Commander to garrison the area,
soon replaced by a Manchu garrison,
establishing a General, Deputy Lieutenant Generals, and others according to regulations.
In the thirteenth year of the Yōngzhèng reign
two subprefectures, three counties, and Tǔsī territories were carved out,
to separately establish Yíchāng and Shīnán prefectures.
In the fifty-sixth year of the Qiánlóng reign
Yuǎn'ān was also placed under the jurisdiction of Jīngmén Subprefecture.
Thus, the territory under Jīngzhōu's jurisdiction
was reduced to only seven counties.
Nevertheless, its strategic importance still surpasses that of other prefectures,
as Jiānglíng inherently commands the crossroads of north and south,
extending eastward and controlling the west,
its interconnectedness remaining as before.
As for adapting to changing circumstances,
the segregation of Manchu and Han cities
prevents disturbance between soldiers and civilians;
the mutual offsetting of grain tribute and commutation
alleviates the labor of transporting military provisions—
systems have indeed been established according to the times.
Only, as the great river flows eastward, its distributaries
have left many old courses silted up,
making river defense, diking, and construction
more critical than in the past.
During the great flood in the year Wùjiǎ of the Qiánlóng reign [1798?],
which inundated the city,
soldiers, civilians, and the city walls suffered severe damage.
The Emperor, looking south with concern and seeking counsel,
specially appointed a high minister,
bearing imperial authority to oversee the situation,
allocating two million taels from the treasury,
for massive engineering projects and major works,
which were successively undertaken.
At that time, I
was ordered to oversee the two Hú provinces,
and day and night I was filled with apprehension and vigilance,
fearing that my considerations might not be thorough enough,
and I would be unable to adequately respond to the imperial decree.
Consulting with the various dignitaries,
inquiring among my colleagues and subordinates,
pooling wisdom and resources,
fortunately, no failures occurred.
And the millions of living souls
all received benevolent grace,
rescued from the deluge and distress—
thus, though Jīngzhōu is ancient, it is as if renewed.
After a year,
the people's vitality gradually revived,
and official affairs became somewhat orderly and peaceful.
The prefect, Zhāng Fānglǐ of Shānyīn,
first intended to organize historical records,
to serve as a guide for future generations;
but he soon left due to other matters.
His successor,
Cuī Lóngjiàn of Yǒngjì,
then gathered the officials of the seven counties to discuss compiling a prefectural gazetteer.
Cuī Lóngjiàn began his career as a distinguished jìnshì,
excelling in scholarship before entering government service.
Regarding this gazetteer,
he was meticulous and not inclined to careless composition.
Moreover, the ancient records of Jīngzhōu
are twice as numerous as those of other prefectures.
Shèng Hóngzhī compiled the *Jīngzhōu Jì*,
Yǔ Zhòngyōng compiled the *Jiāng Jì*,
Zōng Lǐn compiled the *Jīngchǔ Suìshí Jì*,
Emperor Yuán of Liáng compiled the *Jīngnán Zhì*,
and there was also the *Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn*.
Although these books no longer survive,
their categories and contents can be traced,
and their scattered texts and fragments
are still occasionally cited in various works.
The *Jīngzhōu Fǔ Zhì* compiled during the former Míng dynasty
is only recorded in bibliographies but the text itself is lost.
During the Kāngxī reign,
the version compiled by Hú Zàikè
was reputed to be an excellent edition,
but it is also rarely seen in the world.
The extant gazetteer by Yè Yǎnggāo
states that it largely follows Hú's original text.
Its style is rigorous,
and its compilation meticulously cites sources,
which demonstrates the excellence of its method.
As for Cuī Lóngjiàn's work on this gazetteer,
he strictly adhered to historical methodology,
combining comprehensive detail and broad elegance
with independent judgment and distinctive editing principles.
It begins with annals to establish the chronological historical method,
followed by tables to clarify lineages and eras.
Historical records are preserved in various examinations,
and figures are detailed in biographies,
thus achieving a clear structure with well-defined categories.
Furthermore, since historical gazetteers
primarily focus on recording events,
literary works should still be cataloged separately.
However, modern compilers of gazetteers
indiscriminately include poems and miscellaneous writings;
those who attempt to correct this
often truncate poems and prose,
categorizing them under relevant events,
which deviates from the ancient tradition of classification.
Now, following historical precedents to compile the prefectural gazetteer,
he also imitated the principles of anthologies to compile a *Wénzhēng*.
He stated:
"The gazetteer follows the style of the *Guóyǔ* of the Eight Schools,
and the *Wénzhēng* follows the style of the *Guófēng* of the Fifteen States."
Each is an independent work,
allowing them to complement each other without confusion.
Additionally, among the collected materials,
there were trivial anecdotes and unusual remarks
that would be inappropriate to include,
yet regrettable to discard.
Recent compilers have grouped these into "supplementary records,"
but this also deviates from historical methodology.
He thus separately compiled a book titled *Cóngtán*,
incorporating both significant and minor details
in an orderly and systematic manner,
a rare approach among contemporary gazetteer compilers.
In the past, Luó Yuàn compiled the *Xīn'ān Zhì*,
claiming it was a work of Confucian scholarship,
different from mere copied records or ledgers.
Now, Cuī Lóngjiàn's compilation
has profound origins,
and compared to Luó's refined style,
it surpasses rather than falls short.
Coinciding with Húběi's project to compile a provincial gazetteer,
Zhāng Xuéchéng, a diǎnjí from Kuàijī, was invited
to oversee its compilation.
Zhāng Xuéchéng possessed a refined historical insight,
and his views aligned with mine.
Cuī Lóngjiàn also frequently consulted the diǎnjí,
engaging in repeated discussions,
and occasionally sought my opinion as well.
Thus, I am fully acquainted with the entire process
and have composed this preface for the volume.
Preface to the *Shíshǒu Xiàn Zhì*, Written for Governor-General Bì Qiūfān
Shíshǒu is a prominent county in Jīngzhōu.
During the two Hàn dynasties, it was originally part of Huáróng.
After the Jìn dynasty pacified Wú,
it was separated from Huáróng to establish a county,
named Shíshǒu after the mountain.
During the Sòng dynasty, the administrative seat was moved to Tiáohóng,
and the name was changed to Jiànníng.
Later, it was relocated to the left of Xiùlín Mountain,
and the name Shíshǒu was restored.
During the Yuán dynasty's Dàdé reign,
it was moved again to the foot of Chǔwàng Mountain.
From the Míng dynasty to the present,
its cultural heritage and reputation
have been celebrated as flourishing within Jīngzhōu.
The county gazetteer had not been revised
for nearly sixty years.
The old gazetteer was sparse and disorganized,
lacking proper arrangement,
and omitted several decades of historical facts.
The county magistrate, Wáng Wéipíng of Yùtián,
due to my compilation of the provincial gazetteer,
received an official request to submit county records.
He thus organized the county's affairs,
dividing them into eight categories,
combining the beginning and end into ten chapters,
to fulfill the submission requirements,
and requested that I write a preface for it.
As I perused this book,
I came to understand that Mr. Wáng is someone with whom one can discuss governance.
Now, governing must first establish order and discipline,
and compiling a book must clarify its structure and essentials.
In recent times, those who compile local gazetteers for prefectures and counties
either produce mere clerical documents and case files,
cluttered and lacking in judgment;
or they fill them with scenic descriptions and poetic inscriptions,
flashy yet devoid of substance.
If one seeks the underlying principles and meanings,
or the priorities of governance and education,
they are utterly at a loss as to what is being referred to.
Now, governance is about affairs.
A gazetteer is about words.
In the world, there are indeed words that are beautifully crafted
yet fail to capture the affairs;
but one has never heard of words that lack coherence
while the affairs themselves somehow become orderly and well-arranged.
Now, Mr. Wáng’s gazetteer
contains several dozen categories,
grouped into eight sections,
like a net held by its main rope,
orderly and without confusion.
The first is called “Chronicles,”
preserving the methods of history.
A gazetteer is what history draws upon for material,
and history records events;
without chronological arrangement, there can be no order.
The second is called “Geography,”
examining the land and its features.
The county has its origins and establishment,
mountains, rivers, and ancient sites
are arranged by category.
And water conservancy and river defense
occupy a crucial place among them.
The third is called “Establishments,”
recording human efforts and constructions.
City walls, moats, government offices,
down to altars and temples,
are appended in order.
The fourth is called “Civil Administration,”
establishing laws and regulations.
Household registration, land, taxes, and corvée labor, which fall under the Minister of Education,
and postal stations, military defense, which fall under the Minister of War,
are all part of the eight governmental affairs in the *Hóng Fàn*.
The fifth is called “Officials,”
clarifying duties and responsibilities.
Chief officials, deputies, teachers, and scholars—
from them governance and education emanate.
And those of outstanding merit
are thus given biographies.
The sixth is called “Examinations and Selections,”
opening the way for talent and the worthy.
Discussing the excellent and recording promotions is a major aspect of the *Wáng Zhì*;
promoting the virtuous and employing the capable is detailed in the *Zhōu Guān*.
Those who compile local records
cannot afford to omit this.
The seventh is “Biographies,”
the eighth is “Literature and Arts,”
one to examine writings,
the other to investigate contributions,
both gathering what has been scattered and lost,
carefully preserving what might otherwise be forgotten—
especially crucial tasks for capturing the times.
Biographies must be based on verifiable facts,
not on empty fame from praise.
Literature and Arts carefully lists categories and titles,
not padding the pages with poems and essays.
For Biographies follows the tradition of Sīmǎ Qiān’s *Historical Records* biographies,
and Literature and Arts follows the example of Bān Gù and Liú Xiàng’s catalogues.
In matters, one must follow the ancients,
and only then can one set a model for the present age.
Divided into eight parts,
it already has the main rope raised and the meshes spread.
As for the preface, guidelines, and maps,
they are placed at the beginning of the work;
remaining texts and additional remarks
are appended at the end of the scrolls,
separated into their own sections,
not included in the eight parts.
It is like the nine-square well-field system,
or the eight battle formations in marching armies—
the warp and weft are brilliantly clear,
both substance and function are complete.
Then one realizes that a local gazetteer contains the essential governance of a region,
not merely using elegance and literary flair
to adorn officials with a reputation for Confucian refinement.
Moreover, since Shíshǒu was established as a county,
it has moved three times in total.
The current county seat’s topography
is truly unchangeable:
looking around in all directions across the flat plains,
up to the county, mountains surge forth—
to the east is Lónggài,
to the south is Mǎ’ān,
to the west is Xiùlín,
to the north is Chǔwàng.
Positioned centrally and strategically,
government orders are easily evenly implemented.
Thus, from the Míng dynasty to the present,
it has remained the seat of governance.
Now, pacifying and controlling must rely on topography,
governing must depend on order and discipline,
compiling a book must value structure and essentials—
these are one and the same.
Mr. Wáng entered officialdom through Confucian learning,
knowing what tasks come first.
In compiling this book,
he has truly grasped the essentials of structure.
Later generations will follow this,
just as with the county seat.
Moreover, the ancients said:
“Those who sit and speak hope to rise and act.”
If what is now laid out in this book
can indeed be fully realized in governance,
then surely one will not consider mere paperwork and case files sufficient to fulfill one’s duties,
nor literary embellishment sufficient to display one’s reputation.
Thus, even though this is a gazetteer for a single county,
it is Mr. Wáng’s own book on governance.
The finest historians of antiquity
could do no better than this.
I have high hopes for Mr. Wáng.
Written after reading the *Wǔgōng Gazetteer*
Kǎng Hǎi’s *Wǔgōng Gazetteer* consists of three volumes,
further divided into seven chapters,
each with its own title:
first, “Geography”;
second, “Establishments”;
third, “Temples and Sacrifices”;
fourth, “Land and Taxes”;
fifth, “Officials and Teachers”;
sixth, “Biographies”;
seventh, “Examinations and Selections.”
At the beginning, imitating the writings of the ancients,
he separately composed a chapter preface,
placing himself loftily,
almost without humility,
yet many in the world praise it.
Wáng Shìzhèng
also said it was “concise in language, factual in content,
with elegant and classical diction.”
Later generations even wished to uphold it as a model for compiling gazetteers—
this can be considered fortunate indeed.
Now, Mr. Kǎng used just over twenty thousand words
to produce a book of three volumes,
creating a single county gazetteer,
and considered it highly concise.
But looking at his book now,
it is exceptionally cluttered and messy.
This is because he did not understand the methods of historiography
or the forms of literary composition,
and merely thought that reducing the number of volumes and chapters
meant being highly concise—
then who couldn’t be highly concise?
Gazetteers are a form of historical writing.
If they are irrelevant to matters of principle,
it is customary not to indiscriminately include poems and rhapsodies.
Kāng Hǎi, in his account of famous sites and ancient relics,
improperly included useless poetic compositions.
How far is this from the vulgar practice of compiling gazetteers
that treat literary selections as a category of arts and letters?
How far is this from the vulgar practice of compiling gazetteers
Now, feudal lords do not venerate the Son of Heaven as an ancestor,
and high officials do not venerate feudal lords as ancestors—
this is to strictly uphold distinctions in status and title.
Emperors and empresses of successive dynasties
are honored with annals and biographies in the official histories;
they do not rely on local gazetteers.
Those who compile local gazetteers,
when encountering the native places of emperors and empresses,
may indicate and clarify the relevant accounts, and that is sufficient.
To list emperors among the "Personages" section
and record empresses in the "Exemplary Women" section
not only confuses distinctions in status and title,
but also consider: the ruler regards the entire realm as his household—
what special connection does he have with a single county?
Kāng Hǎi, in his "Personages" section,
first listed Hòujì down to King Wén,
excerpting from the Grand Historian's "Annals of Zhōu";
next he listed Táng Gāozǔ and Táng Tàizōng,
again excerpting from the "Basic Annals of Táng"—
such contradictions and inconsistencies are too numerous to question in full.
Local gazetteers should not presumptuously list emperors—
let us leave that aside for now.
Even according to his own practice,
why then did he omit King Wǔ and those after him?
why then did he omit King Wǔ and those after him?
Is it because they later possessed the realm,
and thus were no longer associated with the old territory of Bīn?
But King Tàiwáng once moved to Qí,
and King Wén moved again to Fēng—
why then were they still listed among the personages of Wǔgōng?
Is it because King Wǔ actually possessed the realm,
while King Wén and those before him
were only posthumously honored as kings,
and therefore he recorded them?
Then what principle justifies
the inclusion of Táng Gāozǔ and Táng Tàizōng?
Is it because Gāozǔ and Tàizōng were born and raised there,
and therefore he recorded them?
Then why did he omit
the two ancestors, Xiǎn and Yì?
Among the empresses, from Jiāngyuán above
down to Tàijiāng below,
why is Tàirén alone missing in between?
Jiāng was not a fief within Wǔgōng;
to include her in the "Exemplary Women" section of Wǔgōng—
is this because a woman follows her husband?
Then Táng Gāozǔ's Empress Dòu, the Tàimù Empress,
and Táng Tàizōng's Empress Zhǎngsūn, the Wéndé Empress—
both renowned for their virtue—
why were they not recorded?
Recording what should not be recorded,
resulting in superfluity and presumption,
speaks to a lack of discernment.
Even judging by his own editorial principles,
he acted arbitrarily,
making it impossible to ascertain his intended meaning.
Can such work truly be praised as elevated and concise?
What is even more peculiar is that
the gazetteer is divided into seven chapters,
so why are the maps not included in the chapter sequence?
This, too, follows vulgar convention.
Maps are placed at the beginning of the work;
there are only two maps,
yet Sū Huì's "Star Loom Diagram"
is placed alongside the geographical maps—
this shows a complete lack of categorical sense.
Placing geographical maps at the beginning
may imitate the ancient convention of illustrated treatises,
serving to present the overall layout of the county—
this is still somewhat justifiable.
The "Star Loom Diagram,"
however, is merely the literary work of a single individual.
If one wished to follow Fàn Ye's example of including Cài Yǎn's "Poem of Grief and Indignation,"
it could have been included in the biography of an exemplary woman.
If it is argued that a diagram cannot be included in a biography,
it could have been appended after the biography.
To abruptly place it at the very beginning—
does this mean Wǔgōng County
is distinguished solely because of the woman Sū?
If we extend this principle,
since King Wén is listed among the personages,
why not place the diagram of the Sixty-Four Hexagrams at the beginning?
Since Táng Tàizōng is listed among the personages,
why not place the diagram of the Six Formations at the beginning?
Although this would be pedantic and irrational,
it would still be better than the "Star Loom Diagram," which is famous only because of a single woman.
Only the "Records of Officials" section, which combines praise and criticism,
still upholds the unadulterated Way to some extent,
standing slightly above vulgar conventions.
Postscript to the *Gazetteer of Cháoyì*
Hán Bāngjìng's *Gazetteer of Cháoyì* in two volumes
consists of seven chapters:
first, "General Gazetteer";
second, "Customs";
third, "Products";
fourth, "Land Taxes";
fifth, "Eminent Officials";
sixth, "Personages";
seventh, "Miscellaneous Records."
The entire work totals no more than six or seven thousand characters,
using only sixteen or seventeen sheets of paper.
In terms of conciseness among gazetteers,
none surpasses this one.
Kāng Hǎi, in his *Gazetteer of Wǔgōng*, strove to the utmost for brevity,
yet he falls far behind when compared to this.
Kāng Hǎi wrote a preface for it,
praising it highly.
Now, examining its literary style,
it indeed feels more concise and clean than Kāng's work;
only that within the "General Gazetteer," under ancient sites,
he included several Táng poems, which is superfluous and杂乱.
Both Kāng Hǎi and Hán Bāngjìng were men of literary talent,
but they did not understand historiography.
Moreover, they sought to distinguish themselves from others,
so their works
are unreasonable to this extent—
something that true writers would disdain to discuss.
However, Kāng Hǎi still retained the conventional framework of contemporary gazetteer compilation;
thus, when measured by gazetteer standards,
flaws and errors abound.
Hán's work, on the other hand, cannot even be considered a proper gazetteer;
it is simply an unrhymed "Rhapsody on Cháoyì,"
and also a "Study of Cháoyì" with forcibly divided categories.
If placed among the short records and minor works of the Six Dynasties,
such as the biographies in *Customs of Chénliú* or *Temples and Monasteries of Luòyáng*,
and not judged by the strict standards of historians,
it is not entirely without merit.
Therefore, regarding the two gazetteers by Kāng and Hán,
I consider the *Gazetteer of Cháoyì* slightly superior.
However, although the flaws in the *Gazetteer of Cháoyì* are fewer,
its inclusion of Chéng Jì's involvement with the Jiànwén Emperor's affairs,
indiscriminately drawing from unofficial histories
without verifying the facts,
is the first error.
Combining the "Eminent Officials" section with "Personages,"
yet failing to record the examination years for the presented scholars and advanced scholars,
is the second error.
Recording his father's affairs,
he referred to him as "Hán Jiājūn" (my father, Hán),
so that to this day people do not know his father's actual name.
In the "Exemplary Women" section, there is "Lady Tàiyírén Zhāng of the Hán family,"
who was clearly a respected elder of Bāngjìng's family;
but this leaves people to this day not knowing whose wife
or whose mother she was.
The ancients did not avoid using taboo names in writing.
Some say Sīmǎ Qiān avoided his father's name, Tán, by using "Tóng" instead;
however, in the "Biographies of Jesters," the phrase "tán yán wēi zhòng" (remarks hitting subtly on the truth) appears,
where the character "tán" is not avoided—
so the theory of name avoidance may not be accurate.
Even if he did avoid it,
in narrating his family history,
he must have clearly stated his father's name,
so that later generations could verify it.
Now, Bāngjìng avoided his father's name,
leaving people unaware of who he was;
he referred to his respected elder as "Tàiyírén,"
leaving people unaware of whose wife or mother she was.
This obscures the deeds of his ancestors;
seeking to honor them, he instead diminishes them.
This is the third error.
As for the names of chapters and volumes,
the ancients used bamboo slips for chapters;
when the bamboo slips became too numerous to handle,
they were separately bound into volumes,
marked with the cyclical characters Jia and Yi,
merely for the convenience of verification.
Later generations used silk to form scrolls,
which could hold more than bamboo slips,
so chapters came to denote the beginning and end of a text,
while volumes were generally measured by the capacity of the scroll axis;
this is because chapters have conceptual meaning,
while volumes do not.
In modern times, books are written on paper booklets,
which, compared to scrolls,
can increase the content severalfold;
labeling them as volumes
merely preserves the ancient terminology.
If accumulated papers do not need to be separately bound into booklets,
then for those divided into chapters,
there is no need to further divide them into volumes,
as volumes inherently lack conceptual meaning.
Now, the two gazetteers, *Wǔgōng* and *Cháoyì*,
their intention seems to avoid the vulgar compilation method of dividing into categories,
and both use chapter names for their headings,
which can be said to resemble the ancients’ approach.
*Wǔgōng* uses over sixty sheets of paper,
sufficient for one booklet,
yet it insists on dividing seven chapters into three volumes—
this is conceptually unnecessary.
*Cháoyì* uses only over ten sheets of paper,
insufficient for one booklet,
yet it also divides seven chapters into two volumes—
what is the explanation for this?
Some may say:
“These are minor details,
unrelated to the meaning of the text;
why fuss over them?”
They do not realize that these two authors regard themselves as true writers;
if even such matters as chapter titles and headings
fail to grasp the ancients’ intent,
then their every addition and deletion,
their aspiration to emulate past sages,
without assessing their own virtue and capability,
can generally be inferred.
Postscript to the *Gazetteer of Wújùn*
Fàn Chéngdà’s *Gazetteer of Wújùn* in fifty volumes
is divided into thirty-nine chapters:
namely, Historical Evolution,
Enfeoffments,
Households and Taxes,
Local Tributes,
Customs,
City Walls,
Schools,
Military Camps,
Government Buildings,
Granaries and Storehouses,
with Markets and Offices attached,
Wards and Markets,
Historical Sites,
Noble Titles,
Governors,
List of Names,
Officials,
Temples and Shrines,
Gardens and Pavilions,
Mountains,
Hǔqiū Hill,
Bridges,
Rivers,
Water Conservancy,
Notable Figures,
with Exemplary Women attached,
List of Jìnshì Graduates,
Local Products,
Taoist Temples,
Temples within the Prefectural City,
Temples in the Suburbs,
County Records,
Tombs,
Immortal Affairs,
Buddhist Matters,
Arts and Skills,
Strange Events,
Unusual Tales,
Textual Criticism,
Miscellaneous Poems,
Miscellaneous Records.
At the beginning of the chapters, there is a preface
by Biànrén Zhào Rǔtán from the second year of the Shàodìng era.
It states: “When Shíhú completed the gazetteer,
the prefect prepared woodblocks intending to print it.
At that time, someone who sought to include a certain matter in the records but was refused
exclaimed:
‘This book is not written by Shíhú!’
The prefect dared not proceed with the printing,
so it was stored in the school.
In the first year of Shàodìng,
Lǐ Shòupéng of Guǎngdé, bearing the title of Shàngshū Láng, was appointed prefect.
His ancestor, the former Dùzhī Gōng Lǐ Jiāyán,
was a guest of Shíhú.
Upon inquiring at the school about the old matter,
he exclaimed in surprise:
‘This book has still not been published?’
Another day, while paying respects at Shíhú’s shrine,
he sought surviving writings from his family,
and upon comparison with the school’s copy, found no discrepancies.
However, the book only covers up to the third year of Shàoxī,
and subsequent major developments,
such as the Bǎiwàn Granary, the new county of Jiādìng, the Xǔpǔ Naval Forces, the relocation of the Gùjìng garrison, and the like, were not recorded.
Thereupon, he convened with the collating official Wāng Tàihēng
and scholars of literature for discussion,
following the example of Chǔ Shǎosūn,
to supplement what was missing,
correct errors and falsehoods,
without separately creating a continuation.”
It further states:
“During Shíhú’s lifetime,
he frequently consulted with three local scholars, Gōng Yí, Téng Chéng, and Zhōu Nánhòu,
and Gōng contributed particularly much of what he heard to the master,
hence differing opinions arose.
Yìgōng’s epitaph for the master
records the books he authored,
and the chapter titles can be verified,”
and so on.
Thus, it was highly esteemed by people.
Nowadays, scholars discussing Sòng dynasty local gazetteers
also regard Luó’s *Xīn’ān Gazetteer* and Fàn’s *Gazetteer of Wújùn* as the foremost,
with no dissenting opinions.
I have carefully examined it,
finding its literary style clear and concise;
the vulgar and mediocre tendencies of later local gazetteers
had not yet emerged at that time,
and its compilation is also elegant and neat.
Moreover, its structure details the commandery while being brief about the counties;
categories such as historical changes, city walls and moats, and lists of official titles
all cover the commandery but not the counties.
The two volumes on county records
only document official offices,
occasionally mentioning pavilions and terraces within the compounds,
sometimes quoting inscriptions on stone tablets without recording the names,
resulting in an inconsistent and irregular format.
This reflects the conventions of gazetteer compilation at that time,
which are completely different from
modern prefectural gazetteers that combine prefectural and county records.
I have a separate essay discussing this matter,
so there is no need to elaborate here.
While it is acceptable for other matters to detail the commandery and summarize the counties,
praising its structure is permissible;
however, recording historical changes for the commandery but not the counties
results in a lack of clarity and distinction.
No wonder it mistakenly uses the old name "Wújùn" for the Píngjiāng Circuit Prefecture,
placing it at the beginning of the entire gazetteer
without realizing the error.
Furthermore, when narrating historical changes into the Sòng dynasty,
it states: "In the first year of the Kāibǎo era,
the King of Wúyuè changed the Zhōngwú Army to the Píngjiāng Army.
In the third year of the Tàipíng Xīngguó era,
Qián Chù surrendered the territory."
Consulting historical records,
it is known that Sūzhōu was renamed at that time,
yet the gazetteer text does not mention the change to a prefecture.
It abruptly continues below:
"In the third year of the Zhènghé era,
Sūzhōu was elevated to Píngjiāng Prefecture."
Without any prior mention of Sūzhōu above,
the sudden introduction of the elevation from prefecture to prefecture
makes the text's meaning unclear.
The entire work compiles excerpts from historical records, poetry, essays, and anecdotal writings,
edited together,
with sources still noted under each entry,
which suffices as a method of compilation and categorization,
but is not the style of original composition.
The customs section extensively quotes poetry and anecdotes from the Wú region,
occasionally examining and verifying local dialects,
which is appropriate.
However, gatherings like the Nine Elders of Xú Yòu and others,
or the Gathering of Venerable Elders of Zhāng Gù and others,
were merely occasional grand events of the time
and should not be included in the customs section.
The schools section is in the fourth volume,
while county records are in volumes thirty-seven and thirty-eight;
county administrative offices and official buildings,
already included in the county records,
yet the schools section covers both prefectural and county schools,
meaning schools are mentioned before county names even appear.
Markets and wards are not attached to the city walls and moats section
but to the official buildings section,
which is also illogical.
The lists of names for the Judicial Commissioner's Office and the Salt and Tea Monopoly Commissioner's Office
are not placed in the same category as the lists of prefectural governors,
but are appended after the official buildings section,
which also violates proper norms.
For the Judicial Commissioner's list,
names are written prominently above,
with details of background and tenure dates noted below;
for the Salt and Tea Monopoly Commissioner's list,
official ranks and names are written prominently above,
with details of appointment dates noted below,
showing a lack of uniformity in format.
Prefectural governors include famous individuals,
yet their name lists are placed later,
which is an inversion.
Official positions do not record ranks and quotas,
but only include those with notable deeds,
which is also overly simplistic.
Minor officials and clerks
are intermingled with magistrates and chiefs,
and it is also problematic that magistrates' names appear before the county records.
Ancient sites are rather confused with
temples, official buildings, gardens, pavilions, tombs, Taoist temples, Buddhist monasteries, mountains, and rivers.
Setting apart Hǔqiū as a separate category outside mountains
shows a lack of understanding of the methods of interrelation, detailed and brief cross-referencing,
making the entire work fraught with difficulties.
The biographies section does not compose original entries
but excerpts and condenses historical records,
which is also in line with compilation practices.
Arranged in order across eight volumes,
without using headings or classifications,
it still maintains an elegant style.
However, for prominent clans like the Zhāng and Gù families,
which produced notable figures across generations,
it would be appropriate to group them by clan in one section,
and within each clan,
arrange by generation.
Instead, they are sometimes separated, sometimes combined,
and the chronological order is occasionally disrupted,
unlike the various Lù clans compiled together in one section,
maintaining clear order throughout.
Could it be that the current edition is erroneous,
and not the original arrangement by Fàn?
Immortals, Buddhists, and specialists in arts and crafts
are also branches of the biographies section;
even if one wishes to strictly separate them,
they should still be placed after the biographies section,
with distinct headings.
Yet after the biographies section,
interspersed with lists of successful examination candidates, local products, Taoist temples, city monasteries, suburban monasteries, county records, and tombs,
spanning twelve volumes,
suddenly appear the three categories of immortals and others,
causing material objects and human affairs
to become confused and unclear,
which can be described as extremely disorderly and imprecise.
The local products section is extensively researched,
and the evidential material is also good.
However, swords like Gànjiàng, Mòyé, and Zhúlòu,
and hooks like Wú Hóng and Hù Jī,
though recorded in historical texts as divine artifacts of their time,
are also difficult to fully believe;
now indiscriminately included in local products,
they are not of the same category.
One volume on strange events
and three volumes on unusual tales,
upon careful examination, show no real distinction,
and the research is superficial but not entirely crude.
Poems, rhapsodies, and miscellaneous writings
are already annotated under various categories,
yet those without a clear category
are separately placed under a miscellaneous verses section,
and although the selections are not bad,
it still seems rather disorganized and inappropriate.
Often, when I see modern people compiling gazetteers,
lacking the discernment to make judgments,
yet greedy for the unusual and fond of trivialities,
unwilling to part with anything,
they compile a miscellaneous records section at the end of the volumes,
or call it supplementary chapters.
This is because the entire gazetteer is divided into categories
like placing counting rods,
without any distinctive insight or original design,
so for matters difficult to classify,
they create such a volume
as a catch-all for odds and ends,
which is quite meaningless.
Now observing Fàn's gazetteer,
it also includes a miscellaneous records section at the end,
showing that earlier scholars had already pioneered this.
In fact, the content included
all could belong to existing categories;
it is a pity that Fàn's classification principles were not precise.
Within its fifty volumes,
the use of official titles and place names often does not conform to standards,
and personal names are casually and randomly filled in,
reflecting the style of Sòng dynasty poetry and anecdotal writings,
greatly altering the rules and forms of historical writing;
its inadequacy for specialized local gazetteer studies
and the standards of official historians
goes without saying.
The reason it is praised by the world
is because Shíhú was virtuous and literary,
and also prominent and esteemed in his time;
and though his editing and revisions
do not conform to historical methods,
compared to the vulgar, excessive, mediocre, and reckless works of recent times,
it certainly stands out,
and its fame is not accidental.
However, to consider this an excellent local gazetteer
is not accurate.
Postscript to the *Gūsū Gazetteer*.
Wáng Ào's "Gūsū Zhì" in sixty volumes,
begins with the changes in administrative divisions of the commandery and county,
followed by the ancient and modern governors and magistrates,
and then the imperial examination graduates,
all presented in tables.
Next are the changes in administrative divisions,
followed by astrological divisions,
territorial boundaries,
mountains,
waters,
water conservancy,
customs,
household registration,
local products,
land taxes,
city walls and moats,
wards and alleys,
townships and districts,
bridges,
government offices,
schools,
military defense,
granaries and markets,
post stations and courier services,
altars and temples,
Buddhist and Daoist monasteries,
residences,
gardens and ponds,
historical sites,
tombs and graves,
the lineage of the Wú ruling family,
appended with enfeoffed nobles and clans;
followed by the suppression of rebellions,
achievements of officials,
and biographies of notable figures.
Among the biographies of notable figures,

they are divided into thirteen categories: distinguished ministers, loyal and righteous individuals, filial and fraternal persons, Confucian scholars, literary figures, those of outstanding conduct, recluses, recommended talents, artists, miscellaneous skills, sojourners, exemplary women, and Buddhist and Daoist monks.
In total, there are thirteen categories;
the work concludes with records of anomalies and miscellaneous matters.
However, the number of volumes for each section
does not correspond uniformly to the categories.
The section on distinguished officials is divided into six volumes,
while the distinguished ministers among the biographies of notable figures are divided into ten volumes.
Yet, loyal and righteous individuals are combined with filial and fraternal persons into one volume,
Confucian scholars are combined with literary figures into one volume,
and granaries and markets are combined with post stations and courier services into one volume.
Such arrangements
are numerous and varied.
In total, there are sixty volumes,
which were roughly determined based on the amount of paper,
without any consistent principle.
The naming of "Sū Zhì" is inconsistent;
for instance, Fàn Chéngdà referred to the gazetteer of Sūzhōu as "Wújùn Zhì,"
which was already unreasonable.
Yet, previous critics only reproached Wáng Ào for inappropriately naming the gazetteer of Sūzhōu Prefecture as "Gūsū Zhì,"
which is what is called valuing hearsay over direct observation.
However, among gazetteers of commanderies and counties,
there have always been few excellent editions throughout history.
Works like those of Fàn and Wáng,
though not esteemed by historians,
still stand out
amidst the vulgar and poorly compiled works.
The current edition of "Sūzhōu Fǔ Zhì" has many commendable aspects,
largely because it draws from ample and valuable historical sources.
