Yet, there are absurd and unreasonable elements
that are not even worth a laugh.
Even low-level clerks,
with a basic understanding of document formats,
would certainly not produce such errors,
as seen in the three tables at the beginning.
The first table is titled "Changes in Administrative Divisions of the Commandery and County,"
using "commandery and county" to refer to prefectures and counties,
its absurdity is self-evident.
The table uses provinces, states, commanderies, military prefectures, circuits, and prefectures as headings,
but includes only overarching administrative divisions like provinces and commanderies, omitting counties.
Not only is the style inappropriate,
but even its self-proclaimed title of "commandery and county"
contradicts its content.
Moreover, while the list of officials includes county magistrates,
the table on administrative changes lacks county names.
One wonders to what administrative divisions these county magistrates are attached?
What is even more peculiar is that
the nature of a table
lies in its use of rows and columns to organize information;
for instance, there may be different places in the same year or month,
or different branches within the same generation,
what is called the same warp but different weft,
resulting in uneven and irregular data,
which cannot be clearly presented in ordinary prose.
Hence, rows and columns are used to distinguish them.
For example, in the "Table of Governors and Magistrates,"
the governors, assistant governors, judges, and record-keepers of the commandery,
and the magistrates, assistants, registrars, and sheriffs of the county
should be listed horizontally as the warp;
while the dynasties, years, and months
should be arranged vertically as the weft.
Later readers wishing to check the dates of appointments
could find the era from the vertical headings,
and from the horizontal listings learn which governor, magistrate, assistant, or record-keeper
came earlier or later,
or served simultaneously,
making the table as clear as pointing at one's palm.
If events occurred sequentially
and were not simultaneous,
then it would be straightforward to list them item by item,
and there would certainly be no reason to use a table with rows and columns.
The table divides into columns for provinces, states, commanderies, military prefectures, circuits, and prefectures.
Now, "province" refers to Sūzhōu,
"state" refers to the State of Wú,
"commandery" refers to the commandery,
"military prefecture, circuit, and prefecture" refer to Píngjiāng Circuit and Prefecture.
These are all historical names for the area of Sūzhōu Prefecture over time;
when it was called the State of Wú, there was no Sūzhōu;
when it was called Sūzhōu, there was no Wú Commandery;
when it was called Wú Commandery, there was no Píngjiāng Circuit or Prefecture.
Since there is no simultaneous occurrence of different names causing complexity and inconsistency,
then listing them item by item
would suffice for readers to understand.
Yet now, rows and columns are used to create a table,
shifting up and down arbitrarily,
with no consistent principle,
merely confusing the reader;
even clerks' documents
are not so disorderly.
The "Table of Ancient Governors and Magistrates"
divides into columns for grand administrators, commandants, and acting officials.
Now, grand administrators and commandants
may have served concurrently in the same year or month;
as for acting officials,
they are like temporary officeholders today.
When there is a grand administrator, there is no acting grand administrator;
when there is a commandant, there is no acting commandant.
Acting officials and regular officials
certainly cannot appear simultaneously,
so there is also no reason to use a table with rows and columns.
Now, dividing them into separate columns
needlessly occupies space,
something even clerks would not do.
When listing officials in a table,
titles should conform to the administrative system of the time;
the table of governors and magistrates
should be titled "Table of Prefectural and County Officials,"
using later titles to refer to earlier ones is acceptable.
Now, calling it the "Table of Ancient Governors and Magistrates"
poses no issue in terms of wording;
but as for the "Table of Modern Governors and Magistrates,"
"modern" refers to the current system,
yet still using "governor" and "magistrate" to refer to Míng dynasty prefects and county magistrates
creates a discrepancy between name and reality,
which again is self-evident.
For prefectural officials, only prefects are listed,
omitting vice prefects and below;
for county officials, only county magistrates are listed,
omitting assistants, registrars, and the like.
What is the reasoning for this?
Moreover, tables have rows and columns;
the method of rows and columns
is about grouping similar items together,
precisely to make dissimilar items conform to a category.
Therefore, categories and tables
are inherently incompatible.
A table cannot serve as a category,
and a category has no use for a table—
this is something even clerks understand.
The table for imperial examination graduates
is divided into upper, middle, and lower sections.
Due to differences between ancient and modern systems
and the complexity of the records,
dividing by historical period into separate volumes is acceptable.
Its format should naturally list native places horizontally as the warp,
and list the years of provincial and metropolitan examinations vertically as the weft.
Provincial graduates and metropolitan graduates
are both examination graduates;
yet now, under the name "examination graduates,"
they are further divided into two separate tables for provincial graduates and metropolitan graduates.
This is a method of classification,
not of grouping similar items.
Moreover, those who pass the metropolitan examination
must first have passed the provincial examination.
Now, placing metropolitan graduates before
and provincial graduates after
reverses the actual sequence,
confusing the reader,
something even clerks would not do.
All such errors and absurdities,
like those in Wáng Ào's work,
who is reputed as an erudite scholar,
likely did not originate from his own writing;
rather, he was generally unskilled in historical composition,
and influenced by the habits of literary scholars,
who considered tables lacking in literary elegance,
and thus paid them little attention,
allowing ignorant individuals of the time
to recklessly compile them,
unaware that they would become laughingstocks to the knowledgeable,
to such an extent.
Hence it is said: literary scholars should not be entrusted with compiling gazetteers.
As for the establishment of government offices,
pavilions, towers, and terraces,
the stele inscriptions, prefaces, and postscripts by previous authors that are listed
may retain their original texts.
In the narrative of the gazetteer text regarding the founding and restoration of buildings,
within a single piece,
it is sometimes referred to as a prefecture (zhōu),
sometimes as a commandery (jùn),
largely following the original text of the Fàn Zhì;
not realizing that the Fàn Zhì is not worthy of emulation.
According to history, before the fifth year of the Zhènghé era in the Song dynasty,
it was named Sūzhōu,
and after the fifth year of the Zhènghé era,
it was named Píngjiāng Lùfǔ;
throughout the entire Song dynasty,
there was no name Wújùn.
Since the title of the Fàn Zhì is already erroneous,
the standards and principles of the gazetteer text
are as negligible as those from the state of Kuài, not worth criticizing.
Wáng did not know to make corrections,
which is what is called erroneous.
Moreover, narrating military conflicts since ancient times
and categorizing them under the heading "Píng Luàn" (Suppressing Rebellion)
is also incomprehensible.
Mountains, rivers, fields, and taxes,
wards, alleys, and customs,
households, postal stations, soldiers, and granaries—
these are all categories for recording precedents;
traces of officials and sojourners,
biographies of figures and chaste women—
these are all forms of biographical narration.
Using "Píng Luàn" as a chapter title
neither resembles the recording of precedents in a gazetteer,
nor equals the labeling of individuals in biographies;
it should naturally be recorded separately,
striving for proper order;
otherwise, the entire gazetteer should be revised to resemble a chronicle of events from beginning to end,
so as to avoid criticism of being incongruous.
However, only those well-versed in historical principles
can discern this,
and it is not something to demand of this gazetteer.
As for other minor textual flaws,
occasional errors in compilation,
they are even less worthy of deep scrutiny.
The Sū Zhì is highly praised by the world,
hence it is necessary to clarify this,
not out of deliberate fault-finding,
nor from a fondness for picking on earlier scholars.
Postscript to the Luán Zhì
My family possesses four volumes of the Luán Zhì,
with blurred and worn printing blocks,
missing, disordered, and inverted pages,
making it nearly impossible to read through;
around the forty-seventh year of the Qiánlóng era,
while I was lecturing in Yǒngpíng,
the then-prefect of Luánzhōu, Cài Jūn Xūn of Ānyuè,
wished to entrust me with compiling the prefectural gazetteer,
and thus brought the old gazetteer for me to examine,
which was this very copy.
According to the "Yìwén Zhì" of the Míng Shǐ,
there is Chén Shìyuán's Luánzhōu Zhì in eleven volumes.
Chén, styled Yǎngjūn,
was from Yìngchéng, Húguǎng,
a jìnshì of the Jiājìng era, jiǎchén year,
served as prefect of Luánzhōu,
and had a great reputation;
his writings were abundant,
many are seen in the Míng Zhì,
yet the histories do not include his biography.
The Yìngchéng Xiàn Zhì
has his biography but no bibliography;
however, the local gentry still speak of him with pride to this day.
In my youth, I sojourned in Yìngchéng,
seeking his works,
but found none at all.
I heard that the former county magistrate, Jīn Céng of Jiāngpǔ,
took all the manuscripts from his family collection,
which I deeply regret.
Now, this gazetteer is still referred to as Chén's original version.
During the Kāngxī era,
Prefect Hóu Shàoqí supplemented it following the established format,
although the original sequence of eleven volumes
could no longer be traced,
the categories and principles
remained unchanged.
At the beginning, an unknown author wrote a preface,
stating:
"When I formerly served as an official in Zhōngzhōu,
I met Guō Qīngluó to discuss compiling the Xǔzhōu Zhì.
Guō said:
'Among gazetteers within the realm,
Lǐ Cāngmíng's Qīngzhōu Zhì is the foremost,
and next is the Luán Zhì.'"
This seems to refer to Chén's original version.
Both the book and its author
were highly praised in their time,
which is why Hóu followed it and dared not propose changes.
Now, examining this book,
it is deceptive, far-fetched, and bizarre,
quite tainted by the mid-Míng trend of not reading books yet seeking novelty;
the logic and coherence of the text have reached this point,
making it utterly unworthy of discussion.
Chén was known for his erudition,
yet the Luán Zhì is so mediocre and absurd;
one wonders
what his other writings might be like.
And that Guō Qīngluó offered such baseless praise,
is truly incomprehensible.
The book is divided into four sections:
first, Shì Biān (Chronicles of Ages);
second, Jiāng Lǐ (Boundaries and Territories);
third, Rǎng Zé (Land and Regulations);
fourth, Jiàn Zhì (Establishments).
The Shì Biān uses the chronicle format,
imitating the style of the Chūnqiū,
but is actually wildly unfounded and absurd.
The beginning grandly states:
"Emperor Kù established the Nine Provinces,
our Jì was divided."
The commentary says:
"Why is this recorded?
To mark the beginning."
And so on.
When examining the division of the Nine Provinces,
it again grandly states:
"The Yellow Emperor expelled the Xūnyù."
The commentary says:
"Why record the Xūnyù?
They were our border commanderies."
It again grandly states:
"In the thirteenth year of King Wǔ of Zhōu's reign,
Bóyí and Shūqí starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain,
and Shào Gōng Shì was enfeoffed in Yān,
our Yān was divided."
These are all from Chén's original compilation,
bizarre and absurd, not even worth a laugh.
The Chūnqiū
is a book of the state of Lǔ,
where the phrasing by ministers and subjects
follows principles of internal and external relations,
hence referring to Lǔ as "our state,"
not as a special distinction for rulers of other states.
Moreover, since the Lǔ history is titled by the state's name,
it would be inconvenient within the text to refer to the state as Lǔ again,
a matter of proper grammar,
nothing more.
In the era of commanderies and counties,
the realm was unified under one sovereign;
those who wield the brush to compile prefectural and county gazetteers—
are they not all ministers and subjects of the court?
What "our" is there to speak of?
As for the Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng commentaries on the classics,
they stem from the transmission by classical masters,
where subtle meanings
are difficult to grasp immediately,
so they employ questions and answers to elucidate them—
this is not a historical convention.
Prefectural and county gazetteers,
being the work of a single hand,
are not compilations containing hidden meanings from predecessors
awaiting the author's clarification;
yet to write and explain oneself,
to question and answer oneself—
since this is not a performance by actors,
why engage in a solo dialogue?
Moreover, Liú Zhījī's Shǐ Tōng,
discussing the Jìn Jì and Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū,
strongly criticized predecessors for groundless imitation,
stating that the use of "I" and hypothetical questions and answers
are both to be condemned.
Chén was reputed to be broad and learned,
had he not read this?
National histories are so,
let alone prefectural and county gazetteers?
"In the thirteenth year of King Wǔ of Zhōu's reign"—
the wording is especially erroneous.
The Yīn calendar's years and the Zhōu calendar's years
do not correspond to each other.
The Hóng Fàn was presented by Jīzǐ as categories,
a variation in recording style,
not a standard form of address.
Chén, for the sake of Bóyí and Shūqí,
changed "year" to "year of sacrifice,"
and below, the enfeoffment of Shào Gōng
is covered by the same phrasing—
does he intend to make Shào Gōng a man of Yīn?
Moreover, Bóyí and Shūqí did not eat the grain of Zhōu,
starving to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain—
this means they did not accept official salary and died in poverty and hunger,
not that they stopped eating to sacrifice their lives.
To grandly record their year of death,
is that not extremely absurd?
Just from these few points,
is there any need to examine the rest?
Its chronological compilation is divided into three categories:
the first is called "Previous Dynasties,"
the second "Our Dynasty,"
and the third "Restoration."
The section titled "Our Dynasty"
ends in the twenty-eighth year of the Jiājìng reign of Emperor Shìzōng;
the section titled "Restoration"
begins from the twenty-ninth year of the Jiājìng reign,
which is truly inexplicable.
The categories of geography and territory are six:
called boundaries,
administrative divisions,
mountains and rivers,
scenic spots,
customs,
and historical sites.
The categories of land and regulations are seven:
called household registration,
land taxes,
salt administration,
local products,
horse administration,
military administration,
and postal relay stations.
The categories of establishment and construction are eleven:
called city walls and moats,
government offices,
Confucian schools,
granaries and storehouses,
postal stations,
streets and markets,
archways and plaques,
towers and pavilions,
bridges and ferries,
official sacrifices,
and temples and monasteries.
As for officials, scholars, and notable figures,
as well as civil service examinations and selections,
they are all included within the chronological records.
For officials and scholars, the year and month are prominently recorded,
stating which official and which person assumed office;
if the person has commendable qualities,
it follows the example of the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
annotating their deeds and conduct below.
For civil service examinations, it states:
who was recommended as a tribute student from the school,
who passed the provincial examination,
and who passed the metropolitan examination on which list;
if they have commendable qualities,
it follows the same example as for officials and scholars,
and if not, it is omitted.
Those who were commended for filial piety, righteousness, chastity, and loyalty
are recorded on the day they received the commendation.
However, reclusive scholars,
talented writers,
who did not pass the civil service examinations,
along with chaste and filial women,
virtuous and pure maidens,
who occasionally did not receive commendation,
are not included in the gazetteer according to precedent.
What is particularly unusual
is that Hóu Jūn’s continuation of Chén’s gazetteer,
in the forty-seventh year of the Wànlì reign of the Ming dynasty,
prominently records "the fourth year, Jǐwèi, of the Tiānmìng reign of our Great Ancestor, the High Emperor,"
with the previous Ming reign titles annotated below;
it further prominently records Féng Yùntài passing the metropolitan examination on the same list as Zhuāng Jìchāng,
and also records that Prefect Lín Yīngjù assumed office.
Now, the territory of the previous Ming dynasty
had not yet been incorporated into the territory of our dynasty;
the historical records of our dynasty,
when recording Ming affairs,
if not related to the legitimate calendar,
do not omit the reign titles of Tiānqǐ and Chóngzhēn.
If it is said that out of the duty of a subject,
one should prioritize our dynasty and treat the previous Ming as external,
then since the Tiānmìng reign title is recorded above,
affairs belonging to the previous Ming
should certainly be distinguished by adding the word "Ming";
this would allow readers to understand the distinction between host and guest,
which is also a fixed principle.
Now, Féng Yùntài was a metropolitan graduate of the Ming dynasty,
and Lín Yīngjù was a prefect of the Ming dynasty,
yet they are listed under the reign title of our dynasty,
with no "Ming" character to distinguish them,
which is tantamount to treating Ming metropolitan graduates and prefects
as the examination graduates and officials of our dynasty—
is this not a falsehood!
As for the title of the *Luánzhì*,
it is also quite vulgar and presumptuous.
Luán is the name of a river,
and the prefecture is also named after the river.
Now, removing the character for "prefecture"
and calling it *Luánzhì*
would lead readers of the title label
to suspect it is a gazetteer of the Luán River.
However, the "Treatise on Literature" in the *Míngshǐ* records Chén Shìyuán’s compilation as *Luánzhōuzhì*,
so the removal of the character for "prefecture" in the title
may have been done by Hóu Shàoqí.
In any case, viewing the entire book,
such matters are still minor details,
and not worth censuring.
Postscript to the *Língshòu County Gazetteer*
Some books are valued because of their authors;
one may value the author and overlook the book.
Some writings have good intentions but inadequate expression;
one may value the intention and overlook the expression.
Lù Lǒngqí of Pínghú,
a renowned Confucian scholar of principle studies,
how can he be lightly criticized?
However, he was not deeply versed in historiography.
The *Língshòu County Gazetteer* he compiled
has very good intentions,
but does not deeply understand literary principles.
Thus, valuing Lù as a person
and appreciating the original intent of compiling the gazetteer is acceptable.
Valuing the person
and therefore valuing the book,
considering it a model for gazetteer compilers,
is merely following hearsay.
I note that Lù’s *Língshòu County Gazetteer* has ten volumes:
the first is geography,
with chronicles and local dialects appended;
the second is establishment and construction;
the third is sacrificial ceremonies;
the fourth is disasters and auspicious signs;
the fifth is local products;
the sixth is land taxes;
the seventh is officials and scholars;
the eighth is notable figures;
among notable figures,
it is further divided into empresses and consorts, famous ministers, official achievements, filial piety and righteousness, recluses, and exemplary women;
the ninth is civil service examinations;
the tenth is literature.
Land taxes and literature are divided into upper and lower volumes,
while sacrificial ceremonies, disasters and auspicious signs, and local products are combined into one,
so the division of volumes
lacks any principled rationale.
The book is generally concise,
but land taxes are uniquely detailed,
which can be said to show an understanding of priorities.
The preface and examples all state:
"The land is barren and the people are poor;
those in office should not make frequent changes or impose excessive levies,
and the local inhabitants should not indulge in extravagance or engage in rivalry."
These are particularly benevolent and kind words.
The entire book generally takes this as its guiding principle,
and its conscientiousness truly matches that of the virtuous officials of ancient times.
At the end of the essay, he presents his own proposals to the authorities,
concerning matters of establishment and abolition within the county,
and concludes with a discussion on the principles for compiling the local gazetteer, exchanged with a county resident named Fù Wéiyún.
His proposals on establishment and abolition
are indeed practical and useful;
but his discussion on the principles for compiling the gazetteer
is pedantic, misguided, and inappropriate.
Fearing that people might be swayed by reputation and overlook the substance,
I feel compelled to analyze and clarify these points below.
For instance, regarding the section on geography at the beginning,
it is acceptable to append local dialects,
but appending chronicles is erroneous.
Chronicles
record major events from previous dynasties related to Língshòu,
arranged chronologically,
meaning that within a single county,
they serve the function of basic annals in historical works.
If chronicles could be appended to geography,
then the "Canon of Shùn" could be appended to the "Tribute of Yǔ,"
and the basic annals of history could be incorporated into geographical treatises.
Recording events should prioritize conciseness and proper methodology;
attaching them in such a manner
may be concise,
but can it be considered proper methodology?
In the section on establishments,
he removed the records of memorial arches and tablets,
claiming that the emphasis should be on people,
not on the arches.
This argument is pedantic and far-fetched.
No one is more esteemed than Confucius,
and no one’s details are less reliant on gazetteers for documentation than Confucius.
If it is argued that the emphasis lies elsewhere,
and thus the text is omitted from the gazetteer,
then the gazetteer of Quèlǐ
could be burned and destroyed.
The significance of memorial arches and tablets lies in the people they honor,
just as the significance of schools lies in the Way,
the significance of government offices lies in governance,
and the significance of city walls and moats lies in defense.
If it is argued that because the emphasis lies elsewhere, they should not be recorded,
then schools, government offices, and city walls could all be omitted,
and the entire section on establishments
might as well have its categories abolished.
Removing temples and monasteries without recording them,
under the pretext of rejecting heterodoxy and upholding orthodoxy,
is also pedantic and inappropriate.
The Spring and Autumn Annals emphasized recording constructions and activities;
all inappropriate constructions and activities
were meticulously documented
to serve as warnings.
If we follow Mr. Lù’s argument,
then we need only delete such texts
to reject heterodoxy and uphold orthodoxy.
But after thousands of years,
who would even know what heterodoxy was rejected?
Moreover, within temples and monasteries,
inscriptions on metal and stone can be examined,
and scattered texts and traditions
can be used to investigate ancient matters.
This is the first reason why they should not be omitted.
The offices of monks and Taoist priests
are established by state institutions;
they must have places to reside,
and they must have followers to lead.
This is the second reason why they should not be omitted.
Prayers for rain during droughts,
relief efforts during famines,
the care and adoption of abandoned infants,
and the maintenance of incense and offerings at shrines and tombs of former worthies—
local officials often choose temples and monasteries as public venues
and select monks and Taoist priests as custodians.
These arrangements are greatly relied upon in practical matters
and are frequently mentioned in memorials and official documents,
without ever harming governance.
Thus, institutions like temples, monasteries, monks, and Taoist priests,
which were once viewed as promoting heterodoxy in the past,
now assist in official affairs.
Even if Zhōu Gōng and Confucius were reborn,
they would adapt to circumstances and guide accordingly,
and would surely find ways to manage them appropriately.
They would not necessarily insist on converting the people and repurposing their dwellings.
Mr. Lù, by omitting them without record,
claims to defend the Way.
How narrow is his perspective?
In the sections on officials and the examination system,
he only details the current dynasty,
arguing that this follows the old gazetteer’s practice of beginning with the early Míng.
This is especially erroneous.
The old gazetteer failed to extensively examine earlier dynasties
and began with the early Míng,
which was already a flaw of the old gazetteer.
However, it did not deliberately discard what was already recorded.
Now, Mr. Lù clearly sees the old gazetteer
but deletes the names and surnames from it.
The irrationality of this requires no further argument.
Since ancient times, feudal lords did not include the Son of Heaven in their ancestral temples,
nor did ministers include feudal lords in theirs.
This is a matter of principle and circumstance.
Among the various schools of local gazetteers,
regarding former emperors and empresses of previous dynasties,
they should only note their origins,
and not list them among the biographies of notable figures.
This point has been repeatedly debated by earlier scholars,
yet no consensus has been reached.
In truth, listing them among notable figures
is erroneous.
Without delving into the appropriateness of principle and circumstance,
consider this: if the category of notable figures
includes both ancient and modern individuals,
and local gazetteers list former emperors and empresses
among notable figures,
then those compiling the gazetteer for the capital region
would have to include the current dynasty’s emperors and empresses among notable figures.
This is clearly unacceptable without even asking.
Thus, Mr. Lù’s gazetteer placing empresses at the beginning of the notable figures section
is particularly lacking in rigor.
